en: The Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī and Dharmagupta et al., during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Question Section 1: Chapter on Entrances (Āyatana-varga). First Question:
How many entrances (āyatanas) are there?
Answer: [As follows:]
Twelve. What are the twelve?
The six internal sense bases and the six external sense bases.
What are the six internal sense bases?
They are the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base; these are called the six internal sense bases.
What are the six external sense bases?

They are the sense base of forms, the sense base of sounds, the sense base of odors, the sense base of tastes, the sense base of tangibles, and the sense base of mental phenomena; these are called the six external sense bases.
Thus, the six internal bases and the six external bases are called the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
What is the eye base?
The eye faculty is called the eye base.
What is the eye-base?
The eye-element is called the eye-base.
What is the eye-base?

If it is the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), belonging to the category of "mine" (*ātmiya*), whether past, future, or present, this is called the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*).
What is the eye-base?
If it is the translucent matter belonging to the category of "mine," whether past, future, or present, this is called the eye-base.
What is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*)?

It is that which, being comprised within my own sphere, has seen, now sees, or will see forms—though this is not fixed—or that which, being comprised within my own sphere, has received, now receives, or will receive the light of forms—though this is not fixed. This is called the eye-base.
What is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*)?

It is that which is included within the self’s sphere (*ātmiya*), whether it has already confronted, is currently confronting, or will confront visible forms (*rūpa*), or that which is indeterminate; and that which is unimpeded. This is the eye-base, the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*), the field, the substance, the gate, the storehouse, the world, the pure, the spring, the ocean, the parched wasteland, the whirlpool, the ulcer, the bond, the eye, that which enters into the self’s sphere, this shore, and the internal base (*ādhyātmikam āyatanam*).
The eye seeing forms is called the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*); the ear, nose, tongue, and body bases are likewise.
What is the mind-base?
The faculty of mind is called the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*).
What is the sense-base of mind?
The aggregate of consciousness is called the sense-base of mind.
What is the sense-base of mind?
The mind, consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, and the seven elements of consciousness are called the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*).
What is the sense-base of mind?
Whatever consciousness is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the sense-base of mind.
What are the six groups of consciousness?
They are the group of eye-consciousness, the groups of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, and the group of mind-consciousness.
What is the group of eye-consciousness?

Conditioned by the eye, conditioned by forms, conditioned by light, and conditioned by attention—by these four conditions, consciousness arises; whether it has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate, this is called the group of visual consciousness.
What are the groups of consciousness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?

With the mind as condition, with mental objects as condition, and with attention as condition—conditioned by these three, consciousness has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate; this is called the group of mental consciousness.
These are called the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*).
What are the seven elements of consciousness (*sapta-vijñāna-dhātu*)?
They are the element of eye-consciousness, the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, and the element of mind and the element of mental consciousness.
What is the visual consciousness element?

It is that consciousness which arises from the eye faculty with respect to the objective field of visible forms—whether already arisen, presently arising, about to arise, or indeterminate. This is called the visual consciousness element.
What is the element of ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness?

If consciousness has the body-faculty as its basis and takes contact as its object—whether it has arisen, is arising now, will arise, or is indeterminate—it is called the element of body-consciousness.
What is the mind element (*manodhātu*)?
It is the mind that cognizes phenomena and attends to phenomena; whether it be the initial mind already arisen, now arising, about to arise, or indeterminate, this is called the mind element.
What is the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)?

If consciousness is similar [to its object], not separated from that objective sphere and other similar minds—whether already arisen, presently arising, about to arise, or indeterminate—it is called the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
These are called the seven consciousness elements.
What is past consciousness?
If consciousness has already ceased, it is called past consciousness.
What is future consciousness?
That consciousness which has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged is called future consciousness.
What is present consciousness?
If the mind has arisen but not yet ceased, this is called present consciousness.
What is internal consciousness?
If consciousness is experienced, this is called internal consciousness.
What is external consciousness?
If consciousness is not appropriated, it is called external consciousness.
What is coarse consciousness?
If consciousness is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse consciousness.
What is subtle consciousness?
If consciousness is bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or unbound, it is called subtle consciousness.
What is inferior consciousness?

If consciousness is unwholesome or is the retribution of unwholesome dharmas, or if consciousness is neither retribution nor a dharma leading to retribution and is disagreeable, this is called inferior consciousness.
What is superior consciousness?

If consciousness is wholesome and is the result of wholesome dharmas, or if consciousness is neither a result nor a dharma that leads to results and is agreeable, this is called superior consciousness.
What is distant consciousness?
If various consciousnesses are distant, extremely distant, neither near nor near the boundary, these are called distant consciousnesses.
What are near consciousnesses?
If various consciousnesses are near, extremely near, or near the boundary, these are called near consciousnesses.
What is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*)?
The realm of form is called the sense-sphere of form.
What is the sense-sphere of form?
That which follows the characteristics of form is called the form base (*rūpāyatana*). What is the form base?
If form is visible, possesses resistance, and is cognizable by visual consciousness, it is called the form base.
What is the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*)?

It refers to form that is produced as a retribution born of karma, afflictions, and mental formations, and which is comprised within one’s own continuum (*ātmiya*), such as the beauty or ugliness of the body, its loveliness or lack thereof, its fairness or lack thereof, and its purity or lack thereof; it includes the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from a wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral mind, consisting of going and coming, bending and stretching, and turning about; it also includes external forms known by visual consciousness, such as blue, yellow, red, white, black, purple, coarse or fine, long or short, square or round, water, land, light, shadow, glare, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, vapor, brightness, and darkness, as well as other external forms known by visual consciousness. This is called the sense-base of form.
What is the sense-sphere of sound?
The element of sound is called the sense-sphere of sound.
What is the sense-sphere of sound?
If a form is invisible and resistant, yet is cognizable by the ear-consciousness, this is called the sound-base (*śabda-āyatana*).
What is the sound-base?

If there is sound included within the sense-sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) that is produced as a retribution from karma, mental factors, or afflictions, and is comprised within one’s own continuum—whether it be pleasant or unpleasant, exquisite or not exquisite, soft or not soft; or if it is vocal instruction arising from a wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral mind, consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; or if it is external sound known by the ear-consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*), such as the sound of conchs, large drums, small drums, *vīṇā* lutes, *vallakī* lutes, cymbals, the sound of dancing, singing, instrumental music, lamentation, the voices of men, women, humans, non-humans, sentient beings, non-sentient beings, departing sounds, approaching sounds, sounds of mutual contact, the sounds of wind, rain, water, and the various elements in mutual contact, as well as other external sounds known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere of sound.
What is the odor base (*gandhāyatana*)?
The odor element (*gandhadhātu*) is called the odor base.
What is the odor base?
If a form is invisible and resistant, yet cognizable by olfactory consciousness, this is called the sense-sphere of odor (*gandhāyatana*).
What is the sense-sphere of odor?

It refers to odors produced as retribution from karma, mental factors, and afflictions, which are included within my own continuum—whether they be pleasant or unpleasant odors, soft or harsh odors, agreeable or disagreeable odors; or external odors cognizable by olfactory consciousness, such as the fragrance of tree roots, the fragrance of tree hearts, the fragrance of tree resins, the fragrance of tree bark, the fragrance of flowers, the fragrance of leaves, the fragrance of fruits, whether pleasant or unpleasant, as well as other external odors cognizable by olfactory consciousness. This is called the sense-sphere of odor.
What is the sense-base of taste?
The element of taste is called the sense-base of taste.
What is the sense-base of taste?
If a form is invisible and resistant, and is known by tongue-consciousness, this is called the sense-sphere of taste (*rasāyatana*).
What is the sense-sphere of taste?

It refers to those things produced as retribution by karma, dharmas, and afflictions, which are comprised within my own continuum and consist of the body’s sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or watery phlegm; or external tastes known by tongue-consciousness, whether sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, or bland liquid; and other external tastes known by tongue-consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere of taste.
What is the sense-base of tangibles?
The tangible element is called the sense-base of tangibles.
What is the sense-base of tangibles?
If form is invisible, possesses resistance, and is known by body-consciousness, this is called the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
What is the sense-base of tangibles?

It refers to those tangibles produced as retribution from karma, dharmas, and afflictions, which are included within my own continuum (*ātmiya*)—namely, the cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness of the body; or external tangibles known by body-consciousness, such as cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness, as well as other external tangibles known by body-consciousness. This is called the sense-base of tangibles.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?
The realm of mental objects (dharmadhātu) is called the sphere of mental objects.
What is the sphere of mental objects?
The aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations; if form is invisible and non-resistant, or if it is unconditioned—these are called the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the sphere of mental objects?
It consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of mind, view, wisdom, and liberation.
Non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion; confidence, remorse, absence of remorse, gladness, joy, mental exertion,
mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration,
equanimity of mind, doubt, fear, underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, aging, death, life-force, fetters, and non-existence.

The meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the attainment of the fruits [of the path], the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the non-informative [karmas] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, the impure (*sāsrava*) informative and non-informative [karmas] of bodily and vocal restraint, the impure bodily exertion and impure bodily tranquility, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, and right bodily tranquility;

the cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); and the condition of the persistence of determined phenomena (*dharmasthiti-pratyaya*).

The knowledge of the sphere of infinite space, the knowledge of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the knowledge of the sphere of nothingness, and the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—
these are called the sense-base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Of the twelve sense-bases, how many are material and how many are non-material?
Ten are material, one is non-material, and one is twofold, being either material or non-material.
What are the ten that are material?
The eye-base, the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base; and the visible-form-base, sound-base, odor-base, flavor-base, and tangible-object-base—these are called the ten that are material.
What is the one that is non-material?
The sense-base of mind (manāyatana); this is called the one that is non-material.
What is the one that is twofold, being either material or non-material?
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is called "one part of two," being either material or non-material.
What is the materiality of the sphere of mental objects?

It consists of the unmanifested non-restraint of body and speech; the tainted unmanifested restraint of body and speech; the tainted application of energy (*vīrya*) and the tainted removal of mental afflictions (*praśrabdhi*); and right speech, right action, right livelihood, right application of energy, and right removal of mental afflictions. This is called the materiality of the sphere of mental objects.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is non-material?

Feeling, perception, and so forth up to the attainment of cessation; the knowledge of the exhaustion of conditions up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this is called the sphere of mental objects that is non-material.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are visible and how many are invisible?
One is visible; eleven are invisible. Which one is visible?
The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is what is called "one that is visible.
What are the eleven that are invisible?
The nine sense-bases of form, the sense-base of mind (manāyatana), and the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana); these are called the eleven that are invisible.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
Ten are with resistance; two are without resistance.
What are the ten that are with resistance?
The ten bases of form are called the ten with resistance.
What are the two without resistance?
The mind base and the mental-object base; these are called the two without resistance.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are noble (*ārya*) and how many are non-noble (*anārya*)?
Ten are non-noble; two are twofold, being either noble or non-noble.
What are the ten that are non-noble?
The ten bases of form are called the ten non-noble.
What are the two that are twofold, being either noble or non-noble?
The mind base and the mental-object base are called the two that are twofold, being either noble or non-noble.
What is the sense-sphere of mind that is non-noble?
If the sense-sphere of mind is with-outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called the sense-sphere of mind that is non-noble.
What is the sense-sphere of mind that is non-noble?
If it is the aggregate of feeling associated with the mental consciousness, this is called the non-noble sense-sphere of mind (*mano-āyatana*).
What is the non-noble sense-sphere of mind?

If the sense-sphere of mind is neither that of one in training (*śaikṣa*) nor that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), from eye-consciousness up to mental consciousness, this is called the non-noble sense-sphere of mind.
What is the noble mind-base?
If the mind-base is untainted (*anāsrava*), this is called the noble mind-base.
What is the noble mind-base?

If the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), namely the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), this is called the noble mind-base (*ārya-manāyatana*).
What is the noble mind-base?

It is the mind-base of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); it is when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), enters the noble path with a noble mind; or when those of firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those of firm dharma (*dharmānusārin*), as well as others who have seen the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of nirvāṇa.

Observing suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are, one seeks to attain what has not been attained, to understand what has not been understood, and to realize what has not been realized; thus, free from defilements, one cultivates the path.

For a trainee (*śaikṣa*)—whether a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or non-returner (*anāgāmin*)—when their wisdom of observation is perfected, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of mind through observation, they immediately realize the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they then realize the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*), a destiny (*gati*), the mind-element (*manodhātu*), or the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), these are called the noble mind-base (*mana-āyatana*).
What is the non-noble dharma-base (*dharma-āyatana*)?
If the dharma-base is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called the non-noble dharma-base.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is non-noble?

It refers to the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations; or whatever form is invisible, non-resistant, and with-outflows (sāsrava); or whatever is a non-noble unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). This is called the sphere of mental objects that is non-noble.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is non-noble?
It consists of the sensations, perceptions, and so forth, up to the attainment of non-perception, which belong neither to those in training (śaikṣa) nor to those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, the first four types of form that are non-noble and the seven unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomena are called the sphere of mental objects that is non-noble.
What is the dharma-base that is noble?
If the dharma-base is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the noble dharma-base.
What is the dharma-base that is noble?

If it is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the mental factors associated with the faculty of faith, or any phenomena that are objectless (*anālambana*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), these are called the noble sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-ārya*).
What is the noble sphere of phenomena?

If the factors of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) are those of the learner (śaikṣa) or the one beyond learning (aśaikṣa), then the learner, being free from fetters and proclivities, enters the noble mind and the noble path; or if it be those of one with firm faith and firm dharma, or others who have seen the faults and afflictions of conditioned existence, who contemplate the tranquility of nirvāṇa and the path, who contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are, and who—desiring to attain what has not been attained, desiring to understand what has not been understood, and desiring to realize what has not been realized—cultivate the path while remaining free from defilements.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of mind by means of contemplation, they realize the fruit of asceticism: either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of mind through contemplation—they then realize the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a destination (*gati*), or feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), non-delusion (*amoha*), serene faith (*avetyaprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), gladness (*saumanasya*), mental energy (*cittavīrya*), mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*), the attainment of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech (*samyagvāk*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), right pliancy of body (*kāyapraśrabdhi*), and the certainty of the extinction of conditions through knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): these are called the noble sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-ārya*).
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
Ten are with outflows; two are twofold, being either with outflows or without outflows.
What are the ten that are with outflows?
The ten bases of form are called the ten with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
What are the two that are twofold, being either with-outflows or without-outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*); these are called the two that are twofold, being either with-outflows or without-outflows.
What is the sense-sphere of mind that is with-outflows?
If the sense-sphere of mind is accompanied by craving, it is called the sense-sphere of mind that is with-outflows.
What is the sense-sphere of mind that is with-outflows?
The aggregate of consciousness-feeling is called the sense-base of mind with outflows (*sāsrava*).
What is the sense-base of mind with outflows?
The sense-base of mind consisting of eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*) is called the sense-base of mind with outflows.
What is the mind-base (manāyatana) that is without outflows (anāsava)?
If the mind-base is without craving (niṣtṛṣṇa), this is called the mind-base without outflows.
What is the mind-base without outflows?
If the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), it is called the untainted mind-base (*anāsrava-manāyatana*).
What is the untainted mind-base?

It is the mind-base of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); that is, when a person in training is free from fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) and even realizes the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*), a destiny (*gati*), or the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), these are called the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) mind-base (*manāyatana*).
What is the contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomenon-base (*dharmāyatana*)?
If the phenomenon-base is accompanied by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is called the contaminated phenomenon-base.
What is the dharma-āyatana that is with outflows (sāsrava)?

It is the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations; or whatever form is invisible, non-resistant, and associated with craving—this is called the dharma-āyatana with outflows.
What is the element of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is with outflows (sāsrava)?

If the element of mental objects consists of feeling and perception that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), up to the attainment of non-conceptualization (asaṃjñisamāpatti), and the first four types of form (rūpa), this is called the element of mental objects that is with outflows.
What is the dharma-āyatana that is untainted (*anāsrava*)?
If the dharma-āyatana is free from craving (*tṛṣṇā*), this is called the dharma-āyatana that is untainted.
What is the dharma-āyatana that is untainted?

If it is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) associated with the faculty of faith, or any phenomena that are without objects (*anālambana*) and without craving (*avīta-rāga*), these are called the untainted (*anāsrava*) sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
What is the untainted sphere of phenomena?

If a dharma-element (dharmāyatana) is either of the learner (śaikṣa), of the non-learner (aśaikṣa), or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta)—such that a person in training (śaikṣapudgala) becomes free from fetters and proclivities, even up to the realization of the fruit of arhatship;

or if it pertains to a real person (pudgala) or a destiny (gati); or if it consists of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), initial thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), non-delusion (amoha), serene faith (avetyaprasāda), joy (prīti), mental exertion (cittotsāha), mental pliancy (praśrabdhi), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), equanimity of mind (upekṣā), attainment of the fruit (phalaprāpti), the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), right speech (samyagvāk), right action (samyakkarmānta), right livelihood (samyagājīva), right effort (samyagvyāyāma), right pliancy of body (kāyapraśrabdhi), the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyānirodha), the cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha), the fixed abiding of dharmas (niyata-dharmasthititā), the knowledge of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana-jñāna), the knowledge of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana-jñāna), the knowledge of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana-jñāna), and the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-jñāna)—these are called the untainted (anāsrava) dharma-elements.

The same applies to having craving and being without craving, having seeking and being without seeking, what is to be grasped and what is not to be grasped, having grasping and being without grasping, and having superiority and being without superiority.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated?
Five are appropriated; seven are twofold, being either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What are the five that are appropriated?
The eye-base, and the bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body—these are called the five bases that are associated with feeling (*vedanā*).
What are the seven bases that are twofold, being either associated with feeling or not associated with feeling?

They are the base of visible forms, the bases of sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, the mind-base, and the mental-object-base; these are called the seven bases that are twofold, being either associated with feeling or not associated with feeling.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-base of form?
If the sense-base of form is internal, this is called the feeling associated with the sense-base of form.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-base of form?

If the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) consists of bodily matter—whether beautiful or ugly, exquisite or not exquisite, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, or pure and refined or not pure and refined—that is produced as retribution from karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and is comprised within one's own continuum; or if it consists of the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from feeling and mind, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about—this is called the feeling-aspect (*vedanā*) of the form-base.
What is the sense-base of form that is not feeling?
If the sense-base of form is external, this is called the sense-base of form that is not feeling.
What is the sense-base of form that is not feeling?

The sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) that is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not included within one’s own domain; or that which arises from a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a mind that is neither a result nor subject to fruition, such as the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; or external form known by visual consciousness—this is called the sphere of form that is not felt (*anupātta*).
What is the sound-base as internal?
If the sound-base is an internal sound-base, this is called the sound-base as internal.
What is the sound-base as internal?

If the sound-base (śabdāyatana) produced as retribution from karma, dharmas, or afflictions, which is comprised within one’s own continuum, consists of pleasant sounds or unpleasant sounds, exquisite sounds or non-exquisite sounds, soft sounds or non-soft sounds, and arises from the mind as vocal intimation—the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech—this is called the sound-base as feeling (vedanā).
What is the sound base that is not feeling?
If the sound base is external,
this is called the sound base that is not feeling.
What is the sound-base (śabda-āyatana) that is not felt (anupātta)?

It refers to sounds that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; those not included within one's own sphere; those produced by the mind—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that are neither resultant nor destined to be resultant, consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and vocal expressions; and external sounds known by the ear-consciousness. This is called the sound-base that is not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-sphere of odors?
If the sense-sphere of odors is internal, this is called the feeling associated with the sense-sphere of odors.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-sphere of odors?

If the odorous base (gandhāyatana) produced as retribution from karma, dharmas, and afflictions, which is comprised within my own portion, consists of pleasant odors or unpleasant odors, soft odors or harsh odors, or agreeable odors or disagreeable odors, this is called the experience of the odorous base.
What is the odor-base (gandhāyatana) that is not felt?

If the odor-base is external, or if it is an external odor known by the nose-consciousness—such as the fragrance of tree roots, the fragrance of tree hearts, the fragrance of tree resins, the fragrance of tree bark, the fragrance of leaves, the fragrance of flowers, the fragrance of fruits, pleasant fragrances, unpleasant fragrances, and other external odors known by the nose-consciousness—this is called the odor-base that is not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-base of taste?
If it is the internal sense-base of taste, this is called the feeling associated with the sense-base of taste.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-base of taste?

If the retribution produced by karma, phenomena, or afflictions pertaining to the sense-base of taste—which is comprised within my own continuum—consists of the body’s sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or phlegmatic and bilious sensations, this is called the sense-base of taste as feeling (*vedanā*).
What is the sense-base of taste that is not feeling?

If the taste-base is external, or if it is an external taste known by tongue-consciousness—whether sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, or bland; whether water, juice, or any other external taste known by tongue-consciousness—this is called the taste-base that is not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-base of contact?
If the sense-base of contact is internal, this is called the feeling associated with the sense-base of contact.
What is the feeling associated with the sense-base of contact?

If the tactile base (spraṣṭavyāyatana) produced as a result of karma, mental factors, and afflictions, which is comprised within my own continuum—namely, the body's coldness, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, subtlety, roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness—this is called the feeling of the tactile base.
What is the sense-base of tangibles that is not feeling?

If it is an external sense-base of tangibles known by body-consciousness—whether cold or hot, light or heavy, coarse or subtle, rough or smooth, hard or soft, or whatever other external tangibles are known by body-consciousness—this is called the sense-base of tangibles that is not feeling.
What is the feeling associated with the mind-base?
If the mind-base is internal, this is called the feeling associated with the mind-base.
What is the feeling associated with the mind-base?

If the eye-consciousness up to the mind-consciousness—which arises as a retribution born of karma, mental objects, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own sphere—is called the mind-base as feeling (*vedanā*).
What is the mind-base that is not feeling?
If the mind-base (manāyatana) is external, it is called the mind-base that is not felt (anupātta).
What is the mind-base that is not felt?

If the mind-base—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—is not comprised within my own domain, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called the mind-base that is not felt.
What is the feeling aggregate within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
If it is within the sphere of mental objects, it is called the feeling aggregate within the sphere of mental objects.
What is the feeling aggregate within the sphere of mental objects?

If the phenomena included in the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are produced as retribution from karma and afflictions and are comprised within my own continuum—namely, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, life-force, and the outflow-tainted bodily exertion—these are called the feeling associated with the sphere of mental objects.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not feeling?
If it is a sphere of mental objects that is external, this is called the sphere of mental objects that is not feeling.
What is the sphere of mental objects that is not feeling?

If the dharma-āyatana is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not included within one's own sphere—excluding life-force—the remaining dharma-āyatanas are non-appropriated (*anupātta*); this is called the dharma-āyatana that is non-appropriated.
The same applies to the internal and external [bases].
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
Eight are without retribution; four are of two kinds, being either with or without retribution.
What are the eight that are without retribution?
The eye-base, the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-object-base—these are called the eight that are without retribution.
What are the four that are twofold, being either with retribution or without retribution?

The sense-sphere of form, the sense-sphere of sound, the sense-sphere of mind, and the sense-sphere of phenomena—these are called the four "two-part" bases that are either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the sense-sphere of form with retribution?
If the form base (*rūpāyatana*) is a resultant phenomenon (*vipākadharma*), it is called the form base with retribution (*savipāka*).
What is the form base with retribution?

If the form base arises from a wholesome or unwholesome mind—the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning produced by that wholesome or unwholesome mind—it is called the form base with retribution.
What is the form base (rūpāyatana) that is without retribution?

Whether it be a form base that is retribution or a form base that is not retribution—namely, those non-retribution phenomena consisting of bodily beauty or ugliness, loveliness or lack of loveliness, fairness of skin or lack of fairness, purity or impurity, as well as the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning initiated by an indeterminate mind; or external forms known by the eye-consciousness—this is called the form base without retribution.
What is the sound-base (śabdāyatana) that is retributive?
If the sound-base is of a nature to be retribution, this is called the sound-base that is retributive.
What is the sound-base that is retributive?

The sound-base (śabdāyatana), whether wholesome or unwholesome—namely, the vocal instruction consisting of sounds, syllables, and speech produced by a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind—is called the sound-base with retribution.
What is the sound-base (śabdāyatana) that is without retribution?

If it is the sound-base as retribution, or the sound-base that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution—namely, pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, exquisite sounds and non-exquisite sounds, soft sounds and non-soft sounds; or those vocal communications consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from an indeterminate mind; or external sounds known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sound-base without retribution.
What is the mind-base (manāyatana) that has retribution?
If the mind-base is a dharma subject to retribution, this is called the mind-base that has retribution.
What is the mind-base that has retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the mind-base (*manāyatana*), the remaining mind-base—whether wholesome or unwholesome—as well as the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), are called the mind-base with retribution (*savyābādha*).
What is the mind-base without retribution (*avyābādha*)?

Whether it be the mind-base as retribution or the mind-base as non-retribution, the eye-consciousness up to the mind-consciousness that are non-retribution dharmas—these are called the mind-base without retribution.
What is the dharma-base with retribution?
If a dharma-base is a resultant phenomenon, it is called a dharma-base with retribution (*savipāka*).
What is the dharma-base with retribution?

Excluding the wholesome resultant dharma-base, the remaining wholesome conditioned dharma-bases; the unwholesome [dharma-bases] from feeling and perception up to afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters; the two meditative attainments; and all material phenomena—these are called the dharma-base with retribution.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is non-resultant?

If the sphere of mental objects is a resultant phenomenon or a non-resultant phenomenon, excluding non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, afflictions, proclivities, fetters, and the unmanifested non-restraint of body and speech, the remaining sphere of mental objects is non-resultant.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are mind and how many are not mind?
One is mind; eleven are not mind.
What is the one that is mind?
The mind-base (manāyatana) is called "mind.
What are the eleven that are not mind?
Excluding the mind-base, the remainder are not mind; these are called the eleven that are not mind.
Regarding the twelve bases (āyatana): how many are associated with the mind (citta-saṃprayukta), and how many are not associated with the mind?

Ten are not associated with the mind; one is not said to be either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind; and one is divided into two parts, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the ten that are not associated with the mind?
The ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*); these are called the ten that are not associated with the mind.
What is the one that is said to be neither associated with the mind nor non-associated with the mind?
The mind-base (manāyatana) is called the one that is neither said to be associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind.
What is the one that is divided into two parts, being either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind?
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is called "one part of two," being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What is the sphere of mental objects that is associated with the mind?

If the sphere of mental objects consists of mental factors (*caitasika*), such as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), up to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), this is called the sphere of mental objects associated with the mind.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not associated with the mind?

If a phenomenon within the sphere of mental objects is not produced by the mind, up to and including the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the sphere of mental objects that is not associated with the mind.
Of the twelve bases (āyatana), how many are mental factors (caitta) and how many are not mental factors?
Eleven are not mental factors; one is twofold, being either a mental factor or not a mental factor.
What are the eleven that are not mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta*)?
The ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the mind base (*manāyatana*); these are called the eleven that are not mental factors.
What is the one that is twofold—either a mental factor or not a mental factor?
The sphere of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) is called "one part of two," being either mental concomitants (*caitasika*) or non-mental concomitants.
What is the sphere of mental phenomena that consists of mental concomitants?

If the sphere of mental phenomena possesses an object (*sālambana*), such as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, up to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), this is called the sphere of mental phenomena that consists of mental concomitants.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not associated with the mind?

If the sphere of mental objects arises without an object of perception, up to and including the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the sphere of mental objects that is not associated with the mind.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are conditions (*pratyaya*) and how many are not conditions?
One is a condition, ten are not conditions, and one is twofold—either a condition or not a condition.
What is the one that is a condition?
The mind-base (manāyatana) is called the single object-condition.
What are the ten that lack an object-condition?
The ten material bases (rūpāyatana) are called the ten that lack an object-condition.
What is the one part that is twofold—either with an object-condition (*ālambana*) or without an object-condition?
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), this is called the one part that is twofold—either with an object-condition or without an object-condition.
What is the sphere of mental objects with an object-condition?
If the dharma-base consists of mental factors such as feeling, perception, and even the afflictions and latent tendencies, this is called the conditioned dharma-base.
What is the unconditioned dharma-base?

If the dharma-base consists of non-mental factors, from the arising [of consciousness] up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the unconditioned dharma-base.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are associated with the mind (*cittasamprayukta*) and how many are not associated with the mind?
Eleven are not associated with the mind; one is twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the eleven that are not associated with the mind?
The ten bases of form and the base of mind; these are called the eleven that are not associated with the mind.
What is the one that is twofold—either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind?
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is called "one part of two," being either associated with the mind (*sacittaka*) or dissociated from the mind (*acittaka*).
What is the sphere of mental objects associated with the mind?

If the sphere of mental objects evolves in accordance with the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind—namely, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), up to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the outflowing bodily and vocal precepts; the outflowing bodily exertion (*vīrya*) and the outflowing bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); and right speech, right action, right livelihood, right exertion, and right tranquility—this is called the sphere of mental objects associated with the mind.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not shared with the mind?

If the sphere of mental objects does not follow the mind, does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind—up to and including the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this is called the sphere of mental objects that is not shared with the mind.
The same applies to those that follow the mind and those that do not follow the mind.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are karma and how many are non-karma?
Nine are non-karma; three are twofold, being either karma or non-karma.
What are the nine that are not karma?
The eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, mind-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-object-base; these are called the nine that are not karma.
What are the three that are of two kinds, being either karma or non-karma?

The sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana), the sense-sphere of sound (śabdāyatana), and the sense-sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)—these are called the three that are of two kinds, being either karma or non-karma.
What is the action of the sense-base of form?

It refers to bodily intimation—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—that is initiated by a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind; this is called the action of the sense-base of form.
What is the sense-sphere of form that is not karma?

It refers to the body’s beautiful or ugly color, its exquisite or non-exquisite appearance, its fair skin or lack thereof, and its refinement or lack thereof; or any external form known by visual consciousness—this is called the sense-sphere of form that is not karma.
What is the karma of the sound-base (śabdāyatana)?
It is the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech, which is produced by a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a neutral mind.
This is called the karma of the sound-base.
What is the sense-base of sound that is not karma?

Whether it be pleasant sound or unpleasant sound, exquisite sound or non-exquisite sound, soft sound or non-soft sound, or external sounds known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sense-base of sound that is not karma.
What is the action of the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-karma)?

It refers to the non-informative (avijñapti) aspects of volition (cetanā) regarding body and speech that are non-restraint, as well as the informative and non-informative aspects of restraint regarding body and speech that are with outflows (sāsrava), along with right speech, right action, and right livelihood; these are called the action of the sphere of mental objects.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is not action?

Excluding volition (*cetanā*), the unmanifest forms of bodily and vocal non-restraint, the manifest and unmanifest forms of the tainted (*sāsrava*) bodily and vocal restraint, right speech, right action, and right livelihood—the remaining sphere of mental objects is not action; this is called the sphere of mental objects that is not action.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are associated with karma (*karmasamprayukta*) and how many are not associated with karma?

One is associated with karma; ten are not associated with karma; and one is of three parts—either associated with karma, or not associated with karma, or neither stated to be associated with karma nor not associated with karma.
What is the one that is associated with karma?
The sense-base of mind (manāyatana); this is called the one associated with karma.
What are the ten that are not associated with karma?
The ten sense-bases of form (rūpāyatana) are called the ten that are not associated with karma (karmasaṃprayukta).
What is the one that is threefold—either associated with karma, or not associated with karma, or neither spoken of as associated with nor not associated with karma?

The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is called "one part threefold," meaning it is either associated with karma, not associated with karma, or neither said to be associated nor not associated with karma.
What is the sphere of mental objects that is associated with karma?

If the dharma-āyatana is associated with volition (*cetanā*), excluding volition itself, the remaining factors from sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) up to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are called the dharma-āyatana associated with karma.
What is the dharma-āyatana not associated with karma?

If the dharma-āyatana arises without being associated with volition, up to and including the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-āyatana not associated with karma.
What is the dharma-āyatana that is said to be neither associated with karma nor dissociated from karma?
Volition (cetanā) is called the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana); it is not said to be either associated with karma or dissociated from karma.
Regarding the twelve spheres (āyatanas), how many are common karma (sādhāraṇa-karma) and how many are uncommon karma (asādhāraṇa-karma)?
One is common karma; ten are uncommon karma; and one is twofold, being either common karma or uncommon karma.
What is the one [element] of common karma?
The sense-base of mind (manāyatana); this is called the one of common karma.
What are the ten of non-common karma?
The ten bases of form (rūpāyatana) are called the ten non-common karmas.
What is the one base that is twofold—either common karma or non-common karma? It is the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
This is called the first and second categories: either common karma or non-common karma. What is the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) as common karma?

It refers to those factors of the dharma-base that evolve in accordance with karma, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it—namely: feeling, perception, concentration, volition, contact, up to afflictions, latent tendencies, the attainment of non-perception, and the attainment of cessation; the unmanifest (avijñapti) of the outflow-tainted precepts of body and speech; the outflow-tainted bodily exertion and the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility; and right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, and right bodily tranquility. This is called the dharma-base as common karma.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is not shared with karma?

It refers to those factors of the sphere of mental objects that do not follow along with karma, which arise, abide, and cease independently of it; namely: indeterminate mind, volition, birth, aging, death, life-force, fetters, acquisitions, fruits, non-informative matter of bodily and vocal non-restraint, informative and non-informative matter of impure bodily and vocal restraint, impure bodily vigor, and the nine unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). These are called the sphere of mental objects that is not shared with karma.
The same applies to whether they follow karma or do not follow karma.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are causes and how many are not causes?
One is a cause, seven are not causes, and four are of two kinds, being either causes or not causes.
What is the single cause?
The sense-base of mind (manāyatana); this is called the single cause.
What are the seven non-causes?
The eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, and taste-base—these are called the seven that are not causes.
What are the four that are twofold, being either causes or non-causes?

The sense-base of visible form, the sense-base of sound, the sense-base of tangibles, and the sense-base of mental phenomena—these are called the four "two-part" bases, being either with cause or without cause.
What is the sense-base of visible form with cause?
If the sense-base of visible form is a resultant phenomenon (*vipāka-dharma*), it is called the sense-base of visible form with cause.
What is the cause of the sense-base of form?
The bodily intimation—whether arising from a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about, is called the cause of the sense-base of form.
What is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) that is not a cause?

It refers to the sense-sphere of form that is either a result of maturation (*vipāka*) or not a result of maturation; the non-resultant phenomena of the body such as beautiful or ugly color, dignified or undignified appearance, fair or unrefined skin, and pure or impure adornment; bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from an indeterminate mind, consisting of going, coming, turning around, bending, and stretching; and external forms known by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). These are called the sense-sphere of form that is not a cause.
What is the cause of the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*)?
If the sound-base is a resultant phenomenon (*vipākadharmma*), this is called the cause of the sound-base.
What is the cause of the sound-base?

If the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) is wholesome or unwholesome—namely, the vocal instruction consisting of sounds, syllables, and speech produced by a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind—this is called the cause of the sound-base.
What is the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) that is not a cause?

Whether it be a sound-base that is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), or a sound-base that is not a result of maturation; whether it be a pleasant or unpleasant vocal expression, a refined or unrefined vocal expression, a soft or non-soft vocal expression; whether it be vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*); or whether it be external sound known by the auditory consciousness—this is called the sound-base that is not a cause.
What is the cause of the sense-base of tangibles?
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are called the cause of the sense-base of tangibles.
What is not the cause of the sense-base of tangibles?
Excluding the four great elements, the remaining factors included in the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are called the non-causal sense-sphere of touch (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
What is the causal sense-sphere of mental objects?

It consists of the conditioned factors of the sense-sphere of mental objects, as well as those unconditioned factors that have retribution (*savipāka*), excluding the acquisition of the fruits [of the path]. Furthermore, it includes all other unconditioned wholesome factors with retribution, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), up to and including the afflictions (*kleśa*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and all form (*rūpa*). These are called the causal sense-sphere of mental objects.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not a cause?

If the sphere of mental objects is a condition, is without retribution, and is not shared karma; or if it consists of birth, old age, death, life-force, acquisition, fruition, the nine types of impure bodily progressions, or the unconditioned—this is called the sphere of mental objects that is not a cause.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many have causes and how many are without cause?
Eleven have causes; one is twofold, being either with cause or without cause.
What are the eleven that have causes?
The ten bases of form and the mind-base (manāyatana); these are called the eleven that have causes.
What are the one base that is twofold—either with cause or without cause?
The base of mental phenomena (dharmāyatana); this is called the one base that is twofold, either with cause or without cause.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that has a cause?

If the sphere of mental objects consists of those factors with a basis, such as feeling, perception, and so forth up to right bodily composure, this is called the sphere of mental objects that has a cause.
What is the sphere of mental objects that lacks a cause?

If the dharma-āyatana consists of knowledge that takes as its object the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), this is called the dharma-āyatana without cause.

The same applies to those with a sequence and those without a sequence, those with cause and those without cause, those with conditions and those without conditions, and the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are known and how many are not known?
All are known; they are known and seen as they truly are.
Of the twelve bases, how many are consciousness and how many are not consciousness?
All consciousnesses are consciousnesses that cognize according to their objects.
Among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are objects of understanding and how many are not?
All are objects of understanding, as they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Of the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are fully understood (*parijñāta*) and how many are not fully understood?
All are fully understood through knowledge and vision according to reality.
Of the twelve bases, how many are known by the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) and how many are not known by the knowledge of abandonment?

Eight are not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*); four are twofold, being either to be known through the knowledge of abandonment or not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What are the eight that are not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?
They are the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-base; these are called the eight that are not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What are the four that are twofold, being either to be known through the knowledge of abandonment or not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?

They are the sense-base of visible forms, the sense-base of sounds, the sense-base of mind, and the sense-base of phenomena; these are called the four that are twofold, being either to be known through the knowledge of abandonment or not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the sense-base of form?

If the sense-base of form is unwholesome, consisting of bodily intimation—whether moving forward or backward, bending or stretching—that arises from an unwholesome mind, this is called the knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the sense-base of form.
What is the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) that is not known by the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*)?

It refers to the sphere of form that is either wholesome (*kuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); namely, bodily forms that are beautiful or not beautiful, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, and well-adorned or not well-adorned; or the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about, which arises from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; or external forms cognizable by visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). This is called the sphere of form that is not known by the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the sense-base of sound?

If the sense-base of sound is unwholesome, arising from an unwholesome mind as the collection of sounds, phonemes, and vocal expressions, this is called the knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the sense-base of sound.
What is the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) that is not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

It refers to sounds that are wholesome or indeterminate; pleasant or unpleasant sounds; exquisite or non-exquisite sounds; soft or non-soft sounds; those vocal teachings consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; and external sounds cognized by the ear-consciousness. This is called the sphere of sound that is not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) known through the knowledge of abandonment?

If the sphere of mind consists of the unwholesome mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), this is called the sphere of mind known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the sphere of mind not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
If the mind-base (manāyatana) is wholesome or indeterminate, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called the mind-base known by non-abandoning knowledge (aprahāṇajñāna).
What is the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) known by abandoning knowledge (prahāṇajñāna)?

If the dharma-base consists of unwholesome feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental energy, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-precepts, and tainted mental energy—this is called the dharma-base known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

Excluding the underlying tendencies (anuśaya), the fetters (saṃyojana), and the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, the remaining sphere of mental objects is not known through the knowledge of abandonment; this is called the sphere of mental objects that is not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
The same applies to what is abandoned and what is not abandoned.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and how many are not to be cultivated?
Eight are not to be cultivated; four are of two kinds, being either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What are the eight that are not to be cultivated?
The eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, flavor-base, and tangible-object-base; these are called the eight that are not to be cultivated.
What are the four that are twofold, being either cultivated or not cultivated?
The sense-sphere of form, the sense-sphere of sound, the sense-sphere of mind, and the sense-sphere of phenomena—these are called the four that are twofold, being either cultivated or not cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*)?

If the sense-base of form arises from a wholesome mind as bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning—it is called the cultivation of the sense-base of form.
What is the non-cultivation of the sense-base of form?

If the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is unwholesome or indeterminate; if it consists of bodily forms that are beautiful or ugly, handsome or unhandsome, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, and pure or impure; if it consists of bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti)—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning about—arising from an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; or if it consists of external forms known by visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna)—this is called the sphere of form that is not to be cultivated (abhāvanīya).
What is the cultivation of the sense-base of sound?

If the sense-base of sound is wholesome, consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech—the vocal instruction arising from a wholesome mind—this is called the cultivation of the sense-base of sound.
What is the sense-base of sound that is not cultivated?

It refers to sound that is unwholesome or indeterminate; pleasant sound or unpleasant sound, exquisite sound or non-exquisite sound, soft sound or non-soft sound; sound produced by vocal instruction arising from an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; or external sound known by the auditory consciousness—this is called the sense-base of sound that is not cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the mind-base (*manāyatana*)?
If the mind-base consists of the wholesome mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), this is called the cultivation of the mind-base.
What is the non-cultivation of the mind-base?
If the mind-base (*manāyatana*)—whether unwholesome or indeterminate—consists of eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called the mind-base that is not cultivation (*abhāvanā*).
What is the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) as cultivation?

If the dharma-base consists of wholesome feeling and perception up to mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*), the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*); the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the outflow-tainted precepts of body and speech; the outflow-tainted bodily exertion (*vīrya*) and bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, and right bodily tranquility; and the certainty of the exhaustion of conditions through knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)—this is called the dharma-base as cultivation.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is not to be cultivated?

It refers to those factors of the sphere of mental objects that are unwholesome or indeterminate: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, old age, death, vitality, fetters; as well as the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, the impure mental exertion of the noble ones, and the seven unconditioned phenomena. This is called the sphere of mental objects that is not to be cultivated.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are realized (*sākṣātkṛta*) and how many are not realized?
All are realized, as they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the twelve bases, how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Eight are indeterminate; four are of three kinds—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What are the eight that are indeterminate?
The eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-base; these are called the eight indeterminate [bases].
What are the four bases that are of three kinds—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?

They are the base of visible forms, the base of sounds, the base of mind, and the base of mental phenomena; these are called the four bases that are of three kinds—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is the sense-base of form that is wholesome?

If the sense-base of form arises from a cultivated wholesome mind as bodily intimation—consisting of going, coming, contracting, extending, or turning—it is called the sense-base of form that is wholesome.
What is the sense-base of form that is not wholesome?

If the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—that arises following an unwholesome mind is included within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), this is called the sphere of form that is non-virtuous.
What is the sphere of form that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

If the visible-object base (rūpāyatana) is feeling (vedanā), or if the visible-object base is not a result (avipāka), nor a dharma subject to fruition (avipākadharma); if it is bodily beauty or ugliness, elegance or lack of elegance, loveliness or lack of loveliness, or purity or impurity; if it is the bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning about, produced by an indeterminate mind (avyākṛtacitta); or if it is external form known by visual consciousness—this is called the indeterminate visible-object base.
What is the sound-base (śabdāyatana) that is wholesome?
If the sound-base arises from the collection of sounds, phrases, and speech as an oral instruction produced by a cultivated wholesome mind, this is called the wholesome sound-base.
What is the sound-base that is unwholesome?
If the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) arises from an unwholesome mind as the collection of sounds, phonemes, and verbal expressions through vocal instruction, this is called the unwholesome sound-base.
What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) sound-base?

Whether the sound-base (śabdāyatana) is experienced as a result of maturation (vipāka) or is not a result of maturation; whether it is a pleasant or unpleasant sound, a beautiful or non-beautiful sound, a soft or non-soft sound that is a non-resultant phenomenon (avipākadharma); whether it is vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from an indeterminate mind (avyākṛtacitta); or whether it is an external sound known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the indeterminate sound-base.
What is the sense-sphere of mind that is wholesome?
If the sense-sphere of mind cultivates the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element, this is called the sense-sphere of mind that is wholesome.
What is the sense-sphere of mind that is unwholesome?
If the mind-base (manāyatana) is severed from the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu), this is called the unwholesome mind-base.
What is the indeterminate (avyākṛta) mind-base?

If the mind-base is experienced (vedita), or if the mind-base is neither-result (na-vipāka) nor a dharma that is not-result—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the indeterminate mind-base.
What is the wholesome sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?

If it consists of the cultivated feeling and perception within the sphere of mental objects, up to mental equanimity, the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of fruition, the attainment of cessation; the unmanifest precepts of the body and speech that are with outflows (*sāsrava*); the bodily exertion and bodily tranquility that are with outflows; right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, and right bodily tranquility; and the certainty of the exhaustion of conditions through knowledge—this is called the wholesome sphere of mental objects.
What is the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is unwholesome?

If the mental objects consist of feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the non-informative [actions] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, and tainted mental exertion—this is called the sense-sphere of mental objects that is unwholesome.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

It refers to those factors within the sphere of mental objects that are neither retribution nor productive of retribution, as well as the non-noble unconditioned (*anāsrava-asaṃskṛta*). These include: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, absence of regret, contentment, joy, mental vigor, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, birth, aging, death, life-force, and the outflow-tainted physical vigor that is non-noble, as well as the seven unconditioned phenomena. This is called the sphere of mental objects that is indeterminate.

Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are associated with training (*śaikṣa*), how many are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither associated with training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Ten are neither associated with training nor beyond training; two are threefold, being either associated with training, or beyond training, or neither associated with training nor beyond training.
What are the ten that are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee?
The ten bases of form (rūpāyatana); these are called the ten that are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
What are the two that are threefold—either trainee, or non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee?

The mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*): these two are said to be threefold—either trainee (*śaikṣa*), beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*).
What is the mind-base that is trainee?
If the mind-base is noble (*ārya*) but not beyond-training, this is called the mind-base that is trainee.
What is the mental sense-sphere of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?

If the mental element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) belong to one in training, this is called the mental sense-sphere of one in training.
What is the mental sense-sphere of one in training?

The seeker is free from fetters and proclivities; with the noble mind, they enter the noble path—whether as one of steadfast faith or steadfast Dharma, or as others among the various classes of beings—who perceive the faults and perils of conditioned existence and contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana.

Contemplating suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are, one desires to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, and to realize what has not yet been realized. Having abandoned the defilements and cultivating the path, whether one is a person in training (*śaikṣa*)—such as a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), a once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or a non-returner (*anāgāmin*)—or one who possesses perfected contemplative wisdom, or abides on the stage of knowledge, or has liberated the mind through contemplation, one then realizes the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*): either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
If it refers to a real person or to the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), this is called the mind-base (*manāyatana*) of training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the mind-base of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If the mind-base is noble (*ārya*) and not that of training, this is called the mind-base of no-more-training.
What is the mind-base (manāyatana) that is beyond training (aśaikṣa)?

If the mind-base consists of the mental element (manodhātu) and the mental-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) associated with the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) of one beyond training, this is called the mind-base beyond training.
What is the mind-base beyond training?

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship and has not yet attained the noble dharmas, desiring to attain them through the cultivation of the path, they become fully endowed with insight-knowledge; whether through the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of insight, they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If it is a real person, a destination, or the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, this is called the mind-base that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the mind-base that is neither in training nor beyond training?

If it is the mind-base that is the non-noble aggregate of consciousness and feeling, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called the mind-base that is neither in training nor beyond training.
What is the dharma-base of those in training (*śaikṣa*)?
If a dharma-base is noble (*ārya*) but not that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this is called the dharma-base of those in training.
What is the dharma-base of those in training?

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) associated with the faculty of faith—whether those factors are non-objectified (*anālambana*), untainted (*anāsrava*), or not belonging to the stage of training (*aśaikṣa*)—are called the "dharma-base of the trainee" (*śaikṣa-dharmāyatana*).
What is the dharma-base of the trainee?
When a trainee (śaikṣa) is free from fetters and proclivities, and the noble mind enters the noble path,
