until he immediately attains the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala)— whether it be a real person or a destiny, or feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, serene faith, joy, gladness, mental energy, mental pliancy, confidence, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right pliancy of body, as well as the certainty of the exhaustion of conditions through knowledge— this is called the "dharma-base of the trainee" (śaikṣo dharmāyatanaḥ).
What is the faculty of phenomena that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If the faculty of phenomena is noble and not that of one in training (*śaikṣa*), this is called the faculty of phenomena that is beyond training.
What is the faculty of phenomena that is beyond training?

The faculty of faith of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), as well as the mental factors associated with that faculty of faith, whether they be included within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) or be non-conditioned, untainted (*anāsrava*), and not belonging to training (*aśaikṣa*), are called the sphere of phenomena of one beyond training.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to a person beyond training who has attained the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, or [the factors] such as feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, serene faith, joy, gladness, mental energy, mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right tranquility, as well as the extinction through knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*): these are called the sphere of mental objects that is beyond training.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

It refers to those factors within the sphere of mental objects that are non-noble aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations; or visible form that is invisible and non-resistant, which is tainted, non-noble, and unconditioned, including feeling and perception, up to the attainment of non-perception and the first four types of form, as well as the seven non-noble unconditioned phenomena. This is called the sphere of mental objects that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

Among the twelve bases (āyatana), how many are results of maturation (vipāka), how many are factors that are results of maturation, and how many are neither results of maturation nor factors that are results of maturation?

Five are results of maturation; three are twofold, being either results of maturation or neither results of maturation nor factors that are results of maturation; and four are threefold, being either results of maturation, factors that are results of maturation, or neither results of maturation nor factors that are results of maturation.
What are the five results?
The eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base—these are called the five results.
What are the three that are twofold, being either result or non-result, or the state of not being a result?

The sense-base of odor, the sense-base of taste, and the sense-base of tangibility—these are called the three that are twofold: either resultant (*vipāka*) or neither-resultant-nor-non-resultant (*na-vipāka-na-avipākadharma*).
What are the four that are threefold: either resultant, or the state of being a cause for result (*vipākadharma*), or neither-resultant-nor-non-resultant?

The sense-base of visible forms, the sense-base of sounds, the sense-base of mind, and the sense-base of mental phenomena—these are called the four triads that are either resultants, or productive of resultants, or neither resultant nor productive of resultants.
What is the sense-base of odors that is a resultant?
If the olfactory base (*gandhāyatana*) is experienced, this is called the retribution of the olfactory base.
What is the retribution of the olfactory base?

If the olfactory base is produced as a result of karma, dharmas, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own portion—whether it be a pleasant odor or an unpleasant odor, a soft odor or a harsh odor, a pleasing odor or a displeasing odor—this is called the retribution of the olfactory base.
What is the odor-base (gandhāyatana) that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?

It refers to external odors, those external odors known by the nose-consciousness, such as the fragrance of tree roots, the fragrance of tree hearts, the fragrance of tree resins, the fragrance of tree bark, the fragrance of leaves, the fragrance of flowers, the fragrance of fruits, pleasant fragrances, unpleasant fragrances, and other external odors known by the nose-consciousness. This is called the odor-base that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant.
What is the retribution of the sense-base of taste?
If one experiences the sense-base of taste, this is called the retribution of the sense-base of taste.
What is the retribution of the sense-base of taste?

If the body, which is produced as a retribution born of karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own portion, possesses tastes that are sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or characterized by phlegm and mucus, this is called the retribution of the taste-base (*rasāyatana*).
What is the taste-base that is neither retribution nor a factor subject to retribution?

If it is the external sense-base of taste, or if it is an external taste-base known by tongue-consciousness—whether it be sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, or bland liquid, or any other external taste known by tongue-consciousness—this is called the sense-base of taste that is neither resultant nor a state leading to result.
What is the retribution of the sense-base of touch?
If one experiences the sense-base of touch, this is called the retribution of the sense-base of touch.
What is the retribution of the sense-base of touch?

If the body, which is comprised of the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) and is produced as a retribution born of karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and is included within the category of "mine," and possesses coldness, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, subtlety, roughness, smoothness, hardness, or softness—this is called the retribution of the sphere of tangibles.
What is the sense-base of tangibles that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?

It refers to external tangibles, or those external tangibles known by body-consciousness—such as cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, fineness, roughness, smoothness, hardness, or softness—and whatever other external tangibles are known by body-consciousness; these are called the sense-base of tangibles that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant.
What is the retribution of the sense-base of form?
If the sense-base of form is experienced, this is called the retribution of the sense-base of form.
What is the retribution of the sense-base of form?

If the visible-object base (*rūpāyatana*)—which is produced as a retribution born of karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and is comprised within one’s own continuum; whether it be beautiful or ugly, dignified or undignified, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, pure or impure; and including the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from feeling and mind, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—it is called the retribution of the visible-object base.
What is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) as a result of maturation (*vipākadharmā*)?
If the form-base is subject to maturation, this is called the form-base as a result of maturation.
What is the form-base as a result of maturation?

The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) that is either wholesome or unwholesome, and the bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about, which is produced by a wholesome or unwholesome mind—this is called the sense-base of form as a result of maturation (vipākadharmā).
What is the sphere of form that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?

It is the sphere of form that is indeterminate, not included within one's own continuum, and arises from a mind that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant; it consists of bodily intimation such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, as well as external forms known by visual consciousness. This is called the sphere of form that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant.
What is the sound-base as retribution?
If the sound-base is experienced [as a result of past karma], this is called the sound-base as retribution.
What is the sound-base as retribution?

If the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) arises as a retribution produced by karma, mental factors, or afflictions, and is comprised within one's own continuum—whether it be a pleasant or unpleasant sound, a melodious or non-melodious sound, or a soft or non-soft sound—and consists of vocal instruction arising from the mind through the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech, this is called the retribution of the sound-base.
What is the sound-base as a resultant phenomenon?
If the sound-base is retributive, it is called the sound-base as a resultant phenomenon.
What is the sound-base as a resultant phenomenon?

If the sense-base of sound is wholesome or unwholesome—whether it is the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind—this is called the sense-base of sound that is a result of maturation (*vipākadharmā*).
What is the sound-base (śabdāyatana) that is neither resultant (avipāka) nor subject to result (avipākadharmaka)?

It is the sound-base that is indeterminate (avyākṛta), not included within one's own sphere (asvīkṛta), and produced by a mind that is neither resultant nor subject to result—namely, the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; or external sounds known by the ear-consciousness. This is called the sound-base that is neither resultant nor subject to result.
What is the retribution of the mind-base (*manāyatana*)?
If the mind-base is experienced, or if the mind-base is the wholesome retribution of visual consciousness up to mental consciousness, this is called the retribution of the mind-base.
What is the dharma that is the retribution of the mind-base?
If the mind-base (*manāyatana*) is retribution-born (*vipākaja*), it is called the mind-base as a dharma of retribution (*vipākadharma*).
What is the mind-base as a dharma of retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution-born mind-base, the remaining wholesome or unwholesome mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are called the mind-base as a dharma of retribution.
What is the mind-base (manāyatana) that is neither resultant (avipāka) nor subject to result (avipākadharmaka)?

If the mind-base is indeterminate (avyākṛta) and not included within one's own continuum (asvīkṛta), from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called the mind-base that is neither resultant nor subject to result.
What is the retribution of the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?

It refers to those factors within the sphere of mental objects that are either feelings (*vedanā*) or wholesome retributions (*kuśala-vipāka*), excluding non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*). These include the remaining [mental factors] from feeling and perception (*saṃjñā*) up to equanimity of mind (*citta-upekṣā*), fear (*bhaya*), birth (*jāti*), life-force (*jīvita*), the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of fruition (*phala-prāpti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the outflow-tainted non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of bodily and vocal precepts, the outflow-tainted bodily exertion (*vīrya*), the outflow-tainted bodily pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), right speech (*samyag-vāk*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), right bodily exertion, and right bodily pliancy. This is called the retribution of the sphere of mental objects.
What is the dharma-base as retribution?
If the dharma-base is retribution, this is called the dharma-base as retribution.
What is the dharma-base as retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the dharma-base (dharmāyatana), all other wholesome conditioned dharmas—whether unwholesome, consisting of sensation and perception up to the afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the two meditative attainments, and all matter—are called the retribution-dharmas of the dharma-base.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is neither resultant (*vipāka*) nor of a nature to produce resultants?

It refers to those factors within the sphere of mental objects that are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not included within the category of "mine" (*asvaka*), as well as the noble unconditioned (*āryasaṃskṛta*), feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, birth, aging, death, the outflow-tainted bodily exertion, and the nine unconditioned phenomena. These are called the sphere of mental objects that is neither resultant nor of a nature to produce resultants.

Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*): how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

Eight are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation; four are of three types—either abandoned by insight, or abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the eight that are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

They are the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-object-base; these are called the eight that are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the four bases that are threefold—either abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

They are the base of visible forms, the base of sounds, the base of mind, and the base of mental phenomena; these are called the four bases that are threefold—either abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

If the form-base is unwholesome and arises from a mind associated with afflictions to be abandoned by insight—not being abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)—such as the bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about, this is called the form-base abandoned by insight.
What is the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

If the sense-sphere of form arises from the mind associated with unwholesome defilements (*kleśa*) that are abandoned through cultivation rather than through insight (*darśana*), such as the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) of going, coming, contracting, extending, or turning about, this is called the sense-sphere of form abandoned through cultivation.
What is the sense-base of form that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to those forms of the body that are wholesome or indeterminate—whether they are beautiful or ugly, dignified or undignified, graceful or ungraceful, or pure or impure; or it refers to bodily intimation arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning; or it refers to external forms known by visual consciousness. These are called the sense-base of form that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

If the sound-base is unwholesome, not abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and arises from a mind associated with afflictions abandoned by insight—consisting of sounds, syllables, and vocal expressions—it is called the sound-base abandoned by insight.
What is the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

If the sound-base arises from the vocal instruction of sounds, syllables, and speech produced by a mind associated with unwholesome defilements that are abandoned through cultivation rather than through vision (*darśana-heya*), this is called the sound-base abandoned through cultivation.
What is the sense-base of sound that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation? It is sound that is wholesome or indeterminate;

pleasant or unpleasant bodily sounds, melodious or non-melodious sounds, soft or non-soft sounds; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; and external sounds known by the auditory consciousness. This is called the sense-base of sound that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sense-base of mind that is abandoned by insight?

If the sense-base of mind is unwholesome and not abandoned through cultivation, but is associated with defilements abandoned by insight—namely, the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element—this is called the sense-base of mind abandoned by insight.
What is the sense-sphere of mind (*manāyatana*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

If the sense-sphere of mind consists of the mental element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) associated with unwholesome (*akuśala*) defilements that are abandoned through cultivation rather than through insight (*darśana*), this is called the sense-sphere of mind abandoned through cultivation.
What is the mind-base (manāyatana) that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?
If the mind-base is wholesome or indeterminate—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the mind-base that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is abandoned by vision?

If the sphere of mental objects is unwholesome and is not abandoned through cultivation, but is abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions abandoned by vision—namely: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, and tainted mental exertion—this is called the sphere of mental objects abandoned by vision.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) abandoned by cultivation?

If the sphere of mental objects consists of unwholesome states that are not abandoned by insight, but are abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions abandoned by cultivation—namely: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire-to-act, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, and tainted mental exertion—this is called the sphere of mental objects abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

If a sphere of mental objects is wholesome or indeterminate—excluding doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint—then the remaining spheres of mental objects are called the sphere of mental objects that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the twelve bases (āyatana), how many have the cause of abandonment by insight (darśana-heya-hetu), how many have the cause of abandonment by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-hetu), and how many have neither the cause of abandonment by insight nor the cause of abandonment by cultivation?

All are of three types: either having the cause of abandonment by insight, or having the cause of abandonment by cultivation, or having neither the cause of abandonment by insight nor the cause of abandonment by cultivation.
What is the eye-base that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

If the eye-base is the retribution of phenomena to be abandoned by insight—namely, the eye-base of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—this is called the eye-base that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the eye-base that has its cause in abandonment through cultivation?

If the eye-base is the retribution of a dharma abandoned through cultivation—namely, the eye-base of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—this is called the eye-base that has its cause in abandonment through cultivation.
What is the eye-base that is neither caused by what is abandoned through seeing nor by what is abandoned through cultivation?

If the eye-base is the retribution of wholesome dharmas—the eye-base among gods or humans—this is called the eye-base that is neither caused by what is abandoned through seeing nor by what is abandoned through cultivation.
The ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base are also like this.
What is the mind-base that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

If the mind-base is to be abandoned by insight, or if the mind-base is the retribution of a dharma to be abandoned by insight—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the mind-base that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the mental faculty (manāyatana) that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?

If the mental faculty is the retribution (vipāka) of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—it is called the mental faculty that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the mind-base (*manāyatana*) that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

It refers to the mind-base that is wholesome; or the mind-base that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas; or the mind-base that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution, ranging from eye-consciousness up to mental-consciousness. This is called the mind-base that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the form-base (*rūpāyatana*) that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetuka*)?

It is the form-base that is itself to be abandoned by insight; or the form-base that is the retribution (*vipāka*) of a dharma to be abandoned by insight, which consists of a body that is neither beautiful nor handsome, neither lovely nor pure; and the bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which is produced by a mind that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight. This is called the form-base that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the form base (*rūpāyatana*) whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

It is that form which is abandoned by cultivation, or the body resulting from the retribution of factors abandoned by cultivation, which is neither beautiful nor dignified, neither lovely nor pure; and it includes the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from a mind whose cause is abandoned by cultivation, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about. This is called the form base whose cause is abandoned by cultivation.
What is the form base (*rūpāyatana*) that is neither caused by what is abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) nor by what is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

It refers to: form bases that are wholesome; form bases that are the retribution of wholesome dharmas; or form bases that are neither retribution nor the nature of retribution, such as a beautiful body, an upright and dignified appearance, a fine complexion, or a pure and refined countenance; bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from a mind that is neither abandoned through seeing nor by cultivation, consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; or external forms known by visual consciousness. This is called the form base that is neither caused by what is abandoned through seeing nor by what is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetuka*)?

If the sound-base is to be abandoned by insight, or if it is the unpleasant sound, the non-exquisite sound, or the harsh sound that is the retribution (*vipāka*) of a sound-base to be abandoned by insight; or if it is the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech, which is produced by a mind that has its cause in factors to be abandoned by insight—this is called the sound-base that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

It is the sound-base itself, or that which is to be abandoned by cultivation; it is the unpleasant sound, the non-exquisite sound, or the non-gentle sound that is the retribution of a sound-base to be abandoned by cultivation; and it is the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech, arising from a mind whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation. This is called the sound-base that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sound-base (*śabdāyatana*) that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

It is the sound-base that is wholesome; or the sound-base that is the retribution (*vipāka*) of wholesome dharmas; or the sound-base that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution, consisting of pleasant sounds, exquisite sounds, and soft sounds produced by a mind that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation—namely, the vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*) of collected sounds, phonemes, and speech; or external sounds known by the ear-consciousness. This is called the sound-base that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the fragrance-base that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by seeing?

If the fragrance-base is the retribution of a dharma to be abandoned by seeing—namely, an unpleasant fragrance, an unsoft fragrance, or an disagreeable fragrance—this is called the fragrance-base that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by seeing.
What is the cause for the cessation through contemplation (*bhāvanā-heya*) regarding the sense-base of odors (*gandhāyatana*)?

If the sense-base of odors consists of the retribution of dharmas to be abandoned through contemplation—namely, unpleasant odors, non-soft odors, and disagreeable odors—this is called the cause for the cessation through contemplation regarding the sense-base of odors.
What is the fragrance-base that is neither caused by what is abandoned through vision nor by what is abandoned through cultivation?

It refers to the fragrance-base that is the result of wholesome dharmas; or the fragrance-base that is neither a result nor a dharma leading to a result, such as pleasant fragrances, soft fragrances, and agreeable fragrances of the body; or external fragrances known by the nose-consciousness. This is called the fragrance-base that is neither caused by what is abandoned through vision nor by what is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the gustatory base as a cause that is to be abandoned through insight?

If the gustatory base consists of the retribution of factors to be abandoned through insight—namely, the body's experiences of sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, phlegm, or mucus—it is called the gustatory base as a cause to be abandoned through insight.
What is the cause of the sense-base of taste that is abandoned through cultivation?

If the body resulting from the retribution of dharmas abandoned through cultivation—whether it be sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or characterized by phlegm and mucus—is called the cause of the sense-base of taste that is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the taste-base (*rasāyatana*) that is neither a cause to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

It is the taste-base that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas; or the taste-base that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution, such as the body’s sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or the sensations of phlegm and mucus; or external tastes known by the tongue-consciousness. This is called the taste-base that is neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sphere of tangibles that has the cause of abandonment through insight?

If the sphere of tangibles consists of the cold, heat, heaviness, rigidity, or roughness that is the retribution of factors abandoned through insight, this is called the sphere of tangibles that has the cause of abandonment through insight.
What is the cause of the sense-base of tangibles that is abandoned through cultivation?

If the body of the retribution of the sense-base of tangibles—whether cold, heat, heaviness, rigidity, or roughness—is produced by factors abandoned through cultivation, this is called the cause of the sense-base of tangibles abandoned through cultivation.
What is the sphere of tangibles that has neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to those spheres of tangibles that are the retribution of wholesome dharmas; or those spheres of tangibles that are not retribution, such as the body’s sensations of cold, heat, lightness, subtlety, softness, and smoothness; or external tangibles known by body-consciousness. These are called the spheres of tangibles that have neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by vision?

If a dharma-base has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by vision—whether it be the dharma-base itself, or the retribution of dharmas to be abandoned by vision, namely: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, life-force, fetters, the unmanifest non-restraint of body and speech, and tainted mental exertion—this is called the dharma-base that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by vision.
What is the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) whose cause is abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?

It refers to those factors of the dharma-base that are abandoned by cultivation, as well as the factors that are the retribution of those factors abandoned by cultivation: feeling, perception, volition, contact, vitarka, vicāra, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies (anuśaya), life-force, fetters (saṃyojana), the unmanifested non-restraint of body and speech, and tainted mental exertion. These are called the dharma-base whose cause is abandoned by cultivation.
What is the dharma-base (dharmāyatana) that has neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to those dharma-bases that are wholesome or the retribution of wholesome dharmas; or those dharma-bases that are neither retribution nor productive of retribution, excluding doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, and the non-informative (avijñapti) unwholesome conduct of body and speech. The remaining dharma-bases have neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation; this is called the dharma-base that has neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*): how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

Four are bound to the desire realm; six are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm; two are fourfold, being either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What are the four that are bound to the desire realm?
The tongue-base, the nose-base, the odor-base, and the taste-base—these are called the four that are bound to the desire realm.
What are the six that are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm?

The eye-base, ear-base, body-base, visible-form-base, sound-base, and tangible-object-base—these are called the six bases that are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What are the two bases that are fourfold, being either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or unbound?

The sense-base of mind (manāyatana) and the sense-base of phenomena (dharmāyatana)—these are called the two fourfold groups that are either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the formless realm, or are unbound.
What is the sense-base of the eye (cakṣurāyatana) that is bound to the desire realm?
If the eye-base is subject to the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) or is an outflowing eye-base, this is called the eye-base bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is the eye-base bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
If the eye-base is subject to the outflows of form (*rūpa-āsrava*) or is an outflowing eye-base, this is called the eye-base bound to the form realm.
The ear-base (*śrotra-āyatana*) and body-base (*kāya-āyatana*) are also like this.
What is the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) bound to the desire realm?

If the form-base is associated with the outflows of desire (*kāmāsrava*) or the outflows of existence (*bhavāsrava*), such as bodily forms that are beautiful or unattractive, dignified or undignified, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, and pure or impure; or the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which arise from a mind engaged in desire; or external forms known by the eye-consciousness that are associated with the outflows of desire and existence—this is called the form-base bound to the desire realm.
What is the sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu)?

It is that form which is associated with the outflows of form (rūpāsava) and is subject to outflows (sāsrava), such as the physical beauty, majesty, elegance, and purity of one's own body; the bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) consisting of the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which arise from mental formations; or external forms known by visual consciousness that are associated with the outflows of form and are subject to outflows. This is called the sense-base of form bound to the realm of form.
What is the sound-base (śabda-āyatana) bound to the desire realm?

It is the sound-base that is associated with the outflows of desire (kāma-āsrava) and is impure (sāsrava); namely, pleasant sounds or unpleasant sounds, exquisite sounds or non-exquisite sounds, soft sounds or non-soft sounds; those vocal teachings consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from a mind engaged in desire; and external sounds known by the ear-consciousness that are associated with the outflows of desire and are impure. This is called the sound-base bound to the desire realm.
What is the sound-base (śabdāyatana) bound to the form realm?

It refers to sounds that are outflows of the form realm, tainted, belonging to the body, such as pleasant sounds, exquisite sounds, and soft sounds; those produced by the mind of the form realm through the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech as vocal instruction; or external sounds known by the ear-consciousness that are outflows of the form realm and tainted. This is called the sound-base bound to the form realm.
What is the sense-base of tangibles bound to the desire realm?

If a tangible is a bodily sensation—whether cold or hot, light or heavy, coarse or fine, rough or smooth, hard or soft—that is associated with outflows (āsrava) and is impure; or if it is an external tangible known by body-consciousness that is associated with outflows and is impure, this is called the sense-base of tangibles bound to the desire realm.
What is the sense-base of tangibles bound to the realm of form?

If a tangible is known by body-consciousness as being bound to the outflows of form and subject to outflows—such as cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, fineness, softness, or smoothness—or if it is an external tangible known by body-consciousness as being bound to the outflows of form and subject to outflows, this is called the sense-base of tangibles bound to the realm of form.
What is the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) bound to the desire realm?

If the sense-base of mind consists of eye-consciousness up to mental-consciousness that is associated with the outflows of desire and is tainted by outflows, this is called the sense-base of mind bound to the desire realm.
What is the sense-sphere of mind (manāyatana) bound to the realm of form?

If the sense-sphere of mind consists of visual consciousness, auditory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and mental consciousness that are associated with the outflows of form and are subject to outflows, this is called the sense-sphere of mind bound to the realm of form.
What is the sense-base of mind (manāyatana) bound to the formless realm?

If the sense-base of mind consists of the formless outflows (anāsrava) and the tainted (sāsrava) mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, this is called the sense-base of mind bound to the formless realm.
What is the sense-sphere of mind that is unconditioned?
If the sense-sphere of mind consists of the noble, untainted mind-element and mind-consciousness-element, this is called the sense-sphere of mind that is unconditioned.
What is the sense-sphere of phenomena that is bound to the desire realm?

If the dharma-base consists of desire-taints (*kāmāsrava*), outflows (*āsrava*), feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, confidence, regret, non-regret, gladness, joy, mental energy, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters, the unmanifest non-restraint of body and speech, the outflowing manifest restraint of body and speech, and outflowing bodily energy—this is called the dharma-base bound to the desire realm.
What is the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?

If the sphere of mental objects consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, pliancy, joy, mental vigor, mental serenity, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters, the unmanifest discipline of the body and speech belonging to the outflows (*āsrava*), the outflowing physical vigor, and the outflowing physical serenity—this is called the sphere of mental objects bound to the realm of form.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) bound to the formless realm?

Those factors of the sphere of mental objects that are associated with the outflows of the formless realm and are with-outflow (sāsrava), namely: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, pliancy, mental exertion, mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters, and the unmanifest (avijñapti) bodily and vocal discipline associated with outflows, as well as the manifest bodily exertion and bodily tranquility associated with outflows—these are called the sphere of mental objects bound to the formless realm.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) that is unconditioned by the realms of existence?

Those factors of the sphere of mental objects that are noble, untainted, and unconditioned—namely, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, serene faith, joy, rapture, mental energy, mental tranquility, confidence, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, the attainment of fruition, the attainment of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right tranquility of body, as well as the nine unconditioned phenomena—these are called the sphere of mental objects that is unconditioned by the realms of existence.
Regarding the twelve bases (*āyatana*), how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
Eleven are threefold—either past, future, or present; one is fourfold—either past, future, present, or neither past, nor future, nor present.
What are the eleven bases that are threefold—either past, future, or present?
From the eye-base up to the tangible-object-base; these are called the eleven bases that are threefold—either past, future, or present.
What is the one fourfold category that is either past, future, present, or neither past, future, nor present?
The sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is called the one fourfold category that is either past, future, present, or neither past, future, nor present.
What is the past eye-base?
If the eye-base has arisen and ceased, this is called the past eye-base.
What is the future eye-base?
If the eye-base has not yet arisen and has not yet appeared, it is called the future eye-base.
What is the present eye-base?
If the eye-base has arisen but has not yet ceased, it is called the present eye-base.
The same applies up to the sense-sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*).
What is the past sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?

If the sense-sphere of mental objects has arisen and ceased—namely, sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and so forth, up to right mindfulness of the body (*kāyaprasrabdhi*)—this is called the past sense-sphere of mental objects.
What is the future sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?

If the sphere of mental objects has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged—ranging from sensation and perception up to right mindfulness of the body—this is called the future sphere of mental objects.
What is the present sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
If the sphere of mental objects has arisen but not yet ceased—ranging from feeling and perception up to correct mindfulness of the body—it is called the present sphere of mental objects.
What is the sphere of mental objects that is neither past, nor future, nor present?

If the dharma-base is unconditioned, such as the cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-base that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle One;
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others.
Section Two: The Chapter on Elements (Dhātu-varga). Question:
How many elements are there?
Answer: The eighteen elements (dhātus).
What are the eighteen elements?

The eye element, ear element, nose element, tongue element, body element; the form element, sound element, odor element, taste element, tangible-object element; the eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, body-consciousness element; the mind element, mind-consciousness element, and mental-object element.
What is the eye-element?
The eye-faculty is called the eye-element.
What is the eye-element?
The eye-base is called the eye-element.
What is the eye-element?
That which is the eye, comprised within one’s own continuum, consisting of translucent matter derived from the four great elements—this is called the eye-element.

If the eye is comprised within the category of self, is derived from the four great elements, and consists of pure matter (rūpa) belonging to the past, future, or present, this is called the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*).
What is the eye-element?
If the eye is comprised within the self’s sphere, it is indeterminate whether it has already seen, is currently seeing, or will see forms;
if the eye is comprised within the self’s sphere, it is indeterminate whether the light of forms has already arrived, is currently arriving, or will arrive—this is called the eye element.
What is the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*)?
It is that which belongs to the category of "mine" (*ātmīya*), such that the eye has already encountered, is currently encountering, or will encounter forms (*rūpa*), or is indeterminate;
or, if it belongs to the category of "mine," the form has already encountered, is currently encountering, or will encounter the eye, or is indeterminate. This is called the eye-element.

If the eye is unimpeded, this eye is the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), and the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*). It is the field, the substance, the gate, and the treasury; it is the world, the purity, the spring, and the ocean; it is the wasteland, the whirlpool, the ulcer, and the fetter; it is the eye, that which enters into my own portion, and this shore. When the internal base, the eye, sees forms, this is called the eye-element.
The ear element, nose element, tongue element, and body element are also like this.
What is the form element?
The sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is called the form element.
What is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
If form follows along with the characteristics of form, this is called the realm of form.
What is the realm of form?
If form is visible and resistant, and is cognizable by eye-consciousness, this is called the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*). What is the realm of form?

It refers to the retribution produced by karma, mental factors, and afflictions belonging to the category of "mine," which is the body's beautiful or ugly color, its graceful or ungainly appearance, its fine skin or coarse skin, and its pure or impure state. It also includes the bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*)—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—arising from a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a neutral mind. Furthermore, it includes external forms cognizable by eye-consciousness: blue, yellow, red, white, purple, black; coarse or subtle; long or short; square or round; water, land, light, shadow, smoke, clouds, dust, mist, vapor, brightness, and darkness; and all other external forms cognizable by eye-consciousness. This is called the realm of form.
What is the sound element?
The sound base is called the sound element.
What is the sound element?
If form is invisible and resistant, yet cognizable by the ear-consciousness, this is called the sound element (*śabdadhātu*).
What is the sound element?

If it is sound that arises as a result of karma, mental factors, or afflictions, which is included within one’s own continuum (*ātmiya*)—whether it be a pleasant or unpleasant bodily sound, a melodious or non-melodious sound, or a soft or non-soft sound; or if it is vocal instruction (*vāg-vijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from a wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate mind; or if it is external sound known by the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), such as the sound of chanting, large drums, small drums, *vīṇā* lutes, *vallakī* lutes, cymbals, the sound of dancing, singing, musical performances, or weeping; the voices of men, women, humans, non-humans, sentient beings, or non-sentient beings; the sounds of going, coming, or mutual contact; the sounds of wind, rain, water, and the mutual impact of the great elements; and all other external sounds known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sound-element (*śabda-dhātu*).
What is the fragrance element (*gandhadhātu*)?
If it is the sphere of fragrance (*gandhāyatana*), this is called the fragrance element.
What is the fragrance element?
If a form is invisible and resistant, yet cognizable by olfactory consciousness, this is called the odor-element (*gandhadhātu*).
What is the odor-element?

It refers to those odors produced as retribution from karma, mental factors, and afflictions, which are comprised within my own continuum—whether they be pleasant or unpleasant odors, soft or harsh odors, agreeable or disagreeable odors; or external odors cognizable by olfactory consciousness, such as the odors of tree roots, tree hearts, tree resins, tree bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits—whether they be pleasant or unpleasant odors, and all other external odors cognizable by olfactory consciousness. This is called the odor-element.
What is the taste element (*rasadhātu*)?
If it is the sense-field of taste (*rasāyatana*), it is called the taste element.
What is the taste element?
If it is invisible, possesses resistance, and is cognizable by tongue-consciousness, this is called the taste element (*rasadhātu*).
What is the taste element?

It refers to that which is produced as retribution from karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own continuum—namely, bodily tastes such as sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, saliva, and phlegm; or external tastes cognizable by tongue-consciousness, such as sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, and bland, whether in the form of water or liquid; and whatever other external tastes are cognizable by tongue-consciousness. This is called the taste element.
What is the element of tangibles?
If it is the sense-base of tangibles, it is called the element of tangibles.
What is the element of tangibles?
If form is invisible and resistant, yet cognizable by body-consciousness, this is called the tangible element (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*).
What is the tangible element?

That which is produced as a retribution from karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own continuum—namely, the cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, roughness, fineness, hardness, softness, and so forth of the body; or external tangibles cognizable by body-consciousness—this is called the tangible element.
What is the eye-consciousness element?

If consciousness arises from the faculty of the eye with respect to the objective field of visible forms—whether it has already arisen, is presently arising, will arise, or is indeterminate—it is called the eye-consciousness element.
What is the element of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness?
If consciousness arises from the body-faculty with contact as its object—whether it has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate—it is called the element of body-consciousness.
What is the mind element (*manodhātu*)?

It is that which cognizes phenomena, reflects upon phenomena, and attends to phenomena; whether it be the initial mind that has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate—this is called the mind element.
What is the consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu)?

It refers to consciousness that is similar [to its object] and not separated from its respective sphere, as well as other similar minds—whether already arisen, presently arising, yet to arise, or indeterminate. This is called the consciousness-element.
What is the dharma-element (dharmadhātu)?
If the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) is this, it is called the dharma-element.
What is the dharma-element?

The aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations—whether they are forms that are invisible and non-resistant, or whether they are unconditioned—are called the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
What is the dharma-element?
Feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom,
liberation, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, confidence, remorse, absence of remorse, gladness, joy, mental energy,
mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, and equanimity of mind.
doubt, fear, afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, old age, death, life-force (*jīvita*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*),
the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the unmanifest non-restraint of body and speech,

the manifest and unmanifest restraint of body and speech associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), the outflowing effort of body and the outflowing tranquility of body, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right [livelihood].
The bodily exertion of right bodily composure, the cessation through wisdom and the cessation not through wisdom, the fixed abiding of phenomena, and the spheres of infinite space,
infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception— these are called the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are material (*rūpin*) and how many are non-material (*arūpin*)?
Ten are material; seven are non-material; one is twofold, being either material or non-material.
What are the ten that are material?

The eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, body-element, visible-form-element, sound-element, odor-element, taste-element, and tangible-object-element—these are called the ten material elements.
What are the seven non-material elements?

The eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, body-consciousness element, mind element, and mind-consciousness element—these are called the seven non-material [elements].
What is the one that is twofold, being either material or non-material?
The dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is called "one part of two," being either form (*rūpa*) or non-form (*arūpa*).

What is the form within the dharma-element? It consists of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of bodily and vocal non-precepts; the tainted (*sāsrava*) unmanifest of bodily and vocal precepts; the tainted bodily effort (*vīrya*) and the tainted bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily tranquility. This is called the form within the dharma-element.
What is the non-material dharma-realm?

From sensation and perception up to the attainment of cessation, from the extinction of objects of knowledge up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this is called the non-material dharma-realm.
Of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are visible and how many are invisible?
One is visible; seventeen are invisible. Which one is visible?
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is called the one that is visible.
What are the seventeen that are invisible?
With the exception of the form realm, the remainder are invisible.
Of the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
Ten are with resistance; eight are without resistance.
Which ten are with resistance?
The ten material elements (rūpadhātu) are called the ten with resistance (sapratigha).
What are the eight without resistance?
The seven consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu) and the mental-object element (dharmadhātu); these are called the eight without resistance.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are noble (*ārya*) and how many are non-noble (*anārya*)?
Fifteen are non-noble; three are of two kinds, being either noble or non-noble.
What are the fifteen that are non-noble?
The ten material elements and the five consciousness elements—these fifteen are called non-noble.
What are the three that are twofold, being either noble or non-noble?
The mind element, the mental-consciousness element, and the dharma element—these three are called twofold, being either noble or non-noble.
What is the mind-element that is non-noble?
If the mind-element is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called the non-noble mind-element.
What is the non-noble mind-element?
If the mind-element is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, it is called the non-noble mind-element.
What is the noble mind-element?
If the mind-element is outflow-free (anāsrava), it is called the noble mind-element.
What is the noble mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
If the mind-element is associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), it is called the noble mind-element.
What is the noble mind-element?
Whether it be the mind-element of one in training (*śaikṣa*) or one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*):

when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, enters the noble path with a noble mind—whether as one of steadfast faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or steadfast Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), or others among those in the various realms—who perceives the faults and afflictions of conditioned existence, contemplates the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*, and views suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; who desires to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, and to realize what has not yet been realized, and who practices the path while remaining free from defilements.

When one sees a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—who is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by contemplation, they realize the fruit of asceticism: either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with insight (vipaśyanā-jñāna)—whether through the stage of wisdom or through the liberation of mind through insight—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If it is a real person, a destiny, or the mind-element (*manodhātu*), this is called the noble mind-element.
The mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is also like this.
What is the non-noble dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*)?
If the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is with outflows (sāsrava), it is called the non-noble dharma-element.
What is the non-noble dharma-element?

It refers to the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations; or if it is form that is invisible and non-resistant yet with outflows; or if it is a non-noble unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) phenomenon—this is called the non-noble dharma-element.
What is the dharma-element that is non-noble?

If the dharma-element is neither-learner-nor-non-learner—namely, sensation and perception up to the attainment of non-perception, the first four types of form, and the seven unconditioned phenomena—this is called the dharma-element that is non-noble.
What is the noble dharma-realm?
If a dharma is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the noble dharma-realm.
Why is the dharma-realm called noble?

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and the mental factors associated with the faculty of faith, as well as those phenomena that are non-objective and untainted (*anāsrava*), are called the noble dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu-ārya*).
What is the noble dharma-sphere?
Whether it be the noble dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), or the dharma-realm of those in training (*śaikṣa*), or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*);
when a person in training is free from fetters and proclivities, up until the attainment of the fruit of arhatship;

whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a destiny (*gati*); or feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, confidence, joy, gladness, mental energy, mental serenity, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruits, the attainment of the cessation-concentration (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right serenity of body, as well as the certainty of the exhaustion of conditions through knowledge—these are called the noble dharma-realm.
Of the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
Fifteen are with outflows; three are of two kinds, being either with outflows or without outflows.
What are the fifteen that are with outflows?
The ten material elements and the five consciousness elements—these are called the fifteen with-outflows (*sāsrava*).
What are the three that are of two kinds, being either with-outflows or without-outflows (*anāsrava*)?

The mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*)—these are called the three that are of two kinds, being either with-outflows or without-outflows.
What is the mind-element with outflows?
If the mind-element is accompanied by craving, it is called the mind-element with outflows.
What is the mind-element with outflows?
If the mind-element is neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training, it is called the contaminated mind-element.
What is the uncontaminated mind-element?
If the mind-element is without craving, it is called the uncontaminated mind-element.
What is the mind-element that is without outflows?
If the mind-element is associated with the faculty of faith, it is called the mind-element without outflows.
What is the mind-element without outflows?

Whether it be the mind-element (*manodhātu*) or the case of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who are free from fetters and latencies, up until they attain the fruit of arhatship;
or whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a destiny (*gati*) that constitutes the mind-element—this is called the untainted mind-element (*anāsrava manodhātu*).
The consciousness element is also like this.
What is the dharma element with outflows?
If the dharma element is associated with craving, it is called the dharma element with outflows.
What is the dharma-element with outflows?

The feeling aggregate, the perception aggregate, and the formations aggregate; and whatever form is invisible, non-resistant, and associated with craving—this is called the dharma-element with outflows.
What is the dharma-element that is with outflows (*sāsrava*)?

If the dharma-element is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), comprising feeling, perception, and so forth up to the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), as well as the first four types of form (*rūpa*), this is called the dharma-element that is with outflows.
What is the untainted (anāsrava) dharma-realm?
If the dharma-realm is free from craving, it is called the untainted dharma-realm.
What is the untainted dharma-realm?

The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and its associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), as well as those phenomena that are non-objective and free from craving—these are called the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
What is the untainted dharma-realm?
Whether it be the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), whether it be the trainee (*śaikṣa*) or the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or that which is non-noble and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
when a trainee is detached from the fetters and proclivities, up until the point they attain the fruit of arhatship;

whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a destiny (*gati*); or feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial mental application (*vitarka*), sustained mental application (*vicāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), gladness (*saumanasya*), mental energy (*cittavīrya*), mental serenity (*cittaprasrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*), the attainment of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right effort of body (*samyakvyāyāma*), and right serenity of body (*samyakpraśrabdhi*); the extinction through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), the extinction not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*), the fixed abiding of dharmas (*dharmasthititā*), and the knowledge of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the knowledge of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the knowledge of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)—these are called the untainted dharma-realm (*anāsravadharmadhātu*).

The same applies to having craving and being without craving, having seeking and being without seeking, what is to be grasped and what is not to be grasped, having grasping and being without grasping, and having superiority and being without superiority.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated?
Five are appropriated; thirteen are twofold, being either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What are the five that are appropriated?
The eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, and body-element—these are called the five elements of feeling (*vedanā*).
What are the thirteen that are twofold, being either feeling or not feeling? They are:

the form-element, sound-element, odor-element, taste-element, and tangible-object-element; the eye-consciousness-element, ear-consciousness-element, nose-consciousness-element, tongue-consciousness-element, and body-consciousness-element; and the mind-element, mind-consciousness-element, and mental-object-element. These are called the thirteen that are twofold, being either feeling or not feeling.
What is feeling pertaining to the form realm?
If feeling is internal and pertains to the form realm, it is called feeling pertaining to the form realm.
What is feeling pertaining to the form realm?

If there is bodily form belonging to the category of the self, produced as a retribution from karma, dharmas, and afflictions of the form realm—whether it be beautiful or ugly, dignified or undignified, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, or pure and refined or not pure and refined—as well as the bodily intimation arising from the mind, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about, this is called feeling of the form realm.
What is the form realm that is not felt?
That which is outside the form realm is called the form realm that is not felt.
What is the form realm that is not felt?

If it is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate matter of the form realm that is not included within one's own sphere; or if it is bodily intimation—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning—arisen from a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a mind that is neither resultant nor productive of result; or if it is external matter known by visual consciousness: these are called "matter of the form realm that is not felt."
What is the sound element that is appropriated?
If the sound element is internal, it is called the sound element that is appropriated.
What is the sound element that is appropriated?

If the sound-element produced as retribution from karma, phenomena, or defilements, which is comprised within one's own continuum (*ātmiya*), consists of pleasant or unpleasant sounds, exquisite or non-exquisite sounds, or soft or non-soft sounds; and if it arises from feeling and the mind, and constitutes the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech as vocal instruction—this is called the sound-element of feeling (*vedanā*).
What is the sound-element that is not felt?
That which is external to the sound-element is called the sound-element that is not felt.
What is the sound-element that is not felt?

If the sound-element is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not included within one's own sphere; or if it is the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a mind that is neither resultant nor subject to result; or if it is an external sound known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sound-element that is not felt.
What is the experience of the odor-element?
That which is within the odor-element is called the experience of the odor-element.
What is the experience of the odor-element?

If the fragrance of the body—whether pleasant or unpleasant, soft or not soft, agreeable or not agreeable—which is produced by karma, dharmas, and afflictions, and is comprised within the category of "mine," this is called the experience of the fragrance-element (*gandhadhātu*).
What is the odor-element that is not felt?

If it is an external odor within the odor-element known by the nose-consciousness—such as the fragrance of tree roots, the fragrance of tree hearts, the fragrance of tree resins, the fragrance of tree bark, the fragrance of leaves, the fragrance of flowers, the fragrance of fruits, pleasant odors, unpleasant odors, and other external odors known by the nose-consciousness—this is called the odor-element that is not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the taste element?
That which is within the taste element is called the feeling associated with the taste element.
What is the feeling associated with the taste element?

If the taste-element produced as retribution from karma, phenomena, and afflictions, which is comprised within my own continuum, consists of the body’s sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, phlegmatic, or catarrhal tastes, this is called the "taste-element that is felt" (*vedanīya*).
What is the taste-element that is not felt?

If the taste element is external, known by the tongue-consciousness—whether it be sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, or bland external juices, or any other external tastes known by the tongue-consciousness—this is called the taste element that is not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the element of tangibles?
That which is within the element of tangibles is called the feeling associated with the element of tangibles.
What is the feeling associated with the element of tangibles?

If the tangible element—arising from karma, mental factors, or afflictions, comprised within the category of "mine," and pertaining to the body—is cold, hot, light, heavy, coarse, fine, rough, smooth, hard, or soft, this is called the feeling of the tangible element.
What is the element of tangibles that is not felt?

It refers to external tangibles, or those external tangibles known by body-consciousness—such as cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, fineness, roughness, smoothness, hardness, softness, and whatever other external tangibles are known by body-consciousness. This is called the element of tangibles that is not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the eye-consciousness element?
That which is within the eye-consciousness element is called the feeling associated with the eye-consciousness element.
What is the feeling associated with the eye-consciousness element?

If the eye-consciousness element is produced as a retribution from karma, dharmas, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own sphere, it is called the "appropriated" (upātta) eye-consciousness element.
What is the non-appropriated eye-consciousness element?
If the external eye-consciousness element is not the eye-consciousness element itself, this is called the non-appropriated eye-consciousness element.
The same applies to the ear-consciousness element, the nose-consciousness element, the tongue-consciousness element, and the body-consciousness element.
What is the feeling-element of the mind-element?
That which is internal to the mind-element is called the feeling-element of the mind-element.
What is the feeling-element of the mind-element?

If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is produced as a result of karma, mental objects (*dharma*), or afflictions (*kleśa*), and is comprised within what belongs to the self (*ātmabhāva*), this is called the "mind-element that is sensation" (*vedanā*).
What is the mind-element that is not sensation?
If it is external to the mind-element, this is called the "mind-element that is not sensation."
What is the mind-element that is not associated with feeling?
If the mind-element is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not included within one's own sphere, this is called the mind-element that is not associated with feeling.
The consciousness element is also like this.
What is the feeling of the dharma-element?
Whatever is within the dharma-element is called the feeling of the dharma-element.
What is feeling (vedanā) within the dharma-element (dharmadhātu)?

It refers to that which is produced as retribution by karma and afflictions within the dharma-element, and which is comprised within my own portion: namely, perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), initial application (vitarka), sustained application (vicāra), view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), regret (kaukṛtya), non-regret (akaukṛtya), gladness (saumanasya), joy (prīti), mental exertion (cittavīrya), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), mindfulness (smṛti), fear (bhaya), life-force (jīvita), and the exertion of the contaminated body (sāsrava-kāyavīrya). This is called feeling within the dharma-element.
In what sense is the dharma-dhātu non-sensate?
If it is apart from the dharma-dhātu, that is called the dharma-dhātu being non-sensate.
In what sense is the dharma-dhātu non-sensate?

If the dharma-element is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not included within one's own sphere (*svakīya*), and the remaining dharma-element is not felt (*anupātta*), this is called the dharma-element that is not felt.
The same applies to the internal and external [elements].
Among the eighteen elements (dhātus), how many have retribution (savipāka) and how many are without retribution (avipāka)?
Thirteen are without retribution; five are of two kinds, being either with retribution or without retribution.
What are the thirteen that are without retribution?
The eight form elements and the five consciousness elements—these are called the thirteen that are without retribution (*avipāka*).
What are the five that are of two parts, being either with retribution (*savipāka*) or without retribution?

The form element, the sound element, the mind element, the mental consciousness element, and the phenomena element—these are called the five that are of two parts, being either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the retribution-bound [dharma] of the form realm?
If it is a dharma that is a retribution in the form realm, this is called the retribution-bound [dharma] of the form realm.
What is the retribution-bound [dharma] of the form realm?

Whether it be wholesome or unwholesome in the realm of form, or whether it be bodily intimation arising from a wholesome or unwholesome mind—consisting of going, coming, contracting, extending, or turning about—this is called "retribution-bound" in the realm of form.
What is the form realm that is non-resultant?

It refers to that which is resultant in the form realm and that which is non-resultant in the form realm; specifically, non-resultant phenomena such as the body’s beautiful or ugly complexion, dignified or undignified appearance, fair or unrefined skin, and pure or impure state; the bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which is produced by an indeterminate mind; and external forms known by visual consciousness—these are called the form realm that is non-resultant.
What is the sound-element with retribution?
If the sound-element is of a nature that entails retribution, this is called the sound-element with retribution.
What is the sound-element with retribution?

If the sound-element is wholesome or unwholesome, or if it is vocal instruction arising from a wholesome or unwholesome mind—consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech—this is called the sound-element with retribution.
What is the sound-element that is without retribution (*avipāka*)?

Whether it be the sound-element that is retribution or the sound-element that is not retribution—namely, pleasant or unpleasant sounds, exquisite or non-exquisite sounds, soft or non-soft sounds, which are vocal instructions consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from an indeterminate mind; or whatever external sounds are known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sound-element that is without retribution.
What is the mind-element that is retributive?
If the mind-element is a dharma subject to retribution, this is called the mind-element that is retributive.
What is the mind-element that is retributive?
Excluding the wholesome resultant mental element, the remaining wholesome or unwholesome mental elements are called the mental element with result.
What is the mental element without result?

Whether it be the mind-element that is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), or the mind-element that is not a result of maturation, or the mind-element that is a non-resultant phenomenon (*avipākadharma*), this is called the mind-element without maturation.
The same applies to the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
In what sense does the dharma-realm possess retribution?
