If the dharma-realm is a phenomenon that entails retribution, this is called the dharma-realm possessing retribution.
In what sense does the dharma-realm possess retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the dharma-element, all other wholesome or conditioned phenomena within the dharma-element—whether unwholesome, or comprising sensation and perception up to the afflictions, the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and all matter—are called the dharma-element with retribution.
What is the dharma-element that is non-retribution (*avipāka*)?

Whether it be the dharma-element as retribution or the dharma-element as non-retribution, those dharmas that are non-retribution—excluding non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the non-informative (*avijñapti*) unwholesome conduct of body and speech—the remaining dharma-element is non-retribution. This is called the dharma-element that is non-retribution.
Of the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are mind (*citta*) and how many are non-mind?
Seven are mind; eleven are non-mind.
What are the seven minds?
The seven consciousness elements are called the seven minds.
What are the eleven that are not mind?
The ten material elements and the mental-object element (dharmadhātu) are called the eleven that are not mind.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with the mind?
Ten are not associated with the mind; seven are said to be neither associated with the mind nor dissociated from it; one is of two kinds, being either associated with the mind or dissociated from it.
What are the ten that are not associated with mind?
The ten elements of form (rūpadhātu); these are called the ten that are not associated with mind.
What are the seven that are neither said to be associated with mind nor dissociated from mind?
The seven consciousness elements are called the seven that are neither said to be associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind.
What is the one that is divided into two parts, being either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind?
The dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) is called "partly associated with mind and partly not associated with mind.
What is the dharma-element associated with mind?

If the dharma-element consists of mental factors (*caitasika*), such as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), up to and including the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), this is called the dharma-element associated with mind.
What is the dharma-realm that is not associated with the mind?

If the dharma-realm is not produced by the mind, up to and including the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-realm that is not associated with the mind.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are mental concomitants (*caitta*) and how many are not mental concomitants?
Seventeen are not mental concomitants; one is twofold, being either a mental concomitant or not a mental concomitant.
What are the seventeen that are not mental concomitants (*cittasamprayukta*)?
The ten material elements (*rūpadhātu*) and the seven consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*); these are called the seventeen that are not mental concomitants.
What is the one that is twofold, being either a mental concomitant or not a mental concomitant?
The dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is called "one part of two," being either mental factors (caitta) or non-mental factors (acaitta).
What is the dharma-element that consists of mental factors?

Those factors within the dharma-element that have an object (sālambana), such as feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), up to the afflictions (kleśa) and latent tendencies (anuśaya)—these are called the dharma-element consisting of mental factors.
What is the dharma-element that is not a mental concomitant?

If the dharma-element is not produced by conditions, up to and including the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-element that is not a mental concomitant.
Among the eighteen elements (dhātus), how many have an object (sālambana) and how many are without an object (anālambana)?
Seven have an object; ten are without an object; and one is of two kinds, being either with or without an object.
What are the seven with objects?
The seven consciousness elements; these are called the seven with objects.
What are the ten without objects?
The ten material elements (rūpa-dhātu) are called the ten that are without objects (anālambana).
What is the one element that is twofold—either with an object or without an object?
The mental-object element (dharma-dhātu) is called the one that is twofold—either with an object or without an object.
What is the dharma-element with objects?
Those mental factors associated with the mind within the dharma-element—ranging from feeling and perception up to the afflictions and latent tendencies—are called the dharma-element with objects.
What is the dharma-element without objects?

If the dharma-dhātu is not produced by mental factors, up to and including the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-dhātu being without an object.
Among the eighteen dhātus, how many are associated with the mind, and how many are dissociated from the mind?
Seventeen are exclusively associated with the mind; one is either partially associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the seventeen that are exclusively associated with the mind?
The ten elements of form and the seven elements of consciousness—these are called the seventeen that are exclusively associated with the mind.
What is the "one-and-two-part" which is either associated with mind (*cittasamprayukta*) or dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*)?
The dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is what is called the one-and-two-part which is either associated with mind or dissociated from mind.
What is the dharma-realm that is associated with mind?

If the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) evolves in accordance with the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind—namely, sensation and perception, up to the afflictions and latent tendencies; the unmanifest (avijñapti) of tainted bodily and vocal discipline; tainted bodily exertion and tainted bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility—this is called the dharma-element that is concomitant with the mind.
What is the dharma-realm that does not accompany the mind?

If the dharma-realm does not follow the movement of the mind, and does not arise, abide, or cease together with the mind—up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—this is called the dharma-realm that does not accompany the mind.
The same applies to those that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and those that do not follow the mind (*na cittānuvartin*).
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are karma and how many are not karma?
Fifteen are not karma; three are of two kinds, being either karma or not karma.
What are the fifteen that are not karma?
The eight material elements (*rūpadhātu*) and the seven consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*); these are called the fifteen that are not karma.
What are the three that are twofold, being either karma or not karma?

The visible-form element (*rūpa-dhātu*), the sound element (*śabda-dhātu*), and the mental-object element (*dharma-dhātu*)—these three are called the "two-part" elements, being either karma or non-karma.
What is the visible-form element that is karma?

It refers to bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) consisting of approaching, departing, contracting, extending, and turning, which is initiated by a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a neutral mind; this is called the visible-form element that is karma.
What is the form realm that is not karma?

The body’s being beautiful or not beautiful, dignified or not dignified, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, and pure or not pure; or external forms known by the eye-consciousness—this is called the form realm that is not karma.
What is the action of the sound-element (*śabdadhātu*)?

That which is produced by a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a neutral mind—namely, the gathering of sounds, phonemes, and speech as vocal instruction—is called the action of the sound-element.
What is the sound element that is not karma?

Pleasant bodily sounds and unpleasant bodily sounds, exquisite sounds and non-exquisite sounds, soft sounds and non-soft sounds—whatever external sounds are known by the ear-consciousness are called the sound element that is not karma.
What is the karma of the dharma-element? It consists of volition (*cetanā*);

bodily and vocal non-restraint and non-instruction; tainted bodily and vocal restraint and instruction; and right speech, right action, and right livelihood. These are called the karma of the dharma-element.
What is the dharma-element that is not action (*karma*)?

Excluding volition (*cetanā*), bodily and vocal non-restraint (*avirati-avijñapti*), tainted bodily and vocal restraint (*sāsrava-virati-avijñapti*), right speech, right action, and right livelihood—the remaining dharma-element is not action; this is called the dharma-element that is not action.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are associated with karma (*karmasaṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with karma?

Seven are associated with karma; ten are not associated with karma; and one is of three parts: either associated with karma, or not associated with karma, or neither stated to be associated with nor not associated with karma.
What are the seven associated with karma?
The seven consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu) are called the seven associated with karma.
What are the ten not associated with karma?
The ten material elements (rūpa-dhātu) are called the ten that are not associated with karma (karma-samprayukta).
What is the one that is threefold—sometimes associated with karma, sometimes not associated with karma, or sometimes not stated to be either associated with or not associated with karma?

The dharma-element (dharmadhātu) is called the "one-third" [category], being either associated with karma, not associated with karma, or neither said to be associated with nor not associated with karma.
What is the dharma-element associated with karma?

If the dharma-element is associated with volition (*cetanā*), excluding volition itself, the remaining factors from sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) up to the afflictions (*kleśa*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are called the dharma-element associated with action (*karma-saṃprayukta*).
What is the dharma-element not associated with action?

If the dharma-realm is associated with non-volition, arising up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-realm that is not associated with karma.
What is the dharma-realm that is said to be neither associated with karma nor dissociated from karma?
Volition (cetanā) is called the dharma-element; it is not said to be associated with action or dissociated from action.
Among the eighteen elements, how many are common to action and how many are not common to action?
Seven are common to action, ten are not common to action, and one is of two kinds—either common to action or not common to action.
What are the seven shared activities?
The seven consciousness elements are called the seven shared activities.
What are the ten unshared activities?
The ten material elements (daśa rūpadhātavaḥ) are called the ten non-common karmas (daśāveṇikakarmāṇi).
What is the one element that is twofold—either common karma or non-common karma?
The dharma-element (dharmadhātu), this is called the one element that is twofold—either common karma or non-common karma.
What is the dharma-element of common karma?

If the dharma-element evolves in accordance with karma, such that it arises, abides, and ceases together with common karma—namely, the perception of cessation, mental contact, and so forth, up to the afflictions and latent tendencies; the two meditative attainments; the unmanifest forms of bodily and vocal restraint associated with outflows; the outflow-associated bodily exertion and bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility—this is called the dharma-element of common karma.
What is the non-common karma of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*)?

If the dharma-element does not follow along with karma, and is produced, abides, and ceases independently [of it]—namely, the mental formations of indefinite thought, birth, old age, death, life-force, and acquisitions; the unmanifest non-restraint of body and speech; the manifest and unmanifest restraint of body and speech associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); the manifest effort of body associated with outflows; and the nine unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—this is called the non-common karma of the dharma-element.
The same applies to those that follow karma and those that do not follow karma.
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*): how many are causes and how many are non-causes?
Seven are causes, seven are non-causes, and four are of two kinds, being either causes or non-causes.
What are the seven causes?
The seven consciousness elements (vijñānadhātu) are called the seven causes.
What are the seven non-causes?
The eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, body-element, odor-element, and taste-element—these are called the seven that are not causes.
What are the four that are twofold, being either causes or non-causes?
The visible-object element, sound element, tangible-object element, and mental-object element—these four are called the "two-part" elements, being either with cause or without cause.
What is the visible-object element with cause?
If the visible-object element is a resultant phenomenon (*vipāka-dharma*), it is called the visible-object element with cause.
What is the cause of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?

Whether it be that which belongs to the form realm, whether wholesome or unwholesome, or the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which is produced by a wholesome or unwholesome mind—this is called the cause of the form realm.
What is the form realm that is not a cause? It refers to the retribution of the form realm or that which is not retribution;

the beautiful or ugly physical appearance of the body that is not a retribution-dharma; the dignified or undignified, the fair-skinned or un-fair-skinned, the pure and refined or impure and unrefined; the bodily intimation arising from an indeterminate mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; or external forms known by visual consciousness. These are called the form realm that is not a cause.
What is the cause of the sound-element?
If the sound-element is a resultant phenomenon (*vipāka-dharma*), this is called the cause of the sound-element.
What is the cause of the sound-element?

If the sound-element is wholesome or unwholesome, whether it is produced by a wholesome mind or an unwholesome mind as the vocal instruction consisting of sounds, phonemes, and speech—this is called the cause of the sound-element.
What is the sound-element that is not a cause?

It refers to whether the sound-element is a result of maturation (*vipāka*) or not a result of maturation; whether it is a pleasant or unpleasant sound, a melodious or non-melodious sound, or a soft or non-soft sound that is not a dharma resulting from maturation; whether it is vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech produced by an indeterminate mind; or whether it is external sound known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sound-element that is not a cause.
What is the cause of the element of tangibility?
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and air—are called the cause of the element of tangibility.
What is not the cause of the element of tangibility?
Excluding the four great elements, those phenomena subsumed under the sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*) that are not causes are called the non-causal sphere of tangibles.
What is the causal sphere of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*)?

If a phenomenon of the sphere of mental objects is a condition (*pratyaya*), or if it is a non-condition that has retribution (*savipāka*), excluding the acquisition of the fruit (*phalaprāpti*), the remaining phenomena of the sphere of mental objects that are non-conditions yet have retribution—namely, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), up to the afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and all matter (*rūpa*)—are called the causal sphere of mental objects.
What is the dharma-element that is not a cause?

If it is not a condition, is without retribution, and arises from non-common karma—namely, birth, aging, death, life-force, the attainment of fruits, the progress of the tainted body, and the nine unconditioned phenomena—this is called the dharma-element that is not a cause.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many have causes and how many are causeless?
Seventeen have causes; one is twofold, being either with cause or without cause.
What are the seventeen that have causes?
The ten material elements and the seven consciousness elements—these are called the seventeen that possess causes.
What is the one element that is divided into two parts, being either with cause or without cause?
The mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*)—this is called the one element that is divided into two parts, being either with cause or without cause.
What is the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu) that has a cause?
If the element of phenomena possesses factors such as feeling, perception, and so forth up to right mindfulness of the body, this is called the element of phenomena with a cause.
What is the element of phenomena without a cause?

If the knowledge of the cessation through the condition of the absence of a causal sequence regarding the dharma-realm, up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-realm being without cause.
The same applies to having a causal sequence or lacking one, having conditions or lacking them, and being conditioned or unconditioned.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are cognizable and how many are not cognizable? All are cognizable;
they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Among the eighteen elements, how many are discernible and how many are not discernible?
All consciousnesses are consciousnesses that cognize according to their objects.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are objects of comprehension (*vijñeya*) and how many are not?
All are objects of comprehension, as they are known and seen according to their respective objects.
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are cognized (*vijñāta*) and how many are not cognized?
All are cognized, as they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the eighteen elements, how many are known by the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) and how many are not known by the knowledge of abandonment?

Thirteen are not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*); five are of two kinds, being either to be known through the knowledge of abandonment or not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What are the thirteen that are not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?
The eight elements of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the five elements of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*); these are called the thirteen that are not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What are the five that are of two kinds, being either known through the knowledge of abandonment or known through the knowledge other than the knowledge of abandonment?

They are the form element, the sound element, the mind element, the mental-consciousness element, and the phenomena element; these are called the five that are of two kinds, being either known through the knowledge of abandonment or known through the knowledge other than the knowledge of abandonment.
What is knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the form realm?

If it is unwholesome [matter] of the form realm, or the bodily intimation arising from an unwholesome mind—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—that is called knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the form realm.
What is the form realm that is known by knowledge other than the knowledge of abandonment?

It refers to the wholesome or neutral aspects of the form realm: whether the body’s color is beautiful or not beautiful, dignified or not dignified, graceful or not graceful, or pure and refined or not pure and refined; or the bodily intimation arising from a wholesome or neutral mind, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning; or external forms cognizable by the eye-consciousness—these are called the aspects of the form realm known by knowledge other than the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the sound element known through the knowledge of abandonment?

If the sound element is unwholesome, arising from an unwholesome mind, consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech as vocal instruction—this is called the sound element known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the sound-element that is known by the knowledge of non-interruption (*anantarya-jñāna*)?

It is the sound-element that is wholesome, or indeterminate, whether it be a pleasant or unpleasant bodily sound, a melodious or non-melodious sound, or a soft or non-soft sound; or whatever vocal instruction consisting of sounds, phonemes, and speech is produced by a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; or external sounds known by the auditory consciousness. This is called the sound-element known by the knowledge of non-interruption.
What is the mental element (*manodhātu*) known through the knowledge of abandonment?
If the mental element is unwholesome (*akuśala*), this is called the mental element known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the mental element not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is wholesome or indeterminate, this is called the mind-element known through the knowledge of non-abandonment (*aprahāṇajñāna*).
The same applies to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
What is the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*)?

If the dharma-element consists of unwholesome feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, mental pleasure, joy, mental energy, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, and tainted bodily energy—this is called the dharma-element known through the knowledge of abandonment.
In what sense is the dharma-element known by the knowledge of non-abandonment?

If the dharma-element is wholesome or indeterminate—excluding doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, and the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-precepts—the remainder of the dharma-element is known by the knowledge of non-abandonment.
The same applies to what is abandoned and what is not abandoned.
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are cultivated (*bhāvita*) and how many are not cultivated?
Thirteen are not cultivated; five are of two kinds, being either cultivated or not cultivated.
What are the thirteen that are not cultivated?
The eight elements of form and the five elements of consciousness—these are called the thirteen that are not cultivated.
What are the five that are twofold, being either cultivated or not cultivated?
The form element, sound element, mind element, mental-consciousness element, and phenomena element—these five are called the "two-part" elements, being either cultivated or not cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the form element?

If it is wholesome in the form realm, or if it is bodily intimation—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning—that arises from a wholesome mind, this is called cultivation in the form realm.
What is non-cultivation in the form realm?

If it is unwholesome matter of the form realm, or neutral bodily matter—whether beautiful or ugly, graceful or ungainly, fair-skinned or not, and whether refined or not—; or if it is bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning, produced by an unwholesome mind or a neutral mind; or if it is external matter known by visual consciousness: these are called the non-cultivated [matter] of the form realm.
What is the cultivation of the sound-element?

If the sound-element is wholesome, or if it consists of the vocal instruction arising from a wholesome mind—the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech—this is called the cultivation of the sound-element.
What is the sound-element that is not cultivated?

If the sound-element is unwholesome, or if it is neutral—whether it be a pleasant or unpleasant bodily sound, a melodious or non-melodious sound, or a soft or non-soft sound; or if it is vocal instruction arising from an unwholesome mind or a neutral mind, consisting of sounds, phonemes, and speech; or if it is an external sound known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the sound-element that is not cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
If the mind-element is wholesome, this is called the cultivation of the mind-element.
What is the non-cultivation of the mind-element?
If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is unwholesome or indeterminate, it is called the mind-element that is not to be cultivated.
The same applies to the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
What is the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that is to be cultivated?

If the dharma-realm consists of wholesome sensation and perception, up to mental equanimity, the attainment of the non-percipient state, the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation, the outflow-tainted unmanifest precepts of body and speech, the outflow-tainted bodily exertion and the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, right bodily tranquility, and the certainty of the exhaustion of conditions through knowledge—this is called cultivation of the dharma-realm.
What is the dharma-element that is not cultivated?

The dharma-element that is unwholesome, or indeterminate—namely, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, mental pleasure, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters, bodily and vocal non-restraint (non-informative action), and tainted bodily exertion; as well as the seven unconditioned states of the noble ones—this is called the dharma-element that is not cultivated.
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are realized (*sākṣātkṛta*) and how many are not realized?
All are realized, known, and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the eighteen elements, how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Thirteen are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); five are of three kinds—either wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), or indeterminate.
What are the thirteen that are indeterminate?
The eight elements of form (*rūpadhātu*) and the five elements of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*); these are called the thirteen indeterminate [elements].
What are the five elements that are threefold—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?

They are the element of form, the element of sound, the element of mind, the element of mental consciousness, and the element of phenomena; these are called the five elements that are threefold—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome in the form realm?
If it is bodily intimation—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning—that arises from a wholesome mind cultivated in the form realm, this is called wholesome in the form realm.
What is unwholesome in the form realm?

If bodily intimation—consisting of going, coming, contracting, extending, and turning—that arises from an unwholesome mental state belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) has been abandoned, this is called unwholesome in the realm of form.
What is indeterminate in the realm of form?

Whether it be feeling pertaining to the form realm, or that which pertains to the form realm and is neither a result nor a dharma destined to ripen as a result; whether it be bodily beauty or ugliness, comeliness or lack thereof, elegance or lack thereof, refinement or lack thereof; whether it be the bodily intimation arising from an indeterminate mind—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning—or external forms known by visual consciousness: these are called the indeterminate [forms] of the form realm.
What is the sound-element that is wholesome?
If the sound-element arises from the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech as verbal instruction produced by a cultivated wholesome mind, this is called the wholesome sound-element.
What is the sound-element that is unwholesome?
If the sound-element consists of vocal intimation—the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from an unwholesome mind—this is called the unwholesome sound-element.
What is the indeterminate sound-element?

If it is the sound-element that is experienced (*vedanīya*), or the sound-element that is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor subject to ripening (*avipākadharma*); whether it be a pleasant or unpleasant bodily sound, a melodious or non-melodious sound, or a soft or non-soft sound; arising from an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*) as vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; or whatever external sound is known by the ear-consciousness—this is called the indeterminate sound-element.
What is the wholesome mind-element?
If the mind-element is cultivated, it is called the wholesome mind-element.
What is the unwholesome mind-element?
If the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is severed [from its object], this is called the unwholesome mind-element.
What is the indeterminate mind-element?

If the mind-element is experienced (*vedanīya*), or if the mind-element is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor a dharma that will produce a result (*avipākadharma*), this is called the indeterminate mind-element.
The consciousness element is also like this.
What is the wholesome dharma-element?

If the dharma-element consists of cultivated feeling and perception, up to mental equanimity, the attainment of the fruit of non-perception, the attainment of cessation, the unmanifest precepts of body and speech with outflows, the bodily exertion with outflows and the bodily tranquility with outflows, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, and right bodily tranquility, the extinction through wisdom, and the certainty—this is called the wholesome dharma-element.
What is the unwholesome dharma-element?

If the dharma-element consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, and impure mental exertion—this is called the unwholesome dharma-element.
What is the indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharma-element?

It refers to those factors of the dharma-element that are neither resultant nor subject to result, and which are non-noble unconditioned phenomena; namely: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, absence of regret, contentment, joy, mental vigor, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, birth, old age, death, life-force, impure bodily vigor, and the seven non-noble unconditioned phenomena. These are called the indeterminate dharma-element.
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are trainee (*śaikṣa*), how many are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither trainee nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Fifteen are neither trainee nor beyond training; three are of three kinds—either trainee, or beyond training, or neither trainee nor beyond training.
What are the fifteen that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
The ten material elements and the five consciousness elements; these are called the fifteen that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What are the three that are each of three kinds—either learner, or non-learner, or neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

The mind element (manodhātu), the mind-consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu), and the phenomena element (dharmadhātu)—these are called the three triads that are either trainee (śaikṣa), beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).
What is the mind element that is trainee?
If the mind element (*manodhātu*) is noble but not beyond training, it is called the "mind element of one in training" (*śaikṣa*).
What is the mind element of one in training?
If the mind element is associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and belongs to one in training, it is called the mind element of one in training.
What is the mental element of those in training (*śaikṣa*)?

It refers to a person in training who, having abandoned the fetters and proclivities, enters the noble path with a noble mind; whether one of firm faith or firm Dharma, as well as other persons of similar inclination, they perceive the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality. Desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path free from afflictions.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by contemplation, they realize the fruit of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
If it is a real person or a destination within the mind-element (manodhātu) that is a trainee (śaikṣa), this is called the mind-element of a trainee.
What is the mind-element of one beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
If the mind-element is noble (ārya) and not that of a trainee, this is called the mind-element of one beyond training.
What is the mental element that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If the mental element is associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) that is beyond training, it is called the mental element beyond training.
What is the mental element beyond training?

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, cultivates the path and becomes fully endowed with insight-knowledge—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of mind through insight—he immediately attains the fruit of arhatship.
If it is a real person or a realm of mind (manodhātu) that is beyond training (aśaikṣa), this is called the mind-realm of one beyond training.
What is the mind-realm that is neither in training nor beyond training?
If it is a mind-realm that is not noble (ārya), this is called the mind-realm that is neither in training nor beyond training.
The consciousness element is also like this.
What is the dharma-element of training?
If the dharma-element is noble but not that of one beyond training, it is called the dharma-element of training.
What is training in the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*)?

It is the training in the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and its associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), as well as those dharmas within the dharma-element that take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) but non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) states as their object; this is called training in the dharma-element.
What is training in the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*)?
It is when a person in training (*śaikṣa*), having abandoned the fetters and proclivities, enters the noble mind and the noble path, and even attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny (*gati*), [it includes] feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, serene faith, joy, mental exertion, mental serenity, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruits, the attainment of the cessation-concentration (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right serenity; as well as the certainty of the exhaustion of conditions through knowledge—this is called training in the dharma-element.
What is the dharma-element that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If the dharma-element is noble and not that of one in training (*śaikṣa*), this is called the dharma-element that is beyond training.
What is the dharma-element that is beyond training?

The faculty of faith of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), along with its associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), and those factors within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) that are non-objective (*anālambana*), untainted (*anāsrava*), and not belonging to those in training (*aśaikṣa*): these are called the dharma-element of one beyond training.
What is the dharma-element of one beyond training?
The person beyond training (aśaikṣa) attains even the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, or feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, faith, joy, rapture, mental energy, mental tranquility, confidence, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right tranquility of body, the knowledge of the destruction of the conditions [for suffering]—these are called the dharma-realm of one beyond training.
What is the dharma-element that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

It refers to those factors of the dharma-element that are non-noble sensations within the aggregate of sensation, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations; or form that is invisible, non-resistant, and with-outflow; or non-noble unconditioned phenomena, such as the attainment of cessation of perception and feeling, the first four types of form, and the seven non-noble unconditioned phenomena. This is called the dharma-element that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are results (*vipāka*), how many are subject to fruition (*vipākadharmas*), and how many are neither results nor subject to fruition?

Five are results; eight are twofold, being either results or neither results nor subject to fruition; five are threefold, being either results, subject to fruition, or neither results nor subject to fruition.
What are the five results?
The eye-element, ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, and body-element—these are called the five results.
What are the eight that are twofold, being either results or neither-result-nor-non-result phenomena?

The fragrance element, taste element, and tangible element; and the eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, and body-consciousness element—these are called the eight elements that are of two kinds: either resultant (vipāka) or neither-resultant-nor-non-resultant (na-vipāka-na-avipākadharma).
What are the five elements that are threefold—either resultant (*vipāka*), or productive of result (*vipākadharma*), or neither resultant nor productive of result (*naivavipākanavipākadharma*)?

They are the element of form (*rūpadhātu*), the element of sound (*śabdadhātu*), the element of mind (*manodhātu*), the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). These are called the five elements that are threefold—either resultant, or productive of result, or neither resultant nor productive of result.
What is the retribution of the fragrance-element?
If the fragrance-element is experienced, this is called the retribution of the fragrance-element.
What is the retribution of the fragrance-element?

If the fragrance of the body—whether pleasant or unpleasant, soft or not soft, agreeable or disagreeable—which is produced by the retribution of karma, dharmas, and afflictions belonging to one's own continuum, this is called the retribution of the fragrance-element (*gandhadhātu*).
What is the odor-element that is neither resultant nor subject to result?

It refers to external odors, whether they are known by the nose-consciousness or are external odors known by the nose-consciousness—such as the fragrance of tree roots, the fragrance of tree hearts, the fragrance of tree resins, the fragrance of tree bark, the fragrance of leaves, the fragrance of flowers, the fragrance of fruits, pleasant fragrances, unpleasant fragrances, and other such external odors known by the nose-consciousness. This is called the odor-element that is neither resultant nor subject to result.
What is the retribution of the taste element?
If the taste element is experienced, this is called the retribution of the taste element.
What is the retribution of the taste element?

If the taste-element produced as retribution from karma, mental factors, and afflictions, which is comprised within my own continuum, consists of sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, phlegm, or mucus, this is called the retributive taste-element (*rasa-dhātu-vipāka*).
What is the taste-element that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution (*na-vipāka-na-vipākadharma*)?

If it is an external taste element, or an external taste known by tongue-consciousness—whether it be sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, or bland liquid, or any other external taste known by tongue-consciousness—this is called the taste element that is neither resultant nor a factor leading to result.
What is the retribution of the element of tangibles?
If the element of tangibles is experienced, this is called the retribution of the element of tangibles.
What is the retribution of the element of tangibles?

If the tangible element—arising as retribution from karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and comprised within the category of "self"—consists of the body's coldness, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, subtlety, roughness, smoothness, hardness, or softness, this is called the retribution of the tangible element.
What is the element of tangibles that is neither resultant nor subject to result?

It refers to external tangibles, or those external tangibles known by body-consciousness—such as cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, fineness, roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness—as well as other external tangibles known by body-consciousness. This is called the element of tangibles that is neither resultant nor subject to result.
What is the retribution of the visual consciousness element?
If the visual consciousness element is experienced, this is called the retribution of the visual consciousness element.
What is the retribution of the visual consciousness element?
If the eye-consciousness element is produced as a result of karma, dharmas, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own continuum, it is called the "resultant eye-consciousness element.
What is the eye-consciousness element that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?
If the visual consciousness element is external to the visual consciousness element, it is called the visual consciousness element that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution.
The same applies to the auditory consciousness element, the olfactory consciousness element, the gustatory consciousness element, and the tactile consciousness element.
What is the retribution of the form realm?
If one experiences [the results] of the form realm, this is called the retribution of the form realm.
What is the retribution of the form realm?

If there is bodily form produced as retribution from karma, dharmas, and afflictions of the form realm, which is comprised within my own sphere—whether it be beautiful or ugly, dignified or undignified, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, or pure and refined or not pure and refined—and if there is the bodily intimation arising from the mind, such as coming and going, bending and stretching, or turning about, this is called the retribution of the form realm.
What is the retribution-dharma of the form realm?
If there is retribution within the form realm, this is called the retribution-dharma of the form realm.
What is the retribution-dharma of the form realm?

If bodily intimation—consisting of going, coming, contracting, extending, and turning about—is produced by a wholesome or unwholesome mind of the form realm, whether that mind itself be wholesome or unwholesome, this is called the retributive dharma of the form realm.
What is the form realm that is neither resultant nor a dharma leading to result?

It refers to bodily intimation—such as going, coming, contracting, extending, and turning—which arises from a mind in the form realm that is indeterminate, not included within one's own continuum, and is neither resultant nor a dharma leading to result; or it refers to external forms known by visual consciousness. This is called the form realm that is neither resultant nor a dharma leading to result.
What is the sound element as karmic retribution?
If the sound element is experienced [as a result of past karma], this is called the sound element as karmic retribution.
What is the sound element as karmic retribution?

If the sound-element produced as retribution from karma, dharmas, or afflictions, which is comprised within one's own continuum (*ātmiya*), consists of pleasant or unpleasant sounds, exquisite or non-exquisite sounds, or soft or non-soft sounds; or if it consists of vocal instruction arising from the mind through the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech—this is called the sound-element as retribution.
What is the sound element as a result of maturation (*vipāka-dharma*)?
If the sound element is subject to maturation, this is called the sound element as a result of maturation.
What is the sound element as a result of maturation?

If the sound-element is wholesome or unwholesome, or if it is the vocal instruction consisting of sounds, phonemes, and speech produced by a wholesome or unwholesome mind, this is called the sound-element as a resultant phenomenon.
What is the sound-element that is neither resultant nor productive of result?

It refers to the sound-element that is indeterminate, not included within one's own continuum, and produced by a mind that is neither resultant nor productive of result—namely, the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; or it refers to external sounds known by the ear-consciousness. This is called the sound-element that is neither resultant nor productive of result.
What is the retribution of the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
Whether it be the mind-element itself, its feeling, or the mind-element that is the wholesome retribution of the mind-element—this is called the retribution of the mind-element.
What is the dharma that is the retribution of the mind-element?
If the mind-element (manodhātu) is retributive, it is called the "retributive dharma" of the mind-element.
What is the retributive dharma of the mind-element?
With the exception of the wholesome retribution of the mind-element, all other wholesome or unwholesome mind-elements are called the retributive dharma of the mind-element.
What is the mind element that is neither resultant nor subject to result?
It is the mind element that is indeterminate consciousness and not included within the sphere of "mine"; this is called the mind element that is neither resultant nor subject to result.
The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is also like this.
What is the retribution (*vipāka*) of the dharma element (*dharmadhātu*)?

If the dharma element is wholesome retribution—excluding non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), and the remainder of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) up to mental equanimity (*upekṣā*), fear (*bhaya*), birth (*jāti*), life-force (*jīvita*), the attainment of the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), the fruit of attainment (*phala-prāpti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of the outflow-tainted precepts of body and speech, the outflow-tainted bodily exertion (*vīrya*) and bodily pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), right bodily exertion, and right bodily pliancy—this is called the retribution of the dharma element.
What is the dharma-realm as a resultant phenomenon?
If the dharma-realm has a result, this is called the dharma-realm as a resultant phenomenon.
What is the dharma-realm as a resultant phenomenon?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the dharma-element, all other conditioned wholesome dharmas within the dharma-element—whether unwholesome, or comprising sensation and perception up to the afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the two meditative attainments, and all matter—are called the retributive dharmas of the dharma-element.
What is the dharma-element that is neither result nor the nature of being a result?

It refers to those factors within the dharma-element that are indeterminate and not comprised within the category of "mine," as well as the noble unconditioned, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, birth, aging, death, the outflow-tainted bodily exertion, and the nine unconditioned phenomena. These are called the dharma-element that is neither result nor the nature of being a result.

Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

Thirteen are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation; five are of three parts, being either abandoned by insight, or abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the thirteen that are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?
The eight elements of form and the five elements of consciousness—these are called the thirteen that are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the five that are threefold—either abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

They are the element of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), the element of sound (*śabda-dhātu*), the element of mind (*mano-dhātu*), the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-dhātu*), and the element of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*). These are called the five that are threefold—either abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is that which is abandoned through vision in the form realm?

If it is bodily intimation—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning about—which arises from the mind associated with unwholesome afflictions of the form realm that are abandoned through vision rather than through cultivation, this is called that which is abandoned through vision in the form realm.
What is that which is abandoned through cultivation in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?

If it is the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—that arises from a mind associated with unwholesome afflictions of the realm of form which are abandoned through cultivation rather than through insight, this is called that which is abandoned through cultivation in the realm of form.
What is the form realm that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to whatever is wholesome or indeterminate within the form realm: bodily forms that are beautiful or not beautiful, dignified or not dignified, graceful or not graceful, and pure or not pure; as well as the bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which is originated by a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; and external forms known by visual consciousness. This is called the form realm that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sound-element that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

If the sound-element is unwholesome, not abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and arises from the mind associated with afflictions abandoned by insight—consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and verbal expressions as vocal instruction—this is called the sound-element abandoned by insight.
What is the sound-element that is abandoned through cultivation?

If the sound-element is unwholesome, not abandoned through insight, but arises from a mind associated with afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation—consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and verbal expressions of oral instruction—this is called the sound-element abandoned through cultivation.
What is the sound element that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to sound elements that are wholesome or indeterminate: pleasant bodily sounds or unpleasant bodily sounds, exquisite sounds or non-exquisite sounds, soft sounds or non-soft sounds; or those vocal expressions arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind—consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; or external sounds known by the ear-consciousness. This is called the sound element that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the mind-element that is abandoned by insight?
If the mind-element is unwholesome and not abandoned through cultivation, but is associated with mental states abandoned by insight, this is called the mind-element abandoned by insight.
What is the mind-element (*manodhātu*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

If the mind-element is unwholesome (*akuśala*) and associated with afflictions (*kleśa*) that are not to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) but are to be abandoned by cultivation, this is called the mind-element to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the mind element that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?
If it is a wholesome mind element or an indeterminate mind element, this is called the mind element that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is also like this.
What is the dharma element (*dharmadhātu*) abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

If the dharma element is unwholesome (*akuśala*) and not abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), but is abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions abandoned by insight—namely: feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), vitarka and vicāra, view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), non-regret (*akaukṛtya*), satisfaction (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), fear (*bhaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), the non-informative [actions] of bodily and vocal non-restraint (*asaṃvara-avijñapti*), and tainted mental exertion (*sāsrava-cittavīrya*)—this is called the dharma element abandoned by insight.
What is the dharma-element that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

If the dharma-element consists of unwholesome factors that are not abandoned through vision, but are abandoned simultaneously with the afflictions abandoned through cultivation—namely: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the non-informative matter of bodily and vocal non-precepts, and tainted mental exertion—this is called the dharma-element abandoned through cultivation.
What is the dharma-element that is neither abandoned through vision nor abandoned through cultivation?

If the dharma-element is wholesome or indeterminate—excluding doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, and the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-precepts—the remainder of the dharma-element is called the dharma-element that is neither abandoned through vision nor abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many have the cause of abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu*), how many have the cause of abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-hetu*), and how many have neither the cause of abandonment through seeing nor the cause of abandonment through cultivation?

All are of three types: either having the cause of abandonment through seeing, or having the cause of abandonment through cultivation, or having neither the cause of abandonment through seeing nor the cause of abandonment through cultivation.
What is the eye-element that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by insight?

If the eye-element is the retribution of dharmas to be abandoned by insight—namely, the eye-element of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—this is called the eye-element that has as its cause that which is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the eye-element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation?

If the eye-element is the retribution of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation—namely, the eye-element of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—this is called the eye-element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the eye-element that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation?

If the eye-element is a wholesome dharma resulting from retribution—the eye-element among gods or humans—this is called the eye-element that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation.
The ear-element, nose-element, tongue-element, and body-element are also like this.
What is the form-element that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision?

It is form that is abandoned by vision in the form-element, or the retribution of dharmas abandoned by vision in the form-element, which consists of bodily forms that are not beautiful, not handsome, not lovely, and not pure; and it includes the bodily intimation of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which is produced by a mind whose cause is abandoned by vision. This is called the form-element that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision.
What is the cause for abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)?

It refers to that which belongs to the form realm and is abandoned through cultivation, or the body resulting from the retribution of factors abandoned through cultivation, which is neither beautiful, nor dignified, nor radiant, nor pure; as well as the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from a mind abandoned through cultivation, consisting of going, coming, contracting, extending, and turning about. This is called the cause for abandonment through cultivation in the form realm.
What is the form realm that is neither a cause for abandonment by vision nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation?

It refers to: wholesome states of the form realm; the retribution of wholesome dharmas of the form realm; the beautiful complexion, dignified appearance, and fine skin of the body which are neither retribution nor dharmas subject to retribution in the form realm; bodily intimation arising from a mind that is neither a cause for abandonment by vision nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation—consisting of coming and going, bending and stretching, and turning about; or external forms known by visual consciousness. This is called the form realm that is neither a cause for abandonment by vision nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation.
What is the sound-element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetuka*)?

It is the sound-element that is itself to be abandoned by insight; or the unpleasant sound, the non-exquisite sound, and the harsh sound that are the bodily retribution of factors to be abandoned by insight; or the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech, which is produced by a mind whose cause is to be abandoned by insight—this is called the sound-element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the sound-element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation?

It is the sound-element that is to be abandoned by cultivation; or it is the body resulting from the retribution of a sound-element to be abandoned by cultivation—namely, a sound that is not pleasant, not exquisite, and not soft; or it is the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from a mind whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation. This is called the sound-element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the sound-element that is neither caused by what is abandoned through seeing nor by what is abandoned through cultivation?

It refers to those sounds of the sound-element that are the maturation of wholesome dharmas; or those sounds of the sound-element that are neither maturation nor subject to maturation—namely, pleasant sounds, exquisite sounds, and soft sounds—which arise from a mind not caused by what is abandoned through seeing or cultivation, consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech as vocal instruction; or external sounds known by the ear-consciousness. This is called the sound-element that is neither caused by what is abandoned through seeing nor by what is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the fragrance element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

If the fragrance element is the retribution of a dharma to be abandoned by insight, and is neither a pleasant fragrance, nor a soft fragrance, nor a gratifying fragrance, this is called the fragrance element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the fragrance element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation?

If the fragrance element is the retribution of a dharma to be abandoned by cultivation, and its body is neither pleasant fragrance, nor soft fragrance, nor agreeable fragrance, this is called the fragrance element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the fragrance element that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation?

It refers to those fragrances of the fragrance element that are wholesome karmic results; or those fragrances of the fragrance element that are neither results nor factors leading to results, such as pleasant odors, soft odors, and agreeable odors; or external fragrances known by the olfactory consciousness—this is called the fragrance element that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation.
What is the taste element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

If the taste element is the retribution of a dharma to be abandoned by insight—whether it be sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or characterized by phlegm and mucus—it is called the taste element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the taste element that has its cause in abandonment through cultivation?

If the taste element is the retribution of dharmas abandoned through cultivation—whether it be sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or characterized by phlegm and mucus—it is called the taste element that has its cause in abandonment through cultivation.
What is the taste-element that is neither a cause for abandonment by insight nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation?

It refers to the taste-element that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas; or the taste-element that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution, such as the body’s sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, or the sensations of saliva and phlegm; or external tastes known by tongue-consciousness. This is called the taste-element that is neither a cause for abandonment by insight nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation.
What is the touch-element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

If the touch-element consists of the bodily sensations of cold, heat, heaviness, hardness, or roughness that are the retribution of factors to be abandoned by insight, this is called the touch-element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the cause of the touch-element that is to be abandoned through cultivation?

If the touch-element consists of the coldness, heat, heaviness, rigidity, or roughness of the body as a retribution for dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation, this is called the cause of the touch-element that is to be abandoned through cultivation.
What is the element of tangibles that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation?

It refers to those wholesome resultant tangibles, or those tangibles that are neither resultants nor subject to resultants—such as the body’s sensations of cold, heat, lightness, subtlety, softness, and smoothness—or external tangibles known by body-consciousness. This is called the element of tangibles that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation.
What is the eye-consciousness element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu*)?

If the eye-consciousness element is the retribution (*vipāka*) of factors to be abandoned by insight belonging to the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, this is called the eye-consciousness element that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the eye-consciousness element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation?

If the eye-consciousness element is the retribution of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation—namely, the eye-consciousness element of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—this is called the eye-consciousness element whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the eye-consciousness element that is neither caused by abandonment through insight nor by abandonment through cultivation?

It refers to the eye-consciousness element that is the result of wholesome dharmas, or the eye-consciousness element that is neither a result nor a dharma destined to produce a result among gods or humans; this is called the eye-consciousness element that is neither caused by abandonment through insight nor by abandonment through cultivation.
The ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, and body-consciousness element are also like this.
What is the mind-element that has its cause in what is abandoned by seeing?

It is the mind-element itself, or the mind-element abandoned by seeing, or the mind-element that is the retribution of factors abandoned by seeing; this is called the mind-element that has its cause in what is abandoned by seeing.
What is the mind-element that has its cause in abandonment through cultivation?

The mind-element that is abandoned through cultivation, or the mind-element that is the retribution of factors abandoned through cultivation—this is called the mind-element whose cause is abandonment through cultivation.
What is the mind-element that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to the mind-element that is wholesome, or the mind-element that is the fruition of wholesome dharmas, or the mind-element that is neither fruition nor subject to fruition; this is called the mind-element that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.
The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is also like this.
What is the dharma-element that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya-hetuka*)?

If the dharma-element consists of the retribution of dharmas abandoned by vision—namely, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, vitarka, vicāra, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, life-force, fetters, the unmanifest non-restraint of body and speech, and tainted mental exertion—this is called the dharma-element that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision.
What is the dharma-element that has the cause of abandonment through cultivation?

If the dharma-element is abandoned through cultivation, it consists of the retribution of the dharma-elements abandoned through cultivation: feeling, perception, volition, contact, vitarka, vicāra, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, life-force, fetters, the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, and the contaminated mental exertion. This is called the dharma-element that has the cause of abandonment through cultivation.
What is the dharma-element that is neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to those factors of the dharma-element that are wholesome; or those factors of the dharma-element that are the fruition of wholesome dharmas; or those factors of the dharma-element that are neither fruition nor productive of fruition—excluding doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, and the non-informative matter of bodily and vocal non-restraint—the remaining factors of the dharma-element are causes that are neither to be abandoned by vision nor to be abandoned by cultivation. This is called the dharma-element that is neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.

Of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

Six are bound to the desire realm; nine are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm; three are fourfold, being either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What are the six elements bound to the desire realm?

The nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element—these are called the six elements bound to the desire realm.
What are the nine elements that are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm?

They are the eye element, ear element, body element; the form element, sound element, and tangible-object element; and the eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, and body-consciousness element. These are called the nine twofold elements, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What are the three and four parts that are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound?

The mind element (manodhātu), the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu), and the phenomena element (dharmadhātu)—these are called the three and four parts that are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is the eye-element bound to the desire realm?
If the eye-element is associated with the outflows of the desire realm and is a contaminated eye-element, this is called the eye-element bound to the desire realm.
What is the eye-element bound to the form realm?
If the eye-element is a form-element that is subject to outflows and is an outflow-tainted eye-element, this is called the eye-element being bound to the realm of form.
The same applies to the ear-element and the body-element.
What is meant by the realm of form being bound to the realm of desire?

If there are forms in the realm of form that are desirable outflows (*āsrava*) or tainted (*sāsrava*), whether they are beautiful or not beautiful, dignified or not dignified, graceful or not graceful, or pure or not pure; or if there is bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning about—arisen from a mind engaged in desire; or if there are external forms known by visual consciousness that are desirable outflows or tainted: these are called "bound to the realm of form and the realm of desire."
What is form belonging to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) that is bound to the realm of form?

It refers to the physical beauty, majesty, fine complexion, and purity of the body of one who has outflows (*āsrava*) and is subject to outflows within the realm of form; it also refers to the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—which arises from the mind and its mental factors; and it also refers to external forms known by visual consciousness that possess outflows and are subject to outflows. This is called form belonging to the realm of form that is bound to the realm of form.
What is the sound-element bound to the desire realm?

It refers to those sounds within the sound-element that are associated with the outflows (*āsrava*) and are tainted (*sāsrava*), such as pleasant or unpleasant bodily sounds, exquisite or non-exquisite sounds, soft or non-soft sounds; those vocal instructions arising from a mind engaged in desire, consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; and external sounds cognizable by the ear-consciousness that are associated with the outflows and are tainted. This is called the sound-element bound to the desire realm.
What is the sound element bound to the realm of form?

It refers to those sounds of the sound element that are associated with outflows (āsrava) and are subject to outflows, such as pleasant sounds, various exquisite sounds, and soft sounds; it refers to the vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech arising from the mind and its mental concomitants; or it refers to external sounds known by the ear-consciousness that are associated with outflows and subject to outflows. This is called the sound element bound to the realm of form.
What is the element of tangibles bound to the desire realm?

If the element of tangibles consists of the body’s cold, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, subtlety, roughness, smoothness, hardness, or softness—whether associated with the outflows of desire or being tainted by outflows—or if it is an external tangible known by body-consciousness that is associated with the outflows of desire or is tainted by outflows, this is called the element of tangibles bound to the desire realm.
What is the element of tangibles bound to the realm of form?

If the element of tangibles consists of bodily sensations—whether cold, heat, lightness, subtlety, softness, or smoothness—that are associated with outflows and are subject to outflows; or if it consists of external tangibles known by body-consciousness that are associated with outflows and are subject to outflows, this is called the element of tangibles bound to the realm of form.
What is the eye-consciousness element bound to the desire realm?
If the eye-consciousness element is associated with the outflows of the desire realm and is an outflowing consciousness, this is called the eye-consciousness element bound to the desire realm.
What is the eye-consciousness element bound to the realm of form?
If the eye-consciousness element is associated with the outflows of form and is with-outflow (sāsrava), this is called the eye-consciousness element bound to the realm of form.
The ear-consciousness element and the body-consciousness element are also like this.
What is the mind-element bound to the desire realm?
If the mind-element is associated with the outflows of the desire realm and is an outflowing mind-element, this is called the mind-element bound to the desire realm.
What is the mind-element bound to the form realm?
If the mind-element is associated with the outflows of form or is a mind-element possessed of outflows, this is called the mind-element bound to the form realm.
What is the mind-element bound to the formless realm?
If the mind-element (manodhātu) is formless and is with-outflow (sāsrava), it is called the mind-element bound to the formless realm.
What is the mind-element that is not bound?
If the mind-element is noble and without-outflow (anāsrava), it is called the mind-element that is not bound.
The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is also like this.
What is the dharma element (*dharmadhātu*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātupratisaṃyukta*)?
