If the dharma element consists of desire-outflows (*kāsrava*), outflows of existence (*bhavāsrava*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), absence of regret (*akaukṛtya*), joy (*prīti*), gladness (*saumanasya*), mental energy (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), fear (*bhaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, old age, death, life-force (*jīvita*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), the unmanifest non-restraint of body and speech (*kāyavāg-avijñaptir-aśīla*), the manifest restraint of body and speech with outflows (*kāyavāg-vijñapti-sāsrava-śīla*), and the manifest energy of the body with outflows (*kāyavīrya-sāsrava*); this is called the dharma element bound to the desire realm.
What is the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu)?

It consists of those factors of the dharma-element that are associated with outflows of form (rūpāsrava) and are with-outflow (sāsrava): feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, pliancy, joy, mental exertion, mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters, the unmanifest (avijñapti) of the precepts of body and speech pertaining to the outflows of form, the outflow of bodily exertion, and the outflow of bodily tranquility. These are called the dharma-element bound to the realm of form.
What is the dharma-element bound to the formless realm?

It refers to those factors of the dharma-element that are associated with outflows of the formless realm and are with-outflow (sāsrava): feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, compliance, mental energy, mental pliancy, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters, and the unmanifest precepts of the body and speech associated with outflows, as well as the manifest energy of the body and the pliancy of the body associated with outflows. These are called the dharma-element bound to the formless realm.
What is the dharma-element that is unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

Those dharmas of the dharma-element that are noble, untainted, and unconditioned—namely: feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, serene faith, joy, gladness, mental energy, mental pliancy, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right pliancy of body, as well as the nine unconditioned [dharmas]—these are called the dharma-element that is unconditioned.
Of the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
Seventeen are threefold—being either past, future, or present; one is fourfold—being either past, future, present, or neither past, nor future, nor present.
What are the seventeen elements that are threefold, being either past, future, or present?
From the eye element up to the mind-consciousness element—these are called the seventeen elements that are threefold, being either past, future, or present.
What is the one fourfold [classification] that is either past, or future, or present, or neither past nor future nor present?
The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); this is called the one fourfold [classification] that is either past, or future, or present, or neither past nor future nor present.
What is the past eye-element?
That eye-element which has arisen and ceased is called the past eye-element.
What is the future eye-element?
If the eye-element has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, this is called the future eye-element.
What is the present eye-element?
If the eye-element has arisen but has not yet ceased, this is called the present eye-element.
The same applies up to the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*).
What is the past element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)?
If the element of phenomena has arisen and ceased—ranging from feeling and perception up to right equanimity of body—that is called the past element of phenomena.
What is the future dharma-element?
If the dharma-element has not yet arisen and not yet emerged—ranging from sensation and perception up to right bodily equanimity—that is called the future dharma-element.
What is the present dharma-element?
If the dharma-realm has arisen but its feeling and perception have not yet ceased, up to and including right bodily composure, this is called the present dharma-realm.
What is the dharma-realm that is neither past, nor future, nor present?

If the dharma-realm is unconditioned, such as the knowledge of the exhaustion of conditions up to the knowledge of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the dharma-realm that is neither past, nor future, nor present.

Section 3: The Chapter on the Aggregates (Skandha-varga), Part 3: The Inquiry. Question:
How many aggregates are there?
Answer: The five aggregates (skandhas). Which five?
The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of form?
Any dharma that is form is called the aggregate of form.
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
The ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and that which is form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), this is called the aggregate of form.
What is the aggregate of form?
The four great elements and the matter derived from the four great elements are called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). What is the aggregate of form?
It consists of three types of matter: [matter consisting of the great elements, matter derived from the great elements, and matter consisting of non-manifesting form].
Visible and resistant form, invisible and resistant form, and invisible and non-resistant form—this is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What is the aggregate of form?

Whether form is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near—this is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). What are form-phenomena (*rūpadharma*)?

They are the sense-bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint; the informative and non-informative [matter] of impure bodily and vocal restraint; impure bodily exertion and impure bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility. These are called form-phenomena.
What are the ten bases of form?
The bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the bases of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—these are called the ten bases of form.
What is the form within the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*)?

The non-informative matter of bodily and vocal non-precepts; the informative and non-informative matter of impure bodily and vocal precepts; impure bodily effort and impure bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily tranquility—these are called the form included in the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana-rūpa).
What are the four great elements?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element—these are called the four great elements.
What is matter derived from the four great elements?

The eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; visible forms, sounds, odors, and tastes; the non-informative [matter] of bodily and verbal non-restraint; the informative and non-informative [matter] of impure bodily and verbal restraint; impure bodily effort and impure bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily tranquility—these are called derived matter produced by the four great elements.
What is visible and resistant form?
The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is called visible and resistant form.
What is invisible and resistant form?
The sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and the objects of sound, odor, taste, and touch—these are called invisible, resistant form.
What is invisible, non-resistant form?

The non-informative matter of bodily and vocal non-precepts; the informative and non-informative matter of impure bodily and vocal precepts; impure bodily effort and impure bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily tranquility—these are called invisible and non-obstructive matter.
What is past form? If form has arisen and ceased, this is called past form.
What is future form?
If form has not yet arisen and not yet emerged, this is called future form.
What is present form?
If form has arisen but not yet ceased, this is called present form.
What is internal form?
If form is appropriated, it is called internal form.
What is external form?
If form is not feeling, it is called external form.
What is coarse form?
If form is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse form.
What is subtle matter?
Matter that is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), matter that is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or matter that is unbound—this is called subtle matter.
What is inferior matter?

If form is unwholesome, or if form is the retribution of an unwholesome dharma, or if form is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution and is disagreeable, this is called inferior form.
What is superior form?
If form is wholesome, or if form is the result of wholesome dharmas, or if form is neither a result nor a dharma that leads to results but is agreeable—this is called superior form.
What is distant form?
If various forms are distant, extremely distant, not near, or not near the boundary, these are called "distant forms.
What are "near forms"?
If forms are near, extremely near, or near the boundary, these are called "near forms."
What is the aggregate of feeling?
There is one aggregate of feeling: if there is mental feeling, this is called the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling?
The second is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*): bodily feeling and mental feeling; this is called the aggregate of feeling. What is the aggregate of feeling?
The third [classification] is the aggregate of feeling: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; this is called the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling?

The four types of feeling constitute the aggregate of feeling: feeling bound to the realm of desire, feeling bound to the realm of form, feeling bound to the formless realm, and unconditioned feeling. These are called the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling?

The five feelings constitute the aggregate of feeling: the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; these are called the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling?

The six types of feeling constitute the aggregate of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, and feeling born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is called the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling?

The seven types of feeling belonging to the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha)—namely, feeling associated with the eye-consciousness element, and feelings associated with the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind consciousness—these are called the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling?
The eighteen mental explorations and other mental feelings—this is called the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling?
The thirty-six factors of the sense bases and other mental sensations are called the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).
What is the aggregate of sensation?
The one hundred and eight sensations and other mental sensations are called the aggregate of sensation.
What is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*)?
Whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; distant or near—whatever is felt, this is called the aggregate of feeling.
What is bodily feeling (*kāyikī vedanā*)?
If feeling is associated with body-consciousness, it is called bodily feeling.
What is mental feeling?
If feeling is associated with mind-consciousness, it is called mental feeling.
What is bodily feeling?
Any feeling associated with the group of five consciousnesses—namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness—is called bodily feeling.
What is mental feeling?
Any feeling associated with the mental consciousness is called mental feeling.
What is pleasant feeling?
If there is a pleasant feeling of body or mind, this is called a pleasant feeling.
What is a painful feeling?
If there is a painful feeling of body or mind, this is called a painful feeling.
What is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
If there is a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant within the body or mind, this is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is feeling bound to the desire realm?
If feeling is associated with the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), it is called feeling bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-vedanā*).
What is feeling bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-vedanā*)?
If feeling is associated with the outflow of form (*rūpa-āsrava*) and the outflow of existence, it is called feeling bound to the form realm.
What is feeling associated with the formless realm?
If feeling is characterized by outflows and is subject to the outflows of the formless realm, it is called feeling associated with the formless realm.
What is unconditioned feeling?
If one experiences a noble, untainted feeling, this is called "unbound feeling.
What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?

If it is a pleasant bodily feeling, a pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, or a pleasant feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, or body-contact—that is, the element of pleasure—this is called the faculty of pleasure.
What is the faculty of suffering?

Any bodily painful sensation, any painful sensation born of eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, or body-contact, and the element of suffering—this is called the faculty of suffering.
What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
If there is a pleasant feeling of body or mind, or a pleasant feeling arising from mental contact belonging to the sphere of joy, this is called the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?

If there is a painful feeling of body or mind, or a painful feeling born of mental contact belonging to the sphere of sorrow (*daurmanasya-dhātu*), this is called the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*).
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

If there is a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant of body or mind, or a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant born of visual contact, or a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant born of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, or mental contact, belonging to the sphere of equanimity (*upekṣā-dhātu*), this is called the faculty of equanimity.
What is feeling born of eye-contact?
Any feeling associated with visual consciousness is called feeling born of eye-contact.
What are feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact?
If it is feeling associated with mental consciousness, this is called "feeling born of mind-contact.
What is "feeling born of eye-contact"?

Dependent on the eye and dependent on forms, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors is contact, and the feeling conditioned by that contact is called "feeling born of eye-contact."
What are the feelings arising from contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?

Conditioned by the mind and conditioned by mental objects, mind-consciousness arises; the coming together of these three factors is contact, and conditioned by contact there is feeling—this is called the feeling arising from contact of the mind.
What is feeling associated with the visual consciousness element?
If a feeling arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the visual consciousness element, it is called feeling associated with the visual consciousness element.
What is feeling associated with the consciousness element of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?
If a feeling arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the consciousness element of the mind, it is called feeling associated with the consciousness element of the mind.
What are the eighteen mental explorations?
They are the six explorations of joy, the six explorations of grief, and the six explorations of equanimity.
These six explorations of joy, six explorations of grief, and six explorations of equanimity are called the eighteen mental explorations.
What is the mental feeling apart from the eighteen mental applications?
That which is mental feeling apart from the eighteen mental applications is called "mental feeling apart from the eighteen mental applications."
What are the thirty-six noble phrases? They are:

based on the six kinds of delight in attachment and based on the six kinds of delight in renunciation; based on the six kinds of grief in attachment and based on the six kinds of grief in renunciation; and based on the six kinds of equanimity in attachment and based on the six kinds of equanimity in renunciation.
What is the joy based on the six types of craving?

When the eye perceives a form, there arises love, delight, and mental satisfaction; this love for the form is associated with sensual passion. Whether it is currently being obtained, will be obtained, or has already been obtained, or whether one recollects with joy that which was obtained in the past and has since perished—such joy as this is called joy based on craving.

When one cognizes dharmas with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, there arises love, delight, and satisfaction; this is associated with desire and defilement for the dharma—whether it has been obtained now, will be obtained in the future, or was already obtained in the past—and through recollecting that which has passed and ceased, joy is produced.
To give rise to joy in this way is called joy based on craving.
This is called the six types of joy based on craving.
What is joy based on the six renunciations?

Form is non-self; knowing it to be impermanent, subject to change, detached, and tending toward cessation, one contemplates past form as truly being impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, and thus contemplates the arising of joy as it truly is.
Such joy is called "joy based on emergence.

Regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects as selfless, one knows them to be impermanent, subject to change, detached, and destined for cessation; thus observing these past phenomena as they truly are—impermanent, suffering, and subject to transformation—one gives rise to joy through such true observation.
Such joy as this is called joy based on renunciation.
This is called joy based on the six kinds of renunciation.
What is joy based on the six kinds of craving and grief?

The eye cognizes forms that are lovely, delightful, and pleasing; one feels desire and passion for these lovely forms, thinking, "I have not yet obtained what I shall obtain," and having already obtained them, they change and perish, giving rise to sorrow through recollection.
Such sorrow as this is called sorrow based on craving.

When one perceives sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects with the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, there arises affection, delight, and satisfaction; being associated with attachment to those phenomena and desire for them, one experiences sorrow because of not having obtained what has not yet been obtained, or because of the loss and transformation of what has already been obtained through recollection.
Such sorrow as this is called sorrow based on craving.
This is called sorrow based on the six types of craving.
What is sorrow based on the six types of renunciation?
"Form is non-self"?

One knows it to be impermanent, subject to change, detached, and destined for cessation; one contemplates past form as being thus impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Having contemplated it as it truly is, one yearns for the sublime Dharma of peace and liberation, thinking:
"When shall I enter [this state], such as the practice accomplished by the noble ones?"
Conditioned by this, sorrow arises.
Such sorrow is called sorrow based on the six exits.

Sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are non-self; one knows them to be impermanent, subject to change, disintegrating, and destined for cessation. One contemplates these past phenomena as they truly are—impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—and having contemplated them as they truly are, one yearns for the sublime Dharma of peace and liberation.
"When shall I enter into such practice as that accomplished by the noble ones?"—
this gives rise to sorrow.
Such sorrow is called sorrow based on renunciation.
This is called the six kinds of renunciation based on emergence from sorrow.
What are the six kinds of equanimity based on craving?
When the eye sees forms, an ordinary person gives rise to equanimity; they are as ignorant as small children, failing to see the peril and not knowing the consequences.
Thus, not knowing how to attain equanimity (*upekṣā*), one lacks skillful means regarding form; this is called equanimity based on craving.
When ordinary people experience equanimity toward sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, they are like ignorant children who do not see the danger and do not know the consequences.
Thus, not knowing how to attain equanimity and lacking skillful means regarding the dharmas, this is called equanimity based on craving.
This is called equanimity based on the six types of craving.
What is equanimity based on the six types of renunciation?

Form is non-self; knowing it to be impermanent, subject to change, detached from, and destined for cessation, one contemplates past form as being thus impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Having contemplated it thus as it truly is, equanimity arises.
Knowing thus, one attains equanimity; having skillful means regarding form, this is called equanimity based on emergence.

Sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena are selfless; knowing them to be impermanent, subject to change, detached, and destined for cessation, one contemplates past phenomena as being thus impermanent, suffering, and subject to change. Having contemplated them as they truly are, one gives rise to equanimity.
Thus knowing and attaining equanimity, one possesses skillful means regarding phenomena; this is called "equanimity based on the six renunciations.

Likewise, there is joy arising from the six attachments and joy arising from the six renunciations; likewise, there is grief based on the six attachments and grief based on the six renunciations; likewise, there is equanimity based on the six attachments and equanimity based on the six renunciations. When these are combined, they are called the thirty-six honorable phrases (*ṣaṭtriṃśad-āryapada*).
What is the mental feeling apart from the thirty-six honorable phrases?
Mental feeling apart from the thirty-six honorable phrases is called "mental feeling apart from the thirty-six honorable phrases."
What are the one hundred and eight feelings?
Thirty-six noble phrases of the past, thirty-six noble phrases of the future, and thirty-six noble phrases of the present; when these are combined, they are called the one hundred and eight feelings.
What is the mental feeling remaining after excluding the one hundred and eight feelings?
The mental feeling that remains after excluding the one hundred and eight feelings is called the mental feeling remaining after excluding the one hundred and eight feelings.
What is past feeling?
If feeling has arisen and already ceased, this is called past feeling.
What is future feeling?
If feeling has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, this is called future feeling.
What is present feeling?
If a feeling has arisen but not yet ceased, this is called present feeling.
What is internal feeling?
If feeling is felt, this is called internal feeling.
What is external feeling?
If feeling is not felt, this is called external feeling.
What is coarse feeling?
If feeling is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse feeling.
What is subtle feeling?
If one experiences feelings bound to the form realm, the formless realm, or those that are unbound, these are called subtle feelings (*sūkṣma-vedanā*).
What are base feelings (*hīna-vedanā*)?

If one experiences what is unwholesome (*akuśala*), or the retribution of unwholesome dharmas, or what is neither retribution nor a dharma leading to retribution and is disagreeable, these are called base feelings.
What is superior feeling?
If one experiences the retribution of wholesome dharmas, or experiences that which is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution and is agreeable, this is called superior feeling.
What is distant feeling?
If a feeling is distant, extremely distant, not near, or not at the edge [of the body], it is called a distant feeling (*dūre-vedanā*).
What is a near feeling?
If a feeling is near, extremely near, or at the edge [of the body], it is called a near feeling (*antike-vedanā*).
What is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha)?
Briefly, the aggregate of perception consists of perception, the perception of consciousness, and the ultimate perception of consciousness; this is called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception?
Second, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): perceptions associated with bodily feeling and perceptions associated with mental feeling;
these are called the aggregate of perception.

What is the aggregate of perception? Third, the aggregate of perception: perceptions associated with pleasant feeling, perceptions associated with painful feeling, and perceptions associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; these are called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception?

The four types of perception constitute the aggregate of perception: perception bound to the desire realm, perception bound to the form realm, perception bound to the formless realm, and unconditioned perception. This is called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception?

The five types of perception constitute the aggregate of perception: perception associated with the faculty of pleasure, perception associated with the faculty of pain, perception associated with the faculty of joy, perception associated with the faculty of grief, and perception associated with the faculty of equanimity; these are called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception?
The six perceptions constitute the aggregate of perception: perception of forms, perception of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; these are called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception?

The seventh is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*): perceptions associated with the eye-consciousness element, and perceptions associated with the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and mental-consciousness elements; these are called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha)?

It consists of perception associated with the eighteen mental applications (manopavicāra), as well as other perceptions, the perception of consciousness, and the ultimate perception of consciousness; this is called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception?

It consists of the thirty-six types of perception associated with the noble phrases, as well as other perceptions, perceptions of consciousness, and ultimate perceptions of consciousness; these are called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha)?

It consists of the one hundred and eight perceptions associated with feeling (vedanā), as well as other perceptions, perceptions of consciousness (vijñāna-saṃjñā), and ultimate perceptions of consciousness; this is called the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception?

If one conceives of the past, future, and present; the internal and external; the coarse and subtle; the inferior and superior; the distant and near—this is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
What is perception associated with bodily sensation?
If one conceives of bodily sensation as arising, abiding, and ceasing together with [the mind], this is called the perception associated with bodily sensation.
What is the perception associated with mental sensation?
If one conceives of mental sensation as arising, abiding, and ceasing together with [the mind], this is called the perception associated with mental sensation.
What is the perception associated with pleasant feeling?
If a perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with pleasant feeling, this is called the perception associated with pleasant feeling.
What is the perception associated with painful feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?

If one intends for the feeling of suffering and the feeling that is neither pleasant nor painful to arise together, abide together, and cease together, this is called the perception associated with the feeling that is neither pleasant nor painful.
What is perception bound to the desire realm?

If one’s perception is associated with the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), it is called perception bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-saṃjñā*).
What is perception bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-saṃjñā*)?
If one’s perception is associated with the outflows of form (*rūpa-āsrava*) and the outflows of existence, it is called perception bound to the form realm.
What is perception associated with the formless realm?
If perception is characterized by the outflows of the formless realm and is subject to leakage, it is called perception associated with the formless realm.
What is unassociated perception?
If one contemplates the noble and untainted, this is called the perception of non-attachment (*aniyata-saṃjñā*).
What is the perception associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya-saṃprayukta-saṃjñā*)?
If a perception arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the faculty of pleasure, this is called the perception associated with the faculty of pleasure.
What is the perception associated with the faculty of suffering, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, or the faculty of equanimity?
If a perception arises, abides, and ceases together with the faculty of equanimity, it is called the perception associated with neither-pain-nor-pleasure.
What is the perception of form?
If it is a perception associated with visual consciousness, this is called the perception of form.
What are the perceptions of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena?
If one intends the perception associated with consciousness, this is called the perception of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
What is the perception of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*)?
It is the contemplation of the object of form; if there is perception, perception as consciousness, or ultimate perception as consciousness regarding form, this is called the perception of form.
What are the perceptions of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena?

When one contemplates the sphere of mental phenomena, whatever perception there is—whether it be the perception of consciousness, the perception of thorough knowledge, or the perception of ultimate knowledge—this is called the perception of mental phenomena.
What is the perception associated with the eye-consciousness element?
If a perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the eye-consciousness element, this is called the perception associated with the eye-consciousness element.
What is the perception associated with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element?
If a perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the mind-consciousness-element, this is called the perception associated with the mind-consciousness-element.
What is the perception associated with the eighteen mental applications?
If a perception arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the eighteen mental applications, it is called the perception associated with the eighteen mental applications.

What is the perception of the remainder of perceptions, the perception of consciousness, and the ultimate perception of consciousness, excluding the perceptions associated with the eighteen mental applications?

The perception that remains after excluding the perceptions associated with the eighteen mental applications is called the perception of the remainder of perceptions, the perception of consciousness, and the ultimate perception of consciousness.
What is the perception associated with the thirty-six noble phrases?
If a perception arises, abides, and ceases together with the thirty-six noble phrases, this is called the perception associated with the thirty-six noble phrases.
What is the perception of the remainder, the perception of consciousness, and the perception of ultimate consciousness, after excluding the perception associated with the thirty-six noble phrases?

The perception that remains after excluding the perception associated with the thirty-six noble phrases is called the perception of the remainder, the perception of consciousness, and the perception of ultimate consciousness.
What is perception associated with the one hundred and eight feelings?
If perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the one hundred and eight feelings, it is called perception associated with the one hundred and eight feelings.

What is the perception of the remainder after excluding the perceptions associated with the one hundred and eight feelings, as well as the perception of consciousness and the ultimate perception of consciousness?

The perception that remains after excluding the perceptions associated with the one hundred and eight feelings is called the perception of the remainder after excluding the perceptions associated with the one hundred and eight feelings, as well as the perception of consciousness and the ultimate perception of consciousness.
What is past perception?
If a perception has arisen and ceased, this is called past perception.
What is future perception?
If a perception has not yet arisen and not yet emerged, it is called future perception.
What is present perception?
If a perception has arisen but not yet ceased, it is called present perception.
What is internal perception?
If it is a perception associated with feeling, this is called internal perception.
What is external perception?
If one perceives what is not feeling, this is called external perception.
What is coarse perception?
If a perception is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse perception.
What is subtle perception?
Whether it is perception associated with the form realm, the formless realm, or unconditioned, this is called subtle perception.
What is inferior perception?

If one conceives of an unwholesome thought, or a thought regarding the retribution of unwholesome dharmas, or a thought regarding that which is neither retribution nor a dharma leading to retribution as being disagreeable, this is called an inferior perception.
What is a superior perception?
What is the perception of the wholesome?

What is the perception of the retribution of wholesome dharmas, or the perception of that which is neither retribution nor a cause of retribution and is agreeable? These are called superior perceptions (*viśiṣṭa-saṃjñā*).
What is the distant perception (*dūra-saṃjñā*)?
If one perceives various perceptions as distant, extremely distant, not near, or not near the vicinity, this is called the perception of distance.
What is the perception of proximity?
If one perceives various perceptions as near, extremely near, or near the vicinity, this is called the perception of proximity.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

Excluding the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), all other conditioned phenomena that are not form (*rūpa*) are called the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations?

Volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, confidence, regret, absence of regret, gladness, joy, mental energy, mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, aging, death, life-force, fetters, the attainment of non-perception, the attainment of fruition, and the attainment of cessation—these are called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
The sense-base of mind is called the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
The mind-faculty (manas-indriya) is called the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha).
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
If there is the mind, mentation, and the six groups of consciousness, as well as the seven elements of consciousness—this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
Whatever consciousness is past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—this is called the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the group of six consciousnesses?

The group of visual consciousness, the group of auditory consciousness, the group of olfactory consciousness, the group of gustatory consciousness, the group of tactile consciousness, and the group of mental consciousness.
What is the group of visual consciousness?

Depending on the eye, depending on forms, depending on light, and depending on attention—through these four conditions, consciousness has arisen, arises now, will arise, or is indeterminate; this is called the group of visual consciousness.
What are the groups of consciousness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?

With the mind as condition, with mental phenomena as condition, and with attention as condition, consciousness—having already arisen, arising now, or yet to arise—is indeterminate; this is called the group of mental consciousness.
These are called the six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya).
What are the seven elements of consciousness (sapta-vijñāna-dhātu)?
They are the element of eye-consciousness, the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, the element of mind (manas), and the element of mental consciousness (mano-vijñāna).
What is the eye-consciousness element?

That consciousness which arises from the eye faculty with respect to the objective field of visible forms—whether already arisen, presently arising, about to arise, or indeterminate—is called the eye-consciousness element.
What is the element of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness?
If consciousness arises from the body-faculty with contact as its object—whether it has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate—it is called the element of body-consciousness.
What is the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?

It is that which cognizes mental objects (*dharma*) and reflects upon them; whether the initial mind has already arisen, is presently arising, will arise, or is indeterminate, this is called the mind-element.
What is the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)?

It refers to consciousness that resembles [its object] and does not depart from its respective sphere, as well as other similar minds—whether already arisen, presently arising, yet to arise, or indeterminate. This is called the mental consciousness element.
These are called the seven elements of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).
What is past consciousness?
If consciousness has arisen and then ceased, this is called past consciousness.
What is future consciousness?
If consciousness has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, this is called future consciousness.
What is present consciousness?
If consciousness has arisen but not yet ceased, it is called present consciousness.
What is internal consciousness?
If consciousness is experienced, it is called internal consciousness.
What is external consciousness?
If consciousness is not felt, it is called external consciousness.
What is coarse consciousness?
If consciousness is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse consciousness.
What is subtle consciousness?
If consciousness is bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or is unbound, it is called subtle consciousness.
What is inferior consciousness?

If consciousness is unwholesome, or if consciousness is the retribution of an unwholesome dharma, or if consciousness is neither retribution nor a dharma leading to retribution and is disagreeable—this is called inferior consciousness.
What is superior consciousness?

If consciousness is wholesome, or if it is the retribution of wholesome dharmas, or if it is agreeable consciousness that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution, this is called superior consciousness.
What is distant consciousness?
If a consciousness is distant from the characteristics of other consciousnesses—extremely distant, not near, and not near by their side—it is called distant consciousness.
What is near consciousness?
If consciousness is proximate, extremely proximate, or adjacent, it is called "proximate consciousness.
Of the five aggregates, how many are material and how many are non-material?
One is material; four are non-material.
What is the one form?
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha); this is called the one form.
What are the four non-forms?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are called the four non-material aggregates.
Among the five aggregates, how many are visible and how many are invisible?
Four are invisible; one or two parts may be either visible or invisible.
What are the four that are invisible?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are called the four that are invisible.
What is meant by "one part is twofold, being either visible or invisible"?
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is what is called "one part is twofold, being either visible or invisible.
What is the aggregate of form that is visible?
The sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is called the visible aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What is the invisible aggregate of form?
With the exception of the sense-base of form, the remaining [parts of] the aggregate of form are invisible; this is called the invisible aggregate of form.
Of the five aggregates (*skandha*), how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
Four are without resistance; one is twofold, being either with resistance or without resistance.
Which four are without resistance?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of formations, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are called the four non-resistant [aggregates].
What is meant by the one aggregate that is twofold, being either resistant or non-resistant?
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is called "one part of two," being either with resistance (*sapratigha*) or without resistance (*apratigha*).
What is the aggregate of form with resistance?
The ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), these are called the aggregate of form with resistance.
What is the form aggregate (rūpaskandha) that is non-resistant?
The forms included within the sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana-rūpa); this is called the form aggregate that is non-resistant.
Of the five aggregates, how many are noble (ārya) and how many are non-noble (anārya)?
All [aggregates] are of two kinds: either noble (*ārya*) or non-noble (*anārya*).
What is the aggregate of form that is non-noble?
If the aggregate of form is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called the non-noble aggregate of form.
What is the aggregate of form that is non-noble?
The aggregate of feeling of form—this is called the aggregate of form that is non-noble.
Why is the aggregate of form non-noble?

If the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, consisting of the ten bases of form (rūpāyatana) and the first four types of derived form, this is called the non-noble aggregate of form.
What is the noble aggregate of form?
If the aggregate of form is outflow-free (anāsrava), this is called the noble aggregate of form.
What is the noble aggregate of form?
It is the aggregate of form belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

A person in training, having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies, enters the noble path with a noble mind—whether through firm faith or firm Dharma—and being of another [such] disposition, perceives the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplates the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and views suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are. Not yet having attained what is to be attained, not yet having understood what is to be understood, and not yet having realized what is to be realized, they cultivate the path free from defilements.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with contemplative wisdom, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by contemplation, they realize the fruit of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of the path of cultivation—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the liberation of mind through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If there is a real person or a destination, and right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness—these are called the noble aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What is the non-noble aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*)?
If the aggregate of feeling is with outflows, it is called the non-noble aggregate of feeling.
What is the non-noble aggregate of feeling?
If one experiences the aggregate of feeling, this is called the non-noble aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is non-noble?

If the aggregate of feeling is neither that of one in training nor that of one beyond training—namely, feeling born of eye-contact, and feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—this is called the aggregate of feeling that is non-noble.
What is the noble aggregate of feeling?
If the aggregate of feeling is untainted (*anāsrava*), this is called the noble aggregate of feeling.
What is the noble aggregate of feeling?
The feeling born of mental contact associated with the faculty of faith is called the noble aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha-ārya*).
What is the noble aggregate of feeling?
It is the aggregate of feeling belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
When a practitioner is free from fetters and proclivities, and even seeks to realize the fruit of Arhatship—
whether it be a real person, a destination, or mental contact— this is called the noble aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of perception that is non-noble?
If the aggregate of perception is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called the aggregate of perception that is non-noble.
What is the aggregate of perception that is non-noble?
The aggregate of perception and feeling is called the non-noble aggregate of perception.
What is the non-noble aggregate of perception?

If the aggregate of perception is neither that of a trainee (*śaikṣa*) nor that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), such as the perception of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*), this is called the non-noble aggregate of perception.
What is the noble aggregate of perception?
If the aggregate of perception is noble and untainted, this is called the noble aggregate of perception.
What is the noble aggregate of perception?
If one contemplates the mental formations associated with the faculty of faith within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), this is called the noble aggregate of perception.
What is the noble aggregate of perception?
It refers to the aggregate of perception that is either in training (*śaikṣa*) or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
When a practitioner is freed from the fetters and proclivities, up to and including the immediate realization of the fruit of arhatship—
whether it be the notion of a real person, a destination, or a phenomenon— this is called the noble aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of formations that is non-noble?
If the aggregate of formations is with outflows (*sāsrava*), this is called the aggregate of formations that is non-noble.
Why is the aggregate of formations non-noble?
If one practices the aggregate of formations, this is called the noble-less aggregate of formations.
What is the noble-less aggregate of formations?

If the aggregate of formations is neither that of a learner (*śaikṣa*) nor that of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), ranging from volition (*cetanā*) up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), this is called the noble-less aggregate of formations.
What is the noble aggregate of formations?
If the aggregate of formations is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the noble aggregate of formations.
What is the noble aggregate of formations?

If it is the faculty of faith, or mental factors associated with the faculty of faith, which are conditioned by the taintless (anāsrava) and are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), this is called the noble aggregate of formations.
What is the noble aggregate of formations?

If the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) pertains to those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa), such that a person in training becomes free from fetters and afflictions, even attaining the fruit of arhatship;

or if it pertains to a real person or a destiny (gati); or if it consists of volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), initial and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), non-delusion (amoha), pliancy (prasrabdhi), joy (muditā), mental vigor (cittotsāha), mental serenity (cittaprasāda), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), equanimity of mind (upekṣā), attainment of the fruit (phalaprāpti), and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)—these are called the noble aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is non-noble?
If the aggregate of consciousness is with outflows (*sāsrava*), this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is non-noble.
Why is the aggregate of consciousness non-noble?
The aggregate of consciousness as feeling is called the noble-less aggregate of consciousness.
What is the noble-less aggregate of consciousness?

If the aggregate of consciousness is neither that of a learner (śaikṣa) nor that of one beyond learning (aśaikṣa)—from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the noble-less aggregate of consciousness.
What is the noble aggregate of consciousness?
If the aggregate of consciousness is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the noble aggregate of consciousness.
What is the noble aggregate of consciousness?

If the consciousness aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) associated with the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) is the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu), this is called the noble consciousness aggregate.
What is the noble consciousness aggregate?
It is the consciousness aggregate of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
When a practitioner is freed from the fetters and latent tendencies, they even immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
Whether it be a real person, a destiny, the mind-element, or the mental-consciousness-element—this is called the noble aggregate of consciousness.

The same applies to: the tainted and the untainted; that which is accompanied by craving and that which is not; that which involves seeking and that which does not; that which is subject to appropriation and that which is not; that which is grasped and that which is not; and that which is superior and that which is not.
Of the five aggregates, how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated?
All are of two kinds: either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What is the aggregate of form that is appropriated?
If it is within the aggregate of form, this is called the feeling of the aggregate of form.
What is the feeling of the aggregate of form?

If the form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*) arises as a result of karma, mental factors, and afflictions, and is comprised within the sphere of the self (*ātman*), such as the sense bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the body’s beautiful or unbeautiful color, dignified or undignified appearance, fair or unfair complexion, and pure or impure state; the body’s pleasant or unpleasant sound, various wonderful sounds or non-wonderful sounds, and soft sounds or non-soft sounds; the body’s pleasant or unpleasant odor, mild odors or non-mild odors, and agreeable odors or disagreeable odors; the body’s sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, phlegmatic, or bilious tastes; the body’s cold, hot, light, heavy, coarse, fine, rough, smooth, hard, or soft sensations; and the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning up by the mind; as well as the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech, and the taintful bodily effort (*āśraya-prayoga*): these are called the feeling (*vedanā*) associated with the form aggregate.
What is the aggregate of form that is not feeling?
That which is external to the aggregate of form is called the aggregate of form that is not feeling.
What is the aggregate of form that is not feeling?

If the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not comprised within one’s own domain; or if it consists of bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning—arising from a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or a mind that is neither a result nor a productive cause; or vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; or external forms cognizable by visual consciousness; or sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; or external tangibles cognizable by tactile consciousness; or the non-restraint of body and speech (*avijñapti*); or the impure restraint of body and speech (*avijñapti*); or impure bodily exertion (*vīrya*) and impure bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); or right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, and right bodily tranquility—this is called the aggregate of form that is not feeling (*vedanā*).
What is the appropriation of the aggregate of feeling?
If it is within the aggregate of feeling, this is called the appropriation of the aggregate of feeling.
What is the appropriation of the aggregate of feeling?

If the feeling aggregate is produced as a retribution from karma and afflictions, and is comprised within my own portion—namely, the feelings born of eye-contact, and the feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—this is called the feeling aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is not feeling?
If the aggregate of feeling is external, this is called the aggregate of feeling that is not feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is not feeling?

Whether the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; whether it is not included within one's own domain, such as the feeling born of eye-contact, or the feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact—these are called the aggregate of feeling that is not feeling.
What is the appropriation of the aggregate of perception?
If the aggregate of perception is internal, this is called the appropriation of the aggregate of perception.
What is the appropriation of the aggregate of perception?

If one conceives of the retribution produced by the karma and afflictions of the aggregate of perception as being comprised within my own portion—namely, the perceptions of form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and mental phenomena—this is called the feeling associated with the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception that is not feeling?
If one considers the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) as distinct from feeling (vedanā), this is called the aggregate of perception that is not feeling.
What is the aggregate of perception that is not feeling?

If the aggregate of perception—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—is not comprised within my own domain, such as the perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (dharmas), this is called the aggregate of perception that is not feeling.
What is the appropriation of the aggregate of formations?
If it is within the aggregate of formations, this is called the appropriation of the aggregate of formations.
What is the appropriation of the aggregate of formations?

If the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)—born from karma, dharma, and afflictions, and comprised within my own portion—consist of volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), non-regret (*akaukṛtya*), contentment (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittābhyutsāha*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), fear (*bhaya*), birth (*jāti*), and life-force (*jīvita*), these are called the feeling (*vedanā*) within the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations that is not associated with grasping?
That which is external to the aggregate of formations is called the aggregate of formations that is not associated with grasping.
What is the aggregate of formations that is not associated with grasping?

If the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not included within one's own domain—excluding life-force (jīvita)—the remainder of the aggregate of formations is "not felt" (anupātta); this is called the aggregate of formations that is not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the aggregate of consciousness?
That which is within the aggregate of consciousness is called the feeling associated with the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the feeling associated with the aggregate of consciousness?

If the aggregate of consciousness—arising as a result of karma, dharmas, and afflictions, and comprised within the sphere of "mine," from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the feeling-aspect of the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is not feeling?
If it is outside the aggregate of consciousness, this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is not feeling.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is not feeling?

If the aggregate of consciousness—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—is not comprised within my own domain, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is not feeling.
The same applies to the internal and external.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
All are of two kinds: either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the aggregate of form that is retributive?
If the aggregate of form is of a nature to be retribution, this is called the aggregate of form that is retributive.
What is the aggregate of form that is retributive?

Excluding the wholesome resultant form-aggregate, all other form-aggregates—whether wholesome or unwholesome; the bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, as well as the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phrases, and speech; the non-restraint of body and speech; the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) bodily and vocal restraint; the outflow-tainted bodily effort and bodily exertion; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily exertion—these are called the form-aggregate with resultant.
What is the aggregate of form that is without retribution?

If the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is neither karmic retribution (*vipāka*) nor subject to retribution (*vipākadharmā*), it includes: the sense-bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, odor, taste, and tangibles; bodily beauty and ugliness, comeliness and uncomeliness, elegance and lack of elegance, refinement and lack of refinement; bodily pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, melodious sounds and non-melodious sounds, soft sounds and harsh sounds; the bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of movement, coming and going, bending and stretching, and turning about, which arises from an indeterminate mind; the vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; external forms known by visual consciousness; external sounds known by auditory consciousness; the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) precepts of impure body and speech; impure bodily exertion (*vīrya*) and impure bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility. This is called the aggregate of form that is without retribution.
What is the aggregate of feeling that has retribution?
If the aggregate of feeling is a dharma subject to retribution, this is called the aggregate of feeling that has retribution.
What is the aggregate of feeling that has retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of feeling, any other feeling—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that arises from mental contact is called the aggregate of feeling with retribution.
What is the aggregate of feeling without retribution?

Whether it be the feeling aggregate that is a result of retribution, or the feeling aggregate that is neither a result of retribution nor subject to retribution—namely, feelings born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—these are called the feeling aggregate without retribution.
What is the aggregate of perception that has retribution?
If the aggregate of perception is a phenomenon subject to retribution, this is called the aggregate of perception having retribution.
What is the aggregate of perception that has retribution?
Excluding the wholesome resultant thought-aggregate, any other thought-aggregate that is either wholesome or unwholesome is called the thought-aggregate with result.
What is the thought-aggregate without result?

The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) may be retribution (vipāka), or it may be neither retribution nor subject to retribution (na-vipāka-na-vipākadharmaka). The perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the retribution-free aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of formations that has retribution?
If the aggregate of formations is a dharma subject to retribution, this is called the aggregate of formations having retribution.
What is the aggregate of formations that has retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), all other wholesome or unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*) within the aggregate of formations—including up to the afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—are called the aggregate of formations with retribution (*savipāka*).
What is the aggregate of formations that is without retribution?

If the aggregate of formations is a result of retribution, or if the aggregate of formations is neither a result of retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution—excluding non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, the afflictions (*kleśa*), the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—the remaining aggregate of formations is without retribution; this is called the aggregate of formations that is without retribution.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that has retribution?
If the aggregate of consciousness is a dharma of retribution, this is called the aggregate of consciousness that has retribution.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that has retribution?
Excluding the wholesome resultant consciousness-aggregate, the remaining wholesome or unwholesome mind-element and mind-consciousness-element are called the consciousness-aggregate with resultant.
What is the consciousness-aggregate without resultant?

Regarding the aggregate of consciousness: whether the aggregate of consciousness is karmic retribution, or whether it is neither retribution nor subject to retribution—from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is without retribution.
Among the five aggregates, how many are mental and how many are non-mental?
One is mind; four are not mind.
What is the one mind?
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is called the one mind.
What are the four that are not mind?
The aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of formations—these are called the four that are not mind.
Among the five aggregates, how many are associated with mind, and how many are not associated with mind?

Two are associated with the mind, one is not associated with the mind, one is said to be neither associated with the mind nor dissociated from it, and one is of two kinds, being either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind.
What is meant by "two factors associated with mind"?
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) and the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha); these are called the two factors associated with mind.
What is meant by "one factor not associated with mind"?
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is called the one that is not associated with the mind.
What is the one that is said to be neither associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind?
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is called the one that is said to be neither associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind.
What is meant by "one part belonging to both" (ekāṃśa-ubhayabhāgīya), being either associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) or not associated with the mind (*cittaviprayukta*)?
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is what is called "one part belonging to both," being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What is the aggregate of formations associated with the mind?

If the aggregate of formations consists of mental factors such as volition, up to and including the afflictions and latent tendencies, this is called the aggregate of formations associated with the mind.
What is the aggregate of formations not associated with the mind?

If the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is not a mental factor (caitta), from its arising until the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), this is called the aggregate of formations that is not associated with the mind (cittaviprayukta).
Of the five aggregates, how many are mental factors and how many are not mental factors?
Two are mental concomitants (citta-saṃskāra), two are not mental concomitants, and one is twofold—either a mental concomitant or not a mental concomitant.
What are the two that are mental concomitants?
The aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) and the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha); these are called the two mental concomitants.
What are the two that are not mental factors?
The aggregate of form and the aggregate of consciousness; these are called the two that are not mental factors.
What is the one that is twofold, being either a mental factor or not a mental factor?
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is called "one part of two," being either mental factors (caitta) or non-mental factors.
What is the aggregate of formations that are mental factors?
If the aggregate of formations has as its object volition (cetanā) up to the latent tendencies of the afflictions (kleśānuśaya), these are called the aggregate of formations that are mental factors.
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that is not a mental factor (citta-saṃprayukta)?
The aggregate of formations from those that are not dependently originated up to the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called the aggregate of formations that is not a mental factor.
Of the five aggregates, how many are with an object (sālambana), and how many are without an object (anālambana)?
There are three types of conditions, one that is not a condition, and one that is either a condition or not a condition.
What are the three conditions?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are called the three conditions.
What is the one that is not an object-condition?
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha); this is called the one that is not an object-condition.
What is the one that is twofold—either an object-condition or not an object-condition?
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) is called "one part of two," being either conditioned (sappaccaya) or unconditioned (appaccaya).
What is the aggregate of formations that is conditioned?

If the aggregate of formations consists of mental concomitants such as volition (cetanā), up to the underlying tendencies of the afflictions (kleśānuśaya), this is called the aggregate of formations that is conditioned.
What is the aggregate of formations that is not associated with conditions?
If the aggregate of formations is not a mental factor—from its arising until the attainment of cessation—it is called the aggregate of formations that is not associated with conditions.
Of the five aggregates, how many are associated with the mind, and how many are not associated with the mind?
Two are associated with the mind, one is not associated with the mind, and two are twofold—either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the two associated with the mind?
The aggregate of feeling and the aggregate of perception; these are called the two associated with the mind.
What is the one that is not associated with the mind?
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha); this is called the one that is not associated with the mind.
What are the two that are twofold—either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind?

The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) are called the two "twofold" aggregates, which are either associated with the mind (cittasamprayukta) or dissociated from the mind (cittaviprayukta).
What is the aggregate of form that is associated with the mind?

That which follows the mind, arises together with the mind, abides together with the mind, and ceases together with the mind—namely, the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) non-informative (avijñapti) discipline of body and speech, the outflow-tainted bodily exertion (vīrya), the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility (praśrabdhi), right speech, right action, right livelihood, right bodily exertion, and right bodily tranquility. This is called the aggregate of form associated with the mind.
What is the aggregate of form that is not shared with the mind?

If it does not follow the mind’s turning, does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind—namely, the ten bases of form and the entirety of the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) as form—this is called the aggregate of form that is not shared with the mind.
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that is associated with the mind?

If the aggregate of formations follows the mind in its turning, arises together with the mind, abides together with the mind, and ceases together with the mind—ranging from volition (cetanā) up to the afflictions and latent tendencies (anuśaya)—this is called the aggregate of formations associated with the mind.
What is the aggregate of formations that is not associated with the mind?

If the aggregate of formations does not follow the mind, does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind—from its arising up until the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling—this is called the aggregate of formations that is not associated with the mind.
The same applies to those that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and those that do not follow the mind (*na cittānuvartin*).
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many are karma and how many are not karma?
Three are not karma; two are of two kinds, being either karma or not karma.
What are the three that are not karma?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of consciousness; these are called the three that are not karma.
What are the two that are twofold, being either karma or not karma?

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*): these are called the two pairs that are either karma or not karma. What is the aggregate of form that is karma?

It refers to bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—arising from a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind, or an indeterminate mind; vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*)—such as the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; non-informative action (*avijñapti*) of body and speech that is non-restraint; informative action (*vijñapti*) of body and speech that is restraint with outflows (*sāsrava*); and right speech, right action, and right livelihood. This is called the aggregate of form that is karma.

What is the aggregate of form that is not karma? It consists of the sense-bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the sense-bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles; bodily forms that are beautiful or unattractive, graceful or ungainly, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, and pure or impure; bodily sounds that are pleasant or unpleasant, melodious or unmelodious, and soft or harsh; as well as external forms known by visual consciousness and external sounds known by auditory consciousness; furthermore, it includes tainted bodily exertion and tainted bodily tranquility, as well as right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility. This is called the aggregate of form that is not karma.
What is the kamma of the aggregate of formations?
Volition is called the kamma of the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations that is not kamma?
Excluding volition (*cetanā*), the remaining factors of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) are called the aggregate of formations that are not karma.
Regarding the five aggregates, how many are associated with karma (*karmasaṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with karma?

Three are associated with karma; one is not associated with karma; and one is threefold: it may be associated with karma, not associated with karma, or it is not stated whether it is associated with karma or not associated with karma.
What is meant by the three aggregates associated with karma?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are called the three aggregates associated with karma.
What is the one that is not associated with karma?
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is called one that is not associated with karma.
What is the one that is threefold—either associated with karma, or not associated with karma, or neither said to be associated nor not associated with karma?

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is called "one-third" [of the aggregates], being either associated with karma, not associated with karma, or neither said to be associated nor not associated with karma.
What is the aggregate of formations that is associated with karma?

If the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) consists of contact associated with volition (*cetanā*) up to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions, this is called the aggregate of formations associated with karma.
What is the aggregate of formations not associated with karma?

If the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is not associated with volition (*cetanā*), from birth up to the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), this is called the aggregate of formations that is not associated with karma.
What is the aggregate of formations that is neither said to be associated with karma nor dissociated from karma?
Volition (cetanā) is called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha); it is not said to be either associated with karma or dissociated from karma.
Regarding the five aggregates, how many are common karma (sādhāraṇa-karma) and how many are uncommon karma (asādhāraṇa-karma)?
Three are common karma; two are of two kinds, being either common karma or uncommon karma.
What are the three common karmas?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are called the three common karmas.
What are the two that are twofold, being either common karma or uncommon karma?

The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha) and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) are called the two pairs, which may be either common karma (sādhāraṇa-karma) or uncommon karma (asādhāraṇa-karma).
What is the aggregate of form as common karma?
