The aggregate of form that evolves in accordance with karma, arising together with, abiding together with, and ceasing together with common karma—namely, the unmanifest (avijñapti) of the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) bodily and vocal precepts; the outflow-tainted bodily exertion and the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility—this is called the aggregate of form as common karma.
What is the aggregate of form that is not shared karma?

If the aggregate of form does not follow along with karma, and is not produced together with shared karma, nor abides together with it, nor ceases together with it—namely, the ten bases of form and the first three types of form—this is called the aggregate of form that is not shared karma.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that is common to karma?

If the aggregate of formations follows the turning of karma, arises together with it, abides together with it, and ceases together with it—furthermore, including determinate thought, contact, up to the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and afflictions, as well as the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*)—this is called the aggregate of formations that is common to karma.
What is the aggregate of formations that is non-common karma?

If the aggregate of formations does not follow along with karma, and is not co-arisen, co-abiding, or co-ceasing with it—namely, the mental formations of uncertainty, birth, aging, death, life-force, fetters, and the attainment of fruits—this is called the aggregate of formations that is non-common karma.
The same applies to whether they follow karma or do not follow karma.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many are causes and how many are non-causes?
Three are causes; two are twofold, being either causes or non-causes.
What are the three causes?
The aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, and the aggregate of consciousness—these are called the three causes.
What are the two that are twofold, being either causes or non-causes?
The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) and the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) are called the two "two-part" aggregates, which may be either with cause or without cause.
What is the aggregate of form that has a cause?
If the aggregate of form is a dharma of retribution (vipākadharma), it is called the aggregate of form with a cause.

What is the cause of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)? It refers to the wholesome or unwholesome aggregate of form, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*)—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—arising from a wholesome or unwholesome mind; vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*)—the collection of sounds, phrases, and speech; the great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind; the non-informative (*avijñapti*) discipline of body and speech that is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; the informative discipline of body and speech that is with outflows (*sāsrava*); the wholesome mental application of the body (*kāyasaṃskāra*) and the wholesome removal of the body (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) that are with outflows; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right mental application of the body and right removal of the body. These are called the causes of the aggregate of form.

What is the aggregate of form that is not a cause? It refers to the aggregate of form that is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), and the aggregate of form that is neither a result of maturation nor subject to maturation (*avipākadharma*). This includes the sense-bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the sense-bases of visible forms, odors, and tastes; and bodily qualities such as beautiful or ugly color, dignified or undignified appearance, smooth or coarse skin, and pure or impure complexion; vocal qualities such as pleasant or unpleasant sound, melodious or unmelodious voice, and soft or harsh tone; unmanifest bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from an indeterminate mind—consisting of movements such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; and unmanifest vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; furthermore, external forms known by visual consciousness, external sounds known by auditory consciousness, and the contaminated bodily effort included within the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) excluding the four great elements. This is called the aggregate of form that is not a cause.
What is the cause of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

The aggregate of formations is a condition for the aggregate of formations that is not a condition for [resultant] existence with retribution; excluding the attainment of fruition, the remaining formations that are not conditions for wholesome retribution—ranging from volition (*cetanā*) up to the afflictions (*kleśa*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—are called the cause of the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations that is not a cause?

The aggregate of formations that arises from conditions such as non-retributive, unshared karma, birth, aging, death, life-force, and the acquisition of fruits—this is called the aggregate of formations that is not a cause.
Regarding the five aggregates: how many have causes, and how many are without cause?
All have causes; all have fetters; all have conditions; all are conditioned.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many are known and how many are not known?

All are known; they are known and seen as they truly are. All are cognized; they are cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as they truly are. All are understood; they are known and seen as they truly are. All are realized; they are known and seen as they truly are.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
All of them are twofold: either known through the knowledge of abandonment or not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) that is known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) that is unwholesome, arising from an unwholesome mind—namely, bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; non-informative matter (avijñapti) of body and speech that is not discipline; and impure bodily effort—this is called the aggregate of form known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the aggregate of form that is not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that is wholesome or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), namely: the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-base; bodily beauty and ugliness, comeliness and lack of comeliness, and fairness and lack of fairness; bodily pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, variegated wonderful sounds and non-wonderful sounds, and soft sounds and non-soft sounds; bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of the movement of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; external forms known by visual consciousness; external sounds known by auditory consciousness; the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) morality of the body and speech pertaining to the outflows (*sāsrava*); the outflow-tainted bodily exertion (*vīrya*) and bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility—this is called the aggregate of form that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
What is the knowledge of the abandonment of the aggregate of feeling?

The unwholesome [factors] associated with the aggregate of feeling—namely, volition, contact, attention, vitarka and vicāra, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters—this is called the knowledge of the abandonment of the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The aggregate of feeling that is wholesome or indeterminate—namely, feeling born of eye-contact, and feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—is called the aggregate of feeling that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the aggregate of perception?
Unwholesome perceptions within the aggregate of perception are called the knowledge through the wisdom of abandonment regarding the aggregate of perception.
What is the knowledge regarding the aggregate of perception that is not known through the wisdom of abandonment?

The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) consisting of wholesome and indeterminate perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—this is called the aggregate of perception that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇa-jñāna).
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that is to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The unwholesome factors within the aggregate of formations—namely, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, views, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, mental pleasure, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters—these are called the knowledge of the abandonment of the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that is not known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*)?

The aggregate of formations that is wholesome or indeterminate—excluding doubt, the afflictions (*kleśa*), the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—is the remainder of the aggregate of formations not known through the knowledge of abandonment; this is called the aggregate of formations not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the aggregate of consciousness known through the knowledge of abandonment?
The unwholesome mind-element within the aggregate of consciousness is called the aggregate of consciousness known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the aggregate of consciousness not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*)—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the aggregate of consciousness that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
The same applies to what is abandoned and what is not abandoned.
Regarding the five aggregates, how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) and how many are not to be cultivated?
All [factors] are twofold: either cultivated (*bhāvita*) or uncultivated (*abhāvita*). What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that is cultivated?

The aggregate of form that arises from a wholesome mind—namely, bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) morality of body and speech associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); the faculty of physical vigor (*kāyavīrya*) associated with outflows; the faculty of physical pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*) associated with outflows; right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right pliancy of body—this is called the aggregate of form that is cultivated.

What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that is not to be cultivated? It consists of the unwholesome and indeterminate bases of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the bases of odor, taste, and tangibles; bodily beauty and ugliness, comeliness and lack of comeliness, elegance and lack of elegance, and purity and lack of purity; bodily pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, various wonderful sounds and non-wonderful sounds, and soft sounds and harsh sounds; bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) arising from an unwholesome or indeterminate mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; and external forms known by visual consciousness, external sounds known by auditory consciousness, as well as the non-informative (*avijñapti*) non-restraint of body and speech and the taintful bodily effort (*kāyika vīrya*). This is called the aggregate of form that is not to be cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the aggregate of feeling?
Feeling that arises from wholesome mental contact is called the cultivation of the aggregate of feeling.
What is the non-cultivation of the aggregate of feeling?

The feeling aggregates that are unwholesome or indeterminate—namely, feelings born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—are called the feeling aggregate that is not cultivation.
What is the perception aggregate that is cultivation?
The perception-aggregate that consists of wholesome perceptions is called the cultivation of the perception-aggregate.
What is the perception-aggregate that is not cultivation?

The perception-aggregate that consists of unwholesome and indeterminate perceptions—namely, perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—is called the perception-aggregate that is not cultivation.
What is the cultivation of the aggregate of formations?

The wholesome volitions within the aggregate of formations, up to mental equanimity, the attainment of the meditative absorption of non-perception, the attainment of the fruits [of the path], and the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation—these are called the cultivation of the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that is not to be cultivated?

The unwholesome and indeterminate factors of the aggregate of formations—namely, volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), vitarka and vicāra, view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), non-regret (*akaukṛtya*), satisfaction (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), fear (*bhaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, old age, death, and life-force (*jīvita*)—these are called the aggregate of formations that is not to be cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the aggregate of consciousness?
The wholesome mind-element and mind-consciousness-element are called the cultivation of the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the non-cultivation of the aggregate of consciousness?

The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) that is unwholesome or indeterminate—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the aggregate of consciousness that is not cultivation (abhāvanā).
Regarding the five aggregates, how many are realization (sākṣātkriyā) and how many are not realization?
All are realized as they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*), how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
All are of three types: either wholesome, or unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is the aggregate of form that is wholesome?

If the aggregate of form consists of bodily intimation—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—arising from a cultivated wholesome mind; vocal intimation—such as the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; the unmanifested precepts of body and speech associated with outflows; the wholesome application of energy of one with outflows and the wholesome equanimity of the body; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right equanimity of the body—this is called the aggregate of form that is wholesome.
What is the aggregate of form that is unwholesome?

If the aggregate of form consists of bodily intimation—such as going, coming, contracting, extending, and turning about—which arises from an unwholesome mind; vocal intimation—such as the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; non-informative action of body and speech that is unvirtuous; and tainted bodily effort; this is called the aggregate of form that is unwholesome.

What is the aggregate of form that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? It consists of the aggregate of form that is feeling, and the aggregate of form that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution; namely, the sense-base of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; the sense-bases of odor, taste, and tangibles; bodily beauty and ugliness, the graceful and the ungraceful, the fair-skinned and the un-fair-skinned, the pure and the impure; bodily pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, various wonderful sounds and non-wonderful sounds, soft sounds and harsh sounds; the physical instruction of coming and going, bending and stretching, and turning about, which arises from an indeterminate mind; the vocal instruction of collecting sounds, phonemes, and speech; and external forms known by visual consciousness, external sounds known by auditory consciousness, and the taints associated with bodily exertion—these are called the aggregate of form that is indeterminate.
What is the wholesome aggregate of feeling?
If the aggregate of feeling consists of the feeling born of mental contact through cultivation, this is called the wholesome aggregate of feeling.
What is the unwholesome aggregate of feeling?
The feeling aggregate that consists of the feeling born of mind-contact which has been abandoned is called the unwholesome feeling aggregate.
What is the indeterminate feeling aggregate?

The feeling aggregate that is a feeling, or the feeling aggregate that is neither karmic retribution nor subject to retribution—namely, the feeling born of eye-contact, and the feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—is called the indeterminate feeling aggregate.
What is the aggregate of perception that is wholesome?
If the aggregate of perception consists of the cultivation of wholesome perceptions, this is called the wholesome aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception that is unwholesome?
When the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) abandons the notion of phenomena (dharma-saṃjñā), this is called the unwholesome aggregate of perception.
What is the indeterminate (avyākṛta) aggregate of perception?

The aggregate of perception that is sensation (vedanā), the aggregate of perception that is neither karmic retribution (vipāka) nor a dharma subject to retribution, and the perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—these are called the indeterminate aggregate of perception.
What is the wholesome aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

The aggregate of formations consisting of cultivated volition (*cetanā*) up to mental equanimity (*upekṣā*), the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*), and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*); these are called the wholesome aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations that is unwholesome?

The aggregate of formations consists of volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters; these are called the unwholesome aggregate of formations.
What is the indeterminate (avyākṛta) aggregate of formations?

The aggregate of formations that is feeling, the aggregate of formations that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution—namely: volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, serenity, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire-to-act, mindfulness, fear, birth, aging, death, and life-force—these are called the indeterminate aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is wholesome?
The aggregate of consciousness consisting of the cultivated mind-element and mind-consciousness-element is called the wholesome aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is unwholesome?
The cessation of the aggregate of consciousness—the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element—is called the unwholesome aggregate of consciousness.
What is the indeterminate aggregate of consciousness?

The aggregate of consciousness that is feeling, and the aggregate of consciousness that is neither karmic result nor a dharma leading to result—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the indeterminate aggregate of consciousness.

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many are in training (*śaikṣa*), how many are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither in training nor beyond training (*naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa*)?
All are of three parts: they are either in training, or beyond training, or neither in training nor beyond training.
What is the aggregate of form that is in training (*śaikṣa*)?
If the aggregate of form is noble (*ārya*) but not beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this is called the aggregate of form that is in training.
What is the aggregate of form that is in training?

The seeker is free from fetters and proclivities; with a noble mind, they enter the noble path. Whether through firm faith or firm Dharma, as well as other types of persons, they perceive the faults and perils of conditioned existence and contemplate the tranquility of Nirvāṇa. They contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are. Desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the afflictions.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind through contemplation, they realize the fruit of asceticism: either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
If, for a person who is a trainee (*śaikṣa*), there is right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness, this is called the aggregate of form of a trainee.
What is the aggregate of form of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is noble (*ārya*) but not that of one in training (*śaikṣa*), this is called the aggregate of form of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the aggregate of form of one beyond training?

It is when a person beyond training who desires to attain arhatship, desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, is fully endowed with the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—whether it be the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*) or the mind liberated through insight (*vipaśyanā-vimukta-citta*)—and thereby attains the fruit of arhatship.

If, for a real person or a destination, there is right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness—these are called the aggregate of form pertaining to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the aggregate of form that pertains neither to those in training (*śaikṣa*) nor to those beyond training?

The aggregate of form that is neither noble nor associated with the noble, the aggregate of feeling, the ten bases of form, and the first four elements of form—these are called the aggregate of form that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the aggregate of feeling of the learner?
The aggregate of feeling that is noble but not of one beyond training is called the aggregate of feeling of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the aggregate of feeling of one in training?
The feeling born of mental contact associated with the faculty of faith within the aggregate of feeling of one in training is called the aggregate of feeling of one in training.
What is the training regarding the aggregate of feeling?

When a trainee, having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies, even realizes the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*), whatever feeling arises from the contact of mind with mental objects for that real person or for a destiny—that is called the training regarding the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The aggregate of feeling that is noble and not of one in training—this is called the aggregate of feeling that is beyond training.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is beyond training?
The feeling aggregate associated with the faculty of faith of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), which arises from mental contact, is called the feeling aggregate of one beyond training.
What is the feeling aggregate of one beyond training?
It is when a person beyond training desires to attain arhatship and subsequently attains the fruit of arhatship.
If it is the feeling of contact through the mind belonging to a real person or a destination, this is called the aggregate of feeling of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the aggregate of feeling that is neither of training nor beyond training?

The aggregate of feeling that is non-noble (*anārya*), namely the feeling of contact through the eye, the feelings of contact through the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—this is called the aggregate of feeling that is neither of training nor beyond training.
What is the aggregate of perception that is in training (*śaikṣa*)?
The aggregate of perception that is noble but not beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called the aggregate of perception in training.
What is the aggregate of perception in training?
The perception aggregate that is associated with the faculty of faith in the training is called the perception aggregate of the training.
What is the perception aggregate of the training?
It is when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and proclivities, even attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
If one perceives a real person or the phenomena of the realms (gati) as a conceptualization, this is called the aggregate of perception belonging to those in training (śaikṣa).
What is the aggregate of perception belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
That aggregate of perception which is noble and not belonging to those in training is called the aggregate of perception belonging to those beyond training.
What is the aggregate of perception that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The perception associated with the faculty of faith within the aggregate of perception that is beyond training is called the aggregate of perception that is beyond training.
What is the aggregate of perception that is beyond training?
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship and immediately realizes the fruit of arhatship,
if they perceive a real person or a category of phenomena as a "conceptualization," this is called the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) of one beyond training.
What is the aggregate of perception that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

The non-noble aggregate of perception consists of perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena; this is called the aggregate of perception that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the aggregate of formations that is in training (*śaikṣa*)?
The aggregate of formations that is noble but not beyond training is called the aggregate of formations in training.
What is the aggregate of formations in training?

The mental factors associated with the faculty of faith within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that are in training—namely, those phenomena which are not uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), are included within the aggregate of formations, and are not beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—are called the aggregate of formations in training.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
It is when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), even attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Whether it be a real person, a destiny (*gati*), or [mental factors such as] volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), non-delusion (*amoha*), serene faith (*avetyaprasāda*), joy (*prīti*), rapture (*prāmodya*), mental exertion (*cittotsāha*), mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*), the attainment of the fruit, and the attainment of the cessation-concentration (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—these are called the aggregate of formations of one in training.
What is the aggregate of formations that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The aggregate of formations that is noble and not [the state of] one in training (*aśaikṣa*) is called the aggregate of formations that is beyond training.
What is the aggregate of formations that is beyond training?

The mental factors associated with the faculty of faith of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as those phenomena not conditioned by objects that are included within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) and are not of the state of training (śaikṣa)—these are called the aggregate of formations of one beyond training.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) pertaining to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
It refers to a person beyond training who desires to attain arhatship and thereby immediately attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, [it includes] volition, contact, reflection, initial and sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, faith, pliancy, joy, mental exertion, mental serenity, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruit, and the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). These are called the aggregate of formations pertaining to one beyond training.
What is the aggregate of formations that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

If the aggregate of formations is not noble—ranging from the aggregate of feeling and volition up to the attainment of non-perception—this is called the aggregate of formations that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is in training (*śaikṣa*)?
If the aggregate of consciousness is noble (*ārya*) but not beyond training (*na-asaikṣa*), this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is in training.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is in training?

The aggregate of consciousness associated with the faculty of faith in the state of training (*śaikṣa*), namely the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), is called the aggregate of consciousness in the state of training.
What is the aggregate of consciousness in the state of training?
It is when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, even attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*).

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*), a destiny (*gati*), or the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), these are called the training (*śaikṣa*) aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
What is the beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*) aggregate of consciousness?
If the aggregate of consciousness is noble (*ārya*) but not training, this is called the beyond-training aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?

The aggregate of consciousness that is beyond training consists of the mental element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*); this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is beyond training.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is beyond training?
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship and immediately realizes the fruit of arhatship—
whether it be the real person, the destiny, or the mind-element and mental-consciousness-element— this is called the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) of one beyond training.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

The aggregate of consciousness that is not noble—the aggregate of consciousness and feeling from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the aggregate of consciousness that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Regarding the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), how many are results (vipāka), how many are subject to fruition (vipākadharma), and how many are neither results nor subject to fruition?
All are of three types: they are either results, or subject to fruition, or neither results nor subject to fruition.
What is the aggregate of form as karmic retribution?
The aggregate of form that is the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of form consists of the sense-bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
it includes bodily forms that are beautiful or not beautiful, graceful or not graceful, fair-skinned or not fair-skinned, and pure or impure.
It is neither adorned nor pure; bodily sounds are neither pleasant nor unpleasant, neither manifold nor not manifold, neither soft nor not soft;
bodily odors are neither pleasant nor unpleasant, neither mild nor not mild, neither agreeable nor disagreeable;
there are bodily tastes of sweet, sour, bitter, pungent, salty, bland, phlegmatic, and bilious; and there are bodily sensations of cold, heat, and lightness.
Heavy, coarse, fine, rough, smooth, hard, and soft; bodily intimation arising from the mind consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning;
vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the unmanifested discipline of the outflow-tainted body and speech;
the outflow-tainted bodily effort and the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily tranquility.
This is called the retribution of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What is the retribution-nature of the aggregate of form?
If the aggregate of form possesses retribution, this is called the retribution-nature of the aggregate of form.
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) as a result of maturation (*vipākadharmā*)?

Excluding the wholesome results of maturation within the aggregate of form, the remainder of the aggregate of form—whether wholesome or unwholesome—including bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which arises from a wholesome or unwholesome mind; vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of body and speech that is non-restraint; informative and non-informative matter of body and speech that is impure restraint (*saṃvara*); impure bodily effort (*vīrya*) and impure bodily pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily pliancy—these are called the aggregate of form as a result of maturation.
What is the aggregate of form that is neither karmic retribution nor subject to retribution?

It refers to the aggregate of form that is indeterminate and not comprised within one's own continuum; it includes bodily intimation—such as moving, coming, going, contracting, extending, and turning—which arises from a mind that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution; vocal intimation—such as the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; external forms known by visual consciousness; external sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; and external tangibles known by tactile consciousness, as well as impure bodily exertion. This is called the aggregate of form that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution.
What is the retribution of the aggregate of feeling?

If the aggregate of feeling experiences the wholesome retribution of feeling arising from eye-contact, or feeling arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, this is called the retribution of the aggregate of feeling.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is subject to retribution?
That which has retribution within the aggregate of feeling is called the aggregate of feeling subject to retribution.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is subject to retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of feeling, all other feelings of the aggregate of feeling—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that arise from mental contact are called the aggregate of feeling as retribution-dharma (*vipāka-dharma*).
What is the aggregate of feeling that is neither retribution nor a dharma leading to retribution?

The neutral feelings of the aggregate of feeling that are not comprised within my own portion—namely, the feelings arising from eye-contact, and those arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—are called the aggregate of feeling that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution.
What is the aggregate of perception that is retribution?

Regarding the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), if it is a wholesome retribution consisting of perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena, this is called the retribution of the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception that is of the nature of retribution?
If the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) possesses retribution, it is called the "retributive phenomenon" (*vipāka-dharma*) of the aggregate of perception.
What is the retributive phenomenon of the aggregate of perception?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of perception, all other wholesome and unwholesome perceptions within the aggregate of perception are called the retributive phenomenon of the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of perception that is neither resultant nor subject to result?

It refers to the perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena that are indeterminate and not comprised within one's own sphere; this is called the aggregate of perception that is neither resultant nor subject to result.
What is the retribution of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

The aggregate of formations receives the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of formations, excluding non-greed and non-hatred; it includes the remaining volitions (*cetanā*) up to equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*), fear, birth, old age, death, life-force (*jīvita*), the attainment of the state of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the attainment of the fruit, and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). This is called the retribution of the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations that is subject to retribution?
That which is retributive within the aggregate of formations is called the aggregate of formations that is subject to retribution.
What is the aggregate of formations that is subject to retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), all other formations—whether wholesome or unwholesome, from volition (*cetanā*) up to the afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*)—are called the retributive phenomena of the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?

It consists of those indeterminate formations not included within the category of "mine": namely, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, birth, aging, and death. This is called the aggregate of formations that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant.
What is the aggregate of consciousness as karmic retribution?

If the aggregate of consciousness experiences the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of consciousness—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the aggregate of consciousness as karmic retribution.
What is the aggregate of consciousness as the nature of karmic retribution?
When the aggregate of consciousness has retribution, it is called the "retribution-dharma" of the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the retribution-dharma of the aggregate of consciousness?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the aggregate of consciousness, the remaining wholesome and unwholesome elements of the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) within the aggregate of consciousness are called the retribution-dharma of the aggregate of consciousness.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is neither karmic retribution nor subject to retribution?

It refers to the indeterminate eye-consciousness up to the mental consciousness that is not comprised within my own domain; this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution.

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?
All are of three types: either abandoned by insight, or abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

The aggregate of form that is unwholesome and not abandoned by cultivation, which arises from the mind associated with afflictions abandoned by insight—namely, bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of going, coming, contracting, extending, and turning; vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; the non-informative (*avijñapti*) aspects of bodily and vocal non-restraint; and tainted bodily effort (*kāyavīrya*)—this is called the aggregate of form abandoned by insight.
What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) abandoned through cultivation?

It refers to the bodily intimation (kāyavijñapti) arising from unwholesome defilements abandoned through cultivation—namely, going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; the vocal intimation (vāgvijñapti)—namely, the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech; the non-informative (avijñapti) aspects of bodily and vocal non-restraint; and tainted bodily effort (kāyavīrya). This is called the aggregate of form abandoned through cultivation.
What is the aggregate of form that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that is wholesome or indeterminate: the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base; the odor-base, flavor-base, and tangible-base; bodily beauty and ugliness, comeliness and lack of comeliness, and fairness and lack of fairness of skin; pleasant and unpleasant bodily sounds, various exquisite sounds and lack thereof, and soft sounds and lack thereof; bodily intimation (*kāyavijñapti*) consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind; vocal intimation (*vāgvijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, phrases, and syllables; external forms known by visual consciousness; external sounds known by auditory consciousness; the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) precepts of the body and speech associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); the outflow-associated bodily effort (*vīrya*) and bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); right speech, right action, and right livelihood; and right bodily effort and right bodily tranquility—these are called the aggregate of form that is neither abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) nor abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is the aggregate of feeling that is abandoned through vision?

The aggregate of feeling that is unwholesome, not to be abandoned through cultivation, and associated with the feelings arising from mental contact connected to afflictions abandoned through vision—this is called the aggregate of feeling abandoned through vision.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is abandoned through cultivation?

The aggregate of feeling that is unwholesome, not abandoned through vision, and associated with the feelings arising from mental contact with afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation—this is called the aggregate of feeling abandoned through cultivation.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The aggregate of feeling that is wholesome or indeterminate—the feeling born of eye-contact, and the feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—is called the aggregate of feeling that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of perception that is abandoned by insight?

The aggregate of perception that is unwholesome, not to be abandoned by cultivation, and consists of perceptions associated with afflictions abandoned by insight—this is called the aggregate of perception abandoned by insight.
What is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) abandoned by cultivation?
It refers to unwholesome perceptions associated with defilements that are abandoned by cultivation rather than by insight; this is called the aggregate of perception abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of perception that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The aggregate of perception that is wholesome or indeterminate—namely, perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—is called the aggregate of perception that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

Those unwholesome factors of the aggregate of formations that are not abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), but are abandoned simultaneously with the defilements abandoned by insight—namely: volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), vitarka and vicāra, view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), non-regret (*akaukṛtya*), satisfaction (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), fear (*bhaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and fetters (*saṃyojana*)—these are called the aggregate of formations abandoned by insight.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

It refers to those unwholesome factors of the aggregate of formations that are abandoned simultaneously with the abandonment of afflictions abandoned through cultivation—namely: volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), non-regret (*akaukṛtya*), satisfaction (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire-to-act (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), fear (*bhaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). These are called the aggregate of formations abandoned through cultivation.
What is the aggregate of formations that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

The aggregate of formations that is wholesome or indeterminate, excluding doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and fetters (*saṃyojana*), as well as the remaining formations, is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation; this is called the aggregate of formations that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is abandoned by insight?

If the aggregate of consciousness is unwholesome, not to be abandoned by cultivation, and associated with defilements to be abandoned by insight—namely, the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element—this is called the aggregate of consciousness abandoned by insight.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is abandoned through cultivation?

The aggregate of consciousness that is unwholesome and associated with afflictions abandoned through cultivation—namely, the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element—is called the aggregate of consciousness abandoned through cultivation.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The wholesome and indeterminate aggregates of consciousness, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the aggregate of consciousness that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many have causes that are abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*), how many have causes that are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and how many have causes that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
All [five] are of three types: either having causes abandoned by vision, or having causes abandoned by cultivation, or having causes that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.

What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that has as its cause the factors to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu*)? It refers to the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), the ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base which are the retribution of factors to be abandoned by insight; a body that is not well-colored, not handsome, not beautiful, not refined and pure; a body that does not have a good voice, not a multitude of wondrous sounds, not a soft voice; a body that does not have a multitude of wondrous fragrances, not a good fragrance, not a soft fragrance, not a pleasant fragrance; a body characterized by sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, saltiness, or blandness, and by phlegm and mucus; a body characterized by coldness, heat, heaviness, hardness, or roughness; the bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) consisting of the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which are initiated by a mind that has as its cause factors to be abandoned by insight; the vocal intimation (*vāk-vijñapti*) consisting of sounds, phrases, and speech; the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of bodily and vocal non-restraint; and the impure bodily effort (*kāyika-vīrya*). This is called the aggregate of form that has as its cause factors to be abandoned by insight.

What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)? It consists of the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base that are the retribution of dharmas to be abandoned by cultivation; a body that is not beautiful, not dignified, not fair-skinned, and not pure; a body that does not produce pleasant sounds, wondrous sounds, or soft sounds; a body that does not produce pleasant odors, soft odors, or agreeable odors; the body’s experiences of sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, saltiness, and blandness, or phlegm and mucus; the body’s sensations of cold, heat, heaviness, hardness, and roughness; the bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) arising from the mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; the vocal intimation (*vāk-vijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of bodily and vocal non-restraint; and tainted bodily effort (*kāyika-vīrya*). This is called the aggregate of form whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of form that is neither a cause for abandonment by vision nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation?

It is the wholesome aggregate of form; the retribution of wholesome dharmas within the aggregate of form; and those parts of the aggregate of form that are neither retribution nor subject to retribution, namely:

the sense-base of the eye, the sense-base of the ear, the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of the tongue, and the sense-base of the body; as well as bodily beauty, physical majesty, a fine complexion, and pure refinement; and pleasant bodily sounds.

Various wonderful sounds and gentle sounds; pleasant fragrances, soft fragrances, and agreeable fragrances of the body; the sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, saltiness, and astringency of the body;
the coldness, heat, lightness, subtlety, softness, and smoothness of the body;

bodily intimation arising from the mind as the cause—not to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; and vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech.
Regarding the teaching: external visible forms known by eye-consciousness; external sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles known by body-consciousness;

the outflow-tainted non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of bodily and vocal discipline; the outflow-tainted bodily exertion and the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility; right speech, right action, and right livelihood;

and right bodily exertion and right bodily tranquility—these are called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that is neither abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) nor abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Regarding the cause that is abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu*): what is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) that has as its cause that which is abandoned by insight?

If the aggregate of feeling is abandoned by insight, or if it is the retribution (*vipāka*) of a phenomenon abandoned by insight—namely, feeling born of eye-contact, or feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact—this is called the aggregate of feeling that has as its cause that which is abandoned by insight.
What is the cause of the aggregate of feeling that is abandoned by cultivation?

The aggregate of feeling abandoned by cultivation, the retribution of the aggregate of feeling abandoned by cultivation, and the feelings born of eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—these are called the causes of the aggregate of feeling abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is neither caused by what is abandoned through vision nor by what is abandoned through cultivation?

It is the wholesome aggregate of feeling, the result of wholesome phenomena, and the aggregate of feeling that is neither a result nor a phenomenon destined to result—namely, feeling born of eye-contact, and feeling born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact. This is called the aggregate of feeling that is neither caused by what is abandoned through vision nor by what is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the aggregate of perception that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

The aggregate of perception that is unwholesome, not associated with what is to be abandoned by cultivation, and associated with defilements to be abandoned by insight—this is called the aggregate of perception whose cause is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the aggregate of perception whose cause is abandoned through cultivation?

It is the perception associated with unwholesome phenomena that are not abandoned through insight, but rather through cultivation; this is called the aggregate of perception whose cause is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) that is neither caused by abandonment through vision (darśana-heya) nor by abandonment through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?

It refers to the aggregate of perception that is wholesome, the aggregate of perception that is the result of wholesome dharmas, or the aggregate of perception that is neither a result nor a dharma leading to a result—namely, the perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. This is called the aggregate of perception that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation.
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) that has the cause of being abandoned by insight (darśana-heya-hetu)?

The aggregate of formations abandoned by insight consists of: volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), vitarka and vicāra, view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), regret (kaukṛtya), non-regret (akaukṛtya), contentment (saumanasya), joy (prīti), mental exertion (citta-vīrya), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), mindfulness (smṛti), doubt (vicikitsā), fear (bhaya), afflictions (kleśa), latent tendencies (anuśaya), birth, old age, death, life-force (jīvita), and the fetters (saṃyojana). These are called the aggregate of formations that have the cause of being abandoned by insight.
What is the cause for the cessation through contemplation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

If the aggregate of formations consists of the retribution of formations to be abandoned through contemplation, namely: volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), vitarka and vicāra, view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), absence of regret (*akaukṛtya*), contentment (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), fear (*bhaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth (*jāti*), vitality (*jīvita*), and fetters (*saṃyojana*); these are called the causes for the cessation through contemplation within the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of formations that has as its cause neither what is abandoned by vision nor what is abandoned by cultivation?

Regarding the aggregate of formations: if it is wholesome and is the result of wholesome dharmas; or if it is neither a result nor a dharma subject to ripening—excluding doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and fetters—the remaining aggregate of formations has as its cause neither what is abandoned by vision nor what is abandoned by cultivation. This is called the aggregate of formations that has as its cause neither what is abandoned by vision nor what is abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

If the aggregate of consciousness is a consciousness to be abandoned by insight, or is the retribution of a dharma to be abandoned by insight—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the aggregate of consciousness that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the aggregate of consciousness whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation?

The aggregate of consciousness that is itself to be abandoned by cultivation, and the retribution of the aggregate of consciousness to be abandoned by cultivation—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the aggregate of consciousness whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the aggregate of consciousness that is neither caused by abandonment through insight nor by abandonment through cultivation?

It refers to the wholesome aggregate of consciousness, the retribution of wholesome dharmas within the aggregate of consciousness, and the aggregate of consciousness that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness. This is called the aggregate of consciousness that is neither caused by abandonment through insight nor by abandonment through cultivation.

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
All four parts are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) bound to the desire realm?

It consists of the aggregate of form that is associated with the outflows of desire (kāma-āsrava) and is subject to outflows (sāsrava): the sense-base of the eye, the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body, and the sense-bases of odors and tastes;
as well as bodily forms that are beautiful or ugly, graceful or ungainly, lovely or unlovely, and pure or impure.
Purity; the body’s pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, various wonderful sounds and non-wonderful sounds, soft sounds and non-soft sounds;
the body’s coldness, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, fineness, roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness;

the bodily intimation arising from the mind’s desire to act—namely, going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning around—and the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech. Externally...

Visible forms known by eye-consciousness that are subject to the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*); external sounds and external tangibles known by ear- and body-consciousness that are subject to the outflows of desire and the outflows of existence;

the non-restraint of body and speech (*avijñapti*), the restrained discipline of body and speech (*vijñapti*) associated with the outflows, and the outflow-associated bodily effort—these are called the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).

What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu)? It consists of the aggregate of form that is subject to outflows (āsrava) pertaining to the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) and ear-base (śrotra-āyatana): bodily beauty, dignity, elegance, and pure clarity; bodily pleasant sounds, various wondrous sounds, and soft sounds; bodily qualities of coolness, lightness, subtlety, softness, and smoothness. It includes the bodily intimation (kāya-vijñapti) arising from the mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—and the vocal intimation (vāk-vijñapti)—the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech. It further includes external forms known by visual consciousness that are subject to outflows and have outflows, external sounds and external tangibles known by tactile consciousness that are subject to outflows and have outflows, as well as the unmanifest (avijñapti) discipline of body and speech that has outflows, and the impure bodily elements. This is called the aggregate of form bound to the realm of form.
What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) bound to the formless realm?

It consists of the outflows of form belonging to the formless realm, the informative and non-informative precepts of body and speech that are with outflows, the outflow-possessing bodily effort, and the outflow-possessing bodily tranquility; this is called the aggregate of form bound to the formless realm.
What is the aggregate of form that is unbound?
If the aggregate of form consists of the noble, untainted right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness, this is called the aggregate of form that is unbound.
What is the aggregate of feeling bound to the desire realm?

The feelings arising from eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact that are associated with the outflows of the desire realm and are tainted by the outflows—this is called the aggregate of feeling bound to the desire realm.
What is the aggregate of feeling bound to the realm of form?

The feelings arising from eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact that are associated with outflows and are subject to outflows within the realm of form—this is called the aggregate of feeling bound to the realm of form.
What is the aggregate of feeling bound to the formless realm?

The aggregate of feeling that is the feeling born of mental contact, which is associated with the outflows of the formless realm and is with-outflow—this is called the aggregate of feeling bound to the formless realm.
What is the aggregate of feeling that is unbound?
The noble, untainted feeling born of mental contact within the aggregate of feeling is called the aggregate of feeling that is unbound.
What is the aggregate of perception bound to the realm of desire?

The perception of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these perceptions belonging to the outflows of desire and the outflows of existence within the aggregate of perception—are called the aggregate of perception bound to the realm of desire.
What is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) bound to the realm of form (rūpa-dhātu)?

The perceptions of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena that are associated with the outflows of form and are subject to outflows—this is called the aggregate of perception bound to the realm of form.
What is the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) bound to the formless realm?
The perception of the outflows of the formless realm and of tainted phenomena within the formless realm—this is called the aggregate of perception bound to the formless realm.
What is the aggregate of perception that is unbound?
The noble, untainted perception within the aggregate of perception is called the aggregate of perception that is unbound.
What is the aggregate of formations bound to the desire realm?

If the aggregate of formations consists of volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, pliancy, remorse, lack of remorse, joy, rapture, mental energy, faith, desire-to-do, heedfulness, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, old age, death, life-force, and fetters—this is called the aggregate of formations bound to the desire realm.
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) associated with the realm of form (rūpa-dhātu)?

If the aggregate of formations consists of volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), vitarka, vicāra, view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), non-delusion (amoha), pliancy (prasrabdhi), joy (prīti), mental exertion (citta-vīrya), mental tranquility (citta-praśrabdhi), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), equanimity of mind (citta-upekṣā), doubt (vicikitsā), afflictions (kleśa), latent tendencies (anuśaya), birth, old age, death, life-force (jīvita), fetters (saṃyojana), and the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti)—this is called the aggregate of formations associated with the realm of form.
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) bound to the formless realm?

If the aggregate of formations consists of outflows pertaining to the formless realm, namely: volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), non-delusion (amoha), pliancy (prasrabdhi), mental exertion (citta-vīrya), mental serenity (citta-praśrabdhi), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), equanimity of mind (citta-upekṣā), doubt (vicikitsā), afflictions (kleśa), latent tendencies (anuśaya), birth, old age, death, life-force (jīvita), and fetters (saṃyojana)—this is called the aggregate of formations bound to the formless realm.
What is the aggregate of formations that is not bound?

The noble, untainted (anāsrava) formations—namely, volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), vitarka and vicāra, view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), non-delusion (amoha), serene faith (avetyaprasāda), gladness (saumanasya), joy (prīti), mental exertion (cittotsāha), mental tranquility (praśrabdhi), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), equanimity of mind (citta-upekṣā), the attainment of the fruits [of the path], and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti)—these are called the aggregate of formations that is not bound.
What is the aggregate of consciousness bound to the desire realm?

If the aggregate of consciousness consists of eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness that is associated with the outflows of desire and is subject to outflows, this is called the aggregate of consciousness bound to the desire realm.
What is the aggregate of consciousness bound to the realm of form?

The aggregate of consciousness that is associated with the outflows and is subject to outflows—namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—is called the aggregate of consciousness bound to the realm of form.
What is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) bound to the formless realm?

The aggregate of consciousness that consists of the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) associated with outflows (sāsrava) and belonging to the formless realm; this is called the aggregate of consciousness bound to the formless realm. What is the aggregate of consciousness not bound [to any realm]?

The noble, untainted mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) are called the aggregate of consciousness that is unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Of the five aggregates, how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
All three time periods—past, future, and present—are included.
What is the past aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
That which has arisen and ceased is called the past aggregate of form.
What is the future aggregate of form?
That which has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged is called the future aggregate of form.
What is the present aggregate of form?
The aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) that has arisen but not yet ceased is called the present aggregate of form.
The same applies to the aggregates of feeling (*vedanāskandha*), perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), and consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
*Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle Three.
The Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty,
together with Dharmagupta and others.
Chapter Four: The Four Noble Truths, Section on Questions. Question:
How many noble truths are there?
Answer: [Four.]
Four. What are the four?
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

What is the Noble Truth of Suffering? Birth is suffering; old age is suffering; illness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering; separation from the beloved is suffering; not obtaining what one seeks is suffering; and, in brief, the five aggregates of clinging, which are rooted in craving, are suffering. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.

This noble truth of suffering is real and such as it is, not otherwise, not different, and not a different thing; because it is the truth of the noble ones as correctly taught by the Tathāgata, it is called a "noble truth."
What is birth?

When sentient beings are born among the various classes of beings—being born, being born again, and growing through birth; when the aggregates arise, the sense bases are acquired, and the assembly of constituents comes together—this is called birth.
What is aging?

It refers to when sentient beings, among the various classes of beings, undergo decline and exhaustion, tremble, their faculties mature, and their life-span and activities diminish; this is called aging.
What is illness?

If sentient beings, among the various classes of beings, experience illness as a visitor, illness as suffering, illness caused by heat, illness caused by cold, illness caused by wind, illness due to changes in one's own stage of life, illness due to the unequal increase or decrease of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), or miscellaneous illnesses resulting from karmic retribution—this is called illness.
What is death?

When sentient beings, amidst their respective groups, reach the end of their time, pass away, perish, abandon the body, undergo transformation and cessation, and depart from the assembly—this is called death.
What is association with the unpleasant?

It refers to that which is unloved, undesirable, and disagreeable—such as fierce beasts, venomous insects, and the like; thorns, filth, foul pits, precipices, and mountain crags; or disagreeable forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects. When sentient beings dwell among these, associate with them, do not remain solitary, but instead mingle with them, never parting from them, never being separate from them, corresponding with them, and not being distinct from them—this is called association with the unpleasant.
What is separation from the beloved?

It refers to those who are dear, joyful, and pleasing—whether they be parents, brothers, sisters, wives, or children; or close ministers, retinues, and kinsmen; or pleasing forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—if sentient beings do not dwell with them, do not associate with them, but instead remain alone, unmixed, unjoined, and separated from them, this is called separation from the beloved.
What is the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks?

It refers to when one desires and hopes to certainly obtain something that has not yet been obtained—whether it be forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects—and yet sentient beings fail to obtain them, or having obtained them, lose them again; or they do not value them, lack mastery over them, lack autonomy, and their wishes are not fulfilled. This is called the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks.
How does one eliminate the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging through the removal of craving?
They are the aggregate of form-clinging and the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness-clinging.
What is the aggregate of form-clinging?
If all form (*rūpa*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and subject to grasping (*upādāna*), this is called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).
What are the aggregates of feeling, perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)?
If all consciousness is with outflows and subject to grasping, this is called the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
This is called the removal of craving, which is the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging in their entirety.
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
This craving, further accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
The two types of craving—craving for internal things and craving for external things—are called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
The three cravings—craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—are called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.
What is the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering?
The four attachments—attachment to sensual pleasure, attachment to form, attachment to the formless, and attachment to views—are called the Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering.
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?

It is the six cravings: craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena. This is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.
What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering?
The thirty-six modes of craving—eighteen modes of craving produced internally and eighteen modes of craving produced externally—are called the noble truth of the origin of suffering.

This noble truth of the origin of suffering is real and such as it is, not otherwise, not different, and not a different thing; because it is the truth of the noble ones as correctly taught by the Tathāgata, it is called a "noble truth."
What is internal craving?

Within internal phenomena, it is desire and intense passion, affection and non-aversion, delight and pleasure, that which is desirable, weighty, and consummate; lack of satiety and non-contentment; attachment, intense attachment, and the outflow [of defilements]; intimacy with the web of the branches of craving; that which can produce the root of suffering, generate hope and thirst, dwell upon and tolerate [sensual objects], and extensively incite craving—this is called internal craving.

What is external craving? It is the desire and intense passion for external phenomena; fondness, non-aversion, and delight; pleasure, longing, that which is weighty, that which is ultimate, that which is insatiable and incomplete; attachment, intense attachment, and the outflow of defilements; intimacy with the web of the branches of craving; that which can give rise to the root of suffering, hope, thirst, dwelling, indulgence, and endurance; and that which can extensively incite craving—this is called external craving.

What is sensual craving (*kāmarāga*)? It is the heavy defilement and intense defilement of desire toward phenomena of the desire realm; fondness, non-aversion, and delight; the state of being desirous, which is weighty and ultimate; lack of contentment and lack of fulfillment; attachment, intense attachment, and the outflow (*āsrava*); intimacy with the net of the branches of craving; that which can give rise to the faculty of suffering, hope, thirst, dwelling, indulgence, and endurance; and that which can extensively incite craving—this is called sensual craving.
What is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)?
The desire, defilement, and even extensive craving toward phenomena of the form realm and the formless realm is called craving for existence.
What is non-craving for existence?
If someone insists that there is a self, yet when confronted by threats such as punishment, fear, suffering, or illness, they then long for the self to be severed,
