destroyed, and non-existent— the craving, attachment, and even the extensive proliferation of affection toward those phenomena is called "craving for non-existence" (vibhava-tṛṣṇā).
What is sensual passion (*kāmarāga*)?

Whatever is desire, the grease of desire, delight in desire, craving for desire, attachment to desire, infatuation with desire, thirst for desire, feverish longing for desire, and the net of desire—this is called sensual passion.
What is attachment to form?

If there is desire for form, craving for form, delight in form, affection for form, dependence on form, indulgence in form, infatuation with form, thirst for form, feverish longing for form, or a web of entanglement regarding form—this is called attachment to form.
What is the defilement of the formless?

If there is desire for the formless, attachment to the formless, delight in the formless, craving for the formless, dependence on the formless, indulgence in the formless, infatuation with the formless, thirst for the formless, feverish longing for the formless, and the net of the formless—this is called the defilement of the formless.
What is defilement through views?

If one views with desire, views with attachment, views with delight, views with craving, views as a support, views with indulgence, views with affectation, views with thirst, views with feverish passion, or views as a net—this is called defilement through views.
What is craving for forms (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*)?
When the eye cognizes forms, whatever desire, passion, and so forth, up to extensive craving, arises within those phenomena—that is called craving for forms.
What are cravings for sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma-tṛṣṇā*)?

When the mind cognizes mental phenomena (*dharma*), if within those phenomena there is desire-taint (*rāga*) and so forth, up to extensive craving (*tṛṣṇā*), this is called craving for mental phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).
What are the eighteen modes of craving (*tṛṣṇācarita*) produced internally?

As the Blessed One has said: "Because this exists, that exists; because of that, this comes to be. Thus, there is a cause for difference, a cause for permanence, a cause for impermanence, and a cause for a self. There shall be that self, there shall be such a self, there shall be a different self; there shall be the attainment of that through a cause, the attainment of such an attainment, and the attainment of a different attainment; there shall be hope, and there shall be the hope for that. There shall be that hope.
Thus, there will be hope for future existence; this is called the eighteen modes of craving produced internally.
What are the eighteen modes of craving produced externally?
As the Blessed One has said: "Because this exists, that exists; because this arises, that arises. Thus, there is existence through a cause;

there is existence through a different cause, existence through a future cause, existence through a non-future cause, "I shall have this," and "this I shall have. Likewise, "I shall have this" is distinct from "this I shall have"; there is attainment of this, and there is attainment by that. Thus, there is a difference in attainment, attainment of hope, hope for what is to be, and hope for that which is to be.
In this way, there will be hope for future existence; this is called the eighteen modes of craving produced externally.
What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
When that craving is without remainder—detached, ceased, relinquished, emerged from, liberated, homeless, severed, and no longer arising—this is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.
What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering?
The exhaustion through wisdom (*prajñā-paryādāna*) is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering.

This noble truth of the cessation of suffering is real, such as it is, not otherwise, not different, and not a different thing; it is the noble truth as correctly taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of the noble ones—this is what is called a "noble truth."
What is the cessation through the object of knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
If a phenomenon ceases because its knowledge has ceased, this is called cessation through the object of knowledge.
What is the cessation through the object of knowledge?
If a phenomenon is extinguished by the attainment of the Noble Path, that extinction of the phenomenon is called "cessation through the condition of knowledge" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is meant by "cessation through the condition of knowledge"?
It refers to knowing that when such knowledge knows a phenomenon, those fetters are extinguished; this is called "cessation through the condition of knowledge."
What is the extinction through the condition of knowledge?

The four fruits of the śramaṇa—the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship—these are called the extinction through the condition of knowledge.
What is the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala)?

When the three afflictions to be abandoned through seeing—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa)—are abandoned, this is called the fruit of stream-entry.
What is the fruit of stream-entry?

It is the abandonment of the three afflictions to be eliminated through vision—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—if one attains the deathless, this is called the fruit of stream-entry.
What is the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala)?

When the three afflictions to be abandoned by seeing—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa)—are abandoned, and these afflictions are simultaneously severed by the Noble Path, this is called the fruit of stream-entry.
What is the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala)?

It is the simultaneous abandonment of the three afflictions to be eliminated through vision—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and adherence to rules and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa)—by means of the Noble Path. When one attains the deathless (amṛta), this is called the fruit of stream-entry.
What is the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala)?

If the three afflictions to be abandoned by vision—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—are abandoned; if the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation, namely sensual desire and ill will, are partially abandoned; this is called the fruit of the once-returner.
What is the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala)?

If one has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed by insight—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—and has partially severed sensual desire and ill-will through cultivation, and if one attains the deathless (amṛta), this is called the fruit of the once-returner.
What is the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala)?

If one simultaneously abandons through the Noble Path the three afflictions to be abandoned by vision—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), and attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa)—and abandons through the Noble Path the afflictions to be abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanāheya) such that desire-attachment and ill-will are partially severed, this is called the fruit of the once-returner.
What is the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmiphala)?

Having abandoned the three afflictions to be severed through vision—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—the noble path simultaneously severs these afflictions. Furthermore, having partially severed the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will which are to be severed through cultivation, the noble path simultaneously severs these afflictions. When one attains the deathless (amṛta), this is called the fruit of the once-returner.
What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala)?

If the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa), sensual desire (kāmacchanda), and ill-will (vyāpāda)—are abandoned, this is called the fruit of the non-returner.
What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala)?

It is the abandonment of the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will—and the attainment of the deathless (amṛta); this is called the fruit of the non-returner.
What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala)?

It is the abandonment of the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill-will—when these afflictions are simultaneously severed by the Noble Path; this is called the fruit of the non-returner.
What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala)?

It is the abandonment of the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will. When these afflictions are abandoned all at once by the Noble Path, as if one has attained the deathless nectar (amṛta), this is called the fruit of the non-returner.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
If the afflictions of the form realm and the formless realm, which are to be abandoned through cultivation, are abandoned without remainder, this is called the fruit of arhatship.
What is the fruit of arhatship?

When the afflictions of the form realm and the formless realm have been abandoned through contemplation without remainder, and one attains the nectar of immortality, this is called the fruit of arhatship.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
If all afflictions are exhausted, this is called the fruit of arhatship.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
If all afflictions are exhausted and one attains the nectar of immortality, this is called the fruit of arhatship.
What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering?

It is this eightfold noble path: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; this is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

This is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering; it is as it truly is, not otherwise, not different, and not a different thing. As the Tathāgata has correctly taught it as the truth of the noble ones, it is called a "noble truth."
What is right view?

It is when a trainee (śaikṣa) is free from fetters and proclivities, and with a noble mind enters the noble path; or when those of firm faith and firm Dharma, as well as others, perceive the faults of conditioned formations, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the afflictions.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—possesses the perfection of insight, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of insight, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, and is fully endowed with the wisdom of the contemplation of the path—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the mind liberated through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether regarding a person, a realm of existence, or phenomena, when one contemplates and awakens to their moisture, intense moisture, ultimate moisture, and the moisture of phenomena; when one thoroughly understands their specific characteristics, general characteristics, and common characteristics; and when one possesses the maintenance of thought, analytical observation, progress in discernment, wisdom, knowledge, vision, liberation, skillful means, the flame, the light, the illuminating torch, the eye of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the discernment of phenomena, right awakening, and non-delusion—this is called right view.
What is right awakening?
A practitioner who is free from the fetters and latent tendencies attains the fruit of arhatship immediately.
Whether it be a real person, a realm of existence, or the repeated awakening and correct mindfulness of the mind that takes objects as its focus—this is called right awakening.
What is right speech?
It is when a trainee, having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person, a destiny, or the four types of unwholesome and unpleasant verbal conduct, they are entirely abandoned; having seen their faults, they are restrained by the precepts, do not commit them, and do not tolerate them. Having severed the roots until nothing remains, they are capable of practicing what is wholesome within those unwholesome states. This is called right speech.
What is right action?
It is when a trainee (śaikṣa) is free from fetters and proclivities, even attaining the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person, a realm of existence, or the body, one abandons the three unwholesome [actions] that are not conducive to joy; seeing their faults, one is cautious and does not commit them, nor will one tolerate them. Having severed their roots so that they are exhausted without remainder, one is capable of practicing what is wholesome within those unwholesome states—this is called right action.
What is right livelihood?
It is when a trainee, having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether as a real person or as a realm of existence, one eliminates bodily and verbal unwholesomeness; regarding other forms of wrong livelihood, one does not delight in them but remains detached, seeing their faults, exercising restraint, refraining from them, and not tolerating them. Having severed the roots and exhausted them without remainder, one is capable of practicing what is wholesome amidst those unwholesome dharmas—this is called right livelihood.
What is right effort (*samyag-vīrya*)?
It is when a practitioner, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, the exertion of body and mind that issues forth, the endurance, the non-retrogression, the diligent power, the progress, the non-abandonment, the lack of indolence, the lack of slackness, the lack of laziness, and the faculty of effort, the power of effort, and the awakening factor of effort—this is called right effort.
What is right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*)?
It is when a trainee (*śaikṣa*), having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person, a destiny (*gati*), or the act of recollecting—whether it be subtle recollection, careful recollection, abiding in recollection without forgetfulness, or a continuity of recollection that is as described, which is not lost, not stolen, and not dull; whether it be the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, or the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)—this is called right mindfulness.
What is right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*)?
It is when a person in training (*śaikṣa*), having abandoned the fetters and proclivities, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person, a destiny, or the mind, it is the dwelling in rightness, exclusive dwelling, and one-pointed dwelling; a mind that is single-minded, unified, and undistracted; relying on the mental faculty, it is solitary concentration, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of concentration—this is called right concentration.
Among the Four Noble Truths, how many are material (*rūpa*) and how many are non-material (*arūpa*)?
Two are non-material; two are twofold, being either material or non-material.
Which two are non-material?
The noble truth of origination and the noble truth of cessation—these two are called non-form.
What are the two that are twofold, being either form or non-form?
The noble truth of suffering and the noble truth of the path—these two are called twofold, being either form or non-form.
What is the form (rūpa) of the noble truth of suffering?

It consists of the sense-base of the eye, the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, and body; the sense-bases of visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; the non-informative (avijñapti) matter of bodily and vocal non-restraint; the informative (vijñapti) and non-informative matter of bodily and vocal restraint associated with outflows (sāsrava); and the outflow-associated bodily effort and bodily pliancy. This is called the form of the noble truth of suffering.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is non-material (*arūpa*)?

Feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, confidence, regret, joy, gladness, mental energy, mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, aging, death, life-force, fetters, the attainment of non-perception, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—these are called the noble truth of suffering that is non-material.
What is the form aggregate of the noble truth of the path?
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort—these are called the form aggregate of the noble truth of the path.
What is the non-form [aggregate] of the noble truth of the path?
Right view, right resolve, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are called the Noble Truth of the Path, which is non-material (arūpa).
Of the four noble truths, how many are visible and how many are invisible?
Three are invisible; one and two parts are either visible or invisible.
What are the three that are invisible?
The noble truth of the origin, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path—these are called the three that are invisible.
What is that which is of two parts, being either visible or invisible?
The Noble Truth of Suffering is what is called that which is of two parts, being either visible or invisible.
How is the noble truth of suffering visible?
The sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) is called the noble truth of suffering that is visible.
How is the noble truth of suffering invisible?
Excluding the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), the remaining Noble Truth of Suffering is invisible; this is called the invisible Noble Truth of Suffering.
Among the Four Noble Truths, how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
Three are non-resistant (appaṭigha), and one is twofold, being either resistant (sappaṭigha) or non-resistant.
What are the three that are non-resistant?
The Noble Truth of Origination, the Noble Truth of Cessation, and the Noble Truth of the Path—these are called the three that are non-resistant.
What is the one category that is either with resistance (*sapratigha*) or without resistance (*apratigha*)?
The Noble Truth of Suffering is called the one category that is either with resistance or without resistance.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is with resistance?
The ten bases of form are called the noble truth of suffering with resistance (*sapratigha*).
What is the noble truth of suffering without resistance (*apratigha*)?

The first four [immaterial] aggregates—feeling, perception, and so forth up to the attainment of non-perception—as well as eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, are called the noble truth of suffering without resistance.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many are noble and how many are non-noble?
Two are noble and two are non-noble.
Which two are noble?
The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path—these are called the two that are noble.
What are the two that are not noble?
The noble truth of suffering and the noble truth of the origin—these are called the two that are not noble.

The same applies to: the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*); with craving (*sarāga*) and without craving (*vītarāga*); with seeking (*saiṣaṇa*) and without seeking (*naiṣaṇa*); to be grasped (*upādānīya*) and not to be grasped; with grasping (*sopādāna*) and without grasping; and the superior (*viśeṣa*) and the non-superior (*aviśeṣa*).
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated?
Three are non-appropriated; one is twofold, being either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What are the three that are non-appropriated?
The noble truth of origination, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path—these are called the three that are not felt (*anupāttaka*).
What is the one that is twofold, being either felt or not felt?
The noble truth of suffering (*duḥkha-āryasatya*)—this is called the one that is twofold, being either felt or not felt.
What is the feeling associated with the noble truth of suffering?
If the noble truth of suffering is internal, this is called the feeling associated with the noble truth of suffering.
What is the feeling associated with the noble truth of suffering?
The noble truth of suffering consists of the retribution produced by karma, dharmas, and afflictions, which is comprised within my own sphere:
the sense-base of the eye, the sense-base of the ear, the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of the tongue, and the sense-base of the body;

as well as the body’s beautiful or unbeautiful colors, graceful or ungainly forms, fair or foul skin, and pure or impure appearance; and the body’s pleasant or unpleasant sounds, and various exquisite or... [unpleasant] sounds.
Various wonderful sounds, soft sounds and non-soft sounds; pleasant body odors and non-pleasant body odors, soft odors and non-soft odors, agreeable odors and non-agreeable odors;
bodily sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, saltiness, and blandness; bodily phlegm and mucus;

bodily coldness, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, fineness, roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness; and the movements of coming and going, bending and stretching, as they arise from the mind and are experienced.
The bodily teaching of turning back and returning; the vocal teaching consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech;

and the contaminated body, which is the collection of feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, joy, gladness, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, and dread.
Birth, life, eye-consciousness, and so forth up to mind-consciousness—these are called the feeling aspect of the noble truth of suffering.
What is the non-feeling aspect of the noble truth of suffering?
That which is outside of the noble truth of suffering is called the non-feeling aspect of the noble truth of suffering.

What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not feeling (*vedanā*)? It refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering that is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, and is not included within one’s own sphere; or that which arises from a wholesome or unwholesome mind, being neither a result (*vipāka*) nor a state leading to result, such as bodily intimation consisting of approaching, departing, bending, stretching, or turning, and vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; or external forms known by eye-consciousness, sounds, odors, tastes, or external tangibles known by body-consciousness; or non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of body and speech that is not discipline (*śīla*), or the informative and non-informative matter of the body and speech that is discipline with outflows (*sāsrava*); or the outflowing bodily effort and bodily tranquility; or, excluding life-force, the remaining aggregates of feeling, perception, and so forth up to the attainment of non-perception; and the eye-consciousness up to the mental consciousness. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not feeling.
The internal and external are likewise.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many have retribution and how many are without retribution?
One has retribution, one is without retribution, and two are twofold—either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the one that has retribution?
The noble truth of the origin [of suffering]—this is called the one that has retribution.
What is the one that has no retribution?
The noble truth of cessation is called the one that is without retribution.
What are the two that are twofold, being either with retribution or without retribution?
The noble truth of suffering and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two that are twofold, being either with retribution or without retribution.
In what way does the noble truth of suffering have retribution?
That which is the nature of retribution for the noble truth of suffering is called the noble truth of suffering with retribution.
In what way does the noble truth of suffering have retribution?

Excluding the wholesome resultant [states] within the Noble Truth of Suffering, the remaining states within the Noble Truth of Suffering—whether wholesome or unwholesome—include: bodily intimation arising from an unwholesome or wholesome mind, consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; bodily and vocal non-informative action (avijñapti) that is not discipline; impure (sāsrava) bodily and vocal informative action (vijñapti) and non-informative action that is discipline; impure bodily effort and impure bodily tranquility; feeling and perception up to the afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters; the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñisamāpatti); and the mental element and the mental consciousness element. These are called the Noble Truth of Suffering with resultant.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is without retribution?
It refers to the noble truth of suffering that is either retribution, or neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution;
namely, the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-base; as well as bodily beauty or ugliness, and comeliness or lack thereof.
...beautiful skin is not beautiful skin; pure and clean is not pure and clean; the excellence of the body is not excellence of the body;
the manifold wondrous sounds are not manifold wondrous sounds; soft sounds are not soft sounds;

the bodily intimation arising from a neutral mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—and the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech, [are] external forms for the eye.
That which is known by consciousness: external sounds known by the ear-consciousness; the outflow-tainted non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of bodily and vocal precepts;

the outflow-tainted bodily exertion (*vīrya*) and the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility (*praśrabdhi*); with the exception of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, as well as the afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and fetters (*saṃyojana*);

and all remaining [mental factors] from feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*); and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
The noble truth of cessation is without retribution. What is the noble truth of the path that has retribution?
That which is the nature of retribution within the noble truth of the path is called the noble truth of the path with retribution.
What is the Noble Truth of the Path that has retribution?

It is when a learner (śaikṣa), free from fetters and underlying tendencies, enters the Noble Path with a noble mind; or when those of firm faith and firm Dharma, as well as others who have seen the faults of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; desiring to attain what has not been attained, desiring to master what has not been mastered, and desiring to realize what has not been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the afflictions.
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained,

practices the path— whether it be the person, the destiny, or right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration— this is called the Noble Truth of the Path with retribution.
What is the noble truth of the path that is without retribution?
That the noble truth of the path is without retribution is called the noble truth of the path that is without retribution.
What is the noble truth of the path that is without retribution?

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—possesses the perfection of contemplative wisdom, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by contemplation, they immediately attain the fruits of the ascetic life: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
The person beyond training, the Arhat, being endowed with the wisdom of contemplation—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the mind liberated through contemplation—attains the fruit of Arhatship.
Whether it be the real person or the path of right view up to right concentration, this is called the Noble Truth of the Path, which is without retribution.
Of the Four Noble Truths, how many are mind (*citta*) and how many are non-mind?
Three are non-mind; one is twofold, being either mind or non-mind.
What are the three that are non-mind?
The noble truth of origination, the noble truth of cessation, and the noble truth of the path—these are called the three that are not mind.
What is the one that is twofold, being either mind or not mind?
The noble truth of suffering—this is called the one that is twofold, being either mind or not mind.
What is the mind of the noble truth of suffering?
From eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the mind of the noble truth of suffering.
What is that which is not mind within the noble truth of suffering?

The first four of the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*), from feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), are called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not mental.
Among the Four Noble Truths, how many are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with the mind?

One is associated with the mind; one is not associated with the mind; one is twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind; and one is threefold, being either associated with the mind, or not associated with the mind, or neither described as associated with the mind nor not associated with the mind.
What is associated with the mind?
The noble truth of the origin [of suffering] is called associated with the mind.
What is not associated with the mind?
The noble truth of cessation is called the one that is not associated with the mind.
What is the one that is twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind?
The noble truth of the path is called the one that is twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What is the "one-third" category—whether associated with mind, not associated with mind, or neither stated as associated with mind nor not associated with mind?
The Noble Truth of Suffering is called the one-third category: whether associated with mind, not associated with mind, or neither stated as associated with mind nor not associated with mind.
What is the noble truth of the path associated with the mind?

If the noble truth of the path consists of mental factors—namely, right view, right resolve, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—this is called the noble truth of the path associated with the mind.
What is the noble truth of the path that is not associated with the mind?

The noble truth of the path that is not a mental factor consists of right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right bodily effort; this is called the noble truth of the path that is not associated with the mind.
What is the noble truth of suffering associated with the mind?

If the noble truth of suffering is a mental factor—such as feeling, perception, up to and including the afflictions and latent tendencies—it is called the noble truth of suffering associated with the mind.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is not associated with the mind?

If the noble truth of suffering is not a mental factor (*caitasika*), such as the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the first four types of derived matter, from birth up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), this is called the noble truth of suffering that is not associated with the mind.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is neither said to be associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind?
From eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is neither said to be associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind.
Among the Four Noble Truths, how many are mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*) and how many are not mental factors?
One is a mental factor, one is not a mental factor, and two are twofold, being either mental factors or not mental factors.
What is that which is associated with the mind?
The noble truth of the origin [of suffering] is called that which is associated with the mind.
What is that which is not associated with the mind?
The noble truth of cessation is called the one that is not a mental factor (*cittasamprayukta*).
What are the two that are twofold, being either mental factors or not mental factors?
The noble truth of suffering and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two that are twofold, being either mental factors or not mental factors.
What are the mental factors (caitasika) of the noble truth of suffering?

Excluding the mind itself, the remaining factors associated with the noble truth of suffering—namely, feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), up to afflictions (kleśa) and latent tendencies (anuśaya)—are called the mental factors of the noble truth of suffering.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is not a mental factor (*cittasamprayukta*)?

The noble truth of suffering that is non-objective (*anālambana*), as well as the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*) and the first four [elements] among the material factors, from birth up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the noble truth of suffering that is not a mental factor.
What are the mental factors of the noble truth of the path?

If the noble truth of the path consists of right view, right resolve, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration based on [the noble truth], these are called the mental factors of the noble truth of the path.
What is the noble truth of the path that is not a mental factor?
If the noble truth of the path does not take right speech, right action, right livelihood, or right effort as its object, it is called the noble truth of the path that is not a mental factor.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many have objects and how many are without objects?
One has an object, one is without an object, and two are twofold—either with or without an object.
What is the one that has an object?
The noble truth of origination is called the one with an object.
What is the one without an object?
The noble truth of cessation is called the one without an object.
What are the two pairs that are either with an object or without an object?
The Noble Truth of Suffering and the Noble Truth of the Path—these are called the two pairs that are either with an object or without an object.
What is the noble truth of suffering that has an object?

The noble truth of suffering that consists of mental factors and mind—namely, feeling, perception, and so forth up to the afflictions and latent tendencies; from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the noble truth of suffering with an object.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not an object-condition (*anālambana*)?

Excluding the mind, the remaining factors of the Noble Truth of Suffering that are not mental concomitants (*citta-saṃprayukta*), the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), the first four elements of form, and [the states] from birth up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*): these are called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not an object-condition.
What is the condition for the Noble Truth of the Path?
The mental factors of the Noble Truth of the Path—right view, right resolve, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—are called the conditions for the Noble Truth of the Path.
What is the noble truth of the path that is not an object-condition?

If the noble truth of the path is not a mental factor (*caitasika*), namely right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right bodily effort—this is called the noble truth of the path that is not an object-condition.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many are associated with the mind (*cittasamprayukta*) and how many are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*)?
One is associated with the mind, one is dissociated from the mind, and two are twofold, being either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind.
What is the one shared mental state?
The noble truth of the origin [of suffering] is called the one shared mental state.
What is the one unshared mental state?
The noble truth of cessation is called the one that is not shared with the mind.
What are the two that are twofold—either shared with the mind or not shared with the mind?
The noble truth of suffering and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two that are twofold, being either shared with the mind or not shared with the mind.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is associated with the mind?

If the Noble Truth of Suffering arises in accordance with the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind—namely, the unmanifested discipline of tainted body and speech, tainted bodily exertion, tainted bodily tranquility, feeling, perception, and so forth, up to the afflictions and latent tendencies—this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering associated with the mind.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is not associated with the mind?

The noble truth of suffering does not follow the mind, is not born together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind; namely, the ten bases of form and the first four types of derived matter, from birth up to the attainment of non-perception, and from eye-consciousness up to mental-consciousness—this is called the noble truth of suffering that is not associated with the mind.
What is the noble truth of the path that is associated with the mind?

The noble truth of the path that arises following the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind—from right view up to right concentration—is called the noble truth of the path that is associated with the mind.
What is the noble truth of the path that is not associated with the mind?

The noble truth of the path does not follow the mind, is not born together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind; namely, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort—this is called the noble truth of the path that is not associated with the mind.
The same applies to those that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and those that do not follow the mind (*na cittānuvartin*).
Regarding the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*), how many are karma and how many are non-karma?
Two are non-karma; two are twofold, being either karma or non-karma.
What are the two that are not karma?
The noble truth of the origin and the noble truth of cessation; these are called the two that are not karma.
What are the two that are twofold, being either karma or not karma?
The Noble Truth of Suffering and the Noble Truth of the Path—these are called the two pairs that are either karma or non-karma.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is karma?

It refers to bodily intimation arising from wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral minds—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the non-informative (avijñapti) bodily and vocal non-restraint; and the contaminated (sāsrava) informative and non-informative bodily and vocal restraint, as well as volition (cetanā). This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is karma.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not karma? It consists of the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-base;

bodily forms that are beautiful or ugly, graceful or ungainly, fair-skinned or unattractive, pure or impure; bodily sounds that are pleasant or unpleasant, melodious or unmelodious, soft or harsh; external forms known by eye-consciousness, external sounds known by ear-consciousness, the taintful bodily exertion (*kāyapragraha*) and taintful bodily tranquility (*kāyaprasrabdhi*), with the exception of volition (*cetanā*); all remaining feeling and perception up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*); and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not karma.
What is the action constituent of the noble truth of the path?
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these are called the action constituent of the noble truth of the path.
What is the non-action constituent of the noble truth of the path?
Right view, right resolve, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are called the Noble Truth of the Path and are not karma.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many are associated with karma, and how many are not associated with karma?

One is associated with karma; one is not associated with karma; one is twofold, being either associated with karma or not associated with karma; one is threefold, being either associated with karma, or not associated with karma, or neither said to be associated with nor not associated with karma.
What is that which is associated with a single karma?
The Noble Truth of Origination is called that which is associated with a single karma.
What is that which is not associated with karma?
The noble truth of cessation is called the one that is not associated with karma.
What is the one that is twofold, being either associated with karma or not associated with karma?
The noble truth of the path is called the one that is twofold, being either associated with karma or not associated with karma.
What is the one threefold category that is either associated with action (*karmayoga*), or not associated with action, or is said to be neither associated with action nor not associated with action?

The Noble Truth of Suffering is called the one threefold category that is either associated with action, or not associated with action, or is said to be neither associated with action nor not associated with action.
What is the noble truth of the path associated with action?

If the noble truth of the path consists of right view, right resolve, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration associated with volition (*cetanā*), this is called the noble truth of the path associated with action.
What is the noble truth of the path that is not associated with karma?

If the noble truth of the path consists of right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right bodily effort that are not associated with volition (*cetanā*), this is called the noble truth of the path that is not associated with karma.
What is the noble truth of suffering associated with karma?

If the noble truth of suffering is associated with volition (*cetanā*), then—excluding volition itself—it consists of feeling, perception, and so forth up to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness. This is called the noble truth of suffering associated with karma.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is not associated with karma?

If the noble truth of suffering is not associated with volition (*cetanā*), and consists of the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*), the first four material elements (*rūpadhātu*), and [the states] from birth up to the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), this is called the noble truth of suffering that is not associated with karma.
Why is it that among the Noble Truth of Suffering, karma-associated and non-karma-associated [factors] are not mentioned?
Volition (cetanā) is what is called the Noble Truth of Suffering in which karma-associated and non-karma-associated [factors] are not mentioned.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many are common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*) and how many are uncommon karma (*asādhāraṇa-karma*)?
Two are common karma, one is uncommon karma, and one is twofold—either common karma or uncommon karma.
What are the two common karmas?
The noble truth of the origin and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two common karmas.
What is the one uncommon karma?
The Noble Truth of Cessation is called the first unique karma.
What is the second category, which is either shared karma or unique karma?
The Noble Truth of Suffering is called the second category, which is either shared karma or unique karma.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is common karma?

If the noble truth of suffering evolves in accordance with karma, arising, abiding, and ceasing together with that karma—namely, the outflow-tainted non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of bodily and vocal discipline, the outflow-tainted bodily exertion, the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility, feeling, perception, concentration, mental attention, contact, and so forth, up to the afflictions and latent tendencies, the attainment of non-perception, and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—this is called the noble truth of suffering that is common karma.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is not shared karma?

That which does not follow from karma, nor arises together with it, nor abides together with it, nor ceases together with it—namely, the ten bases of form (*daśa rūpāyatanāni*), the non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal non-restraint, the impure informative and non-informative [matter] of bodily and vocal restraint, the impure bodily effort, the indeterminate mental consciousness, birth, aging, death, life-force, and the fetters (*saṃyojanāni*)—this is called the noble truth of suffering that is not shared karma.
The same applies to those that follow karma and those that do not follow karma.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many are causes and how many are not causes?
Two are causes, one is not a cause, and one is either a cause or not a cause depending on its division.
What are the two causes?
The noble truth of the origin and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two causes.
What is the one that is not a cause?
The noble truth of cessation is called "one that is not a cause.
What is the "one that is twofold, being either a cause or not a cause"?
The noble truth of suffering is called "the one that is twofold, being either a cause or not a cause."

What is the cause of the noble truth of suffering? It is the condition for the noble truth of suffering; the non-conditioned retribution of the noble truth of suffering; the conditioned wholesome retribution of the noble truth of suffering; bodily intimation arising from the four great elements through wholesome or unwholesome minds—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element; the non-informative [karma] of body and speech that is neither moral nor immoral; the contaminated informative and non-informative [karma] of body and speech; contaminated bodily effort and contaminated bodily tranquility; feeling and perception up to the afflictions and latent tendencies; the attainment of non-perception; and visual consciousness up to mental consciousness. These are called the cause of the noble truth of suffering.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not a cause? It refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not a condition, is without retribution, and is non-common karma:

the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base; the odor-base, flavor-base; the body’s beautiful color and non-beautiful color, the dignified and non-dignified, the fair skin and non-fair skin, the pure and non-pure; the body’s beautiful sound and non-beautiful sound, the various wondrous sounds and non-wondrous sounds, the soft sounds and non-soft sounds; the bodily intimation arising from an indeterminate mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; and the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phrases, and speech; external forms known by eye-consciousness, external sounds known by ear-consciousness; excluding the four great elements, the remaining factors included in the touch-base; and the impure bodily effort, birth, aging, death, and vitality. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not a cause.
Of the four noble truths, how many have causes and how many are causeless?
Three have causes; one is causeless.
What are the three that have causes?
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], and the noble truth of the path—these are called the three causes of existence.
What is the one that is without cause?
The noble truth of cessation—this is called the one without cause.

The same applies to that which has a causal sequence and that which lacks a causal sequence, that which has conditions and that which lacks conditions, and that which is conditioned and that which is unconditioned.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many are to be known and how many are not to be known?
All-knowingness knows and sees the four noble truths as they truly are.
How many are consciousness and how many are not consciousness? All are consciousness;
consciousness-consciousness knows them as they truly are.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many are understood (*parijñāta*) and how many are not understood?
All are understood; they are understood as they are.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many are fully realized (*parijñāta*) and how many are not fully realized?
All four noble truths are understood as they are.
Of these, how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

One is known through the knowledge of abandonment; two are not known through the knowledge of abandonment; and one is twofold, being either known through the knowledge of abandonment or not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is known by one type of knowledge of abandonment?
The noble truth of the origin [of suffering] is called that which is known by one type of knowledge of abandonment.
What are the two types not known by knowledge of abandonment?
The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path—these are called the two that are known by knowledge that does not involve abandoning.
What is the one that is twofold, being either known by knowledge that involves abandoning or known by knowledge that does not involve abandoning?
The Noble Truth of Suffering is called "one part" which is either to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) or not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is to be known through the knowledge of abandonment? It refers to the Noble Truth of Suffering consisting of:

unwholesome bodily intimation arising from an unwholesome mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of body and speech that is non-restraint; tainted bodily effort (*vīrya*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), absence of regret, satisfaction (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), mental effort (*citta-vīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), fear (*bhaya*), afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), the mind-element (*manodhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*). This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The Noble Truth of Suffering consists of the wholesome and indeterminate eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-base; bodily beautiful and non-beautiful colors, graceful and non-graceful forms, fair and non-fair complexions, pure and non-pure appearances; bodily pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, soft sounds and harsh sounds; bodily intimation arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind—namely, going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; external visible form known by eye-consciousness, external sound known by ear-consciousness; the outflow-tainted non-intimations of bodily and verbal precepts; the outflow-tainted bodily effort and bodily tranquility; the latent tendencies, fetters, and bonds of doubt and affliction; all remaining feeling and perception up to the attainment of non-perception; and eye-consciousness up to mental consciousness. These are called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
The same applies to what is abandoned and what is not abandoned.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and how many are not to be cultivated?
Two are to be cultivated, one is not to be cultivated, and one is partially to be cultivated and partially not to be cultivated.
What are the two cultivations?
The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path—these are called the two cultivations.
What is the one that is not cultivation?
The noble truth of origination is called "one that is not to be cultivated.
What is the one that is twofold—either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated?
The noble truth of suffering is called "the one that is twofold—either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated."
What is the cultivation of the noble truth of suffering?

It consists of wholesome bodily intimation arising from wholesome states of mind—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the contaminated unmanifested discipline of body and speech; contaminated bodily exertion and contaminated bodily pliancy; feeling and perception, up to doubt; and, excluding the attainment of non-perception, the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element. This is called the cultivation of the noble truth of suffering.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is not to be cultivated?

It is the noble truth of suffering that is unwholesome or indeterminate: the sense-base of the eye, the sense-base of the ear, the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of the tongue, the sense-base of the body;
and the sense-base of odors, the sense-base of tastes, and the sense-base of tangibles; as well as bodily forms that are beautiful or ugly, graceful or ungainly, and fair-skinned or otherwise.
Beautiful skin and non-beautiful skin; pure and non-pure bodies; pleasant voices and non-pleasant voices;

various wondrous sounds and non-wondrous sounds; soft voices and non-soft voices; bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, arising from an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind;
vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; and external forms cognizable by the eye-consciousness.
The knowable; external sounds known by the ear-consciousness; non-informative matter (avijñapti) that is neither bodily nor vocal discipline;

tainted bodily effort; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial mental application, sustained mental application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, absence of regret, contentment, joy, mental effort, faith, desire-to-act, and mindfulness.
Doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters (*saṃyojana*),
and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness— these are called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is not to be cultivated.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many are realized and how many are not realized?
All are realized and known as they are seen in reality.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
Two are wholesome, one is unwholesome, and one is threefold—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What are the two that are wholesome?
The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two that are wholesome.
What is the one that is unwholesome?
The noble truth of the origin [of suffering] is called the one that is unwholesome.
What is the one that is threefold—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
The Noble Truth of Suffering is called "one part threefold," meaning it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate. What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is wholesome?

It refers to the bodily intimation arising from a wholesome mind cultivated through the Noble Truth of Suffering—namely, going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the contaminated (sāsrava) bodily and vocal non-intimations (avijñapti); contaminated bodily effort and contaminated bodily pliancy; up to mental equanimity, the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), the mind-element (manodhātu), and the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu). This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering that is wholesome.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is unwholesome?

It refers to the feelings, perceptions, volitions, contacts, thoughts, initial and sustained mental applications, views, wisdom, liberations, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, and mental exertion that arise from an unwholesome mind; as well as the bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the non-informative matter of bodily and vocal non-restraint; tainted bodily exertion; faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, fetters, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element. This is called the noble truth of suffering that is unwholesome.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is indeterminate?
It is the noble truth of suffering that is neither a result nor subject to becoming a result: the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base;
the odor-base, taste-base, and tangible-base; and bodily forms that are beautiful or ugly, and those that are graceful or ungraceful.
Magnificence is not magnificence; exquisite purity is not exquisite purity; the bodily excellence of beautiful voice is not beautiful voice;
the manifold wonderful sounds are not manifold wonderful sounds; the soft tones are not soft tones;

the bodily intimation arising from an indeterminate mind—consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about—and the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech, are external forms.
That which is known by eye-consciousness; external sound known by ear-consciousness;

and the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) bodily formations of effort, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, vitarka, vicāra, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, satisfaction, joy, mental effort, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, birth, and aging.
Death, life, eye-consciousness, and so forth up to mind-consciousness—these are called the indeterminate Noble Truth of Suffering.
Regarding the Four Noble Truths, how many are trainee (śaikṣa), how many are beyond training (aśaikṣa), and how many are neither-trainee-nor-beyond-training?
Two are neither-learner-nor-non-learner; two are twofold, being either learner or non-learner.
What are the two that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
The noble truth of suffering and the noble truth of the origin—these are called the two that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What are the two that are twofold, being either trainee (*śaikṣa*) or beyond-training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path—these are called the two that are twofold, being either trainee or beyond-training.
What is the training regarding the noble truth of cessation?
The fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning—these are called the training regarding the noble truth of cessation.
What is the state beyond training regarding the noble truth of cessation?
The fruit of arhatship is called the noble truth of cessation pertaining to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the noble truth of the path pertaining to those in training (*śaikṣa*)?

It is when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies, enters the noble path with a noble mind—whether through steadfast faith or steadfast Dharma—and likewise other persons who, seeing the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*, and correctly contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; they desire to attain what has not yet been attained, desire to understand what has not yet been understood, and desire to realize what has not yet been realized, practicing the path to abandon the afflictions.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with insight-knowledge, whether through the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of insight, they immediately attain the fruit of recluseship: either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
If a person in training possesses right view up to right concentration, this is called the noble truth of the path in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the noble truth of the path beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?

It is when a person beyond training, desiring to attain arhatship and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of the contemplation of the cultivation of the path; whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation, they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
Whether it be a real person or a realm, from right view up to right concentration—this is called the Noble Truth of the Path for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Among the Four Noble Truths, how many are results (*vipāka*), how many are things that produce results (*vipākadharmas*), and how many are neither results nor things that produce results?

One is a resultant dharma (*vipāka-dharma*); one is neither-resultant-nor-non-resultant dharma (*na-vipāka-na-avipāka-dharma*); one is twofold, being either resultant or non-resultant dharma; and one is threefold, being either resultant, non-resultant dharma, or neither-resultant-nor-non-resultant dharma.
What is the single dharma that is a result?
The noble truth of the origin [of suffering] is called the single dharma that is a result.
What is the single dharma that is neither a result nor a cause of a result?
The noble truth of cessation is called the one that is neither resultant nor a cause of result.
What is the one that is twofold, being either resultant or a cause of result?
The noble truth of the path is called the one that is twofold, being either resultant or a cause of result.
What is the single category that is threefold—namely, result (*vipāka*), the nature of being a result (*vipākadharma*), or neither result nor the nature of being a result?
The Noble Truth of Suffering is called this single category that is threefold: result, the nature of being a result, or neither result nor the nature of being a result.
What is the result of the noble truth of the path?
The noble truth of the path is itself without result; this is called the result of the noble truth of the path.
What is the result of the noble truth of the path?

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—possesses the perfection of insight-knowledge, whether through the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of insight, they immediately attain the fruit of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
Whether it be a real person or the path consisting of right view up to right concentration, this is called the fruition of the Noble Truth of the Path.
What is the noble truth of the path as a resultant phenomenon?
The noble truth of the path that is wholesome and a result—this is called the noble truth of the path as a resultant phenomenon.
What is the noble truth of the path as a resultant phenomenon?

The seeker is freed from the fetters and latent tendencies; with a noble mind, they enter the noble path. Whether it be those possessing firm faith and firm Dharma, or others who have seen the faults and perils of conditioned existence, who contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana, and who contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality—they desire what has not yet been attained, desire to understand what has not yet been understood, and desire to realize what has not yet been realized, practicing the path to abandon the afflictions.
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, or when one who has not yet attained the noble dharmas desires to attain them and cultivates the path—
whether it be the right view up to the right concentration of a real person or a destiny— this is called the fruition-dharma of the Noble Truth of the Path.
What is the result of the Noble Truth of Suffering?
The wholesome result of the Noble Truth of Suffering consists of the sense-bases of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
as well as bodily forms that are beautiful or ugly, graceful or ungainly, radiant or non-radiant, and pure or impure.
The body has pleasant sounds and unpleasant sounds, exquisite sounds and non-exquisite sounds, soft sounds and non-soft sounds;
the body has pleasant odors and unpleasant odors, mild odors and non-mild odors, agreeable odors and disagreeable odors;
the body has sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, saltiness, and blandness, as well as phlegm and mucus; the body has coldness, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, and fineness.
Roughness, smoothness, hardness, and softness; bodily intimation arising from feeling, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning;
vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the unmanifested discipline (*avijñapti*) of the outflow-tainted body and speech;

the outflow-tainted bodily effort and the outflow-tainted bodily pliancy—excluding non-greed and non-hatred; and all other [mental factors] from feeling and perception up to mental equanimity and fear.
Birth, life, the attainment of non-perception, and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness— these are called the fruition of the Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is the dharma that is the fruition of the Noble Truth of Suffering?
The noble truth of suffering has a result; this is called the noble truth of suffering as a dharma that has a result.
What is the noble truth of suffering as a dharma that has a result?
It consists of all other wholesome and unwholesome states within the noble truth of suffering, excluding the wholesome results of the noble truth of suffering itself.

Wholesome mental states, unwholesome mental states, the bodily intimation of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; the vocal intimation of collecting sounds, syllables, and speech; bodily and vocal non-restraint (avijñapti); impure bodily and vocal restraint (vijñapti); impure bodily effort and impure bodily tranquility; feeling, perception, and so forth, up to the afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters; the attainment of non-perception; the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element—these are called the dharma of retribution for the Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor of a nature to ripen as a result?

It is the neutral (*avyākṛta*) bodily intimation—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—which is not included within the sphere of the self and is produced by a mind that is neither a result nor of a nature to ripen as a result; it is also vocal intimation—the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech—and external forms known by visual consciousness, external sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles known by body-consciousness; furthermore, it includes the contaminated (*sāsrava*) bodily vigor, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained thought, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, non-regret, contentment, joy, mental vigor, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, birth, old age, death, and everything from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness. This is called the noble truth of suffering that is neither a result nor of a nature to ripen as a result.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

Two are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation; one is divided into two parts, being either abandoned by vision or abandoned by cultivation; and one is divided into three parts, being either abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the two that are neither abandoned through vision nor abandoned through cultivation?
The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two that are neither abandoned through vision nor abandoned through cultivation.
What is that which is twofold, being either abandoned by vision or abandoned by cultivation?
The Noble Truth of Origination is what is called that which is twofold, being either abandoned by vision or abandoned by cultivation.

What is the one tripartite category that is either abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

The Noble Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-āryasatya*) is called the one tripartite category that is either abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the noble truth of the origin that is abandoned by vision?
If the noble truth of the origin is abandoned by vision, it is called the noble truth of the origin abandoned by vision.
What is the noble truth of the origin that is abandoned by cultivation?

The Noble Truth of Origination that is abandoned through reflection is called the Noble Truth of Origination abandoned through reflection; this is what is meant by "the Noble Truth of Origination abandoned through reflection. What is the Noble Truth of Suffering abandoned through vision?

It refers to the bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which arises from the mind associated with unwholesome defilements abandoned through vision; the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the non-informative (avijñapti) bodily and vocal non-restraint; tainted bodily effort; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, lack of regret, mental ease, joy, mental effort, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters; as well as the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element. This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering abandoned through vision.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is abandoned through cultivation?

It consists of bodily intimation arising from the mind associated with unwholesome, non-view-abandoned defilements to go, come, bend, stretch, or turn; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; bodily and vocal non-restraint (avijñapti); tainted bodily effort; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, absence of regret, satisfaction, joy, mental effort, faith, desire, mindfulness, fear, defilement, latent tendencies, and fetters; as well as the mental faculty and the mental consciousness-faculty. This is called the noble truth of suffering that is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
It is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is wholesome or indeterminate: the sense-base of the eye, the sense-bases of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and the sense-bases of odors, tastes, and tangibles;
as well as bodily forms that are beautiful or ugly, graceful or ungraceful, and fair-skinned or not fair-skinned.
Whether pure or impure, beautiful or not beautiful, manifold or not manifold, soft or not soft;
whether arising from a wholesome mind or an indeterminate mind, the bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning,
as well as the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech— all these are external forms known by visual consciousness.
External sounds known by the ear-consciousness; the unmanifested discipline of the out-flowing body and speech; the out-flowing bodily exertion and the out-flowing bodily tranquility;
the removal of the latent tendencies, fetters, and bonds of doubt and affliction;

and all remaining [mental factors] from feeling and perception up to the attainment of non-perception, as well as the visual consciousness up to the mental consciousness—these are called the Noble Truth of Suffering, which is neither abandoned through vision nor abandoned through cultivation.

Regarding the Four Noble Truths: how many have causes that are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu*), how many have causes that are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-hetu*), and how many have causes that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

Two have causes that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation; one is of two parts, having either causes abandoned by vision or causes abandoned by cultivation; and one is of three parts, having either causes abandoned by vision, or causes abandoned by cultivation, or causes that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the two that are neither causes to be abandoned by vision nor causes to be abandoned by cultivation?
They are the noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two that are neither causes to be abandoned by vision nor causes to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is that which is twofold, being either a cause for abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) or a cause for abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
The Noble Truth of Origination (*samudaya-āryasatya*); this is called that which is twofold, being either a cause for abandonment through seeing or a cause for abandonment through cultivation.

What is that which is one part of three, being either a cause for abandonment by vision, a cause for abandonment by cultivation, or neither a cause for abandonment by vision nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation?

The noble truth of suffering is called that which is one part of three, being either a cause for abandonment by vision, a cause for abandonment by cultivation, or neither a cause for abandonment by vision nor a cause for abandonment by cultivation.
What is the cause for the noble truth of origination that is abandoned by vision?
The noble truth of origination that is abandoned by vision regarding the noble truth of origination is called the cause for the noble truth of origination abandoned by vision.
What is the cause for the noble truth of origination that is abandoned by cultivation?
The noble truth of origination that is abandoned through reflection is called the cause abandoned through reflection regarding the noble truth of origination.
What is the cause abandoned through vision regarding the noble truth of suffering?

It is the noble truth of suffering abandoned through vision, and the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base which are the retribution of those factors abandoned through vision regarding the noble truth of suffering.
Upon entry, the body is neither of good color, nor handsome, nor beautiful, nor pure;
the body is neither of good sound, nor of various wondrous sounds, nor of soft sounds; the body is neither of good fragrance, nor of soft fragrance, nor of pleasing fragrance;
the body has sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, saltiness, blandness, phlegm, and mucus; the body has cold and heat.
Coarseness and rigidity; bodily intimation arising from the mind that is the cause of abandonment through insight, such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning;
vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; non-informative action (avijñapti) of body and speech that is not discipline;
