and the contaminated factors of bodily effort, feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, view, wisdom, and understanding.
Vitality, regret, non-regret, rapture, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, doubt, fear,
afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, life-force, fetters, and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—
these are called the causes for the abandonment through vision of the Noble Truth of Suffering.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that has its cause in abandonment through reflection?
It is the Noble Truth of Suffering abandoned through reflection, and the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base,

and body-base that are the retribution of dharmas abandoned through reflection regarding the Noble Truth of Suffering— namely, bodily forms that are not beautiful, not dignified, not lovely, and not...
It is purified and refined: the body is not of pleasant sound, nor of manifold wonderful sounds, nor of soft sounds;

the body is not of pleasant fragrance, nor of soft fragrances, nor of agreeable fragrances; the body possesses sweetness, sourness, saltiness, blandness, bitterness, and pungency, as well as saliva and phlegm, coldness, heat, coarseness, heaviness, hardness, and roughness;
it is that which arises from the mind through the causes of volitional abandonment, and which performs coming and going, bending and stretching, and turning about.
The teaching of bodily turning; the teaching of vocal sounds, syllables, and speech; non-informative action (avijñapti) of body and speech that is not discipline;

tainted bodily effort, sensation, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial mental application, sustained mental application, view, wisdom, liberation, regret, absence of regret, gladness, joy, mental effort, and faith.
Desire, mindfulness, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, life-force, fetters, and from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—
these are called the causes for the noble truth of suffering that are to be abandoned through reflection.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is neither a cause to be abandoned by vision nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation?

It is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is wholesome; the Noble Truth of Suffering that is the fruition of wholesome dharmas; and the Noble Truth of Suffering that is neither fruition nor subject to fruition, namely:
the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, and body-base; as well as bodily beauty, majesty, and fine complexion.
It is pure and adorned; it possesses a beautiful body-sound, a multitude of wondrous sounds, and gentle sounds; it possesses a beautiful body-fragrance, soft fragrances, and pleasing fragrances;
it possesses sweetness, sourness, bitterness, pungency, saltiness, and blandness, as well as phlegm and mucus; it possesses coldness, heat, lightness, subtlety, softness, and smoothness;
and its coming, going, bending, stretching, and turning arise from the mind, being neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.

Physical instruction, and vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phrases, and speech; external forms known by eye-consciousness, and external sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles known by body-consciousness;
the unmanifest (avijñapti) discipline of the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) body and speech; the outflow-tainted bodily exertion and the outflow-tainted bodily tranquility;
the removal of doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, and fetters; and all remaining [mental factors] from feeling and perception up to the absence of [discrimination].
If one conceives of eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering whose cause is neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.
Among the Four Noble Truths, how many are bound to the desire realm, how many are bound to the form realm, how many are bound to the formless realm, and how many are unbound?
Two are non-bound, and two are threefold—either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
What are the two that are non-bound?
The noble truth of cessation and the noble truth of the path; these are called the two that are non-bound.
What are the two or three parts that are either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
The Noble Truth of Suffering and the Noble Truth of the Origin [of Suffering] are called the two or three parts that are either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
What is the Noble Truth of Suffering associated with the desire realm?

It consists of the Noble Truth of Suffering that is subject to the outflows of desire and the outflows of existence: the sense-base of the eye, the sense-base of the ear, the sense-base of the nose, the sense-base of the tongue, the sense-base of the body, the sense-base of odors, and the sense-base of tastes;
as well as bodily forms that are beautiful or not beautiful, graceful or not graceful, and fair-skinned or not fair-skinned.
Pure and impure bodies; pleasant and unpleasant voices; manifold and non-manifold sounds;
soft and non-soft sounds; the body’s coldness, heat, lightness, heaviness, coarseness, fineness, hardness, softness, roughness, and smoothness;
the bodily intimation arising from the mind’s desire to act—namely, going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning around; and the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech.
Vocal intimation; external visible form known by eye-consciousness; the outflow of desire and the outflow of existence known by body-consciousness as external contact;

the non-restraint of body and speech consisting of the outflow of desire and the outflow of existence, the restraint of body and speech consisting of the outflow of existence, and the outflow of existence consisting of bodily vigor, feeling, perception, volition, contact, view, wisdom, and understanding.
Freedom from delusion, clear confidence, remorse, absence of remorse, gladness, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness,
doubt, fear, afflictions, latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, old age, death, life-force, fetters, and the three pairs of consciousnesses—
eye-consciousness with its corresponding forms— this is called the Noble Truth of Suffering.
Bound to the desire realm.
What is the noble truth of suffering bound to the form realm?

It consists of the noble truth of suffering that is a taint of form and a taint of outflows (*āsrava*), namely: the eye-base, the ear-base, and the body-base; as well as bodily beauty and physical majesty.
Beautiful skin, pure and clean; pleasant bodily sounds, various wondrous sounds, and soft sounds; a body that is cool, warm, light, subtle, soft, and smooth;
the bodily intimation arising from the mind through the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning;
the vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, phrases, and speech; and external forms known by the eye-consciousness—these are the outflows of form and the outflows of existence.
Whether it be sound or external tangibles known by body-consciousness, the non-informative (avijñapti) precepts of body and speech that are form-leakage (rūpāsrava) and outflowing (sāsrava),
the outflowing bodily exertion (vīrya) and outflowing bodily tranquility (praśrabdhi), feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa),

attention (manasikāra), initial inquiry (vitarka), sustained investigation (vicāra), view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), non-delusion (amoha), pliancy (prasrabdhi), joy (prīti), and so forth.
Joy, mental energy, mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, concentration, equanimity of mind,
doubt, afflictions, latent tendencies, birth, aging, death, life-force, fetters, the attainment of non-perception,
eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness— these are called the form-aspect of the Noble Truth of Suffering.

Regarding the realms of attachment (*dhātu-saṃyukta*): what is the Noble Truth of Suffering that is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu-saṃyukta*)? The Noble Truth of Suffering that is bound to the formless realm consists of: outflows pertaining to the formless realm (*ārūpyāsrava*);

tainted non-informative matter of body and speech (*sāsravā-vijñapti-kāya-vāk-śīla*); tainted bodily exertion (*sāsrava-kāya-pradāna*) and tainted bodily tranquility (*sāsrava-kāya-praśrabdhi*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), mental exertion (*citta-pradāna*), mental tranquility (*citta-praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā-citta*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), afflictions (*kleśa*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), birth, old age, death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*), life-force (*jīvita*), fetters (*saṃyojana*), the mind-element (*mano-dhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*). This is called the Noble Truth of Suffering bound to the formless realm.
What is the noble truth of the origin that is bound to the desire realm?

The craving for sensual pleasures (*kāma-cchanda*) that is an outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and an outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), this is called the noble truth of the origin bound to the desire realm.
What is the noble truth of the origin that is bound to the form realm?
The noble truth of origination consists of craving for form that is subject to outflows and subject to the taints; this is called the noble truth of origination bound to the realm of form.
What is the noble truth of origination bound to the formless realm?

The noble truth of origination consists of formless outflows (*anāsrava*), with outflows (*sāsrava*), and craving for formless formations; this is called the noble truth of origination bound to the formless realm.
Regarding the four noble truths, how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
One is neither past, nor future, nor present; three are each of three kinds—either past, or future, or present.
What is the one that is neither past, nor future, nor present?
The noble truth of cessation is called "one that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Why are the [remaining] three each divided into three—either past, future, or present?
The noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin [of suffering], and the noble truth of the path—these are called the three triads that are either past, future, or present.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is past?
The noble truth of suffering that has arisen and ceased is called the past noble truth of suffering.
What is the future noble truth of suffering?
The noble truth of suffering that has not yet arisen and has not yet appeared is called the future noble truth of suffering.
What is the noble truth of suffering that is present?
The noble truth of suffering that has arisen but not yet ceased is called the noble truth of suffering that is present.
The same applies to the noble truth of origination and the noble truth of the path.

Chapter Five: The Section on Inquiry, Chapter on the Faculties (Indriya-varga). Question:
How many faculties are there?
Answer: Twenty-two faculties.
What are these twenty-two faculties?

The eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty; the female faculty, male faculty, life faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, mind faculty, faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known."
What is the eye faculty?
The eye base is called the eye faculty.
What is the eye faculty?
The eye-element is called the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). What is the eye-faculty?
That which is the translucent matter (*rūpa-prasāda*) derived from the four great elements, belonging to the category of the self, is called the eye-faculty.
What is the eye faculty?
That which is the pure matter (rūpa-prasāda), derived from the four great elements, belonging to the category of the self, whether past, future, or present—this is called the eye faculty.
What is the eye faculty?

If the eye, being comprised within the sphere of the self, has seen, is seeing, or will see forms—though this is not fixed—and if the eye, being comprised within the sphere of the self, has received, is receiving, or will receive the light of forms—though this is not fixed—it is called the eye faculty (cakṣur-indriya).
What is the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?

It is that which, being comprised within the sphere of the self, has already confronted, is currently confronting, or will confront forms (*rūpa*), or is indeterminate; or that which, being comprised within the sphere of the self, has already confronted, is currently confronting, or will confront forms, or is indeterminate—this is called the eye-faculty.

If the eye is unobstructed, it is the eye, the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), and the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*); it is the field, the object, the gate, and the treasury; it is the world, the purification, the spring, and the ocean; it is the parched wasteland, the whirlpool, the ulcer, and the fetter; it is the eye, that which enters into my portion, this shore, and the internal base that sees forms—this is called the eye-faculty.
The ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, and the body faculty are also like this.
What is the female faculty?
That which is the female nature, the female form, and the female characteristic—this is called the female faculty.
What is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)?
That which is male nature, male form, and male characteristic—this is called the male faculty.
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
Longevity is called the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
What is the life-faculty?
If sentient beings abide, this is called the life-faculty.
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?

That which, among all sentient beings, does not end, does not regress, is not lost, and does not die; that which has not yet passed its time, remains active, and is sustained—this is called the life-faculty.
What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?

Any pleasant bodily sensation, pleasant sensation arising from eye-contact, or pleasant sensation arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, or body-contact—that is, the element of pleasure—is called the faculty of pleasure.
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?

If there is a painful bodily sensation, a painful sensation born of eye-contact, or a painful sensation born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, or body-contact—that is, the element of suffering—it is called the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
If there is a pleasant mental sensation, a pleasant sensation born of mind-contact, or the element of joy, it is called the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?
Any mental painful feeling, a painful feeling born of mental contact, or the element of grief—this is called the faculty of grief.
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

If there is a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling of body and mind, or a neither-painless-nor-pleasant feeling arising from eye-contact, or a neither-painless-nor-pleasant feeling arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, this equanimity-element is called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
What is the faculty of mind?
The sphere of mind is called the faculty of mind.
What is the faculty of mind?
The aggregate of consciousness is called the mind-faculty (*manendriya*).
What is the mind-faculty?
Whatever is mind, mentation, consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, or the seven elements of consciousness—this is called the mind-faculty.
What is the faculty of mind?
That which cognizes the past, future, and present; the internal and external; the coarse and subtle; the inferior and superior; the distant and near—this is called the faculty of mind.
What is the group of six consciousnesses?
The group of eye-consciousness, and the groups of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness.
What is the group of eye-consciousness?

Depending on the eye, depending on forms, depending on light, and depending on attention, consciousness arises—having arisen, arising now, to arise in the future, or being indeterminate. This is called the group of eye-consciousness.
What are the groups of consciousness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind?

Having the mind as their object, phenomena as their object, and attention as their object—when consciousness has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate through these three conditions, it is called the group of mental consciousness.
These are called the six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya).
What are the seven elements of consciousness (sapta-vijñāna-dhātu)?

They are the element of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, the mind-element (manas-dhātu), and the mind-consciousness-element (mano-vijñāna-dhātu).
What is the element of eye-consciousness?

If consciousness arises from the eye-faculty with respect to the objective field of visible forms—whether it has already arisen, is arising now, will arise in the future, or is indeterminate—it is called the element of eye-consciousness.
What are the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness?

If the body-sense faculty (*kāyendriya*) has arisen, and contact with its object has arisen, is arising, or will arise—whether determinate or indeterminate—this is called the body-consciousness element (*kāyavijñānadhātu*).
What is the mind element (*manodhātu*)?

It is the mind that knows phenomena (*dharma*) and attends to phenomena; if the initial moment of mind has arisen, is arising, or will arise—whether determinate or indeterminate—this is called the mind element.
What is the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)?

It refers to consciousness that resembles [its object] and does not depart from its respective sphere, as well as other similar mental consciousnesses—whether already arisen, currently arising, yet to arise, or indeterminate—which are termed the mental consciousness element.
These are called the seven consciousness elements.
What is past consciousness?
If a consciousness has arisen and ceased, it is called past consciousness.
What is future consciousness?
If consciousness has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, it is called future consciousness.
What is present consciousness?
If consciousness has arisen but not yet ceased, it is called present consciousness.
What is internal consciousness?
If consciousness is experienced, it is called internal consciousness.
What is external consciousness?
If consciousness is not associated with feeling, it is called external consciousness.
What is coarse consciousness?
If consciousness is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse consciousness.
What is subtle consciousness?
If consciousness is bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or is unbound, it is called subtle consciousness.
What is inferior consciousness?

If consciousness is unwholesome, or if consciousness is the retribution of unwholesome dharmas, or if consciousness is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution and is disagreeable, it is called inferior consciousness.
What is superior consciousness (*viśiṣṭa-vijñāna*)?

Consciousness that is wholesome, or consciousness that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas, or consciousness that is neither retribution nor a dharma leading to retribution and is agreeable—this is called superior consciousness.
What is distant consciousness (*dūra-vijñāna*)?
If consciousness is distant in its characteristics, extremely distant, not near, and not near the boundary, it is called "distant consciousness.
What is "near consciousness"?
If consciousness is near in its characteristics, extremely near, and near the boundary, it is called "near consciousness."
What is the faculty of faith?

It is when a trainee (śaikṣa) is free from fetters and proclivities, and with a noble mind enters the noble path; or when others—whether those of firm faith or firm dharma, or those of other dispositions—perceive the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of nirvāṇa, and contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; desiring to understand what is not yet understood, desiring to attain what is not yet attained, and desiring to realize what is not yet realized, they cultivate the path to become free from afflictions and views.

If a practitioner—whether a stream-enterer, once-returner, or non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, then whether on the stage of wisdom or through the liberation of the mind by means of contemplation, they immediately attain the fruit of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) seeks to attain the fruit of arhatship, desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, they cultivate the path to abandon the afflictions; when their wisdom of contemplation is perfected—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of mind through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If, regarding a real person or a realm of existence, there is faith in entry, faith in ultimate entry, faith in truth, and purity of mind—this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
What is the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*)?
When a practitioner is free from the fetters and latent tendencies, they may even immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, the exertion of body and mind that issues forth as endurance, non-retrogression, diligent application, non-abandonment, non-laxity, non-slackness, non-indolence, the power of exertion, the awakening of exertion, and right exertion—this is called the faculty of exertion (*vīryendriya*).
What is the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
It is when a practitioner, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), even attains the fruit of Arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a realm of existence, that which is mindfulness, recollection, subtle mindfulness, conformable mindfulness, abiding mindfulness, continuous mindfulness, non-forgetting, non-loss, non-seizure, non-dullness, non-dull faculties, the power of mindfulness at every thought-moment, the awakening factor of mindfulness, and right mindfulness—this is called the faculty of mindfulness.
What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?
It is when a person in training (*śaikṣa*), having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), even attains the fruit of Arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, when the mind abides, abides rightly, abides exclusively, with a one-pointed mind, a unified mind, and an undistracted mind, relying on mindfulness—this concentration of solitude, the power of concentration, the awakening-factor of concentration, and right concentration—is called the faculty of concentration.
What is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)? It is when a trainee (*śaikṣa*), having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a realm of existence, within phenomena (*dharma*), it is the thorough discernment, the repeated discernment, and the ultimate discernment; the discernment of phenomena through reflection, the awakening to and penetration of specific characteristics, general characteristics, and common characteristics; the retention of thought, the eloquence of speech, the progress of wisdom, knowledge, vision, and the skillful means of liberation; the torch, the flame, the light, and the illuminating lamp; the eye of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the non-neglect of the correct awakening that discerns phenomena—this is called the faculty of wisdom.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?

For one who possesses firm faith and the nature of a person of firm practice, any dharma that is noble, untainted, and not [previously] a faculty but is designated as a faculty—excluding, within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the factors of volition, perception, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, liberation, satisfaction, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, and right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right pliancy of body—this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*)?

It refers to those noble learners (*śaikṣa*) for whom certain dharmas—though they are noble, untainted, and not [originally] faculties—are designated as faculties. Excluding from within the faculty of knowing: perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, liberation, contentment, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruit, the cessation-attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right pliancy of body; these are called the faculty of knowing.
What is the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*)?

It refers to those dharmas that are noble, untainted (*anāsrava*), and not [previously] faculties, yet are designated as faculties for an Arhat who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). Excluding from within the faculty of one who has already known: perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, liberation, serenity, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of the cessation-concentration (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right pliancy of body—these are called the faculty of one who has already known.
Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are material (*rūpa*) and how many are non-material (*arūpa*)?
Seven are material; eleven are non-material; four are twofold, being either material or non-material.
What are the seven that are material?
The eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, female faculty, and male faculty are called the seven material [faculties].
What are the eleven that are non-material?

The life-faculty, the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity, the mental faculty, the faculty of faith, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—these eleven are called non-material.
What are the four that are twofold, being either material or non-material?

The faculty of exertion (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)—these are called the four that are twofold, being either material or non-material.
What is the form (rūpa) of the faculty of energy (vīryendriya)?
The bodily exertion that leads to transcendence is called the form of the faculty of energy.
What is the non-form of the faculty of energy?
The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) that is not form or mind, but is the exertion of transcending, is called the faculty of energy that is not form.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that is form?
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort (*samyak-prahāṇa*) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is form.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is non-material?

Perception, volition, contact, attention, initial mental application, sustained mental application, liberation, serenity, joy, tranquility of mind, desire, heedfulness, and equanimity of mind—these are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is non-material.
What is the form of the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*)?
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort are called the form of the faculty of knowledge.
What is the non-form of the faculty of knowledge?

Perception, volition, contact, attention, vitarka and vicāra, liberation, serenity, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, attainment of the fruit, and the meditative absorption of cessation—these are called the faculty of knowledge that is non-material.
What is the form (rūpa) of the faculty of one who has already known?
Right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort are called the form of the faculty of one who has already known.
What is the non-form (arūpa) of the faculty of one who has already known?

Perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of mind, liberation, serenity, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, attainment of the fruit, and the attainment of cessation—these are called the faculty of one who has already known, and they are non-material.
Of the twenty-two faculties, how many are visible and how many are invisible?
All are invisible.
Of the twenty-two faculties, how many are with resistance and how many are without resistance?
Seven are with resistance (*sapratigha*); fifteen are without resistance (*apratigha*).
What are the seven that are with resistance?
From the eye faculty up to the male faculty—these are called the seven that are with resistance.
What are the fifteen that are non-obstructive?
The life-faculty up to the faculty of "already known" are called the fifteen non-obstructive faculties.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are noble and how many are non-noble?
Eight are noble, eleven are non-noble, and three are twofold, being either noble or non-noble.
What are the eight that are noble?
The faculty of faith up to the faculty of one who has already known are called the eight noble faculties.
What are the eleven that are non-noble?
The eye faculty up to the suffering faculty, as well as the grief faculty—these are called the eleven that are non-noble.
What are the three that are twofold, being either noble or non-noble?

The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the mental faculty (*manendriya*) are called the three "two-part" faculties, being either noble (*ārya*) or non-noble (*anārya*).
What is the faculty of joy that is non-noble?
The faculty of joy that is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called the faculty of joy that is non-noble.
What is the faculty of joy that is non-noble?
The feeling of pleasure arising from mental contact that is neither in training nor beyond training is called the faculty of joy that is non-noble.
What is the faculty of joy that is noble?
The faculty of joy that is untainted is called the noble faculty of joy.
What is the noble faculty of joy?
The pleasant feeling arising from mental contact associated with the faculty of faith is called the noble faculty of joy.
What is the noble faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*)?

It is the faculty of joy belonging to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). When a person in training is free from fetters and proclivities, enters the noble mind and the noble path, or when one of firm faith and firm Dharma, as well as others who have seen the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; desiring to attain what has not been attained, to understand what has not been understood, and to realize what has not been realized, they cultivate the path to become free from fetters and proclivities. This is the noble faculty of joy.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of the mind through contemplation, they immediately attain the fruit of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, and is fully endowed with the wisdom of the contemplation of the path—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If it refers to a real person, a realm of existence, or the pleasant feeling resulting from mental contact, it is called the noble faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*).
What is the faculty of equanimity that is non-noble?
It is the faculty of equanimity that is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The faculty of equanimity is called non-noble (*anārya*).
What is the faculty of equanimity that is non-noble?

The faculty of equanimity that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), namely: the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of eye-contact, and the sensations of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-contact—this is called the faculty of equanimity that is non-noble.
What is the noble faculty of equanimity?
The faculty of equanimity that is untainted (anāsrava) is called the noble faculty of equanimity.
What is the noble faculty of equanimity?
The feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from mental contact associated with the faculty of equanimity and the faculty of faith is called the noble faculty of equanimity.
What is the noble faculty of equanimity?

It is the faculty of equanimity of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); it is that by which a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and proclivities, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a realm (*gati*), or the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), these are called the noble faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya-ārya*).
What is the non-noble faculty of mind?
The faculty of mind that is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called the non-noble faculty of mind.
What is the faculty of mind that is non-noble?
The aggregate of consciousness and feeling is called the faculty of mind that is non-noble.
What is the faculty of mind that is non-noble?
The mental faculty (*manendriya*) that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, is called the non-noble mental faculty.
What is the noble mental faculty?
The mental faculty that is outflow-free (*anāsrava*) is called the noble mental faculty.
What is the noble faculty of mind?
The mind-element and mind-consciousness-element associated with the faculty of faith are called the noble faculty of mind.
What is the noble faculty of mind?
The faculty of mind (*manendriya*) is either of the trainee (*śaikṣa*) or the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

When a person in training becomes free from the fetters and latent tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) and even attains the fruit of Arhatship—whether as a real person (*pudgala*) or a destiny (*gati*), or as the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*)—it is called the noble faculty of mind (*ārya-manendriya*).

The same applies to: the tainted and the untainted; that which is accompanied by craving and that which is not; that which involves seeking and that which does not; that which is subject to appropriation and that which is not; that which is grasped and that which is not; and that which is surpassable and that which is unsurpassable.
Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated?
Eight are appropriated, eight are non-appropriated, and six are twofold—either appropriated or non-appropriated.
Which eight are appropriated?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty are called the eight faculties that are feeling (vedanā).
What are the eight that are not feeling?
The faith faculty up to the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) are called the eight faculties that are not feeling.
What are the six that are twofold, being either experienced (*vedita*) or not experienced?

The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity, and the mental faculty—these are called the six that are twofold, being either experienced or not experienced.
What is the feeling of the faculty of pleasure?
That which is internal to the faculty of pleasure is called the feeling of the faculty of pleasure.
What is the feeling of the faculty of pleasure?

The sensation of pleasure born as retribution from the factors of karma and afflictions, which is included within my own sphere—namely, the pleasant sensation arising from eye-contact and the pleasant sensations arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact—is called the sensation of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) that is not feeling (*vedanā*)?

The pleasant feelings arising from eye-contact external to the faculty of pleasure, and the pleasant feelings arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact, are called the faculty of pleasure that is not feeling.
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) that is feeling?
The faculty of suffering within is called the feeling of the faculty of suffering.
What is the feeling of the faculty of suffering?

The retribution produced by the karma, dharmas, and afflictions of the faculty of suffering, which is comprised within my own portion—namely, the painful feeling born of eye-contact, and the painful feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact—is called the feeling of the faculty of suffering.
What is the faculty of suffering that is not feeling?

The painful feelings arising from eye-contact external to the faculty of suffering, and the painful feelings arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact, are called the faculty of suffering that is not feeling.
What is the faculty of joy that is feeling?
The faculty of joy that is internal is called the feeling of the faculty of joy.
What is the feeling of the faculty of joy?

The pleasant feeling born of mental contact, which is the maturation produced by karma, dharmas, and afflictions, and which is comprised within my own portion—this is called the feeling of the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of joy that is not feeling?
That which is external to the faculty of joy is called the faculty of joy that is not feeling.
What is the faculty of joy that is not feeling?

The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) that is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral, and which is not included within one’s own sphere (*asvaka*), namely the pleasant feeling born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja sukhavedanā*), is called the faculty of joy that is not feeling (*na-vedanā*).
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) as feeling?
The faculty of grief that is internal is called the faculty of grief as feeling.
What is the feeling of the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)?

The painful feeling born of mental contact, which is produced as a retribution by karma, dharmas, and afflictions, and is comprised within my own portion, is called the feeling of the faculty of grief.
What is the faculty of grief that is not feeling?
Excluding the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), what is called the faculty of grief that is not feeling (*vedanā*)?
What is the faculty of grief that is not feeling?

The faculty of grief—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—that is not included within my own domain (*asvīkṛta*) and is the painful feeling born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja duḥkhavedanā*), is called the faculty of grief that is not feeling.
What is the feeling of the equanimity faculty?
That which is internal to the equanimity faculty is called the feeling of the equanimity faculty.
What is the feeling of the equanimity faculty?

The feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from eye-contact that is produced by karma, phenomena, and afflictions, and which is included within one’s own continuum, as well as the feelings of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, are called the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
What is the faculty of equanimity that is not feeling?
That which is apart from the faculty of equanimity is called the faculty of equanimity that is not feeling.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is not feeling?

The faculty of equanimity that is indeterminate, wholesome, unwholesome, or not included within one’s own sphere—namely, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation born of eye-contact, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—is called the faculty of equanimity that is not feeling.
What is the feeling associated with the mind-faculty?
That which is internal to the mind-faculty is called the feeling associated with the mind-faculty.
What is the feeling associated with the mind-faculty?

The eye-consciousness up to the mind-consciousness that is produced as retribution from the karma and afflictions of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) and is comprised within my own portion is called "the feeling associated with the mind-faculty" (*manas-indriya-vedanā*).
What is the mind-faculty that is not feeling?
If the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) is external, it is called the mind-faculty that is not associated with feeling (*vedanā*).
What is the mind-faculty that is not associated with feeling?

The mind-faculty—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate—that is not comprised within my own sphere, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, is called the mind-faculty that is not associated with feeling.
The same applies to the internal and external [factors].
Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
One has retribution; ten are without retribution; eleven are of two kinds, being either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the one faculty that has retribution?
The faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" is called the one faculty that has retribution.
What are the ten faculties that have no retribution?
The eye faculty up to the pain faculty are called the ten that are without retribution.
What are the eleven that are twofold, being either with retribution or without retribution?

Excluding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the remaining faculties from the faculty of joy up to the faculty of "one who has already known" are called the eleven that are twofold, being either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the faculty of joy that has retribution?
The faculty of joy whose nature is to have retribution is called the faculty of joy with retribution.
What is the faculty of joy that has retribution?

The faculty of joy that is the result of the eradication of wholesome karma is without retribution; the remaining faculties of joy, which are pleasant feelings arising from mental contact and are either wholesome or unwholesome, are called the faculty of joy with retribution.
What is the faculty of joy without retribution?

If the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) is a result (*vipāka*), or if the faculty of joy is neither a result nor a dharma that will become a result (*na-vipāka-dhamma*)—namely, the pleasant feeling born of mental contact (*manosamphassa-ja-sukha-vedanā*)—this is called the faculty of joy that is without result (*avipāka*).
What is the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*) that has a result?
The faculty of grief that is of the nature of retribution is called the faculty of grief with retribution.
What is the faculty of grief with retribution?
The painful feeling resulting from mental contact that is wholesome or unwholesome is called the faculty of grief with retribution.
What is the faculty of grief that is without retribution?

If the faculty of grief is a retribution, or if it is a faculty of grief that is neither a retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution—namely, the painful feeling born of mental contact—it is called the faculty of grief that is without retribution.
What is the faculty of equanimity that has retribution?
That which is the faculty of equanimity as a dharma subject to retribution is called the faculty of equanimity with retribution.
What is the faculty of equanimity with retribution?

The faculty of equanimity that is eliminated through cultivation and is a result of wholesome karma; and the remaining faculty of equanimity, which is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mental contact and is either wholesome or unwholesome—these are called the faculty of equanimity with retribution (*savyābādha*).
What is the faculty of equanimity without retribution (*avyābādha*)?

The faculty of equanimity that is retribution, the faculty of equanimity that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations arising from eye-contact, as well as those arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—these are called the faculty of equanimity without retribution.
In what sense does the mind-faculty possess retribution?
That which is a mind-faculty of the nature of retribution is called the mind-faculty possessing retribution.
In what sense does the mind-faculty possess retribution?

Excluding the wholesome resultant mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*), the remaining wholesome and unwholesome mind-elements (*mano-dhātu*) and mind-consciousness-elements (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*) are called the mind-faculty with retribution (*sābhisamskāra*).
What is the mind-faculty without retribution (*anabhisamskāra*)?

The faculty of mind that is a result of maturation (*vipāka*), and the faculties of mind that are neither results of maturation nor subject to maturation (*na-vipāka-dharma*), from eye-consciousness up to mental-consciousness, are called the faculty of mind without retribution (*avipāka*).
What is the faculty of faith with retribution?
The faculty of faith that is a dharma with retribution is called the "faculty of faith with retribution.
What is the faculty of faith with retribution?

It is when a trainee (śaikṣa), having abandoned the fetters and proclivities, enters the noble path with a noble mind; or when one who possesses firm faith and firm Dharma, as well as other persons in the various realms of existence, perceive the faults and afflictions of conditioned formations, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; and, desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the afflictions. This is the faculty of faith with retribution.
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, practices the path of cultivation—

whether as a real person or as a destiny— if they enter with faith, enter with ultimate faith, have faith in the truth, and their mind is purified by faith, this is called the faculty of faith with retribution.
What is the faculty of faith that is without retribution?
That which is the retribution of the faculty of faith is called the faculty of faith without retribution.
What is the faculty of faith without retribution?

When one sees a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—who is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of mind gained through contemplation, they immediately attain the fruits of the ascetic life: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, if they possess the perfection of insight-knowledge—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of mind through insight—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

If, regarding a real person or a realm of rebirth, one has faith and enters therein, has faith and fully entered therein, has faith in the truth, and has a pure mind of faith, this is called the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) without retribution.
The same applies to the faculty of vigor (vīryendriya), the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya), the faculty of concentration (samādhīndriya), and the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya).
What is meant by "the faculty of knowing has retribution"?
The faculty of knowing that is of a nature to have retribution is called "the faculty of knowing has retribution.
What is meant by "the faculty of knowing has retribution"?

The learner (śaikṣa) perceives the faults and afflictions of conditioned activities, contemplates the tranquility of nirvāṇa, and contemplates suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path. Desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to become free from the afflictions.

Whether it be a real person or a realm, or [states such as] perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, liberation, satisfaction, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, the attainment of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right mental pliancy—these are called the faculty of knowledge with retribution.
What is the faculty of knowing that is without retribution?
The retribution of the faculty of knowing is called the faculty of knowing without retribution.
What is the faculty of knowing without retribution?

When one sees a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—who is fully endowed with the wisdom of insight, whether in the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of insight, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

Whether it be a real person or a destination, or [the mental factors of] perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, liberation, satisfaction, joy, tranquility of mind, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, attainment of the fruit, the meditative absorption of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right tranquility of body—these are called the faculty of knowledge without outflow (*anāsrava*).
In what sense does the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) possess retribution?
The state of the faculty of one who has already known being a phenomenon subject to retribution is called the faculty of one who has already known possessing retribution.
In what sense does the faculty of one who has already known possess retribution?
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, or when one who has not yet attained the noble dharmas desires to attain them, they cultivate the path.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, the factors consisting of perception, volition, contact, attention, vitarka and vicāra, liberation, serenity, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, the attainment of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right bodily pliancy—these are called the faculty of "I have known" (ājñātendriya) with retribution.
What is the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya) that is without retribution?
The retribution of the faculty of one who has already known is called the faculty of one who has already known that is without retribution.
What is the faculty of one who has already known that is without retribution?

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) seeks to attain the fruit of arhatship, through the perfection of insight-knowledge—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the mind liberated by insight—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a realm of existence (*gati*), or [the mental factors of] perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), vitarka and vicāra, liberation (*vimukti*), satisfaction (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), tranquility of mind (*praśrabdhi-citta*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā-citta*), attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), right speech (*samyag-vāk*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), and right tranquility of body (*kāya-praśrabdhi*): these are called the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) and are without retribution (*avipāka*).
Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are mind (*citta*) and how many are non-mind?
One is mind; twenty-one are non-mind. Which one is mind?
The mind-faculty (manas-indriya) is called "one mind.
What are the twenty-one that are not mind?
With the exception of the mind-faculty, all others are not mind.
Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with the mind?

Nine are associated with the mind; eight are not associated with the mind; one is not stated to be either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind; and four are of two parts, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the nine associated with mind?
Excluding the faculty of mind and the faculty of energy, the remaining faculties from the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of wisdom are called the nine associated with mind.
What are the eight not associated with mind?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty are called the eight that are not associated with the mind (*citta-viprayukta*).
Why is one [faculty] not described as either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind?
The mind faculty (*manas-indriya*) is what is called the one not described as either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the four that are twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind?

The faculty of exertion (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), and the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*)—these are called the four that are twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What is the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) associated with the mind?
The faculty of energy that is a mental factor (*caitasika*), which issues forth from the mind as exertion, is called the faculty of energy associated with the mind.
What is the faculty of energy not associated with the mind?
The faculty of exertion (*vīryendriya*) is not a mental factor; because it consists of bodily and vocal intimation, it is called the faculty of exertion that is not associated with the mind.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that is associated with the mind?

If the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) is a mental factor (caitasika), then its associated factors—namely, perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), vitarka and vicāra, liberation (vimukti), serenity (praśrabdhi), joy (prīti), mental pliancy (cittapraśrabdhi), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), and equanimity of mind (upekṣā)—are called the mental associations of the faculty of desiring to know the unknown.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that is not associated with the mind?

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is not a mental concomitant (caitta); right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort (samyak-prahāṇa) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not associated with the mind.
What is the faculty of knowledge associated with the mind?

If the faculty of knowledge is a mental factor—namely, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, liberation, satisfaction, joy, tranquility of mind, desire, heedfulness, and equanimity of mind—it is called the faculty of knowledge associated with the mind.
How is it that the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) is not associated with the mind?

The faculty of knowing is not a mental factor (*caitasika*). Its attainment, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right bodily exertion (*kāyapraśrabdhi*)—these are called the faculty of knowing that is not associated with the mind.
The faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya) is also like this.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are mental concomitants (citta-saṃprayukta) and how many are not mental concomitants?
Nine are mental concomitants; nine are not mental concomitants; four are of two kinds, being either mental concomitants or not mental concomitants.
What are the nine mental factors?
Excluding the faculty of mind and the faculty of energy, the remaining faculties from the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of wisdom are called the nine mental factors.
What are the nine non-mental factors?
The eye faculty through to the life faculty and the mind faculty are called the nine that are not mental concomitants (*citta-saṃprayukta*).
What are the four that are twofold, being either mental concomitants or not mental concomitants?

The faculty of vigor, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known—these are called the four that are twofold, being either mental concomitants or not mental concomitants.
What is the faculty of energy that is a mental factor?
If the faculty of energy takes the mind as its object and issues forth exertion, this is called the faculty of energy that is a mental factor.
What is the faculty of energy that is not a mental factor?
The faculty of vigor that does not have the body as its object, nor its arising or departure, is called the faculty of vigor that is not a mental factor (*citta-saṃskāra*).
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that is a mental factor?

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that has as its objects perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is a mental factor.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that is not a mental factor?

That which is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," excluding right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort, is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not a mental factor.
What are the mental factors associated with the faculty of knowing?

The mental factors associated with the faculty of knowing are: perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, liberation, satisfaction, joy, tranquility of mind, desire, heedfulness, and equanimity of mind; these are called the mental factors associated with the faculty of knowing.
How is it that the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*) is not a mental concomitant (*caitasika*)?

The faculty of knowledge is not a mental concomitant when it attains its fruit through non-conditioning, or when it constitutes the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, or right exertion of the body; this is called the faculty of knowledge being a non-mental-concomitant.
The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) is also like this.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are conditions (*pratyaya*) and how many are not conditions?
Ten are conditions; eight are not conditions; four are of two parts, being either conditions or not conditions.
What are the ten conditions?

Excluding the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*), the remaining faculties from the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), as well as the mental faculty (*manendriya*), are called the ten conditions.
What are the eight non-conditions?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty are called the eight non-objective (anālambana).
What are the four that are twofold—either objective or non-objective?

The faculty of exertion (vīryendriya), the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya), and the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya) are called the four that are twofold—either objective or non-objective.
What is the condition for the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*)?
The mental factor of energy that issues forth as exertion is called the condition for the faculty of energy.
What is not the condition for the faculty of energy?

The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) that is not a mental factor (*caitasika*) and consists of bodily or vocal manifestation (*kāyavāgvijñapti*) is called the faculty of energy that is non-objective (*anālambana*).
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*) as an object?

Those factors associated with the mind—namely, perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial and sustained application (*vitarkavicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental pliancy (*cittakarmaṇyatā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" as an object.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) that is not a condition?

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" is not a mental factor (caitasika); right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right effort (samyak-prahāṇa) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not a condition.
What is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of the faculty of knowing (ājñendriya)?

The mental factors associated with the faculty of knowing—namely, perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manasikāra), initial inquiry (vitarka), sustained investigation (vicāra), liberation (vimukti), serenity (praśrabdhi), joy (prīti), mental pliancy (citta-praśrabdhi), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), and equanimity of mind (upekṣā)—are called the object-conditions of the faculty of knowing.
What is the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya) that is not a condition?

The faculty of knowledge is not a mental concomitant (caitta); its attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right exertion of the body—these are called the faculty of knowledge that is not a condition.
The faculty of one who has already known is also like this.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are associated with the mind and how many are not associated with the mind?
Ten are associated with the mind; nine are not associated with the mind; three are of two kinds, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the ten faculties associated with the mind?

Excluding the faculty of mind and the faculty of vigor, the remaining faculties from the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" are called the ten faculties associated with the mind.
What are the nine faculties not associated with the mind?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty, together with the mind faculty, are called the nine non-common mental faculties.
What are the three that are twofold—either common to the mind or not common to the mind?
The faculty of vigor, the faculty of knowledge, and the faculty of one who has already known are called the three that are twofold, being either common to the mind or not common to the mind.
What is the faculty of energy associated with the mind?

If the faculty of energy evolves in accordance with the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind, such that the mind exerts itself toward transcendence, this is called the faculty of energy associated with the mind.
What is the faculty of energy that is not associated with the mind?

The faculty of energy does not follow the mind, is not born together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind; it is the exertion and transcendence of the body, which is called the faculty of energy that is not associated with the mind.
What is the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) that is concomitant with the mind?

The faculty of knowing turns in accordance with the mind; it arises together with the mind, abides together with the mind, and ceases together with the mind. These are: perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*), right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), and right physical pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*). This is called the faculty of knowing that is concomitant with the mind.
What is the faculty of knowing (ājñendriya) that is not associated with the mind?

If the faculty of knowing does not follow the mind, does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind—namely, the attainment of the fruit, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right exertion of the body—it is called the faculty of knowing that is not associated with the mind. The faculty of having already known (ājñātāvīndriya) is also like this.
The same applies to those that follow the mind (*cittānuvartin*) and those that do not follow the mind (*na cittānuvartin*).
Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are karma and how many are non-karma?
Nineteen are non-karma; three are of two parts, being either karma or non-karma.
What are the nineteen that are not karma?
The eye faculty up to the wisdom faculty are called the nineteen that are not karma.
What are the three that are of two parts, being either karma or not karma?
The faculty of "desiring to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "having known" are called the three twofold faculties, which may be either karma or non-karma.
What is the faculty of desiring to know the unknown that is karma?

Volition (*cetanā*), right speech (*samyag-vāk*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*) are called the activity (*karma*) of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not activity?

Perception (*saṃjñā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental pliancy (*citta-praśrabdhi*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity of mind (*citta-upekṣā*), and right bodily pliancy (*kāya-praśrabdhi*) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not activity.
What is the faculty of knowledge as action?
Volition, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are called the faculty of knowledge as action.
What is the faculty of knowledge that is not action?

Perception, contact, volition, applied thought, sustained thought, liberation, rapture, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, attainment of fruition, the attainment of cessation, and right bodily pliancy are called the faculty of knowledge that is not karma.
The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) is also like this.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are associated with karma (*karmasamprayukta*) and how many are not associated with karma?

Ten are associated with karma; eight are not associated with karma; one is of two parts, being either associated with karma or not associated with karma; and three are of three parts, being either associated with karma, not associated with karma, or not stated to be either associated with or not associated with karma.
What are the ten faculties associated with karma?
Excluding the faculty of vigor, the remaining faculties from the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of wisdom, as well as the mental faculty, are called the ten faculties associated with karma.
What are the eight not associated with karma?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty are called the eight that are not associated with karma.
What is the one that is twofold—either associated with karma or not associated with karma?
The vigor faculty is called the one that is twofold—either associated with karma or not associated with karma.
What are the three triads that are either associated with karma, dissociated from karma, or neither described as associated nor dissociated from karma?

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known" are called the three triads that are either associated with karma, dissociated from karma, or neither described as associated nor dissociated from karma.
What is the faculty of energy associated with action?
The exertion of the mind associated with volition through the faculty of energy is called the faculty of energy associated with action.
What is the faculty of energy not associated with action?
The faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*) that is not associated with volition (*cetanā*) and consists of bodily and vocal intimation is called the faculty of vigor not associated with karma.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) associated with karma?

The factors associated with the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown"—namely, volition, perception, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, liberation, serenity, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, and equanimity of mind—are termed the activity associated with the faculty of desiring to know the unknown.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that is not associated with karma?

The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not associated with volition (*cetanā*), namely right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right exertion of the body, is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" that is not associated with karma.
Why is the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) not described as either associated with karma or dissociated from karma?
Volition (cetanā) is what is called the faculty of desiring to know the unknown, and it is not described as either associated with karma or dissociated from karma.
What is the association of the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) with its activity?

The association of the faculty of knowing with volition (*cetanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained examination (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*), joy (*prīti*), rapture (*prāmodya*), mental pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*) is called the association of the faculty of knowing with its activity.
How is it that the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*) is not associated with action?

The faculty of knowledge is not associated with volition (*cetanā*) when it attains the fruit, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right exertion of the body; this is called the faculty of knowledge being non-associated with action.
How is it that the faculty of knowing (ājñendriya) is said to be neither associated with karma nor dissociated from karma?
Volition (cetanā) is what is called the faculty of knowing that is neither associated with karma nor dissociated from karma.
The faculty of one who has already known is also like this.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many share in common karma and how many do not share in common karma?
Twelve share in common karma; eight do not share in common karma; and two are of two kinds, being either shared in common karma or not shared in common karma.
What are the twelve common activities?
The faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" are called the twelve common activities.
What are the eight uncommon activities?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty are called the eight uncommon karmas.
What are the two that are twofold, being either common or uncommon karmas?
The faculty of knowing and the faculty of having known are called the two that are twofold, being either common or uncommon karmas.
What is the shared activity (*sahakārikarma*) of the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*)?

The faculty of knowing follows after activity; it arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with activity. These include: perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental pliancy (*cittapraśrabdhi*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), right speech (*samyagvāc*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), right livelihood (*samyagājīva*), and right bodily pliancy (*kāyapraśrabdhi*). These are called the shared activity of the faculty of knowing.
What is the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) as its non-common karma?

The faculty of knowing does not follow along with karma; it arises, abides, and ceases independently of common [karma], and attains its fruit independently. This is called the faculty of knowing as its non-common karma.
The faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*) is also like this.
Whether it follows the transformation of karma or does not follow the transformation of karma is also like this.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are causes and how many are not causes?
Twelve are causes, eight are not causes, and two are twofold, being either causes or not causes.
What are the twelve causes?
From the faculty of pleasure up to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," these are called the twelve causes.
What are the eight that are not causes?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty are called the eight that are not causes.
What are the two that are twofold, being either causes or not causes?
The faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) are called the two "two-part" faculties, being either causes or non-causes.
What is the cause of the faculty of knowing?

Regarding the faculty of knowing, that which is conditioned by the faculty of knowing and has retribution (*savipāka*), excluding the attainment of the fruit (*phala-prāpti*), as well as the remaining factors of the faculty of knowing—namely, perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*), joy (*prīti*), rapture (*prāmodya*), tranquility of mind (*praśrabdhi*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), right speech (*samyag-vāk*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), and right tranquility of body (*kāya-praśrabdhi*)—are called the cause of the faculty of knowing.
What is meant by the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) not being a cause?

When the faculty of knowing is neither a condition nor has a retribution, and one attains the fruit through non-common karma (*asādhāraṇa-karman*), this is called the faculty of knowing not being a cause.
The faculty of having already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is also like this.
Of the twenty-two faculties, how many have causes and how many are causeless?
All have causes; all have conditions; all have objects; all are conditioned.
Among the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are cognitions (*jñāna*) and how many are not cognitions?
All are cognitions; they know and see according to their respective objects.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and how many are not consciousnesses?
All consciousnesses are cognized by the mental consciousness according to their respective objects.
Regarding the twenty-two faculties, how many are resolved and how many are not resolved?
All are resolved, as they are known and seen according to their respective objects.
Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are fully understood (*parijñāta*) and how many are not fully understood?
All are fully understood, for they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Of the twenty-two faculties, how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

Eighteen [faculties] are not known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*); four are of two kinds, being either known through the knowledge of abandonment or not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What are the eighteen that are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

They are the faculty of the eye up to the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of faith up to the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*); these are called the eighteen that are not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What are the four that are twofold, being either known through the knowledge of abandonment or not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

They are the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity, and the faculty of mind; these are called the four that are twofold, being either known through the knowledge of abandonment or not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) known through the knowledge of abandonment?
