The faculty of joy that is an agreeable feeling born of mental contact and is unwholesome is called the faculty of joy known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the faculty of joy not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) that is wholesome or indeterminate, arising from mental contact and consisting of pleasant feeling, is called the faculty of joy not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
How is the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*) to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?
The faculty of grief that is unwholesome, arising from mental contact and consisting of painful feeling, is called the faculty of grief to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the faculty of grief that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The faculty of grief that is wholesome or indeterminate, arising from mental contact as a painful feeling—this is called the faculty of grief that is not to be known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is to be known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The faculty of equanimity that is unwholesome and consists of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mental contact is called the faculty of equanimity known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*).
What is the faculty of equanimity not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The faculty of equanimity that is wholesome or indeterminate and consists of the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, as well as the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact, is called the faculty of equanimity not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the faculty of mind known through the knowledge of abandonment?
The unwholesome mind-faculty, mind-element, and mind-consciousness-element are called the mind-faculty known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the mind-faculty not known through the knowledge of abandonment?

The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that is wholesome or indeterminate, as well as the visual consciousness up to the mental consciousness, is called the mental faculty known through the knowledge of the non-abandoned (*aprahīṇa-jñāna*).
The same applies to what is abandoned and what is not abandoned.
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are to be cultivated (*bhāvayitavya*) and how many are not to be cultivated?
Eight are to be cultivated; ten are not to be cultivated; four are twofold, being either to be cultivated or not to be cultivated.
What are the eight that are to be cultivated?
The faculty of faith up to the faculty of one who has already known—these are called the eight that are to be cultivated.
What are the ten that are not cultivated?
The eye faculty up to the pain faculty are called the ten that are not cultivated.
What are the four that are of two parts, being either cultivated or not cultivated?

The faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*), and the faculty of mind (*manindriya*) are called the four "twofold" faculties, meaning they are either cultivated (*bhāvita*) or not cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the faculty of joy?
If the faculty of joy is associated with wholesome mental contact and pleasant feeling, it is called the cultivation of the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of joy that is not cultivated?
The faculty of joy that is neither wholesome nor indeterminate, being the pleasant feeling born of mental contact, is called the faculty of joy that is not cultivated.
What is the faculty of grief that is cultivated?
The faculty of grief that is a painful feeling arising from contact with a wholesome mind is called the cultivated faculty of grief.
What is the faculty of grief that is not cultivated?
The faculty of grief that is a painful feeling arising from contact with an unwholesome or indeterminate mind is called the uncultivated faculty of grief.
What is the cultivation of the faculty of equanimity?
The pleasant mental contact and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling associated with the faculty of equanimity are called the cultivation of the faculty of equanimity.
What is the non-cultivation of the faculty of equanimity?

The faculty of equanimity that is unwholesome or indeterminate—the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation arising from eye-contact, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—is called the faculty of equanimity that is not to be cultivated.
What is the cultivation of the faculty of mind?
The wholesome mind-element and consciousness-element are called the cultivation of the faculty of mind.
What is the non-cultivation of the faculty of mind?

The mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) that is unwholesome or indeterminate, as well as the visual consciousness up to the mental consciousness, are called the mental faculty that is not cultivation (*abhāvanā*).
Among the twenty-two faculties, how many are realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) and how many are not realization?
All are realized, known, and seen as they truly are.
Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Eight are wholesome; ten are indeterminate; four are of three kinds—either wholesome, or unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What are the eight wholesome factors?
The faculty of faith up to the faculty of having already known are called the eight wholesome factors.
What are the ten indeterminate factors?
The eye faculty up to the suffering faculty are called the ten indeterminate [faculties].
What are the four that are threefold—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate?
The joy faculty, the grief faculty, the equanimity faculty, and the mind faculty are called the four that are threefold—either wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is the faculty of joy that is wholesome?
If the faculty of joy is the pleasant feeling arising from mental contact that has been cultivated, this is called the wholesome faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of joy that is unwholesome?
The pleasant feeling born of mental contact that is severed from the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) is called the unwholesome faculty of joy.
What is the indeterminate faculty of joy?

The pleasant feeling born of mental contact that is the faculty of joy, which is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor a dharma subject to ripening (*vipākadhamma*), is called the indeterminate faculty of joy.
What is the wholesome faculty of grief?
If the faculty of grief is a painful feeling resulting from mental contact that is cultivated, it is called the wholesome faculty of grief.
What is the unwholesome faculty of grief?
The faculty of grief that is a painful feeling born of mental contact, when it is severed [from its roots], is called the unwholesome faculty of grief.
What is the indeterminate faculty of grief?

The faculty of grief, the feeling of grief, which is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor a dharma subject to ripening (*vipākadharmatā*), and which is a painful feeling born of mental contact, is called the indeterminate faculty of grief.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is wholesome?
The feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from mental contact through the cultivation of the faculty of equanimity is called the wholesome faculty of equanimity.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is unwholesome?

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) that is a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja*), when it is unwholesome (*akuśala*), is called the unwholesome faculty of equanimity.
What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) faculty of equanimity?

The faculty of equanimity that is a feeling of equanimity which is neither a result of maturation (*vipāka*) nor a factor leading to maturation (*vipākadharma*), as well as the feelings of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from visual contact and the feelings of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental contact—these are called the indeterminate faculty of equanimity.
What is the faculty of mind that is wholesome?
The mental faculty, the mental element, and the mental consciousness element when cultivated—this is called the wholesome faculty of mind.
What is the faculty of mind that is unwholesome?
The faculty of mind (*manendriya*) that is severed, as well as the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), are called the unwholesome faculty of mind.
What is the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) faculty of mind?

If the faculty of mind is experienced (*vedita*) and is neither a result of maturation (*vipāka*) nor a dharma that will produce maturation (*vipākadharman*), including from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, it is called the indeterminate faculty of mind.
Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are of training (*śaikṣa*), how many are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither of training nor beyond training?

Two are of training, one is beyond training, eleven are neither of training nor beyond training, five are of two parts—either of training or beyond training—and three are of three parts—either of training, beyond training, or neither of training nor beyond training.
What are the two trainings?
The faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and the faculty of "knowing" are called the two trainings.
What is the one beyond training?
The faculty of one who has already known is called the faculty of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What are the eleven faculties that are neither of training nor beyond training?
The eye faculty up to the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief are called the eleven faculties that are neither of training nor beyond training.
What are the five faculties that are twofold, being either *śaikṣa* or *aśaikṣa*?

They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom; these are called the five twofold faculties, being either *śaikṣa* or *aśaikṣa*.
What are the three triads that are either trainee (śaikṣa), beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither trainee nor beyond training?

The faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), and the mental faculty (manendriya) are called the three triads that are either trainee, beyond training, or neither trainee nor beyond training.
What is the faculty of faith in training?

It is when a person in training (śaikṣa) has severed the fetters and proclivities, and with a noble mind enters the noble path; or when those of firm faith and firm dharma, as well as others who have seen the faults and afflictions of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of nirvāṇa, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; desiring to attain what has not been attained, to understand what has not been understood, and to realize what has not been realized, they cultivate the path to become free from defilements.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with insight through contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by contemplation, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

Whether it be a real person or a realm, if there is faith in entry, faith in ultimate entry, faith in reality, faith in entering reality, and purity of mind, this is called the faculty of faith in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the faculty of faith of one beyond training?

It is when a person in training desires to attain arhatship; desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, they fulfill the wisdom of contemplation through the cultivation of the path. Whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation, they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destination, if there is faith in entry, faith in ultimate entry, faith in truth, faith in entering truth, and purity of mind, this is called the faculty of faith of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom are also like this.
What is the faculty of joy that is in training (*śaikṣa*)?
If the faculty of joy is a noble dharma (*āryadharma*) but not that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is called the faculty of joy that is in training.
What is the faculty of joy that is in training (*śaikṣa*)?
The pleasant feeling arising from mental contact associated with the faculty of faith, which is the faculty of joy that is in training—this is called the faculty of joy that is in training.
What is the faculty of joy that is in training?

The seeker is free from fetters and proclivities; with a noble mind, they enter the noble path. Whether it be those with firm faith or firm Dharma, as well as others who have seen the faults of conditioned existence, they contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana. They contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are. Desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the defilements.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of contemplation, they immediately attain the fruit of recluseship: either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
If it pertains to a real person or a realm, and the pleasant feeling born of mental contact is called the faculty of joy of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the faculty of joy of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If the faculty of joy is noble (*ārya*) and not that of one in training, it is called the faculty of joy of one beyond training.
What is the faculty of joy that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The pleasant feeling born of mental contact associated with the faculty of faith that is beyond training is called the faculty of joy that is beyond training.
What is the faculty of joy that is beyond training?

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of the path and its contemplation—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the mind liberated through contemplation—they then attain the fruit of arhatship.

If it is a real person (*pudgala*), or a destination (*gati*), or the pleasant feeling born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-sukha-vedanā*), it is called the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the faculty of joy that is neither in training nor beyond training?
The pleasant feeling born of mental contact that is not noble (*ārya*) is called the faculty of joy that is neither in training nor beyond training.
What is the faculty of equanimity of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
If the faculty of equanimity is noble (*ārya*) but not that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is called the faculty of equanimity of one in training.
What is the faculty of equanimity of one in training?
The equanimity faculty associated with the faculty of faith that is linked to mental contact and is neither painful nor pleasant is called the "equanimity faculty of one in training" (*śaikṣa*).
What is the equanimity faculty of one in training?
It is when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and proclivities, even attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a destination (*gati*), if there is a sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from mental contact, it is called the faculty of equanimity of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the faculty of equanimity of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The faculty of equanimity that is noble (*ārya*) but not of one in training is called the faculty of equanimity of one beyond training.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from mental contact associated with the faculty of faith that is beyond training is called the faculty of equanimity that is beyond training.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is beyond training?
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship and immediately attains it—
whether as a real person or as a destiny— the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from mental contact is called the faculty of equanimity of one beyond training.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

It refers to the faculty of equanimity that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arising from contact with the eye, which is not noble; and the faculty of equanimity that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arising from contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, which is not noble. This is called the faculty of equanimity that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the faculty of mind that is in training (*śaikṣa*)?
The faculty of mind that is noble (*ārya*) but not beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called the faculty of mind in training.
What is the faculty of mind in training?

The mental faculty (*manendriya*) associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) that is in training (*śaikṣa*), namely the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), is called the "mental faculty in training.
What is the mental faculty in training?
It is when a person in training, having abandoned the fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), even attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*), a realm of existence (*gati*), or the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), these are called the faculty of mind in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the faculty of mind beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The faculty of mind that is noble (*ārya*) but not in training is called the faculty of mind beyond training.
What is the faculty of mind that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?

The mind-element (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) that is beyond training are called the faculty of mind that is beyond training.
What is the faculty of mind that is beyond training?
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) seeks to attain the fruit of arhatship and even immediately attains the fruit of arhatship—
whether as a real person or as a destiny— the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mental-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu) are called the faculty of mind (manendriya) of one beyond training.
What is the faculty of mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?

The faculty of mind consisting of non-noble consciousness and the aggregate of feeling—ranging from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—is called the faculty of mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are fruition (*vipāka*), how many are factors that lead to fruition (*vipākaja*), and how many are neither fruition nor factors that lead to fruition?

Eight are fruition; one is a factor that leads to fruition; seven are twofold, being either fruition or factors that lead to fruition; two are twofold, being either fruition or neither fruition nor factors that lead to fruition; and four are threefold, being either fruition, factors that lead to fruition, or neither fruition nor factors that lead to fruition.
What are the eight resultant factors?
The eye faculty up to the life faculty are called the eight resultant factors.
What is the single resultant factor?
The faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is called a single dharma that is a result (*vipāka*).
What are the seven [faculties] that are twofold—either results or dharmas that produce results?

Excluding the faculty of desiring to know the unknown, the remaining faculties from the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) up to the faculty of "one who has already known" (*ājñendriya*) are called the seven twofold dharmas, being either results or dharmas that produce results.
What are the two pairs that are either retribution (*vipāka*) or neither-retribution-nor-non-retribution-dharmas?
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) are called the two pairs that are either retribution or neither-retribution-nor-non-retribution-dharmas.
What are the four that are threefold—either resultant (*vipāka*), or productive of result (*vipākadharma*), or neither resultant nor productive of result?

The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the mental faculty (*manendriya*) are called the four that are threefold—either resultant, or productive of result, or neither resultant nor productive of result.
What is the retribution of the faculty of faith?
The absence of retribution for the faculty of faith is called the retribution of the faculty of faith.
What is the retribution of the faculty of faith?

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by contemplation, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) seeks to attain the fruit of arhatship, if they possess the perfection of insight—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the mind liberated through insight—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a realm, if there is faith in entry, faith in ultimate entry, faith in truth, faith in entering truth, and purity of mind, this is called the retribution of the faculty of faith.
What is the faculty of faith as a resultant dharma?
The faculty of faith that possesses fruition is called the faculty of faith as a resultant dharma.
What is the faculty of faith as a resultant dharma?

The seeker is free from fetters and proclivities; with a noble mind, they enter the noble path. Possessing firm faith and firm Dharma, as well as other persons who have entered this course, they perceive the faults and perils of conditioned existence and contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana. They contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality. Desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to become free from defilements.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, practices the path of cultivation—whether as a real person or as a destiny;

whether through faith-entry, ultimate faith-entry, faith in reality, faith-entry into reality, or the purification of the mind of faith—this is called the dharma that is the fruition of the faculty of faith.
The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) are also like this.
What is the retribution of the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*)?
The faculty of knowledge is without retribution; this is called the retribution of the faculty of knowledge.
What is the fruition of the faculty of knowledge?

It refers to those in training—stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and non-returners (*anāgāmin*)—who possess perfected insight (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*). Whether through the stage of knowledge or through the mind liberated by insight, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning.

Whether it be a real person or a realm, or whether it be perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, liberation, joy, rapture, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, attainment of fruit, the meditative absorption of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, or right mental pliancy—these are called the fruits of the faculty of knowledge.
What is the faculty of knowledge that is of the nature of resultant?
The faculty of knowledge that has a result is called the faculty of knowledge that is of the nature of resultant.
What is the faculty of knowledge that is of the nature of resultant?

The practitioner, seeing the faults and perils of conditioned activities, contemplates the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*. He contemplates, in accordance with reality, the origin of suffering, its cessation, and the path leading to that cessation. Desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized, he cultivates the path to become free from afflictions.

Whether it be a real person or a destination, or [states such as] perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of mind, liberation, pleasure, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, the attainment of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right bodily pliancy—these are called the factors to be known through the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*).
What is the retribution of the faculty of one who has already known?
The faculty of one who has already known is without retribution; this is called the retribution of the faculty of one who has already known.
What is the retribution of the faculty of one who has already known?

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, through the perfection of contemplative wisdom—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated by contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person (*pudgala*) or a destiny (*gati*), or [mental factors] such as perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), vitarka and vicāra, liberation (*vimukti*), satisfaction (*saumanasya*), joy (*prīti*), serenity of mind (*praśrabdhi-citta*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), equanimity of mind (*upekṣā-citta*), attainment of fruit (*phala-prāpti*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), right speech (*samyag-vāk*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), and right serenity of body (*samyak-kāya-praśrabdhi*): these are called the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*).
What is the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātendriya) that is of a nature to be retributed?
The faculty of one who has already known which possesses retribution is called the faculty of one who has already known that is of a nature to be retributed.
What is the faculty of one who has already known that is of a nature to be retributed?

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, practices the path of cultivation—whether it be a real person or a destiny;

whether it be perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, liberation, serenity, joy, mental pliancy, desire, heedfulness, equanimity of mind, the attainment of cessation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, or right bodily pliancy—these are called the faculty of "I have known" (ājñātendriya), which is of the nature of a result.
What is the retribution of the faculty of pleasure?
The experience of the faculty of pleasure is called the retribution of the faculty of pleasure.
What is the retribution of the faculty of pleasure?

The pleasant sensations born of the karma of the faculty of pleasure, produced by afflictions, and comprised within my own portion—namely, the pleasant sensation from eye-contact and the pleasant sensations from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact—are called the retribution of the faculty of pleasure.
What is the faculty of pleasure that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?

The neutral faculty of pleasure that is not included within the sphere of the self—namely, the pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, and the pleasant feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact—is called the faculty of pleasure that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant.
What is the retribution of the faculty of suffering?
The experience of the faculty of suffering is called the retribution of the faculty of suffering.
What is the retribution of the faculty of suffering?

The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) consists of the retribution born from karma, phenomena, and afflictions that is comprised within my own portion: the painful sensation arising from eye-contact, and the painful sensations arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact; this is called the retribution of the faculty of suffering.
What is the faculty of suffering that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution?

It refers to the neutral faculty of suffering arising from eye-contact that is not comprised within one's own sphere, as well as the faculties of suffering arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact; this is called the faculty of suffering that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution.
What is the retribution of the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*)?
The pleasant feeling born of mental contact that is the wholesome retribution of the faculty of joy is called the retribution of the faculty of joy.
What is the phenomenon that is the retribution of the faculty of joy?
The faculty of joy that is retributive is called the "retributive factor of the faculty of joy.
What is the retributive factor of the faculty of joy?

With the exception of the wholesome retribution of the faculty of joy, all other pleasant feelings arising from mental contact that are associated with the faculty of joy—whether wholesome or unwholesome—are called the retributive factors of the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of joy that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?

The indeterminate faculty of joy consisting of the pleasant feeling born of mental contact that is not included within the sphere of the self—this is called the faculty of joy that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant.
What is the faculty of grief as a result of maturation (*vipāka*)?
The experience of the faculty of grief is called the faculty of grief as a result of maturation.
What is the faculty of grief as a result of maturation?

The sorrow faculty (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is a resultant phenomenon produced by karma and afflictions, belonging to the category of "mine," and consisting of the painful feeling born of mental contact, is called the sorrow faculty as a result (*vipāka*).
What is the sorrow faculty as a resultant phenomenon?
The sorrow faculty that possesses a result is called the sorrow faculty as a resultant phenomenon.
What is the faculty of grief that is a result of maturation (*vipāka-dharma*)?
The faculty of grief that is a painful feeling arising from contact with the mind, whether wholesome or unwholesome—this is called the faculty of grief that is a result of maturation.
What is the faculty of grief that is neither a result of maturation nor a factor leading to maturation (*na-vipāka-na-vipāka-dharma*)?

The faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), not included within my own domain, and the painful feeling arising from mental contact—this is called the faculty of grief that is neither resultant (*vipāka*) nor subject to result.
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) that is resultant?

The faculty of equanimity, the feeling of equanimity, the pleasant-neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arising from eye-contact, and the pleasant-neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—these are called the faculty of equanimity that is resultant.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is of the nature of retribution?
That which has retribution is called the faculty of equanimity that is of the nature of retribution.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is of the nature of retribution?

Excluding the equanimity faculty that is wholesome and resultant, the remaining equanimity faculty—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that arises from mental contact as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is called the equanimity faculty of the resultant type (*vipākadharmā*).
What is the equanimity faculty that is neither resultant nor of the resultant type?

The faculty of equanimity that is indeterminate and not comprised within one's own portion—namely, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation arising from eye-contact, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—is called the faculty of equanimity that is neither fruition nor a dharma subject to fruition.
What is the retribution of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*)?
The experience of the mind-faculty that constitutes the wholesome retribution of the mind-faculty, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, is called the retribution of the mind-faculty.
What is the dharma that is the retribution of the mind-faculty?
The mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) that possesses retribution is called the "mind-faculty as a dharma of retribution.
What is the mind-faculty as a dharma of retribution?

Excluding the wholesome retribution of the mind-faculty, the remaining wholesome and unwholesome mind-elements (*manodhātu*) and mind-consciousness-elements (*manovijñānadhātu*) are called the mind-faculty as a dharma of retribution.
What is the faculty of mind that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant?

If the faculty of mind is indeterminate and not comprised within one's own continuum—from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness—it is called the faculty of mind that is neither resultant nor subject to becoming resultant.

Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

Eighteen are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation; four are of three kinds: either abandoned by vision, or abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the eighteen that are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The eye faculty up to the pain faculty, and the faith faculty up to the faculty of one who has already known—these are called the eighteen that are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.

What are the four factors that are each threefold—either abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?

They are the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the faculty of mind (*manendriya*); these are called the four factors that are each threefold—either abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, or neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) that is abandoned by insight (darśana-prahātavya)?

The faculty of joy that is unwholesome, not abandoned by cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya), and is a pleasant sensation born of mental contact associated with afflictions abandoned by insight—this is called the faculty of joy abandoned by insight.
What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

The faculty of joy that is unwholesome (*akuśala*), not abandoned through insight (*na dṛṣṭi-prahātavya*), and associated with the pleasant feeling arising from mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-sukha-vedanā*) due to afflictions abandoned through cultivation—this is called the faculty of joy abandoned through cultivation.
What is the faculty of joy that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The faculty of joy consisting of pleasant feeling born of mental contact that is wholesome or indeterminate is called the faculty of joy that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the faculty of grief that is abandoned by insight?

The faculty of grief that is unwholesome, not to be abandoned by cultivation, and which is the painful feeling arising from mental contact associated with afflictions abandoned by insight—this is called the faculty of grief abandoned by insight.
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

The faculty of grief that is unwholesome (*akuśala*), not abandoned through insight (*na dṛṣṭi-heya*), and associated with the suffering sensation arising from mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*) with afflictions abandoned through cultivation—this is called the faculty of grief abandoned through cultivation.
What is the faculty of grief that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The faculty of grief consisting of a painful feeling born of mental contact that is wholesome or indeterminate is called the faculty of grief that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is abandoned by insight?

The faculty of equanimity that is unwholesome, not abandoned by cultivation, and associated with the mental contact of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling that is abandoned by insight—this is called the faculty of equanimity abandoned by insight.
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

The faculty of equanimity that is unwholesome (*akuśala*), not abandoned by insight (*na dṛṣṭi-prahātavya*), and associated with the mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*) of equanimous feeling arising from afflictions abandoned by cultivation—this is called the faculty of equanimity abandoned by cultivation.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The faculty of equanimity that is wholesome or indeterminate, consisting of the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from eye-contact, and the feelings of neither-pain-nor-pleasure arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact—this is called the faculty of equanimity that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the faculty of mind that is abandoned by insight?

The faculty of mind that is unwholesome and not abandoned by cultivation, but is associated with defilements abandoned by insight—namely, the mind-element and the mind-consciousness-element—is called the faculty of mind abandoned by insight.
What is the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) that is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?

The mental element (*manodhātu*) and the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) associated with unwholesome (*akuśala*) defilements (*kleśa*) that are abandoned through cultivation rather than through insight (*darśana-heya*), which are associated with the faculty of mind, are called the faculty of mind abandoned through cultivation.
What is the faculty of mind that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?

The faculty of mind that is wholesome or indeterminate, from eye-consciousness up to mental-consciousness, is called the faculty of mind that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.

Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many have the cause of abandonment by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu*), how many have the cause of abandonment by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-hetu*), and how many have neither the cause of abandonment by seeing nor the cause of abandonment by cultivation?

Nine have neither the cause of abandonment by seeing nor the cause of abandonment by cultivation; thirteen are of three kinds: either having the cause of abandonment by seeing, or having the cause of abandonment by cultivation, or having neither the cause of abandonment by seeing nor the cause of abandonment by cultivation.
What are the nine that are neither causes for abandonment through vision nor causes for abandonment through cultivation?

The faculty of pleasure, the faculty of faith, and so forth up to the faculty of "one who has already known"—these are called the nine that are neither causes for abandonment through vision nor causes for abandonment through cultivation.

What are the thirteen [faculties] that are of three types—either having the cause of abandonment through vision (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu*), or having the cause of abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-hetu*), or having neither the cause of abandonment through vision nor the cause of abandonment through cultivation?

Excluding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the remaining faculties from the eye-faculty up to the mind-faculty are called the thirteen that are of three types—either having the cause of abandonment through vision, or having the cause of abandonment through cultivation, or having neither the cause of abandonment through vision nor the cause of abandonment through cultivation.
What is the eye-faculty that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

The eye-faculty that is the retribution of dharmas to be abandoned by insight—namely, the eye-faculty of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts—is called the eye-faculty that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the eye-faculty that has its cause in abandonment through contemplation?

The eye-faculty that is the retribution of dharmas abandoned through contemplation—namely, the eye-faculties of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts—is called the eye-faculty that has its cause in abandonment through contemplation.
What is the eye-faculty that is neither a cause for abandonment through seeing nor a cause for abandonment through cultivation?

The eye-faculty that is a wholesome dharma-result (vipāka) among gods or humans is called the eye-faculty that is neither a cause for abandonment through seeing nor a cause for abandonment through cultivation.
The same applies to the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as the female and male faculties.
What is the faculty of suffering that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision?

The faculty of suffering that is the retribution for phenomena abandoned by vision—namely, the painful feeling resulting from eye-contact, and the painful feelings resulting from contact with the ear, nose, tongue, and body—is called the faculty of suffering that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision.
What is the faculty of suffering that has its cause in abandonment through contemplation?

The faculty of suffering that is the retribution of factors abandoned through contemplation—namely, the painful sensation resulting from eye-contact and the painful sensations resulting from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact—is called the faculty of suffering that has its cause in abandonment through contemplation.
What is the faculty of suffering that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation?

It refers to the faculty of suffering that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas, as well as the faculty of suffering that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution—namely, the painful feeling resulting from eye-contact, and the painful feelings resulting from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact. This is called the faculty of suffering that is neither caused by abandonment through vision nor by abandonment through cultivation.
What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) that has its cause in what is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*)?

If the faculty of joy is the pleasant feeling born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-sukha-vedanā*) that is abandoned by seeing, it is called the faculty of joy whose cause is abandoned by seeing.
What is the faculty of joy whose cause is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
The pleasant feeling born of mental contact associated with the faculty of joy that is abandoned through cultivation is called the cause abandoned through cultivation of the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of joy that has neither a cause abandoned through vision nor a cause abandoned through cultivation?

The faculty of joy that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas, as well as the faculty of joy that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution—namely, the pleasant feeling arising from mental contact—is called the faculty of joy whose cause is neither to be abandoned by insight nor to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the faculty of grief that has the cause of abandonment through insight?

The faculty of grief, the faculty of grief abandoned through insight, and the painful feeling born of mental contact that is the retribution of factors abandoned through insight—these are called the faculty of grief that has the cause of abandonment through insight.
What is the cause for the abandonment through contemplation (*vitarka-prahāṇa*) of the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*)?

The faculty of sorrow, the sorrow that is abandoned through contemplation, and the painful feeling born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-duḥkhavedanā*) which is the retribution of those factors abandoned through contemplation—these are called the causes for the abandonment through contemplation of the faculty of sorrow.
What is the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is neither caused by abandonment through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) nor by abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

The wholesome faculty of grief, the faculty of grief that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas, and the faculty of grief consisting of the painful feeling born of mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśaja-duḥkhavedanā*)—which is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution—is called the faculty of grief that is neither caused by abandonment through insight nor by abandonment through cultivation.
What is the faculty of equanimity that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision?

The faculty of equanimity that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision refers to the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, as well as the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact that are the retribution of those factors abandoned by vision; these are called the faculty of equanimity that has its cause in what is abandoned by vision.
What is the faculty of equanimity that has its cause in abandonment through contemplation?

The faculty of equanimity that has its cause in abandonment through contemplation, as well as the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling resulting from eye-contact that is the retribution of phenomena abandoned through contemplation—this is called the faculty of equanimity having its cause in abandonment through contemplation.
What is the faculty of equanimity that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation?

It refers to the wholesome faculty of equanimity, the faculty of equanimity that is the fruit of retribution for wholesome dharmas, and the faculty of equanimity that is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution; namely, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation born of eye-contact, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensations born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact. These are called the faculty of equanimity that has neither a cause to be abandoned by insight nor a cause to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the faculty of mind that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight?

The faculty of mind that is to be abandoned by insight, and the eye-consciousness up to the mental consciousness that are the retribution of factors to be abandoned by insight—these are called the faculty of mind that has its cause in what is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the mental faculty (*manendriya*) that has the cause of abandonment through reflection?

The mental faculty that has the cause of abandonment through reflection, and the eye-consciousness up to the mind-consciousness which are the retribution of dharmas having the cause of abandonment through reflection—these are called the mental faculty that has the cause of abandonment through reflection.
What is the mental faculty that is neither a cause for abandonment through vision nor a cause for abandonment through cultivation?

It refers to the wholesome mental faculty, the mental faculty that is the retribution of wholesome dharmas, and the mental faculty that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution—from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness. These are called the mental faculties that are neither causes for abandonment through vision nor causes for abandonment through cultivation.

Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*): how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?

Six are bound to the desire realm; eight are unbound; four are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm; one is threefold, being either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm; another is threefold, being either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, or unbound; and two are fourfold, being either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What are the six factors bound to the desire realm?
The nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of grief—these are called the six factors bound to the desire realm.
What are the eight that are non-bound?
The faculty of faith up to the faculty of "one who has already known" are called the eight that are non-bound.
What are the four that are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm?
The eye faculty, the ear faculty, the body faculty, and the pleasure faculty are called four that are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What is the one that is threefold, being either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm?
The life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is called "one part and three divisions," being either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Furthermore, what is that which is "one part and three divisions," being either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or unconditioned (unbound)?
The faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*) is further classified as threefold: either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, or unbound.
What are the two fourfold divisions—either bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, or unbound?

The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) are called the two fourfold sets, which are either bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
What is the faculty of eye (*cakṣurindriya*) bound to the desire realm?
The eye-faculty that is a leakage of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and a leakage of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is called the eye-faculty bound to the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is the eye-faculty bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The eye-faculty that is a leakage of form (*rūpa-āsrava*) and a leakage of existence is called the eye-faculty bound to the realm of form.
The ear faculty and the body faculty are also like this.
What is the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) bound to the desire realm?

The faculty of pleasure bound to the desire realm refers to the pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, and the pleasant feelings born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, and body; these are called the faculty of pleasure bound to the desire realm.
What is the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu)?

The faculty of pleasure bound to the form realm refers to the pleasant feeling arising from eye-contact and the pleasant feelings arising from ear- and body-contact that are associated with the outflows of form (rūpāsrava) and are tainted (sāsrava). This is called the faculty of pleasure bound to the form realm.
What is the life-faculty bound to the desire realm?
The life-force, the outflows of the desire realm, the outflows of existence, and the longevity of the desire realm are called the life-faculty bound to the desire realm.
What is the life-faculty bound to the form realm?
The life-faculty that is material, outflowing, and subject to outflows, being the vitality of material formations, is called the life-faculty bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃyojita*).
What is the life-faculty bound to the formless realm?

The life-faculty that is immaterial, outflowing, and subject to outflows, being the vitality of immaterial formations, is called the life-faculty bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-saṃyojita*).
What is the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*) bound to the desire realm?
The pleasant feeling arising from mental contact that is associated with the outflows of the desire realm and is itself an outflow—that is called the faculty of joy bound to the desire realm.
What is the faculty of joy bound to the form realm?

The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) that is a pleasant feeling born of mental contact, which is associated with the outflows of form and is subject to outflows, is called the faculty of joy bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃyukta*).
What is the faculty of joy that is unbound?
The faculty of joy that is a pleasant feeling born of mental contact, which is noble and without outflows (*ārya-anāsrava*), is called the faculty of joy that is unbound.
What is the faculty of equanimity bound to the desire realm?

The faculty of equanimity that is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arising from eye-contact, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact, which are associated with the outflows of desire and are tainted by outflows—this is called the faculty of equanimity bound to the desire realm.
What is the faculty of equanimity bound to the realm of form?

The faculty of equanimity that is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling resulting from eye-contact, ear-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, which is associated with the outflows of form and is tainted by outflows—this is called the faculty of equanimity bound to the realm of form.
What is the faculty of equanimity bound to the formless realm?

The faculty of equanimity that is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling arising from mental contact, which is associated with outflows and is tainted by the outflows of the formless realm, is called the faculty of equanimity bound to the formless realm.
What is the faculty of equanimity that is unconditioned?

The faculty of equanimity consisting of the noble, untainted mind-element, mind-consciousness-element, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mind-contact is called the faculty of equanimity that is unconditioned.
What is the mind-faculty bound to the desire realm?
The mind-faculty that is associated with the outflows of desire and is an outflow, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, is called the mind-faculty bound to the desire realm.
What is the mind-faculty bound to the form realm?

The faculty of mind (*manendriya*) that is associated with the outflows of form (*rūpāsrava*) and the outflows of the outflows (*sāsrava*), namely eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mental consciousness—this is called the faculty of mind bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is the faculty of mind bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
The faculty of mind that is formless, outflowing, and with-outflows—namely, the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element—is called the faculty of mind bound to the formless realm.
What is the faculty of mind that is unbound?
The faculty of mind that is noble and without-outflows—namely, the mind-element and mind-consciousness-element—is called the faculty of mind that is unbound.
Of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
All are of three divisions: they are either past, or future, or present.
What is the past eye-faculty?
That which has arisen and ceased is called the past.
What is the future eye-faculty?
When the eye-faculty has not yet arisen and not yet emerged, it is called "future.
What is the eye-faculty that is "present"?
When the eye-faculty has arisen but not yet ceased, it is called "present."
This continues up to the faculty of "already known" (ājñātendriya), which is also thus.

Chapter Six: The Section on Inquiry into the Seven Factors of Enlightenment. Question:
How many types of awakening are there?
The answer is:
seven.
What are the seven?

They are the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of energy, the awakening factor of tranquility, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness?

The seeker is free from fetters and proclivities; with the noble mind, they enter the noble path. Whether it be those possessing firm faith and firm Dharma, or persons of other dispositions who perceive the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are—they desire what has not yet been attained, desire to understand what has not yet been understood, and desire to realize what has not yet been realized, practicing the path to abandon the afflictions.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of the mind through contemplation, they immediately attain the fruit of the ascetic life: either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation through the cultivation of the path—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destination, whether it be mindfulness, recollection, subtle mindfulness, conformable mindfulness, abiding, non-forgetfulness, continuous mindfulness, non-loss, non-seizure, non-dullness, the mindfulness of those with non-dull faculties, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, or right mindfulness—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness.

What is the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? It is when a practitioner, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person, a destiny, or among phenomena, it is the investigation, repeated investigation, and ultimate investigation; the discernment of phenomena through reflection that realizes and penetrates specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and common characteristics (*sādhāraṇalakṣaṇa*); the retention, analysis, observation, exertion, discrimination, wisdom, knowledge, vision, liberation, skillful means, arts, flames, and luminosity; the eye of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and non-deluded right view—this is called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena.
What is the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It is when a practitioner, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, the exertion that issues forth from body and mind—characterized by endurance, non-retrogression, and diligent effort; an energy that is not abandoned, not lax, not slack, and not indolent; the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the power of energy (*vīryabala*), and right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*)—this is called the awakening factor of energy.
What is the awakening factor of joy?
It is when a practitioner, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a [rebirth] destiny, there is exultation, leaping for joy, intense leaping for joy, ultimate leaping for joy, purification, fulfillment, and mental gladness; this is called the awakening factor of joy.
What is the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It is when a trainee (*śaikṣa*), having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny (*gati*), whether it be physical and mental pliancy, physical and mental flexibility, physical and mental lightness, physical and mental softness, or physical and mental tranquility—this is called the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
What is the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
It is when a practitioner, having abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destiny, the mind abides, dwells correctly, and dwells exclusively; the mind is single-minded, unified, joyful, and undistracted; it is based on the mental faculty, solitary, and concentrated—this is the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and right concentration.
This is called the awakening factor of concentration.
What is the awakening factor of equanimity?
It is when a practitioner, having abandoned the fetters and underlying tendencies, even attains the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a realm of existence, if one practices equanimity and non-attachment, with a mind that is upright and straightforward, free from guile, and does not prize or accept [sensory objects], this is called the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Among the seven awakening factors, how many are material (*rūpa*) and how many are non-material (*arūpa*)?
Five are non-material; two are twofold, being either material or non-material.
What are the five that are non-material?

The awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity—these are called the five that are non-material.
What are the two factors that are each twofold, being either material or non-material?
The factor of exertion (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are the two factors that are each twofold, being either material or non-material.
What is the factor of exertion that is material?
The exertion that issues from the body is called the enlightenment factor of energy with form.
What is the enlightenment factor of energy without form?
The exertion that issues from the mind is called the enlightenment factor of energy without form.
