The mind being joyful, pliant, light, malleable, and free from hindrances—this is called the factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga), which is non-material (arūpa).
Of the seven factors of awakening, how many are visible (sanidarśana) and how many are invisible (anidarśana)?
All are invisible.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are with resistance and how many are without resistance?
All are without resistance.
Of the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are noble (*ārya*) and how many are non-noble? All are noble.
Of the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
All are untainted; all are without sensation; all are without seeking; all are not destinations to be reached; all are without grasping; all are without superiority.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
All are non-appropriated; all are external (*bāhya*).
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
All [factors] are of two kinds: either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness with retribution?
That which is the dharma of the retribution of the awakening factor of mindfulness is called the awakening factor of mindfulness with retribution.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that has retribution?

It is when a practitioner who has abandoned the fetters and latent tendencies enters the noble path with a noble mind; whether it be one of firm faith and firm Dharma, or others in the various realms of existence, they perceive the faults and afflictions of conditioned formations, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are. Desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to become free from defilements.
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) seeks to attain the fruit of arhatship, and seeking to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, cultivates the path—whether as a real person or as a destiny;

whether it be mindfulness, recollection, subtle mindfulness, compliant mindfulness, established mindfulness, abiding in the characteristic of non-forgetfulness, continuous mindfulness, mindfulness that is not lost, not stolen, not dull, nor of dull faculties, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, or right mindfulness—this is called the awakening factor of mindfulness with retribution.
What is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that is without retribution?
The retribution of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness is called the enlightenment factor of mindfulness without retribution.
What is the enlightenment factor of mindfulness without retribution?

When one sees a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—who is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether in the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of mind by contemplation, they immediately attain the fruit of asceticism: either the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, through the perfection of contemplative wisdom—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the liberation of mind through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destination, if there is mindfulness, recollection, subtle mindfulness, and compliant mindfulness; if there is abiding mindfulness, continuous mindfulness, non-forgetting, non-seizure, non-dullness, and mindfulness of those with non-dull faculties; and if there is the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and right mindfulness—this is called the enlightenment factor of mindfulness that is without retribution.
The same applies to the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Regarding the seven enlightenment factors, how many are mental and how many are non-mental?
All are non-mental.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are associated with the mind and how many are not associated with the mind?
Five are associated with the mind; two are twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the five factors associated with the mind?

The awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of joy, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity—these are called the five factors associated with the mind.
What are the two factors that are twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind?

The enlightenment factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are called the two factors that are either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What is the enlightenment factor of energy associated with the mind?
If the enlightenment factor of energy is a mental factor (*caitasika*) that issues forth as exertion, it is called the enlightenment factor of energy associated with the mind.
What is the enlightenment factor of effort that is not associated with the mind?
If the enlightenment factor of effort is a bodily or vocal exertion rather than a mental factor (*caitasika*), it is called the enlightenment factor of effort that is not associated with the mind.
What is the enlightenment factor of discernment that is associated with the mind?

Regarding the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): if it is a mental concomitant (*caitasika*), such that it brings joy to the mind, makes the mind supple, light, pliant, and tranquil, this is called the factor of tranquility associated with the mind.
What is the factor of tranquility not associated with the mind?

If the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) is not a mental concomitant (*caitasika*), such that there is bodily ease, bodily suppleness, bodily lightness, bodily softness, and bodily tranquility, this is called the factor of tranquility that is not associated with the mind.
Among the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), how many are mental concomitants and how many are not mental concomitants?
Five factors are mental concomitants; two are twofold, being either mental concomitants or not mental concomitants.
What are the five mental concomitants?

Mindfulness-enlightenment-factor, investigation-of-dharmas-enlightenment-factor, joy-enlightenment-factor, concentration-enlightenment-factor, and equanimity-enlightenment-factor—these are called the five mental concomitants.
What are the two factors that are each twofold, being either mental concomitants (caitta) or non-mental concomitants?

The factor of vigor (vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga) and the factor of equanimity (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga): these are called the two factors that are each twofold, being either mental concomitants or non-mental concomitants.
What is the mental factor of the enlightenment factor of energy?
If the enlightenment factor of energy arises from the mind as its object and issues forth, it is called the mental factor of the enlightenment factor of energy.
What is the enlightenment factor of energy that is not a mental factor?

If the awakening factor of effort (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) arises conditioned by the body and issues forth as deliverance, it is called the awakening factor of effort that is not a mental factor (*caitasika*).
What is the awakening factor of rapture (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) as a mental factor?

If the awakening factor of rapture is conditioned by mental pleasure, mental pliancy, mental lightness, mental softness, and mental tranquility, it is called the awakening factor of rapture as a mental factor.
What is the perception of removal that is not a mental factor?

If the perception of removal is not associated with bodily pleasure, bodily pliancy, bodily lightness, bodily softness, or bodily removal, it is called the perception of removal that is not a mental factor.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many have objects and how many do not?
Five have objects; two are twofold, being either with objects or without objects.
What are the five that have objects?

The awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity—these are called the five conditions.
What are the two that are twofold, being either conditions or non-conditions?

The enlightenment factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) are called the two factors that are either with-object (*sālambana*) or without-object (*anālambana*).
What is the enlightenment factor of energy with-object?
If the enlightenment factor of energy is a mental concomitant (*caitasika*) that issues forth as exertion.
This is called the enlightenment factor of energy with an object.
What is the enlightenment factor of energy without an object?
If the enlightenment factor of energy is not a mental concomitant (caitta), but consists of the exertion of body and speech, it is called the enlightenment factor of energy without an object.
What is the condition for the awakening-factor of rapture (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

If the awakening-factor of rapture is a mental factor (*caitasika*), such that the mind is joyful, pliant, light, malleable, and composed, this is called the condition for the awakening-factor of rapture.
What is the non-condition for the awakening-factor of rapture?

If the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is not a mental concomitant (*caitasika*), then bodily bliss, bodily pliancy, bodily lightness, bodily softness, and bodily tranquility are called the factor of tranquility that is non-objective (*anālambana*).
Among the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), how many are associated with the mind (*cittasamprayukta*) and how many are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*)?
Five are associated with the mind; two are twofold, being either associated with the mind or not associated with the mind.
What are the five associated with the mind?

The awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, the awakening factor of rapture, the awakening factor of concentration, and the awakening factor of equanimity—these are called the five associated with the mind.
What are the two factors that are each twofold, being either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind?
The factor of exertion (*vīrya*) and the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) are called the two factors that are each twofold, being either associated with the mind or dissociated from the mind.
What is the awakening factor of energy associated with the mind?

The awakening factor of energy follows the mind, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it; because the mind initiates exertion, it is called the awakening factor of energy associated with the mind.
What is the awakening factor of energy that is not associated with the mind?

If the awakening factor of energy does not follow the mind in its turning, and does not arise, abide, or cease together with the mind, but rather issues forth from the body, it is called the awakening factor of energy that is not associated with the mind.
What is the factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) associated with the mind?

If the factor of tranquility follows the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind—namely, physical ease and mental ease, physical pliancy and mental pliancy, physical lightness and mental lightness, physical softness and mental softness, physical tranquility and mental tranquility—this is called the factor of tranquility associated with the mind.
What is the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that is not associated with the mind?

If the factor of tranquility does not follow the mind, nor arises, abides, or ceases together with the mind, yet consists of bodily pleasure, bodily suppleness, bodily lightness, bodily softness, and bodily tranquility—this is called the factor of tranquility that is not associated with the mind.
The same applies to those that follow the mind and those that do not follow the mind.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are karma and how many are not karma? All are not karma.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are associated with karma and how many are not associated with karma?
Five are associated with karma; two are twofold, being either associated with karma or not associated with karma.
What are the five factors associated with activity?

Mindfulness-enlightenment-factor, investigation-of-dharmas-enlightenment-factor, joy-enlightenment-factor, concentration-enlightenment-factor, and equanimity-enlightenment-factor are called the five factors associated with activity.
What are the two factors that are twofold—either associated with activity or not associated with activity?

The enlightenment factor of energy (*vīrya-sambodhyaṅga*) and the enlightenment factor of investigation (*mīmāṃsā-sambodhyaṅga*) are called the two factors that are either associated with karma or not associated with karma.
What is the enlightenment factor of energy associated with karma?
The enlightenment factor of energy associated with volition (*cetanā*), which is the mental exertion and striving, is called the enlightenment factor of energy associated with karma.
What is the awakening factor of energy that is not associated with karma?
If the awakening factor of energy is not associated with volition (*cetanā*), yet involves bodily and vocal exertion, it is called the awakening factor of energy that is not associated with karma.
What is the application of the factor of investigation of renunciation (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

If the investigation of renunciation is associated with volition (*cetanā*), such that the mind is joyful, supple, buoyant, pliant, and renounced, this is called the application of the factor of investigation of renunciation.
What is the factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not associated with karma?

If the factor of tranquility is not associated with volition (cetanā), then bodily ease, bodily pliancy, bodily lightness, bodily softness, and the removal of bodily rigidity are called the factor of tranquility that is not associated with karma.
Of the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are common karma and how many are non-common karma?
All are common karma; all follow along with karma.
Of the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are causes and how many are non-causes?
Regarding all causes:
among the seven factors of enlightenment, how many have causes and how many are without cause?
All have causes; all have a thread [of continuity]; all have conditions; all are conditioned.
Of the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are cognitions and how many are not cognitions?
All are cognitions, known and seen according to their respective objects.
Of the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are consciousnesses and how many are not consciousnesses?
All consciousnesses are like the consciousness of objects.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment,
how many are liberations?
How many are not understanding?
All are understanding, as they know and see things as they are.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are penetration and how many are not penetration?
All are fully understood, known and seen according to reality.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
All are not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are to be cultivated and how many are not to be cultivated?
All are to be cultivated.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are to be realized and how many are not to be realized?
All are realized, known, and seen as they truly are.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
All are wholesome.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are *śaikṣa*, how many are *aśaikṣa*, and how many are neither *śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa*?
All are twofold: either *śaikṣa* or *aśaikṣa*.
What is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that is *śaikṣa*?

The seeker is freed from the fetters and latent tendencies; with a noble mind, they enter the Noble Path. Whether it be those with firm faith and firm Dharma, or persons of other dispositions, they perceive the faults and dangers of conditioned existence and contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana. They contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are. Desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the defilements.

When one sees a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—who is either fully endowed with insight-knowledge, established on the plane of knowledge, or has attained liberation of mind through insight, they then realize the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

Whether it be a real person or a destination, if there is mindfulness, recollection, subtle mindfulness, and compliant mindfulness; if there is abiding mindfulness, continuous mindfulness, non-forgetting, non-seizure, non-dullness, and mindfulness of those with non-dull faculties; and if there is the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and right mindfulness—this is called the training in the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is beyond training?

When a person beyond training desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of the path and contemplation—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they then attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person or a destination, if there is mindfulness, recollection, subtle mindfulness, and compliant mindfulness; if there is abiding mindfulness that is unforgetting and continuous; if there is mindfulness that is not lost, not stolen, not dull, and possesses non-dull faculties; and if there is the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and right mindfulness—this is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness belonging to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The same applies to the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Among the seven enlightenment factors, how many are results (*vipāka*), how many are things that lead to results (*vipākadhamma*), and how many are neither results nor things that lead to results?
All [factors] are of two kinds: either fruition (*vipāka*) or that which has the nature of fruition (*vipākadharmaka*).
What is the fruition of the awakening-factor of mindfulness?
The awakening-factor of mindfulness is itself without fruition; this is termed the "fruition of the awakening-factor of mindfulness."
What is the fruit of the awakening factor of mindfulness?

It is when a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—possesses the perfection of contemplative knowledge; whether through the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind through contemplation, they immediately attain the fruits of śrāmaṇya: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training who has attained the fruit desires to realize the fruit of arhatship—whether as a real person or as a destiny—the mindfulness that is mindful, recollective, subtle mindfulness, compliant mindfulness, abiding mindfulness, continuous mindfulness, unimpaired, unrobbed, non-dull, and possessed of non-dull faculties; this mindfulness faculty, the power of mindfulness, and right mindfulness are called the result of the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that is retributive?
Mindfulness-enlightenment has retribution; thus it is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that is retributive.
What is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness that is retributive?

The practitioner is free from fetters and proclivities; with a noble mind, they enter the noble path. Whether it be those with firm faith and firm Dharma, or persons of other dispositions, they perceive the faults and afflictions of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are. Desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the defilements.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain the fruit of arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, practices the cultivation of the path—whether it be a real person or a destiny—if there is mindfulness, recollection, subtle mindfulness, and compliant mindfulness;

if there is abiding mindfulness that is continuous and uninterrupted; if there is mindfulness that is not lost, not stolen, not dull, and not of dull faculties; and if there is the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and right mindfulness—this is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga), which is a dharma resulting from retribution.
The same applies to the enlightenment factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
Regarding the seven enlightenment factors, how many are abandoned by vision, how many are abandoned by cultivation, and how many are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
All [factors] are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.

Among the seven factors of enlightenment, how many have insight as their cause of abandonment, how many have cultivation as their cause of abandonment, and how many have neither insight nor cultivation as their cause of abandonment?
All [factors] have as their cause neither those abandoned by seeing nor those abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, how many are bound to the desire realm, how many are bound to the form realm, how many are bound to the formless realm, and how many are unbound?
All are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Of the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
All three categories are either past, future, or present.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness that is past?
If the awakening factor of mindfulness has arisen and already ceased, it is called past.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness in the future?
When the awakening factor of mindfulness has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, it is called the awakening factor of mindfulness in the future.
What is the awakening factor of mindfulness in the present?
When the awakening factor of mindfulness has arisen and not yet ceased, it is called the present awakening factor of mindfulness.
The same applies to the awakening factors from the investigation of dharmas up to equanimity.
Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Unwholesome Roots From the Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra, Question Section, Chapter Seven: The Chapter on Unwholesome Roots. Question:
How many unwholesome roots are there?
Answer: Three.
What are the three?
They are the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
What is the unwholesome root of greed?
Hope is called the unwholesome root of greed.
What is the unwholesome root of greed?
It is the continuous succession of attachment, delight, and mental satisfaction toward the five objects of desire, as well as the craving for and defilement by attractive forms.

When visual consciousness encounters forms that are pleasing, delightful, and agreeable, there arises a continuity of craving for those forms, characterized by desire and defilement; when auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses encounter tangibles that are pleasing, delightful, and agreeable, there arises a continuity of craving for those tangibles, characterized by desire and defilement. Furthermore, regarding the desires of others, their forms, their wealth, their wives, their daughters, or whatever they require—when one harbors the hope of obtaining these, and if there is greed, attachment, and a mind associated with greed, a longing, a heart of love, defilement, heavy defilement, and ultimate defilement, as well as other objects of greed—if there is greed, heavy greed, and ultimate greed, a longing, a heart of love, defilement, heavy defilement, and ultimate defilement—this is called the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha-akuśalamūla*).
What is the unwholesome root of ill will?
Anger is called the unwholesome root of ill will.
What is the unwholesome root of ill will?

Whether toward few sentient beings or many sentient beings, they inflict various harms, injuries, and sufferings; or they harbor anger, intense anger, ultimate anger, associated anger, and impetuous rage; they feel hatred and resentment in their hearts, harboring mutual animosity, lacking compassion, lacking pity, and lacking the intent to benefit sentient beings and other objects of their anger.

If there is resentment, intense resentment, ultimate resentment, associated anger, or violent rage; if one harbors hatred, distresses the mind, and feels malice, lacking loving-kindness, compassion, and beneficial qualities—this is called the unwholesome root of ill-will (*vyāpāda-akuśalamūla*).
What is the unwholesome root of delusion?
Ignorance is called the unwholesome root of delusion.
What is the unwholesome root of delusion?

They do not know suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path; they do not know the past, they do not know the future, and they do not know both the past and the future; they do not know the internal, they do not know the external, and they do not know both the internal and the external; they do not know the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact; they do not know reality as it is, they do not know suchness, and they do not know karmic retribution; they do not know conditions, nor what is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; nor what is black or white; nor what has conditions or lacks conditions; nor what is luminous or non-luminous; nor what is done or not done; nor what is friendly or unfriendly.

In those phenomena, if delusion (moha) seizes the mind—seizing it, obstructing it, covering it, darkening it, defiling it, and entangling it; if there is the turbidity of delusion, the ignorance (avidyā), the flow of ignorance, the abyss of ignorance, and the latent tendency of ignorance; if there is lack of knowledge and lack of vision, lack of liberation and lack of deliverance, and lack of skillful means—and if, in other phenomena as well, delusion seizes the mind, seizing it, obstructing it, covering it, and darkening it, up to lack of knowledge and lack of vision, lack of liberation and lack of deliverance, and lack of skillful means—this is called the unwholesome root of delusion.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are material and how many are non-material?
All are non-material.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are visible and how many are invisible?
All are invisible.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
All are without resistance.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are noble (ārya) and how many are non-noble?
All are non-noble.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?

All that is with outflows, all that is with craving for existence, all that is sought in existence, all that is to be sought in existence, all that is grasped in existence, and all that is surpassed in existence.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
All are non-appropriated; all are external (*bāhya*).
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
All [factors] have retribution.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are mental and how many are non-mental?
All are non-mental.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*), how many are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with the mind?
All are associated with the mind.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are mental factors (*caitasika*) and how many are not mental factors?
Regarding all mental factors and the three unwholesome roots: how many are conditions and how many are not conditions?
All are conditions.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*): how many are concomitant with the mind (*cittasahabhū*), and how many are not concomitant with the mind?
All are concomitant with the mind; all follow the movement of the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are karma (*karman*), and how many are not karma?
All are not karma.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are associated with karma and how many are not associated with karma?
All are associated with karma.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are common karma and how many are uncommon karma?
All are common karma; all follow along with karma.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many have causes and how many are without causes?
All things have a cause, all have a thread [of continuity], all have conditions, and all are conditioned.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are objects of knowledge and how many are not objects of knowledge?
All-knowing knowledge perceives and sees things as they truly are; all consciousness and mental cognition perceive things as they truly are; all is understood, and all is fully comprehended.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment, and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
All are known through the knowledge of abandonment; all are abandoned.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are to be cultivated and how many are not to be cultivated?
All are not to be cultivated.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are realized (*sākṣātkṛta*) and how many are not realized?
All are realized, being known and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Regarding all unwholesome states and the three unwholesome roots:
how many are associated with training (*śaikṣa*), how many are associated with no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither associated with training nor associated with no-more-training?
All are neither associated with training nor associated with no-more-training.
Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are results (*vipāka*), how many are subject to results (*vipākadharmāḥ*), and how many are neither results nor subject to results?
All are subject to results.

Regarding the three unwholesome roots: how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
All [factors] are of two types: either abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is the unwholesome root of greed that is abandoned by seeing?
The unwholesome root of greed that is abandoned by seeing due to the cause of the unwholesome root of greed—this is called the unwholesome root of greed abandoned by seeing.
What is the unwholesome root of greed that is abandoned through cultivation?

The unwholesome root of greed is abandoned through cultivation because it has the unwholesome root of greed as its cause; thus, it is called the unwholesome root of greed abandoned through cultivation.
Hatred and delusion are also like this.

Regarding the three unwholesome roots, how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Two are bound to the desire realm; one is of three parts—that is, it may be bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
What are the two that are bound to the desire realm?
The unwholesome root of greed and the unwholesome root of hatred are called the two that are bound to the desire realm.
What is the one that is threefold—either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm?
The unwholesome root of delusion is said to be of one part and three divisions, being either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
What is the unwholesome root of delusion that is bound to the desire realm?

The unwholesome root of delusion that is associated with the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is called "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is the unwholesome root of delusion bound to the form realm?
The unwholesome root of delusion that is associated with the outflow of form (*rūpa-āsrava*) and the outflow of existence is called "bound to the form realm."
What is the unwholesome root of delusion bound to the formless realm?
The outflows of the formless realm and the unwholesome root of delusion that is with-outflow are called "bound to the formless realm.
Of the three unwholesome roots, how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
All [unwholesome roots] are of three kinds: past, future, or present.
What is the unwholesome root of greed that is past?
The unwholesome root of greed that has arisen and ceased is called past.
What is the unwholesome root of greed that is future?
The unwholesome root of greed that has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged is called future.
What is the unwholesome root of greed that is present?

When the unwholesome root of greed has arisen and not yet ceased, it is called "present. The same applies to hatred and delusion.
