How many roots of goodness are there? Answer:
Three.
What are the three?
They are the wholesome root of non-attachment, the wholesome root of non-hatred, and the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What is the wholesome root of non-attachment?
The absence of longing is called the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*).
What is the wholesome root of non-attachment?
When the mind is capable of enduring and remaining free from attachment, this is called the wholesome root of non-attachment.
What is the wholesome root of non-attachment?
It is the continuity of attachment to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), characterized by delight, pleasure, and agreeable passion for forms.

Specifically, it is the continuity of attachment to forms through visual consciousness, characterized by delight, pleasure, and agreeable passion for forms; and likewise through auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness, characterized by attachment to contact, delight, pleasure, and agreeable passion for forms.

Regarding the continuity of sensual desire: with respect to others' desires, others' forms, others' wealth, others' wives and daughters, others' maidens, and whatever others require, one does not hope to obtain them;

one is without greed and without attachment of mind; one does not crave or hope for them, does not love or desire them with sensual passion, does not value a mind of sensual passion, and is ultimately free from sensual passion; and as for other phenomena, it is likewise.
Not being heavy with greed, ultimately not being greedy, not longing for, not loving, not desiring to be stained by,
not being heavy with the desire to be stained by, ultimately not being greedy, not longing for, not loving,
not desiring to be stained by, not being heavy with the desire to be stained by, and ultimately not desiring to be stained by— this is called the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*).
What is the wholesome root of non-ill will?
The absence of anger is called the wholesome root of non-ill will.
What is the wholesome root of non-ill will?
The mind’s capacity for forbearance and freedom from ill will is called the wholesome root of non-ill will (*avyāpāda*).
What is the wholesome root of non-ill will?

If, toward few beings or many beings, one does not harm these beings, does not bind them, does not confine them, and does not inflict various sufferings upon them; if one is not angry, not intensely angry, and ultimately without anger; if the mind should not be angry, if one is not wrathful, not crossly angry, not hateful, not agitated in mind, and not mutually hostile; if one feels compassion and seeks the benefit of beings, and regarding other phenomena as well, is not angry, not resentful, not intensely resentful, and ultimately without resentment; if the mind should not be resentful, if one is not wrathful, not crossly angry, not hateful, not agitated in mind, and if the mind is neither angry nor resentful, being without mutual hostility and feeling compassion and seeking the benefit of phenomena—this is called the wholesome root of non-resentment (*avyāpāda*).
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion?
Being free from ignorance is called the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion?

The mind’s capacity for endurance and freedom from delusion is called the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha-kuśalamūla*). What is the wholesome root of non-delusion? It is knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path;

knowing the past, knowing the future, and knowing both the past and the future; knowing the internal, knowing the external, and knowing both the internal and external; knowing the arising, cessation, gratification, danger, and escape regarding the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*); knowing things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*); knowing suchness (*tathatā*); knowing karmic retribution; knowing conditions (*pratyaya*); knowing the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate; and knowing what is black and white, what has conditions and what is without conditions, what is luminous and what is without light, and what is done and what is not done, as well as what is friendly and what is unfriendly.

Within past phenomena, there is non-delusion, non-stealing, and non-stealing associated with the mind; it is unobstructed, uncovered, free from darkness, free from confusion, and free from mental entanglements. It is not deluded and not turbid; it is the radiant illumination of light, the knowledge and vision of the skillful means of liberation, the eye of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the discernment of phenomena, right awakening, and right view. Furthermore, within other phenomena, there is non-delusion, non-stealing, and non-stealing associated with the mind; it is unobstructed, uncovered, and free from darkness, up to and including right awakening and right view. This is called the wholesome root of non-delusion.
Regarding the three roots of goodness: how many are material (*rūpa*) and how many are non-material (*arūpa*)?
All are non-material.
Regarding the three roots of goodness: how many are visible (*sanidarśana*) and how many are invisible (*anidarśana*)?
All are invisible.
Among the three wholesome roots, how many are with resistance (*sapratigha*) and how many are without resistance (*apratigha*)?
All are without resistance.
Regarding the three wholesome roots, how many are noble (ārya) and how many are non-noble (anārya)?
Two are non-noble; one is twofold, being either noble or non-noble.
What are the two that are non-noble?
Non-greed and non-hatred are called the two that are non-noble.
What is the one that is twofold, being either noble or non-noble?
Non-delusion as a root of goodness is called the one that is twofold, being either noble or non-noble.
What is the non-noble root of goodness that is non-delusion?
The root of goodness that is non-delusion which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called the non-noble root of goodness that is non-delusion.
What is the non-noble root of goodness that is non-delusion?
The wholesome root of non-delusion that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner is called the wholesome root of non-delusion that is non-noble.
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion that is noble?
The wholesome root of non-delusion that is untainted is called the wholesome root of non-delusion that is noble.
What is the noble root of non-delusion?
The root of non-delusion associated with the faculty of faith is called the noble root of non-delusion.
What is the noble root of non-delusion?

The seeker is free from fetters and proclivities; with a noble mind, they enter the noble path. Possessing firm faith and firm Dharma, as well as other types of persons, they perceive the faults and perils of conditioned formations, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana, and observe suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality. Desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to become free from afflictions.

When one sees a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—who is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether in the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of mind by contemplation, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

If a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, wishes to achieve the fullness of the wisdom of contemplation through the path of cultivation—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they shall immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
Whether it be a destination (*gati*) or non-delusion (*amoha*), these are called the noble roots of goodness of non-delusion.

The same applies to whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), with craving (*sarāga*) or without craving, with seeking (*saiṣaṇa*) or without seeking, to be grasped (*upādānīya*) or not to be grasped, with clinging (*sopādāna*) or without clinging, and with superiority (*saviśeṣa*) or without superiority.
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
All are non-appropriated; all are external (*bāhya*).
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many have retribution (*savipāka*) and how many are without retribution (*avipāka*)?
Two are with retribution; one is twofold, being either with retribution or without retribution.
What are the two that are with retribution?
Non-greed and non-hatred are called the two that are with retribution.
What is the twofold wholesome root of non-delusion that is either with retribution or without retribution?
The wholesome root of non-delusion is called the twofold [root] that is either with retribution or without retribution.
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion that has retribution?
The non-delusion wholesome root that is a resultant phenomenon is called the "non-delusion wholesome root with retribution.
What is the non-delusion wholesome root with retribution?

It refers to a trainee who has abandoned the fetters and proclivities, whose noble mind enters the noble path; or other persons of various dispositions who possess firm faith and firm Dharma, who perceive the faults and perils of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*, and contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; who, not yet having attained what they desire to attain, not yet having understood what they desire to understand, and not yet having realized what they desire to realize, cultivate the path to become free from afflictions.
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, or when one who has not yet attained the noble dharmas desires to attain them and cultivates the path—
whether as a real person or as a destiny— if there is non-delusion, this is called the wholesome root of non-delusion with retribution.
What is the non-delusive root of goodness that is without retribution?
That which is the retribution of the non-delusive root of goodness is called the non-delusive root of goodness without retribution.
What is the non-delusive root of goodness without retribution?

When one sees a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—who is fully endowed with insight, whether in the stage of knowledge or in the liberation of mind through insight, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, if they possess the perfection of insight-knowledge—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of mind through insight—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If there is no delusion regarding either a real person or a realm of existence, it is called the wholesome root of non-delusion without retribution.
Among the three wholesome roots, how many are mental and how many are non-mental?
All are non-mental.
Regarding the three wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*): how many are associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with the mind?
All are associated with the mind.
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are mental factors (*caitasika*) and how many are not mental factors?
Regarding all mental factors and the three roots of goodness: how many have objects as conditions, and how many do not?
All have objects as conditions.
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are associated with the mind (*cittasamprayukta*), and how many are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*)?
All are associated with the mind; all follow the movement of the mind (*cittānuparivartin*).
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are karma (*karman*), and how many are not karma?
All are non-action (*akarma*).
Of the three roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), how many are associated with action (*karmasamprayukta*) and how many are not associated with action?
All are associated with action.
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are common karma and how many are not common karma?
All are common karma; all follow along with karma.
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are causes and how many are not causes?
Regarding all causes:
among the three wholesome roots, how many have a cause and how many are without a cause?
All have a cause; all have a nexus; all have an object-condition; all are conditioned.
Regarding the three wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*): how many are cognitions (*jñāna*) and how many are not cognitions?
All are cognitions, as they are known and seen according to their respective objects.
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) and how many are not consciousnesses?
All consciousnesses are cognized by the mental consciousness according to their objects;
all understandings are fully comprehended.
Regarding the three wholesome roots, how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
All are not known by the knowledge of abandonment; all are not abandoned.
Regarding the three wholesome roots, how many are cultivated and how many are not cultivated?
All are cultivated.
Regarding the three roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*): how many are realized (*sākṣātkṛta*) and how many are not realized?
All are realized; they are known and seen as they truly are.
Regarding the three roots of goodness: how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
All are wholesome.

Regarding the three wholesome roots, how many are of the trainee (*śaikṣa*), how many are of the non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither of the trainee nor the non-trainee (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Two are neither of the trainee nor the non-trainee; one is threefold, being either of the trainee, or of the non-trainee, or neither of the trainee nor the non-trainee.
What are the two that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Non-greed and non-hatred are called the two that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the one that is threefold—either learner, or non-learner, or neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
The wholesome root of non-delusion is designated as "one-third" [of the three trainings], being either *śaikṣa*, *aśaikṣa*, or neither *śaikṣa* nor *aśaikṣa*.
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion that is *śaikṣa*?
The wholesome root of non-delusion that is noble (*ārya*) but not *aśaikṣa* is called the wholesome root of non-delusion that is *śaikṣa*.
What is the training in the wholesome root of non-delusion?
Training in the wholesome root of non-delusion associated with the faculty of faith is called the training in the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What is the training in the wholesome root of non-delusion?

The practitioner leaves behind the fetters and proclivities; with the noble mind, they enter the noble path. Whether it be those with firm faith and firm Dharma, or persons of other dispositions, seeing the faults and perils of conditioned formations, they contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana. Contemplating suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path as they truly are, they desire to attain what has not yet been attained, desire to understand what has not yet been understood, and desire to realize what has not yet been realized, practicing the path to abandon the afflictions.

When a trainee—whether a stream-enterer, a once-returner, or a non-returner—possesses the perfection of insight, whether through the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of insight, they immediately attain the fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.
If the wholesome root of non-delusion pertains to a real person or a destiny, it is called the wholesome root of non-delusion of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If the wholesome root of non-delusion is noble and not that of one in training, it is called the wholesome root of non-delusion of one beyond training.
What is the root of non-delusion that is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
The root of non-delusion associated with the faculty of faith that is beyond training is called the root of non-delusion that is beyond training.
What is the root of non-delusion that is beyond training?

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of the contemplation of the path—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If, regarding either a real person or a destiny, there is non-delusion, this is called the non-delusion wholesome root of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
What is the non-delusion wholesome root that is neither of training nor beyond training?
Non-delusion that is not noble (*ārya*) is called the non-delusion wholesome root that is neither of training nor beyond training.
Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many are results (*vipāka*), how many are factors that produce results (*vipākadharmas*), and how many are neither results nor factors that produce results?
Two are factors that produce results; one is twofold, being either a result or a factor that produces results.
What are the two factors that result in maturation?
Non-greed and non-hatred are called the two factors that result in maturation.
What is the one factor that is twofold—either resulting in maturation or being a factor that results in maturation?
The wholesome root of non-delusion is called "one part of two," being either fruition (*vipāka*) or the dharma that leads to fruition (*vipākadharmatā*).
What is the fruition of the wholesome root of non-delusion?
The wholesome root of non-delusion is itself without fruition; this is termed the fruition of the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What is the retribution for the wholesome root of non-delusion?

It is when a trainee—whether a *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, or *anāgāmin*—is endowed with the perfection of contemplative wisdom; whether in the stage of knowledge or through the mind liberated by contemplation, they immediately attain the fruits of the ascetic life: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, through the perfection of insight-knowledge—whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of mind through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.
If a person or a realm is free from delusion, it is called the retribution of the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What is the phenomenon that is the retribution of the wholesome root of non-delusion?
When the wholesome root of non-delusion possesses retribution, it is called the phenomenon that is the retribution of the wholesome root of non-delusion.
What is the retributive dharma of the wholesome root of non-delusion?

It refers to a practitioner who has abandoned the fetters and proclivities, whose noble mind enters the noble path, possessing firm faith and firm Dharma; as well as other persons who, seeing the faults and afflictions of conditioned existence, contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana, and contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the defilements.
When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, or when one who has not yet attained the noble dharmas desires to attain them and cultivates the path—
if such a person or such a destiny is free from delusion, this is called the dharma that is the fruition of the wholesome root of non-delusion.

Regarding the three wholesome roots, how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
All are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the three wholesome roots: how many have the cause of abandonment by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many have the cause of abandonment by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many have neither the cause of abandonment by insight nor the cause of abandonment by cultivation?
All of them have neither the cause of abandonment by insight nor the cause of abandonment by cultivation.

Regarding the three roots of goodness: how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
Two are bound to the desire realm; one is fourfold, being either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What are the two that are bound to the desire realm?
Non-greed and non-hatred are called the two that are bound to the desire realm.
What is the one that is fourfold—either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound?
The wholesome root of non-delusion is said to be of four parts: either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm, or unbound.
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion that is bound to the desire realm?
The roots of wholesome non-delusion that are outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) are termed "bound to the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What are the roots of wholesome non-delusion bound to the form realm?
The roots of wholesome non-delusion that are outflows of form (*rūpa-āsrava*) and outflows of existence are termed "bound to the form realm."
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion bound to the formless realm?
The wholesome root of non-delusion that is associated with the outflows of the formless realm and is subject to outflows is called "bound to the formless realm.
What is the wholesome root of non-delusion that is unbound?
The noble, untainted, non-deluded wholesome roots are called "unbound" (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Among the three wholesome roots, how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
All things belong to three periods: either past, future, or present.
What is the past root of non-attachment?
When the root of non-attachment has arisen and ceased, it is called past.
What is the future root of non-attachment?
The root of non-attachment that has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged is called "future.
What is the present root of non-attachment?
When the wholesome root of non-greed has arisen and not yet ceased, it is called "present.
The same applies to non-hatred and non-delusion.
Chapter Nine: The Great Section Śāriputra Abhidharma Śāstra, Question Section, Great Section, Chapter Nine Question:
How many great [elements] are there?
The answer is: four.
What are the four?
They are the great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
What is the great element of earth?
The second is the great element of earth, comprising the internal great element of earth and the external great element of earth.
What is the internal great element of earth?

Whatever within the body is distinct, solid, and perceived as solid—namely, the bones, teeth, nails, hair of the head, hair of the body, skin, flesh, muscles, tendons, spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, heart, intestines, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, abdomen, lower abdomen, and excrement—and whatever else within the body is solid and perceived as solid: this is called the internal great element of earth.
What is the external earth element?

Whatever is external and not appropriated that is solid—such as copper, iron, lead, tin, white bronze, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, precious gems, jewels, sand, stones, soil, salt flats, refuse heaps, ash, earth, grass, trees, branches, leaves, stalks, nodes, and other such external things that are not appropriated but are solid—is called the external earth element.
In this way, the internal earth element and the external earth element are called the earth element.
What is the water element?
There are two water elements: the internal water element and the external water element.
What is the internal water element?

Whatever water is received within the body—such as phlegm, saliva, mucus, bile, liver, fat, marrow, brain, grease, tears, nasal mucus, pus, blood, urine, and other such moistening waters received within the body—is called the internal water element.
What is the external water element?

Whatever is external moisture that is not appropriated—such as ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, dark molasses, milk, curd, whey, fermented grain liquor, sugarcane wine, honey-wine, and other such external moistures that are not appropriated—is called the external water element.
Thus, the internal water element and the external water element are called the water element.
What is the fire element?
There are two fire elements: the internal fire element and the external fire element.
What is the internal fire element?

It refers to the heat experienced within the body—whether it is hot, capable of making things hot, or causing the body to burn internally; it includes the digestion of food, drink, and so forth, as well as other distinct fires experienced within the body. This is called the internal fire element.
What is the external fire element?

External fire that is not experienced as heat—namely, the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, the heat of jewels, the heat of houses, the heat of walls, the heat of mountains, the heat of grain vapors, the heat of grass, the heat of wood, the heat of cow dung, and other such external heats that are not experienced—is called the external fire element.
In this way, the internal fire element and the external fire element are called the fire element.
What is the wind element?
There are two wind elements: the internal wind element and the external wind element.
What is the internal wind element?

Winds experienced within the body—upward winds, downward winds, winds dependent on the joints, winds causing convulsions or lameness, winds moving through the bones and joints, the winds of exhalation and inhalation, and other distinct internal winds experienced within—are called the internal wind element.
What is the external wind element?

External winds that are not appropriated—east winds, south winds, west winds, north winds; winds with dust and winds without dust; cold winds and hot winds; black winds, whirlwind-gales, and earth-shaking winds, as well as other external winds that are not appropriated—are called the external wind element.
Thus, the internal wind element and the external wind element are called the wind element.
Of these four great elements, how many are form and how many are non-form? All are form.
Of the four great elements, how many are visible and how many are invisible?
All are invisible.
Of the four great elements, how many are resistant and how many are non-resistant?
All that is impingible consists of the four great elements. How many are noble (ārya) and how many are non-noble (anārya)?
All are non-noble.
Regarding the four great elements (mahābhūta), how many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)?

All of them are with outflows, all are accompanied by craving (tṛṣṇā), all involve seeking (prārthana), all are subject to grasping (upādāna), all involve clinging (parigraha), and all are surpassed by others.
Of the four great elements, how many are appropriated (*upātta*) and how many are non-appropriated (*anupātta*)?
All are of two kinds: either appropriated or non-appropriated.
What is the earth element that is appropriated?
If the earth element is internal, it is called the "appropriated earth element" (*pṛthivīdhātu-upātta*).
What is the appropriated earth element?
That which is produced as a retribution from karma and afflictions, and is comprised within the sphere of the self, is called the appropriated earth element.
What is the earth element that is not appropriated?
The external earth element is called the earth element that is not appropriated.
The same applies to the water, fire, and wind elements.
Of the four great elements, how many are retributive and how many are non-retributive?
All are non-retributive.
Of the four great elements, how many are mental and how many are non-mental?
All are non-mental.
Of the four great elements, how many are associated with the mind and how many are not associated with the mind?
All are not associated with the mind.
Of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many are mental concomitants (*cittasamprayukta*) and how many are not mental concomitants?
All are not mental concomitants.
Of the four great elements, how many are objects (*ālambana*) and how many are not objects?
All [of these] are non-conditions.
Among the four great elements, how many are associated with the mind and how many are not associated with the mind?
All are not associated with the mind; all do not follow the mind.
Of the four great elements, how many are karma and how many are not karma?
All are not karma. Of the four great elements, how many are associated with karma and how many are not associated with karma?
All [of these] are not associated with karma.
Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many are common karma and how many are uncommon karma?
All are uncommon karma; all do not follow along with karma.
Of the four great elements, how many are causes and how many are not causes? All are causes.
Of the four great elements, how many have causes and how many are causeless?
All things have causes; all things have conditions; all things have objects; all things are conditioned.
Of the four great elements, how many are cognizable and how many are non-cognizable?
All are "knowing," as they are known and seen according to their respective objects.
Regarding the four great elements, how many are consciousness and how many are non-consciousness?
All are consciousness, as they are cognized according to their respective objects.
All are fully understood, known and seen according to reality.
Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
All are not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
Regarding the four great elements (mahābhūta), how many are cultivated (bhāvita) and how many are not cultivated? All are not cultivated.
Regarding the four great elements, how many are realized (sākṣātkṛta) and how many are not realized?
All are realized as they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the four great elements, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
All are indeterminate.
Of the four great elements, how many are trainee (śaikṣa), how many are beyond training (aśaikṣa), and how many are neither trainee nor beyond training?
All are neither trainee nor beyond training.
Of the four great elements, how many are fruition (vipāka), how many are subject to fruition (vipākadharmā), and how many are neither fruition nor subject to fruition?
All [elements] are of two kinds: either retribution (*vipāka*) or neither-retribution-nor-non-retribution-dharma (*na-vipāka-na-avipāka-dharma*).
What is the earth element as retribution?
That which is experienced as the earth element is called the earth element as retribution.
What is the retribution of the earth element?
That which is produced by the karma and afflictions of the earth element, and is comprised within my own portion, is called the retribution of the earth element.
What is the earth element that is neither retribution nor subject to retribution?
The external earth element is called the earth element that is neither resultant nor a cause of result.
The water, fire, and wind elements are also like this.
Of these four great elements, how many are abandoned by vision, how many are abandoned by cultivation, and how many are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
All [factors] are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.

Regarding the four great elements, how many have insight as their cause of abandonment, how many have cultivation as their cause of abandonment, and how many have neither insight nor cultivation as their cause of abandonment?

All three categories are either causes for abandonment through seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*), causes for abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), or causes for neither abandonment through seeing nor abandonment through cultivation.
What is the earth element that is a cause for abandonment through seeing?
If the great earth element that is the retribution of a dharma abandoned by seeing is called the great earth element with the cause of being abandoned by seeing.
What is the great earth element with the cause of being abandoned by cultivation?
The great earth element that is the retribution of a dharma abandoned by cultivation is called the great earth element with the cause of being abandoned by cultivation.
What is the earth element that is neither a cause for abandonment by insight nor for abandonment by cultivation?

The earth element that is a result of wholesome dharmas, being neither a result nor a dharma subject to ripening, is called the earth element that is neither a cause for abandonment by insight nor for abandonment by cultivation.
The same applies to the elements of water, fire, and wind.

Regarding the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), and how many are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*)?
All [elements] are twofold, being either bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) bound to the desire realm?
The earth element that is associated with the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and is tainted (*sāsrava*) is called "bound to the desire realm."
What is the earth element bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃyukta*)?
The earth element that is associated with the outflows of form (*rūpāsrava*) and is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) is called "bound to the realm of form.
The same applies to the water, fire, and wind elements.
Of the four great elements, how many are past, how many are future, and how many are present?
All are threefold: either past, or future, or present.
What is the past earth element?
When the earth element has arisen and ceased, it is called "past.
What is the earth element that is "future"?
When the earth element has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, it is called "future."
What is the present earth element?
That which has arisen from the earth element but has not yet ceased is called "present.
The same applies to the water, fire, and wind elements.
Chapter Ten: On the Upāsaka. From the *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Question Section, Chapter Ten on the Upāsaka.
Question: Is this one an upāsaka?
Answer: Yes. Who is an upāsaka?
These are lay followers (upāsaka) of that Buddha.
Of which Buddha? Of Śākyamuni Buddha.
What is the merit of a lay follower?
It is the Dharma.
What is this Dharma?
Detachment from desire.
What is detachment from desire?
It is cessation.
What is cessation? Nirvana.
To what extent is one designated as an upāsaka?

If a person possesses the male faculties and characteristics, whose mind is not deranged, who is not oppressed by suffering, and who desires to become an upāsaka, he turns toward the Exalted One with his mind directed toward him as his master; relying on equanimity and finding joy therein, at a time when the Wheel of Dharma has not yet been turned and the Saṅgha does not yet exist, he receives the two teachings orally:
taking refuge in the Buddha and taking refuge in the Dharma.
Having received these two words, one is immediately named an upāsaka.
As a verse says:
"Free from the stains of afflictions and latent tendencies, One realizes the foremost, eternal tranquility."
The Subduer, known as Immeasurable, spoke thus for the sake of Trapusa:
"Take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma; these are the stainless, unsurpassed jewels.
Since there is no third jewel, he taught that one should rely upon these two jewels."
"It is not that he wishes to harm them; the Great Sage has nothing with which to be stingy.
This is the proper meaning of this Dharma; the Great Sage does not disparage the Saṃgha.
Once the Wheel of Dharma had been turned, there was a community of noble ones; he then spoke the Three Utterances, whereby they received the Three Teachings orally:
"I take refuge in the Buddha, I take refuge in the Dharma, and I take refuge in the Saṃgha.
Having received these three utterances, one is immediately called an upāsaka.
As the Buddha said:
“There are many places of refuge—mountains and crags, trees, groves, and shrines;
these are sought because one is oppressed by suffering.
But this refuge is not secure; this refuge is not supreme.”
By taking refuge in this place, one cannot escape all suffering.
But by taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and by correctly contemplating the Four Noble Truths—
that suffering arises from its origin— one can extinguish both suffering and its origin.
The Eightfold Noble Path is the secure and peaceful way that leads inevitably to the state of the Deathless;
this refuge is the most secure, this refuge is the supreme.
By taking refuge in this place, one is able to leave behind all suffering.
Question: How many precepts does an upāsaka have? Answer:
Five. What are the five?
Refraining from taking life for as long as one lives is the precept of an upāsaka.
To refrain from stealing for the duration of one's life is a lay follower’s precept.
To refrain from sexual misconduct for the duration of one's life is a lay follower’s precept.
To refrain from false speech for the duration of one's life is a lay follower’s precept.
To refrain from drinking alcohol for as long as one lives is a precept of an upāsaka.
Thus, these five precepts of an upāsaka must be received and observed for the duration of one's life without transgression.
To what extent does one become an upāsaka who maintains the precepts?

If an upāsaka constantly maintains these five precepts—practicing them with protection, with proximity, without deficiency, without confusion, without turbidity, and without admixture—and acts in accordance with the precepts, he is called an upāsaka who maintains the precepts.
As the verse says:
"The wise person who upholds the precepts, Hoping for the three kinds of happiness,
Honors them and gains benefit, Ultimately receiving the bliss of the heavens."
"Seeing such places as these, the wise are able to abandon evil;
those of sharp faculties who uphold the pure precepts shall always attain the foremost bliss.
What is the taking of life?

If, conceiving the notion that they are living beings, one intentionally severs the life of a living being—whether the time of death has not yet arrived or the time has arrived but death has not yet occurred—one instructs them to kill, sever their life, and not allow them to live; and having heard those words, once that time has passed and that life has been extinguished, [the victim] falls to the ground.

Such bodily and verbal actions, being those of sentient beings, constitute the taking of life—whether one has already taken the life of a sentient being, is about to take it, or is not yet certain to take it; that is the karmic action of killing.
One who performs that action is called a person who takes life.
What is the precept of an upāsaka regarding non-killing?

If one does not delight in that action, but rather distances oneself from it, refrains from doing it, guards against its violation, cuts off its root, abandons what is unwholesome, and practices what is wholesome with endurance, this is called non-killing; this is the precept of an upāsaka.
As the Buddha said:
"Neither killing nor inciting others to kill, nor encouraging others to kill;
through all forms of meditative concentration, through fearlessness, and through great renown,"
"Towards all sentient beings, I completely renounce all weapons and staves.
What is taking what is not given?
If there is someone who takes what is not given—whether in a village or in the mountains and marshes—if another has not given it, one takes that other's property with a thieving mind.

Whether traveling with others or interacting with them, if one perceives another's property as belonging to oneself, gives rise to a mind of theft, harbors longing, cherishes it, and treats it as one’s own;

and if through such bodily and verbal actions one takes it away or brings it here, removes it from its original place, shifts its location, destroys seals or markers, or carries it across a boundary—such action constitutes taking what is not given (*adattādāna*).
One who performs that action is called a person who takes what is not given.
What is non-stealing as an upāsaka precept?

It is to take no pleasure in that action, to distance oneself from it, to refrain from performing it, to guard the precept without transgression, to sever its roots, to abandon the unwholesome roots, and to endure while practicing virtue; this is called the upāsaka precept of non-stealing.
As the Buddha said:
"Neither stealing nor inciting others to steal, neither taking nor carrying away,
nor even encouraging others to take— thus one is free from all forms of taking what is not given."
What is sexual misconduct?

If there is one who engages in illicit conduct with those protected by their mother, father, brother, sister, paternal aunt, maternal uncle, or by themselves, by the Dharma, by clan, by relatives, by a formal agreement, or even by a garland of flowers;
or if one engages in sexual intercourse with one’s own wife through an improper orifice—such karma constitutes illicit conduct.
If one performs those actions, one is called a person of wrong conduct.
What is non-sexual misconduct as a lay follower’s precept?

If one does not delight in those actions, but rather distances oneself from them, does not perform them, guards the precepts without transgression, cuts off their root, abandons what is unwholesome, and perseveres in performing what is wholesome—this is called non-sexual misconduct as a lay follower’s precept.
As the Buddha said:
"Abandoning unchaste conduct, one views desire as a pit of fire;
though one may not yet be free from desire, one's feet shall not trespass upon another's wife."
What is false speech?

If a person speaks falsely—whether among companions, in an assembly, among kinsmen, before noble persons, or in the presence of a ruler—or if someone requests another to bear witness, they speak according to what they know.

That person claims to know what he does not know, claims not to know what he knows, claims to have seen what he has not seen, and claims not to have seen what he has seen. Whether acting for himself or for another, or for the sake of wealth, he deliberately utters false speech among the assembly. He conceals what he has endured, what he has desired, what he has perceived, what he has conceived, and what his mind has known. Not having seen, he says he saw; having seen, he says he did not see. Not having heard, he says he heard; having heard, he says he did not hear. Not having perceived, he says he perceived; having perceived, he says he did not perceive. Not having cognized, he says he cognized; having cognized, he says he did not cognize. First he intends to speak falsely, while speaking he knows it is false, and after speaking he knows it is false.
Thus, with a deceitful mind, for the sake of wealth, if one collects sounds, syllables, phrases, and verbal instructions through the mouth, this is the karma of false speech.
One who practices such actions is called a person of false speech.
What is the precept of refraining from false speech for a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?

It is to take no pleasure in that karma, to distance oneself from it, not to commit it, to guard the precepts without transgression, to sever its roots, to abandon what is unwholesome, and to endure while practicing what is wholesome; this is called the precept of refraining from false speech for a lay follower.
As the Buddha said:
"Whether in a companion's company or among a multitude, may each and every one refrain from false speech;
neither speaking it oneself nor encouraging others to do so, may one be free from all falsehood."
What is the basis for negligence that is drinking intoxicants?

If there is the basis for negligence that is drinking intoxicants—whether it be liquor, fermented grain spirits, sugarcane wine, grape wine, honey wine, or other types of alcohol—if one drinks such intoxicants or takes pleasure in them, even to the extent of sprinkling a single drop upon the body or onto a blade of grass, that action constitutes the basis for negligence that is drinking intoxicants.
If one engages in those actions, such a person is called one who drinks alcohol and is heedless.
What is the abstention from drinking alcohol and heedlessness that constitutes the precept of an upāsaka?

If one does not delight in those actions, but rather distances oneself from them, refrains from committing them, guards the precepts without transgression, cuts off their roots, abandons the unwholesome roots, and is capable of enduring while practicing virtue—this is called the state of abstaining from drinking alcohol and being heedless, which constitutes the precept of an upāsaka.
As the Buddha said:
"The noble one should abstain from liquor, nor should they give it to others;
neither drinking it nor encouraging its enjoyment—know this to be a ground for heedlessness."
Knowing this to be an unwholesome path, the arrogant fool persists in it;
knowing this state to be unwholesome, one guards oneself through the virtue of precepts.
One does not kill nor steal, speaks truthfully, and abstains from intoxicants.
Abstaining from sexual misconduct and severing the dharma of desire, Not eating at night or at improper times;
Being humble and not using high beds, Finding delight in tranquility, listening, and the joy of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
Not using flower garlands or scented ointments— These are called the eight precepts of the fast (*aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa*).
Observing the fast at that time, the wise person gives food as alms and makes offerings of food and drink to the Saṅgha, without negligence or craving.
They honor their parents and seek wealth and goods in accordance with the Dharma.
"By personally cultivating one's household duties, one attains birth in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Regarding the five precepts, how many are form (rūpa) and how many are non-form (arūpa)? All are form.
Of the five precepts, how many are visible and how many are invisible?
All are invisible.
Of the five precepts, how many are with resistance and how many are without resistance?
All are non-reactive.
Regarding the five precepts, how many are noble and how many are non-noble?
All are non-noble.
Regarding the five precepts: how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?

All are with outflows; all are accompanied by craving (*tṛṣṇā*); all involve seeking (*prārthana*); all are subject to appropriation (*upādāna*); all involve grasping (*parigraha*); and all are subject to surpassing.
Regarding the five precepts: how many are acquired and how many are not acquired?
All are not acquired; all are external.
Regarding the five precepts: how many have retribution and how many are without retribution?
All [these] have retribution.
Regarding the five precepts, how many are mental and how many are non-mental?
All are non-mental.
Of the five precepts, how many are associated with the mind (*citta-saṃprayukta*) and how many are not associated with the mind?
All are not associated with the mind.
Of the five precepts, how many are mental factors (*caitasika*) and how many are not mental factors?
All are not mental concomitants (*citta-saṃskāra*).
Of the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), how many have objects (*sālambana*) and how many are without objects?
All are without objects.
Of the five precepts, how many are associated with the mind (*cittasamprayukta*) and how many are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*)?
All are dissociated from the mind; all do not follow the mind in their transformation (*na cittānuvartin*).
Of the five precepts, how many are karma (*karman*) and how many are not karma?
Regarding all actions:
among the five precepts, how many are associated with action (*karmasamprayukta*) and how many are not associated with action?
All are not associated with action.
Of the five precepts, how many are common karma and how many are not common karma?
All are non-common karma; all do not follow along with karma.
Of the five precepts, how many are causes and how many are not causes?
Regarding all causes:
among the five precepts, how many have causes and how many are causeless?
All have causes; all have origins; all have conditions; all are conditioned.
Regarding the five precepts, how many are known and how many are not known?
All are known, as they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the five precepts, how many are cognized and how many are not cognized?
Regarding all consciousnesses, mental consciousness cognizes according to the object;
it understands everything and comprehends everything.
Of the five precepts, how many are known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), and how many are not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
All are known by the knowledge of non-interruption (*anuccheda-jñāna*).
Regarding the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), how many are cultivated (*bhāvita*) and how many are not cultivated?
All are cultivated.
Regarding the five precepts: how many are realized (*sākṣātkṛta*) and how many are not realized?
All are realized, as they are known and seen according to their actual nature.
Regarding the five precepts: how many are wholesome (*kuśala*), how many are unwholesome (*akuśala*), and how many are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
All are wholesome.
Regarding the five precepts, how many are trainings (*śaikṣa*), how many are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and how many are neither training nor beyond training?
All are neither training nor beyond training.
Regarding the five precepts: how many are results (*vipāka*), how many are subject to results (*vipākadharmas*), and how many are neither results nor subject to results?
All are subject to results. Regarding the five precepts:
how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and how many are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
All [factors] are neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding the five precepts, how many have insight as their cause, how many have cultivation as their cause, and how many have neither insight nor cultivation as their cause?
All [factors] have as their cause neither what is abandoned by insight nor what is abandoned by cultivation.
Regarding the five precepts: how many are bound to the desire realm, how many are bound to the form realm, how many are bound to the formless realm, and how many are unbound?
Regarding all factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*),
among the five precepts (*pañca-śīla*), how many are past, how many are future, how many are present, and how many are neither past, nor future, nor present?
All [precepts] consist of three temporal divisions: past, future, or present.
What is meant by the past non-killing precept?
Once the non-killing precept has arisen and subsequently ceased, it is called "past."
What is the precept of non-killing in the future?
The precept of non-killing that has not yet arisen and not yet emerged is called "future.
What is the precept of non-killing in the present?
When the precept against killing has arisen but not yet ceased, it is called "present.
This applies likewise to the precepts up to and including the precept against drinking alcohol and the precept of non-negligence.

Non-Question Section 1: Chapter on Elements (Dhātuvarga), Part One. The realm of form and the realm of non-form.
The visible realm and the invisible realm.
The realm of resistance and the realm without resistance;
the noble realm and the non-noble realm;
the tainted realm and the untainted realm.
There is the realm of craving and the realm free from craving.
There is the realm of seeking and the realm free from seeking.
There is the realm to be grasped and the realm not to be grasped.
There is the realm with grasping and the realm without grasping.
There is the superior realm and the non-superior realm.
There is the realm of sensation and the realm that is not sensation.
The internal sphere and the external sphere;
the sphere of retribution and the sphere without retribution;
the mental sphere and the non-mental sphere.
The realm associated with the mind and the realm not associated with the mind;
the realm that is a mental factor and the realm that is not a mental factor;
the realm that is an object-condition and the realm that is not an object-condition.
The realm associated with the mind and the realm not associated with the mind;
the realm that follows the mind and the realm that does not follow the mind;
the realm of karma and the realm that is not karma.
The realm of karmic retribution and the realm not of karmic retribution;
the realm associated with karma, the realm not associated with karma, and the realm neither associated with nor dissociated from karma.
The realm of common karma and the realm of uncommon karma;
the realm that evolves in accordance with karma and the realm that does not evolve in accordance with karma;
the causal realm and the non-causal realm.
There is the realm with cause and the realm without cause.
There is the realm with continuity and the realm without continuity.
There is the realm with conditions and the realm without conditions.
The conditioned realm and the unconditioned realm;
the realm of wisdom and the realm of non-wisdom;
the realm of consciousness and the realm of non-consciousness.
The realm of liberation and the realm not of liberation;
the realm of full comprehension and the realm not of full comprehension;
the realm known through the knowledge of abandonment and the realm not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
The realm of abandonment and the realm of non-abandonment;
the realm of cultivation and the realm of non-cultivation;
the realm of realization and the realm of non-realization.
There is the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder and the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.
There is the wholesome realm, the unwholesome realm, and the indeterminate realm.
There is the realm of those in training, the realm of those beyond training, and the realm of neither those in training nor those beyond training.
The realm of retribution, the realm of dharmas that are retribution, and the realm of dharmas that are neither retribution nor productive of retribution;
the realm of abandonment through vision, the realm of abandonment through cultivation, and the realm of dharmas that are neither abandoned through vision nor abandoned through cultivation.
The realm of causes abandoned by vision, the realm of causes abandoned by cultivation, and the realm of causes neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation;
the inferior realm, the middling realm, and the superior realm.
The coarse element, the subtle element;

the minute element, the arising element, the emerging element, the transcending element, the diligent element, the sustaining element, the exiting element, the abandoning element, the element of dispassion, and the element of cessation.
The realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
The realm of form and the non-form realm.
The realm of cessation and the three realms of transcendence.
The past element, the future element, the present element, and the element that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
The past objective-element, the future objective-element, the present objective-element, and the objective-element that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
The realm bound to the desire realm, the realm bound to the form realm, the realm bound to the formless realm, and the unbound realm.
The realm of form, the realm of feeling, the realm of perception, the realm of formations, and the realm of consciousness.
The five elements of departure and the six elements of departure:
the earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element;
the element of pleasure, the element of pain, the element of joy, the element of grief, and the element of equanimity.
The element of ignorance, the element of desire, the element of ill will, and the element of harmfulness;
the element of renunciation, the element of non-ill will, the element of non-harmfulness, the element of light, and the element of purity.
The realm of form, the realm of infinite space, the realm of infinite consciousness, the realm of nothingness, and the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are the eighteen realms.
What is the realm of form?
If a phenomenon is form, it is called the realm of form.
What is the non-form realm?
If a phenomenon is not form, it is called the non-form realm.
What is the visible realm?
The sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*); this is called the visible realm.
What is the invisible realm?
Excluding the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), all other phenomena are called the invisible element (*anidarśana-dhātu*).
What is the resistant element (*sapratigha-dhātu*)?
The ten bases of form are called the resistant element.
What is the non-resistant element (*apratigha-dhātu*)?
The sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*); these are called the non-resistant element.
What is the noble element (*ārya-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the noble realm (*āryadhātu*).
What is the non-noble realm?
If a phenomenon is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called the non-noble realm.
What is the realm with outflows (*sāsrava-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is accompanied by craving, it is called the realm with outflows.
What is the realm without outflows (*anāsrava-dhātu*)?
If phenomena are free from craving, they are called the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
What is the realm with craving?
If phenomena involve seeking, they are called the realm with craving (*sāsrava-dhātu*).
What is the realm of non-craving?
If a phenomenon is without seeking, it is called the realm of non-craving.
What is the realm of seeking?
If a phenomenon is subject to appropriation, it is called the realm of seeking (*saiṣaṇā-dhātu*).
What is the realm of non-seeking (*naiṣaṇā-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is not subject to appropriation, it is called the realm of non-seeking.
What is the sphere of what-is-to-be-appropriated (*upādānīya-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is subject to appropriation, it is called the sphere of what-is-to-be-appropriated.
What is the sphere of what-is-not-to-be-appropriated (*anupādānīya-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is without grasping, it is called the sphere of the non-graspable.
What is the sphere of the graspable?
If a phenomenon possesses excellence, it is called the sphere of the graspable.
What is the element without superiority?
If a phenomenon lacks superiority, it is called the element without superiority.
What is the element with superiority?
If a phenomenon involves grasping, it is called a realm with excellence.
What is a realm without excellence?
If a phenomenon does not involve grasping, it is called a realm without excellence.
What is the "element with a superior"?
If there is another element that is more excellent, sublime, and surpassing than a given dharma-element, this is called the "element with a superior.
What is the "element without a superior"?
If the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) has no other realm that is more excellent, sublime, or superior to it, this is called the unsurpassed realm (anuttara-dhātu).
What is the realm of sensation (vedanā-dhātu)?
If a dharma is internal, this is called the realm of sensation.
What is the non-appropriated element (*anupātta-dhātu*)?
Any phenomenon that is external is called the non-appropriated element.
What is the internal element (*ādhyātma-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is appropriated, it is called an internal element (*ādhyātmika-dhātu*).
What is an external element?
If a phenomenon is not appropriated, it is called an external element (*bāhya-dhātu*).
What is the realm with retribution?
If a phenomenon is a phenomenon that entails retribution, this is called the realm with retribution.
What is the realm without retribution?
If a phenomenon is retribution, or if it is neither retribution nor a phenomenon that leads to retribution, this is called the element of non-retribution (*avipāka-dhātu*).
What is the mental element (*citta-dhātu*)?
The sense-base of mind (*mano-āyatana*), this is called the mental element.
What is the non-mental element (*acittadhātu*)?
With the exception of the mind-base (*manāyatana*), all other phenomena are called the non-mental element.
What is the element associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayuktadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is a mental concomitant (*caitta*), it is called the "sphere associated with mind" (*cittasaṃprayukta-dhātu*).
What is the sphere not associated with mind?
If a phenomenon is not a mental concomitant, it is called the "sphere not associated with mind."
What is the mental concomitant element (*caitasika-dhātu*)?
With the exception of mind, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are called the mental concomitant element.
What is the non-mental-concomitant element?
If a phenomenon is neither an object-condition nor the mind, it is called the non-mental-factor element (*acaitasika-dhātu*).
What is the object-element (*ālambana-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon involves the grasping of marks and the mind, it is called the object-element.
What is the non-object-conditioned element (*anālambana-dhātu*)?
With the exception of mind, all other mental factors (*caitta*) are called the non-object-conditioned element.
What is the element associated with mind (*sacittaka-dhātu*)?

If a dharma evolves in accordance with the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind, it is called the "mind-associated element" (*sacittaka-dhātu*).
What is the "non-mind-associated element"?

If a dharma does not evolve in accordance with the mind, nor arises together with the mind, nor abides together with the mind, nor ceases together with the mind, it is called the "non-mind-associated element."
What is the realm that functions in accordance with the mind?
If a phenomenon arises together with the mind, abides together with the mind, and ceases together with the mind, it is called the realm that functions in accordance with the mind.
What is the realm that does not function in accordance with the mind?

If a phenomenon does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind, it is called the element that does not turn in accordance with the mind.
What is the element of action?
Bodily action, verbal action, and mental action; these are called the element of action.
What is the non-karmic sphere?
Excluding bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, all other phenomena are called the non-karmic sphere.
What is the sphere of karmic retribution?
If a phenomenon is a craving for phenomena or a wholesome fruition of phenomena, this is called the realm of karmic retribution (*karmavipāka-dhātu*).
What is the non-retribution realm?
If a phenomenon is a fruition, or neither a fruition nor a dharma subject to fruition, this is called the non-retribution realm.
What is the sphere associated with karma?
If a phenomenon is associated with volition (*cetanā*), it is called the sphere associated with karma.
What is the sphere not associated with karma?
If a dharma is not associated with volition (*cetanā*), it is called the element that is not associated with karma.
What is the element that is neither associated with karma nor not associated with karma?
Volition itself is called the element that is neither associated with karma nor not associated with karma.
What is the sphere of common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma-viṣaya*)?
If a phenomenon follows along with karma, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called the sphere of common karma.
What is the sphere of uncommon karma (*asādhāraṇa-karma-viṣaya*)?
If a phenomenon does not follow the transformation of karma, and does not arise, abide, or cease together with karma, this is called the non-common sphere of karma.
What is the sphere that follows the transformation of karma?
If phenomena arise, abide, and cease together with karma, these are called the elements that follow the transformation of karma.
What are the elements that do not follow the transformation of karma?
If phenomena do not arise, abide, or cease together with karma, these are called the elements that do not follow the transformation of karma.
What is the causal element (*hetudhātu*)?

Whether a phenomenon is a condition (*pratyaya*) or not a condition, if it has retribution (*savipāka*), or if it is not a condition—excluding the attainment of fruition (*phalaprāpti*)—the remaining wholesome retribution and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are called the causal element.
What is the non-causal realm (*ahetudhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is not a condition, is without retribution, and is the fruit obtained from non-common karma, this is called the non-causal realm.
What is the causal realm (*hetudhātu*)?
If a phenomenon has a continuity, it is called the realm with cause.
What is the realm without cause?
If a phenomenon lacks continuity, it is called the realm without cause.
What is the realm with a causal nexus (*sanidāna-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon has an object-condition (*sālambana*), it is called the realm with a causal nexus.
What is the realm without a causal nexus (*anidāna-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is without an object-condition (*ālambana*), it is called the realm of the non-sequential (*anantarya-dhātu*).
What is the realm with an object-condition?
If a phenomenon is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is called the realm with an object-condition.
What is the objectless realm (*anālambana-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called the objectless realm.
What is the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛta-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon has an object-condition, it is called the conditioned realm (*saṃskṛtadhātu*).
What is the unconditioned realm?
If a phenomenon lacks an object-condition, it is called the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*).
What is the knowledge of the elements (*dhātu*)?
To know all phenomena as they truly are through knowledge and vision—this is called the knowledge of the elements.
What is the non-knowledge of the elements?
There is no non-cognitive element (*avijñānadhātu*).
Furthermore, it is said that all phenomena are not known through a cognition that perceives them as they truly are; this is called the non-cognitive element.
What is the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*)?
All phenomena are consciousness; the consciousness that cognizes objects as they are is called the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).
What is the non-element of consciousness?
There is no such thing as a non-element of consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said: all phenomena are not consciousnesses that cognize objects as they truly are; this is called the non-consciousness element (*avijñānadhātu*).
What is the element of understanding (*vijñānadhātu*)?
All phenomena are understood through knowledge and vision as they truly are; this is called the element of understanding.
What is the non-analytical element (*apratisaṃkhyā-dhātu*)?
There is no such thing as a non-analytical element.
Furthermore, it is said: all phenomena are not analytically discerned; knowing and seeing them as they truly are is called the non-analytical element.
What is the realm of thorough comprehension (*parijñeya-dhātu*)?
To thoroughly comprehend all phenomena by knowing and seeing them as they truly are—this is called the realm of thorough comprehension.
What is the realm that is not thoroughly comprehended (*aparijñeya-dhātu*)?
The non-cognizable realm (*aparijñeya-dhātu*).
Furthermore, it is said that all phenomena are not cognizable in the sense of being known and seen as they truly are; this is called the non-cognizable realm.
What is the realm known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*)?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome, it is called the realm known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the realm not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
If a phenomenon is wholesome or indeterminate, it is called the realm not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the realm of abandonment (*prahāṇadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome, it is called the realm of abandonment.
What is the non-realm of abandonment?
Whether a phenomenon is wholesome or indeterminate, it is called the non-abandonment realm (*aprahāṇadhātu*).
What is the cultivation realm (*bhāvanādhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is wholesome, it is called the cultivation realm.
What is the non-cultivated element (*abhāvitadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome (*akuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is called the non-cultivated element.
What is the realized element (*sākṣātkṛtadhātu*)?
To realize all phenomena as they truly are through knowledge and vision is called the realm of realization (*adhigama-dhātu*).
What is the non-realm of realization?
There is no such thing as a non-realm of realization.
Furthermore, it is said: all phenomena are not realized through knowledge and vision as they truly are; this is called the "unrealized realm" (*apratisaṃvid-dhātu*).
What is the realm of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?
As the Blessed One has said:
What are those two nirvāṇa realms? Which two?
The nirvāṇa realm with remainder and the nirvāṇa realm without remainder.
What is *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*?
It refers to this bhikṣu who is an arhat, whose taints are exhausted, who has accomplished what was to be done, who has laid down the heavy burden, and who has attained his own benefit.

This is the exhaustion of all afflictions through right knowledge; one attains liberation regarding the aggregates, elements, and sense bases. Because one still dwells due to the conditions of past karma, the mind experiences various forms of suffering and pleasure, including what is agreeable and disagreeable; this is called the realm of nirvana with remainder.
What is the realm of nirvana without remainder?
It refers to the extinction of the five aggregates of a bhikṣu, such that the five aggregates of the future no longer continue to arise; this is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
What is the wholesome realm?
If a phenomenon is cultivated, it is called the wholesome realm.
What is the unwholesome realm?
If a phenomenon is to be abandoned, it is called the unwholesome element (*akuśala-dhātu*).
What is the indeterminate element (*avyākṛta-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is either a feeling (*vedanā*) or a phenomenon that is neither a karmic result (*vipāka*) nor a cause for a karmic result (*avipāka-dharma*), this is called the indeterminate element.
What is the realm of training (*śaikṣadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is noble (*ārya*) but not beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is called the realm of training.
What is the realm of no-more-training (*aśaikṣadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is noble but not that of one in training, it is called the realm of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadhātu*).
What is the realm of neither-training-nor-beyond-training?
If a phenomenon is not noble, it is called the realm of neither-training-nor-beyond-training.
What is the realm of retribution (*vipākadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is felt (*vedita*) or is a wholesome retribution, this is called the realm of retribution.
What is the realm of phenomena that are retribution (*vipākadharmadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon has retribution, it is called the dharma-realm of retribution.
What is the dharma-realm that is neither retribution nor a phenomenon subject to retribution?
If a phenomenon is indeterminate and is not comprised within my own sphere, it is called the dharma-realm that is neither retribution nor a phenomenon subject to retribution.
What is the realm of abandonment through vision (*darśana-prahātavya-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome and is not abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), it is called the realm of abandonment through vision.
What is the realm of abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome and not abandoned through insight, it is called the realm of abandonment through cultivation.
What is the realm that is neither abandoned through insight nor abandoned through cultivation?
If a phenomenon is wholesome or indeterminate, it is called the realm that is neither abandoned through insight nor abandoned through cultivation.
What is the element of causes abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetu-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is the retribution of a phenomenon abandoned by insight, this is called the element of causes abandoned by insight.
What is the element of causes abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-hetu-dhātu*)?
If a dharma is abandoned through reflection, or if a dharma is the retribution of a dharma abandoned through reflection, this is called the element of causes abandoned through reflection.
What is the element of causes that is neither abandoned through seeing nor abandoned through reflection?

Whether a phenomenon is wholesome, or a phenomenon that is the fruit of a wholesome phenomenon, or a phenomenon that is neither a fruit nor a cause for a fruit—this is called the element of causes that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the inferior realm?
Any phenomena that are unwholesome are called the inferior realm.
What is the intermediate realm?
If a phenomenon is indeterminate, it is called the intermediate realm (*madhyadhātu*).
What is the superior realm (*viśiṣṭadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is wholesome, it is called the superior realm.
What is the inferior realm?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome or indeterminate, it is called the inferior realm.
What is the intermediate realm?
If a phenomenon is not noble and wholesome, it is called the intermediate realm (*madhyadhātu*).
What is the superior realm (*viśeṣadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is noble and untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the superior realm.
What is the coarse realm (*audārika-dhātu*)?
Those phenomena that are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are called the coarse realm.
What is the subtle realm (*sūkṣma-dhātu*)?
If phenomena are bound to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or are unbound, these are called the subtle realm (*sūkṣma-dhātu*).
What is the minute realm (*aṇu-dhātu*)?
If phenomena are bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, these are called the minute realm.

Furthermore, the coarse realm (*audārika-dhātu*) refers to those phenomena that are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-pratisaṃyukta*); these are called the coarse realm.
Furthermore, regarding the subtle realm (*sūkṣmadhātu*): if a phenomenon is unconditioned by the realms of existence, it is called the subtle realm.
What is the minute realm (*saudhārmadhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is called the minute realm.
What is the element of exertion (*vyāyāma-dhātu*)?
When one exerts oneself, correctly generates, brings forth, contacts, and realizes [the goal], this is called the element of exertion.
What is the element of emergence (*niḥsaraṇa-dhātu*)?
If one advances but has not yet crossed over the broad expanse, this is called "leaving the boundary.
How does one cross over the boundary?
If one advances and has already crossed over the broad expanse, this is called "crossing over the boundary."
What is the element of diligence?
The power of diligence is called the element of diligence.
What is the element of maintenance?
To maintain the realm through total retention is called "maintaining the realm.
What is "exiting the realm"?
To exit from exiting the realm is called "exiting the realm."
Furthermore, the element of exertion (*vīrya-dhātu*) refers to the exertion of diligence (*vīrya*). What is diligence?
It is when the body and mind give rise to transcendence, applying the mind without regression, and proceeding with diligent effort and right progress; this is called the element of exertion.
Furthermore, the "holding of the elements" (dhātudhara) refers to mindfulness (*smṛti*).
What is this mindfulness?

It is the holding of those dharmas as they have been heard and studied, maintaining them correctly so that they remain; it is the non-forgetfulness of the mental image (*saṃjñā*) and the continuous succession of moments of mindfulness—this is called the holding of the elements.

Furthermore, "the realm of emergence" refers to the abandonment of all outflows (*āsrava*), the exhaustion [of defilements], the cessation of craving, and *nirvāṇa*; this is called the realm of emergence.
What is the "realm of abandonment"?

If a bhikṣu, in the shade of trees or in an open space, contemplates the body in this way—observing the evil of bodily conduct and its retribution, both in the present life and in future lives—and abandons unwholesome bodily conduct while cultivating wholesome bodily conduct; this is the realm of abandonment.

Thus, one contemplates the evil retributions for evil conduct of speech and mind—both retributions in this life and in future lives—and abandons evil conduct of speech and mind while cultivating good conduct of speech and mind; this is called the "realm of abandonment."
What is the realm of detachment?
