The exhaustion of craving, detachment, and nirvana—this is called the realm of detachment.
What is the realm of cessation?
The exhaustion of craving, detachment, cessation, and nirvāṇa—this is called the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
What is the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)?

From the Avīci Great Hell above, up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmitavaśavartin*), whatever constitutes the divisions of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called the realm of desire.
What is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
From the Brahma heavens up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, whatever constitutes the divisions of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called the realm of form.
What is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?

From the Ākāśānantyāyatana heaven up to the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana heaven, if there are the constituents of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, these are called the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
What is the form realm (rūpadhātu)?
If a dharma is material, it is called the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
What is the non-material realm?
Excluding the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), the remaining non-material dharmas constitute the realm of non-form; this is called the non-material realm.
What is the element of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*)?

There are two cessations: cessation through the object of knowledge (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through the object of knowledge (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); this is called the element of cessation.
What is the triple element of emergence (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*)?
As the Blessed One has said:
"There are three realms of transcendence.
What are these three realms of transcendence?
This refers to emerging from the desire realm to reach the form realm, and emerging from the form realm to reach the formless realm.
When that which has been performed and accumulated is extinguished, this is called "emerging.
What is meant by "emerging from the desire realm to reach the form realm"?
If there is a defiled fever arising from conditions related to desire, and that does not exist within form, this is called "emerging from desire and reaching form.
What is meant by "emerging from form and reaching the formless"?
If there is a defiled fever arising from conditions related to form, and that does not exist within the formless, this is called "emerging from form and reaching the formless."
What is the cessation of what has been done and accumulated?
If there is the feverish distress of outflows arising conditioned by formations, and that [distress] is absent in nirvāṇa, this is called the cessation of what has been done and accumulated.
This is called emergence.
These are known as the three realms of emergence.
What is the past realm?
If a phenomenon has arisen and then ceased, this is called the past realm (*atīta-dhātu*).
What is the future realm (*anāgata-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon has not yet arisen and has not yet appeared, this is called the future realm.
What is the present element?
If a phenomenon has not yet ceased, it is called the present element.
What is that which is neither past, nor future, nor present element?
If a phenomenon is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called the realm that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
What is the realm of the past object?
To contemplate the past, or for a phenomenon to arise [in relation to the past], this is called the realm of the past object.
What is the sphere of future objects?
To contemplate the future, or any phenomena that have not yet arisen—this is called the sphere of future objects.
What is the sphere of present objects?
Contemplating present phenomena: if a phenomenon arises, this is called the sphere of the present realm.
What is the sphere of the realm that is neither past, nor future, nor present?
Contemplating that which is neither past, nor future, nor present—whatever phenomenon arises is called the sphere of the realm that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
What is the element bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is associated with the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called the element bound to the desire realm.
What is the element bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon is subject to the outflows of form (*rūpāsrava*) and is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called the element bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dhātu*).
What is the element bound to the realm of formlessness?
If a phenomenon is subject to the outflows of formlessness (*ārūpyāsrava*) and is with outflows, it is called the element bound to the realm of formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dhātu*).
What is the realm that is not bound (*apratisaṃyukta-dhātu*)?
If a phenomenon within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is noble and untainted (*anāsrava*), this is called the realm that is not bound.
What is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
The aggregate of form is called the element of form.
What is the element of feeling?
The aggregate of feeling is called the element of feeling.
What is the element of perception?
The aggregate of perception is called the element of perception.
What is the element of formations?
The aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) is called the element of formations (saṃskāra-dhātu).
What is the element of consciousness (vijñāna-dhātu)?
The aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) is called the element of consciousness.
What are the five elements of transcendence?
As the Blessed One has taught the five elements of transcendence.
What are the five?
It means that when a bhikṣu contemplates desire, his mind does not incline toward it;

he is not impure, does not abide in it, and does not understand it. He contemplates the mind of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa-citta*); with a mind of renunciation, he inclines toward purity, abides in it, and understands it. His mind becomes well-directed, well-tamed, and well-cultivated. If, regarding desire, there arises a mind of renunciation and understanding, then the outflows (*āsrava*), burning fevers, and attachments born of the object of desire are renounced and abandoned; he does not undergo such suffering. This is called "renouncing the realm of desire" (*kāmadhātu-niḥsaraṇa*).

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu contemplates ill-will, his mind does not incline toward it; he does not dwell in impurity, nor does he understand it. When he contemplates non-ill-will, his mind is free from anger;

his mind inclines toward purity, dwells in it, and understands it. His mind becomes virtuous, exceedingly well-tamed, and well-cultivated. If his mind emerges from, understands, and arises above ill-will—if, by taking ill-will as its object, he gives rise to the emergence and detachment from the outflows (*āsrava*) and the burning heat born of it—he does not experience that suffering. This is called "emerging from the realm of ill-will."
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu contemplates harm, at the time of contemplating harm, his mind does not incline toward harm; it is not pure, does not abide, and is not liberated.

When he contemplates non-harm, his non-harming mind inclines toward purity, abides, and is liberated. His mind becomes well-directed, exceedingly well-tamed, and well-cultivated. If his mind emerges from and is liberated regarding harm, and if the outflows, torments, and fevers arising from the condition of harm are abandoned through that emergence and liberation, and he does not experience such suffering, this is called the element of emergence from harm.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu contemplates form, his mind does not incline toward form; it is not clear, does not abide, and is not liberated. When he contemplates the formless, his mind inclines toward the formless;

it becomes clear, abides, and is liberated. His mind becomes well-directed, well-tamed, and well-cultivated. The mind emerges from and is liberated regarding form; through the emergence and liberation from the outflows, the burning heat arising conditioned by form, he does not experience this suffering. This is called "emerging from the realm of form."
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates his own body; his mind does not incline toward it, does not become defiled, does not remain attached, and does not fail to understand it.

He contemplates the cessation of his own body; as he ceases [attachment to] his own body, his mind inclines toward purity, remains settled, and understands. His mind becomes well-directed, well-tamed, and well-cultivated. If, regarding his own body, a liberation arises from emergence, and through that emergence he gives rise to a liberation that is free from the outflows, the burning heat, and the emergence [of attachment] based on his own body, he does not experience such suffering. This is called "emerging from the sphere of one's own body."
These are called the five elements of transcendence.
What are the six elements of transcendence?
They are as the Blessed One has taught regarding the six elements of transcendence.
Suppose a bhikkhu were to say this to another bhikkhu: "Bhikkhu!

I have approached and frequently cultivated a mind of loving-kindness, making it my vehicle and my practice, being diligent, mindful, and well-resolved; yet I am still overwhelmed by a mind of ill will."
That bhikṣu rebuked this bhikṣu: "Bhikṣu!
Do not speak in such a manner; do not slander the Blessed One."
"It is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak thus.
Monks! This is not a ground for expectation."

If one has drawn near to and extensively cultivated the mind of loving-kindness, having made it a vehicle and a practice, having been diligent, mindful, and well-advanced, it is impossible that the mind would be shrouded by ill-will.
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus!
Having emerged from a mind of ill will, one should cultivate and frequently practice the wholesome, liberated mind of loving-kindness until it becomes immeasurable."
Furthermore, a bhikkhu says this to another bhikkhu: "Bhikkhu!
I have cultivated the mind of compassion through frequent practice; I am diligent, attentive, conscious, and well-advancing, yet I am still overcome by a harmful state of mind."
That bhikkhu rebuked this bhikkhu, saying: "Bhikkhu!
Do not speak in such a manner; do not slander the Blessed One."
"It is not good to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak thus.
Monks! This is not a ground for hope."

If, having cultivated and frequently practiced a mind of compassionate understanding, having established it as a vehicle and made it one's own, having been diligent, having attained clear comprehension, and having advanced with skill, one would then allow a mind of harm to cover [the heart], such a thing is impossible.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks! Having eliminated a mind of malice, one should cultivate and extensively train in a mind of compassion or an immeasurable state."
Furthermore, a bhikkhu says this to another bhikkhu:

"I am one who delights in liberation of mind, who approaches it and practices it extensively, who acts as a vehicle and acts as a foundation, who is prudent, mindful, and well-energetic; yet, for that reason, I am still overwhelmed by a lack of joy."
That bhikkhu rebuked this bhikkhu, saying: "Bhikkhu!
Do not speak in such a way; do not slander the Blessed One."
"It is not good to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak thus.
Monks! This is not a basis for hope."

If one has approached with a mind of joyful understanding, has practiced extensively, has made it a vehicle and a practice, has been conscientious, has possessed discernment, and has exerted oneself well, it is impossible that such a person would be overcome by a mind of dissatisfaction.
The Blessed One said:
"Monks! One should abandon the mind that finds no delight; rather, one should well cultivate and extensively train in the mind of joy and liberation, which is immeasurable."
Furthermore, a bhikkhu says this to another bhikkhu:

"I have abandoned and relinquished my mind of attachment, drawing near to and frequently practicing its cultivation; I am diligent, alert, and well-advanced. Yet, I am still overwhelmed by a mind of lust and hatred."
That bhikṣu rebuked this bhikṣu, saying:
"Do not speak thus; do not slander the Blessed One.
It is not good to slander the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not speak in such a way."
"Monks! This is not a possibility.

If one has cultivated and approached a mind of relinquishment, practiced it extensively and learned it well, mastered it as a vehicle and as an activity, been diligent, discerning, and well-exerted, it is impossible that there should still be craving or aversion to shroud the mind."
The World-Honored One said:
"O bhikṣus!
Having emerged from a mind of attachment and aversion, if one well cultivates and extensively trains in the immeasurable mind of equanimity and liberation."
Furthermore, a bhikṣu says this to him:

"I have closely approached and frequently cultivated the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), making it my vehicle and my practice; being diligent, conscious, and well-advanced, I therefore possess mindfulness, perception, and consciousness."
That bhikṣu rebuked this bhikṣu, saying: "Bhikṣu!
Do not speak in such a manner; do not slander the Blessed One."
"It is not good to slander the Blessed One; the Blessed One does not speak thus.
Monks, this is not a possibility.

If one has cultivated the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), has practiced it extensively, has mastered it, has applied oneself to it with care, has fully understood it, and has made excellent progress in it, it is impossible for there to be any perception, ideation, or consciousness."
The Blessed One said:
"Bhikṣus!
Having emerged from all perceptions, if one has well cultivated and extensively practiced the mind of the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) and the immeasurables (apramāṇa)."
Furthermore, a bhikṣu says this to another bhikṣu:
"Because I have not extinguished the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' the arrow of doubt covers my mind.
That bhikṣu then rebukes this bhikṣu:
"Monks! Do not speak thus; do not slander the Blessed One.
It is not good to slander the Blessed One, for the Blessed One does not speak in such a way."
"Monks! This is not a ground for expectation.
It is impossible that one whose mind is shrouded by the arrow of doubt would [persist] because of the cessation of 'I' and 'mine'."
The Blessed One said:
"Monks! Extract the arrow of doubt, and sever the conceit of 'I am'."
These are called the six elements of emergence.
What is the earth element?
There are two types of earth element: the internal earth element and the external earth element.
What is the internal earth element?

Whatever is solid within this body—such as bones, teeth, hair of the head, hair of the body, thin skin, flesh, sinews, veins, spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, heart, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, large abdomen, and small abdomen—and whatever else is solid within this body, this is called the internal earth element.
What is the external earth element?

Whatever is external and not appropriated that is solid—such as copper, iron, lead, tin, white bell-metal, gold, silver, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, coral, coins, precious gems, sand, stones, grass, trees, branches, leaves, stalks, nodes, and other such external things that are not appropriated and are solid—this is called the external earth element.
Thus, the internal earth element and the external earth element are called the earth element.
What is the water element?
There are two water elements: the internal water element and the external water element.
What is the internal water element?

Whatever water is received within this body—saliva, phlegm, bile, sweat, fat, marrow, brain, grease, lymph, mucus, spittle, pus, blood, urine, and whatever else constitutes the moisture and watery components received within this body—is called the internal water element.
What is the external water element?

Whatever is the external water element that is not appropriated—such as ghee, oil, honey, rock sugar, dark stone honey, milk, curd, buttermilk, fermented grain wine, sugarcane wine, honey-wine, and other external waters that are not appropriated—this is called the external water element.
Such internal and external water elements are called the water element.
What is the fire element?
There are two fire elements: the internal fire element and the external fire element.
What is the internal fire element?

Whatever fire is experienced within this body—whether it is heat, or that which causes heat, causes the body to become hot, or causes internal burning; whatever digests food, drink, and so forth; and whatever other fire is experienced within this body—this is called the internal fire element.
What is the external fire element?

Whatever external fire is not experienced as heat—whether it be the heat of fire, the heat of the sun, the heat of a fire-gem, the heat of a house, the heat of a wall, the heat of a mountain, the heat of grain, the heat of grass, the heat of wood, the heat of cow dung, or any other external fire that is not experienced—it is called the external fire element.
Thus, the internal fire element and the external fire element are called the fire element.
What is the wind element?
There are two wind elements: the internal wind element and the external wind element.
What is the internal wind element?

Whatever winds are experienced within this body—the upward-moving wind, the downward-moving wind, the winds residing in the joints, the winds causing contraction and lameness, the winds moving through the bones and joints, the winds of exhalation and inhalation, and whatever other internal winds there may be—this is called the internal wind element.
What is the external wind element?

Whatever external wind is not appropriated—whether it be east wind or west wind, north wind or south wind, dust-laden wind or dust-free wind, cold wind or hot wind, black wind, *vairambha* wind, earth-shaking wind, or any other external wind that is not appropriated—this is called the external wind element.
Thus, internal wind and external wind are called the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
What is the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*)?
There are two space elements: the internal space element and the external space element.
What is the internal space element?

Whatever within this body is experienced as space and is not covered by the four great elements—whether it be the cavities of the ears, nose, and mouth, or the passages through which food and drink enter, or where they abide, or from which they exit, or whatever else within this body is experienced as space and is not covered by the four great elements—this is called the internal space element.
What is the external space element?

Whatever is external space that is not felt and is not covered by the four great elements—such as mounds, wells, jars, pots, pits, valleys, and other such external spaces that are not felt and are not covered by the four great elements—is called the external space element.
Thus, the internal space element and the external space element are called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*).
What is the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*)?
The six groups of consciousness—the visual consciousness group, the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness groups—are called the consciousness element.
What is the realm of pleasure (*sukha-dhātu*)?
The pleasant feelings arising from eye-contact, and the faculty of pleasure arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact—this is called the realm of pleasure.
What is the realm of suffering (*duḥkha-dhātu*)?

The painful feelings arising from eye-contact, and the painful feelings arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact, which constitute the faculty of suffering—these are called the element of suffering (*duḥkha-dhātu*).
What is the element of joy (*saumanasya-dhātu*)?
If it is a pleasant feeling of the mind that constitutes the faculty of joy, this is called the element of joy.
What is the element of sorrow (*daurmanasyadhātu*)?
If it is a mental painful feeling that constitutes the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*), this is called the element of sorrow.
What is the element of equanimity (*upekṣādhātu*)?

The neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings of body and mind—namely, the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings arising from eye-contact, and the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact, which constitute the faculty of equanimity—are called the element of equanimity (*upekṣā-dhātu*).
What is the element of ignorance?
Delusion, the unwholesome root, is called the element of ignorance.
What is the element of desire?
The realm of desire is called the desire realm.
What is the realm of ill will?
The realm of ill will is called the realm of ill will.
What is the element of harm?
The harming of the element of harm is called the element of harm.
What is the element of desire?

If there is desire for desires, craving for desires, delighting in desires, dependence on desires, longing for desires, thirst for desires, burning for desires, and entanglement in desires—this is called the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
What is the element of ill will (*vyāpādadhātu*)?
If one deceives and harasses sentient beings, violating their hopes and expectations without severing the life-faculty, this is called the element of ill will.
What is the element of cruelty (*vihiṃsādhātu*)?
If one deceives and harms sentient beings, hoping to invade and destroy their life-faculties, this is called the element of harm (*vihimsā-dhātu*). What is the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)?

It is the continuity of attachment to the five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), the delight in them, the pleasure in them, the craving for their forms, and the defilement by desire. It is the continuity of attachment to forms through eye-consciousness, the delight in them, the pleasure in them, the craving for their forms, and the defilement by desire; it is the continuity of attachment to touch through ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness, the delight in them, the pleasure in them, the craving for their forms, and the defilement by desire. It is the hope and defilement by desire regarding another’s possessions, another’s domain, another’s wife, or another’s goods, wishing: "May I obtain these. It is greed, intense greed, ultimate greed, and its association with hope, love, defilement, heavy defilement, ultimate defilement, and other dharmas that are objects of greed. It is greed, intense greed, ultimate greed, and the hope, love, defilement, heavy defilement, and ultimate defilement associated with them. This is called the realm of desire.
What is the element of ill will (*vyāpādadhātu*)?

If one harms few or many sentient beings, binds them, and causes them to undergo various sufferings; if there is ill will, intense ill will, ultimate ill will, associated with anger, hatred, a troubled mind, perversity, lack of loving-kindness, lack of compassion, and lack of benefit—this is called the element of ill will.
What is the element of harm (*vihiṃsā-dhātu*)?

If one afflicts sentient beings by means of hands, fists, tiles, stones, swords, staves, or other such instruments of affliction; if one thus deceives and harms sentient beings, invades and torments their hopes, or takes their lives—this is called the element of harm.
What is the element of emergence (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*)?
With the exception of loving-kindness and compassion, all other wholesome factors of emergence are called the element of emergence.
What is the element of non-ill will (*avyāpādadhātu*)?
Loving-kindness (maitrī) is called the element of non-ill will.
What is the element of non-harming?
Compassion (karuṇā) is called the element of non-harming.
What is the realm of light?
It is the light of form and the light of wisdom.
What is the light of form?

The light of fire, the light of the sun, the light of the moon, the light of jewels, the light of the stars, the light of the Buddha, the light of sentient beings, and other illuminations produced by the four great elements—these are called material lights.
What is the light of wisdom?
The three kinds of wisdom—wisdom derived from reflection, wisdom derived from hearing, and wisdom derived from cultivation—are called the light of wisdom.
These, namely the light of form and the light of wisdom, are called the realm of light.
What is the pure element (*śubhadhātu*)?
The pure liberation (*śubhavimokṣa*) and other pure forms that can purify form, which are pleasing to the eye and never cause weariness—this is called the pure element.
What is the form element (*rūpadhātu*)?
The sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*): these are called the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
What is the realm of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-dhātu*)?
There are two types of the realm of the sphere of infinite space: either the conditioned realm of the sphere of infinite space or the unconditioned realm of the sphere of infinite space.
What is the conditioned sphere of infinite space?
It is the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space and birth in the sphere of infinite space.
What is the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space?
If a bhikṣu, having transcended all perceptions of form, extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity, attains the sphere of infinite space.
What is birth in the sphere of infinite space?

If, through intimacy with this concentration and extensive cultivation of it, one is reborn among the gods of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), possessing the fourfold aggregates of self—namely, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called "birth in the sphere of infinite space.

Such concentration of the sphere of infinite space and such birth in the sphere of infinite space are called the conditioned realm of the sphere of infinite space (*saṃskṛta-ākāśānantyāyatana-dhātu*).
What is the unconditioned sphere of infinite space?
If, by means of wisdom, the sphere of infinite space is abandoned, this is called the [unconditioned] sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the unconditioned spheres of infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

What are the eighteen elements? They are the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element; the ear element, the sound element, and the ear-consciousness element; the nose element, the odor element, and the nose-consciousness element; the tongue element, the taste element, and the tongue-consciousness element; the body element, the tangible-object element, and the body-consciousness element; and the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. These are called the eighteen elements.

2. Chapter on Karma, from the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Section on Non-Inquiry, Chapter Two: Karma. It consists of karma of volition (*cetanā-karma*) and karma after having willed (*cetayitvā-karma*);
karma that is intentional (*saṃcetanika-karma*) and karma that is unintentional (*asaṃcetanika-karma*).
Karma that is experienced and karma that is not experienced;
karma that is experienced to a small degree and karma that is experienced to a great degree;
matured karma and karma that is not yet matured.
Material action and non-material action;
visible action and invisible action;
resistant action and non-resistant action.
Noble karma and non-noble karma;
contaminated karma and uncontaminated karma;
karma associated with craving and karma not associated with craving.
There is karma with seeking and karma without seeking;
karma that is to be grasped and karma that is not to be grasped; karma with appropriation and karma without appropriation.
There are superior karmas and non-superior karmas;
karmas that are experienced and karmas that are not experienced;
internal karmas and external karmas.
There is karma with retribution and karma without retribution.
There is karma associated with the mind and karma not associated with the mind.
There is karma that is a mental factor and karma that is not a mental factor.
Karma that is conditioned and karma that is not conditioned;
karma associated with the mind and karma dissociated from the mind;
karma that follows the mind and karma that does not follow the mind.
Karma that is not associated with karma; karma that is neither associated with karma nor non-associated with karma.
Common karma; uncommon karma.
Karma that evolves in accordance with karma; karma that does not evolve in accordance with karma.
Karma that has a cause and karma that does not have a cause;
there is karma with a cause, karma with a continuity, karma with conditions, and conditioned karma;
karma that is known and karma that is not known.
Karma of consciousness and non-karma of consciousness;
karma of understanding and non-karma of understanding;
karma of realization and non-karma of realization.
Karma known through the knowledge of abandonment and karma not known through the knowledge of abandonment;
abandoned karma and non-abandoned karma;
cultivated karma and non-cultivated karma.
Action realized through direct knowledge (*abhijñā-karman*) and action not realized through direct knowledge;
action based on instruction (*anuśāsana-karman*) and action not based on instruction;
bodily action consisting of informative and non-informative [matter] (*vijñapti-avijñapti-karman*), and vocal action consisting of informative and non-informative [matter].
Karma of body, karma of speech, and karma of mind.
Karma of morality, karma of non-morality, and karma that is neither moral nor immoral.

Karma of bodily morality, non-morality, and that which is neither moral nor immoral; karma of verbal morality, non-morality, and that which is neither moral nor immoral; and karma of mental morality, non-morality, and that which is neither moral nor immoral.
Wholesome karma, unwholesome karma, and neutral karma;
karma of those in training, karma of those beyond training, and karma of those who are neither in training nor beyond training;
karma that is a result, karma that is subject to resulting, and karma that is neither a result nor subject to resulting.
Karma abandoned by vision, karma abandoned by cultivation, and karma abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation;
karma with causes abandoned by vision, karma with causes abandoned by cultivation, and karma with causes abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation.
Inferior karma, middling karma, and superior karma;
coarse karma, subtle karma, and minute karma;
karma resulting in pleasant feeling, karma resulting in painful feeling, and karma resulting in neutral feeling.
Karma resulting in pleasant feeling, karma resulting in painful feeling, and karma resulting in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Karma that leads to joy, karma that leads to grief, and karma that leads to equanimity.
Karma that leads to joy, karma that leads to grief, and karma that leads to neither-joy-nor-grief.
Karma to be experienced in the present life, karma to be experienced upon rebirth, and karma to be experienced in subsequent lives;
karma that yields pleasure, karma that yields suffering, and karma that yields neither suffering nor pleasure;
and karma with pleasant results, karma with painful results, and karma with results that are neither painful nor pleasant.
Karma resulting in pleasant retribution, karma resulting in painful retribution, and karma resulting in neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution.
Past karma, future karma, and present karma.
Karma with past objects, karma with future objects, karma with present objects, and karma with objects that are neither past, nor future, nor present.
There are four types of karma: karma bound to the desire realm, karma bound to the form realm, karma bound to the formless realm, and unbound karma.
There are also four types of karma according to their experience.
The five fears,
the five enemies,
and the five deeds of immediate retribution.
The five precepts and the transgression of the five precepts;
karma caused by greed, karma caused by hatred, and karma caused by delusion;
and karma caused by non-greed, karma caused by non-hatred, and karma caused by non-delusion.

Karma leading to the hells, karma leading to the animal realm, karma leading to the realm of hungry ghosts, karma leading to the human realm, karma leading to the celestial realms, and karma leading to nirvana.
The seven unwholesome factors.
The seven wholesome dharmas;
the eight noble modes of speech and the non-eight noble modes of speech;
and bodily, vocal, and mental actions caused by greed.
Bodily, verbal, and mental actions arise conditioned by hatred;
bodily, verbal, and mental actions arise conditioned by delusion;
and bodily, verbal, and mental actions arise conditioned by non-attachment.
Because of non-anger, there are bodily, verbal, and mental actions;
because of non-delusion, there are bodily, verbal, and mental actions.
These include the ten unwholesome courses of action and the ten wholesome courses of action.
The accomplishment of ten dharmas leads to falling into hell as swiftly as a javelin is cast; the accomplishment of ten dharmas leads to birth in heaven as swiftly as a javelin is cast.
The accomplishment of twenty dharmas leads to falling into hell as swiftly as a javelin is cast; the accomplishment of twenty dharmas leads to birth in heaven as swiftly as a javelin is cast.
The accomplishment of thirty dharmas leads to falling into hell as swiftly as a spear is cast; the accomplishment of thirty dharmas leads to birth in heaven as swiftly as a spear is cast.
The accomplishment of forty dharmas leads to falling into hell as swiftly as a spear is cast; the accomplishment of forty dharmas leads to birth in heaven as swiftly as a spear is cast.
What is the karma of volition?
Mental karma is called the karma of volition.
What is the karma after having willed?
Bodily action and verbal action are called "intentional action" (*cetayitvā-karman*).
What is "deliberate action"?
If an action is performed intentionally and one experiences its retribution, this is called "deliberate action."
What is unintentional karma?
If karma is not performed and its retribution is not experienced, this is called unintentional karma.
What is experienced karma?
If karma has a retribution, it is called "karma to be experienced.
What is "karma not to be experienced"?
If karma has no retribution, it is called "karma not to be experienced."
Furthermore, regarding "action to be experienced" (vedanīya-karma): if an action involves volition that has either a retribution or no retribution, it is called action to be experienced.
Furthermore, regarding "action not to be experienced" (avedanīya-karma): if an action is bodily or vocal action that has no retribution, it is called action not to be experienced.
What is karma with little result?
If karma yields little retribution, it is called karma with little result.
What is karma with much result?
If karma does not receive even a small retribution, it is called "karma that receives much.
What is "ripened karma"?
If karma receives its retribution soon, it is called ripened karma.
What is non-ripening karma?
If karma is not to be experienced as retribution in the near term, it is called non-ripening karma.
What is material karma?
Bodily action and verbal action are called material action.
What is non-material action?
Mental action is called non-material action.
What is visible action?
If an action is included within the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is called visible action.
What is invisible action?
If an action is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is called invisible action.
What is resistant action?
If an action is subsumed under the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*) or the sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*), it is called resistant action.
What is non-resistant karma?
If karma is subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is called non-resistant karma.
What is noble karma?
If karma is untainted (anāsrava), it is called noble karma (ārya-karma).
What is non-noble karma?
If karma is tainted (sāsrava), it is called non-noble karma.
What is karma with outflows (*sāsrava-karman*)?
If karma is accompanied by craving (*tṛṣṇā*), it is called karma with outflows.
What is karma without outflows (*anāsrava-karman*)?
If karma is without craving, it is called untainted karma (*anāsrava-karma*).
What is karma with craving?
If karma involves seeking, it is called karma with craving (*sāsrava-karma*).
What is karma without craving?
If karma is without seeking, it is called karma without craving.
What is karma with seeking?
If karma is to be grasped, it is called "karma with seeking.
What is "karma without seeking"?
If karma is not to be grasped, it is called "karma without seeking."
What is karma that is subject to grasping?
If karma is accompanied by grasping, it is called karma subject to grasping.
What is karma not subject to grasping?
If karma is without grasping (*anupādāna*), it is called non-appropriative karma (*anupādānīya-karman*).
What is karma with grasping?
If karma possesses excellence (*viśeṣa*), it is called karma with grasping (*sopādāna-karman*).
What is action without grasping?
If an action is without excellence, it is called action without grasping.
What is action with excellence?
If karma is accompanied by grasping, it is called superior karma.
What is non-superior karma?
If karma is without grasping, it is called non-superior karma.
Furthermore, there is karma that has a superior [karma]; if this karma has another karma that is more excellent, sublime, or surpassing it, this is called karma with a superior.
Furthermore, there is karma without a superior; if this karma has no other karma that is more excellent, sublime, or surpassing it, this is called karma without a superior.
What is appropriated karma?
If karma is internal, it is called appropriated karma.
What is non-appropriated karma?
If an action is external, it is called non-appropriated action.
What is internal action?
If an action is appropriated, it is called internal action.
What is external karma?
If karma is not experienced [in this life], it is called external karma.
What is karma that has retribution?
If karma has a retribution, it is called "karma with retribution.
What is "karma without retribution"?
If karma is not a retribution, it is called "karma without retribution."
What is karma associated with the mind?
If karma is a mental factor (*caitasika*), it is called karma associated with the mind.
What is karma not associated with the mind?
If an action is not a mental factor (*caitasika*), it is called an action that is not associated with the mind (*cittaviprayukta-karman*).
What is an action that is a mental factor?
If an action is a condition (*pratyaya*), it is called an action that is a mental factor.
What is non-mental concomitant karma?
If karma is not a condition, it is called non-mental concomitant karma.
What is conditional karma?
If an action is a mental factor (*caitasika*), it is called "action that is an object-condition" (*ālambana-karma*).
What is "action that is not an object-condition"?
If an action is not a mental factor, it is called "action that is not an object-condition."
What is karma that is concomitant with the mind?
If karma follows the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind, this is called karma concomitant with the mind.
What is karma not concomitant with the mind?

If karma does not arise together with the mind, does not arise simultaneously with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind, it is called non-concomitant karma.
What is karma that arises in accordance with the mind?
If karma arises together with the mind, abides together with the mind, and ceases together with the mind, it is called "karma that follows the mind.
What is "karma that does not follow the mind"?
If karma does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind, it is called "karma that does not follow the mind."
What is karma that is not associated with karma?
If karma is not associated with volition (*cetanā*), it is called karma that is not associated with karma.
What is karma that is neither associated with karma nor non-associated with karma?
Volition (*cetanā*) is called karma that is neither associated with karma nor dissociated from karma.
What is co-existent karma?
If karma follows along with karma, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called co-existent karma.
What is non-common karma?
If karma does not follow along with [other] karma, and is not born together with, does not abide together with, and does not cease together with [other] karma, this is called non-common karma.
What is karma that evolves in accordance with karma?
If karma arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with [another] karma, this is called karma that evolves in accordance with karma.
What is karma that does not evolve in accordance with karma?
That which arises not in common with karma, does not abide in common with it, and does not cease in common with it—this is called "karma that does not follow the turning of karma.
What is "karma as cause"?
If karma is a condition for karma, or if karma is a non-condition for wholesome existence, this is called "karma as cause."
What is non-causal karma?
If karma is not a condition for retribution, and its retribution is not shared with others, this is called non-causal karma.
What is causal karma?
If karma has a continuity, it is called "karma with a cause.
What is karma with a continuity?
If karma proceeds by way of conditions, or if karma is concomitant [with other factors], this is called "karma with a continuity."
What is karma with an object?
If karma is conditioned, it is called karma with an object.
What is conditioned karma?
If karma has conditions, it is called conditioned karma.
How does one know karma?
To know all karma as one knows and sees phenomena is called knowing karma.
What is non-cognitive action?
There is no such thing as non-cognitive action.
Furthermore, it is said that all actions are not known through cognitive knowledge and vision of things as they are; this is called non-cognitive action.
What is the karma of consciousness?
All karma that is cognized by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as it is, is called the karma of consciousness.
What is not the karma of consciousness?
There is no karma that is not consciousness.
Furthermore, it is said: all karma is not the consciousness that cognizes objects as they are; this is called non-consciousness karma.
What is resolving karma?
To know and see things as they truly are is called the "understanding of karma.
What is the "non-understanding of karma"?
There is no such thing as non-understanding of karma.
Furthermore, it is said: all karma that is not understood through knowledge and vision as it truly is is called "uncomprehended karma.
What is "comprehended karma"?
All karma that is comprehended through knowledge and vision as it truly is is called "comprehended karma."
What is the karma that is not fully understood?
There is no such karma as that which is not fully understood.
What is the karma known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*)?
If karma is unwholesome, it is called karma known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
What is karma not known through the knowledge of abandonment?
If karma is wholesome or indeterminate, it is called karma not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
What is the severance of karma?
If karma is unwholesome, this is called the severance of karma.
What is not the severance of karma?
If karma is wholesome or indeterminate, it is called non-abandonable karma.
What is cultivated karma?
If karma is wholesome, it is called cultivated karma.
What is non-cultivated karma?
If karma is unwholesome or neutral, it is called non-cultivated karma.
What is realized karma?
When all karma is realized through knowledge and vision exactly as it is, this is called "realized karma" (*kṛtābhisamaya-karman*).
What is "non-realized karma"?
There is no such thing as non-realized karma.
Furthermore, it is said: all karma that is not known through direct realization as it truly is is called non-realized karma.
What is informative karma?
Bodily action and verbal action are called informative karma.
What is non-informative action?
Mental action is called non-informative action.
What is bodily informative action?
If bodily action is included within the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is called bodily informative action (*kāya-vijñapti-karma*).
What is bodily non-informative action?
If bodily action is included within the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is called bodily non-informative action (*kāyāvijñapti-karma*).
What is vocal informative action (*vāgvijñapti-karma*)?
If vocal action is included within the sphere of sound (*śabdāyatana*), it is called vocal informative action.
What is vocal non-informative action (*vāgavijñapti-karma*)?
If an action of speech is included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), it is called unmanifest action of speech (*vāg-avijñapti-karman*).
What is bodily action?
If an action is neither mental nor an action of speech, it is called bodily action (*kāya-karman*).
What is vocal action?
If an action is neither based on conditions nor bodily action, it is called vocal action.
What is mental action?
If it is karma conditioned by the mind, it is called mental karma (*manas-karman*). What is the karma of morality (*śīla-karman*)?

If it is karma arising from a wholesome mind—namely, bodily intimation (*kāya-vijñapti*) consisting of going, coming, bending, and stretching; vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*) consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) of impure bodily and vocal morality; right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*); and wholesome volition (*kuśala-cetanā*)—this is called the karma of morality.
What is non-virtuous karma?

It refers to unwholesome karma arising from an unwholesome mind, including bodily intimation such as coming, going, bending, and stretching; vocal intimation such as the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; as well as non-restraint in body and speech, non-informative action (*avijñapti*), and unwholesome volition (*cetanā*). This is called non-virtuous karma.
What is action that is neither discipline nor non-discipline?

It refers to unwholesome-neutral bodily intimation—such as going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning—that is produced by an unwholesome-neutral mind; vocal intimation consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech; and unwholesome-neutral volition (*cetanā*). This is called action that is neither discipline nor non-discipline.
What is bodily karmic restraint?

It refers to wholesome bodily karma arising from a wholesome mind—namely, the bodily intimation of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; the informative and non-informative aspects of impure bodily restraint; right action; and right livelihood. This is called bodily karmic restraint.
What is bodily non-restraint action?

If bodily action is unwholesome—namely, the bodily intimation consisting of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, which is initiated by an unwholesome mind, as well as the bodily non-intimation that is not restraint—this is called bodily non-restraint action.
What is bodily action that is neither discipline nor non-discipline?

It refers to neutral bodily action—namely, the physical intimation of coming and going, bending and stretching, and turning about, which is initiated by a neutral mind. This is called bodily action that is neither discipline nor non-discipline.
What is the karmic action of verbal restraint?

If verbal karma is wholesome, arising from a wholesome mind, consisting of vocal instruction—the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech—and includes the unmanifested verbal restraint that is with outflows, as well as right speech and right livelihood, this is called the karmic action of verbal restraint.
What is non-restraint of speech?

If there is unwholesome vocal karma—vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, phrases, and words arising from an unwholesome mind, as well as vocal non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that is not restraint—this is called non-restraint of speech.
What is verbal action that is neither discipline nor non-discipline?

It refers to verbal action that is indeterminate, consisting of vocal instruction arising from an indeterminate mind—the gathering of sounds, phonemes, and speech; this is called verbal action that is neither discipline nor non-discipline.
What is the karmic action of mental restraint?
If a mental action is wholesome—that is, volition associated with a wholesome mind—this is called the karmic action of mental restraint.
What is the karmic action of non-restraint of the mind?
If mental karma is unwholesome—that is, volition associated with an unwholesome mind—this is called mental non-restraint karma.
What is mental karma that is neither restraint nor non-restraint?
If mental karma is indeterminate—that is, volition associated with an indeterminate mind—this is called mental karma that is neither discipline nor non-discipline.
What is wholesome karma?
If karma is cultivated, this is called wholesome karma.
What is unwholesome karma?
If karma is abandoned, it is called unwholesome karma.
What is neutral karma?
If an action or sensation is neither a result nor subject to the law of ripening, it is called neutral action (*avyākṛta-karma*).
What is training action (*śaikṣa-karma*)?
If an action is noble (*ārya*) but not that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is called training action.
What is the karma of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)? If karma is noble (*ārya*) but not that of one in training (*śaikṣa*), it is called the karma of one beyond training.
What is the karma that is neither of one in training nor of one beyond training?
If karma is non-noble, it is called karma that is neither of training nor beyond training.
What is retributive karma?
If karma is experienced or if karma is wholesome with a result, it is called retributive karma.
What is karma that is of the nature to be experienced as retribution?
If karma has retribution, it is called karma that is of the nature to be experienced as retribution.
What is karma that is neither retribution nor of the nature to be experienced as retribution?
If karma is indeterminate and not included within one's own portion, it is called karma that is neither a result nor a dharma leading to a result.
What is karma abandoned by vision?
If karma is unwholesome and not abandoned through cultivation, it is called karma abandoned by vision.
What is karma to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
If karma is unwholesome but not to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*), this is called karma to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is karma that is neither to be abandoned by insight nor to be abandoned by cultivation?
If an action is wholesome or neutral, it is called an action that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is an action whose cause is abandoned by vision?
If an action is abandoned by vision, or if it is the retribution of a phenomenon abandoned by vision, this is called an action whose cause is abandoned by vision.
What is karma whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
If karma is to be abandoned by cultivation, or if it is the retribution of factors to be abandoned by cultivation, this is called karma whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is karma that has neither the cause of being abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) nor the cause of being abandoned by cultivation?

If an action is wholesome, or an action that is the result of wholesome dharmas, or an action that is neither a result nor a dharma destined to produce a result—this is called an action whose cause is neither to be abandoned by vision nor to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is inferior karma?
If karma is unwholesome, it is called inferior karma.
What is middling karma?
If karma is neutral (avyākṛta), it is called middling karma.
What is superior karma?
If karma is wholesome (kuśala), it is called superior karma.
Furthermore, regarding inferior action: if an action is unwholesome or indeterminate, it is called inferior action.
Furthermore, regarding middling action: if an action is not noble and wholesome, it is called middling action.
Furthermore, regarding superior karma: if karma is noble and untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called superior karma.
What is coarse karma?
If karma is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), it is called coarse karma.
What is subtle karma?
If karma is bound to the form realm or is unbound, it is called subtle karma.
What is minute karma?
If karma is bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), it is called subtle karma.
Furthermore, coarse karma refers to karma that is bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu); this is called coarse karma.

Furthermore, subtle karma refers to karma bound to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or that which is unbound; this is called subtle karma.
Furthermore, minute karma refers to karma bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called minute karma.

Furthermore, coarse karma refers to karma that is bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness; this is called coarse karma.
Furthermore, regarding subtle karma: if karma is unconditioned by the realms of existence, it is called subtle karma.
Furthermore, regarding minute karma: if karma is conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is called minute karma.
What is karma associated with pleasant feeling?
If karma is associated with pleasant feeling, it is called karma associated with pleasant feeling.
What is karma associated with painful feeling?
If karma is associated with painful feeling, it is called karma experienced as suffering.
What is karma experienced as equanimity?
If karma is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is called karma experienced as equanimity.
What is karma that results in pleasant feeling?
If karma receives a pleasant retribution, it is called karma resulting in pleasant feeling.
What is karma that results in painful feeling?
If karma results in the experience of painful retribution, it is called karma of painful feeling.
What is karma of neutral feeling?
If karma results in the experience of neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution, it is called karma of neutral feeling.
What is karma that results in pleasant feeling?

Excluding karma that results in painful feeling and karma that results in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, any other karma that is wholesome and has a retribution is called karma that results in pleasant feeling.
What is karma that results in painful feeling?
If karma is unwholesome, it is called karma of painful feeling.
What is karma of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
Excluding karma of pleasant and painful feeling, whatever other karma there is, that is called karma of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is karma that is a ground for joy?
If karma, once produced, gives rise to joy, it is called karma that is a ground for joy.
What is karma that is a ground for sorrow?
If an action, once initiated, gives rise to sorrow, it is called an action that has sorrow as its basis.
What is an action that has equanimity as its basis?
If an action, once initiated, results in equanimity, it is called an action that has equanimity as its basis.

Furthermore, regarding karma associated with the sphere of joy (*saumanasya-sthānīya-karma*): excluding karma associated with the sphere of equanimity (*upekṣā-sthānīya*), any other karma associated with the spheres that is wholesome and has a ripened result (*savipāka*) is called karma associated with the sphere of joy.
Furthermore, regarding karma associated with the sphere of grief (*daurmanasya-sthānīya-karma*): if karma is unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is called karma associated with the sphere of grief.

Furthermore, regarding the karma of the sphere of equanimity (*upekṣā-sthānīya-karman*): excluding the karma of the sphere of joy (*prīti-sthānīya-karman*), any other karma that is wholesome and has a retribution is called the karma of the sphere of equanimity.
Furthermore, regarding the karma of the sphere of joy: if a karma is wholesome and has a retribution, it is called the karma of the sphere of joy.
Furthermore, regarding karma that pertains to the sphere of sorrow (*daurmanasya-sthānīya*): if karma is unwholesome and has a retribution, it is called karma pertaining to the sphere of sorrow.

Furthermore, regarding karma that pertains neither to the sphere of joy nor to the sphere of sorrow: excluding karma pertaining to the sphere of joy and karma pertaining to the sphere of sorrow, whatever other karma there is, that is called karma pertaining neither to the sphere of joy nor to the sphere of sorrow.
What is karma to be experienced in the present life?

It is that karma which, having arisen within one's own continuum, is performed and accomplished by oneself as a child or an adult, and for which the retribution is experienced by the body of this very self as a child or an adult in this same life; this is called karma to be experienced in the present life.
What is karma to be experienced upon rebirth?

If karma belongs to one's own continuum and is accomplished through the actions of those who are young or old, such that its retribution is experienced upon rebirth, this is called karma to be experienced upon rebirth.
What is karma to be experienced in subsequent lives?

If karma belongs to one's own continuum, and whether performed by the young or the old, this karma is accomplished such that its retribution is experienced in the third or fourth birth, or even later; this is called karma to be experienced in subsequent lives.
What is karma that bestows pleasure?
If karma results in a pleasant fruit, it is called karma that bestows pleasure.
What is karma that bestows suffering?
If an action results in the fruit of suffering, it is called an action that gives suffering.
What is an action that neither gives pleasure nor gives suffering?
Any action other than those that give pleasure or give suffering is called an action that neither gives pleasure nor gives suffering.
What is karma with pleasant results?
If karma is wholesome and has a pleasant retribution, it is called karma with pleasant results.
What is karma with painful results?
If karma is unwholesome, it is called karma that has a painful fruit.
What is karma that has neither a pleasant fruit nor a painful fruit?
Excluding karma that has a pleasant fruit or a painful fruit, whatever other karma there is, this is called karma that has neither a pleasant fruit nor a painful fruit.
What is karma with pleasant retribution?
If karma has a pleasant fruit, it is called karma with pleasant retribution.
What is karma with painful retribution?
If an action has a painful fruit, it is called an action with a painful retribution.
What is an action with neither pleasant nor painful retribution?
Excluding actions with pleasant retribution and actions with painful retribution, whatever other actions remain are called actions with neither pleasant nor painful retribution.
What is karma with pleasant retribution?
If karma is wholesome and possesses retribution, it is called karma with pleasant retribution.
What is karma with painful retribution?
If karma is unwholesome, it is called karma with a painful retribution.
What is karma with a retribution that is neither pleasant nor painful?
With the exception of karma with a pleasant retribution and karma with a painful retribution, whatever other karma there is is called karma with a retribution that is neither pleasant nor painful.
What is past karma? If karma has arisen and ceased, it is called past karma.
What is future karma?
If karma has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, it is called future karma.
What is present karma?
If karma has arisen but has not yet ceased, it is called present karma.
What is karma with a past object?
If karma arises through contemplating past phenomena, this is called karma with a past object.
What is karma with a future object?
If one contemplates future phenomena and karma arises, this is called karma with a future object.
What is karma with a present object?
If one contemplates present phenomena and karma arises, this is called karma with a present object.
What is karma with an object that is neither past, nor future, nor present?
If karma arises through contemplating dharmas that are neither past, nor future, nor present, this is called karma with an object that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
What is karma bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma*)?
If karma is characterized by the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) or is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called karma bound to the desire realm.
What is karma bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma*)?
If an action is characterized by the outflows of form (*rūpāsrava*) and is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called an action bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma*).
What is an action bound to the formless realm?
If an action is characterized by the outflows of the formless (*ārūpyāsrava*) and is subject to outflows, it is called an action bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-karma*).
What is non-bound karma?
If karma is noble and untainted, this is called non-bound karma.
What are the four types of karma?

There is black karma with black retribution, white karma with white retribution, black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution, and non-black-non-white karma with non-black-non-white retribution.
What is black karma with black retribution?
If an action is unwholesome and has a result, it is called black action with black result.
What is white action with white result?
If an action is wholesome and has a result, it is called white action with white result.
What is black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution?

There is no single karma that is both black and white and yields black-and-white retribution; rather, it refers to cases where black karma yields black retribution and white karma yields white retribution—this is called black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution.
What is non-black, non-white karma with non-black, non-white retribution?
If it is the noble one’s karma that has retribution and which abandons the afflictions, this is called non-black, non-white karma with non-black, non-white retribution.
What is black karma with black retribution?
If karma is unwholesome and has a retribution, this karmic retribution is called black karma with black retribution.
What is white karma with white retribution?
If an action is wholesome and possesses a result, this karmic result is called "white action with white result.
What is "black-and-white action with black-and-white result"?

There is no single action that is both black and white and possesses a black-and-white result. Rather, when there is a black action with a black result, or a white action with a white result—these combined results are what is called "black-and-white action with black-and-white result."
What is non-black, non-white karma with non-black, non-white retribution?
Any dharma that is noble, has retribution, and abandons the afflictions—this is called non-black, non-white karma with non-black, non-white retribution.
What is black karma with black retribution?
As the Blessed One said:
"I myself, having realized it through direct knowledge, declare four types of karma."
What are the four?

Black karma with black retribution; white karma with white retribution; black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution; and non-black, non-white karma with non-black, non-white retribution, which is the karma that brings an end to all karma.
What is black karma with black retribution?
It is when a person performs impure bodily actions, performs impure verbal actions, and performs impure mental actions, thereby accomplishing impure karma.
Having engaged in impure conduct of body, speech, and mind, and having accomplished impure karma, he is born in an impure place.
Having been born in that impure place, he experiences impure contacts.

Having experienced an impure contact, one experiences an impure feeling that is entirely painful, entirely burning with suffering, entirely unwholesome, entirely unpleasant, disagreeable, and undesirable—something loathed by all and not hoped for by gods or humans.
Just as with the beings in hell, these beings are reborn according to the karma they have performed; once born, they encounter [suffering] at every touch.
I know that these beings experience suffering through their karma; this is called black karma with black retribution.
What is white karma with white retribution?
It is when a person performs pure bodily conduct, performs pure verbal conduct, and performs pure mental conduct, thereby accomplishing pure karmic actions.
Having purified the conduct of body, speech, and mind, and having accomplished pure karma, one is born in a pure place.
Having been born in a pure place, one experiences pure contact.
Having experienced pure contact, one experiences pure feeling—exclusively pleasant, lovely, joyful, and agreeable, never loathsome, and longed for by gods and humans.
It is just as with the beings of the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven: when beings are reborn there, they are born according to the karma they have performed; once born, they experience contact after contact.
I know that these beings obtain happiness through their karma; this is called white karma with white retribution.
What is black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution?
It is when a person performs pure and impure bodily actions, performs pure and impure verbal actions, and performs pure and impure mental actions, thereby accomplishing pure and impure karma.
Having practiced pure and impure conduct of body, speech, and mind, and having accomplished pure and impure karma, they are born in pure and impure places.
Having been born in a pure or impure place, one experiences pure or impure contacts.
Having experienced pure or impure contacts, one feels pure or impure feelings, experiencing a mixture of suffering and pleasure.
Whether as humans or devas, if sentient beings are reborn, they are born according to the karma they have performed; having been born, they encounter their respective experiences.
I know that sentient beings experience pleasure and pain through karma; this is called black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution.
What is the action that is neither black nor white, which does not have a black or white retribution, and which is capable of exhausting all karma?
It is the thought of abandoning black action with its black retribution,
and the thought of abandoning white action with its white retribution.

If there is black-and-white karma with black-and-white retribution, or if one cuts off volition, this is called non-black-and-white karma with non-black-and-white retribution, which is the karma capable of exhausting all karma.
These are called the four types of karma.
What are the four types of karmas that result in experience?
As the Blessed One has taught, there are four types of karma that result in experience.
What are these four?

There is karma that is painful in the present and results in a painful retribution in the future; there is karma that is pleasant in the present and results in a painful retribution in the future; there is karma that is painful in the present and results in a pleasant retribution in the future; and there is karma that is pleasant in the present and results in a pleasant retribution in the future.
What is the karma that is painful both in its present experience and results in pain in the future?
It is when a person, enduring sorrow and enduring pain, takes life; because of that act of killing, they experience sorrow and pain with various states of mind.

Enduring sorrow and enduring pain, they likewise engage in stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous talk, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view. Because of those wrong views, they experience sorrow and pain with various states of mind, and at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the miserable realms of hell. This is karma that is painful both in its present experience and results in pain in the future.
What is the karma that brings happiness in the present life but results in suffering in the future?

It is when a person, with patience and delight, with patience and pleasure, commits killing; because of that killing, they experience joy and pleasure with various states of mind. They likewise practice stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view, experiencing joy and pleasure with various states of mind because of those wrong views. When their body breaks up and their life ends, they fall into the miserable realms of hell. This is karma that brings happiness in the present life but results in suffering in the future.

What is the karma that is painful in the present but yields a pleasant retribution in the future? It is when a person endures sorrow and endures suffering while abstaining from taking life; because of this abstinence from killing, they experience various forms of sorrow and suffering through their mind.

Enduring sorrow and enduring suffering, they also abstain from stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; they are without covetousness, without ill will, and possess right view. Because of this right view, they experience various forms of sorrow and suffering through their mind. At the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world. This is karma that is painful in the present but yields a pleasant retribution in the future.
What is the karma that results in happiness in the present life and a happy retribution in the future?

If a person endures with joy and delights in not killing, then by virtue of that non-killing, they experience joy and delight through various states of mind. Enduring with joy and delighting in not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, not using double-tongued speech, not using harsh words, not engaging in frivolous chatter, not being covetous, not harboring ill will, and holding right view—by virtue of that right view, they experience joy and delight through various states of mind. At the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavens. This is the karma that results in happiness in the present life and a happy retribution in the future.
These are called the four types of karmic results experienced through feeling.
What are the five fears?
If one kills living beings, because of that act of killing, fear arises in this life and fear arises in future lives.

Stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the state of heedlessness through drinking intoxicants—because of this state of heedlessness through drinking intoxicants, one experiences fear in this life and fear in future lives.
These are called the five fears.
What are the five enemies?
If one kills living beings, because of that act of killing, enmity arises in this life and enmity arises in future lives.

Stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the state of intoxication through drinking liquor—because of this state of intoxication through drinking liquor, enmity arises in this life and enmity arises in future lives.
These are called the five enemies. What are the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?

They are: the immediate retribution of killing one’s mother; the immediate retribution of killing one’s father; the immediate retribution of killing an Arhat; the immediate retribution of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; and the immediate retribution of shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with an evil mind.
What is the immediate retribution of killing one’s mother?
If one intentionally takes the life of one’s mother while perceiving her as one’s mother, this is called the immediate retribution of killing one’s mother.
What is the immediate retribution of killing one’s father?
If one intentionally takes the life of one's father while perceiving him as one's father, this is called the immediate transgression of killing a father.
What is the immediate transgression of killing an Arhat?
If one intentionally takes the life of an Arhat Śrāvaka, this is called the immediate transgression of killing an Arhat.
What is the immediate offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha?

When one faction invites four or more bhikṣus and the second faction invites four or more bhikṣus, and they cast voting tallies and issue proclamations, this is called the immediate offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha.
What constitutes the immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) of shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with an evil mind?

If one intentionally sheds the blood of a Tathāgata with an evil mind, even to the extent of wounding him as little as a hair-tip, this is called the immediate retribution of shedding the blood of a Tathāgata with an evil mind.
These are called the five ānantarya [sins].
What are the five precepts?

Refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from false speech, and refraining from drinking intoxicants which lead to heedlessness—these are called the five precepts.
What is meant by transgressing the five precepts?
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants as a basis for negligence—these are called transgressing the five precepts.
What is karma caused by greed?
If bodily, verbal, and mental karma have greed as their cause, greed as their sequence, greed as their origin, and greed as their condition, this is called karma caused by greed.
What is action caused by hatred?

If an action—whether an action of body, speech, or mind—is caused by hatred, has hatred as its sequence, arises from the accumulation of hatred, and has hatred as its condition, it is called action caused by hatred.
What is karma caused by delusion?
If bodily, verbal, or mental karma has delusion as its cause, delusion as its sequence, delusion as its origin, and delusion as its condition, this is called karma caused by delusion.
What is action caused by non-greed?

If one’s bodily, verbal, and mental actions have non-greed as their cause, non-greed as their sequence, non-greed as their origin, and non-greed as their condition, this is called action caused by non-greed.
What is action caused by non-ill will?

If bodily, verbal, and mental actions have non-ill will as their cause, non-ill will as their sequence, non-ill will as their origin, and non-ill will as their condition, these are called actions caused by non-ill will.
What is action caused by non-delusion?

If bodily, vocal, and mental actions have non-delusion as their cause, non-delusion as their sequence, non-delusion as their origin, and non-delusion as their condition, these are called actions caused by non-delusion.
What is karma that leads to rebirth in hell?
If unwholesome karma increases such that it can cause birth in hell, this is called karma leading to hell.
What is karma leading to rebirth as an animal?
If among unwholesome karmas there is that which can cause birth among animals, this is called karma leading to the animal realm.
What is karma leading to the hungry ghost realm?
If there is unwholesome karma that is mild, which can cause birth among hungry ghosts, this is called karma directed toward the hungry ghost realm.
What is karma that leads to rebirth among humans?
If karma is wholesome yet does not increase [in strength], it can cause one to be born among humans; this is called karma leading to rebirth among humans.
What is karma that leads to rebirth among devas?
If karma is wholesome and predominant, such that it can cause rebirth in the heavens, this is called "karma leading to the heavens.
What is "karma leading to nirvana"?
If karma is noble and possesses retribution, and is capable of severing the afflictions, this is called "karma leading to nirvana."
What are the seven unwholesome factors?
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—these are called the seven unwholesome factors.
What are the seven wholesome dharmas?

They are: refraining from killing, refraining from stealing, refraining from sexual misconduct, refraining from false speech, refraining from divisive speech, refraining from harsh speech, and refraining from frivolous speech. These are called the seven wholesome dharmas.
What are the eight non-noble modes of speech?

To say one has seen when one has not seen, to say one has not seen when one has seen; to say one has heard when one has not heard, to say one has not heard when one has heard; to say one has sensed when one has not sensed, to say one has not sensed when one has sensed; to say one has cognized when one has not cognized, to say one has not cognized when one has cognized—these are called the eight non-noble modes of speech.

What are the eight noble modes of speech? To say one has not seen when one has not seen; to say one has seen when one has seen; to say one has not heard when one has not heard; to say one has heard when one has heard; to say one has not cognized when one has not cognized; to say one has cognized when one has cognized; to say one has not known when one has not known; to say one has known when one has known—these are called the eight noble modes of speech.
What is bodily action caused by greed?

If a bodily action is unwholesome, arising from greed, not being free from greed, and with the mind covered by greed—such as the bodily intimation of going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning about, as well as bodily non-restraint and non-intimation—this is called bodily action caused by greed.
What is verbal karma caused by greed?

If verbal karma is unwholesome, arising from greed, not being free from greed, and with the mind enveloped by greed, it consists of the instruction of verbal karma—the collection of sounds, phonemes, and speech—as well as verbal non-restraint and non-informative action (*avijñapti*); this is called verbal karma caused by greed.
What is mental action caused by greed?
If mental action is unwholesome and caused by greed—not being free from greed, with the mind covered by greed and associated with volition—it is called mental action caused by greed.
