What is bodily action caused by hatred?

If unwholesome bodily action arises from hatred, not being free from hatred, and with the mind covered by hatred—consisting of the bodily intimation of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning about, as well as bodily non-informative matter that is not part of the precepts—this is called bodily action caused by hatred.
What is verbal action caused by hatred?

If verbal action is unwholesome, arising from hatred, not free from hatred, with the mind covered by hatred, consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and speech as verbal instruction—whether manifest verbal non-restraint or non-manifest verbal non-restraint—this is called verbal action caused by hatred.
What is mental action caused by hatred?
If mental action is unwholesome, caused by hatred, not free from hatred, and associated with volition whose mind is shrouded by hatred—this is called mental action caused by hatred.
What is bodily action caused by delusion?

If bodily action is unwholesome, caused by delusion, not free from delusion, and arises with a mind shrouded by delusion—consisting of the bodily intimation of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, as well as bodily non-intimation that is not restraint—this is called bodily action caused by delusion.
What is vocal karma caused by delusion?

If vocal karma is unwholesome, arises from delusion, is not free from delusion, and is produced when the mind is shrouded by delusion—consisting of the vocal instruction that gathers sounds, phonemes, and speech, as well as vocal non-restraint and non-informative action—this is called vocal karma caused by delusion.
What is mental action caused by delusion?
If a mental action is unwholesome, caused by delusion, not free from delusion, and associated with volition whose mind is shrouded by delusion, this is called mental action caused by delusion.
What is bodily action caused by non-greed?

If bodily action is wholesome, arising from non-greed—being free from greed and not obscured by greed—and consists of informative and non-informative bodily discipline (*kāya-śīla*) that is tainted (*sāsrava*), including the movements of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning, this is called bodily action caused by non-greed.
What is verbal action caused by non-greed?

If verbal action is wholesome and arises from non-greed—being free from greed and not covered by greed—and consists of the vocal instruction of sounds, phonemes, and speech that has accumulated, as well as the informative and non-informative aspects of impure verbal restraint, this is called verbal action caused by non-greed.
What is mental action caused by non-greed?

If mental action is wholesome, having non-greed as its cause—being free from greed and associated with volition (*cetanā*) whose mind is not obscured by greed—this is called mental action caused by non-greed.
What is bodily action caused by non-ill will?

If bodily action is wholesome, caused by non-ill will, free from ill will, and not covered by ill will, arising as the informative and non-informative bodily discipline—whether it be the movement of going, coming, bending, stretching, or turning—it is called bodily action caused by non-ill will.
What is verbal action caused by non-ill will?

If verbal action is wholesome, caused by non-ill will, free from ill will, and not covered by ill will; that which arises from the collection of sounds, phrases, and speech as vocal instruction, including the informative and non-informative aspects of impure verbal restraint—this is called verbal action caused by non-ill will.
What is the mental action caused by non-hatred?

If a wholesome mental action is caused by non-hatred—being free from hatred and not having the mind obscured by hatred—and is associated with volition (*cetanā*), this is called the mental action caused by non-hatred.
What is bodily action caused by non-delusion?

If wholesome bodily action arises from non-delusion, free from delusion, and not obscured by delusion—consisting of the bodily intimation of going, coming, bending, stretching, and turning; the contaminated bodily discipline of both informative and non-informative types; right action; and right livelihood—this is called bodily action caused by non-delusion.
What is verbal action caused by non-delusion?

If verbal action is wholesome, caused by non-delusion, free from delusion, and arises from a mind not obscured by delusion—consisting of vocal instruction through the collection of sounds, phrases, and words; including both the informative and non-informative aspects of impure verbal restraint; and comprising right speech and right livelihood—this is called verbal action caused by non-delusion.
What is mental action caused by non-delusion?

If a wholesome mental action is caused by non-delusion, is free from delusion, and is associated with volition (*cetanā*) that is not obscured by delusion, this is called mental action caused by non-delusion.
What are the ten unwholesome courses of action?
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—these are called the ten unwholesome courses of action.
What are the ten paths of wholesome action? They are:

abstaining from killing, abstaining from stealing, abstaining from sexual misconduct, abstaining from false speech, abstaining from divisive speech, abstaining from harsh speech, abstaining from frivolous speech, abstaining from covetousness, abstaining from ill will, and practicing right view. These are called the ten paths of wholesome action.
What are the ten dharmas that, when accomplished, cause one to fall into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear?
Killing, up to and including wrong view—these ten dharmas, when accomplished, cause one to fall into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear.
What are the ten dharmas that, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a hurled spear?
They are the practice of non-killing up to right view; these ten, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a hurled spear.
What are the twenty dharmas by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear? They are:

killing oneself, inciting others to kill, and so on, up to holding wrong views oneself and inciting others to hold wrong views. These are called the twenty dharmas by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear.
What are the twenty dharmas that, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a hurled spear?

They are: personally refraining from taking life and teaching others to refrain from taking life, up to and including personally maintaining right view and teaching others to practice right view. These are the twenty dharmas that, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a hurled spear.
What are the thirty factors by which one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear?

They are: committing killing oneself, inciting others to kill, and praising killing; and so on, up to: holding wrong views oneself, inciting others to hold wrong views, and praising wrong views. These are the thirty factors by which one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear.
What are the thirty factors that, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a thrust spear?

They are: refraining from killing oneself, teaching others not to kill, and praising the abstention from killing; and so on, up to: maintaining right view oneself, teaching others right view, and praising the practice of right view. These are called the thirty factors that, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a thrust spear.
What are the forty factors by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear?

They are: killing oneself, inciting others to kill, praising killing, and taking delight in killing; and so on, up to: holding wrong views oneself, inciting others to hold wrong views, praising wrong views, and taking delight in wrong views. These are the forty factors by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear.
What are the forty factors that, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a hurled spear? They are:

not killing oneself, teaching others not to kill, praising the abstention from killing, and not taking pleasure in killing; and so on, up to: having right view oneself, teaching others right view, praising right view, and taking pleasure in the practice of right view. These are the forty factors that, when accomplished, lead to rebirth in a good destination as swiftly as a hurled spear. This concludes the Chapter on Karma.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Scroll Seven;
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others.
Chapter Three: The Chapter on Persons (Pudgala-varga), Part Two: The Non-Interrogative Section. There are ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and non-ordinary persons;
persons by nature (*prakṛti-pudgala*), śrāvaka persons, bodhisattva persons, pratyekabuddha persons, and perfectly awakened persons (*samyaksaṃbuddha-pudgala*).
Those who are persons entering the realization of the fruit of stream-entry and those who are stream-enterers;
those who are persons entering the realization of the fruit of once-returning and those who are once-returners;
those who are persons entering the realization of the fruit of non-returning and those who are non-returners.
Those who are persons realizing the fruit of arhatship and those who are arhats;
persons who are self-sufficient and those who are sufficient for others;
persons in training, persons beyond training, and persons who are neither in training nor beyond training.
Those fixed in the right, those fixed in the wrong, and those who are unfixed;
the blind, the one-eyed, and the two-eyed;
those who practice loving-kindness, those who practice compassion, those who practice sympathetic joy, and those who practice equanimity.
The practitioner of emptiness, the practitioner of signlessness, and the practitioner of wishlessness.
The practitioner who does not cause affliction.
The practitioner of the superior entry and the practitioner of the universal entry.
Those who have cultivated the eight liberations;
those who possess the six supernormal powers;
those who have reached the limit in this world; and those who have reached the limit in that world.
One liberated in part, one liberated in both parts;
one liberated by wisdom, one who has attained realization through the body, one who has attained vision, one liberated by faith, one of firm conviction, and one of firm dharma.
One who has severed the five factors,
one who has accomplished the six factors,
and one who possesses the single protection.
The four reliances:
the person who has extinguished divergent conditions, the real person,
and the person who seeks the most excellent.
One who is not turbid in thought;
one who has removed bodily conduct;
one whose mind is well-liberated; and one whose wisdom is well-liberated.
Those liberated both ways and those not liberated both ways;
those subject to regression and those not subject to regression;
and those who possess deliberation.
Those who protect slightly;
those who contemplate non-retrogression but do not contemplate retrogression;
and those who protect non-retrogression but do not protect retrogression.
There are those who shoot at people;
by law, they shall not be initiated, nor shall they be permitted to reside during the kalpa.
The vanguard;
those who cross the moat, those who breach the moat;
and those who advance on horseback.
There are no defiled persons and no indolent or arrogant persons. What,
then, is an ordinary person?
If a person has not yet entered into the state of right determination, they are called an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
How is one not an ordinary person?
If a person has entered into the state of right determination, they are called one who is not an ordinary person.
Furthermore, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is one who has not yet attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); such a person is called an ordinary person.
Furthermore, a non-ordinary person is one who has attained right determination; such a person is called a non-ordinary person.
Furthermore, as for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*): if a person has not yet attained, nor ever before attained, the five noble faculties (*āryendriya*), they are called an ordinary person.
Furthermore, what is a non-ordinary person?
If a person has attained or previously attained the five noble faculties, they are called a non-ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
What is a person by nature (*prakṛtipudgala*)?

If a person dwells successively in the superior dharmas of an ordinary person, and if those dharmas immediately cease before reaching the stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), such a person is called a person by nature.
What is a person of natural disposition?
It is a person who accomplishes the qualities of natural disposition.
What are the qualities of natural disposition?
If one contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and reflects upon the tranquility of nirvana;

for a person who is not yet established in the certainty of the right path but practices according to reality—whether it be feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial and sustained application of thought, view, wisdom, liberation, non-delusion, faith, joy, gladness, mental energy, confidence, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, the sphere of mental consciousness, the mind-sphere, or the bodily and verbal precepts practiced according to reality—these are called natural phenomena (*dharmas by nature*).
If a person accomplishes this Dharma, they are called a person by nature (*prakṛti-pudgala*).
What is a person who is a śrāvaka?

If a person hears from another, receives instruction from another, requests another to speak, and listens to the Dharma from another—rather than through their own reflection, their own awakening, or their own contemplation reaching the supreme right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)—and thereby attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), such a person is called a śrāvaka.
What is a person who is a bodhisattva?

If a person is endowed with the thirty-two marks, and without hearing from others, receiving instruction from others, requesting others to speak, or listening to the Dharma from others, they contemplate for themselves, awaken for themselves, and observe for themselves; they possess unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena; they shall attain the sovereign power and noble majesty of self-mastery; they shall attain the knowledge and vision of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; and they shall accomplish the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata, achieve great compassion, and turn the wheel of the Dharma—this is called a person who is a bodhisattva.
What is a person who is a pratyekabuddha?

It refers to a person who does not possess the thirty-two marks, who has not heard from another, received instruction from another, requested another to speak, or listened to the Dharma from another; yet, through his own reflection, his own awakening, and his own contemplation, he attains the supreme and correct resolve, and realizes the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat. Regarding all dharmas, he lacks unobstructed knowledge and vision, has not attained mastery, has not attained mastery through power, has not attained mastery as a noble and exalted being, has not attained the unsurpassed, most excellent, and perfect awakening of knowledge and vision, and has not achieved the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and great compassion to turn the wheel of Dharma. Such a person is called a pratyekabuddha.
What is a person who is a pratyekabuddha?

It is one who does not possess the thirty-two marks, nor has heard from another, nor received instruction from another, nor requested another to speak, nor listened to the Dharma from another; yet, through self-reflection, self-awakening, and self-contemplation, he attains the supreme and correct resolve, realizing the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat. Regarding all dharmas, his mind possesses unobstructed knowledge and vision; his mind attains mastery, his mind attains sovereign power, and his mind is noble, eminent, and exalted. However, he does not possess the unsurpassed, most excellent, and perfectly awakened knowledge and vision, nor does he achieve the Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, and great compassion to turn the wheel of the Dharma—this is called a person who is a pratyekabuddha.
What is a person of perfect enlightenment?

It is one who, having accomplished the thirty-two marks, does not hear from others, does not receive instruction from others, does not request others to speak, and does not listen to the teachings of others; but through self-reflection, self-awakening, and self-contemplation, attains unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena, achieves mastery over the powers, and possesses sovereign, noble, and supreme excellence; having attained the unsurpassed, most excellent, and perfect enlightenment, accomplishes the ten powers and four fearlessnesses of a Tathāgata, and achieves great compassion; thus, with sovereignty, he turns the wheel of Dharma—this is called a person of perfect enlightenment.
What is one who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry?

If a person has attained the path leading to the realization of the fruit of stream-entry, but has not yet attained, touched, or realized the fruit of stream-entry itself, this is called one who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of stream-entry.
What is a person who is a stream-enterer (srotāpanna)?

It is one who has realized the fruit of stream-entry and abides in that fruit, but has not yet attained the higher path leading toward the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin); such a person is called a stream-enterer.
What is one who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*?

If a person has attained the path to the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, but has not yet attained the direct realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* itself, this is called one who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
What is a sakṛdāgāmin?
If a person, having attained and realized the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, abides in that fruit but has not yet attained the higher path leading to the fruit of an anāgāmin, this is called a sakṛdāgāmin.
Who is the person proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of anāgāmin?

If a person has attained the path to the realization of the fruit of anāgāmin, but has not yet attained the fruit of anāgāmin nor touched its realization, this is called a person proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of anāgāmin.
What is a non-returner (anāgāmin)?
If a person has attained and realized the fruit of non-returning, abides in that fruit, and has not yet attained the higher path leading toward the fruit of arhatship, this is called a non-returner.
Who is the person progressing toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship?

It is one who has attained the path leading to the realization of the fruit of arhatship, yet has not yet attained the fruit of arhatship nor touched its realization; such a person is called one progressing toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship.
What is a person who is an Arhat?
If a person has attained the fruit of Arhatship and has realized it through direct contact with the path, they are called a person who is an Arhat.

Furthermore, those who are proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of Srotāpanna—those of steadfast faith and steadfast Dharma—are called persons proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of Srotāpanna.
What is a *srotāpanna*?

If a person has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed by vision—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—and through the Noble Path has simultaneously severed those afflictions and abides in that abandonment; yet has not yet attained the higher path and has only partially severed the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will which are to be severed by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), such a person is called a *srotāpanna*.

Furthermore, regarding the person who is a candidate for the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*: if a person has abandoned three afflictions to be severed through vision—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—and having simultaneously severed those afflictions by means of the Noble Path, attains the higher path while still partially severing, yet not fully severing, the portion of the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will (*kāmacchanda* and *vyāpāda*) to be severed through cultivation, such a person is called a candidate for the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Furthermore, regarding the *sakṛdāgāmin*: if a person has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed by vision—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—by severing them all at once through the Noble Path; and if they have also partially severed the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will to be severed by cultivation, severing them all at once through the Noble Path and abiding in that abandonment, yet have not attained the higher path; and while the remaining afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will to be severed by cultivation have not been fully severed, they are called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Furthermore, regarding the person who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of Anāgāmin: if a person has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed by vision—namely, the view of a self, doubt, and attachment to precepts—and has simultaneously severed them through the Noble Path; and if they have simultaneously severed through the Noble Path the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will to be severed by cultivation, yet among the remaining afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will to be severed by cultivation, some have been completely severed while others have not yet been severed—such a person is called one who is proceeding toward the fruit of Anāgāmin.

Furthermore, regarding the person who is a non-returner (anāgāmin): if the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill-will—are abandoned simultaneously by means of the Noble Path, and he abides in that abandonment; yet, having not yet attained the higher path, he has not completely abandoned the afflictions pertaining to the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya), such a person is called a non-returner.

Furthermore, regarding the person who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of Arhatship: if a person has abandoned the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill-will—and has severed them all simultaneously by means of the Noble Path; and having attained the higher path, they have abandoned the afflictions pertaining to the form realm and the formless realm that are to be abandoned through cultivation, such that they are either completely severed or not yet severed, this person is called one who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of Arhatship.

Furthermore, an Arhat is one who, through contemplation, has completely and without remainder abandoned the afflictions pertaining to the realm of form and the afflictions pertaining to the formless realm; such a person is called an Arhat.
Furthermore, regarding the Arhat: if a person has severed all afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called an Arhat.
When all afflictions are exhausted, it is the fruit of Arhatship; if a person attains direct realization of this, they are called an Arhat.
What is a person who is self-sufficient?
As the Blessed One said:
"Two persons in the world are difficult to find."
What are the two?
Self-sufficiency and sufficiency for others.
What is sufficiency for others?

If a person gives to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, to those who are greedy and insatiable, and to poor beggars—food and drink, vehicles, clothing, incense, flowers, ointments, beds, mats, bedding, dwellings, and lamps for reliance—this is called "one who satisfies others."
What is a person who is self-sufficient?
If a bhikṣu has exhausted all outflows, up to having accomplished what was to be done and no longer returning to this state of existence—he is called a self-sufficient person.
Of these two persons,
which one is it that speaks of the Tathāgata-nature?
The reason is as follows:
"One who brings fulfillment to both oneself and others is extremely rare in this world;
a donor who is like a clear pool, who constantly abides in the body of pure precepts,
and who is further able to give food and drink— such a person is exceedingly difficult to find."
"Free from desire and having severed ill will, Having extinguished delusion and attained the outflow-free state,
Self-sufficient through the noble Dharma— Such a person is exceedingly rare.
What is a trainee?

Those who are persons realizing the fruit of stream-entry, stream-enterers; those who are persons realizing the fruit of once-returning, once-returners; those who are persons realizing the fruit of non-returning, non-returners; and those who are persons realizing the fruit of arhatship—these are called persons in training (*śaikṣa*).
Who is the person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
An Arhat is called a person beyond training.
Who is the person who is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*)?
Ordinary worldlings are called persons who are neither in training nor beyond training.
What is a person of right determination?
If a person has attained the supreme right determination, they are called a person of right determination.
What is a person of wrong determination?
If a person enters into wrong determination, they are called a person of wrong determination.
What is a person of no fixed determination?

If a person has not ascended to right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and has not entered into wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyāma*), they are called an indeterminate person (*aniyata-pudgala*).
What is a person of right determination?
If a person has attained right determination, they are called a person of right determination.
What is a person of wrong determination?
If a person has attained wrong determination, they are called a person of wrong determination.
What is a person of no fixed determination?
If a person has neither attained right determination nor attained wrong determination, they are called an indeterminate person.
What is a person of right determination?
If a person has attained the five noble faculties and has previously attained them, they are called a person of right determination.
What is a person of wrong determination?
It refers to a person who has committed one or more of the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and, having accomplished them, has not yet experienced their maturation;
or one who has accomplished one or two of the five deeds of immediate retribution and has not yet experienced their maturation—this is called a person of wrong determination.
What is a person of indeterminate status?

It refers to a person who has not yet attained the five noble faculties (*āryendriya*), has never before attained them, does not commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), and does not bring them to completion; nor does he incur their karmic retribution. Regarding the five deeds of immediate retribution, he has not accomplished them, and whether one or two of them have been committed, he does not undergo their retribution. Such a person is called one of indeterminate status.
What is meant by a blind person?
If a person possesses eyes, yet is unable to acquire wealth and treasures that have not been acquired, or is unable to increase those already acquired;
or if a person possesses eyes, yet is unable to give rise to wholesome dharmas that have not arisen, or is unable to expand those already arisen—such a person lacks these eyes and is called "blind."
What is meant by a person with one eye?
It refers to a person who possesses eyes such that they are able to acquire wealth and treasures not yet obtained, and having acquired them, increase and expand them;

yet, though possessing such eyes, they lack the capacity to give rise to wholesome dharmas not yet arisen, or, having given rise to them, to cause them to increase and expand—such a person is called one with one eye.
What is one who possesses two eyes?
If a person is endowed with eyes such that they can acquire wealth and treasures not yet obtained, and having acquired them, can increase and expand them—possessing such eyes;

or if a person is endowed with eyes such that they can produce wholesome states not yet arisen, and having produced them, can increase and expand them—possessing such eyes, this is called one who possesses two eyes.
What is one who practices loving-kindness?
If a person attains a mind resolved upon loving-kindness and frequently engages in this practice, they are called one who practices loving-kindness.
What is one who practices compassion?
If a person attains a mind resolved upon compassion and frequently practices this conduct, they are called a practitioner of compassion.
What is a practitioner of sympathetic joy?
If a person attains a mind resolved upon sympathetic joy and frequently practices this conduct, they are called a practitioner of sympathetic joy.
What is the person who practices equanimity (*upekṣā-carita*)?
If a person attains the mind of equanimous understanding and frequently practices this conduct, they are called a person who practices equanimity.

Furthermore, regarding the person who practices loving-kindness (*maitrī-carita*): if a person, having attained the mind of loving-kindness and mental pliancy, and having cultivated gentleness, subsequently enters right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), they are called a person who practices loving-kindness.

Furthermore, regarding the practitioner of compassion (*karuṇā-carita*): if a person, having attained the liberation of the mind through compassion and having cultivated mental pliancy, successively ascends to right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), this is called a practitioner of compassion.

Furthermore, regarding the person who practices through joy (*ratisaṃhita*): if a person, having attained joyful understanding and tamed the mind, and having cultivated pliancy, sequentially ascends to right determination and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), such a person is called one who practices through joy.
What is one who practices through equanimity?

If a person, having attained equanimity and having trained and disciplined the mind, and having cultivated pliancy, sequentially ascends to right determination and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), this is called one who practices through equanimity.
What is one who practices emptiness?
If a person attains the concentration of emptiness and frequently engages in this practice, they are called one who practices emptiness.
What is one who practices signlessness?
If a person attains the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*) and frequently practices this cultivation, they are called a practitioner of signlessness.
What is a practitioner of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-prayogin*)?
If a person attains the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) and frequently practices this cultivation, they are called a practitioner of wishlessness.

Furthermore, regarding the practitioner of emptiness: if a person attains the practice of emptiness and enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), thereby realizing the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), such a person is called a practitioner of emptiness.

Furthermore, regarding the practitioner of the signless: if a person attains the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), enters the supreme right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and realizes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), this is called a practitioner of the signless.
What is a practitioner of the wishless (apraṇihita)?

If a person attains the concentration of the wishless, enters the supreme certainty, and realizes the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin), or the fruit of arhatship, this is called a practitioner of the wishless.
What is the practitioner who is free from affliction?
It is one who has attained the dharma of being free from affliction.
What is the dharma of being free from affliction?
That is to say, if a person knows what is praise-worthy and knows what is not praise-worthy;
having known what is praise-worthy and what is not praise-worthy, they neither praise nor do not praise, but teach the Dharma with clarity and understand the Dharma with clarity.

Having understood the Dharma, he delights inwardly in diligence; he does not speak of evil behind one's back nor praise goodness to one's face. He proclaims the Dharma in full measure rather than incompletely; he need not regard the customs of a region, nor follow the etiquette of non-humans, but teaches the Dharma according to the local circumstances.

Furthermore, one cultivates the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, dhyānas, and liberations; having cultivated them, one attains noble, untainted equanimity. If one possesses such equanimity, one accords with the Dharma and Vinaya.

He does not engage in the base conduct of ordinary people who pursue sensual pleasures, nor does he engage in the non-noble and meaningless asceticism of suffering; always abandoning these two extremes, he enters and practices the Middle Way, knowing what is to be commended and what is not to be commended.

Having understood that there is neither exhortation nor non-exhortation, he neither exhorts nor does not exhort; he teaches the Dharma with clarity and understands the Dharma with clarity. Having understood the Dharma, he delights in internal diligence;

he does not speak of evil behind one’s back, nor does he praise goodness in one’s presence. His teaching of the Dharma is complete and not incomplete; he need not look toward the directions, nor does he engage in the etiquette of censuring others. He teaches the Dharma according to the circumstances, free from affliction and detached from affliction, liberated from affliction and entering the state of non-affliction.
Furthermore, this is that which has been collectively established by those people as "non-affliction.
One who practices this is called a practitioner of non-affliction.
What is a practitioner of superior entry?
If a person attains the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and frequently practices them, this is called one who practices the bases of mastery.
What is one who practices the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
If a person attains the ten universal bases and frequently practices them, this is called one who practices the universal bases.
What is one who cultivates the eight liberations?
If a person attains the eight liberations and frequently practices this practice, they are called one who cultivates the eight liberations.
What is one with the six supernormal powers?
If a person has accomplished the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and frequently practices these activities, they are called a person of the six supernormal powers.
What are the five types of persons who have reached the end?

They are: the person of seven births (*saptakṛdbhavaparama*), the family-to-family person (*kulaṃkula*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the one-interval person (*ekavīcika*), and the person who attains arhatship in the present life.
What is a person who will be reborn seven times at most?
A *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is called a person who will be reborn seven times at most.

Furthermore, regarding the person who will be reborn seven times at most: if a person has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed by vision—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—these are all severed simultaneously through the Noble Path.

Abiding in that abandonment, though not yet having attained the higher path, one performs the work of partially severing the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will through contemplation; such a person will necessarily undergo seven more births as a god and seven more births as a human. Having completed these seven divine and seven human existences, they reach the end of suffering; this is called a "seven-times-born" person (*saptakṛtvah-parama*).
What is meant by a "householder who dwells at home"?

It refers to a person who has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed through vision—namely, the view of a self, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—having severed them all simultaneously through the Noble Path. Such a person attains the higher path and partially severs the afflictions of sensual desire and ill will that are to be severed through cultivation, yet has not yet fully severed their karmic activity. They are destined to be reborn once, or to undergo two or three human existences; having experienced those two or three human lives, they will reach the end of suffering. This is called a householder who dwells at home.

Furthermore, regarding the "householder" (gahapati): if a person has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed by vision—namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—and has simultaneously severed them through the Noble Path; yet, regarding the afflictions to be severed by cultivation (*bhāvanāheya*), such as sensual desire and ill-will, has only partially severed them and has not yet attained the state of a *sakṛdāgāmin*; and who, having necessarily been reborn once more, or having experienced two or three human existences, will reach the end of suffering after completing those two or three human lives—such a person is called a householder.
What is a *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner)?

It is a person who has abandoned the three afflictions to be abandoned by vision—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—abandoning them all simultaneously through the Noble Path; and who has partially abandoned the afflictions of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and ill-will (*vyāpāda*) to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), abandoning them all simultaneously through the Noble Path and abiding in that abandonment. Having not yet attained the higher path that effects the complete abandonment of the remaining sensual desire and ill-will to be abandoned by cultivation, such a person will necessarily be born once more in a single celestial or human body. Having experienced and traversed that single celestial or human existence, they will reach the end of suffering. This is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.

Furthermore, regarding the *sakṛdāgāmin*: if a person has abandoned three afflictions to be severed through vision—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—having severed them all at once by means of the Noble Path; and if they have partially severed the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will (*rāga* and *pratigha*) to be severed through cultivation; and if they have "transcended the state of one who belongs to a family" (*kulaṃkula*), such that they do not necessarily undergo birth as a single type of being in a single heaven or a single human body, but rather, having experienced existence in one heaven or one human body, they reach the end of suffering—this is called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
What is the person of one birth (*ekabījī*)?

It is a person who, having abandoned the three afflictions to be abandoned by vision—namely, the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)—abandons them all simultaneously through the Noble Path; and who, having abandoned a portion of the afflictions of sensual desire and ill-will to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), abandons them all simultaneously through the Noble Path and attains the higher path. Having abandoned the remaining portions of sensual desire and ill-will to be abandoned by cultivation without remainder, yet not having abandoned the karma that must necessarily result in birth, such a person will take birth in only one more human body. Having experienced and lived out that single human life, they reach the end of suffering. This is called the person of one birth.

Furthermore, there is a person of one type: if a person has abandoned the three afflictions to be severed by vision—namely, the view of a self, doubt, and attachment to precepts—and abandons them all at once through the Noble Path; and if they have largely abandoned the craving for sensual desire and ill-will to be severed by cultivation, surpassing the stage of a Sakṛdāgāmin; yet they do not perform the karma of an Anāgāmin, but must necessarily be born once more as a single human body, and having experienced that single human existence, they will reach the end of suffering. This is called a person of one type.
What is meant by one who attains arhatship in the present body?

If a person, through my emanation—whether appearing as old or young—enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and that person, in this very life and through this very emanation of mine, whether old or young, attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), or attains the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*), such a person is called one who attains the fruit of arhatship in the present body.
These are called the five persons who reach the limit here.
What are the five persons who reach the limit there?

They are: one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, one who attains parinirvāṇa quickly after birth, one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion, one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion, and one who attains parinirvāṇa by ascending the stream.
What is one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state?

It is a person who has abandoned the five lower fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will—having severed them all simultaneously by means of the Noble Path. Possessing the most excellent proficiency in the five noble faculties—the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—if they attain swift liberation through this pleasant path, or if, having cultivated that path, they attain the fruit of arhatship.

He encounters obstacles such that he does not attain the fruit of arhatship in his present body; or, due to many conditions, he practices loving-kindness toward his relatives, and by the force of past karma, he will necessarily be reborn with a celestial body. Therein, he experiences dissatisfaction, is born into dissatisfaction, dwells in dissatisfaction, and acts with dissatisfaction, before attaining parinirvāṇa within that celestial body.
What is meant by "parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state" (antarā-parinirvāṇa)?

Having passed away from the desire realm and been reborn among the devas of the form realm, one attains parinirvāṇa within the lifespan of those devas and within the cessation of phenomena there; this is called parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.

Furthermore, this is a designation collectively established by those people; it is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state," and such a person is called one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
What is a person who attains parinirvāṇa quickly?

If a person has abandoned the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will—and abandons them all simultaneously through the Noble Path, this noble one possesses sharp faculties and is thus not equal to one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state.
What are the five?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Whether this path is one of swift liberation through suffering, or whether by cultivating that path one attains the fruit of arhatship.

He encounters obstacles such that he does not attain the fruit of arhatship in his present body. Because he has practiced loving-kindness toward his relatives for many reasons, he will necessarily receive the body of a certain deity due to his past karma. In that state, there will be what is disagreeable to him; he will experience what is disagreeable in its arising, its abiding, and its activity. From that celestial body, he will quickly pass into parinirvāṇa.
What is meant by "swift parinirvāṇa"?

One who, at the end of life in the desire realm, is reborn in a heaven of the form realm, and because that heaven has a short lifespan and much pleasure, attains parinirvāṇa quickly; this is called swift parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, this is a designation established by common consensus among those people, called "one who attains parinirvāṇa quickly"; such is called "one who attains parinirvāṇa quickly.
What is "one who attains parinirvāṇa without application" (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin)?

If a person has abandoned the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will—and has severed them all simultaneously through the Noble Path, this noble one possesses weak faculties.
What are the five?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of concentration, the faculty of wisdom, and the faculty of mindfulness.
Whether this path is pleasant yet difficult to realize, or whether one cultivates that path to attain the fruit of arhatship.

He encountered obstacles such that he could not attain the fruit of Arhatship in his present body; because he practiced compassion toward his relatives for many reasons, he will, due to his past karma, necessarily be reborn to receive the body of a deva.

Therein, one experiences pleasure, gives rise to pleasure, dwells in displeasure, and acts with displeasure; yet, within that celestial body, one attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyī*).
What is meant by "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion"?

If one passes away from the desire realm and is reborn in the heavens of the form realm, and there attains the path of non-interval (ānantarya-mārga) without exertion, and having attained it, attains parinirvāṇa right there in that interval, this is called "parinirvāṇa without exertion" (anabhisamskāra-parinirvāṇa).
Furthermore, this is what is collectively designated by those people as "attaining parinirvāṇa without exertion," and such a person is called one who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion.
What is a person who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion?

If a person has abandoned the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will—and has severed them all simultaneously by means of the Noble Path, yet their five faculties of the noble ones are weak.
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Whether this path is difficult to realize or, having cultivated that path, one has attained the fruit of arhatship.

He encounters obstacles such that he does not attain the fruit of arhatship in his present body; because he has performed many acts of compassion toward his relatives, he will, by virtue of his past karma, necessarily be reborn with the body of a certain deva. While in that deva-body, he experiences pleasure when entering, pleasure when born, and pleasure while dwelling, yet experiences displeasure when moving about; therein, within that deva-body, he attains parinirvāṇa through practice.
What is meant by parinirvāṇa through effort?

One who, at the end of life in the desire realm, is reborn in a celestial realm of the form realm, and who—possessing effort and finding it difficult to attain the path of non-interval—attains it and thereupon enters parinirvāṇa; this is called parinirvāṇa through effort.

Furthermore, this is a designation collectively established by those people, called "one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion," and such a person is termed "one who attains parinirvāṇa with exertion.
What is a person who is an "upstreamer" (ūrdhva-srotas) reaching as far as Akaniṣṭha?

If a person has abandoned the five lower-tier fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill-will—and abandons them all simultaneously through the Noble Path, this person’s five faculties of the noble ones are the weakest.
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
Whether this path is pleasant yet difficult to realize or painful yet difficult to realize, by cultivating that path one attains the fruit of arhatship.

He encountered obstacles such that he could not realize the fruit of arhatship in his present body; because he practiced loving-kindness toward his relatives for many reasons, by virtue of his past karma he will certainly be reborn to receive a body in the five heavens, where he will experience pleasure upon entering, pleasure upon being born, pleasure while dwelling, and pleasure while moving about.
If such a person passes away from here, they will ascend to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
What is meant by "ascending to the Akaniṣṭha"?
It means that after passing away in the desire realm, one is born among the Unsurpassed Gods (Akanistha) of the form realm and dwells there for the full lifespan of those gods.
Having lived their full lifespan as those devas, they pass away and are reborn among the gods of the Heatless Heaven (Atapa).
Having been born among the gods of the Heatless Heaven, they pass away and are reborn among the gods of the Clearly Visible Heaven (Sudṛśa).
Having been born among the Sudarśana devas, at the end of that life they are reborn among the Sudarśanīya devas.
Having been born among the Sudarśanīya devas, at the end of that life they are reborn among the Akaniṣṭha devas, where they remain for the full lifespan of those gods.
Having lived for the full lifespan of those gods, they attain the path of non-interruption and realize the fruit of arhatship.
Having realized the fruit of arhatship, they enter parinirvāṇa right there; this is called the "upward-streamer" who reaches Akaniṣṭha.
Furthermore, this is a designation collectively established by those people: one who flows upward as far as Akaniṣṭha is called a person who flows upward as far as Akaniṣṭha.
These are called the five types of persons who have reached the ultimate limit.
What is a person liberated by one part?

It refers to a person who, while still in training, attains the eight liberations and the attainment of cessation, but does not attain the eight liberations and the attainment of cessation at the later stage of being beyond training.
Subsequently, at the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), one attains the eight liberations and the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
One who attains the eight liberations and the attainment of cessation at the stage of learning (śaikṣa) is called a person liberated by one part (ekadeśavimukta).
What is the person liberated in both ways?

If a person, while still in training, attains the eight liberations and the attainment of cessation, and later, when no longer in training, also attains the eight liberations and the attainment of cessation, this is called a person liberated in both ways.

Furthermore, regarding those liberated in one part (*ekadeśavimukta*): if a person has produced the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) but not the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), this is called a person liberated in one part.

Furthermore, regarding those liberated in both parts (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*): if both the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising have been produced, this is called a person liberated in both parts.
What is a person liberated by wisdom (paññāvimutta)?

If a person, having attained peaceful liberation beyond the realms of form and the formless, does not personally touch it with the body, but through the practice of insight (vipassanā) abandons the outflows (āsava), this is called a person liberated by wisdom.
What is a person who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*)?

If a person, having attained peaceful liberation beyond the realm of form and the formless realm, cultivates the bodily contact and practice [of that liberation], yet does not abandon the outflows (*āsrava*) through the vision of wisdom, this is called a person who has realized through the body.
What is one who attains through vision?

If a person, having attained tranquility and liberation beyond the realms of form and formlessness, does not proceed by bodily contact, nor does he abandon the outflows through the vision of wisdom, but rather practices primarily through the discernment of wisdom according to the Dharma disseminated by the Blessed One—this is called one who attains through vision.
What is a person liberated through faith?

It is a person who has attained peaceful liberation beyond the realms of form and formlessness, yet has not personally touched it with the body nor severed the outflows through the vision of wisdom; following the Dharma as promulgated by the Blessed One, they have attained vision through the practice of discernment by means of wisdom, but have not yet reached [the higher stage]. This is called a person liberated through faith.
What is one who has attained through vision?

If a person attains the firm Dharma, enters the supreme and correct determination, and realizes the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), yet has not yet attained the eight liberations or the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), this is called one who has attained through vision.
What is a person liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta)?

If a person has attained firm faith, entered into the supreme and right determination, and has realized the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti), the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmin), or the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin), yet has not yet attained the eight liberations or the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), this is called a person liberated through faith.
What is a person of firm faith?

If a person has attained the peaceful liberation that transcends the realms of form and formlessness, yet has not personally touched it with the body nor severed the outflows through the vision of wisdom, but instead accepts it through faith in the Blessed One—this is called a person liberated through firm faith.
What is one who is a person of firm dharma?

If a person, having attained the peaceful liberation that transcends the realms of form and formlessness, does not physically touch and practice it, nor does he abandon the outflows through the vision of wisdom; yet, regarding the Dharma as promulgated by the Blessed One, he contemplates it with wisdom and attains patient acceptance—this is called a person of firm dharma.
What is a person of firm faith?

It refers to a person whose nature is inclined toward faith and who possesses abundant faith; they have attained the supreme right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), yet have not yet personally realized each of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya—whether it be the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding the five faculties, such a person possesses a predominance of the faculty of faith while the other four faculties are weak; they have not yet attained the eight liberations or the meditative absorption of cessation. This is called a person of steadfast faith.
What is one who is a person of firm nature?

It refers to a person whose disposition is such that they take pleasure in discerning the Dharma and frequently discern the Dharma, having attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), yet not having realized each of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya—namely, the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, or the fruit of arhatship.

Regarding these five faculties, his faculty of wisdom is predominant while the other four are slight; he has not yet attained the eight liberations or the attainment of cessation. This is called a person of steadfast nature.
What is the person who has severed the five factors?
If a person has severed the five hindrances—the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—this is called a person who has severed the five factors.

Furthermore, regarding the person who has severed five factors: if a person has severed the five lower fetters—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will—they are called a person who has severed five factors.
What is a person accomplished in the six bases?

It is one who is accomplished in the six kinds of equanimity (*upekṣā*): when seeing forms with the eye, they are without sorrow or joy, dwelling in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware; when hearing sounds with the ear, smelling odors with the nose, tasting flavors with the tongue, feeling tangibles with the body, or cognizing mental phenomena with the mind, they are without sorrow or joy, dwelling in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware. This is called a person accomplished in the six bases.
What is the person who possesses one protection?
If a person accomplishes the guarding of the mind through mindfulness, this is called the person who possesses one protection.
What is the person who relies on the four supports?
If a person knows forbearance, knows intimacy, knows detachment, and knows relinquishment, they are called a person who relies on the four reliances.
How does one eliminate the notion of a real person through various conditions?
If, apart from this, there are certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who hold views based on other conditions, such as: "The self and the world are eternal—this alone is true, all else is false";
"The self and the world are non-eternal—this alone is true, all else is false";
or "The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal—this alone is true, all else is false."
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
The self and the world are finite; this alone is true, all else is false.
The self and the world are infinite; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The world has an end and is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
"The world is neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, all else is false.
"The body is the soul; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The life-principle is the body; this is true, and all else is false.
"The life-principle is one thing and the body another; this is true, and all else is false.
"There is neither life-principle nor body; this is true, and all else is false."
That the Tathāgata exists after parinirvāṇa—this is true, all else is false;
that the Tathāgata does not exist after parinirvāṇa—this is true, all else is false;
that the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after parinirvāṇa—this is true, all else is false.
There is a Nirvāṇa that is neither the going nor the non-going; this is real, while all else is false.
When all of that has been extinguished, harmed, relinquished, released, vomited out, detached from, and exhausted, this is called the extinction of the person who is distinct from conditions.
How does one seek the most excellent person?
It is when a person seeks the cessation of desire and seeks the cessation of existence, seeking the holy life (*brahmacarya*) with the task already accomplished.
What is meant by "seeking desire"?

Regarding the phenomena of the desire realm that have not yet been awakened to or fully known, and those of the desire realm that have not yet been abandoned—whether they be the aggregates, elements, or sense-bases of the desire realm; or forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; or sentient beings or phenomena—if one seeks them, yearns for them, accumulates them, exhaustively seeks them, craves them, and having sought them, yearned for them, accumulated them, and exhaustedly sought them—this is called the seeking of sensual desires (*kāma-tṛṣṇā*).
What is the seeking of existence (*bhava-tṛṣṇā*)?

It is when the realm of form and the formless realm have not been awakened to or known, and the realm of form and the formless realm have not been abandoned; whether it be the aggregates, elements, and bases of the realm of form and the formless realm, or the dhyānas, liberations, meditative concentrations, or attainments—if one seeks these, yearns for them, accumulates them, and exhaustively pursues them with craving and longing—having yearned, accumulated, and exhaustively pursued them, this is called the seeking of existence.
What is the pursuit of the holy life of purity?
It refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.

If one pursues that, seeks after it, accumulates it, exhausts it, seeks it through craving, and having sought, accumulated, and exhausted it, one is called a person who pursues the holy life of purity.

If a person seeks the cessation of desire, seeks the cessation of existence, and seeks the holy life (*brahmacarya*) until what was to be done is accomplished, this is called a person who seeks the most excellent.
What is a person whose thoughts are not turbid?
Turbid perceptions refer to the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, and the perception of cruelty.
Non-turbid perceptions refer to the perception of renunciation, the perception of non-ill will, and the perception of non-cruelty.

If a person abandons the perception of sensual desire and recollects the perception of renunciation; abandons the perception of ill will and recollects the perception of non-ill will; and abandons the perception of cruelty and recollects the perception of non-cruelty, such a person is called one who possesses non-turbid perceptions.
What is one who practices the cultivation of the body through its removal?
"Body" refers to the out-breath and in-breath.
If these enter into a state of tranquility and are eliminated, such a person is called one who practices the cultivation of the body through its removal.

Furthermore, setting aside those who practice the removal of bodily sensations: if a bhikṣu, having abandoned both suffering and pleasure, and with the prior cessation of sorrow and joy, dwells in equanimity and mindfulness purified, neither suffering nor pleasant, and thus accomplishes the fourth dhyāna—this is called one who practices the removal of bodily sensations.
What is a person whose mind is well-liberated?
If a person’s mind is liberated from desire, and their mind is liberated from hatred and delusion, this is called a person whose mind is well-liberated.
What is a person well-liberated through wisdom?

If a person knows for themselves regarding the Dharma: "I desire that what is to be abandoned will certainly not arise; that hatred and delusion, once abandoned, will certainly not arise," this is called a person well-liberated through wisdom.
What is a person whose mind is well-liberated?
If a person’s mind is liberated from desire, and having attained the contact of being free from desire, they have realized it for themselves—this is called a person whose mind is well-liberated.
What is a person well-liberated through wisdom?
If a person is free from ignorance and, having attained the realization of liberation through wisdom, has touched it with direct experience, they are called a person well-liberated through wisdom.
What is a person whose mind is well-liberated?
If a person has produced the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) but not yet the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), this is called a person whose mind is well-liberated.
What is a person whose wisdom is well-liberated?
If a person has produced the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they are called one whose wisdom is well-liberated.
What is one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)?
If a person dwells having initiated a mind that is liberated both ways, they are called one liberated both ways.
What is one who possesses non-common liberation?
If a person dwells in a mind of non-common liberation and does not give rise to [further afflictions], this is called one who possesses non-common liberation.
What is one who is subject to falling away?

If a person, having initiated an abiding in a mind of common liberation, experiences a falling away or transformation from that mind of common liberation, this is called a person subject to falling away.
What is a person not subject to falling away?

If a person dwells in the uncommon mind of liberation without wavering or arising [from it], and does not fall back or change from that common mind of liberation, such a person is called one who is non-retrogressive.
What is meant by "one who possesses volition"?

If a person, while abiding in a mind of common liberation, gives rise to volition, and that volition exists within the mind of common liberation such that it causes me not to end [the path], nor to fall back, nor to change—this is called "one who possesses volition."
What is a person who possesses subtle protection?
It is when a person, having initiated an abiding in the mind of shared liberation, protects it, thinking: "May I not fall away from or change this mind of shared liberation."
One who does not fall back from nor change their shared mind of liberation is called a person of subtle protection.
What kind of person is it who, when reflecting, does not fall back, but when not reflecting, does fall back?

If a person, while abiding in a mind of shared liberation, should give rise to the thought, "May he not harm me, so that I may not fall away or change from this mind of shared liberation," then that person will not fall away or change from the mind of shared liberation,
and the thought "may he not harm me" will not arise, so that he does not fall away or change from the mind of shared liberation.
He falls away from the common liberation; this is called the person who does not fall away when reflecting, but falls away when not reflecting.
What is the person who does not fall away if they guard even slightly, but falls away if they do not guard even slightly?

If a person, while abiding in a mind of shared liberation, generates the aspiration: "May I protect myself so that I do not fall back from or change this mind of shared liberation," then they shall indeed not fall back from or change that mind of shared liberation.

If one does not guard it, may I not fall away or change from the shared mind of liberation, while he neither falls away nor changes from the shared mind of liberation; yet he falls away and changes from the shared mind of liberation—this is called the case where some people do not fall away when they guard even slightly, but do fall away when they do not guard even slightly.
What is meant by a person who has a "target" (*sappatigha*)?

If a person has produced the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) but not yet the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they will necessarily produce the knowledge of non-arising; as long as they have this "target," they will never give rise to a mind of liberation (*vimuktacitta*). Such a person is called one who has a target.
What is meant by a person who does not initiate [unwholesome] states?
If a person’s mind is liberated from desire, ill-will, and delusion, such a person is called one who does not initiate [unwholesome] states.
What is meant by a person who does not initiate [unwholesome] states?
One who does not give rise to desire, nor gives rise to hatred or delusion, is called a person who does not give rise to [defilements].
What is a person who abides through the eon (*kalpa*)?
One who possesses firm faith and firm Dharma, or who further possesses virtuous conduct, or a person who attains Arhatship in the present life—this is called a person who abides through the eon.
What is meant by the *sthāyikappa* (the abiding eon)?

It refers to those until the afflictions of all worlds have not yet been destroyed, who will certainly cause that person to attain the four fruits of the ascetic life—namely, the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*)—and who have attained the three contacts of realization; these are called people of the abiding eon.
What is one who is "equal to the head" (śūra-samāna)?
It refers to a person who, while not yet having practiced the Path, has both their outflows (*āsrava*) and their life-force severed simultaneously.
Furthermore, it refers to one for whom the life-force is severed immediately after the severance of the outflows; such a person is called "equal to the head."
What is meant by "one who has crossed the moat"?
If a person has severed ignorance, they are called one who has crossed the moat.
What is meant by "one who has destroyed the moat"?
If a person has severed birth and death, they are called one who has destroyed the moat.
What is a person who advances by means of a vehicle?
If a person has severed craving, they are called a person who advances by means of a vehicle.
What is a person who is undefiled?
If a person has abandoned the five lower fetters, they are called a person who is undefiled.
What is a person who is indolent and arrogant?
If a person has severed their conceit (*māna*), they are called a person who has abandoned pride.
*Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Volume Eight;
*Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Volume Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Dharmagupta and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Section Four: The Chapter on Knowledge (Jñāna-varga), Part One of the First of the Non-Questioned Divisions. Right View.
Right knowledge,
the faculty of wisdom,
and the power of wisdom.
The discernment of phenomena as right awakening;
the knowledge of liberation;
and the knowledge of right awakening and wrong knowledge.
Noble wisdom and non-noble wisdom;
outflowing wisdom and non-outflowing wisdom;
wisdom accompanied by craving and wisdom free from craving.
There is knowledge seeking [something] and knowledge not seeking [anything].
There is knowledge that should be grasped and knowledge that should not be grasped.
There is knowledge involving grasping and knowledge free from grasping.
There is superior knowledge and non-superior knowledge.
Knowledge that is felt and knowledge that is not felt.
Internal knowledge and external knowledge.
There is wisdom with retribution and wisdom without retribution;

there is wisdom shared by ordinary persons and wisdom not shared by ordinary persons; there is wisdom shared by those who are not ordinary persons and wisdom not shared by those who are not ordinary persons.
Wisdom shared with śrāvakas, wisdom not shared with śrāvakas, wisdom not shared with those who are not śrāvakas, and wisdom not shared with those who are not śrāvakas;
wisdom like lightning, and wisdom like a vajra.
Knowledge of indeterminate attainment and knowledge of determinate attainment;
knowledge of superior maintenance with effort and knowledge of superior maintenance without effort;
knowledge cultivated in one part and knowledge cultivated in two parts.
The knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, and the knowledge of nirvana;
skillful means regarding the elements, skillful means regarding contemplation;
skillful means regarding what is not the Dharma, and skillful means for removing what is not the Dharma.
The method for entering meditative concentration and the method for emerging from meditative concentration;
wisdom with applied thought and wisdom without applied thought;
wisdom with sustained examination and wisdom without sustained examination.
There is knowledge with joy and knowledge without joy;
there is knowledge with attachment to flavor and knowledge accompanied by equanimity;
there is luminous knowledge and non-luminous knowledge.
Wholesome knowledge, unwholesome knowledge, and indeterminate knowledge;
knowledge of those in training, knowledge of those beyond training, and knowledge of those who are neither in training nor beyond training;
resultant knowledge, knowledge of the nature of resultants, and knowledge that is neither resultant nor of the nature of a resultant.
Knowledge of what is abandoned by vision, knowledge of what is abandoned by cultivation, and knowledge of what is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
Knowledge of the causes abandoned by vision, knowledge of the causes abandoned by cultivation, and knowledge of the causes that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
Inferior wisdom, middling wisdom, and superior wisdom;
coarse wisdom, subtle wisdom, and minute wisdom;
the three types of clear knowledge (vidyā).
The three types of wisdom and the three eyes:
the knowledge of observing the body internally, the knowledge of observing the body externally, and the knowledge of observing the body both internally and externally.
The wisdom that contemplates internal feelings as feelings; the wisdom that contemplates external feelings as feelings; the wisdom that contemplates both internal and external feelings as feelings.
The wisdom that contemplates the internal mind as mind; the wisdom that contemplates the external mind as mind; the wisdom that contemplates both internal and external minds as mind.

The wisdom that contemplates internal phenomena among internal phenomena; the wisdom that contemplates external phenomena among external phenomena; the wisdom that contemplates both internal and external phenomena among both internal and external phenomena.
The wisdom of internal objects, the wisdom of external objects, the wisdom of both internal and external objects, and the wisdom of the realm of sentient beings.
Knowledge of the realm of form, knowledge of the realm of non-form, and knowledge of the realm of sentient beings.
Knowledge of the conditioned realm, knowledge of the unconditioned realm, and knowledge of the realm of sentient beings.
Wisdom regarding the realm of phenomena, wisdom regarding the non-realm, and wisdom regarding the realm of sentient beings;
lesser wisdom, middling wisdom, and immeasurable wisdom;
and wisdom regarding a lesser realm, wisdom regarding a middling realm, and wisdom regarding an immeasurable realm.
Limited wisdom with limited objects, limited wisdom with intermediate objects, and limited wisdom with immeasurable objects;
intermediate wisdom with limited objects, intermediate wisdom with intermediate objects, and intermediate wisdom with immeasurable objects.
Infinite wisdom with a limited range, infinite wisdom with a medium range, and infinite wisdom with an infinite range.
Limited-duration wisdom, medium-duration wisdom, and infinite-duration wisdom.
Limited wisdom dwelling for a short time, limited wisdom dwelling for a medium length of time, and limited wisdom dwelling for an immeasurable length of time.
Medium wisdom dwelling for a short time, medium wisdom dwelling for a medium length of time, and medium wisdom dwelling for an immeasurable length of time.
Immeasurable wisdom abides briefly, immeasurable wisdom abides for a medium duration, and immeasurable wisdom abides for an immeasurable duration.
There are skillful means regarding the good paths and skillful means regarding the evil paths;
there are skillful means that are wholesome and skillful means that are unwholesome.
The skillful means of diligence and the skillful means of tranquility;
the skillful means of grasping and the skillful means of relinquishing;
knowledge of the past, knowledge of the future, and knowledge of the present.
Knowledge of the past realm, knowledge of the future realm, knowledge of the present realm, and knowledge of that which is neither past, nor future, nor present.
Knowledge bound to the desire realm, knowledge bound to the form realm, knowledge bound to the formless realm, and unbound knowledge;
knowledge of suffering, knowledge of the origin, knowledge of cessation, and knowledge of the path.
Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and knowledge of the minds of others;
the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of expression, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence;

the knowledge of activity but not the knowledge of detachment, the knowledge of detachment but not the knowledge of activity, the knowledge of both activity and detachment, and the knowledge of neither activity nor detachment.
Wisdom that neither grasps nor issues forth;

wisdom that has defilement but is not mixed, and wisdom that is neither mixed nor has defilement; wisdom that both has defilement and is free from defilement, and wisdom that neither has defilement nor is free from defilement.
