Knowledge of the yokes is not knowledge apart from the yokes; knowledge apart from the yokes is not knowledge of the yokes; there is knowledge of both the yokes and that which is apart from the yokes; and there is knowledge that is neither of the yokes nor apart from the yokes.

Knowledge of the fruits of knowledge is not knowledge of the fruits of abandonment; knowledge of the fruits of abandonment is not knowledge of the fruits of knowledge; there is knowledge of both the fruits of knowledge and the fruits of abandonment; and there is knowledge that is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the fruit of abandonment.

The fruit of knowledge is not the attainment of the fruit; the attainment of the fruit is not the fruit of knowledge; there is the fruit of knowledge that is the attainment of the fruit; and there is that which is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the attainment of the fruit.

The knowledge of exhaustion is not awakening; the knowledge of awakening is not exhaustion; there is the knowledge of exhaustion that is awakening; and there is the knowledge that is neither exhaustion nor awakening.

The knowledge of understanding is not liberation; the knowledge of liberation is not understanding; there is the knowledge of liberation, and the knowledge that is neither understanding nor liberation.
There is the knowledge of the stage of decline, the knowledge of the stage of maintenance, the knowledge of the stage of increase, and the knowledge of the stage of penetration.

The wisdom of the stage of decline is not the wisdom of the stage of maintenance; the wisdom of the stage of maintenance is not the wisdom of the stage of decline; there is the wisdom of both the stage of maintenance and the stage of decline;

and there is the wisdom that is neither the stage of decline nor the stage of maintenance. The wisdom of the stage of decline is not the wisdom of the stage of increase; the wisdom of the stage of increase is not the wisdom of the stage of decline; there is the wisdom of both the stage of decline and the stage of increase; and there is the wisdom that is neither the stage of decline nor the stage of increase.
The wisdom of the stage of decline is not the wisdom of penetration; the wisdom of penetration is not the wisdom of decline; there is the wisdom of both decline and penetration;

and the wisdom that is neither decline nor penetration. The wisdom of the stage of maintenance is not the wisdom of increase; the wisdom of increase is not the wisdom of maintenance; there is the wisdom of both maintenance and increase; and the wisdom that is neither maintenance nor increase.
The wisdom of the stage of abiding is not the wisdom of liberation; the wisdom of liberation is not the wisdom of abiding; there is the wisdom of both abiding and liberation;

and there is the wisdom that is neither abiding nor liberation. The wisdom of increase is not the wisdom of liberation; the wisdom of liberation is not the wisdom of increase; there is the wisdom of both increase and liberation; and there is the wisdom that is neither increase nor liberation.
The five knowledges,
the six supernormal powers,
and the seven expedient means.
The dharma-knowledge of suffering and the subsequent knowledge of suffering;
the dharma-knowledge of origin and the subsequent knowledge of origin;
the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the subsequent knowledge of cessation.
The knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*).
The nine preparatory stages (*navopāya*).
The ten powers of the Tathāgata (*tathāgatadaśabala*).
The nature of ten knowledges;
the nature of forty-four knowledges;
the nature of seventy-seven knowledges.
What is right view?
If one’s seeing is wholesome, compliant, and not contrary, this is called right view.
What is right knowledge?
If wisdom is well-conforming and not contrary, it is called right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).
What is right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*)?
If acceptance is well-conforming and not contrary, it is called right view.
What is right knowledge?
If knowledge is wholesome, compliant, and not contrary, it is called right knowledge.
What is right view?

Excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), if any other views are wholesome, compliant, and non-opposing, these are called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
What is right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*)?
The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising are called right knowledge.
What is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)?

It is when a trainee (*śaikṣa*), having become free from the fetters and underlying tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), enters the noble mind and the noble path; whether it be one of steadfast faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) or one of steadfast Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), as well as others who have seen the faults and perils of conditioned existence, who contemplate the tranquility of *nirvāṇa*, and who contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality; who, not yet having attained, desires to attain; not yet having understood, desires to understand; not yet having realized, desires to realize; and who cultivates the path to become free from the afflictions (*kleśa*). This is the faculty of wisdom.

When a learner—whether a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), a once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), or a non-returner (anāgāmin)—is fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation, whether on the plane of knowledge or through the liberation of mind by contemplation, they realize each respective fruit of the ascetic life: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

When a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) desires to attain arhatship, and desiring to obtain the noble dharmas not yet obtained, becomes fully endowed with the wisdom of the contemplation of the path—whether it be the stage of wisdom or the mind liberated through contemplation—they immediately attain the fruit of arhatship.

Whether it be a real person, a realm of existence, or a phenomenon—through discernment, thorough discernment, and ultimate discernment—one discerns phenomena; through the contemplation of phenomena, one awakens to and penetrates their specific characteristics, other characteristics, and common characteristics. One reflects upon, distinguishes, and contemplates them, giving rise to sovereign wisdom, insight, analytical skill, artistry, brilliance, radiance, and illumination.
The eye of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the right awakening of the investigation of phenomena, and right view free from delusion—these are called the faculty of wisdom.
What is the power of wisdom?
The faculty of wisdom is called the power of wisdom.
What is the right awakening of the discernment of phenomena?
The power of wisdom is called the right awakening of the discernment of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of liberation?

If, within liberation, one possesses the wisdom and vision that perceives the means to liberation, and the mind is liberated from greed and hatred, thinking "my mind is liberated," and regarding that very greed and hatred, one possesses the wisdom and vision of the means to their liberation—this is called the "knowledge of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna*). In this treatise, the term for "liberation" (*vimukti*) is rendered as "shooting" (*śe*); in the Dandain (Dan) edition of the canon, it is consistently written as "shooting."
What is awakening?

When the Tathāgata’s wisdom arises, he attains mastery, autonomy, power, sovereignty, supreme nobility, and sovereign knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena through unimpeded wisdom and insight; he realizes unsurpassed perfect awakening, accomplishes the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four fearlessnesses, and achieves great compassion and the sovereign turning of the wheel of Dharma—this is called awakening.
What is right knowledge?
If knowledge is wholesome, compliant, and not contrary, it is called right knowledge.
What is wrong knowledge?
If wisdom is neither wholesome nor compliant, but contrary [to the Dharma], it is called wrong wisdom (*mithyājñāna*).
What is noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*)?
If wisdom is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called noble wisdom.
What is non-noble wisdom?
If wisdom is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called non-noble wisdom.
What is wisdom with outflows?
If knowledge is accompanied by craving, it is called tainted knowledge (*sāsrava-jñāna*).
What is untainted knowledge?
If knowledge is free from craving, it is called untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
What is knowledge associated with craving?
If knowledge involves seeking, it is called knowledge associated with craving.
What is knowledge free from craving?
If wisdom is without seeking, it is called the wisdom of non-attachment.
What is the wisdom of seeking?
If wisdom involves grasping, it is called the wisdom of seeking.
What is the wisdom of non-seeking?
If wisdom is not something to be grasped, it is called the wisdom of non-seeking.
What is the wisdom of that which is to be grasped?
If wisdom involves grasping, it is called "wisdom that should be grasped.
What is wisdom that should not be grasped?
If wisdom is without grasping, it is called "wisdom that should not be grasped."
What is knowledge with grasping?
If knowledge possesses superiority, it is called knowledge with grasping.
What is knowledge without grasping?
If wisdom is without superiority, it is called non-appropriating wisdom.
What is wisdom with superiority?
If wisdom involves appropriation, it is called wisdom with superiority.
What is non-surpassable knowledge?
If knowledge is without grasping, it is called non-surpassable knowledge.
What is surpassable knowledge?
If, regarding this knowledge, there exists another knowledge that is superior, more excellent, and surpassing it, this is called "knowledge with something superior.
What is "knowledge with nothing superior"?
Regarding this knowledge, if there is no other knowledge that is superior, more excellent, and surpassing it, this is called "knowledge with nothing superior."
What is superior wisdom?

It is when the Tathāgata gives rise to wisdom such that he possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena; he attains mastery, autonomy, power, majesty, sovereign nobility, and sovereign knowledge and vision; he achieves the unsurpassed, most excellent, and perfect enlightenment; he accomplishes the ten powers of a Tathāgata and the four fearlessnesses; and through the mastery of great compassion, he accomplishes the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Excluding that knowledge, any other knowledge is called superior knowledge (*viśeṣajñāna*).
What is non-superior knowledge?
Any remaining knowledge prior to that is called non-superior knowledge.
What is the knowledge of feeling?
If knowledge is internal, it is called the knowledge of feeling.
What is the knowledge that is not feeling?
If knowledge is external to feeling, it is called non-feeling-knowledge.
What is internal knowledge?
If knowledge is associated with feeling, it is called internal knowledge.
What is external knowledge?
If knowledge is not feeling, it is called external knowledge.
What is knowledge with retribution?
If knowledge is a result or a dharma that is subject to ripening, it is called knowledge with ripening.
What is knowledge without ripening?
If knowledge is neither a result nor a dharma subject to ripening, it is called knowledge without ripening.
What is the knowledge common to ordinary persons?
Knowledge that is not acquired at birth by ordinary persons, yet is acquired at birth by ordinary persons—this is called knowledge common to ordinary persons.
What is the knowledge uncommon to ordinary persons?

If a wisdom is not acquired by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and is not attained by ordinary persons who have not yet been born [into that state], it is called the "wisdom exclusive to ordinary persons.
What is the "wisdom shared with non-ordinary persons"?
If a wisdom is acquired by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and also arises in those who are not ordinary persons, it is called "wisdom common to those who are not ordinary persons.
What is "wisdom uncommon to those who are not ordinary persons"?
If a wisdom is acquired by ordinary persons but not acquired by those who are not ordinary persons, it is called the "unshared wisdom of those who are not ordinary persons.
What is the "shared wisdom of śrāvakas"?
If wisdom is not acquired by birth among Śrāvakas, yet is acquired by birth among Śrāvakas as well, this is called wisdom common to Śrāvakas.
What is wisdom uncommon to Śrāvakas?
If wisdom is not acquired by birth among Śrāvakas, and is not acquired by birth among Śrāvakas, this is called wisdom uncommon to Śrāvakas.
What is wisdom not shared with śrāvakas?
If a wisdom is acquired by birth among śrāvakas and also acquired by birth among those who are not śrāvakas, this is called wisdom not shared with śrāvakas.
What is the wisdom not shared with śrāvakas?
If a wisdom is acquired by birth by śrāvakas, but is neither acquired nor produced by those who are not śrāvakas, this is called the wisdom not shared with śrāvakas.
What is knowledge like lightning?
It is knowledge that abides for only a brief moment and lasts for only a short interval.

Just as lightning abides for only a brief moment and lasts for only a short interval, so too does this knowledge abide for only a brief moment and last for only a short interval; this is called knowledge like lightning.
What is wisdom like a vajra?

If wisdom abides immeasurably and for immeasurable durations, just as a vajra abides immeasurably and for immeasurable durations, so too does this wisdom abide immeasurably and for immeasurable durations; this is called wisdom like a vajra.
Furthermore, regarding "knowledge like lightning" (*vidyut-sama-jñāna*):

if a knowledge arises that severs a small portion of the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is like lightning flashing from amidst the clouds to illuminate a small area before quickly vanishing; knowledge is likewise in severing a small portion of the afflictions. This is called knowledge like lightning.

Furthermore, it is like vajra-wisdom (*vajrajñāna*). If this wisdom arises, it cuts off all afflictions (*kleśa*) without exception; there is not even the most subtle [affliction] that is not swiftly severed.

Just as when a vajra is hurled at pearls or stones, there is nothing it does not shatter or crush, so too is this wisdom: once it has arisen, it cuts off all afflictions, such that there is nothing—whether coarse or subtle—that is not severed or exhausted. This is called vajra-like wisdom.

Furthermore, there is the lightning-like knowledge (*vidyut-jñāna*), which refers to the knowledge arising that attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), and the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*); this is called lightning-like knowledge.

Furthermore, as for diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*): if wisdom arises and one attains the fruit of arhatship, this is called diamond-like wisdom. Furthermore, as for lightning-like wisdom (*vidyut-jñāna*):

this refers to the wisdom that arises when one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), the fruit of arhatship, or [the realization of] a pratyekabuddha; this is called lightning-like wisdom.

Furthermore, regarding adamantine wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*): the Tathāgata is said to have given birth to this wisdom, which possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena; it attains sovereign and autonomous power, noble and supreme mastery, and the wisdom and vision of unsurpassed enlightenment. The Tathāgata accomplishes the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, and through great compassion, he achieves the sovereignty of turning the wheel of Dharma. Such wisdom is called "wisdom like a vajra."
What is knowledge of non-attainment?
If a knowledge is attained that is not certain to be attained and is difficult to attain, this is called knowledge of non-attainment.
What is knowledge of attainment?
If knowledge is attained with certainty, without difficulty, it is called "knowledge attained with certainty" (*niyata-prāpta-jñāna*).
What is "knowledge maintained through the exertion of effort" (*vīrya-pratipatti-parigṛhīta-jñāna*)?

It is knowledge that is not attained with certainty, but is difficult to attain; it is not achieved through one's own power, nor is it honorable or sovereign; it does not occur where one desires, nor as one desires, nor to the full extent one desires; its attainment through the exertion of effort is as difficult as a boat going against the current.

If one attains such wisdom, it is not easily obtained even through meditative concentration; it is not attained by power, nor by sovereign mastery, nor in a desired place, nor as one desires, nor to the full extent of one's desire. Its cultivation and arising are difficult to attain; this is called the wisdom of the protection and maintenance of application.
What is the knowledge that maintains progress without effort?

It is the knowledge that attains concentration without difficulty, characterized by mastery, power, and sovereignty; it reaches whatever place is desired, in whatever manner is desired, and to whatever extent is desired; it is easily practiced and attained without hardship, just as a boat going with the current does so without difficulty.

If one attains such wisdom—wherein concentration and wisdom are not difficult to attain, and one possesses the noble sovereignty of autonomous power—then wherever one desires, in whatever manner one desires, and for as long as one desires, the practice arises effortlessly and spontaneously; this is called the wisdom of maintaining non-practice progress.
What is the cultivation of wisdom in one part?
If wisdom arises such that there is the perception of light but no seeing of forms, or if forms are seen but there is no perception of light, this is called the cultivation of wisdom in one part.
What is the cultivation of wisdom with two parts?
If wisdom arises accompanied by the perception of light and also sees forms, this is called the cultivation of wisdom with two parts.

Furthermore, what is the cultivation of wisdom with one part? If wisdom does not sever the afflictions, or if it severs the afflictions but does not give rise to wisdom, this is called the cultivation of wisdom with one part.
Furthermore, there is the cultivation of wisdom with two aspects: if the arising of wisdom also involves the abandonment of afflictions, this is called the cultivation of wisdom with two aspects.

Furthermore, there is the cultivation of wisdom with one aspect: if the wisdom is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arising rather than the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), this is called the cultivation of wisdom with one aspect.

Furthermore, there is twofold cultivation of knowledge (*jñāna-bhāvanā*). If knowledge arises that is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), this is called twofold cultivation of knowledge.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion?

When greed, hatred, and delusion have been exhausted, one realizes: "My greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted. That very knowledge which perceives liberation as the means is called the knowledge of exhaustion.
What is the knowledge of non-arising?

When greed, hatred, and delusion have been extinguished and do not arise again, one realizes: "My greed, hatred, and delusion are exhausted and will not arise again. To possess this very knowledge and vision regarding the means of liberation is called the knowledge of non-arising.
What is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna)?
If knowledge has the conditioned (saṃskṛta) as its noble object, this is called the knowledge of the stability of phenomena.
What is the knowledge of nirvāṇa?
If wisdom has the realm of the noble nirvāṇa as its object, this is called "wisdom of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, regarding the wisdom of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*): setting aside the conditionality of suchness (*tathatā*), if other phenomena are such as they are, not otherwise, neither different nor distinct entities, being permanent phenomena, real phenomena, the stability of phenomena, the fixed nature of phenomena, and non-conditions—this is called the wisdom of the stability of phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of nirvana: that nirvana is peaceful; it is relinquishment, protection, realization, and reliance; it is non-sinking, crossing-over, non-heating, and non-burning; it is without sorrow, without affliction, and without pain. When, through the contemplation of other formations, knowledge arises regarding such nirvana, this is called the knowledge of nirvana.
What is the realm of skillful means (*upāya-dhātu*)?

It consists of the realm of the multitude, the realm of comparison, the realm of contact, and the realm of reflection; this is the realm of form and this is the realm of the formless; this is the realm of the visible and this is the realm of the invisible; this is the realm of resistance and this is the realm of non-resistance; this is the noble realm and this is the non-noble realm. This very realm is the skillful means for liberation within that very realm; this is called the realm of skillful means.
What is the application of skillful means regarding reflection?

If one reflects, reflects extensively, reflects by comparison, or reflects through recollection of contact—reflecting that "this is wholesome," "this is unwholesome," "this is right mindfulness," or "this is wrong mindfulness"—and if, through such recollection, one attains liberation via knowledge and vision regarding those very objects, this is called the application of skillful means regarding reflection.
What is the improper method?

It is the assembly of the unrighteous, the association with the unrighteous, the mental engagement with the unrighteous, and the unrighteous reflection that "this is a light offense" or "this is a heavy offense," "this is an offense with remainder" or "this is an offense without remainder," "this is an evil deed" or "this is not an evil deed," or "this is a multitude of offenses. To then claim knowledge, vision, or liberation regarding such a method is called the improper method.
What is the removal of improper means?

It is the removal of improper means from the assembly, the removal of improper means from comparison, and the removal of improper means from conceptual reflection; it is the removal of improper means such that one is cleared of minor offenses of improper means, and likewise cleared of grave offenses; it is the removal of both offenses with remainder and those without remainder; it is the removal of committed evils and the removal of uncommitted evils—thus is there the removal of all offenses.

Having thus eliminated all transgressions, when this supreme Dharma eliminates those transgressions, one then understands the skillful means for liberation through knowledge and vision; this is called the skillful means for eliminating unrighteousness.
What is the method for entering meditative concentration?

It consists of the assembly for entering concentration, the comparison for entering concentration, the contact for entering concentration, and the reflection for entering concentration. These include: entering the concentration of perception and the concentration of non-perception; entering the concentration that conforms to perception and the concentration that does not conform to perception; entering the concentration free from form; entering the superior entry concentration; and entering the universal entry concentration—thus one enters these various concentrations.

Having thus entered these meditative absorptions, one enters them through such superior dharmas; this very application regarding knowledge, vision, and liberation is called the "application for entering meditative absorption."
What are the skillful means for emerging from meditative absorption? These are:

emerging from absorption through the assembly, emerging through comparison, emerging through contact, and emerging through reflection; likewise, emerging from the attainment of cessation and the attainment of non-perception; likewise, emerging from a conforming attainment and not emerging from a non-conforming attainment; likewise, emerging from an attainment free from form and not emerging from an attainment not free from form; and likewise, emerging from superior entry into absorption and entering into all-encompassing entry into absorption—such are the ways of emerging from various absorptions.

Having thus emerged from those meditative absorptions, when one emerges from such superior dharmas and immediately realizes the skillful means for knowledge, vision, and liberation therein, this is called the skillful means of emerging from absorption.
What is wisdom accompanied by vitarka?
If wisdom is associated with vitarka, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called wisdom accompanied by vitarka.
What is wisdom without vitarka?
If wisdom is not associated with applied thought (*vitarka*), and does not arise, abide, or cease together with applied thought, it is called wisdom without applied thought (*avitarkajñāna*).
What is wisdom with sustained thought (*savicārajñāna*)?
If wisdom is associated with contemplation (vipassanā), arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called wisdom with contemplation.
What is wisdom without contemplation?
If wisdom is not associated with contemplation, not arising together with it, not abiding together with it, and not ceasing together with it, this is called wisdom without contemplation.
What is knowledge accompanied by joy (*sappītika-ñāṇa*)?
If knowledge is associated with joy, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called knowledge accompanied by joy.
What is knowledge without joy (*nippītika-ñāṇa*)?
If knowledge is not associated with joy, does not arise together with it, does not abide together with it, and does not cease together with it, this is called knowledge without joy.
What is knowledge of attachment?
If knowledge is associated with pleasant feeling, this is called knowledge of attachment.
What is the knowledge of equanimity (*upekṣājñāna*)?
If knowledge is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*), it is called the knowledge of equanimity.
What is useful knowledge (*upayajñāna*)?
If wisdom has an objective domain, it is called "wisdom with utility.
What is "wisdom without utility"?
If wisdom arises without an objective domain, it is called "wisdom without utility."
Furthermore, if wisdom arises that severs ignorance, it is called "wisdom of non-action.
What is "wholesome wisdom"?
If wisdom is cultivated, it is called wholesome wisdom.
What is unwholesome knowledge?
If knowledge is abandoned, it is called unwholesome knowledge.
What is indeterminate knowledge?
If knowledge is either receptive or is neither a result nor a dharma that will produce a result, this is called neutral knowledge (*avyākṛta-jñāna*).
What is knowledge of training (*śaikṣa-jñāna*)?
If knowledge is noble (*ārya*) but not that of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this is called knowledge of training.
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*)?
If knowledge is noble (*ārya*) and not that of one in training (*śaikṣa*), it is called the knowledge of one beyond training.
What is the knowledge that is neither of one in training nor of one beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣajñāna*)?
If wisdom is not noble, it is called wisdom that is neither of training nor beyond training.
What is retributive wisdom?
If wisdom is experienced or if wisdom is the result of wholesome karma, it is called retributive wisdom.
What is the knowledge of phenomena that are retribution (*vipākadharmajñāna*)? If a knowledge has retribution, it is called the knowledge of phenomena that are retribution.
What is the knowledge of phenomena that are neither retribution nor subject to retribution (*naivavipākanavipākadharmajñāna*)?
If knowledge is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not included within one's own portion, it is called "knowledge that is neither resultant nor a cause of result" (*na-vipāka-na-vipāka-dharma-jñāna*).
What is knowledge to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya-jñāna*)?
If knowledge is unwholesome (*akuśala*) and not to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it is called knowledge to be abandoned by vision.
What is the knowledge to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-jñāna*)?
If a knowledge is unwholesome (*akuśala*) but not to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), this is called the knowledge to be abandoned by cultivation.
What is the knowledge that is neither to be abandoned by vision nor to be abandoned by cultivation?
If knowledge is indeterminate, it is called knowledge that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is knowledge whose cause is abandoned by vision?
If knowledge is itself abandoned by vision, or if knowledge is the retribution of a dharma abandoned by vision, this is called knowledge whose cause is abandoned by vision.
What is the knowledge of the cause that is abandoned through cultivation?

It is the knowledge that abandons through cultivation, or the knowledge that is the fruition of a dharma abandoned through cultivation; this is called the knowledge of the cause abandoned through cultivation.
What is the knowledge that has as its cause neither what is abandoned by vision nor what is abandoned by cultivation?

It is knowledge that is wholesome, or knowledge that is the result of wholesome dharmas, or knowledge that is neither a result nor a dharma leading to a result; this is called the knowledge that has as its cause neither what is abandoned by vision nor what is abandoned by cultivation.
What is inferior wisdom?
If wisdom is unwholesome, it is called inferior wisdom.
What is middling wisdom?
If wisdom is indeterminate, it is called middling wisdom.
What is superior wisdom?
If wisdom is wholesome, it is called superior wisdom.
Furthermore, inferior wisdom refers to wisdom that is either unwholesome or indeterminate; this is called inferior wisdom.
Furthermore, middling wisdom refers to wisdom that is not noble and wholesome; this is called middling wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding superior knowledge: if knowledge is noble and untainted, it is called superior knowledge.
What is coarse knowledge?
If knowledge is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse knowledge.
What is subtle wisdom?
If wisdom is bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu) or is unbound, this is called subtle wisdom.
What is minute wisdom?
If knowledge is bound to the formless realm, it is called subtle knowledge.
Furthermore, regarding coarse knowledge: if knowledge is bound to the desire realm or the form realm, it is called coarse knowledge.

Furthermore, subtle wisdom (*sūkṣmajñāna*) refers to wisdom that is bound to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, or is unbound; this is called subtle wisdom.
Furthermore, minute wisdom (*aṇujñāna*) refers to wisdom that is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called minute wisdom.

Furthermore, regarding coarse knowledge (*audārika-jñāna*): if knowledge is bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or bound to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), or the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), this is called coarse knowledge.
Furthermore, subtle wisdom (*sūkṣmajñāna*): if wisdom is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is called subtle wisdom.
Furthermore, minute wisdom (*aṇujñāna*): if wisdom is unbound (*anupādhi*), it is called minute wisdom.
What are the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*)?

They are the clear knowledge of the realization of recollecting past lives, the clear knowledge of the realization of the death and rebirth of sentient beings, and the clear knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava*).
What is the clear knowledge of the realization of recollecting past lives?

If, through the arising of wisdom, one recollects immeasurable past lives—recollecting one birth, two, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, ten thousand births, a hundred thousand births, immeasurable hundreds of births, immeasurable thousands of births, immeasurable tens of thousands of births; or immeasurable eons of dissolution, or immeasurable eons of formation—one thinks: "I was formerly there, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, and such a lifespan; my life was thus short or my life lasted thus long; I experienced such suffering and pleasure in that place; passing away from there, I was reborn there; passing away from there, I was again reborn there. Thus, being fully endowed with the recollection of various past lives, this is called the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
What is the realization through direct knowledge of the birth and death of sentient beings?

It is when, through the arising of wisdom, one possesses the purified divine eye that surpasses the human eye, and sees sentient beings being born and dying—whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, in evil or good realms, lowly or exalted—and knows sentient beings according to their karma: "These sentient beings, having accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind; having reviled noble ones, held wrong views, and performed actions based on wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in the evil realms of hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts."

These sentient beings have accomplished wholesome conduct of body, accomplished wholesome conduct of speech, and accomplished wholesome conduct of mind; they do not revile the noble ones, possess right view, and perform actions based on the cause of right view. At the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a happy destination, among the devas or among humans.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, one sees beings passing away and being reborn—of beautiful or ugly appearance, in good or bad destinations, high or low—and knows beings according to their karma; this is called the realization of the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings.
What is the clear knowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyājñānadarśana*)?

It is when, through the arising of wisdom, the outflows are destroyed and untainted liberation arises; there is liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom; one realizes for oneself in this very life, attaining the perfection of practice: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence. This is called the clear knowledge of the realization of the destruction of the outflows.
These are called the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
What are the three kinds of wisdom?
They are the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
What is wisdom born of reflection?

It is when, without hearing from others, receiving instruction from others, requesting others to speak, or listening to the Dharma from others, one reflects upon, awakens to, and contemplates for oneself; if such knowledge arises without being derived from formal cultivation, this is called wisdom born of reflection.
What is the wisdom derived from hearing?

It is when, having heard from another, received instruction from another, requested another to speak, or listened to the Dharma from another—rather than through one's own reflection, one's own awakening, or one's own contemplation—if knowledge arises, this is called the wisdom derived from hearing.
What is the cultivation of wisdom?

If one cultivates the faculties, the powers, the factors of awakening, the dhyānas, the liberations, the concentrations, and the attainments; or if, through such cultivation, wisdom has already been cultivated or arises—this is called the cultivation of wisdom.
These are called the three types of wisdom.
What are the three eyes?
The fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye.
What is the fleshly eye?
If the eye is comprised within the self’s sphere and is the translucent matter derived from the four great elements, it is called the fleshly eye.
What is the divine eye?
If the divine eye is comprised within one's own constituent parts, it is called the divine eye.
What is the wisdom eye?
The three types of wisdom—wisdom derived from reflection, wisdom derived from hearing, and wisdom derived from cultivation—are called the wisdom eye.

Furthermore, regarding the fleshly eye (*māṃsacakṣus*): excluding that which is included within the sphere of my own [karmic] portion and is the divine eye, any other eye produced from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and characterized by purity is called the fleshly eye.

Furthermore, regarding the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*): that which is included within the sphere of my own [karmic] portion as the divine eye, as well as that which is attained through the cultivation of the divine eye, is called the divine eye.

Furthermore, regarding the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*): excluding the cultivation of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*), the remaining three types of wisdom—namely, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)—are called the wisdom-eye.
These are known as the three eyes.
What is the wisdom of contemplating the internal body within the internal body?

It is the wisdom that arises when one contemplates all internal material bodies comprised of the four great elements, or a single portion of such internal material bodies comprised of the four great elements, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called the wisdom of contemplating the internal body within the internal body.
What is the knowledge of observing the external body as the external body?

It is the knowledge that arises when one contemplates all external physical bodies comprised of the four great elements, or even a single portion of an external physical body comprised of the four great elements, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called the knowledge of observing the external body as the external body.
What is the knowledge of observing the internal and external body as the internal and external body?

It is the knowledge that arises when one contemplates all internal and external material bodies composed of the four great elements, or a single instance of such internal and external material bodies composed of the four great elements, as being impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called the knowledge of observing the internal and external body as the internal and external body.
What is the knowledge of observing internal feelings within internal feelings?

When knowledge arises from observing all internal feelings, or a portion of internal feelings, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, this is called the knowledge of observing internal feelings within internal feelings.
What is the knowledge of observing external feelings as external feelings?

When, regarding all external feelings or a portion of external feelings, there arises the knowledge that observes them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—this is called the knowledge of observing external feelings as external feelings.
What is the knowledge of observing internal and external feelings as internal and external feelings?

It is the knowledge that arises when one observes all internal and external feelings, or feelings in a single instance of the internal and external, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this is called the knowledge of observing internal and external feelings as internal and external feelings.
What is the knowledge that contemplates the internal mind with respect to the internal mind?

When, regarding all internal minds and a single instance of internal mind, there arises the knowledge that contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—this is called the knowledge that contemplates the internal mind with respect to the internal mind.
What is the knowledge of observing the external mind with respect to the external mind?

When, regarding all external minds or a single instance of an external mind, the knowledge that observes them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self arises, this is called the knowledge of observing the external mind with respect to the external mind.
What is the wisdom that contemplates the internal and external mind as the internal and external mind?

When wisdom arises from contemplating all internal and external minds, or a single instance of internal and external mind, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, this is called the wisdom that contemplates the internal and external mind as the internal and external mind.
What is the knowledge that contemplates internal phenomena as internal phenomena?

Excluding the four great elements and those phenomena comprised by the physical body, when there arises knowledge that contemplates all other internal phenomena—or a specific portion of internal phenomena—as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, this is called the knowledge that contemplates internal phenomena as internal phenomena.
What is the knowledge of observing external phenomena as external phenomena?

Excluding the four great elements, the physical body, and the phenomena comprised by sensation and mind, when there arises a knowledge that observes all other external phenomena—or any single instance of external phenomena—exactly as they are, namely as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, this is called the knowledge of observing external phenomena as external phenomena.
What is the knowledge of observing internal and external phenomena (dharmas) regarding internal and external phenomena?

Excluding the four great elements, the physical body, and the phenomena subsumed under sensation, mind, and mental factors, when there arises the knowledge that observes all other internal and external phenomena—or any single instance of internal or external phenomena—as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self according to their actual nature, this is called the knowledge of observing internal and external phenomena regarding internal and external phenomena.
What is knowledge of internal objects?
When wisdom arises from contemplating internal phenomena, this is called knowledge of internal objects.
What is knowledge of external objects?
When the knowledge of contemplating external phenomena arises, this is called the knowledge of external objects.
What is the knowledge of both internal and external objects?
When the knowledge of contemplating both internal and external phenomena arises, this is called the knowledge of both internal and external objects.
What is the knowledge of the realm of sentient beings?
It is the knowledge that there is no realm of sentient beings.

Furthermore, when the wisdom of contemplation arises through the practice of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings, this is called the knowledge of the realm of sentient beings.
What is the knowledge of the realm of form?
When the knowledge arises through contemplating form-phenomena, this is called the knowledge of the realm of form.
What is the knowledge of the realm of the formless?
When the knowledge of the formless phenomena arises through contemplation, this is called the knowledge of the formless realm.
What is the knowledge of the realm of sentient beings?
There is no such thing as the knowledge of the realm of sentient beings.
Furthermore, when knowledge arises from the practice of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings, this is called "knowledge of the realm of sentient beings.
What is "knowledge of the conditioned realm"?
When knowledge arises from contemplating conditioned phenomena, this is called "knowledge of the conditioned realm."
What is the knowledge of the unconditioned realm?
When the knowledge of contemplating unconditioned phenomena arises, it is called the knowledge of the unconditioned realm.
What is the knowledge of the realm of sentient beings?
There is the wisdom regarding the sphere of non-sentient beings.

Furthermore, when the wisdom of contemplation arises through the practice of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings, this is called the wisdom regarding the sphere of sentient beings.
What is the knowledge of the sphere of phenomena (dharmaviṣayajñāna)?
When the knowledge of phenomena arises through contemplation, it is called the knowledge of the sphere of phenomena.
What is the knowledge without a sphere (anālambanajñāna)?
There is no object and no cognition of an object.
Furthermore, when the cognition of past and future phenomena arises through contemplation, this is called the cognition of no object.
What is the cognition of the sphere of sentient beings?
There is the wisdom regarding the realm of non-sentient beings.
Furthermore, the practice of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward sentient beings is called the wisdom regarding the realm of sentient beings.
What is limited wisdom?
If it abides for a short duration or for a brief interval, this is called limited wisdom (*parīttā prajñā*).
What is intermediate wisdom?
If wisdom abides in a middling manner or for an intermediate duration, this is called intermediate wisdom (*madhyamā prajñā*).
What is immeasurable knowledge (*apramāṇa-jñāna*)?
If knowledge is immeasurable, abiding immeasurably and dwelling for immeasurable intervals, this is called immeasurable knowledge.
Furthermore, regarding limited knowledge (*parītta-jñāna*): if knowledge is limited in its duration, limited in its intensity, and limited in its objective sphere, this is called limited knowledge.
Furthermore, regarding middling wisdom: if wisdom abides in the middle, is middling-soft, and has a middling object, this is called middling wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding immeasurable wisdom: if wisdom abides in the immeasurable, is immeasurably sharp, and has an immeasurable object, this is called immeasurable wisdom.
What is knowledge of limited scope?

If a knowledge pertains to a single sentient being, a single phenomenon, or the initial arising of a single mental formation—excluding the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—this is called knowledge of limited scope.
What is knowledge of the intermediate realm?
If a knowledge that enumerates sentient beings or phenomena as they first arise—excluding the nirvana of the Tathāgata—is called knowledge of the intermediate realm.
What is the wisdom of immeasurable objects?
If a wisdom [perceives] immeasurable sentient beings, or the initial arising of dharmas, or the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata, this is called the wisdom of immeasurable objects.
What is limited wisdom with a limited object?

It is when wisdom dwells for a short time, is slight, or concerns a single sentient being, a single dharma, or a single formation that has just arisen—excluding the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; this is called limited wisdom with a limited object.
What is the limited range of inferior wisdom?

It refers to wisdom that dwells for only a short time, is weak, or pertains to the enumeration of sentient beings or phenomena that have only recently arisen—excluding the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa. This is called the limited range of inferior wisdom.
What is limited wisdom with an immeasurable object?

When wisdom dwells on a small scale, is slight, or weak, yet its objects are immeasurable sentient beings, dharmas just arising, or the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata—this is called limited wisdom with an immeasurable object.
What is middle-range wisdom with a limited scope?

If wisdom abides within the middle range—whether it be of middling-soft intensity, or if it concerns a single sentient being, a single phenomenon, or a single activity that has just arisen, yet does not pertain to the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata—this is called middle-range wisdom with a limited scope.
What is intermediate wisdom with an intermediate object?

If wisdom abides in the intermediate, is intermediate-soft, concerns a multitude of sentient beings, or concerns phenomena that have just arisen, yet does not pertain to the nirvana of a Tathāgata—this is called intermediate wisdom with an intermediate object.
What is the immeasurable sphere of middle-level wisdom?

If one abides in the middle, whether with middling-soft faculties, or if there are immeasurable sentient beings, or when dharmas first arise, or at the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata—this is called the immeasurable sphere of middle-level wisdom.
What is immeasurable knowledge with a limited scope?

If knowledge is immeasurable yet abides in a limited manner or possesses limited benefit—whether directed toward a single sentient being, a single phenomenon, or a single practice at its initial arising, excluding the parinirvāṇa of a Tathāgata—this is called immeasurable knowledge with a limited scope.
What is the objective sphere within immeasurable wisdom?

If wisdom is immeasurable in its abiding and immeasurable in its benefit—whether it enumerates sentient beings or the initial arising of phenomena, with the exception of the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa—this is called the objective sphere within immeasurable wisdom.
What is immeasurable wisdom and its immeasurable sphere?

If wisdom is immeasurable in its abiding, immeasurable in its benefit, or if it concerns immeasurable sentient beings, the initial arising of dharmas, or the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata—this is called immeasurable wisdom and its immeasurable sphere.
What is knowledge that abides for a short time?
If knowledge abides for a brief interval—whether for the duration of a finger-snap or more, but not for the duration of milking a cow or more—it is called knowledge that abides for a short time.
What is knowledge abiding for an intermediate duration?
If knowledge abides for an intermediate period—such as the time it takes to milk a cow, or more, but not seven days or more—it is called knowledge abiding for an intermediate duration.
What is immeasurable abiding wisdom?
If wisdom abides for an immeasurable interval—whether for seven days or more—it is called immeasurable abiding wisdom.
What is limited wisdom with limited abiding?

If the object is slight and weak, or if it abides for a short duration—whether for the snap of a finger or slightly longer, but not for the duration of milking a cow or longer—this is called "slight wisdom and slight abiding."
What is meant by "dwelling in middling [concentration] with limited wisdom"?

If wisdom has a limited object, is limited and weak, yet dwells for a middling duration—such as the time it takes to milk a cow, or slightly more—this is called dwelling in middling [concentration] with limited wisdom.
What is "limited wisdom with immeasurable abiding"?
If wisdom has limited objects and is limited and weak, yet abides for an immeasurable duration—whether seven days or more—this is called "limited wisdom with immeasurable abiding."
What is intermediate wisdom dwelling for a short time?

If wisdom has an intermediate object, is intermediate-soft, and dwells for a brief interval—whether for the snap of a finger, or for the time it takes a cow to yield milk, or more than that—it is called intermediate wisdom dwelling for a short time.
What is intermediate wisdom abiding in the intermediate state?

If wisdom has an intermediate object, is intermediate-soft, and abides for the duration of a cow’s lowing or more, but not for seven days or more, this is called intermediate wisdom abiding in the intermediate state.
What is the immeasurable abiding of middling wisdom?
If the wisdom has a middling object, is middling-soft, or abides for an immeasurable interval of seven days or more, this is called the immeasurable abiding of middling wisdom.
What is immeasurable wisdom dwelling for a short time?

If wisdom has an immeasurable object and immeasurable benefit, yet dwells for only a brief interval—whether for the duration of a finger-snap or more, but not for the duration of milking a cow or more—this is called immeasurable wisdom dwelling for a short time.
What is dwelling within immeasurable wisdom?

If wisdom has immeasurable objects, immeasurable benefit, and dwells for an intermediate duration—whether for as long as it takes to milk a cow or more, but not for seven days or more—this is called dwelling within immeasurable wisdom.
What is immeasurable wisdom and immeasurable abiding?
If wisdom has immeasurable objects, immeasurable benefit, or if it abides for immeasurable intervals—such as seven days or more—this is called immeasurable wisdom and immeasurable abiding.
What is the skillful means of the wholesome path?

The wholesome path refers to wholesome phenomena as well as humans and devas; if one possesses the wisdom and vision that constitute the skillful means for liberation, this is called the skillful means of the wholesome path.
What is the skillful means regarding the evil realms?

The evil realms refer to unwholesome dharmas, as well as the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts; if one possesses the wisdom and vision that liberates from these, this is called the skillful means regarding the evil realms.

What is skillful means? It is when, through this cause and this condition, there is form; through this cause and this condition, there are feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; through this cause and this condition, one enters the first dhyāna, and enters the second, third, and fourth dhyānas; and by abandoning evil and unwholesome states, one accomplishes wholesome states. If there is wisdom and vision regarding the means of liberation, this is called skillful means.
What is the skillful means of tranquility?
Tranquility refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*); if one possesses the wisdom and vision that constitute the skillful means for liberation, this is called the skillful means of tranquility.
What is the skillful means of grasping?
"Grasping" (*ādāna*) refers to exertion; if one possesses the knowledge and vision of the means for liberation, this is called the "means of grasping.
What is the "means of relinquishing" (*prahāṇa*)?

There are two types of relinquishing: the faculty of relinquishing and the mind of relinquishing; if one possesses the knowledge and vision of the means for liberation, this is called the "means of relinquishing."

Furthermore, regarding the method of tranquility (*śamatha-upāya*): when the mind is agitated, it is thus stilled through the cessation of its characteristics; if one perceives with wisdom the means for liberation, this is called the method of tranquility.

Furthermore, regarding the application of effort (*upāya*), if one’s progress is weak, one should apply oneself with diligence in this way: taking [the object] according to conditions, taking it correctly, exhorting oneself, correctly exhorting oneself, and correctly rejoicing; if there is wisdom and vision regarding the means of liberation, this is called the application of effort.

Furthermore, regarding the method of relinquishment (*prahāṇa-vidhi*): when the concentrated mind thus relinquishes greed, hatred, and delusion until they are exhausted, and if there is the wisdom and vision that constitutes the method of liberation, this is called the method of relinquishment.
What is past knowledge?
If knowledge has arisen and ceased, this is called past knowledge.
What is future knowledge?
If wisdom has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, this is called future wisdom.
What is present wisdom?
If wisdom has arisen but has not yet ceased, this is called present wisdom.
What is the knowledge of past objects?
When the knowledge that contemplates past phenomena arises, it is called the knowledge of past objects.
What is the knowledge of future objects?
When the knowledge of future phenomena arises through contemplation, this is called the knowledge of the future realm.
What is the knowledge of the present realm?
When the knowledge of present phenomena arises through contemplation, this is called the knowledge of the present realm.
What is the knowledge of objects that are neither past, nor future, nor present?

It is the arising of the knowledge of phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present through contemplation; this is called the knowledge of objects that are neither past, nor future, nor present.
What is knowledge bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-jñāna*)?
If knowledge is characterized by the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called knowledge bound to the desire realm.
What is knowledge bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-jñāna*)?
If knowledge is associated with the outflows of form and is subject to outflows, it is called knowledge bound to the realm of form.
What is knowledge bound to the formless realm?
If knowledge is associated with the outflows of the formless and is subject to outflows, it is called knowledge bound to the formless realm.
What is non-bound knowledge?
If knowledge is noble and untainted, it is called non-bound knowledge.
What is knowledge of suffering?
Regarding this Noble Truth of Suffering, if there is knowledge and vision that serves as the means for liberation, this is called the knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of origination?
Regarding this Noble Truth of Origination, if there is knowledge and vision that serves as the means for liberation, this is called the knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of cessation?
Regarding this noble truth of cessation, if there is knowledge that sees the means of liberation, this is called the knowledge of cessation.
What is the knowledge of the path?
Regarding this Noble Truth of the Path: if one possesses the wisdom and vision that constitutes the means for liberation, this is called "knowledge of the path" (*mārga-jñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of suffering: if one possesses the wisdom and vision that constitutes the means for liberation concerning the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of encountering the unpleasant, the suffering of separation from the beloved, the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks, and the suffering of the five aggregates of clinging in their entirety—this is called "knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-jñāna*).

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*): this craving further possesses the characteristic of being stained by desire and continues in succession, manifesting as longing for various objects. If one possesses the wisdom that perceives the means of liberation, this is called the knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of cessation?

It is the knowledge that views the liberation through the detachment from craving, its cessation, its exhaustion, its relinquishment, its transcendence, and its deliverance—being without dependence, forever severed without remainder; this is called the knowledge of cessation.
Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*):

the Noble Eightfold Path consists of right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. The wisdom that perceives and understands the means for liberation is called the knowledge of the path.

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*): all conditioned, outflow-tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-saṃskṛta-dharma*) subsumed under the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), or if, with respect to a single instance of such conditioned, outflow-tainted phenomena subsumed under the truth of suffering, one perceives suffering, perceives non-self, and contemplates suffering; and if there is wisdom that perceives the means of liberation—this is called the knowledge of suffering.

Furthermore, as for the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*): all causes of suffering and the origination of suffering—whether they be the cause of suffering in a single instance, the conditions for suffering, or the origination of suffering—are seen as origination, seen as non-self, and contemplated as origination. These causes and these conditions bring about all suffering; if one possesses the wisdom that perceives the means of liberation, this is called the knowledge of origination.

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*): it is the exhaustion of all suffering, the exhaustion of all afflictions (*kleśa*), and the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*). If, in every respect, there is the exhaustion of suffering, the exhaustion of afflictions, and the exhaustion of outflows—perceiving cessation, perceiving non-self, and contemplating cessation—and if one possesses the wisdom that perceives the means of liberation, this is called the knowledge of cessation.

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*): it is the noble path that is the essential means for the correct cessation of suffering. Whether it be the noble path that is the essential means for the correct cessation of suffering in a single instance—the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the vision of non-self (*anātman*), or the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—it is by this cause and this condition that all suffering is exhausted. If one possesses the wisdom that perceives the skillful means for liberation, this is called the knowledge of the path.
What is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
If a noble, untainted knowledge that does not depend on inference and encompasses all aspects, this is called the knowledge of phenomena.
What is subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?

If knowledge is noble, untainted, inferential, and encompasses all aspects without exception, it is called inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). What is mundane knowledge (*loka-jñāna*)? It is the knowledge of sentient beings;

the knowledge of the names, words, and languages of phenomena; the knowledge of past speech, future speech, and present speech; the speech of male, female, and neither-male-nor-female; single speech, dual speech, triple speech, manifold speech, immeasurable speech, and all speech; and the knowledge that perceives the means of liberation—this is called mundane knowledge.
What is the knowledge of others' minds?
If one knows another's mind through wisdom, or if there is wisdom that perceives and penetrates the skillful means [of others], this is called the knowledge of others' minds.

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*): if there are conditioned, out-flowing phenomena subsumed under the truth of suffering, one perceives suffering, perceives non-self, and contemplates suffering.
If it concerns the cause of suffering, the source of suffering, or the accumulation of suffering, one contemplates the accumulation, sees non-self, and reflects upon the accumulation;
if it concerns the exhaustion of suffering, the exhaustion of afflictions, or the exhaustion of outflows, one contemplates cessation, sees non-self, and reflects upon cessation;
if it concerns the noble path, one sees non-self and reflects upon the path as well as other dharmas.

If, regarding that noble, untainted knowledge, it is not an inferential knowledge of all aspects, it is called dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*). Furthermore, regarding inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*):

if a person has produced dharma-knowledge with respect to phenomena already practiced, then with respect to other phenomena, [knowing] how they arise in their respective ways, according to their respective characteristics, through such analogy—thinking "this is like that" or "that is like this"—if it is a noble, untainted knowledge that is an inferential knowledge of all aspects, it is called inferential knowledge.

Furthermore, worldly knowledge (*loka-jñāna*) refers to knowing sentient beings, knowing the enumeration of phenomena (*dharma-saṃkhyā*), knowing conventional designations, words, and names; or knowing form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; or knowing suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; or knowing the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; or knowing the wisdom that perceives the means of liberation—this is called worldly knowledge.

Furthermore, regarding the knowledge of others' minds: if one uses this knowledge to know the mental factors and the mind of another sentient being or another person, one knows a mind with attachment as it truly is—a mind with attachment;
one knows a mind without attachment as it truly is—a mind without attachment;
one knows a mind with aversion as it truly is—a mind with aversion; and one knows a mind without aversion as it truly is—a mind without aversion.
With a mind of hatred, he knows as it truly is a mind of hatred; with a mind free from hatred, he knows as it truly is a mind free from hatred.
With a mind of envy, he knows as it truly is a mind of envy; with a distracted mind, he knows as it truly is a distracted mind;
with a narrow mind, he knows as it truly is a narrow mind; with a broad mind, he knows as it truly is a broad mind.
He knows an unconcentrated mind as it truly is an unconcentrated mind, and he knows a concentrated mind as it truly is a concentrated mind;
he knows an unliberated mind as it truly is an unliberated mind, and he knows a liberated mind as it truly is a liberated mind;
he knows a surpassable mind as it truly is a surpassable mind, and he knows an unsurpassable mind as it truly is an unsurpassable mind.
If one possesses the wisdom that perceives the means of liberation, this is called the knowledge of others' minds.

What is the analytical eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*)? It is the assembly of phenomena, the inference of phenomena, and the contact with phenomena; when noble wisdom is complete and without remainder, this is called the analytical eloquence regarding phenomena.
What is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*)?
The multitude of meanings, the comparison of meanings, and the contact with meanings—when noble wisdom is complete and without remainder, this is called the analytical knowledge of meaning.
What is the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*)?
To master the assembly, to master the comparison, and to master the contact—if one possesses such noble wisdom without remainder, this is called eloquence in expression (*nirukti-pratibhāna*).
What is eloquence in application (*pratipatti-pratibhāna*)?

To apply oneself to the assembly, to apply oneself to the comparison, and to apply oneself to the contact—if one possesses such noble wisdom without remainder, this is called eloquence in application.

Furthermore, regarding the discrimination of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid): excluding the discrimination of language and the discrimination of eloquence, if there is any other noble, untainted knowledge that knows the characteristics of phenomena without exception through non-analogical cognition, this is called the discrimination of phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*): excluding the analytical knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), if there is any other noble, untainted wisdom that knows the characteristics of all things through inferential knowledge without exception, this is called the analytical knowledge of meaning.

Furthermore, regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna*): whether it concerns form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; or suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; or hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or devas—if one speaks thus, uses such words, and makes such distinctions, or possesses the wisdom and vision that constitutes the skillful means for liberation, this is called eloquence.

Furthermore, one should analyze *pratibhāna* (eloquence). "Should" (*pratibhā*) means wisdom; knowing by means of such wisdom—specifically, the wisdom that perceives the means for liberation—is called *pratibhāna*. Furthermore, regarding *dharma-pratibhāna* (analytical knowledge of phenomena):

whether it be form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; or suffering, origin, cessation, or the path; if one knows, through noble, untainted wisdom rather than inferential wisdom, the characteristics [of these] without remainder—not as contact with objects, not as contact with causes, not as contact with conditions, and not as contact with dependencies—this is called *dharma-pratibhāna*.

Furthermore, regarding analytical eloquence concerning meaning (*arthapratibhāna*): it is the contact with meaning, the contact with causes, the contact with continuities, and the contact with conditions. By means of this meaning—whether it be form, sensation, perception, formations, or consciousness; or suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; or through the knowledge of the outflows-free (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and the subsequent inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)—one knows the characteristics of phenomena without remainder. This is called analytical eloquence concerning meaning.
Furthermore, regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna*):

by attaining the three forms of eloquence—eloquence of phenomena (*dharma-pratibhāna*), eloquence of meaning (*artha-pratibhāna*), and eloquence of expression (*nirukti-pratibhāna*)—if one’s speech is analytical, unimpeded, free from entanglement, and without obstruction; if it is clear and lucid; and if one knows and perceives the skillful means of liberation—this is called eloquence of expression.
Furthermore, one should explain "appropriate eloquence" (*pratibhāna*), by which one attains three forms of eloquence:

eloquence regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratibhāna*), eloquence regarding meaning (*artha-pratibhāna*), and eloquence regarding expression (*nirukti-pratibhāna*). Whether it be the unimpeded, unentangled, boundless, immeasurable, inexhaustible, inconceivable, and incalculable [eloquence] that follows from such exposition, or the knowledge and vision of the skillful means of liberation—this is called appropriate eloquence.
Furthermore, regarding the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*): the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena.
Furthermore, regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is called the analytical knowledge of meaning.
Furthermore, if one discerns phenomena as inconceivable, this is called the analytical knowledge of phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*): if one reflects upon and discriminates the meaning through reflection, this is called the analytical knowledge of meaning.
What is meant by "analytical knowledge" (*pratisaṃvid*)? Analytical knowledge refers to wisdom that takes [the object] as its condition; it refers to the power of wisdom.
Wisdom refers to supreme wisdom; that is, vajra-wisdom and non-remainder wisdom.

Through these, one accomplishes the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): the skillful means of phenomena, the skillful means of meaning, the skillful means of scriptures, and the skillful means of expression; as well as the skillful means of application, the skillful means of the past, the skillful means of the future, and the skillful means of both the past and the future.
If one accomplishes these four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), it is impossible for anyone to exhaust the meaning of this sutra.
These are called the four analytical knowledges.
What is the knowledge that acts but is not divorced from wisdom?
If it is not noble and possesses retribution, this is called knowledge of action (*kriyājñāna*), not knowledge of detachment (*vairāgyajñāna*).
What is knowledge of detachment that is not knowledge of action?
If it is noble, possesses retribution, and is capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called knowledge of detachment, not knowledge of action.
What is the knowledge of both activity and detachment? There is no single knowledge that is either activity or detachment.
If it were knowledge of activity, it would not be knowledge of detachment; if it were knowledge of detachment, it would not be activity. This is called the knowledge of both activity and detachment.
What is knowledge that is neither of action nor of separation?
Any knowledge other than the knowledge of action and the knowledge of separation is called knowledge that is neither of action nor of separation.
Furthermore, there is knowledge of action that is not of separation; if it pertains to the desire realm and is retributive, this is called knowledge of action that is not of separation.
What is the non-activity of the knowledge of detachment (*viveka-jñāna*)?
If the noble one possesses retribution (*vipāka*) that is capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called the non-activity of the knowledge of detachment.

Furthermore, regarding the activity of the knowledge of detachment: if the knowledge arises and severs the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) while still receiving existence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called the activity of the knowledge of detachment.

Furthermore, there is knowledge that is neither produced nor abandoned. If knowledge is without retribution, or if it is noble knowledge with retribution that does not sever the afflictions, this is called knowledge that is neither produced nor abandoned.
The same applies to being with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows, and being with fetters (*yoga*) or without fetters.
What is knowledge that is the fruit of knowledge but not the fruit of abandonment?
If, once knowledge has arisen, it gives rise to further knowledge but does not abandon afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called knowledge that is the fruit of knowledge but not the fruit of abandonment.
What is the knowledge of the fruit of abandonment that is not the fruit of knowledge?

If knowledge arises and abandons the afflictions, yet this abandonment does not arise from that [specific] knowledge, this is called the knowledge of the fruit of abandonment that is not the fruit of knowledge.
What is the knowledge of the fruit of abandonment that is the fruit of knowledge?
If knowledge has arisen, and through the arising of that knowledge afflictions are abandoned, this is called the knowledge of the fruit of knowledge and the fruit of abandonment.
What is the knowledge that is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the fruit of abandonment?

With the exception of the knowledge of the fruit of knowledge and the fruit of abandonment, any other knowledge is called the knowledge that is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the fruit of abandonment.

Furthermore, the fruit of knowledge (*jñāna-phala*) is not the fruit of abandonment (*prahāṇa-phala*). If knowledge arises and one attains the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) that are not noble, or if one attains one or two of those non-noble five supernormal powers, this is called the fruit of knowledge that is not the fruit of abandonment.

Furthermore, there is the knowledge of the fruit of abandonment that is not the fruit of knowledge. If, when knowledge arises, one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, this is called the knowledge of the fruit of abandonment that is not the fruit of knowledge.

Furthermore, there is the knowledge of the fruit of abandonment that is the fruit of knowledge. If, when knowledge arises, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fruit of *anāgāmin*, or the fruit of *arhat*, this is called the knowledge of the fruit of abandonment that is the fruit of knowledge.

Furthermore, there is knowledge that is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the fruit of abandonment. This refers to knowledge that is either without retribution or with retribution, and which is neither produced by knowledge nor capable of abandoning afflictions; this is called knowledge that is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the fruit of abandonment.
The attainment of the fruits of wisdom is also like this.
What is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) that is not awakening?

If a knowledge arises that exhausts the afflictions but is not the knowledge of awakening—excluding the knowledge of exhaustion itself—if it is any other knowledge, this is called the knowledge of exhaustion that is not awakening.
What is knowledge of awakening that is not exhaustive?
If knowledge arises such that one attains the five non-noble supernormal powers, whether one or two of them, this is called knowledge of awakening that is not exhaustive.
What is exhaustive knowledge of awakening?

If wisdom arises such that one attains the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship, this is called the knowledge of the awakening to exhaustion.
What is the wisdom that is neither exhaustion nor awakening?

If there is no retribution, or if the wisdom has retribution, and it is neither capable of severing afflictions nor giving rise to wisdom, this is called the wisdom that is neither exhaustion nor awakening.
Liberation is also like this.
*Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle Nine.
2. *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Dharmagupta and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Part Two of the Fourth Chapter, the Section on Knowledge (*Jñāna-varga*), from the Non-Questioned Division (*Apraśnaka-vibhaṅga*): What is knowledge of the regressive portion (*hāna-bhāgīya-jñāna*)?
If wisdom is unwholesome, it is called wisdom of the regressive type (*hānabhāgīya*).
What is wisdom of the stationary type (*sthityaṃśabhāgīya*)?
If wisdom is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is called wisdom of the stationary type.
What is the knowledge pertaining to the stage of increase?
If knowledge is mundane yet wholesome, it is called the knowledge pertaining to the stage of increase.
What is the knowledge pertaining to penetration?
If knowledge is noble, possesses fruition, and is capable of severing the afflictions, it is called the knowledge of the factor of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-jñāna*).
What is the knowledge of the factor of decline (*hānabhāgīya-jñāna*)?
