If knowledge arises such that one declines from non-noble wholesome states, does not abide in them, and does not increase them, this is called the knowledge of the factor of decline.
What is the knowledge of the station (sthiti-bhāgīya-jñāna)?
If knowledge arises such that one abides in, does not fall back from, and does not increase in unwholesome but noble dharmas, this is called the knowledge of the station.
What is the knowledge of the side of increase?
If a knowledge arises that increases un-noble, unwholesome dharmas, and neither retreats nor remains stable, this is called the knowledge of the side of increase.
What is the knowledge of the factor of penetration?
If it is associated with penetration and conjoined with penetration, this is called the knowledge of the factor of penetration.
What is the knowledge of the factor of decline and not the knowledge of the factor of stability?
If there is falling away and not abiding, this is called knowledge of the stage of falling away and not the stage of abiding.
What is knowledge of the stage of abiding and not the stage of falling away?
If there is abiding and not falling away, this is called knowledge of the stage of abiding and not the stage of falling away.
What is the knowledge of the stage of decline and the stage of stability?
There is no single knowledge that is both the stage of decline and the stage of stability.

If it is knowledge of the stage of stability, it is not the stage of decline; if it is the stage of decline, it is not the stage of stability. This is called the knowledge of the stage of decline and the stage of stability.
What is knowledge that is neither of the category of decline nor of the category of stability?

Excluding knowledge of the category of decline and knowledge of the category of stability, any other knowledge or vision is termed knowledge that is neither of the category of decline nor of the category of stability.
What is knowledge of the category of decline that is not of the category of increase?
If there is regression and no growth, this is called "knowledge of the regressive portion" (hānabhāgīya-jñāna) and not growth.
What is "knowledge of the progressive portion" (viśeṣabhāgīya-jñāna) and not regression?
If knowledge grows and does not regress, this is called "knowledge of the progressive portion" and not regression.
What is the knowledge of the regressive portion and the progressive portion?
There is no single knowledge that is both regressive and progressive.

If a certain knowledge is regressive and not progressive, while another knowledge is progressive and not regressive, these are called the knowledge of the regressive portion and the progressive portion.
What is knowledge that is neither of the nature of retrogression nor of the nature of increase?

Excluding knowledge of the nature of retrogression and knowledge of the nature of increase, any other knowledge is termed knowledge that is neither of the nature of retrogression nor of the nature of increase.
What is the knowledge of the factor of stability that is not the factor of liberation?
If there is stability without liberation, this is called the knowledge of the factor of stability that is not the factor of liberation.
What is the knowledge of the factor of liberation that is not the factor of stability?
If wisdom involves liberation but not abiding, this is called "wisdom of the factor of liberation that does not abide.
What is "wisdom of the factor of abiding that is a factor of liberation"?
There is no single wisdom that is both a factor of abiding and a factor of liberation.
If the wisdom of the stage of abiding is not the wisdom of penetration, and the wisdom of penetration is not the wisdom of abiding, this is called the wisdom of the stages of abiding and penetration.
What is the wisdom that is neither of the stage of abiding nor of penetration?
Excluding the knowledge of the stage of abiding and the stage of penetration, any other knowledge is called the knowledge that is neither of the stage of abiding nor of the stage of penetration.
What is the knowledge of the stage of increase that is not of the stage of penetration?
If there is growth that is not liberation, this is called "knowledge of the factor of growth, not the factor of liberation.
What is knowledge of the factor of liberation, not the factor of growth?
If knowledge involves liberation but not growth, this is called "knowledge of the factor of liberation, not the factor of growth."
What is the knowledge of the increase and the analysis of parts?
There is no single knowledge that constitutes both the increase and the analysis of parts.
If the knowledge of increase is not the analysis of parts, and the knowledge of the analysis of parts is not the increase, this is called the knowledge of the increase and the analysis of parts.
What is knowledge that is neither conducive to growth nor conducive to penetration?
With the exception of knowledge conducive to growth and knowledge conducive to penetration, any other knowledge is called knowledge that is neither conducive to growth nor conducive to penetration.
What are the five knowledges?
As the Blessed One said:

"When one cultivates the concentration of the mind on immeasurable meanings so that it is equally and clearly illumined, and when a bhikṣu has cultivated this concentration and the concentration of the mind on immeasurable meanings is equally and clearly illumined, five knowledges arise within."
What are the five?

This concentration produces internal knowledge that it brings happiness in the present life and will result in the experience of happiness as its future retribution; this concentration produces internal knowledge that it is noble and undefiled; this concentration produces internal knowledge that it is what noble ones cultivate; this concentration produces internal knowledge that through its tranquility, excellence, and sublimity, the noble mind attains liberation and eliminates unwholesome states; and this concentration produces internal knowledge that one enters it with mindfulness and emerges from it with mindfulness.

The immeasurable and boundless illumination of the mind through the cultivation of meditative concentration: once a bhikṣu has cultivated concentration, these five kinds of knowledge arise from the immeasurable and boundless illumination of the mind; these are called the five knowledges.

What are the six supernormal powers? They are: the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the bases of psychic power; the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the divine ear; the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of observing the minds and mental factors of others; the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of recollecting past lives; the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the death and rebirth of sentient beings; and the supernormal power of realization through knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.
What is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhividhi-jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*)?

It is the wisdom that arises when one experiences immeasurable bases of psychic power: shaking the great earth; making one into many and many into one; passing through walls, mountains, and cliffs without obstruction as if through empty space; sitting cross-legged, coming and going through the air like a bird; entering the earth as if it were water and walking upon water as if it were earth; emitting smoke and flames from the body like a great mass of fire; and having the power and majesty to touch the sun and moon with the hand, even reaching as far as the Brahma-heaven, attaining mastery over the body—this is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the bases of psychic power.
What is the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear?
It is the wisdom that arises as the divine ear, surpassing the human ear, by which one hears two kinds of sounds:
those of humans and those of non-humans. This is called the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the divine ear.
What is the supernormal knowledge of realization through wisdom that contemplates the mind and mental factors?
It is when wisdom arises such that one knows the minds and mental factors of other sentient beings and others: if there is a mind with desire, one knows it as it truly is as a mind with desire;
if there is a mind without desire, one knows it as it truly is as a mind without desire; if there is a mind with hatred, one knows it as it truly is...
He knows as it truly is a mind with hatred as a mind with hatred, and a mind without hatred as a mind without hatred;
he knows as it truly is a mind with delusion as a mind with delusion, and a mind without delusion as a mind without delusion;
he knows as it truly is a swift mind as a swift mind, a distracted mind as a distracted mind, a small mind as a small mind, and a noble mind as a noble mind.
He knows the noble mind as it truly is; he knows the unsettled mind as it truly is an unsettled mind, and the settled mind as it truly is a settled mind;
he knows the unliberated mind as it truly is an unliberated mind, and the liberated mind as it truly is a liberated mind;
he knows the surpassable mind as it truly is a surpassable mind, and the unsurpassable mind as...
Truly knowing the unsurpassed mind is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the wisdom that contemplates the mind and mental factors.
What is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the wisdom of recollecting past lives?
It is the wisdom that arises when one recollects immeasurable and various past lives—recollecting one life, two, three, four, five... [and so forth].
Ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, hundreds, thousands of births, ten thousand births, a hundred thousand births, immeasurable tens of births,
immeasurable hundreds of births, immeasurable thousands of births, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of births;
even through the formation of kalpas, the destruction of kalpas, or both the formation and destruction of kalpas, and immeasurable kalpas of formation and immeasurable kalpas of destruction.
Throughout immeasurable eons of world-formation and destruction, I was formerly there, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food,
such a lifespan, such longevity, such brevity of life,
and experiencing such suffering and pleasure; dying from that place, I was born there, and after dying from that place, I was born yet again.
Passing away from there and being born here, thus possessing such accomplished conduct, one recollects various past lives;
this is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the recollection of past existences (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).
What is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the birth and death of sentient beings?

It is the wisdom that gives rise to the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, by which one sees sentient beings being born and dying, whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, in good or bad destinies, lowly or exalted; and one knows sentient beings according to the karma they have created: how those sentient beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind; how they have reviled noble ones and held wrong views; and how, conditioned by these wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the miserable states of hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.

When sentient beings accomplish wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind; do not revile the noble ones; and practice right view—due to that right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a good destination, among the devas or among humans.
Such divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the death and rebirth of sentient beings.
What is the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows?

It is when, through the arising of wisdom, there is the attainment of the exhaustion of outflows, the liberation of mind from outflows, and the liberation by wisdom; one realizes for oneself in the present life, having achieved the practice, knowing: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further state of existence. This is called the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows.
These are called the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
What are the seven preparatory practices (*saptopāya*)?
As the Blessed One said:
A bhikṣu who possesses the seven bases of mastery and the three types of contemplation is pure and virtuous within this Dharma, and his fame spreads afar; he is called a "noble person.
What is meant by a bhikṣu possessing the seven bases of mastery?

Just as a bhikkhu knows form, knows the arising of form, knows the cessation of form, knows the path leading to the cessation of form, knows the gratification of form, knows the danger in form, and knows the escape from form.

One knows feeling, knows the origin of feeling, knows the cessation of feeling, knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling; one knows the gratification of feeling, knows the danger of feeling, and knows the escape from feeling.

One knows perception, knows the origin of perception, knows the cessation of perception, knows the path leading to the cessation of perception; one knows the gratification of perception, knows the danger of perception, and knows the escape from perception.
Volitional formations: their origin, their cessation, the path leading to their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the escape from them. Consciousness:
its origin, its cessation, the path leading to its cessation, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it.
How does a bhikṣu know form?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements as they truly are, so does a bhikṣu know form.
How does a bhikṣu know the arising of form?
Just as a bhikṣu knows form through the arising of craving, so does a bhikṣu know form and the arising of form.
How does a bhikṣu know the cessation of form?
When a bhikṣu’s craving ceases, he knows the cessation of form through the cessation of craving; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the cessation of form.
How does a bhikṣu know, as it truly is, the path to the cessation of form?
It is when a bhikṣu knows, as they truly are, the Eightfold Noble Path:

right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; in this way, a bhikṣu knows, as it truly is, the path to the cessation of form.
How does a bhikṣu know the gratification (*āsvāda*) of form?
That which is the joy and pleasure arising conditioned by form is the gratification of form; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the gratification of form.
How does a bhikṣu know the danger (*ādīnava*) of form?
If form is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the peril of form; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the peril of form.
How does a bhikṣu know the escape from form?
If one subdues the defilement of desire for form and brings about the cessation of that desire for form, this is the escape; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the escape from form.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who thus know form, know the origin of form, know the cessation of form, know the path leading to the cessation of form, know the gratification of form, know the danger of form, and know the escape from form, they will become weary of form, become dispassionate toward it, bring it to cessation, and proceed upon the path.

Whether it be those in the happy realms or the people of the happy realms who have clear understanding of this Dharma, as well as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—who thus know form, know the origin of form, know the cessation of form, know the path leading to the cessation of form, know the gratification of form, know the peril of form, and know the escape from form; who, through weariness with form, become dispassionate toward it, realize its cessation, and attain liberation, no longer subject to rebirth; who are well-liberated or persons well-liberated; who are purely virtuous or persons purely virtuous—there is for them no further place of birth.
How does a bhikṣu know feeling?
There are six groups of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact, and feeling born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six groups of feeling.
In this way, a bhikṣu knows feeling.
How does a bhikṣu know the arising of feeling?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the arising of feeling through the arising of contact, in this way he knows the arising of feeling.
How does a bhikṣu know the cessation of feeling?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the cessation of feeling through the cessation of contact, in this way a bhikṣu knows the cessation of feeling.
How does a bhikṣu know the path leading to the cessation of feeling?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is—

namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration— in this way, a bhikṣu knows the path leading to the cessation of feeling.
How does a bhikṣu know the gratification of feeling?
If joy and pleasure arise conditioned by feeling, that is the gratification of feeling; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the gratification of feeling.
How does a bhikṣu know the danger of feeling?
That feelings are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the danger in feelings; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the danger in feelings.
How does a bhikṣu know the escape from feelings?
The subduing of the defilement of feeling, the eradication of the defilement of feeling, and the emergence from feeling—thus does a bhikṣu know the emergence from feeling.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who thus know feeling, know the origination of feeling, know the cessation of feeling, know the path leading to the cessation of feeling, know the gratification of feeling, know the danger of feeling, and know the emergence from feeling, they will become weary of feeling, detach from desire for it, realize its cessation, and proceed upon the path.

Whether one is in a happy destination or is a person in a happy destination, if they have clear understanding regarding this Dharma—and likewise other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—knowing feeling, knowing the origin of feeling, knowing the cessation of feeling, knowing the path leading to the cessation of feeling, knowing the gratification of feeling, knowing the danger of feeling, and knowing the escape from feeling; then, through disenchantment with feeling, detachment, the realization of its cessation, liberation, they will not be born again.
One who is well-liberated, or a person who is well-liberated; one who is purely wholesome, or a person who is purely wholesome—such a one has no further place of rebirth.
How does a bhikṣu understand perceptions?
There are six classes of perception:

The perception of forms, the perception of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six groups of perception (*ṣaḍ-saṃjñā-kāya*). In this way, a bhikṣu knows perception.
How does a bhikṣu know the arising of perception?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the arising of perception through the arising of contact, in this way a bhikṣu knows the arising of perception.
How does a bhikṣu know the cessation of perception?
A bhikṣu knows the cessation of perception through the cessation of contact; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the cessation of perception.
How does a bhikṣu know the path to the cessation of perception?
It is when a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is—
from right view up to right concentration— in this way, a bhikṣu knows the path to the cessation of perception.
How does a bhikṣu know the gratification of perception?
If the joy and pleasure that arise conditioned by perception are the gratification of perception—in this way, a bhikṣu knows the gratification of perception.
How does a bhikṣu know the danger in perception?
To perceive that perception is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is to know the danger of perception; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the danger of perception.
How does a bhikṣu know the escape from perception?
If one wishes to tame the defilement of desire and sever the defilement of desire, this is the emergence from perception; thus, a bhikṣu knows the emergence from perception.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who thus know perception, know the origin of perception, know the cessation of perception, know the path leading to the cessation of perception, know the gratification of perception, know the danger in perception, and know the emergence from perception, they will become weary of perception, become dispassionate toward it, realize its cessation, and proceed upon the path.

Whether they be those in the happy realms or those among humans who are clear regarding this Dharma, as well as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, they thus know perception, know the origin of perception, know the cessation of perception, know the path leading to the cessation of perception, know the gratification of perception, know the danger of perception, and know the escape from perception; through disenchantment with perception, detachment, realization of its cessation, and liberation, they shall not be born again.
One who is well-liberated, or a person who is well-liberated; one who is purely wholesome, or a person who is purely wholesome—such a one has no further place of rebirth.
How does a bhikṣu know the course of action?
There are six groups of volition:
Volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six groups of volition. In this way, a bhikṣu knows volition.
How does a bhikṣu know the arising of volition?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the origin of formations through the origin of ignorance, so does a bhikṣu know the origin of formations.
How does a bhikṣu know the cessation of formations?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the cessation of formations through the cessation of ignorance, so does a bhikṣu know the cessation of formations.
How does a bhikṣu know the path leading to the cessation of formations?
It is when a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is—
from right view up to right concentration— in this way, a bhikṣu knows the path leading to the cessation of formations as it truly is.
How does a bhikṣu know the gratification of conditioned formations?
If joy and pleasure arise conditioned by formations, that is the gratification of formations; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the gratification of formations.
How does a bhikṣu know the danger in conditioned formations?
That formations are impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is the danger inherent in formations; in this way, a bhikkhu understands the danger in formations.
What is a bhikkhu’s understanding of the escape from formations?
If one practices the subduing of sensual defilement and the eradication of sensual defilement, such a bhikṣu is said to know the escape from formations.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who thus know formations, know the origin of formations, know the cessation of formations, know the path leading to the cessation of formations, know the gratification of formations, know the danger of formations, and know the escape from formations, they will become weary of formations, detach from desire, realize cessation, and proceed toward the path.

Whether one is in a happy destination or is a person in a happy destination, if they are clear regarding this Dharma—and likewise regarding other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—thus knowing the nature of formations (saṅkhāra), the origin of formations, the cessation of formations, the path leading to the cessation of formations; knowing the gratification of formations, the danger of formations, and the escape from formations; and having become disenchanted with formations, detached from desire for them, realized their cessation, and attained liberation, they will not be born again.
One who is well-liberated, or a person who is well-liberated; one who is purely wholesome, or a person who is purely wholesome—such a one has no further place of rebirth.
What is a bhikṣu’s knowledge of consciousness?
It is the six groups of consciousness:

The body of visual consciousness, and the bodies of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness—these are the six bodies of consciousness. In this way, a bhikṣu knows consciousness.
How does a bhikṣu know the arising of consciousness?
Just as a bhikṣu understands the arising of consciousness through the arising of name-and-form, in this way a bhikṣu understands the arising of consciousness.
How does a bhikṣu understand the cessation of consciousness?
Just as a bhikṣu understands the cessation of consciousness through the cessation of name-and-form, in this way a bhikṣu understands the cessation of consciousness.
What is the bhikṣu’s knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of consciousness?
It is when a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is—right view through to right concentration; in this way, the bhikṣu knows the path leading to the cessation of consciousness.
How does a bhikṣu know the gratification of consciousness?
The joy and pleasure that arise conditioned by consciousness are the gratification of consciousness; in this way, a bhikṣu knows the gratification of consciousness.
How does a bhikṣu know the danger of consciousness?
That consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change—this is the peril of consciousness; in this way, a bhikṣu understands the peril of consciousness.
What is a bhikṣu’s understanding of the escape from consciousness?

If one tames the defilement of craving for consciousness and brings about its cessation, this is the transcendence of consciousness; in this way, a bhikṣu understands the transcendence of consciousness.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who thus understand consciousness, the arising of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, the gratification of consciousness, the danger of consciousness, and the transcendence of consciousness, they will become disenchanted with consciousness, become free from desire for it, realize its cessation, and proceed upon the path.

Whether they belong to the happy realms or are persons of the happy realms who have clear understanding of this Dharma, as well as other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas—[they understand] consciousness, the origin of consciousness, the cessation of consciousness, the path leading to the cessation of consciousness, the gratification of consciousness, the danger of consciousness, and the escape from consciousness; through disenchantment with consciousness, dispassion, the realization of its cessation, and liberation, they shall not be born again.
One who is well-liberated, like one who is well-liberated; one who is purely virtuous, like one who is purely virtuous—such a person has no further place of rebirth.
Thus, bhikṣus, is the method of the seven stations.
What are the three kinds of contemplation for a bhikṣu?

They are as follows: a bhikṣu contemplates the elements (dhātu), contemplates the sense bases (āyatana), and contemplates conditions (pratyaya); such are the three kinds of contemplation for a bhikṣu.
Through these seven stations of skillful means and three kinds of contemplation, a bhikṣu becomes purely virtuous and far-renowned within this Dharma, being called a "Noble Man" (mahāpuruṣa).
This is called the sevenfold application of skillful means (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*).
What is the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*)?

If there are impure, conditioned phenomena subsumed under the truth of suffering, and one perceives them as suffering, perceives them as non-self, or contemplates them as suffering—such that, through noble, untainted wisdom, one realizes their characteristics without remainder by way of direct perception rather than inference—this is called the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering.
What is the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*)?

If a person has already practiced the knowledge of the dharma of the arising of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), and regarding other phenomena subsumed under the truth of suffering, [perceives] their arising as it is, their characteristics as they are, and through analogy that "this is like that" and "that is like this," and if, with respect to those noble, untainted knowledges, there is no remainder of the characteristics of analogical knowledge—this is called the subsequent knowledge of suffering.
What is the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*)?

If one perceives the cause of suffering, the sequence of suffering, and the origination of suffering; if one perceives origination, perceives non-self, and contemplates origination; and if, regarding this, there is the noble, untainted knowledge that is not inferential, whose characteristic is the absence of remainder—this is called the knowledge of the dharma regarding origination.
What is the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*)?

If a person, having generated the knowledge of the dharma of origination through practice, and regarding other phenomena subsumed under the truth of origination, generates [knowledge] in that manner, with that characteristic, and by way of that analogy—thinking "this is like that" or "that is like this"—such that the characteristics of the analogical knowledge within noble, untainted wisdom are complete without remainder, this is called the subsequent knowledge of origination.
What is the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*)?

It is when, regarding the phenomena of the exhaustion of suffering, the exhaustion of afflictions, and the exhaustion of outflows, one perceives cessation, perceives non-self, and contemplates cessation; it is that noble, untainted knowledge which is not inferential and is characterized by the absence of remainder—this is called the knowledge of the dharma of cessation.
What is the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*)?

If a person has already practiced the knowledge of the dharma of arising and cessation, and regarding other phenomena subsumed under the truth of cessation, [perceives] them as they arise, as they are characterized, and by analogy—thinking "this is like that" or "that is like this"—and if, within the noble, untainted knowledge, the characteristics of this analogical knowledge are complete without remainder, this is called the subsequent knowledge of cessation.
What is the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*)?

When, within the noble path that is the definitive departure which correctly extinguishes the dharmas of suffering, one perceives the path, perceives non-self, and contemplates the path—such that it is the noble, untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), not a knowledge based on inference, and characterized by the absence of remainder—this is called the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path.
What is the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*)?

If a person, by means of the dharma-practice, gives rise to the dharma-knowledge of the path, and regarding other phenomena subsumed under the truth of the path, [perceives] their arising as it is, their characteristics as they are, and their analogies as they are—thinking "this is like that" or "that is like this"—then the complete characteristic of analogy within noble, untainted knowledge is called the subsequent knowledge of the path.

What are the nine skillful means? They are: the skillful means of concentration upon concentration; the skillful means of entering concentration from concentration; the skillful means of abiding in concentration; the skillful means of emerging from concentration; the skillful means of the objective sphere of concentration; the skillful means of the range of activity of concentration; the skillful means of the bliss of concentration; and the skillful means of transforming concentration. These involve the favorable and unfavorable dharmas, as well as the thorough contemplation and thorough understanding of the characteristics of wholesome dharmas.
What is the skillful means of concentration upon concentration?

It consists of the assembly of concentration upon concentration, the designation of concentration upon concentration, the contact of concentration upon concentration, and the mental attention of concentration upon concentration. This includes concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought, concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought, the concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, and the concentration of wishlessness. Such concentration is the skillful means of knowledge, vision, liberation, and penetration.
What is the method for entering meditative concentration?

It consists of the assembly for entering concentration, the names for entering concentration, the contact of entering concentration, and the mental attention of entering concentration; it includes concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought, concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought, and the entry into the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—thus one enters these concentrations.
Having entered this concentration, one enters this supreme state of the dharma; if one knows and sees the skillful means of penetration, this is called the skillful means for entering concentration.
What is the skillful means for abiding in concentration?

They are the abiding in the assembly, the abiding in names, the abiding in contact, and the abiding in reflection; they are the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation, the concentration without directed thought but with sustained evaluation, the concentration without directed thought and without sustained evaluation, and the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
This is the stabilization.
Having stabilized, this dharma is the supreme stabilization; if one knows and sees the application of skillful means for penetration, this is called the application of stabilization.
What is the application of emerging from stabilization?

The emergence from concentration, the names of the emergence from concentration, the contact of the emergence from concentration, and the mental application of the emergence from concentration—whether this emergence from concentration is with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka and with vicāra, or without vitarka and without vicāra; whether it is emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness—this is the emergence from concentration.

Having emerged from this meditative absorption, this dharma excels upon emerging; if one knows, sees, and masters the skillful means [of emergence], this is called the skillful means of emerging from absorption.
What is the skillful means regarding the objective sphere of absorption?

If one contemplates a dharma that is necessarily produced by concentration, or if a dharma is the objective domain of concentration, or if one possesses the knowledge, vision, and skillful means of penetration, this is called the "skillful means regarding the objective domain of concentration.
What is the "skillful means regarding the sphere of activity of concentration"?

The practice of concentration refers to the four foundations of mindfulness; if one possesses the skillful means of knowledge, vision, and penetration, this is called the skillful means regarding the sphere of the practice of concentration.
What is the skillful means regarding the pleasure of concentration?

The bliss of concentration refers to the removal of the group of [sensual] pleasures; it is the name of the bliss of concentration, the contact of the bliss of concentration, and the mental attention to the bliss of concentration. It is the bliss of concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, that with no directed thought and only sustained thought, and that with neither directed thought nor sustained thought; it is the concentration of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—this is the bliss of concentration.

This is the skillful means (*upāya*) for the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi-sukha*). If one knows, sees, and masters this skillful means, it is called the "skillful means for the bliss of concentration.

What is the "skillful means for the transformation of concentration"? It is when, arising from the mind of the first dhyāna, one enters and abides in the mind of the second dhyāna; arising from the mind of the first dhyāna, one enters and abides in the mind of the third dhyāna; arising from the mind of the first dhyāna, one enters and abides in the mind of the fourth dhyāna; arising from the mind of the second dhyāna, one enters and abides in the mind of the third dhyāna; arising from the mind of the second dhyāna, one enters and abides in the mind of the fourth dhyāna; and arising from the mind of the third dhyāna, one enters and abides in the mind of the fourth dhyāna. If one knows, sees, and masters this skillful means, it is called the "skillful means for the transformation of concentration."
What is meant by "properly grasping"?
It is the thorough contemplation and thorough understanding of the characteristics of phenomena that are either conducive or non-conducive [to liberation].
What are phenomena that are not definitively conducive?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome, it is called "not definitely conforming to the Dharma.
What is "definitely conforming to the Dharma"?
If a phenomenon is wholesome, it is called "definitely conforming to the Dharma."
Furthermore, regarding "not invariably conforming to the Dharma": if a dharma has a superior [counterpart], it is called a dharma that does not invariably conform to the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding "invariably conforming to the Dharma": if a dharma has no superior [counterpart], it is called a dharma that invariably conforms to the Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding those factors that are not necessarily conducive: if, when one contemplates these factors, they do not necessarily arise, these are called factors that are not necessarily conducive.
Furthermore, regarding those factors that are necessarily conducive: if, when one contemplates these factors, they necessarily arise, these are called factors that are necessarily conducive.

To skillfully grasp the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), to reflect upon them skillfully, and to understand them skillfully—this is called skillfully grasping the characteristics of phenomena that are favorable or unfavorable, reflecting upon them skillfully, and understanding them skillfully.
These are known as the nine preliminary applications (*upāya*).

What are the ten powers of the Tathāgata? They are: the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the causes and results of actions performed in the past, future, and present; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings and individuals; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the various inclinations of other sentient beings and individuals; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the various elements and immeasurable worlds; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the paths leading to all destinations; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the defilement, purification, and emergence from meditative concentrations, liberations, samādhis, and attainments; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the realization of past lives; the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the realization of the death and rebirth of sentient beings; and the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows.
What is the Tathāgata’s power regarding the possible and the impossible?
What is meant by the possible and the impossible?

"Impossible" refers to the following: that one who practices evil with the body, evil with speech, and evil with the mind should receive a retribution that is pleasant, delightful, and agreeable—this is impossible.
If one engages in evil conduct of body, evil conduct of speech, and evil conduct of mind, and consequently receives a retribution that is unpleasant, unloved, and disagreeable—this is possible.
To say that one who engages in good conduct of body, good conduct of speech, and good conduct of mind would receive a retribution that is unpleasant, unloved, and disagreeable—this is impossible.
If one practices wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, it is possible that one will experience the retribution of being beloved, joyful, and pleasing; such a case exists.

It is impossible—that is, out of place—to say that one who practices unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, having accomplished the karma of slandering the noble ones and holding wrong views, would, by reason of those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, be reborn among gods or humans in the good destinations; such a case does not exist.

If one engages in unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind, and accomplishes the practice of wrong views that revile the noble ones, then by reason of those karmas based on wrong views and through those causes and conditions, at the breaking up of the body after death, one will be reborn in the miserable states, in the hells; such a thing is possible, it is within the realm of possibility.

If one engages in wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and accomplishes right view that does not revile the noble ones, yet because of the causal conditions of karma based on such right view, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is born in the miserable states within the hells—this is impossible.

If one practices wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and accomplishes right view that does not revile the noble ones, then by reason of the causal conditions of karma associated with such right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, one will be reborn among the virtuous—among humans or devas; this is possible, for it is a logical possibility.
If one were to intentionally take the life of a mother who is an Arhat, such a thing is impossible; it is not possible.
If an ordinary person were to intentionally take the life of a mother, such a thing is possible; it is both possible and impossible [depending on the status of the mother].
It is impossible, it cannot be, that one who has attained the perfection of vision would intentionally take the life of his father; such a thing is not possible.
It is possible, it is within the realm of possibility, that an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) would intentionally take the life of his father; such a thing is possible.
If one kills an Arhat or a Śrāvaka because they are endowed with [right] views, that is impossible; it is not possible.
If one kills an Arhat because they are an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), that is possible; it is possible.
If one sees a person endowed with [right] view break the Saṃgha, such a thing is impossible;
if an ordinary person breaks the Saṃgha, such a thing is possible. This is the distinction between the possible and the impossible.
If one sees a person endowed with right view shedding blood from the body of the Tathāgata with an evil mind, such a thing is impossible; it is not possible.
If an ordinary person sheds blood from the body of the Tathāgata with an evil mind, such a thing is possible; it is possible.
If one who is endowed with vision seeks some other superior excellence outside of this Dharma, such a thing is impossible; it is not possible.
If an ordinary person seeks some other superior excellence outside of this Dharma, such a thing is possible; it is possible.
If one sees a person who is fully endowed [with the Dharma] seeking further offerings outside of this Dharma, such a thing is impossible;
it is not possible. If an ordinary person seeks further offerings outside of this Dharma, such a thing is possible; it is possible.
If one who is endowed with vision seeks elsewhere outside this Dharma for other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas to explain right view, such a thing is impossible; it is not possible.
If an ordinary person seeks elsewhere outside this Dharma for other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas to explain right view, such a thing is possible; it is possible.

If one sees a person who is fully endowed [with wisdom] speaking outside of this Dharma, or if other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas speak of the Dharma and praise it, saying, "This one is all-knowing and all-seeing," such a thing is impossible; there is no such case.

If an ordinary person, outside of this Dharma, hears other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas preaching and praising them, saying, "This one is omniscient and all-seeing," there is both the possibility and the impossibility of such a thing.

If one sees a person who is complete in their faculties, and if there are among those outside this Dharma any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, based on different conditions, maintain that "the self and the world are eternal—this alone is true, all else is false";
or "the self and the world are non-eternal—this alone is true, all else is false";
or "the self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal—this alone is true, all else is false"; [or "neither eternal nor non-eternal"]...
"The self and the world are neither eternal nor non-eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
The self and the world are finite; this alone is true, all else is false.
The self and the world are infinite; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The world has an end and is infinite; this alone is true, all else is false";
"The world is neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, all else is false";
"Life is the same as the body; this alone is true, all else is false."
"The body is the life-force; this is true and all else is false.
"The body and the life-force are different; this is true and all else is false.
"There is neither life-force nor body; this is true and all else is false."
"The Tathāgata exists after parinirvāṇa; this is true and all else is false.
"The Tathāgata does not exist after parinirvāṇa; this is true and all else is false.
"The Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after parinirvāṇa; this is true and all else is false."

Nirvana is neither the existence of the Tathāgata nor the non-existence of the Tathāgata; this alone is real, while all else is false. To claim that there is a reality distinct from these conditions—that would be impossible; such a thing cannot exist.

If there were ordinary persons, or outside this Dharma, or śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, who held a different basis for the view that "the self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false," and so on, up to "neither exists nor does not exist after death is nirvāṇa"—if they held such a different basis as being truly real, it would be a case of what is possible and what is impossible.

If an ordinary person, through the theft of precepts regarding purity and seeking auspiciousness through false conditions, falls into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, and then receives an eighth human body—such a thing is possible; such a case exists.
It is impossible, it cannot happen, that two wheel-turning sage-kings (cakravartin-rājas) should appear in the world simultaneously; such a thing has never occurred.
It is possible, it can happen, that one wheel-turning sage-king appears in the world; such a thing has occurred.
It is impossible, it cannot happen, that a Wheel-Turning Sage King should be born in a borderland;
it is possible, it can happen, that a Wheel-Turning Sage King should be born in a central land.

If a Wheel-Turning Sage King were born into a lowly family, such as the family of a *caṇḍāla* or various artisans; or if he were deaf, blind, mute, crippled, lame, or paralyzed, lacking physical completeness due to such ailments or other diseases—this is impossible, this cannot be.

If a Wheel-Turning Sage King is born into a noble family, or a great Kṣatriya clan, or a great Brāhmaṇa clan, or a great householder clan, and possesses a body that is upright, exquisite, and endowed with auspicious marks—such a thing is possible; it is within the realm of possibility.
If a Wheel-Turning Sage King were born into a poor and lowly family, lacking many things and possessing no property, food, drink, or clothing—this is impossible; this cannot be.

If a Wheel-Turning Sage King is born into a wealthy family, possessing gold, silver, money, treasures, jade, shells, coral, mani-jewels, pearls, and lapis lazuli; elephants, horses, carriages, and servants; and granaries and treasuries filled with grain and silk—such a thing is possible, for it is within the realm of possibility.
It is impossible, it cannot be, that two Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas should appear in the world simultaneously; such a thing has never occurred.
It is possible, it can be, that one Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world; such a thing has occurred.
It is impossible, it cannot be, that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha should be born in a borderland;
it is possible, it can be, that a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha should be born in a central land.

If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were born into a lowly family—such as a family of caṇḍālas or various craftsmen—or were deaf, blind, mute, crippled, lame, paralyzed, deficient in limb, or afflicted by other such ailments, this would be impossible; it could not be.

If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is born into a noble family—whether into a great Kṣatriya clan or a great Brāhmaṇa clan—and possesses a most excellent and beautiful countenance with the supreme accomplishment of physical marks, such a possibility exists.
If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha were born into a poor and lowly family, lacking in food, drink, clothing, and other necessities—such a thing is impossible; it cannot be.

If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is born into a family of great wealth and treasure—where gold, silver, money, gems, shells, coral, maṇi-jewels, pearls, lapis lazuli, elephants, horses, carriages, servants, grain, silks, and storehouses overflow—is such a thing possible or impossible? It is possible.
That a woman should become a wheel-turning sage king (cakravartin) is impossible; that it is possible is not the case.
That a man should become a wheel-turning sage king is possible; that it is possible is the case.
That a woman should become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—this is impossible; this is not possible.
That a man should become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—this is possible; this is possible.
If a woman were to become Śakra, Lord of Devas, or Māra, the King, or Brahmā, the King—that is impossible; there is no such possibility.
If a man were to become Śakra, Lord of Devas, or Māra, the King, or Brahmā, the King—that is possible; there is such a possibility.
Just as there is no cause, no door, no object, no expectation, and no existence, so too there is no such thing as a "possible place" (*sthāna*).
Knowing cause, door, object, and expectation as they truly are—just as they exist—the Tathāgata knows, according to reality, what is a possible place and what is an impossible place (*asthāna*).

In this way, the Tathāgata’s correct discrimination and correct understanding of what is possible and what is impossible, as well as his skillful means of insight, knowledge, vision, and penetration based on conditions—this is called the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the Tathāgata is supreme, sovereign, victorious, most excellent, and unsurpassed by virtue of his power of wisdom; as a virtuous and great person, the Tathāgata has accomplished such power that, in whatever place and in whatever manner he desires, he enters and emerges from meditative concentration exactly as he intends. This is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What is the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the causes, retributions, and the spheres of experience for past, future, and present karma?
What is past karma? If karma has arisen and subsequently ceased, it is called past karma.
What is future karma?
If karma has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, it is called future karma.
What is present karma?
If karma has arisen but not yet ceased, it is called present karma. What is this karma?

It is karma of volition (*cetanā*) and karma subsequent to volition; karma performed intentionally and karma not performed intentionally; karma that is experienced and karma that is not experienced; karma experienced to a small degree and karma experienced to a great degree; matured karma and non-matured karma; material karma and immaterial karma; visible karma and invisible karma; resistant karma and non-resistant karma; noble karma and non-noble karma. These are called karma.
What is the karma of feeling?
As the Blessed One has said:

there are four types of karma of feeling—karma of feeling that is painful in the present and results in a painful retribution in the future; karma of feeling that is pleasant in the present and results in a painful retribution in the future; karma of feeling that is painful in the present and results in a pleasant retribution in the future; and karma of feeling that is pleasant in the present and results in a pleasant retribution in the future.
What is the karma that is painful both in its present experience and results in a painful retribution in the future?
Suppose there is a person who, enduring grief and enduring suffering, commits killing; because of that act of killing, they experience various forms of grief and suffering with their mind.

Enduring grief and enduring suffering, they likewise engage in stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and wrong view; because of those wrong views, they experience various forms of grief and suffering with their mind. At the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the miserable states, the hells. This is karma that is painful both in its present experience and results in a painful retribution in the future.
What is the karma that is pleasant in its present experience but results in a painful retribution later?

If a person, with a mind of patience, joy, and delight, commits the taking of life; and because of that act of killing—with various states of mind—patiences, rejoices, and delights, even up to the point of holding wrong views; and because of those wrong views—with various states of mind—patiences, rejoices, and delights, then at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they fall into the miserable realms of hell. This is the karma that is pleasant in its present experience but results in a painful retribution later.
What is the karma that is painful in the present but results in a pleasant retribution later?

If a person endures sorrow and endures suffering while refraining from taking life—and because of that non-killing, they endure various mental states of sorrow and suffering; if they likewise endure sorrow and suffering while refraining from stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, ill will, and by maintaining right view—and because of practicing right view, they endure various mental states of sorrow and suffering, then at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in the heavens. This is karma that is painful in the present but results in a pleasant retribution later.
What is the karma that results in happiness in the present life and a happy retribution in the future?

If a person, with patience and joy, with patience and delight, refrains from taking life, then because of that non-killing, they experience various states of joy and delight through their mind; and so it continues through patience and joy, up to right view. Because of that right view, they experience various states of patience, joy, and delight through their mind. At the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly realm. This is the karma that results in happiness in the present life and a happy retribution in the future.
This is called the "kamma that is experienced" (*vedanīya-kamma*).

Furthermore, when one takes up kamma through the teaching of "taking up kamma," and having taken it up, experiences its result—this is called past, future, and present kamma that is to be experienced.
What is meant by "condition"?
If there is misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, resulting in an undesirable, unpleasant, and disagreeable retribution—this is called a condition.
If one engages in good conduct of body, speech, and mind, one receives a retribution that is pleasant, joyful, and agreeable; this is called a "basis.

If one engages in evil conduct of body, speech, and mind, and accomplishes the practice of false views that revile the noble ones, then by reason of the causal conditions of those actions rooted in false views, at the breaking up of the body after death, one falls into the miserable states of existence, the hells; this is called a "basis."

If one practices wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and accomplishes right view that does not revile the noble ones, then by reason of the causal conditions of karma based on right view, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in a happy destination, in the heavens; this is called a "station."

If an ordinary person intentionally takes the life of their mother, intentionally takes the life of their father, intentionally takes the life of an Arhat or a Śrāvaka, intentionally causes a schism in the Saṃgha, or intentionally draws blood from the body of a Tathāgata with an evil mind—this is called a "basis."

If an ordinary person seeks outside of these teachings for some other superior being, seeks some other recipient of offerings, seeks some other śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who proclaims right view, or praises some other śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, saying, "He is all-knowing and all-seeing," this is called a ground.

If an ordinary person, outside of these teachings, or certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through a different basis, maintain that there is a real self and the world is eternal—claiming "this alone is true, all else is false," and so on, up to "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death"—and they take this different basis as the ultimate reality, this is called a "position."

If an ordinary person regards the grasping after precepts as purification and seeks auspiciousness through wrong conditions, they fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts; when they subsequently receive an eighth human existence, this is called a "station."

If there is a single wheel-turning sage king, or if a wheel-turning sage king is born in the central land, or if a wheel-turning sage king is born into a noble family—whether a great clan of Kṣatriyas, a great clan of Brahmins, or a great clan of householders; if he is handsome and possesses excellent physical marks; or if a wheel-turning sage king is born with abundant wealth and treasures such as gold, silver, conch shells, coral, mani jewels, pearls, and lapis lazuli, and with elephants, horses, carriages, servants, and granaries and treasuries filled to overflowing—this is called the "place."

If a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha appears in the world; if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is born in a central land; if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is born into a noble family, such as a great Kṣatriya clan or a great Brāhmaṇa clan; if he possesses a body that is upright, exquisite, and endowed with excellent physical marks; or if a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is born into a family of great wealth and treasure, possessing gold, silver, money, and property, jade and shells, elephants, horses, carriages, servants, and granaries filled to overflowing with grain and silk—these are called the "circumstances."
Whether a man becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King, or a man becomes a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, or a man becomes Śakra, Lord of Devas, or Māra, or Brahmā—these are called the stations.
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has said:

"Dwelling for such a time in the hells, dwelling for such a time among animals, dwelling for such a time among hungry ghosts, dwelling for such a time among humans, and dwelling for such a time in the heavens"—this is called the locus.
What is meant by cause?

If an action is caused by greed, or if an action is caused by hatred, or if an action is caused by delusion; or if an action is caused by non-greed, or if an action is caused by non-hatred, or if an action is caused by non-delusion—this is called cause.

Furthermore, form has this cause and this means; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness have this cause and this means for entering the first dhyāna concentration; they have this cause and this means for entering the second, third, and fourth dhyāna concentrations; and for abandoning unwholesome states and accomplishing wholesome states—this is called the cause.
What is meant by "retribution" (*vipāka*)?

If karma and the experience of karma receive their retribution within the five destinies—namely, hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and gods—including their form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—this is called retribution.
The Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the causes, retributions, and the bases for the undertaking of karma in the past, future, and present.

Thus, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the causes, retributions, and the bases for the undertaking of karma in the past, future, and present; he discerns them as they truly are and understands them as they truly are. Through such wisdom, knowledge, vision, comprehension, and skillful means, this is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the causes, retributions, and the bases for the undertaking of karma in the past, future, and present.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the Tathāgata is supreme, sovereign, victorious, most excellent, and unsurpassed by virtue of his power of wisdom; having accomplished such powers as a virtuous person, a great man, and a Tathāgata, he enters and emerges from meditative absorption at will, in whatever place, and in whatever manner he desires—this is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What is the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the superior and non-superior faculties of other sentient beings and other persons?
What are "other sentient beings" and "other persons"?
With the exception of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, all other sentient beings are called "other sentient beings" and "other persons."
What are the faculties (*indriya*)?
There are twenty-two faculties:

the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, male faculty, female faculty, life faculty, pleasure faculty, pain faculty, joy faculty, grief faculty, equanimity faculty, mind faculty, faith faculty, energy faculty, mindfulness faculty, concentration faculty, wisdom faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known. These are called the faculties.
What is a non-superior faculty?
If a faculty is unwholesome, it is called a non-superior faculty.
What is a superior faculty?
If a faculty is wholesome, it is called a superior faculty (*viśiṣṭendriya*).
Furthermore, regarding non-superior faculties: if a faculty is not noble (*ārya*), it is called a non-superior faculty.
Furthermore, regarding superior faculties: if a faculty is noble, it is called a superior faculty.
Furthermore, as for non-superior faculties: if a faculty is noble yet dull, it is called a non-superior faculty.
Furthermore, as for superior faculties: if a faculty is noble and sharp, it is called a superior faculty.

The Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings and persons; he knows that such-and-such a being has sharp or dull faculties, is well-honoring and well-understanding, yet fears future sinking like a diamond, and would fall back were they not to hear the Dharma.

There shall be those who know the Dharma, just as there are ponds of *utpala* flowers, ponds of *padma* flowers, ponds of *kumuda* flowers, and ponds of *puṇḍarīka* flowers, or as there are the *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers themselves.
There are utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka lotuses that have emerged from the mud but have not yet risen above the water.
There are utpala, padma, kumuda, and puṇḍarīka lotuses that have emerged from the mud and are level with the water.
There were blue lotuses, red lotuses, yellow lotuses, and white lotuses, which had emerged from the water and remained suspended in mid-air without clinging to it.

In this way, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings and other persons: that these sentient beings have sharp or dull faculties, are well-reverent and well-understanding, yet fear future sinking like a diamond; that if they do not hear the Dharma, they will immediately regress, but there shall be those who understand the Dharma.

If these sentient beings possess the necessary faculties, they may take the life of their mother, take the life of their father, take the life of an Arhat Śrāvaka, cause a schism in the Saṃgha, or with an evil mind draw blood from the body of a Tathāgata.

If these sentient beings, despite having their faculties perfected, seek some other superior being outside of this Dharma, or seek someone else to receive offerings—namely, other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who can preach right view—and they praise those other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, saying, "These are all-knowing and all-seeing."

If these sentient beings possess the faculties for accomplishment, there may be outside of this Dharma other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through different perspectives, claim that the self and the world are eternal, while all else is false; or even that nirvāṇa is neither existent nor non-existent after death, claiming this alone is true and all else is false—meaning they take their own divergent views to be the ultimate reality.

If these sentient beings possess mature faculties, yet regard the clinging to precepts as purification and seek auspiciousness through false conditions, they will fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, and subsequently receive an eighth human body.
If these sentient beings possess the matured faculties, they are born into great clans of kṣatriyas, great clans of brahmins, or great clans of householders.

If these sentient beings possess the matured faculties, they are born among the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, or the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
If these sentient beings possess the requisite faculties, they are born in the Brahmā realm, as Brahmā-purohita, Brahmā-pārṣadya, or Mahābrahmā.
If these sentient beings possess the requisite faculties, they are born in the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, or Ābhāsvara-heavenly-sound realms.
If these beings possess the perfection of faculties, they are born among the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Parīttaśubha Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven.
If these beings possess the perfection of faculties, they are born among the Bṛhatphala Heaven, the Parīttabṛhatphala Heaven, the Apramāṇabṛhatphala Heaven, and the Bṛhatphala Heaven.
If these beings have perfected their faculties, they are born in the Heaven of Non-perception.

If these beings have perfected their faculties, they are born in the Heaven of No-Superiority, the Heatless Heaven, the Clearly Visible Heaven, the Beautifully Clearly Visible Heaven, or the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

If these sentient beings have perfected their faculties, they are born in the Heaven of Infinite Space, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness, or the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.

If these sentient beings have their faculties perfected, they may dwell having transcended sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, and thus achieve the practice of the first dhyāna.

If these sentient beings have their faculties perfected, and possess the cessation of applied and sustained thought, internal clarity, faith, and one-pointedness of mind, they achieve the practice of the second dhyāna, which is characterized by concentration free from applied and sustained thought and born of joy and bliss.

If these sentient beings have their faculties perfected, they dwell detached from joy with equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body; as the noble ones describe it, "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness," they achieve the practice of the third dhyāna.

If these sentient beings have their faculties perfected, they abandon pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, they enter and abide in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

If these sentient beings have their faculties perfected, they transcend all perceptions of form, extinguish perceptions of aversion, do not attend to perceptions of diversity, and achieve the practice of the sphere of infinite space.
If these beings have perfected their faculties, they transcend the sphere of infinite space and achieve practice in the sphere of infinite consciousness.
If these beings have perfected their faculties, they transcend the sphere of infinite consciousness and achieve practice in the sphere of nothingness.
If these sentient beings have perfected their faculties, they may transcend all the sphere of nothingness and achieve the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

If these sentient beings have perfected their faculties, they may attain immeasurable and manifold supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), being able to shake the great earth, making one into many and many into one, and even attaining mastery over their bodies as far as the Brahma-heaven.

If these sentient beings possess the faculties of accomplishment, they have the purified divine ear that surpasses that of humans, by which they hear two kinds of sounds: human sounds and non-human sounds.

If these sentient beings possess the faculties of accomplishment, they possess the knowledge of the minds of other sentient beings and others; they know a mind with desire as it truly is—a mind with desire—and they know a mind without desire as it truly is—a mind without desire; and so on, up to knowing a superior mind as it truly is—a superior mind—and knowing a non-superior mind as it truly is—a non-superior mind.

If these sentient beings have perfected their faculties and possess the recollection of various past lives—recalling one birth, two births, three births, and so forth until they have perfected this practice.

If these sentient beings possess perfected faculties, they see with the pure divine eye, surpassing that of humans, the birth and death of beings—their beautiful and ugly forms, their rebirth in good or evil destinies, and their superior or inferior states—even knowing, as it truly is, the karma created by those beings.

If these sentient beings possess the faculties for the supreme and correct determination, they will attain the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship.
If these sentient beings possess accomplished faculties and power, they act through the accomplishment of power and mastery.
If these sentient beings possess accomplished faculties and do not take the life of their mother, they act even unto the accomplishment of power and mastery.

When the Tathāgata, in this manner, accurately discerns and distinguishes the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings and other persons, through the wisdom of discernment, knowledge, vision, and skillful means, this is called the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings and other persons.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the Tathāgata is preeminent through the power of wisdom, supreme through the power of mastery, the most excellent, the highest, and unsurpassed; having accomplished this power, the Tathāgata—the Great Person, the Noble One—is able, wherever he desires and in whatever manner he desires, to emerge from and enter meditative absorption at will. This is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What is the Tathāgata’s power of knowing the various inclinations of other sentient beings and other persons?
What are "other sentient beings" and "other persons"?
With the exception of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, all other sentient beings are called "other sentient beings" and "other persons."
What is liberation?
If the mind inclines toward that, reaches that, honors that, and is liberated by that, this is called liberation.
The Tathāgata, regarding other sentient beings and other persons, knows their various liberations as they truly are, [knowing]: "This sentient being possesses liberation."

There are those who understand inferior things and those who understand superior things; among sentient beings, there are those who understand evil, those who understand good, those who understand birth and death, and those who understand nirvāṇa.
Among sentient beings, there are those who understand forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (dharmas);
among sentient beings, there are those who understand the great clans of the kṣatriyas, the great clans of the brāhmaṇas, and the great households of the householders.

There are sentient beings who understand the Four Great Heavenly Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven;
there are sentient beings who understand the Brahmā Heaven, the Brahmapurohita Heaven, the Brahmapārṣadya Heaven, and the Mahābrahmā Heaven;
and there are sentient beings who understand the Ābhāsvara Heaven and the Parīttābha Heaven.
There are the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Heaven of Immeasurable Light, and the Heaven of Radiant Sound;
there are sentient beings who understand the Heaven of Purity, the Heaven of Limited Purity, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, and the Heaven of Universal Purity;

there are sentient beings who understand the Heaven of Reality, the Heaven of Limited Reality, the Heaven of Immeasurable Reality, and the Heaven of Fruition; and there are sentient beings who understand the Heaven of Non-conception.

There are sentient beings who understand the Heaven of No Strife (Abṛha), the Heaven of No Heat (Atapa), the Heaven of Good Vision (Sudṛśa), the Heaven of Excellent Vision (Sudarśana), and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven;

there are sentient beings who understand the Heaven of Infinite Space (Ākāśānantyāyatana), the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness (Vijñānānantyāyatana), the Heaven of Nothingness (Ākiṃcanyāyatana), and the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana); and there are sentient beings who understand entering the first dhyāna and the second.

In the third and fourth dhyānas, there are sentient beings who understand and enter the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the concentration of the sphere of nothingness,
and the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; there are sentient beings who understand and realize the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power,

those who understand and realize the supernormal power of the divine ear, those who understand and realize the supernormal power of discerning the minds of others, and those who understand and realize the supernormal power of recollection.
The knowledge and realization of past lives; the knowledge and realization of the births and deaths of sentient beings who possess understanding;

the knowledge that there are sentient beings who, through understanding, attain the supreme and correct determination and realize the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and the fruit of arhatship;

the knowledge that there are sentient beings who, through understanding, attain power, honor, and sovereignty; and the knowledge that if sentient beings can understand and see, they will abandon [the defilements].
There are those who take the life of their mother; there are those who take the life of their father; there are those who take the life of an Arhat Śrāvaka;
there are those who cause a schism in the Saṃgha; there are those who, with an evil mind, draw blood from the body of a Tathāgata.
If sentient beings understand that apart from these dharmas, they seek another who is more venerable, superior, or worthy of receiving offerings; or if they praise other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas...
The Gate is able to explain right view and praise other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas as being omniscient and all-seeing;

it holds that if there were any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas outside of this Dharma who, through different conditions, truly maintain that the self and the world are eternal— claiming "this alone is true and all else is false," up to "neither does the Tathāgata exist after death nor does he not exist after death in nirvāṇa"— then [the former] would be real and the others false.

If sentient beings understand that there are those who, through the theft of precepts as a means of purification and seeking auspiciousness through false conditions, fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, and receive an eighth human birth;
if sentient beings understand that there are those born into great clans of the Kṣatriyas, great clans of the Brāhmaṇas, or great families of householders;

and if sentient beings understand that there are those born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
If sentient beings understand that there is birth in the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika, and Mahābrahmā heavens;
if sentient beings understand that there is birth in the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, and Ābhāsvara-heaven-of-radiance heavens;
if sentient beings understand that there is birth in the Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna heavens;
