If sentient beings understand that there are the Heaven of Actual Birth, the Heaven of Limited Actualities, the Heaven of Immeasurable Actualities, and the Heaven of Actual Fruits;
if sentient beings understand that there is the Heaven of Non-perception;
and if sentient beings understand that there are the Heaven of No Superiority, the Heatless Heaven, the Heaven of Good Vision, the Heaven of Excellent Vision, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

If sentient beings understand that there exist the heavens of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;

if sentient beings understand that there exists the practice of attaining the first dhyāna, which is characterized by the separation from desires, evil, and unwholesome states, and consists of applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and the joy and bliss born of seclusion; if sentient beings understand that there exists the practice of attaining the second dhyāna, which is characterized by the cessation of applied and sustained thought, internal tranquility, confidence, and one-pointedness of mind, consisting of the joy and bliss born of concentration, free from applied and sustained thought; if sentient beings understand that there exists the practice of attaining the third dhyāna, which is characterized by the fading away of joy, dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing bliss with the body as the noble ones describe it, saying "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and happy"; and if sentient beings understand that there exists the practice of attaining the fourth dhyāna, which is characterized by the abandoning of both pleasure and pain, and the prior disappearance of grief and joy, consisting of neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and the purity of equanimity and mindfulness;

If sentient beings understand that there are those who, having abandoned all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), extinguished perceptions of aversion (*pratigha-saṃjñā*), and ceased attending to perceptions of diversity (*nānātva-saṃjñā*), achieve the practice of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); or those who, having abandoned the sphere of infinite space, achieve the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); or those who, having abandoned the sphere of infinite consciousness, achieve the practice of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); or those who, having abandoned the sphere of nothingness, achieve the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

If sentient beings understand that there are those who attain various supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*) capable of shaking the great earth, making one into many and many into one, and even attaining mastery over their bodies as far as the Brahma-heaven;
and if sentient beings understand that there are those with the purified divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) that transcends that of humans, hearing two kinds of sounds:
The sounds of humans and non-humans;

if sentient beings understand that there are other sentient beings and others know the minds of other sentient beings—knowing as it truly is a mind with desire as a mind with desire, and knowing as it truly is a mind without desire as a mind without desire, up to knowing as it truly is a superior mind as a superior mind and a mind without superiority as a mind without superiority;
and if sentient beings understand the recollection of various past lives, recollecting one life, two lives, three lives, and so forth, up to the full accomplishment of such practice.

If sentient beings understand that there is a pure divine eye surpassing that of humans, by which they see the birth and death of sentient beings—whether their appearance is beautiful or ugly, whether they are in good or evil realms, or whether they are lowly or superior—and even know sentient beings according to the karma they have created;

if sentient beings understand that there is the supreme, right determination through which one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmin*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*);
and if sentient beings understand that there is power, honor, and sovereignty; [then they shall attain this samādhi].
If sentient beings understand that there is no such thing as severing a mother’s life;
if sentient beings understand that there is nothing up to and including power, supremacy, or sovereignty [to cause such harm];

in this way, the Tathāgata, regarding the various understandings of other sentient beings and other persons, discerns and distinguishes them according to reality through the wisdom of discernment, knowledge, vision, understanding, and skillful means—this is called the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge of the various understandings of other sentient beings and other persons.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the Tathāgata is supreme by the power of wisdom, possessing sovereign power, superior power, the most excellent, the highest, and unsurpassed; having accomplished this power, the Tathāgata—the virtuous one, the great person—enters and emerges from meditative absorption at any desired place, in any desired manner, and for as long as desired. This is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What are the various realms (*nānā-dhātu*), the immeasurable realms (*apramāṇa-dhātu*), and the Tathāgata’s power of worldly knowledge?
What are the various realms?

They are the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*), the realm of the formless (*arūpa-dhātu*), and so on up to the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*), as explained in the *Dhātu-varga*; these are called the immeasurable realms.
What is the world?
There are two kinds of worlds:
the world of sentient beings and the world of formations.
What is the world of sentient beings?
"Sentient beings" refers to those born within the five destinies:
hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; this is called the world of sentient beings.
What is meant by "wandering in the world"?
"Wandering" refers to the five aggregates of clinging:
the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; these are called wandering in the world.
The Tathāgata knows these various immeasurable realms and worlds as they truly are.

Thus, regarding these various and immeasurable realms and worlds, the Tathāgata selects and discerns them through wisdom that perceives conditions, and through the skillful means of insight and vision; this is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding various and immeasurable realms and worlds.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

Regarding this matter, the Tathāgata’s knowledge is supreme by virtue of power, sovereign power, superior power, most excellent power, and unsurpassed power; it is beyond reproach. The Tathāgata, a virtuous person and a Great Man, has accomplished this power such that, in whatever place he desires, according to his wish and to the full extent of his desire, he enters and emerges from meditative concentration. This is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What is called the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge that reaches all paths?
What is meant by "reaching all paths"?

There is not a single sentient being, a single dharma, a single knowledge, or a single path that can reach all paths; only the fruition-dharma (*vipākadharma*) of the Tathāgata is designated as reaching all paths.
The Tathāgata knows, as it truly is, all paths leading to every destination: that by practicing such a path one may be led to a short life or a long life;
that by practicing such a path one may be led to much illness or little illness;
and that by practicing such a path one may be led to a lowly or a noble status.
If one accomplishes this path of practice, it can lead to the ugly or the beautiful;
if one accomplishes this path of practice, it can lead to the lowly or the noble;
if one accomplishes this path of practice, it can lead to little majesty and power or great majesty and power.
If one accomplishes this practice of the path, it leads one to the state of being without wisdom or with wisdom;
if one accomplishes this practice of the path, it can lead one to the great clans of the Kṣatriyas, the great clans of the Brāhmaṇas, or the great households of the Gṛhapatis;

if one accomplishes this practice of the path, it leads one to the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.
By practicing this path extensively, one is led to the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Brahmakāyika, and Mahābrahmā heavens;
by practicing this path extensively, one is led to the Ābhāsvara, Parīttābhā, Apramāṇābhā, and Ābhāsvara heavens;
by practicing this path extensively, one is led to the Śubhakṛtsna, Parīttaśubha, Apramāṇaśubha, and Śubhakṛtsna heavens.
By practicing this path extensively, one is led to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven, and the Puṇyaprasava Heaven;
by practicing this path extensively, one is led to the Āsaṃjñika Heaven;
by practicing this path extensively, one is led to the Avṛha Heaven, the Atapa Heaven, the Sudarśana Heaven, the Sudṛśa Heaven, and the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

By practicing this path extensively, one is led to the heavens of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
by practicing this path extensively, one is able to enter the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna;

by practicing this path extensively, one is able to enter the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

By practicing this path extensively, one attains the realization-knowledge of the supernormal powers (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), the realization-knowledge of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-jñāna*), the realization-knowledge of the discernment of minds (*cetaḥparyāya-jñāna*), the realization-knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), and the realization-knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna*). One understands: "This path is painful and slow to resolve," "this path is painful and quick to resolve," "this path is pleasant and slow to resolve," and "this path is pleasant and quick to resolve.

By practicing this path extensively, one is able to ascend to right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*).
By practicing the path extensively, one attains sovereignty through power and mastery.

If sentient beings commit such acts as taking the life of their mother, taking the life of their father, taking the life of an Arhat Śrāvaka, causing a schism in the Saṅgha, or with an evil mind drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata;

or if sentient beings seek other objects of veneration superior to these dharmas, seek other forms of offerings, seek other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas capable of preaching right view, or praise other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, saying they are omniscient and all-seeing; or if they commit such acts as seeking outside these dharmas for other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who maintain different views, such as that there is a real self or that the world is eternal, claiming "this alone is true and all else is false"—[these constitute offenses].

"The world is finite," "this alone is true and all else is false," and so on, up to "the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death in nirvāṇa"—"this alone is true and all else is false," they say, regarding their own particular views as the ultimate reality.

If sentient beings practice with the theft of precepts as their purification and seek auspiciousness through false conditions, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, and receive an eighth human existence.
If sentient beings practice [the path], they may be born into great kṣatriya families, great brāhmaṇa families, or great householder families;

if sentient beings practice, they may be born among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, the Yāma heaven, the Tuṣita heaven, the Nirmāṇarati heaven, or the Paranirmitavaśavartin heaven;

if sentient beings practice, they may be born in the Brahmā heavens—namely, the Brahmakāyika, Brahmapurohita, Mahābrahmā, and Ābhāsvara heavens—or in the Parīttābha, Apramāṇābha, and Ābhāsvara heavens.
If sentient beings practice, they are born in the Heaven of Pure Abode, the Heaven of Limited Purity, the Heaven of Immeasurable Purity, or the Heaven of Universal Purity;
or if sentient beings practice, they are born in the Heaven of Real Existence, the Heaven of Limited Reality, the Heaven of Immeasurable Reality, or the Heaven of Ultimate Fruit;

or they are born in the Heaven of Non-perception. Furthermore, if these sentient beings practice, they are born in the Heaven of No Superiority, the Heatless Heaven, the Heaven of Good Vision, the Heaven of Excellent Vision, or the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
If sentient beings practice so as to be born in the Heaven of Infinite Space, the Heaven of Infinite Consciousness, the Heaven of Nothingness, or the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception;

or if they practice so as to achieve the first dhyāna, which is free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, accompanied by directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and characterized by the joy and happiness born of seclusion; or if they practice so as to achieve the second dhyāna, which is the cessation of directed and sustained thought, characterized by internal clarity, single-mindedness, and the joy and happiness born of concentration; or if they practice so as to achieve the third dhyāna, which is free from joy and characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing physical happiness such that the noble ones describe it as "dwelling in happiness through mindfulness and equanimity"; or if they practice so as to achieve the fourth dhyāna, which is the abandonment of both suffering and pleasure, the prior extinction of sorrow and joy, and is characterized by neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, purity of equanimity, and mindfulness.

If sentient beings practice by being free from all perceptions of form, by extinguishing perceptions of aversion, and by not attending to perceptions of diversity, they achieve the sphere of infinite space. Some, being free from the entire sphere of infinite space, achieve the sphere of infinite consciousness. Some, being free from the entire sphere of infinite consciousness, achieve the sphere of nothingness. If sentient beings practice by being free from the entire sphere of nothingness, they achieve the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

If sentient beings practice with receptivity, they may attain immeasurable and manifold supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) capable of shaking the great earth; they can make one into many and many into one, and even attain mastery over their bodies as far as the Brahma-heaven.
They possess the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*), purified and surpassing that of humans, by which they hear two kinds of sounds:
those of humans and those of non-humans.

There is the knowledge of the minds of other sentient beings and others: one knows a mind with desire as it truly is as a mind with desire; one knows a mind without desire as it truly is as a mind without desire; and so on, up to knowing a superior mind as it truly is as a superior mind, and knowing an inferior mind as it truly is as an inferior mind.
Furthermore, one recollects various immeasurable past lives—whether one birth, two births, three births, or even until the accomplishment of the practice of the Dharma.

Moreover, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, one observes the birth and death of sentient beings—their beautiful and ugly forms, their wholesome and unwholesome desires, their lowly and exalted states—and even knows sentient beings according to the karma they have created.

If sentient beings practice, they may attain the supreme certainty of rightness and realize the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, or the fruit of arhatship.
If sentient beings act, they may obtain power, supremacy, and mastery;
yet if sentient beings act, there is no case where they do not sever their mother’s life, nor is there any who obtains power, supremacy, and mastery [without such consequences].

Thus, the Tathāgata’s path that reaches all places is a discernment and differentiation according to reality; through the skillful means of wisdom, knowledge, vision, and insight, this is called the Tathāgata-power of the knowledge of the path that reaches all places.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the Tathāgata is preeminent through the power of wisdom, possessing sovereign power, superior power, the most excellent, the supreme, and the unsurpassed; having accomplished this power, he is a virtuous person, a great man, and a Tathāgata. Wherever he desires, in whatever manner he desires, and to whatever extent he desires, he emerges from and enters meditative absorption at will. This is called the power of the Tathāgata.

What is called the Tathāgata’s power of knowledge regarding the defilement, purification, and emergence from the meditative absorptions (dhyāna), liberations (vimokṣa), concentrations (samādhi), and attainments (samāpatti)? What are the meditative absorptions? They are as follows:

when a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra), attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss; when, with the subsiding of directed and sustained thought, through internal tranquility and one-pointedness of mind, he attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from directed and sustained thought and born of concentration, characterized by joy and bliss; when, through detachment from joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly conscious, experiencing bliss with the body, attaining and dwelling in the third dhyāna, of which the noble ones declare: "He dwells in bliss who has equanimity and mindfulness"; and when, having abandoned both pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of elation and dejection, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness—these are called the meditative absorptions.
What are the liberations?
Contemplating forms while possessing form is the first liberation;
not perceiving forms internally while contemplating forms externally is the second liberation.
The pure liberation is the third liberation;

being free from all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory reaction, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one achieves the practice of the sphere of infinite space—this is the fourth liberation;
being free from the entire sphere of infinite space, one achieves the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness—this is the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one achieves the practice of the sphere of nothingness; this is the sixth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one achieves the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is the seventh liberation.
Transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one achieves the cessation of feeling and perception; this is the eighth liberation.
This is called liberation.
What is concentration?

Concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought, concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought, the concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, and the concentration of wishlessness—these are called concentration.
What is entry into meditative concentration (*samāpatti*)?

It refers to entering the concentration of perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*), the concentration of non-perception (*asaṃjñā-samāpatti*), the concentration that follows perception and the concentration that does not follow perception, the concentration not shared with form (*arūpa-samāpatti*) and the concentration shared with form (*rūpa-samāpatti*), the unsurpassed concentration (*anuttara-samāpatti*), and the universal bases of mastery (*kṛtsnāyatana-samāpatti*). This is called entry into meditative concentration.
What is defilement?

It refers to the defilement of desire, the defilement of hatred, the defilement of delusion, the defilement of afflictions, and the defilement of hindrances, coverings, fetters, and unwholesome conduct; as well as other defiled phenomena, such as the defilements of dhyāna, liberation, concentration, and meditative absorption—namely, impurity, non-arising, lack of clarity, lack of excellence, polluting karma, and the absence of radiance. These are called defilements.
What is purity?

It is the exhaustion of desire, the exhaustion of hatred, the exhaustion of delusion, the exhaustion of afflictions, and the exhaustion of hindrances, coverings, fetters, and unwholesome conduct, as well as the exhaustion of all other defiled dharmas. Furthermore, when there is the stainless purity of meditative absorption, liberation, concentration, and entry into meditative states, giving rise to pure, sublime, and undefiled karma that possesses radiance—this is called purity.

What is "arising"? It is as when one arises from the first dhyāna with a mind that enters the second dhyāna; as when one arises from the first dhyāna with a mind that enters the third dhyāna; as when one arises from the first dhyāna with a mind that enters the fourth dhyāna; as when one arises from the second dhyāna with a mind that enters the third dhyāna; as when one arises from the second dhyāna with a mind that enters the fourth dhyāna; and as when one arises from the third dhyāna with a mind that enters the fourth dhyāna. This is called arising.
Furthermore, if purity is itself arising, and if arising is itself purity, this is called "the arising of purity.
That Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, the defilement and purity of the arising [of states] when entering into meditative absorption, liberation, and concentration.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s discernment, differentiation, and analytical investigation regarding the arising of impurities and purity within the meditative absorptions, liberations, and concentrations—his wisdom, knowledge, vision, and skillful application in directing them—is called the Tathāgata-power of the knowledge of the arising of impurities and purity within the meditative absorptions, liberations, and concentrations.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

It is the power of knowledge regarding this matter that is venerable, sovereign, superior, most excellent, supreme, and unsurpassed; it is a power achieved by the Tathāgata, a virtuous and great person. In whatever place he desires, and in whatever manner he desires, he enters and emerges from meditative concentration as he wishes; this is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What is the Tathāgata’s power of the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives? The Tathāgata recollects his own and others’ various past lives;

he recollects one birth, two births, three, four, five, ten, twenty, thirty, forty, fifty, a hundred births, a thousand births, a hundred thousand births, immeasurable hundreds of births, immeasurable thousands of births, an eon of formation, an eon of destruction, or an eon of both formation and destruction; he recollects immeasurable eons of formation, immeasurable eons of destruction, or immeasurable eons of both formation and destruction, thinking: "I was formerly there, with such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food and drink, such a lifespan, such a duration of life, and such experiences of suffering and pleasure; passing away from there, I was born there; passing away from there, I was born here."

Having accomplished the practice of recollecting various past lives, it is like a person who goes from his own village to another village, where he may walk, stand, sit, speak, or remain silent; then from that village he goes to yet another village, where he may walk, stand, sit, speak, or remain silent; and from that village he goes to yet another village, where he may walk, stand, sit, speak, or remain silent.

At a later time, this person returns to his own village; he recalls everything regarding the previous villages without any difficulty, thinking: "I went from my own village to another village; while in that village, I walked thus, stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus. From that village I went to yet another village; while in that village, I walked thus, stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus. From that village I went again to yet another village; there I walked thus, stood thus, sat thus, spoke thus, and remained silent thus. Now I have returned to my own village."

In this way, the Tathāgata recollects his own and others' immeasurable and manifold past lives—recollecting one birth, two births, three births, and so on, up until the accomplishment of his current conduct.

Thus, the Tathāgata’s realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives consists of selecting and discerning according to reality, through the skillful means of wisdom, insight, and vision; this is called the Tathāgata’s power of the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the Tathāgata is preeminent through the power of wisdom, possessing sovereign power, superior power, the most excellent, the highest, and unsurpassed power. O noble ones, O great beings, it is by the accomplishment of this power of the Tathāgata that he enters and emerges from meditative absorption at whatever place, in whatever manner, and to whatever extent he desires. This is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What is the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge and realization of the birth and death of sentient beings?

With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the Tathāgata sees sentient beings’ births and deaths—their beautiful and ugly forms, their good and evil destinies, and their lowly or exalted states—and he knows sentient beings according to the karma they have created. He knows those sentient beings who engage in misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, and misconduct of mind, who hold wrong views and revile the noble ones; because of the karma resulting from such wrong views, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the evil destinies of hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.

These sentient beings, having practiced wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind, and having accomplished right view that does not revile the noble ones, through the karma conditioned by right view, at the breaking up of the body after death, are reborn in a good destination, among the devas or among humans.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—of beautiful or ugly appearance, in good or bad destinations, low or exalted—and he knows beings according to their karma.

Suppose there were a high tower within a village or city, and a person with clear vision stood upon it; they would see sentient beings from the east coming and going, moving about, and circulating toward the west; they would see sentient beings from the west coming and going, moving about, and circulating toward the east; they would see sentient beings from the south coming and going, moving about, and circulating toward the north; they would see sentient beings from the north coming and going, moving about, and circulating toward the south; and they would see the people at the base of the tower themselves entering and exiting, coming and going, and moving about.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s divine eye is purified and surpasses that of humans; he sees sentient beings passing through birth and death—whether they possess beautiful or ugly forms, whether they are in good or evil destinies, or whether they are lowly or exalted—and even knows sentient beings according to the karma they have created.

In this way, the Tathāgata’s realization of the wisdom regarding the birth and death of sentient beings involves selecting and discerning according to reality, and employing the skillful means of insight, knowledge, vision, and penetration; this is called the Tathāgata’s power of the realization of wisdom regarding the birth and death of sentient beings.
What is meant by the powers of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, the Tathāgata is the venerable one, the one possessing the power of wisdom, the one of sovereign power, the one of superior power, the most excellent, the supreme, the unsurpassed, the great man, and the noble being.

When the Tathāgata has accomplished this power, he enters and emerges from meditative absorption at any desired place, in any desired manner, and for as long as he desires; this is called the power of the Tathāgata.
What is meant by the power of the Tathāgata consisting of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*)?
What are the outflows (*āsrava*)?
There are seven outflows:

the outflow to be abandoned by vision, the outflow to be abandoned by patience, the outflow to be abandoned by association, the outflow to be abandoned by dissociation, the outflow to be abandoned by subduing, the outflow to be abandoned by precepts, and the outflow to be abandoned by cultivation; these are called outflows.
What is the exhaustion of the outflows?

When there is the exhaustion of the outflows, the exhaustion of conditions, the subduing of conditions, the subduing and departing from them, right departure, relinquishment, vomiting up, cutting off, and emergence—this is called the exhaustion of the outflows.

In this way, the Tathāgata knows his own body and the bodies of others who have exhausted their outflows as they truly are. It is like a spring of water that is pure and not turbid; if there are within it sand, stones, shells, clams, turtles, fish, or tortoises moving about, a person with clear vision standing by the side of the spring sees them all with perfect clarity.

If sand, gravel, snails, clams, soft-shelled turtles, tortoises, fish, and turtles move about within it, that person sees those sands, gravels, snails, clams, soft-shelled turtles, tortoises, fish, and turtles moving about therein.
In this way, the Tathāgata knows, as they truly are, both his own and others' exhaustion of the outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).

This Tathāgata’s knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows—his discernment and analysis according to reality, his wisdom, knowledge, vision, and skillful means—is called the Tathāgata’s power of the knowledge of the exhaustion of the outflows.
What is called the power of the Tathāgata?

In this regard, it is that which is supreme by the power of wisdom, sovereign power, superior power, most excellent, highest, and unsurpassed; it is the power achieved by the Tathāgata—the virtuous one, the great person—by which he enters and emerges from meditative absorption at his will, in the place of his choosing, and to the full extent of his desire. This is called the power of the Tathāgata.
These are the ten powers of the Tathāgata.
What are the twelve natures of knowledge?
As the Blessed One has said:
"O bhikṣus! I shall speak of the twelve modes of knowledge.
Listen closely, listen closely; attend well and reflect well upon it, for I shall speak."
The bhikṣu said: "So it is.
All you bhikṣus, listen with a sincere mind."
The Blessed One spoke thus:
"What are the twelve knowledges? Monks!"
"This is the Noble Truth of Suffering; regarding this Dharma previously unheard, knowledge arose, vision arose, awakening arose, clarity arose, skill arose, wisdom arose, and understanding arose.

Monks, you should know: regarding this Noble Truth of Suffering, regarding this Dharma previously unheard, knowledge arose, vision arose, awakening arose, clarity arose, skill arose, wisdom arose, and understanding arose."

"Monks! Having known this Noble Truth of Suffering, for me—regarding dharmas unheard before—there arose knowledge, there arose vision, there arose awakening, there arose clarity, there arose skill, there arose wisdom, and there arose understanding."

“Monks! Regarding this noble truth of the origin [of suffering], through the Dharma not heard before, there arose in me knowledge, there arose vision, there arose awakening, there arose clarity, there arose skill, there arose wisdom, and there arose understanding.

Monks, you should know: ‘This noble truth of the origin must be abandoned’; regarding this Dharma not heard before, there arose in me knowledge, there arose vision, there arose awakening, there arose clarity, there arose skill, there arose wisdom, and there arose understanding.”

“Monks! Having abandoned this Noble Truth of the Origin of Suffering, for me—who had not heard this Dharma before—there arose knowledge, there arose vision, there arose awakening, there arose clarity, there arose skill, there arose wisdom, and there arose understanding.”

"Monks! Regarding this noble truth of the cessation [of suffering], through the Dharma unheard before, knowledge arose in me, vision arose, awakening arose, light arose, skill arose, wisdom arose, and understanding arose. Monks!"

When this noble truth of cessation was realized, for me—having not heard it before—there arose knowledge, there arose vision, there arose awakening, there arose clarity, there arose skill, there arose wisdom, and there arose understanding. Monks!
"Monks, having realized this noble truth of cessation, there arose in me— regarding the Dharma unheard before— knowledge, vision, awakening, clarity, skill, wisdom, and understanding."

"Regarding this noble truth of the path, O bhikṣus, through the Dharma previously unheard by me, there arose knowledge, there arose vision, there arose awakening, there arose clarity, there arose skill, there arose wisdom, and there arose understanding."

"Monks! When this Noble Truth of the Path is cultivated, for one who has not heard the Dharma before, there arises knowledge, there arises vision, there arises awakening, there arises clarity, there arises skill, there arises wisdom, and there arises understanding."
"Monks! Having cultivated this Noble Truth of the Path, in me—previously unheard of—arose knowledge, arose vision, arose awakening, arose clarity, arose skill, arose wisdom, and arose understanding."

"These Four Noble Truths consist of three aspects and twelve modes; if I had not known them as they truly are, I would not have attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, nor would I have declared that I had attained it."

"Monks! Because I have known these Four Noble Truths in their three aspects and twelve modes as they truly are, I have now attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; thus I declare that I have attained it."
These are called the twelve natures of knowledge.
What are the forty-four natures of knowledge?
As the Blessed One said:
"Monks! I shall speak of the forty-four modes of knowledge.
Listen closely, listen closely, and attend well and reflect thoroughly; I shall speak."
The bhikṣu said: "So it is,
World-Honored One!"
"Listen with a focused mind, O bhikṣus.
Thus has the Blessed One spoken:
What are the forty-four knowledges?"
In this way, bhikṣu!

One knows old age and death, one knows the origin of old age and death, one knows the cessation of old age and death, and one knows the path leading to the cessation of old age and death; likewise for birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness; and one knows formations, one knows the origin of formations, one knows the cessation of formations, and one knows the path leading to the cessation of formations.
How does a bhikṣu know old age and death?
What is old age?

It refers to the decline and exhaustion of all sentient beings among the various classes of beings, their trembling, their wrinkled faces, the maturation of their faculties, and the shortening of their life-span and course; this is called old age.
What is death?

It refers to the passing away, the cessation, the exhaustion, the dissolution, and the relinquishing of the aggregates by sentient beings; it is the transformation of these things and their departure from the world—this is called death.
"Monks! Thus one understands old age and death.
How does a monk understand the arising of old age and death?"
Just as a bhikṣu knows the origin of old age and death through the origin of birth, so does a bhikṣu know the origin of old age and death.
How does a bhikṣu know the cessation of old age and death?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the cessation of old age and death through the cessation of birth, so does a bhikṣu know the cessation of old age and death.
How does a bhikṣu know the path leading to the cessation of old age and death?
It is when a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is:

right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. In this way, a bhikṣu knows the path leading to the cessation of old age and death.

If a bhikṣu knows old age and death, knows the origin of old age and death, knows the cessation of old age and death, and knows the path leading to the cessation of old age and death, this is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).
The bhikṣu possesses clear and constant understanding through present-knowledge, and by means of this, he draws analogies for the past and the future.

Just as those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past who had already known old age and death, already known the origin of old age and death, already known the cessation of old age and death, and already known the path leading to the cessation of old age and death—all that they knew, I have known myself;

and just as those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the future will know old age and death as suffering, will know the origin of old age and death, will know the cessation of old age and death, and will know the path leading to the cessation of old age and death—all that they shall know, I have known myself.
This is inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). Bhikṣus!

If two knowledges are clear and distinct—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and inferential knowledge—then it is said that the bhikṣu is endowed with vision and understanding; he has attained endurance, attained the supreme Dharma, and attained fearlessness. He is directed toward this Dharma, knows the taming of this Dharma, and sees the taming of this Dharma. Having learned the training and mastered the flow toward the Dharma, he will certainly be able to abide permanently in the holy life of purity, attaining mastery in the penetration of the gate of the Deathless (*amṛta*).
How does a bhikṣu know and understand birth, becoming, grasping, craving, feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness?
What are the volitional formations (saṃskāra)?
The three formations:
bodily formation, verbal formation, and mental formation—these are called formations; in this way, a bhikṣu knows formations.
How does a bhikṣu know the arising of formations?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the origin of formations through the origin of ignorance, so does a bhikṣu know the origin of formations.
How does a bhikṣu know the cessation of formations?
Just as a bhikṣu knows the cessation of formations through the cessation of ignorance, so does a bhikṣu know the cessation of formations.
How does a bhikṣu know the path leading to the cessation of suffering?
It is when a bhikṣu knows the Noble Eightfold Path as it truly is:

right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. In this way, a bhikṣu knows the path leading to the cessation of suffering.

"Monks! Thus one knows formations, knows the arising of formations, knows the cessation of formations, and knows the path leading to the cessation of formations; this is called the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna). Monks!"
With clear and constant understanding through present-knowledge, one draws analogies based on the past and the future.

Just as those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the past already knew suffering, already knew the origin of suffering, already knew the cessation of suffering, and already knew the path leading to the cessation of suffering—all that they knew, I too know;

and just as those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas of the future will know suffering, will know the origin of suffering, will know the cessation of suffering, and will know the path leading to the cessation of suffering—all that they will know, I too know.
This is called inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*). Bhikṣu!

If these two knowledges are clear and lucid—namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and inferential knowledge—then this bhikṣu is said to be complete in vision and understanding. He has attained endurance, attained the supreme Dharma, and attained fearlessness. He is directed toward this Dharma for self-mastery; he knows this mastery and sees this mastery of the Dharma. Having mastered the training and perfected the course of practice, he will certainly abide permanently in the Dharma of pure and holy conduct, attaining mastery in the penetration of the gate of the Deathless (*amṛta*).
This is called the nature of the forty-four knowledges.
What is the nature of the seventy-seven knowledges?
As the Blessed One said:
"Monks! I shall speak of the seventy-seven modes of knowledge.
Listen closely, listen closely; attend well and reflect well upon what I shall say."
The bhikṣu said: "So it is,
World-Honored One!"
"Listen with a focused mind, O bhikṣus.
Thus has the Blessed One spoken:
What are the seventy-seven knowledges?"

The knowledge that volitional formations have ignorance as their condition, and the knowledge that in the absence of ignorance there are no volitional formations; just as there is knowledge that volitional formations have ignorance as their condition and that in the absence of ignorance there are no volitional formations in the past, so too there is knowledge that volitional formations have ignorance as their condition and that in the absence of ignorance there are no volitional formations in the future. Whatever is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), that too is a phenomenon subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to dispassion, and subject to cessation. Likewise, the knowledge that aging and death have birth as their condition, and the knowledge that in the absence of birth there is no aging and death; just as there is knowledge that aging and death have birth as their condition and that in the absence of birth there is no aging and death in the past, so too there is knowledge that aging and death have birth as their condition and that in the absence of birth there is no aging and death in the future. Whatever is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena regarding those, that too is a phenomenon subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to dispassion, and subject to cessation.
This concludes the Chapter on the Nature of the Seventy-Seven Knowledges.
*Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle Eleven. *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle Twelve.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Dharmagupta and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty. Chapter Five:
The Section on Conditions (Pratyaya-varga), Part Two: Non-Questioning. The Section on Conditions, Fifth: Skillful Application of Conditions and Skillful Understanding of Conditions.

There is noble patience (*āryakṣānti*) that takes conditions as its object and functions as a skillful means, yet is not knowledge (*jñāna*); there is noble knowledge that takes conditions as its object and functions as a skillful means, yet is not patience; and there is the reception of questions and answers regarding conditions as skillful means, based on co-arising phenomena (*sahajātadharma*), such that: "if this exists, that exists; if this cause is absent, that is absent; if this arises, that arises; if this ceases, that ceases."

If there is ignorance as a condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to birth as a condition for aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair, then this mass of suffering is brought to completion; thus, there is the fullness of pure suffering.
With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, up to the cessation of birth, whereby the mass of aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair ceases.
In this way, the cessation of this mass of suffering is the accomplishment of the skillful means of dependent origination.
If one harbors doubt regarding past conditions, thinking:
"Did I exist in the past? Or did I not exist in the past?"
What is the nature of past existence, and what is the cause of past existence?
If one harbors doubt regarding the future, thinking:
"Do I exist in the future? and so on, up to: "What is the cause of existence in the future?"
If, due to those causes and conditions, one harbors doubt and uncertainty:
"How do I exist? How do I not exist? By what cause do I exist?
From what place of birth do I arise?"
From where do these sentient beings come, and to where do they go?
If one harbors doubt regarding the Buddha, wondering:
"Is this the World-Honored Buddha, or is he not the Buddha?"
Does the Blessed One teach the Dharma well? Does the Blessed One not teach the Dharma well?
Does the community of the Blessed One’s disciples fare well? Does the community of the Blessed One’s disciples not fare well?
Is it a practice of permanence or a practice of impermanence?
Is it a practice of suffering or a practice that is not suffering?
Is it my dharma or not my dharma?
Is it the nirvana of tranquility or the nirvana that is not tranquil?
Is there giving or no giving?
Is there generosity or no generosity?
Is there sacrifice, or is there no sacrifice?
Are there the fruits and retributions of wholesome and unwholesome karma, or are there no fruits and retributions of wholesome and unwholesome karma?
Is there this present world, or is there no present world?
Is there a future life, or is there no future life?
Are there parents, or are there no parents?
Is there a heavenly realm, or is there no heavenly realm?
Are there beings born by transformation, or are there no beings born by transformation?

Are there śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who have correctly set out and correctly attained, and who, having realized for themselves both this world and the world beyond, proclaim it; or are there no such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who have correctly set out and correctly attained, and who, having realized for themselves both this world and the world beyond, proclaim it?
If one harbors doubt regarding the Dharma and the mind lacks certainty, being hesitant, dual-minded, and uncertain, with immeasurable doubts that are not exhausted, there is no liberation;
at such a time, it does not exist.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through some other basis, maintain that "the self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false," up to and including [the views] that the Tathāgata exists after death or does not exist after death—such views did not exist at that time either.
How much more so for one who has accomplished the skillful means of the Noble Conditions—such a person will ultimately never have these defilements of affliction.
What are these conditions?
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
I shall now explain conditions and dependently arisen phenomena.
What are conditions?
Ignorance is the condition for volitional formations.
Whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, the Dharma abides in the Dharma-realm.

Having perfectly awakened to and perfectly understood that Dharma-realm, the Tathāgata expounds, reveals, analyzes, and elucidates it, teaching: "Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations," and so on, up to "conditioned by birth are aging and death."

If this dharma is such that it is just so and not otherwise, not different and not a different thing, being a constant dharma, a real dharma, a dharma-abiding, and a dharma-fixed—conditioned by such as this, it is called a condition (*pratyaya*).
What are dependently arisen phenomena?
Old age and death are impermanent; they are conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to dispassion, and subject to cessation.

Even down to ignorance, which is impermanent—a conditioned, dependently arisen phenomenon, a phenomenon subject to exhaustion, a phenomenon subject to change, a phenomenon subject to dispassion, and a phenomenon subject to cessation—this is called a dependently arisen phenomenon.
What is the skillful means regarding conditions?

Whether it be those conditions or these conditions that give rise to phenomena, if one perceives and understands the skillful means [of their arising], this is called the skillful means regarding conditions,
O Bhikṣu!
To what extent is it called "skillful means regarding conditions"?
When one knows and sees, as they truly are, the dharmas that arise conditioned by those very conditions, to that extent it is called skillful means regarding conditions.
What is ignorance?
Delusion, the unwholesome root—this is called ignorance.
What is the condition of ignorance for volitional formations?
With ignorance as condition, there are meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and imperturbable formations.
What are non-meritorious formations?
They are unwholesome bodily formations, unwholesome verbal formations, and unwholesome mental formations.
What are unwholesome bodily actions?
If a person lacks wisdom and has not severed ignorance, yet engages in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and other such unwholesome bodily actions, these are called unwholesome bodily actions.
What is unwholesome verbal conduct?

If a person lacks wisdom, possesses ignorance that has not been severed, and engages in false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, frivolous speech, and other such unwholesome verbal acts, this is called unwholesome verbal conduct.
What are unwholesome mental formations?
If a person lacks wisdom, possesses ignorance that has not been severed, and gives rise to sensual desire, ill will, and wrong views, these are called unwholesome mental formations.
These unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called non-meritorious formations (*apuṇyābhisaṃskāra*); they have ignorance as their condition for present-life formations.
What are meritorious formations?
They are wholesome actions of body, wholesome actions of speech, and wholesome actions of mind.
What is wholesome conduct of the body?

If a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, yet refrains from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, as well as other forms of bodily wholesome conduct—this is called wholesome conduct of the body.
What is wholesome verbal conduct?

If a person, though lacking wisdom and having not yet severed ignorance, refrains from false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech, as well as other wholesome verbal actions, this is called wholesome verbal conduct.
What is wholesome conduct of the mind?
If a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, yet possesses non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view—this is called wholesome conduct of the mind.
These wholesome conducts of body, speech, and mind are called meritorious formations; they are formations conditioned by ignorance in the present life.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they may—detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and possessing the joy and happiness born of seclusion—achieve the practice of the first *dhyāna*. Their bodily action consists of non-informative (*avijñapti*) morality included within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and known by the mental consciousness; their vocal action consists of non-informative morality included within the sphere of mental objects and known by the mental consciousness; and their mental action consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind.
Such wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind is called meritorious action conditioned by ignorance as a present-life formation.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they attain the second dhyāna—characterized by the absence of vitarka and vicāra, internal clarity of faith, and the joy and bliss born of concentration—through the cessation of vitarka and vicāra. Their bodily action, consisting of non-informative (avijñapti) discipline included within the sphere of mental consciousness, and their vocal action, consisting of non-informative discipline included within the sphere of mental consciousness, both being known by the mental consciousness; and their mental action, arising from the mind through feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—such wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind is called meritorious action conditioned by ignorance as a present-life formation.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they—free from joy and practicing equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing bliss with the body as the noble ones describe it, and attaining the third dhyāna characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and bliss—possess bodily karma that is unmanifest (avijñapti), subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), and known by the mental consciousness; vocal karma that is unmanifest, subsumed under the sphere of mental objects, and known by the mental consciousness; and mental karma consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind. Such wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called meritorious formations (puṇyābhisaṃskāra) conditioned by ignorance in the present life.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they attain the fourth dhyāna—characterized by the abandonment of pleasure and pain, and the prior cessation of sorrow and joy, wherein there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and which is purified by equanimity and mindfulness—and their bodily action consists of non-informative (avijñapti) discipline included within the sphere of mental objects and known by the mental consciousness; their verbal action consists of non-informative discipline included within the sphere of mental objects and known by the mental consciousness; and their mental action consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind. Such wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called meritorious formations (puṇyābhisaṃskāra), which are formations of the present life conditioned by ignorance.
This is called meritorious action (*puṇyābhisaṃskāra*).
What is immovable action (*āniñjyābhisaṃskāra*)?

If a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, having abandoned all perceptions of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*), extinguished perceptions of ill-will (*vyāpādasaṃjñā*), and not attending to perceptions of diversity (*nānātvasaṃjñā*), they achieve the practice of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Their bodily action, which is unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and included within the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and known by the mental consciousness; their vocal action, which is unmanifest and included within the base of mental phenomena and known by the mental consciousness; and their mental action—consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind—such wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called immovable action conditioned by ignorance, which manifests in the present life.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they dwell having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness while detached from the sphere of nothingness. Their bodily action, which is unmanifest and subsumed under the dharma-base of precepts, is known by the mental consciousness; their vocal action, which is unmanifest and subsumed under the dharma-base of precepts, is known by the mental consciousness; and their mental action consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind. Such wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called "immovable formations" (āneñjya-saṃskāra), which are formations of the present life conditioned by ignorance.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they may dwell in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) while having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Their bodily action, which is unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and included within the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), is known by the mental consciousness; their vocal action, which is unmanifest and included within the base of mental phenomena, is known by the mental consciousness; and their mental action consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind. Such wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called "immovable formations" (*āneñjya-saṃskāra*) conditioned by ignorance that manifest in the present life.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they leave behind all the spheres of nothingness and achieve the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Their bodily action, consisting of non-informative discipline (*avijñapti-śīla*) included within the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and known by the mental consciousness; their vocal action, consisting of non-informative discipline included within the base of mental phenomena and known by the mental consciousness; and their mental action—arising from the mind as feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—these wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called "immovable formations" that are conditioned by ignorance and manifest in the present life.
This is called immovable karma.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind. Because they have performed unwholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, they fall into hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts to receive a body composed of the five aggregates.
Thus, conditioned by present formations, one experiences future formations; this is called "ignorance conditions future formations.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to birth in the desire realm, perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to birth in the desire realm, and having performed these wholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, if they are born among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm, they receive a body composed of the five aggregates within those human or desire-realm heavenly states due to causes, antecedents, and conditions.
In this way, conditioned by present formations, one undergoes future formations; this is called "ignorance conditions future formations.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to birth in the form realm, or perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to birth in the form realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are born among the devas of the form realm.
By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, they receive a body composed of the five aggregates within the heavens of the form realm.
Thus, conditioned by present formations, one experiences future formations; this is called "ignorance conditions future formations.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind that lead to birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Having performed these wholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens of the formless realm. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, they experience a body consisting of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) in the heavens of the formless realm.
In this way, conditioned by present formations, one undergoes future formations; this is called "ignorance conditions future formations.
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda!"
Volitional formations have craving as their condition.
Thus, Ānanda, having asked the question, the answer has been given.
What is the condition for volitional formations?
"Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition. This is the answer, Ānanda!
"If there were no ignorance, would there be volitional formations?
"No, World-Honored One."
Ānanda! Conditioned by causes and conditions, there is volitional formation (*saṃskāra*). If there is no ignorance (*avidyā*) as a condition for volitional formation, it is as previously explained.
For this reason, it is so said.
What is consciousness conditioned by formations?

When volitional thoughts accompanied by desire arise, consciousness accompanied by desire arises; thus, when present formations condition present consciousness, this is called "consciousness conditioned by present formations."

There is [volition] associated with hatred, there is that associated with delusion; there is no [volition] associated with desire, no [volition] associated with hatred, and no [volition] associated with delusion. There is wholesome, unwholesome, and conditioned indeterminate volition (*cetanā*), and there is indeterminate consciousness at birth. Thus, conditioned by present formations (*saṃskāra*), present consciousness arises; this is called "formations as condition for present consciousness."

Conditioned by the eye and conditioned by forms, consciousness arises; that eye-activity and form-activity, when taken as conditions for consciousness, thus condition present activity to produce present consciousness. This is what is meant by "present activity conditions present consciousness."
When the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental objects as conditions, consciousness arises;

those mental formations and mental objects, if they condition that consciousness—thus, when present formations condition present consciousness, this is called "present formations as condition for present consciousness."

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not severed ignorance, they engage in unwholesome bodily actions, unwholesome verbal actions, and unwholesome mental actions. Having performed these unwholesome deeds, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. Due to causes, antecedents, and conditions, the initial consciousness arises in those realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. Through the accumulation of conditions based on the antecedents of karmic causes, eye-consciousness arises, and so on up to mind-consciousness and the subsequent discerning consciousness.
In this way, conditioned by present formations (*saṃskāra*), future consciousness arises; this is what is meant by "formations as condition for future consciousness.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom, has not severed ignorance, and performs wholesome bodily actions with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are to be experienced in a birth within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or performs wholesome verbal and mental actions that are to be experienced in a birth within the desire realm—having performed these wholesome actions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, whether they are born among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm—then by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, if they are born among humans or in the six heavens of the desire realm, their initial consciousness arises. Through the accumulation of conditions based on the antecedent cause of karma, eye-consciousness arises, and so on up to mind-consciousness and the subsequent discerning consciousness.
In this way, conditioned by present formations (*saṃskāra*), future consciousness (*vijñāna*) arises; this is "formations as condition for consciousness.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows (*sāsrava*) that lead to birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to birth in the form realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are born in the heavens of the form realm. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, the initial consciousness is experienced in the heavens of the form realm; through the accumulation of the causal antecedents of karma, eye-consciousness arises, and so on up to mind-consciousness and subsequent cognitive awareness.
Thus, conditioned by present formations (*saṃskāra*), future consciousness arises; this is called "formations as condition for future consciousness.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows (*sāsrava*) that lead to rebirth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the formless realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens of the formless realm. Due to the causal nexus and conditions, the initial consciousness arises in those heavens of the formless realm; through the accumulation of the causal nexus of karma, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and subsequent cognitive awareness arise.
In this way, conditioned by present formations (*saṃskāra*), future consciousness arises; this is called "formations as the condition for future consciousness.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom, has not severed ignorance, and performs unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, then after performing such unwholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they fall into the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts. Due to these causes, antecedents, and conditions, there exists within the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts an unwholesome volition that co-exists with that consciousness.
Thus, conditioned by future formations, one experiences future consciousness; this is called "formations as condition for future consciousness.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that will lead to birth in the desire realm, or perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that will lead to birth in the desire realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the breaking up of the body after death, if they are born among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm, then by way of cause, connection, and condition, there is wholesome volition among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm, and the consciousness that accompanies that volition.
Thus, conditioned by future formations, one experiences future consciousness; this is called "formations as condition for future consciousness.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to birth in the form realm, or perform wholesome vocal and mental actions with outflows that lead to birth in the form realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they are born in the heavens of the form realm. Due to causes, antecedents, and conditions, there arises in the heavens of the form realm consciousness accompanied by volition and co-existent with volition.
In this way, conditioned by future formations, future consciousness arises; this is called "formations as condition for future consciousness.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the formless realm, or perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the formless realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens of the formless realm. Due to causes, antecedents, and conditions, there exists in those heavens of the formless realm an immovable volition together with the consciousness associated with that volition.
In this way, future consciousness arises conditioned by future formations; this is called "formations as condition for future consciousness.

Furthermore, if the final formations cease while remaining unknown, or if, after the formations have ceased without interval, consciousness continues to arise in another path, those formations serve as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for that [consciousness].
If, due to consciousness, one is reborn in another realm, those formations are the condition for that consciousness as its causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
If, through volitional formations, one is reborn in another realm due to that consciousness, those formations are the condition for that consciousness as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
If those formations cause consciousness to continue into another realm of existence, those formations are the condition for that consciousness as a supporting condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*).
If retributive formations cause consciousness to continue into another realm of existence, those formations are the condition for that consciousness as a retribution condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*).

If the active consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) arises in continuation from another path of existence, those formations (*saṃskāra*) are the condition for that consciousness by way of being its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

If the consciousness associated with the formations arises in continuation from another path of existence, those formations are the condition for that consciousness by way of being a distinct condition (*anya-pratyaya*).
If a formation (saṃskāra) proceeds with consciousness as its dominant condition to arise in another path of existence, that formation serves as the dominant condition for that consciousness.

When this final consciousness ceases and the initial consciousness arises in the subsequent path of existence, the final consciousness having ceased, the initial consciousness arises immediately, with no interval between them.
It is like the shifting of a shadow and the continuity of the sun, or the shifting of the sun and the continuity of the shadow; between the shadow and the sun there is no interval.

In the same way, when the final consciousness ceases, the initial consciousness continues as it arises in another realm; once the final consciousness has ceased, the initial consciousness is immediately received, with no interval in between.
Whether it be the initial consciousness or the final consciousness, the mental factors associated with them do not persist into the subsequent consciousness.
This is analogous to how, once visual consciousness has ceased, auditory consciousness arises; and once auditory consciousness has ceased, visual consciousness arises again.
Dharmas associated with eye-consciousness do not reach ear-consciousness, and dharmas associated with ear-consciousness do not reach eye-consciousness.

In this manner, the final consciousness and the dharmas associated with the final consciousness do not reach the initial consciousness, and the dharmas associated with the initial consciousness do not reach the final consciousness.

After the final consciousness has ceased, the initial consciousness arises immediately. One says that this time has passed; one says that this ceases and that arises, that this ends and that begins. It is not that the life is that body, nor is it that the life is different from the body. It is neither eternal nor annihilated; it neither departs nor arrives, nor undergoes transformation. It is not without cause, nor is it without action. It is not that one performs an action and another receives its fruit, nor that one performs an action and a different one receives its fruit. One knows there is going and coming; one knows there is birth and death; one knows there is the continuity of karma; one knows there is the teaching of the Dharma; one knows there are conditions. Yet, there is no one who goes from here to there, and there is no one who comes from there to here.
Why is this? Because they arise through the continuous succession of karmic conditions.
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda! Consciousness has a condition.
Thus, Ānanda, having asked, there was this answer.
What is the condition for consciousness?
It is conditioned by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). This is the answer.
"Ānanda, if there were no volitional formations (saṃskāra), would there be consciousness (vijñāna)?
"World-Honored One, there would not."
"No, Ānanda. For this reason, consciousness arises through these causal conditions;
whether it is 'volitional formations as condition for consciousness' or as previously explained."
It is for this reason that it is said:
how is it that consciousness conditions name-and-form?
Conditioned by craving, consciousness arises; conditioned by craving, bodily action arises; conditioned by craving, vocal action arises; and conditioned by craving, mental action arises.
The bodily and vocal actions associated with the desire realm are called "form" (rūpa).
The mental action associated with the desire realm, along with the feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind, are called "name" (nāma).
In this way, present consciousness gives rise to present name-and-form; this is called "present name-and-form conditioned by consciousness.

It is accompanied by hatred and accompanied by delusion, yet it is without shared desire, without shared hatred, and without shared delusion; it is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate consciousness with conditions, as well as indeterminate bodily, verbal, and mental actions.
Neutral bodily and vocal actions are called "form" (rūpa).
Neutral mental action consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind; these are called "name" (nāma).
In this way, conditioned by present consciousness, present name-and-form arises; this is called "present consciousness conditions present name-and-form.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they produce unwholesome consciousness. Having produced that unwholesome consciousness, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they fall into hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, name-and-form arises in hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements constitute "form" (*rūpa*); that which arises from the mind—namely, feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—is called "name" (*nāma*).
This is called "conditioned by present consciousness, future name-and-form arises"; this constitutes "consciousness as the condition for future name-and-form.

Furthermore, if a person possesses no wisdom and their ignorance is not yet severed, they perform a contaminated wholesome consciousness that will lead to birth in the desire realm. Having performed such a wholesome consciousness, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, if they are born among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm, they receive name-and-form among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm due to causes, antecedents, and conditions. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements constitute "form. That which arises from the mind—feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—is called "name."
In this way, conditioned by present consciousness, future name-and-form arises.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they may—detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and possessing the joy and happiness born of seclusion—achieve and dwell in the first dhyāna; they honor, esteem, and endure that joy and happiness of the first dhyāna.

Having attained the endurance of the noble first dhyāna, consciousness takes up reliance upon pleasure; at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is reborn in the heavens of the form realm. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, name-and-form arise in the heavens of the form realm: the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements constitute "form," while feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind constitute "name."
In this way, conditioned by present consciousness, future name-and-form arises; this is called "consciousness conditions future name-and-form.

Furthermore, next, if a person lacks wisdom and ignorance has not been abandoned, they dwell having attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having transcended the sphere of nothingness; they find joy in that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, regarding it as supreme, abiding therein with endurance and delighting in that joy.

Having attained mastery in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and having dwelt there extensively, one practices with a mind that relies upon and delights in grasping; at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the heavenly realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. By reason of these causes, conditions, and links, one is born in the heaven of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. What is called "name" consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention produced by the mind.
In this way, conditioned by present consciousness, future name-and-form arises; this is called "consciousness conditions future name-and-form.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they engage in unwholesome bodily conduct, unwholesome verbal conduct, and unwholesome mental conduct.
