Having engaged in such unwholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, the initial consciousness arises in those realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, together with that consciousness is name-and-form. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements constitute "form"; that which arises from the mind—feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—constitutes "name."
In this way, conditioned by future consciousness, future name-and-form arises; this is called "consciousness conditions future name-and-form.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind that are subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) and destined for birth in the desire realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, if they are reborn among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm, then due to causes, antecedents, and conditions, there arises—among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm—the initial consciousness. Together with that consciousness is name-and-form: the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements constitute "form" (*rūpa*); that which arises from the mind—feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—is called "name" (*nāma*).
In this way, with future consciousness as condition, future name-and-form arises; this is called "consciousness conditions future name-and-form.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the form realm, or perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the form realm. Having performed these wholesome actions, at the breaking up of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens of the form realm. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, the initial consciousness of the form realm arises, together with which there is name-and-form: the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements constitute "form," while feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention produced by the mind constitute "name."
In this way, conditioned by future consciousness, future name-and-form arise; this is called "conditioned by consciousness, there is future name-and-form.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom, has not yet severed ignorance, and performs wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the formless realm, or performs wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the formless realm, then having performed these wholesome actions, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, they are born in the heavens of the formless realm. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, the first consciousness arises in the heavens of the formless realm; together with that consciousness is "name," consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention produced by the mind—this is called "name."
In this way, conditioned by future consciousness, future name-and-form arises; this is called "conditioned by consciousness, there is future name-and-form.
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda!"
"Name-and-form has a condition.
Thus, Ānanda, having asked the question, there was this answer:
"What is the condition for name-and-form?"
"Consciousness conditions name-and-form;
this is the answer, Ānanda!"
"If consciousness did not enter the womb, would name-and-form arise?
World-Honored One, it would not."
"Ānanda! If consciousness were not to enter the womb and emerge from it, would there be the arising of name-and-form?
"World-Honored One, there would not."
"No, Ānanda! If the consciousness of an infant were severed and destroyed so as to no longer exist, would that name-and-form grow and expand?"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Ānanda!"
“World-Honored One, if all consciousness were absent, would name-and-form exist? No,
World-Honored One.”
Therefore, Ānanda!
It is by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions that name-and-form comes to be. Ānanda!
If consciousness conditions name-and-form, as previously explained,
for this reason it is said:
What is the conditioning of name-and-form for the six sense bases?

Conditioned by edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), the present eye faculty is moistened, benefited, and increased; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties are likewise moistened, benefited, and increased.

Edible food refers to form (*rūpa*); that which arises from the mind—namely, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and mental application (*manasikāra*)—is called name (*nāma*).

In this way, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), there arise the present six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the present six sense bases arise.

Conditioned by clothing, bathing, and the regulation of the body, the present eye faculty is moistened, benefited, and increased; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties are likewise moistened, benefited, and increased.
Clothing, bathing, physical regulation, and solid food are called "form" (rūpa). Mental volition, sensation, perception, intention, contact, and attention are called "name" (nāma).
Thus, conditioned by present name-and-form, present six sense bases arise; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the six sense bases arise in the present."

Conditioned by forms that are a basis for joy, the present eye faculty is moistened, benefited, and increased; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties are likewise moistened, benefited, and increased.
Forms that are a basis for joy refer to "form" (rūpa); that which arises from the mind—namely feeling, perception, volition, contact, and mental application—is called "name" (nāma).
In this way, name-and-form conditions the present six sense bases.

Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu who is an arhat—one whose taints are exhausted, who has accomplished what was to be done, who has laid down the heavy burden, who has attained his own benefit, whose fetters of existence are destroyed, who is rightly liberated, and who has experienced the supreme attainment—he experiences the moistening, benefiting, and growth of the present eye faculty, as well as the moistening, benefiting, and growth of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties.

If, in reality, bodily action and verbal action are called "form" (rūpa), and mental action—consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind—is called "name" (nāma);
then, conditioned by such present name-and-form, there arises present sixfold sense-basis (ṣaḍāyatana). This is what is meant by "conditioned by name-and-form, there is present sixfold sense-basis."

Furthermore, if there is a bhikṣu of great supernormal power and great majesty who, directing his mind toward his own body, manifests another physical form, complete with all its limbs, joints, and sense faculties; in this present state, he causes the eye faculty to be moistened, benefited, and increased, and causes the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties to be moistened, benefited, and increased.

If one considers the bodily and vocal actions of a real person as "form" (rūpa), and the mental action of a real person—consisting of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), and attention (manasikāra) arising from the mind—as "name" (nāma).
In this way, conditioned by present name-and-form, there arise the present six sense bases; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the present six sense bases arise.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu attains the power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*) and mastery over his mind and life-span, remaining for one kalpa or less than one kalpa, his present eye faculty will be moistened, benefited, and increased, and his ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties will likewise be moistened, benefited, and increased.

If one considers the bodily and vocal actions of a real person as "form" (rūpa), and the mental action of a real person—consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind—as "name" (nāma).
Thus, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the present six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the present six sense bases arise.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind. Unwholesome bodily and vocal actions are called "form" (*rūpa*); unwholesome mental actions consist of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*) arising from the mind, which are called "name" (*nāma*).

Having produced unwholesome name-and-form, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, one is born in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; by way of causes, antecedents, and conditions, one produces the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind in those realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts.
Thus, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the future six sense-bases arise.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom, their ignorance being unsevered, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows (*sāsrava*) that lead to birth in the desire realm, and they perform wholesome verbal and mental actions that lead to birth in the desire realm. Wholesome bodily and verbal actions are termed "form" (*rūpa*); wholesome mental actions consist of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*) arising from the mind—these are termed "name" (*nāma*).

Having performed wholesome name-and-form, at the dissolution of the body after death, if one is reborn among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm, then by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind arise among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm.
In this way, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the future six sense-bases arise.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet abandoned ignorance, they may—detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion—achieve the practice of the first dhyāna. In this case, the practitioner’s bodily and vocal actions are called "form" (*rūpa*), while the practitioner’s mental action—the feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*) arising from the mind—is called "name" (*nāma*).

Having performed wholesome name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); by reason of those causes, conditions, and links, the faculties of eye, ear, body, and mind arise within the heavens of the form realm.
In this way, conditioned by present name-and-form, future sixfold sense-bases arise; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the future sixfold sense-bases arise.
Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance:

With the cessation of applied and sustained thought, and through inner serenity and confidence, one accomplishes the practice of the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss. In this state, the practitioner’s bodily and vocal karma is called "form" (rūpa), while the practitioner’s mental karma—consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind—is called "name" (nāma).

Having performed wholesome name-and-form, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the heavens of the Form Realm; by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, the faculties of eye, ear, body, and mind arise within those heavens of the Form Realm.
In this way, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the future six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, the future bases.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and their ignorance (*avidyā*) is not yet severed, they—detached from joy and dwelling in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body as the noble ones experience it, having attained the third dhyāna—performs bodily and vocal actions which are called "form" (*rūpa*); the mental action of that person consists of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*) arising from the mind, which are called "name" (*nāma*).

Having produced that wholesome name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), with it as cause, antecedent, and condition, the eye, ear, body, and mind-faculties arise within the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Thus, conditioned by present name-and-form, future sense-bases (*āyatana*) arise; this is called "name-and-form as the condition for future sense-bases."

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they sever suffering and pleasure, first extinguishing grief and joy, and achieve the fourth dhyāna—equanimity, mindfulness, and purity. In this practice, the practitioner’s bodily and vocal karma is called "form" (rūpa); the practitioner’s mental karma, consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind, is called "name" (nāma).

Having performed wholesome name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), at the breaking up of the body after death, one is reborn in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); by reason of causes, conditions, and links, the faculties of eye, ear, body, and mind arise in the heavens of the form realm.
In this way, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future entry [into existence] arises; this is called "name-and-form as the condition for future entry.
Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they may think:

"Perception (*saṃjñā*) is my affliction, it is a boil and an arrow; non-perception (*asaṃjñā*) is peaceful and sublime. Thus, they are able to accomplish the practice of the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*). In this case, the practitioner's bodily and vocal actions are termed "form" (*rūpa*), while the attainment of non-perception is termed "name" (*nāman*).

Having performed wholesome deeds of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in the Heaven of Non-perception (*asaṃjñisattva-deva*). By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*) arises within his body in the Heaven of Non-perception.
Thus, with present name-and-form as condition, future sense-bases arise; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future sense-bases.

Furthermore, if a person, relying on the noble realization shared by the wise, dwells having attained the first dhyāna—which is accompanied by applied and sustained thought, born of seclusion, and characterized by joy and bliss—then their actual bodily and vocal actions are called "form," while their actual mental action, consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind, is called "name."

Having performed wholesome name-and-form, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, he was reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, he was born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens possessing the faculties of eye, ear, body, and mind.
In this way, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future entry [into existence] arises; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future entry.

Furthermore, if a person, relying on the noble common awakening, having stilled discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*), with internal clarity and faith, without discursive thought or investigation, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss—if, in that true person, bodily and vocal actions are called "form" (*rūpa*), and in that true person, mental action consists of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind, these are called "name" (*nāman*).

Having performed wholesome name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, he obtains the faculties of eye, ear, body, and mind in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Thus, with present name-and-form as condition, future sense-bases arise; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future sense-bases.

Furthermore, if a person, relying on the noble common awakening, dwells in equanimity, free from joy, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing happiness with the body—just as the noble ones describe "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness"—and accomplishes the third dhyāna: therein, the actual bodily and vocal actions are called "form"; the actual mental action, consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind, is called "name."

Having performed wholesome deeds of name-and-form, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, he obtains the faculties of eye, ear, body, and mind in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
In this way, with present name-and-form as condition, future sense-bases arise; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future sense-bases.

Furthermore, if a person, relying on the noble common awakening, abandons pleasure and pain, and with the prior cessation of grief and joy, dwells in the fourth dhyāna—accomplished in equanimity, mindfulness, and purity—if one considers the actual bodily and vocal actions of that person as "form," and their actual mental action, consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind, as "name."

Having performed wholesome name-and-form, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens; by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, he obtains the faculties of eye, ear, body, and mind in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens.
Thus, with name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as condition, future sense-bases (*āyatana*) arise; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future sense-bases.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom, lacks clarity, and has not yet severed ignorance, they transcend all perceptions of form (*rūpasaṃjñā*), extinguish perceptions of sensory reaction (*pratighasaṃjñā*), do not attend to perceptions of diversity (*nānātvasaṃjñā*), and achieve the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). In this case, the practitioner’s bodily and vocal actions are called "form," while the practitioner’s mental action—consisting of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*) arising from the mind—is called "name."

Having performed wholesome deeds, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the Heaven of Infinite Space. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, he obtains the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) in the Heaven of Infinite Space.
Thus, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future entry [into existence] arises; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future entry."

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they dwell having attained the sphere of infinite consciousness while being detached from the sphere of nothingness. In this case, the practitioner’s bodily and vocal actions are called "form" (rūpa), while the practitioner’s mental action—consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind—is called "name" (nāma).

Having performed wholesome deeds, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, he obtains the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) in the Heaven of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness.
Thus, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future entry [into existence] arises; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future entry."

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they may achieve the practice of the sphere of nothingness while remaining apart from the sphere of infinite consciousness. In this case, the practitioner’s bodily and vocal actions are called "form" (rūpa), while the practitioner’s mental action—consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind—is called "name" (nāma).

Having performed wholesome deeds of name-and-form, at the dissolution of the body after death, he is reborn in the Heaven of Nothingness; by means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, he obtains the mental faculty of the Heaven of Nothingness.
Thus, with present name-and-form as condition, future entry [into existence] arises; this is called "name-and-form conditions future entry.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having transcended the sphere of nothingness. In that case, the person's bodily and vocal actions are called "form," while the person's mental action—consisting of feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention arising from the mind—is called "name."

Having performed wholesome name-and-form, at the breaking up of the body and the end of life, he is reborn in the heavenly realm of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; through causes, antecedents, and conditions, he obtains the mental faculty of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in that heavenly realm.
Thus, conditioned by present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future entry [into existence] arises; this is called "conditioned by name-and-form, there is future entry.

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom, has not abandoned ignorance, and performs unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind—having performed these unwholesome actions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts. By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, they obtain the name-and-form of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts. The four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements constitute "form" (*rūpa*); that which arises from the mind—sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and mental application (*manasikāra*)—is called "name" (*nāma*).
As name-and-form increases, one acquires the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind faculties of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
Thus, conditioned by future name-and-form, future six sense bases arise; this is called "name-and-form conditions the future six sense bases."

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to birth in the desire realm, and they perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to birth in the desire realm.

Having performed wholesome deeds, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, one obtains name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) as a human or in the heavens of the desire realm: the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements; and that which arises from the mind—namely, feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*)—is called "name" (*nāma*).
As name-and-form increases, one obtains the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind among humans or in the heavens of the desire realm.
Thus, conditioned by future name-and-form, future six sense bases arise; this is called "name-and-form conditions future six sense bases."

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the form realm, and they perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the form realm.

Having performed wholesome deeds, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). By means of causes, antecedents, and conditions, one obtains name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the heavens of the form realm: the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements are called "form" (*rūpa*); that which arises from the mind—feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*)—is called "name" (*nāma*).
As name-and-form increases, one obtains the eye, ear, body, and mind-faculties belonging to the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Thus, conditioned by future name-and-form, there arises future sense-bases (*āyatana*); this is called "name-and-form conditions future sense-bases."

Furthermore, if a person lacks wisdom and has not yet severed ignorance, they may perform wholesome bodily actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the formless realm, or perform wholesome verbal and mental actions with outflows that lead to rebirth in the formless realm.

Having performed wholesome deeds, at the dissolution of the body after death, one is reborn in the heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); by reason of these causes, conditions, and links, one obtains the designation "heavenly being of the formless realm. That which arises from the mind—feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and mental application (*manasikāra*)—is called "name" (*nāman*).
It is called "increase," whereby one attains the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) in the heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, conditioned by future name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), future entry [into the womb] arises; this is called "name-and-form as condition for future entry."
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda! The six sense bases have conditions."
Thus, having asked the question, Ānanda received this answer:
"What is the condition for the six sense bases?
Name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases."
This is the answer: "Ānanda,
if there were no name-and-form at all, would the six sense bases exist?"
“No, World-Honored One!
It is so, Ānanda!”
With the causal sequence as condition, there are the six sense bases. Ānanda!
With name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases, as previously explained.
For this reason it is said:
What is contact conditioned by the six sense bases?
Contact is twofold, conditioned by the six sense bases: bodily contact and mental contact; this is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases."

Furthermore, conditioned by the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) arise three types of contact: pleasant contact, painful contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact; this is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases.

Furthermore, conditioned by the six sense bases arise three types of contact: contact bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), contact bound to the form realm (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta), and contact bound to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta); this is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases."
Furthermore, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) condition the five types of contact; contact associated with the five faculties of feeling is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases.

Furthermore, the six sense bases condition the six types of contact: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact; these are called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases."

Furthermore, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) condition the seven types of contact (sparśa): contact associated with the eye-consciousness element, and contact associated with the elements of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness; this is called "contact conditioned by the six sense bases."

Furthermore, the six sense bases condition the eighteen types of contact: pleasant contact, painful contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact of the eye; pleasant contact, painful contact, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is called "the six sense bases as the condition for contact."
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda! Contact has a condition."
Thus, having asked the question, Ānanda received this answer:
"What is the condition for contact?
Contact is conditioned by the six sense bases."
This is the answer: "Ānanda!
If there were no six sense bases, would there be contact?"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Ānanda!"
With contact as its cause, condition,
and nexus, Ānanda!
Contact is conditioned by the six sense bases, as previously explained.
For this reason it is said:
What is feeling conditioned by contact?
There are two kinds of feeling conditioned by contact: bodily feeling and mental feeling; these are called feeling conditioned by contact.

Furthermore, conditioned by contact (sparśa), there arise three types of feeling (vedanā): pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; this is called "feeling conditioned by contact.
This continues up to eighteen types of feeling conditioned by contact, as explained above.
This is called "feeling conditioned by contact.
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda!..."
Feeling has a condition.
Ānanda asked, and having already received the answer, he further inquired:
"What is the condition for feeling?"
"Feeling has contact as its condition.
This is the answer, Ānanda!
"If there were no contact at all, would there be feeling?
World-Honored One, there would not."
Ānanda! Feeling arises with conditions as its cause. Ānanda!
Contact conditions feeling, as previously explained.
For this reason, it is said:
What is the way in which feeling conditions craving?
Conditioned by a pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, there arises a pleasant feeling born of eye-contact.

Having experienced that pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, one delights in it, takes pleasure in it, becomes attached to it, and remains steadfastly clinging to it; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, conditioned by a pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, there arises a pleasant feeling born of eye-contact.

Having experienced that pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, one craves for another pleasant feeling born of eye-contact—whether it be similar or superior. This is called craving conditioned by feeling.
Having experienced a pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, one craves that pleasant feeling born of eye-contact; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, conditioned by a painful feeling born of eye-contact, there arises a painful feeling born of eye-contact.
Having experienced a painful feeling born of eye-contact, one craves for a pleasant feeling born of eye-contact; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, conditioned by a painful feeling born of eye-contact, a painful feeling born of eye-contact arises.
If, having experienced a painful sensation born of eye-contact, one wishes for it to be severed, destroyed, and non-existent, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, conditioned by a painful sensation born of eye-contact, there arises a painful sensation born of eye-contact.
If, having experienced a painful feeling born of eye-contact, one craves for a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, conditioned by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact arises.

Having experienced a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, one dwells with delight, joy, and attachment toward pleasant feelings born of eye-contact; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, conditioned by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact, there arises a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of eye-contact.

If, having experienced a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant born of eye-contact, one craves for another feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant born of eye-contact—whether it be similar or superior—then, with such a feeling as condition, craving arises.
Furthermore, conditioned by eye-contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, there arises eye-contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
If, having experienced eye-contact that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one craves for eye-contact that is pleasant feeling, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."

Furthermore, when the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind take mental contact as a condition for pleasant feeling, and having given rise to this pleasant feeling from mental contact, one experiences joy and delight toward that pleasant feeling from mental contact, becoming attached to it and dwelling therein with endurance—this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, when one experiences delight, pleasure, attachment, endurance, and persistence based on the pleasant feeling born of mental contact, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, based on the pleasant feeling born of mental contact, there arises the pleasant feeling born of mental contact.

If, having experienced a pleasant feeling born of mental contact, one craves for another pleasant feeling born of mental contact—whether similar or superior—that is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, conditioned by a pleasant feeling born of mental contact, there arises a pleasant feeling born of mental contact.
Having experienced that pleasant feeling born of mental contact, one craves for a feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, conditioned by a painful feeling born of mental contact, there arises a painful feeling born of mental contact.
Having experienced that painful feeling born of mental contact, one craves for a pleasant feeling born of mental contact; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, conditioned by a painful feeling born of mental contact, there arises a painful feeling born of mental contact.
Having experienced that painful feeling born of mental contact, one craves: "May I be severed from it, may it perish, may it not exist. This is called craving conditioned by feeling.
Furthermore, conditioned by a painful feeling born of mental contact, there arises a painful feeling born of mental contact.
Having experienced that painful feeling born of mental contact, one craves for a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mental contact; this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, conditioned by the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of mental contact, there arises a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of mental contact.

If, once that feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of mental contact has arisen, one harbors longing for it, endures it, and remains attached to it, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, conditioned by the feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of mental contact, there arises a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of mental contact.

If, having experienced this feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure born of mental contact, one craves for such a feeling of neither-pain-nor-pleasure—whether for its likeness or for something superior to it—this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
Furthermore, conditioned by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mind-contact, there arises a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mind-contact.
If, having been conditioned by a neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling born of mind-contact, one craves for a pleasant feeling born of mind-contact, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling."
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda, craving has a condition."
When Ānanda had asked this, he received the answer:
"What is the condition for craving?
Craving is conditioned by feeling."
This is the answer: "Ānanda!
If there were no one who experiences any feeling at all, would craving exist?"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Ānanda!"
With craving as its cause and condition,
Ānanda! Craving has feeling as its condition, just as was previously explained.
For this reason it is said:
What is grasping conditioned by craving?

When craving has not been abandoned, there arise the grasping for sensual desire, the grasping for views, the grasping for precepts and observances, and the grasping for a self; this is called grasping conditioned by craving.
What is the clinging to sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*)?
With the exception of the initial contact of craving for the realm of desire, any further expansion of craving for the realm of desire is called the clinging to sensual desire.
What is the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭi-upādāna*)?
Excluding the attachment to precepts and rituals, there is the attachment to other views.
What is the attachment to precepts and rituals?
The attachment to precepts and paths is called the attachment to precepts and rituals.
What is the grasping of self (*ātmagrāha*)?
Excluding the initial contact of craving for the form and formless realms, if there is further extensive craving for the form and formless realms, this is called the grasping of self.
What is the grasping of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-grāha*)?

Excluding the craving for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-tṛṣṇā*), initial contact (*sparśa*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), whatever other afflictions (*kleśa*) there are in the realm of desire are called the grasping of desire (*kāyagrāha*).
What is the grasping of views?
The sixty-two views and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are called the grasping of views.
What is the clinging to precepts?

It is the desire and craving for those [precepts] that are considered purification through precepts, purification through the path, purification through both, liberation, non-reliance, or the end of suffering.
"Precepts" refers to the precepts of body and speech.

"The Way" refers to seeking auspiciousness through improper conditions, such as growing one's hair, entering water, serving fire, serving the sun and moon, practicing the cow-walk, the deer-walk, the dog-walk, or the silent-walk; or practicing asceticism for the sake of power, or practicing the conduct of great men—these various forms of asceticism and other methods of seeking improper auspiciousness are called "the Way."

If that precept and this path are sought, sought again, and thoroughly sought, to this extent it is called purity, called liberation, called purity of precept, called my liberation, called noble, called an arhat, and called parinirvāṇa.
If one has a strong desire for, a persistent desire for, and an endurance for those [objects], this is called *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances).
What is *ātmagrāha* (clinging to a self)?

Excluding the initial contact with craving for the form and formless realms, as well as *śīlavrataparāmarśa* and *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*, whatever other afflictions exist in the form and formless realms are called *ātmagrāha*.
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda! What is the condition for grasping?"
Thus, having been asked by Ānanda, the answer was given:
"By what condition does grasping arise?
Grasping has craving as its condition."
This is the answer: "Ānanda,
if there were no craving at all, would there be clinging?"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Ānanda!"
By means of these causal factors, there is grasping.
Ānanda! Grasping has craving as its condition, just as was explained previously.
For this reason it is said:
What is "existence conditioned by clinging"?

When the clinging to sensual desire, clinging to views, clinging to precepts and rituals, and clinging to a self have not been abandoned, and one performs actions pertaining to the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm, resulting in karmic retribution through body, speech, and mind—this is called "existence conditioned by clinging."
Furthermore, conditioned by grasping, there are the three realms of existence: the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
What is the realm of desire?
There are two kinds of the realm of desire: either the realm of desire as karmic existence (*karmabhava*) or the realm of desire as rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
What is the existence of desire (kāma-bhava) as the existence of karma (karma-bhava)?

When the performance of desire is not yet completed, its nature is not yet known, and it is not yet abandoned, if one performs bodily, verbal, or mental karma that has retribution as its result through the performance of desire, this is called the existence of desire as the existence of karma.
What is the existence of desire that is itself the existence of birth?

When karma has been performed and completed, one receives the fivefold aggregates of self—the form, sensation, perception, formations, and consciousness—within the heavens of the desire realm; this is called the existence of desire that is itself the existence of birth.
This is called the existence of grasping (*upādānabhava*), this is called the existence of retribution (*vipākabhava*), and this is called the existence of renewed becoming (*punarbhavabhava*).
Thus, the karmic existence of the desire realm (*kāmabhava*) and the birth-existence of the desire realm (*kāmajanmabhava*) are termed "existence in the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-bhava*).
What is the existence of form (*rūpabhava*)?
There are two kinds of existence of form: either the existence of form is itself the existence of karma (*karmabhava*), or the existence of form is itself the existence of birth (*upapattibhava*).
What is the existence of form that is itself the existence of karma?

When the formations of form (*rūpa-saṃskāra*) have not yet been completed, and while they are neither fully known nor abandoned, if one performs formations of form that result in retribution through bodily, vocal, or mental karma, this is called "existence of form" (*rūpa-bhava*), which is identical to "existence as karma" (*karma-bhava*).
What is "existence of form" as "existence as birth" (*jāti-bhava*)?

If, once the karma has been accomplished, one receives the fivefold aggregates of self—form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—in the heavens of the form realm, this is called "existence as form" (*rūpabhava*), which is identical to "birth-existence" (*upapattibhava*).
This is called existence by way of grasping (*upādānabhava*), this is called existence as retribution (*vipākabhava*), and this is called renewed existence (*punarbhavabhava*).
Thus, with such formative action (*saṃskāra*) as existence, and with such formative action as birth-existence (*upapattibhava*), this is termed "existence by way of form" (*rūpabhava*).
What is formless existence (*ārūpyabhava*)?
There are two kinds of formless existence: either formless existence is itself karmic existence (*karmabhava*), or formless existence is itself birth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
What is formless existence as karmic existence?

When the practice of the formless realm is not yet completed, not yet known, and not yet abandoned—if one performs informative acts of body, speech, and mind that have retribution within the formless realm—this is called "existence in the formless realm," which is precisely "karmic existence."
What is the existence of the formless realm that is itself the existence at birth?

When karma has been fully accomplished, one receives the fourfold aggregates of self—the body, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—within the heavens of the formless realm; this is called the existence of the formless realm that is itself the existence at birth.
This is called existence as feeling, this is called existence as retribution, and this is called renewed existence.
Thus, there is existence as formless karmic activity, and thus there is existence as birth in the formless realm; this is termed "formless existence."
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda! There is existence that has a condition."
Thus, having been questioned by Ānanda, the answer was given:
"By what condition does existence arise? Existence arises with grasping as its condition."
This is the answer: "Ānanda!
If there were no grasping at all, would there be existence?"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Ānanda!"
By way of causal sequence,
Ānanda! Conditioned by grasping (upādāna), there is existence (bhava), as previously explained.
For this reason it is said:
What is birth with conditions?

When sentient beings undergo repeated births within the various realms of existence, enter the womb and emerge from the womb, acquire the aggregates of birth, and possess the assembly of the sense bases—this is called birth.
As the Buddha said:
"Ānanda! Birth has its conditions."
When Ānanda asked this, he received the answer:
"With what as condition does birth arise? Birth arises with existence as its condition."
This is the answer: "Ānanda!
If all that exists did not exist, would there be birth?"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Ānanda!"
Because with causes, conditions, and dependencies there is arising, as previously explained.
For this reason it is said:
"How is it that with birth as condition there arise aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—this great mass of suffering?"
What is old age?
It refers to the senescence of sentient beings, characterized by trembling, the maturation of the sense faculties, the decline of mindfulness, and the diminution of conduct; this is called old age.
What is death?

When sentient beings reach their end, pass away, and die; when the time has passed, the aggregates (skandhas) disintegrate and they relinquish the body; when these aggregates undergo transformation and there is separation from the multitude—this is called death.
What is sorrow?

When sentient beings encounter various painful phenomena—whether it be sorrow (*śoka*), profound sorrow, or ultimate sorrow; whether it be internal fever or mental distress—this is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
What is lamentation (*parideva*)?

Being bound and oppressed by sorrow, fully consumed by grief, with a mind agitated by distress, one utters exhausted sighs, weeps, laments, and speaks at random; or one strikes oneself and raves—this is called *śoka* (sorrow).
What is suffering?
If one experiences physical pain—ranging from the painful feeling born of eye-contact up to the painful feeling born of body-contact—this is called suffering.
What is affliction?
If the mind perceives suffering and the mental contact results in a painful feeling, this is called affliction (*upāyāsa*).
What is the great mass of suffering?
Whether it be various sufferings, the suffering of insults and humiliation, or mental instability—this is called the great mass of suffering (*mahā-duḥkha-skandha*).
As the Buddha said: "Ānanda!
This great mass of suffering—the sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair of old age and death—has a condition."
When Ānanda asked this question, he received the answer:
"What is the condition for this mass of great suffering—the aging, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair?
Aging, death, grief, lamentation, pain, and despair have birth as their condition."
This is the answer: "Ānanda, if there were no birth,
would there be old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair— that great mass of suffering?"
"No, World-Honored One!
No, Ānanda!"
By way of causes, conditions, and links, there arises this great mass of suffering— the aggregate of old age, death, sorrow,
lamentation, pain, and despair— as previously explained regarding how birth conditions this great mass of suffering.
What is this arising of the entire mass of suffering?
It refers to the seven factors of suffering: aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, affliction, and the great mass of suffering; these are called the pure aggregate of suffering.

Furthermore, there are eleven factors of suffering: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth; these are called the pure mass of suffering.

Furthermore, there are eighteen factors of suffering: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and the great mass of suffering; these are called the pure aggregate of suffering.
Thus this entire mass of suffering arises through its origination, through its combination, and through its co-arising.
Having arisen and having co-arisen, it emerges and co-emerges.
Having emerged and having co-emerged, it reaches fulfillment; this is called the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
How is it that with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease?
If ignorance arises, volitional formations arise; if ignorance ceases, volitional formations cease. This is called "with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease."
...up to: if there is birth, there is aging and death; if birth ceases, then aging and death cease. This is called "the cessation of aging and death through the cessation of birth.
What is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering?
The "pure mass of suffering" refers to the seven factors of suffering: old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, distress, and the great mass of suffering; this is called the pure mass of suffering.
Furthermore, the eleven types of suffering are called the "pure aggregate of suffering.
Furthermore, the eighteen factors of suffering, from ignorance up to the great mass of suffering, are called the "pure aggregate of suffering."
Thus, this entire mass of suffering—its exhaustion, transformation, tranquility, cessation, and disappearance—is called the cessation of the entire mass of suffering.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle 12; *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle 13.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kaśmīra and others, including Dharmagupta, during the Yao Qin dynasty. Chapter Six:

The Foundations of Mindfulness (Smṛtyupasthāna), Part of the Non-Questioning Section. Practicing the One Path, sentient beings become pure; they remain far removed from sorrow and lamentation, bring an end to suffering and affliction, and realize Nirvana. Having severed the five hindrances, they cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness.

What is called the one path? It is to dwell alone in seclusion and quietude, delighting in diligent effort; not delighting in various worldly activities nor in non-activities; not engaging in meaningless speech nor delighting in meaningless speech; not engaging in sleep nor delighting in sleep; not engaging in socializing nor delighting in socializing; not engaging in dependence nor delighting in dependence; not engaging in negligence nor delighting in negligence; not engaging in intimacy nor delighting in intimacy. Such a path is born, rightly born; it arises, rightly arises; it is touched and realized—this is called the one path.

Furthermore, being solitary and remote, detached from and abandoning evil, secluded and free from defilement, and separated from all desires and evils—such that the Path arises, arises correctly, originates, originates correctly, and is touched and realized—this is called the One Path.

Furthermore, that which arises, arises correctly; originates, originates correctly; and is touched and realized—being free from the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion that are not shared [with others], and free from the obstructive, obscuring, and binding unwholesome conducts—this is called the One Path.

Furthermore, when one practices the conduct of seclusion alone through heedfulness, diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension—such that this path is born, rightly born, arisen, rightly arisen, and is touched and realized—this is called the single path.

Furthermore, dwelling alone in seclusion and quietude, associating with and sitting alongside [others], or in wilderness places, empty locations, mountain valleys, cliff caves, open spaces, or grass-seated spots; being in forests, thickets, among burial mounds, or by the water's edge, far removed from inhabited villages—such is the path that is born, rightly born, arisen, rightly arisen, touched, and realized. This is called the one path.
Furthermore, when the mind dwells alone, dwells correctly, rests correctly, and enters into meditative concentration, this is called the one path.
Furthermore, that which is consistently supple, tamed, and pure is called the one path.
Furthermore, the complete exhaustion of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the afflictions, hindrances, obscurations, coverings, and fetters of unwholesome conduct—this is called the One Path.
Furthermore, the departure from desire, tranquility, the cultivation of right awakening, the cessation of evil, and the attainment of nirvana—this is called the One Path.
What is the path?
The one-branch path up to the eleven-branch path—this is called the path.

This path is a bridge, a cause, a gate, a root, an arising, a preeminence, a continuity, and an accomplishment; it is the birth of what is rightly born, the arising of what is rightly arisen, and the emergence of what is rightly emerged; it is the harmonious fulfillment of wholesome qualities. This is called the path.
What is meant by the purification of sentient beings?
"Sentient beings" refers to those born within the five realms of existence.

For the sake of sentient beings among humans and devas, it is taught that they should draw near to the four foundations of mindfulness and practice extensively to attain the purification of precepts, the purification of mind, the purification of view, the purification through the prediction of enlightenment and the crossing over of doubt, the purification of knowing the path and what is not the path, the purification of the knowledge and vision of entering the path, and the purification of the attainment of knowledge and vision.
To cause impure sentient beings to become pure and to cause defiled sentient beings to become free from defilement—this is called the purification of sentient beings.
What is meant by being far removed from sorrow and lamentation?
What is sorrow (*daurmanasya*)?
When sentient beings encounter various painful phenomena, they experience sorrow, heavy sorrow, internal burning, and mental fever; this is called sorrow.
What is lamentation (*parideva*)?

It refers to sentient beings who are oppressed by the entanglement of sorrow, fully possessed by the arrows of grief, and whose minds are distracted by distress; they sigh deeply, wail, weep, lament, and speak incoherently, or even strike themselves and utter confused words—this is called *karuṇā* (compassion/sorrow).
Cultivating and training in the four foundations of mindfulness brings one close to the removal of sorrow and lamentation; this is called "removing sorrow and lamentation.
What is meant by "extinguishing suffering and affliction"?
Suffering refers to whatever bodily sensations are painful, from the painful feeling born of eye-contact up to the painful feeling born of body-contact; this is called suffering.
What is vexation?
If the mind perceives suffering and the mental contact results in a painful feeling, this is called vexation.
By drawing near to and practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, suffering and vexation are extinguished; this is called the extinction of suffering and vexation.
What is meant by attaining *nirvāṇa*?
*Nirvāṇa* refers to the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
By drawing near to, practicing, and training in the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one attains the four fruits of the ascetic life; this is what is meant by attaining *nirvāṇa*.
What is meant by abandoning the five hindrances?
To extinguish the five hindrances is what is meant by abandoning the five hindrances.
What is meant by cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness?
That is to say: observing the body within the body, he dwells with diligence, right knowledge, and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow;
observing the body without the body, he dwells with diligence, right knowledge, and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
One dwells contemplating the body as a body internally and externally, with diligence and ardor, with right wisdom and mindfulness, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
It is the same for feelings, the mind, and phenomena.
What is meant by "dwelling contemplating the body as a body"?

The "body" refers to the physical body composed of the four great elements, produced through the causes and conditions of one's parents; it is sustained by food and drink, maintained by appropriate clothing, and nourished by the application of oils. It is a phenomenon subject to impermanence, destruction, and transformation; this is what is called the body.
Furthermore, the "name-body" (nāmakāya) refers to the form-body (rūpakāya).
Furthermore, the earth-body, water-body, fire-body, and wind-body are called name-bodies.
Furthermore, the multitude of elephants, the multitude of horses, the multitude of chariots, and the multitude of infantry are called name-bodies.

Furthermore, the six groups of consciousness, the six groups of contact, the six groups of feeling, the six groups of perception, the six groups of volition, the six groups of craving, the six groups of applied thought, and the six groups of sustained thought—these are called "groups" (kāya).
What is the practice of observing the body in the internal body?

It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all internal physical forms comprised of the four great elements, or certain internal parts of the body comprised of the four great elements, contemplates them as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent; thus, through such diligent observation, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and remains rightly established. This is called the practice of observing the body in the internal body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all internal bodily phenomena comprised within the four great elements and physical form, or those internal phenomena comprised within the four great elements and physical form in a single location, as suffering, an affliction, an abscess, an arrow, a craving for flavors, a disease, dependent on conditions, subject to disintegration, unstable, unsatisfactory, perishable, suffering, empty, and non-self; he contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and accepts their conditions—namely, that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, up to name-and-form being the condition for the six sense bases—and this is called the contemplation of the body in the internal body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates, knows, understands, and accepts the cessation of all internal bodily phenomena comprised within the four great elements and physical form, or the phenomena comprised within the four great elements and physical form in a single internal part: that is, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; and so on, up to the cessation of name-and-form, whereby the six sense bases cease. This is called the contemplation of the body in the internal body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows the pleasure of walking as the pleasure of walking, and so on, up to knowing the pleasure of lying down as the pleasure of lying down; he knows the pleasure of the body’s abiding as it truly is. This is called the internal contemplation of the body in the body.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu goes out or comes in, bends or stretches, turns around, or moves about, he knows it correctly as it occurs; even up to sleeping or waking, speaking or remaining silent, he knows it correctly as it occurs. This is called the contemplation of the body within the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, when breathing out long, knows it is long; when breathing in long, knows it is long; when breathing out short, knows it is short; when breathing in short, knows it is short—just as a turner of a lathe knows when the cord is long and knows when the cord is short. This is called "contemplating the body within the body."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu perceives all manner of impurities from the crown of his head to his feet, and from his feet to the crown of his head; he contemplates that within the body there are hair of the head, hair of the body, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, blood, flesh, sinews, veins, spleen, kidneys, heart, lungs, the large and small excremental organs, feces, urine, mucus, saliva, pus, blood, fat, brain, membranes, tears, sweat, marrow, and bones.

Just as a person with clear vision, looking into a granary through two doors, sees various grains—sesame, black beans, small beans, mung beans, large wheat, and small wheat—so too does a bhikṣu contemplate his own body from the crown of the head to the feet, and from the feet to the crown of the head, seeing it filled with all manner of impurities. This is called the practice of contemplating the body within the internal body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the elements of the body: within this body there are only the elements of earth, water, fire, and air. It is like a skilled butcher or a butcher’s apprentice who, having slaughtered an ox, divides it into four parts; whether sitting, standing, walking, or staying, he sees only those four parts.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates these great elements: this body consists only of the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element. Yet these great elements merely depend on water and fire to arise; they are mutually contradictory, nourished by food and drink, and are feeble and powerless. They are not solid, lack strength, and do not abide for even a single moment. This is called "contemplating the bodily formations within the internal body."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates that the body subsists on food and arises from the accumulation of food; it persists by depending on food and ceases to persist in the absence of food, just as fire burns when dependent on fuel and is extinguished when there is no fuel.

In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as subsisting through nutriment and arising from the accumulation of nutriment; it persists by depending on nutriment and does not persist without nutriment.
As the Buddha said:
"Contemplating the suffering accumulated by the body, one sees that all of it has nutriment as its condition."
If one can eliminate craving for food, then these various sufferings will not exist.
Knowing thus the perilous faults— that food is the accomplishment of suffering—
a bhikṣu who has extinguished craving for food will certainly attain nirvāṇa.
This is called the internal contemplation of the body’s activities.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as entirely empty and universally empty; through mindfulness, he fully knows and understands its practice. This, too, is called the internal contemplation of the body’s activities.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as a festering ulcer. This body has nine orifices that leak fluids, and whatever fluids they discharge are all impure. As Mahākāśyapa said:
"The physical body of the four great elements is characterized by decay, contradiction, and leakage, even unto the brevity of life. This is called the internal contemplation of the body's formations.

Furthermore, regarding all other formations—those phenomena comprised within the internal four great elements of the physical body, or those phenomena comprised within a single part of the internal four great elements of the physical body—one contemplates them so as to attain concentration, and the mind abides and remains correctly established; this is called the practice of observing the body within the internal body.
What is the internal body?
Regarding the body, if it is experienced as being produced from internal conditions, belonging to one's own nature and one's own portion, this is called "internal.
What is the contemplation?
That is to say, when a person of true reality minutely contemplates the understanding of the contemplation of conditions through perfect awakening, this is called "contemplation" (vipaśyanā).
What is "practice" (caryā)?
When such minute contemplation is accomplished, practicing in accordance with the Dharma, maintaining the practice, and practicing subtly—this is called "practice."
What is diligent exertion?
It refers to a person who accords with reality and practices diligence extensively in accordance with the Dharma; this is called diligent exertion.
Furthermore, if one initiates, manifests, transcends, and does not retreat in body and mind, this is called diligent exertion.
What is right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*)?
It refers to the knowledge, vision, understanding, and skillful means of a person who knows reality as it is; this is called right knowledge.
What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?

It refers to the mindfulness of a person who acts in accordance with reality—mindfulness that recollects, subtly recollects, takes as its object, abides in, does not forget, continues uninterruptedly, does not lose, and does not accumulate; this is called mindfulness.
What is mundane [mindfulness]?
There are two kinds of worlds:
the world of sentient beings and the world of formations.
Rebirth within the five destinies is called the world of sentient beings.
The five aggregates of clinging are called the world of formations.
What is greed?
Greed as an unwholesome root is called greed.
What is sorrow (*daurmanasya*)?
The painful sensation born of mental contact is called sorrow.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
Covering, turning away from, understanding, severing, vomiting out, and casting off—this is called "removal.
What is the practice of observing the body in the external body?

If a bhikṣu, regarding all external physical bodies comprised of the four great elements, or a single portion of an external physical body comprised of the four great elements, contemplates impermanence, knows impermanence, understands impermanence, and accepts impermanence; thus practicing this observance with heedfulness, he attains concentration, and his mind dwells in right abiding—this is called the practice of observing the body in the external body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all external phenomena comprised within the four great elements of the physical body, or certain external phenomena comprised within the four great elements of the physical body, as suffering, a boil, an arrow, attachment, a disease, a dependency, a conditioned phenomenon, impermanent, unsatisfactory, subject to decay, suffering, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and perceives their conditions: namely, that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, up to name-and-form being the condition for the six sense bases. This is called the contemplation of the body in terms of the external body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates, knows, understands, and accepts the cessation of all external phenomena comprised within the physical body of the four great elements, as well as those external phenomena comprised within the physical body of the four great elements in a single location: that with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; and so on, up to with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. This is called the contemplation of the body in external bodies.

Furthermore, when one contemplates all other external phenomena comprised by the four great elements and physical bodies, or those phenomena comprised by a single external location and physical body, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells correctly, this is called the contemplation of the body in the external body.
What is the external body?
It refers to that which is not felt, not internal, not dependently arisen, not of intrinsic nature, and not one's own portion; this is called "external.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
What is the practice of observing the body in the internal and external body?

It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all the phenomena comprised within the physical body of the four great elements internally and externally, or even a single portion thereof, observes them as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent; thus observing with heedfulness, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and dwells rightly. This is called the practice of observing the body in the internal and external body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all internal and external material bodies comprised of the four great elements, or a single instance of an internal or external material body comprised of the four great elements, as suffering, a boil, an arrow, attachment, a disease, a dependency on conditions, a disintegrating phenomenon, unstable, incomplete, subject to destruction, suffering, empty, and non-self; he contemplates its conditions, knows its conditions, understands its conditions, and accepts its conditions—from ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, up to contact as the condition for feeling—and this is called the contemplation of the body in terms of the internal and external body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates, knows, understands, and accepts the cessation of all internal and external physical bodies comprised of the four great elements, or the cessation of the physical bodies comprised of the four great elements in a single instance: through the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; and so on, up to the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. This is called the contemplation of the body within the internal and external body.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees a corpse discarded in a cemetery, having been there for one day up to three days, this is called the internal and external contemplation of the body as a body.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees a corpse discarded in a cemetery, bloated and livid for one to three days, this is called "contemplating the body within and without by observing bodily activities."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse discarded in a cemetery, having been there for one to three days, being devoured by crows, birds, tigers, wolves, and various other beasts; this is called the internal and external contemplation of the body’s activities.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse with its bones and joints still connected, bluish-red, putrefied, and corrupted by pus and blood—impure, foul-smelling, loathsome, and disgusting. This is called the internal and external contemplation of the body as a body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse whose skeletal joints are still connected, covered with remaining blood and skin, and whose sinews and veins have not yet severed; this is called the internal and external contemplation of the body’s formations.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose skeletal joints are still connected, though the flesh and blood have already detached while the sinews and veins have not yet severed—this is called the internal and external contemplation of the body within the practice of observing the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse whose bones and joints have already fallen apart but have not yet left their original positions; this is called the practice of observing the body within and without the internal and external body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse whose bones and joints are broken and separated from their original positions, such that the bones of the feet, shins, calves, thighs, hips, spine, ribs, sides, hands, feet, shoulders, arms, neck, and skull each lie in a different place; this is called the practice of observing the body within and without the internal and external body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse whose bones and joints have long been weathered, white as a conch shell, blue as a pigeon, decayed, and shattered; this is called the internal and external contemplation of the body’s movements.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse being burned upon a pyre of fire, where the hair, body hair, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, veins, marrow, and bones—all from the hair down to the marrow—gradually dissolve and vanish. He contemplates this phenomenon as not remaining in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above or below. This phenomenon was originally non-existent and has arisen; having arisen, it returns to extinction. This is called the internal and external contemplation of the body regarding bodily activities.

Furthermore, regarding all other formations comprised within the physical body of the four great elements, or those internal and external formations comprised within the physical body of the four great elements in a single location—when one contemplates these and attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established, this is called "contemplating the body as a body internally and externally."
What is the internal-external body?
Whether it be felt or unfelt, this is called the internal-external body.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.

A bhikṣu contemplates the conditioned arising of the body-dharmas and contemplates the conditioned cessation of the body-dharmas. As a bhikṣu thus contemplates the conditioned arising and conditioned cessation of the body-dharmas, there arises within him mindfulness of the body; through wisdom and clear comprehension, he does not rely on the body, and by practicing without reliance, he does not grasp at the world.
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells contemplating the body within the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world.
He likewise dwells contemplating the body externally and both internally and externally.
What is the practice of observing feelings as feelings?
"Feelings" refers to the six feelings: from feeling born of eye-contact up to feeling born of mind-contact; these are called feelings.
What is the practice of observing internal feelings as feelings?

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates all internal feelings, or internal feelings in a single instance, as impermanent—knowing them to be impermanent, understanding them to be impermanent, and accepting them as impermanent—and thus, through such heedful observation, attains concentration, a settled mind, and right abiding; this is called the practice of contemplating feelings within internal feelings.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all internal feelings, or internal feelings in a specific instance, as suffering, an affliction, a boil, an arrow, a disease, a wound, a calamity, a conditionality, a phenomenon subject to disintegration, unstable, unsatisfactory, perishable, painful, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and experiences their conditions—namely, that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to contact being the condition for feeling. This is called the practice of contemplating feelings by observing internal feelings.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, whether regarding all internal feelings or a specific portion of internal feelings, contemplates their cessation, knows their cessation, understands their cessation, and experiences their cessation: namely, with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; continuing thus, with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. This is called the practice of contemplating feelings within internal feelings.

Furthermore, regarding all other formations, one contemplates all internal feelings and a specific category of internal feelings; by means of this contemplation, one attains concentration, and the mind becomes settled and rightly established. This is called the practice of contemplating feelings within internal feelings.
What is meant by "internal"?
Feeling is called internal; that which is internal, that which is a condition, that which is its own nature, and that which belongs to oneself—this is called internal.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
What is a bhikṣu’s practice of contemplating feelings in external feelings?

It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all external feelings or a certain portion of external feelings, contemplates them as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent; thus practicing with heedfulness, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and remains rightly established. This is called the practice of contemplating feelings in external feelings.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all external feelings, or a single instance of external feeling, as suffering, a calamity, an ulcer, an arrow, a disease, a taste [of pain], dependent on conditions, subject to destruction, unstable, unsatisfactory, perishable, painful, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and experiences their conditions: that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to contact being the condition for feeling. This is called the practice of contemplating feelings regarding external feelings.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all external feelings, or feelings in a single external location, contemplating their cessation, knowing their cessation, understanding their cessation, and experiencing their cessation: that is, with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; continuing in this way until, with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases. This is called the practice of contemplating feelings regarding external feelings.

Furthermore, regarding all other formations and all external feelings—whether it be a single instance of an external feeling—one contemplates them and attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called the practice of contemplating feelings with respect to external feelings.
What is the external?
That which is experienced, practiced, or received is called external; it is not internal, not a condition, not of one's own nature, and not one's own portion—this is termed "external."
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
What is the practice of observing internal and external feelings (*vedanā*)?
