It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all internal and external feelings—or even a single instance of internal or external feeling—contemplates them as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent; thus, through diligent observation, he attains concentration, and his mind becomes settled and rightly established. This is called the practice of observing internal and external feelings.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, whether contemplating all internal and external feelings, or feelings in a single instance internally or externally, contemplates them as suffering, affliction, an ulcer, an arrow, attachment, a disease, dependent on conditions, subject to destruction, impermanent, unsatisfactory, fragile, painful, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and experiences their conditions—namely, that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to contact being the condition for feeling. This is called the practice of observing feelings through the contemplation of internal and external feelings.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all internal and external feelings, or feelings in a single instance, both internally and externally, contemplating their cessation, knowing their cessation, understanding their cessation, and the cessation of feeling itself. That is to say, with the cessation of ignorance, up to the cessation of contact, there is the cessation of feeling; this is called the practice of observing feelings regarding internal and external feelings.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu experiences a pleasant feeling, he knows, "I am experiencing a pleasant feeling";
the same applies to painful feelings and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
If he experiences a defiled pleasant feeling, he knows, "I am experiencing a defiled pleasant feeling."
If one experiences an undefiled pleasant feeling, one knows, "I am experiencing an undefiled pleasant feeling.
It is the same for painful feelings and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
This is called the practice of observing feelings internally and externally.

Furthermore, regarding all other formations—the internal and external feelings, or the feelings of a single location, both internal and external—by contemplating these, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells correctly; this is called the practice of observing feelings through the contemplation of internal and external feelings.
What are internal and external feelings?
If feeling is not [inherently] feeling, this is called "internal and external.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the conditioned arising of the phenomena of feeling and contemplates the conditioned cessation of the phenomena of feeling.

Thus, a bhikṣu contemplates the conditioned arising and cessation of the phenomena of feeling with mindfulness of feeling; internally, through wisdom and clear comprehension, he does not rely on feeling, being without reliance, and practices without grasping at anything in the world.
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells contemplating feelings internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
It is the same for external feelings and for internal-external feelings.
What is the contemplation of the mind’s activities?
What is the mind?
That which is mind, mentation, consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, and the seven elements of consciousness—this is called the mind.
What is the practice of observing the mental states within the internal mind?

It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all internal minds or a portion of the internal mind, contemplates impermanence, knows impermanence, understands impermanence, and accepts impermanence. By thus contemplating with heedfulness, he attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called the practice of observing the mental states within the internal mind.

Furthermore, regarding all internal states of mind, or a single instance of internal state of mind, one contemplates them as suffering, an affliction, an ulcer, an arrow, a disease, a conditionality, a dharma subject to disintegration, unstable, unsatisfactory, perishable, suffering, empty, and non-self; and one contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and experiences their conditions—namely, that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*), and so forth. This is called the contemplation of the mental activities within the internal mind.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all internal states of mind, or a single instance of an internal state of mind, reflecting upon their cessation, knowing their cessation, understanding their cessation, and accepting their cessation: namely, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases. This is called a bhikṣu’s contemplation of the mental activities within the internal mind.

Furthermore, regarding all other mental states or a single mental state, through reflection he attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; in this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the mental activities within his own mind.
What is internal?
If the mind or mental feeling is called internal—being internal, being an object-condition, being intrinsic nature, and being one's own portion—it is termed "internal.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
What is a bhikṣu’s contemplation of the mind by means of the external mind?

It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all external minds or a certain portion of the external mind, contemplates them as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent; thus, through diligent contemplation, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and remains rightly established. This is called the contemplation of the mind by means of the external mind.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all external minds, or a single instance of an external mind, as suffering, an affliction, an ulcer, an arrow, a disease, a taste of pain, dependent on conditions, subject to destruction, unstable, unsatisfactory, perishable, suffering, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and experiences their conditions: namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations, volitional formations condition consciousness, and so forth. This is called the contemplation of the mind’s activities regarding external minds.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all external minds and a single instance of an external mind, contemplating their cessation, knowing their cessation, understanding their cessation, and experiencing their cessation: that is, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases, and so on. This is called the contemplation of the mental formations of the external mind.

Furthermore, regarding all other mental activities—the external mind, the mind focused on a single external object—one contemplates them and attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called the contemplation of the mental activities of the external mind.
What is the external?
That which is not experienced by the mind is called external; it is not internal, not a condition, not of its own nature, and not one's own portion. This is termed "external.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
What is the bhikṣu’s contemplation of the mind with respect to the internal and external mind?

It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all internal and external minds, or a single instance of internal and external mind, contemplates impermanence, knows impermanence, understands impermanence, and accepts impermanence. Through such vigilant observation, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and dwells rightly; this is called the contemplation of the mind with respect to the internal and external mind.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, regarding all internal and external minds, or a single instance of internal or external mind, contemplates them as suffering, an affliction, a boil, an arrow, a disease, a taste [of pain], dependent on conditions, subject to disintegration, unstable, unsatisfactory, perishable, and as suffering, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and accepts their conditions—namely, that ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), and volitional formations condition consciousness, and so forth. This is called the contemplation of the mental activities of internal and external minds.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all internal and external minds, or a single instance of internal and external mind, contemplating their cessation, knowing their cessation, understanding their cessation, and experiencing their cessation: namely, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases, and so on, up to this being called the contemplation of the mental activities of internal and external minds.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu who has a mind with desire knows as it truly is a mind with desire; he knows as it truly is a mind without desire. Even up to a mind that is superior, he knows as it truly is a mind that is superior; a mind that is not superior, he knows as it truly is a mind that is not superior. Thus, through diligent observation, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and remains rightly established. This is called the contemplation of the mind’s activities regarding the internal and external mind.

Furthermore, regarding all other formations—the internal and external mind, or the mind in a single instance, whether internal or external—when one contemplates them and attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells correctly, this is called the contemplation of the mind’s activity with respect to the internal and external mind.
What is the internal-external mind?
It is the mind that is either experienced or not experienced.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the conditioned arising of mental phenomena and the conditioned cessation of mental formations.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the arising and cessation of mental formations, there may arise within him a thought; yet, through wisdom and clear comprehension, he does not rely on that mind, he acts without dependence, and he does not grasp at the world.
In this way, a bhikṣu observes the mind within the mind with diligent effort, with right knowledge and right mindfulness, removing worldly greed and sorrow.
It is the same for observing the mind externally and both internally and externally.
What is the practice of contemplating phenomena (dharma-anupaśyanā)?

"Phenomena" refers to all things other than the physical body composed of the four great elements, including the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations; as well as all else, whether material or immaterial, visible or invisible, resistant or non-resistant, noble or non-noble. These are called phenomena.
What is a bhikṣu’s practice of contemplating phenomena as internal phenomena?

It is when a bhikṣu, setting aside the material body comprised of the four great elements, contemplates all other internal phenomena—or any one category of internal phenomena—as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent. Contemplating thus with heedfulness, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and remains rightly established; this is called the practice of contemplating phenomena as internal phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sets aside the four great elements, the physical body, and the phenomena subsumed under sensation and mind; he then contemplates all other internal phenomena, or any single category of internal phenomena, as suffering, affliction, a boil, an arrow, a disease, a wound, a calamity, conditioned by dependence, subject to destruction, unstable, insatiable, perishable, and as suffering, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and experiences their conditions: namely, that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to birth being the condition for aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—the massing of this entire collection of suffering. This is called the practice of contemplating internal phenomena as phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sets aside the material body comprised of the four great elements, as well as the aggregates of sensation, perception, and consciousness, and all other internal phenomena, or any single instance of an internal phenomenon; he contemplates their cessation, knows their cessation, understands their cessation, and experiences their cessation: namely, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—the entire mass of suffering—cease. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena within internal phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding other formations—excluding those phenomena comprised within the physical body of the four great elements, such as feeling, perception, and mind—if one contemplates all internal phenomena, or a single portion of internal phenomena, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells correctly, this is called the practice of contemplating phenomena as internal phenomena.
What are internal phenomena?
Phenomena that are appropriated are called internal; being internal, being a condition, being one's own nature, and being one's own portion—these are termed "internal.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
What is a bhikṣu’s practice of contemplating phenomena as external phenomena?

It is when a bhikṣu, setting aside the physical body composed of the four great elements and the phenomena included within sensation, mind, and mental factors, contemplates all external phenomena—or phenomena in a particular external location—as impermanent, knowing them as impermanent, understanding them as impermanent, and accepting them as impermanent. By observing thus with heedfulness, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and dwells rightly; this is called the practice of contemplating phenomena as external phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sets aside the four great elements, the physical body, and the phenomena comprised of feeling and mind; he then contemplates all other external phenomena, or any single instance of an external phenomenon, according to reality as being suffering, a boil, an arrow, a malady, a danger, a dependency, a conditioned dharma, unstable, insatiable, subject to decay, painful, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and experiences their conditions: namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, up to birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—the massing of this entire aggregate of suffering. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena by observing external phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sets aside the physical body composed of the four great elements, as well as the phenomena pertaining to feeling and mind, and all other external phenomena, or even a single instance of an external phenomenon. He contemplates them according to reality: he contemplates their cessation, knows their cessation, understands their cessation, and accepts their cessation. Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; and so on, until with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and despair—the entire mass of suffering—cease. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena by way of external phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding other formations—excluding the four great elements, the physical body, and the factors subsumed under sensation and mind—one contemplates all external phenomena, or external phenomena in a single location, as they actually are; by so reflecting, one attains a concentrated mind that abides and dwells correctly. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena through external phenomena.
What are external phenomena (*bahirdhā-dharma*)?
Phenomena that are not felt are called "external"; they are not internal, not conditioned by [the self], not of one's own nature, and not part of one's own domain. This is termed "external.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
What is a bhikṣu’s practice of contemplating phenomena regarding internal and external phenomena?

It is when a bhikṣu, setting aside the material body composed of the four great elements, contemplates all internal and external phenomena—or a specific portion of them—according to their actual nature as impermanent; he knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent. Thus, through diligent contemplation, he attains concentration such that his mind abides and is rightly established. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena regarding internal and external phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sets aside the four great elements, the physical body, and the phenomena subsumed under feeling and mind; he then contemplates all other internal and external phenomena, or any specific internal or external phenomenon, as they truly are: as suffering, affliction, an ulcer, an arrow, a sting, a calamity, dependent origination, the nature of conditions that lead to disintegration, instability, insatiability, perishability, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. He contemplates the conditions, knows the conditions, understands the conditions, and experiences the conditions—namely, ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, and so on, up to birth as the condition for aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair, the massing of all these sufferings. This is called the practice of the contemplation of phenomena regarding internal and external phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sets aside the physical body composed of the four great elements, as well as the phenomena of feeling, perception, and volition, along with all other internal and external phenomena, or any single instance of internal or external phenomena. He contemplates them according to reality: their cessation, knowing their cessation, understanding their cessation, and experiencing their cessation. Thus, with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease; and so on, until with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, grief, and the mass of suffering all cease. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena regarding internal and external phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows as it truly is when there is desire within him: "There is desire within me," and he knows as it truly is when there is no desire within him: "There is no desire within me. He knows as it truly is when desire has not yet arisen: "Desire has not yet arisen"; he knows as it truly is when desire is about to arise: "Desire is about to arise"; he knows as it truly is when desire has arisen: "It should be abandoned"; and he knows as it truly is when desire has been abandoned: "It will not arise again. It is the same for ill-will, delusion, torpor, restlessness, regret, and doubt. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena regarding internal and external phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, when there is eye-consciousness, desire, and anger regarding forms within himself, knows as it truly is: "There is eye-consciousness, desire, and anger regarding forms within me";
when there is no eye-consciousness, desire, and anger regarding forms within himself, he knows as it truly is: "There is no eye-consciousness, desire, and anger regarding forms within me."

When desire and ill will have not yet arisen regarding the eye’s consciousness of forms, one knows as it truly is that they have not yet arisen; when desire and ill will have not yet arisen regarding the eye’s consciousness of forms, one knows as it truly is that they will arise; when desire and ill will have presently arisen regarding the eye’s consciousness of forms, one knows as it truly is that they should be abandoned; when desire and ill will have already been abandoned regarding the eye’s consciousness of forms, one knows as it truly is that they will not arise again. It is the same for the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena with respect to internal and external phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, when there is the awakening-factor of mindfulness within him, knows as it really is: "There is the awakening-factor of mindfulness within me"; when there is no awakening-factor of mindfulness within him, he knows as it really is: "There is no awakening-factor of mindfulness within me. He knows as it really is that the awakening-factor of mindfulness which has not yet arisen has not arisen; he knows as it really is that the awakening-factor of mindfulness which has not yet arisen will arise; and he knows as it really is that the awakening-factor of mindfulness which has already arisen is present and being fully cultivated. It is the same for the remaining six awakening-factors. This is called the practice of observing internal and external phenomena by way of phenomena.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows as they truly are suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering; he knows as they truly are the taints, the origin of the taints, the cessation of the taints, and the path leading to the cessation of the taints. This is called the practice of contemplating phenomena regarding internal and external phenomena.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu becomes weary of and detached from all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and enters the realm of the deathless (*amṛta-dhātu*); this is tranquility.

This is the supreme cessation, the extinction of craving for all conditioned formations, which is nirvāṇa. This is called the practice of observing phenomena by way of internal and external phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding all other formations—excluding the material body comprised of the four great elements, as well as sensation, perception, and consciousness—and all other internal and external phenomena, or any single instance of internal or external phenomena, to contemplate them according to their actual nature so that the concentrated mind abides and dwells correctly: this is called the practice of contemplating phenomena through the observation of internal and external phenomena.
What are internal and external phenomena?
Whether a phenomenon is appropriated or unappropriated, these are called internal and external phenomena.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates the practice of the dependent origination of phenomena and contemplates the practice of the dependent cessation of phenomena.

Thus, a bhikṣu contemplates the practice of the arising and ceasing of phenomena; when a phenomenon arises within his mindfulness, he—through wisdom and clear comprehension—does not rely on that phenomenon, practices without dependence, and does not grasp at the world.
In this way, a bhikṣu dwells contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed worldly greed and sorrow.
He does the same for external phenomena and for both internal and external phenomena.

If one practices and trains in the four foundations of mindfulness as they truly are, such fear will arise; one should always practice the mode of non-self toward all worlds, with a mind that is neither elated nor depressed and has no place of abiding. It is impossible for there to be notions of a self, a sentient being, a life-force, or a person; one should always practice the foremost conduct of emptiness.

If one attains this subsequent mind, one does not engage in what is useless, nor does one receive or cling to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles; being unimpeded regarding the three periods of time, one is liberated from the realm of desire and liberated from the realms of form and formlessness, such that cessation occurs and there is no further rebirth—this is the end of suffering.
Just as in the last month of spring, during the height of the summer heat when there are no clouds or mist, a small amount of water in an earthenware vessel quickly boils away and vanishes;

so too, if a bhikṣu attains the subsequent mind, he does not engage in what is unbeneficial, nor does he receive or cling to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, until they are extinguished and do not arise again.
This is called the end of suffering.
Just as a fierce flame blown by the wind is extinguished without moving to another place,
so too, when name-and-form is fanned out by awakening, its exhaustion likewise reaches no destination.
Like a smith forging hot iron, A shooting star vanishes without trace;
As the smelting and casting gradually return to nothingness, Seeking conviction is difficult to attain.
Like rain falling into the ocean, How could the original drops remain?
What liberation could there even be? Because it is empty, it is a serene bliss.
Having relinquished the body and departed from conceptualization, no sensations are perceived;
all activities are utterly stilled, and consciousness likewise ceases of its own accord.
Chapter Seven: Right Exertion (*Samyak-pradhāna*) From the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Section on Non-Inquiry, Chapter Seven: Right Exertion. Question:
How many types of right exertion are there?
Answer: [There are four.]
Fourth. What are the four?
If a bhikṣu wishes that unwholesome and evil states that have not yet arisen do not arise, he arouses desire, exerts himself, strives for excellence, and applies right effort to restrain the mind.

One should apply right effort (*samyakprahāṇa*) by generating desire, exerting oneself, striving forward, and concentrating the mind to surely abandon unwholesome and evil states that have already arisen;
one should apply right effort by generating desire, exerting oneself, striving forward, and concentrating the mind so that wholesome states not yet arisen may arise;

and one should apply right effort by generating desire, exerting oneself, striving forward, and concentrating the mind so that wholesome states already arisen may remain, be perfected through cultivation, not be forgotten, and be further increased and expanded.
How does one desire that unwholesome states which have not yet arisen do not arise?
Unwholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind is called unwholesome and non-virtuous states.
Furthermore, the ten paths of unwholesome action are called unwholesome and non-virtuous states.

Furthermore, the unwholesome roots, that which is associated with the unwholesome roots, and that which arises from the unwholesome roots—whether it be non-object-conditioned or non-sensory—are called evil and unwholesome phenomena (*pāpakā akuśalā dharmāḥ*).

Furthermore, covetousness, ill will, and delusion; anger, resentment, and malice; hypocrisy, envy, parsimony, and stinginess; flattery, guile, deceit, and concealment of faults; lack of shame and lack of dread of blame; self-exaltation and contentious dispute; stubbornness and negligence; pride, arrogance, and overweening pride—all these are called evil and unwholesome phenomena.
Furthermore, the ten unwholesome factors are called evil and unwholesome dharmas.

When such evil and unwholesome dharmas have not yet arisen, have not yet emerged, and have not yet come together, to cause them not to arise, not to emerge, and not to come together within me—this is called "desiring that evil and unwholesome dharmas which have not yet arisen shall not arise."
What is meant by "arousing desire"?
If one desires, intensely desires, wishes to act, wishes to arise, wishes to manifest, wishes to transcend, wishes to attain, wishes to touch, or wishes to realize—this is called arousing desire.
What is called self-exertion?

It is the power of endurance and vigor; desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized—this is called self-exertion.
What is called "exertion" (*vīrya*)?
It is the arousal, manifestation, transcendence, endurance, non-retrogression, diligent application, and cultivation of progress within body and mind; this is termed exertion.
This progressive arising, correct arising, correct birth, contact, and realization is called "superior progress" (*viśeṣa-gāmin*).
What is meant by "collecting the mind"?
Mind, mental consciousness, the six groups of consciousness, and the seven elements of consciousness—these are called "mind."
This mind is gathered, rightly gathered; it is gathered through its objects, urged, and rightly exhorted; it leaps with joy—this is called the gathering of the mind.
What is meant by "right"?
Right cause, right intention, and right effort—these are called "right."
What is meant by "abandonment"?

It is the relinquishing of unwholesome dharmas, the arising of wholesome and pure dharmas, the practice of what is pleasant in the present life, and the abandonment of the outflows through knowledge, vision, wisdom, and discernment, reaching the end of all suffering—this is called abandonment.

"Unwholesome and unskillful states that have already arisen must certainly be abandoned"—this is also said regarding the right effort of exertion, striving, and uplifting the mind with desire, but with the distinction that [in this case] they have already arisen.
What is meant by "desiring that wholesome dharmas not yet arisen may arise"?
Wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind is called wholesome dharmas.
... And what is meant by "abandoning"?

Abandoning unwholesome states and giving rise to wholesome, pure states, practicing for happiness in the present life, and through knowledge, vision, wisdom, and discernment, severing the outflows and exhausting the limit of all suffering—this is called "severance."
What is meant by "desiring that wholesome phenomena which have arisen remain"?
Wholesome conduct of body, speech, and mind is called wholesome phenomena.
Furthermore, there are the ten right factors, from right view up to right knowledge, as well as other factors that accord with the right factors; these are called wholesome phenomena.

When such wholesome qualities arise and come together, causing me to abide in them without loss or forgetfulness and leading me to ultimate perfection—this is called "wholesome qualities having arisen and being established."
What is meant by "fulfillment"?

It refers to the desire to bring fulfillment to the aggregate of ethical discipline that has not yet been fulfilled, and so on, up to the desire to bring fulfillment to the aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation that has not yet been fulfilled; this is called fulfillment.
What is meant by cultivation (*bhāvanā*)?
If one approaches wholesome dharmas, correctly approaches them, relies upon them, and diligently practices and trains in them, this is called cultivation.
What is meant by non-forgetfulness?
To cause wholesome dharmas not to be lost or taken away, and to maintain their continuity so that mindfulness does not forget them—this is called "non-forgetfulness.
What is meant by "increasing and expanding"?
To cause wholesome dharmas to grow, expand, and advance—this is called "increasing and expanding."
Furthermore, what is meant by "abandonment"?

It is the relinquishing of unwholesome states, the arising of wholesome and pure states, practicing for happiness in the present life, and through knowledge, vision, wisdom, and discernment, severing all taints and reaching the end of all suffering—this is called abandonment.
Chapter 8: The Chapter on the Bases of Psychic Power (Ṛddhipāda) from the Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra, Section on Non-Questions. Question:
How many bases of psychic power are there?
Answer: [The following follows].
The four are:

the basis for spiritual power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of desire accompanied by the factors of exertion; the basis for spiritual power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of energy; the basis for spiritual power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of mind; and the basis for spiritual power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of wisdom accompanied by the factors of exertion.
What is desire (*chanda*)?

It refers to the wish to revere, the wish to act, the wish to initiate, the wish to manifest, the wish to transcend, the wish to attain, the wish to touch, the wish to understand, and the wish to realize; this is called desire.
What is concentration?
If the mind abides and dwells correctly, this is called concentration.
Such desire and such concentration are called "desire-concentration" (*chanda-samādhi*).

Furthermore, when one attains concentration by taking desire as the primary factor—desiring it, inclining toward it, relying on it, tending toward it, and increasing it—and the mind abides and remains rightly established, this is called concentration through desire (*chanda-samādhi*).
Furthermore, when wholesome desire arises and brings about concentration, the mind abides and remains rightly established;
when unwholesome desire arises and brings about concentration, the mind abides and remains rightly established;
and when neutral desire arises and brings about concentration, the mind abides and remains rightly established—this is called concentration through desire (*chanda-samādhi*).
Furthermore, when one does not wish to practice virtue, one reflects to oneself:
"This is not what is good for me, nor what I delight in, nor what is appropriate, nor what should be practiced, nor the time for my practice; why then do I not wish to practice virtue?"
One thus attains concentration by taking desire as the primary factor; the mind abides and remains correctly established—this is called concentration through desire (*chanda-samādhi*).
Furthermore, when one practices wholesome dharmas through desire, one reflects to oneself:
"This is what is wholesome for me; this is what I prefer; this is what is appropriate; this is what I am practicing; this is the time for my practice; I desire to practice the wholesome."
When one attains concentration through desire as the primary factor, the mind abides and remains rightly established; this is called "concentration through desire" (*chanda-samādhi*).
Furthermore, when wholesome desire does not arise, and unwholesome desire arises after wholesome desire has ceased, one acts in conjunction with greed, hatred, and delusion.

Then, one reflects to oneself: "This is not what is good for me, not what I prefer, not what is appropriate, not my proper conduct, nor the time for such conduct. Why do I not desire to practice what is wholesome, yet instead act in conjunction with greed, hatred, and delusion?"
Venerable sir, when one wishes to attain concentration and the mind abides in right abiding, this is called "concentration through desire.

Furthermore, when unwholesome desires do not arise, and having ceased unwholesome desires, wholesome desire arises, such that one does not act in association with greed, hatred, or delusion, but reflects to oneself:

"This is what is wholesome for me; this is what I prefer; this is what I ought to do; this is my practice; this is the time for my practice. I wish to practice what is wholesome, acting without association with greed, hatred, or delusion."
Taking wholesome desire as supreme, one attains concentration; the mind abides and is rightly established—this is called "concentration through desire.
What is "abandonment"?

Drawing the mind toward wholesome states, drawing it toward correctness, and drawing it toward pliancy; being rightly pliant, rightly stilled, not losing [the object], and not shifting—this is called "abandonment."
Furthermore, the arousal, manifestation, transcendence, endurance, exertion, and non-retrogression of body and mind is called abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Furthermore, the cultivation of the four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*) is called abandonment.

Furthermore, the abandoning of evil and unwholesome states, the arising of wholesome states, practicing for happiness in the present life, and through knowledge, vision, wisdom, and discernment, severing all taints and exhausting the very limit of suffering—this is called abandonment.
What are the formations of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃskāra*)?
Pleasure, joy, faith, equanimity, mindfulness, and right knowledge—these are called the formations of abandonment.

Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment of the basis for spiritual power through the concentration of desire and the formations of abandonment: with the exception of desire, diligence, mind, and wisdom, the remaining concomitant factors—feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, applied thought, sustained thought, liberation, serene confidence, pleasure, joy, mental confidence, heedfulness, mindfulness, equanimity of mind, bodily diligence, and the remaining concomitant forms—are called the formations of abandonment.
What is accomplishment?

It is the full possession of the arising together, the concurrent arising, the correct arising, the experiencing, and the generation of the concentration of desire for abandonment along with the formative forces of abandonment; this is called accomplishment.
What is cultivation?

This is the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration through desire, accomplished by the formative forces of abandonment; to approach it, to approach it correctly, to rely upon it, to rely upon it correctly, and to practice it with diligent application and training—this is called cultivation.
What is the supernormal power (*ṛddhi*)?
It refers to the supernormal power of the mind, the transformation of the mind, and the mastery of the mind through which one performs various transformations; this is called supernormal power.

Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu who possesses great supernormal power, capable of immeasurable transformations and shaking the great earth; he can turn one into many and many into one, and whether regarding near or distant objects, or walls and high mountains, he passes through them without obstruction as if walking through empty space.

Sitting cross-legged, he traverses the void like a bird; he enters and emerges from the earth as if entering and emerging from water; he treads upon water as if on land; his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire; with his hand he touches the sun and moon in their majestic splendor; and even up to the Brahma Heaven, his body attains mastery—this is called supernatural power (*ṛddhi*).
What is meant by "basis" (pāda)?

It is that which is like the application of energy for the sake of attaining concentration; it is the basis, the equality, the cause, the gateway, the function, the path, the arrival, the condition, the sequence, and the power.
The divine power arises rightly, is produced rightly, is brought forth rightly, and issues forth rightly; it is as one wishes and exactly as intended—this is called the basis.

If a bhikṣu, desiring to cultivate the basis of psychic power through the accomplishment of concentration and the exertion of effort, should wish: "May my desire be neither too high nor too low, neither sinking nor scattering; may I maintain constant mindfulness of what precedes and follows, so that the former is like the latter and the latter is like the former, as by day is by night and as by night is by day, and my mind is awakened and free from obscuration."

In the clear understanding of practice, one steadies the mind with the body and steadies the body with the mind; with perceptions of joy and perceptions of lightness, one acts throughout the entire body.
What is inferior desire?

If one desires that which is associated with indolence—failing to exert effort, failing to encourage oneself, abandoning what is wholesome, and retreating from the Dharma—this is called inferior desire.
What is indolence?
To be slothful, lethargic, and mentally dull regarding wholesome dharmas, thereby falling away from them—this is called indolence.
If one wishes to associate with indolence, failing to exert effort, failing to encourage oneself, and falling away from wholesome dharmas—this is called inferior desire.
What is high desire (*uddhacca-chanda*)?
If desire is associated with agitation (*auddhatya*) and not associated with tranquility (*śamatha*), and it accomplishes distracted conduct, this is called high desire.
What is agitation?
If the mind is distracted and not tranquil, this is called agitation (*auddhatya*).
If one desires that which is associated with agitation and not associated with tranquility, thereby accomplishing a distracted course of action, this is called high desire (*unnata-chanda*).
What is the submergence of desire?

If desire is associated with sleep and not associated with the cessation of mindfulness, such that wisdom is not accomplished and wholesome dharmas are not distinguished, this is called the submergence of desire.
What is sleep?
When afflictions have not been severed, the body is neither at ease, nor composed, nor light, nor supple, nor free from [impurities]; this is called sleep.
What is torpor (*middha*)?
When defilements have not been abandoned, the mind is dazed and obscured; this is called torpor.

If one desires to associate with sleep and dissociate from mindfulness, such that wisdom is not accomplished and wholesome phenomena are not distinguished, this is called being submerged in desire (*līnacchanda*).
What is the scattering of desire?

It is the arising of desire-taint, being associated with desire-taint; having much desire and viewing things as pure while failing to contemplate their defects, the mind scatters toward the five external sense-objects, becoming attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—this is called the scattering of desire.
What is sensual attachment?

Whatever is desire for sensual pleasures, craving for sensual pleasures, affection for sensual pleasures, delight in sensual pleasures, the branch of sensual pleasures, the net of sensual pleasures, the endurance of sensual pleasures, the acquisition of sensual pleasures, the accumulation of sensual pleasures, and the longing for sensual pleasures—this is called sensual attachment.

If one desires to incline toward sensual defilement, being associated with and conjoined to sensual defilement; if one has much desire and views [objects] as pure while failing to contemplate their faults; and if the mind is distracted by the five external sense objects, becoming attached to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—this is called "distracted desire."
What is the constant practice of walking meditation before and after [other activities]?

If a bhikṣu, having walked in the morning, reflects upon the matter as it is, enters into wholesome dharmas, enters the supramundane state, and attains nirvāṇa, being associated with the concentration of detachment;

having finished walking in the morning, he walks at midday; having finished walking at midday, he walks in the afternoon; having finished walking in the afternoon, he walks on the upper terrace; having finished walking on the upper terrace, he walks on the lower terrace; having finished walking on the lower terrace, he enters his room; having entered his room, he walks during the first watch of the night; having finished walking during the first watch of the night, he walks during the last watch of the night; and having finished walking during the last watch of the night, he reflects upon the matter as it is, enters into wholesome dharmas, enters the supramundane state, and attains nirvāṇa, being associated with the concentration of detachment—this is called the constant practice of walking meditation before and after.
What is meant by "the former being like the latter, and the latter being like the former"? It is as follows:

a bhikṣu practices in accordance with the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and meditative attainments before he enters concentration; he practices in accordance with the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and meditative attainments after he has entered concentration.

Having practiced in accordance with the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and meditative attainments after entering concentration, he then practices in accordance with the faculties, powers, factors of awakening, dhyānas, liberations, concentrations, and meditative attainments both before and after entering concentration. This is called "the former being like the latter, and the latter being like the former."
What is meant by "day as night and night as day"?
It is when a bhikṣu, having taken up the perception of light and properly cultivated the perception of day, subsequently contemplates the perception of light during the day as he does at night;
and just as he does at night, so too does he do during the day. This is called "day as night and night as day."
What is meant by "the mind being awakened and free from obscuration"?

If there are the stains of greed, hatred, and delusion; the stains of afflictions; the obscurations, coverings, fetters, and stains of unwholesome conduct—these are what obstruct the mind, do not open the mind, cover the mind, veil the mind, give rise to a bound and impure mind, and constitute a mind that is neither bright nor clear. This is called the obscured mind.
If the mind is free from the stains of greed, hatred, and delusion, up to and including the clarity of mind, this is called the mind being awakened and devoid of obscuration.
How does one cultivate the mind that possesses luminosity?

If a bhikṣu cultivates a mind accompanied by the radiance of wisdom, he cultivates a mind possessed of clarity; he cultivates a mind accompanied by the perception of clarity, he cultivates a mind possessed of clarity.
What is the mind accompanied by the radiance of wisdom?
If one illuminates with the three types of wisdom—namely, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation—this is called the mind of common wisdom-light.
If one draws near to, closely attends to, and diligently practices and trains in this, it is called the cultivation of the mind of common wisdom-light, the cultivation of the luminous mind.
What is the mind associated with the perception of light?

If a bhikṣu takes up various signs of light—such as the light of fire, the light of the sun and moon, the light of jewels, or the light of the stars—and having taken up these signs of light, contemplates the light while under a tree or in the open air, knowing the light, understanding the light, and experiencing the light; whatever perception, recollection, or cognition of perception such a person of reality possesses, this is called the mind of the perception of light.
If it arises together with the perception of light, abides together with it, and ceases together with it, this is called the mind associated with the perception of light.

If one draws near to it, approaches it closely, and diligently practices and trains in it, this is called the cultivation of the mind associated with the perception of light, the cultivation of the mind possessed of light.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in an open space, with a pure mind, practices the universal liberation and possesses a superior mind of clarity—whatever perceptions, recollections, or cognitions such a person of reality has—this is called the perception of clarity of mind.
If it arises together with the perception of light, abides together with it, and ceases together with it, this is called the mind associated with the perception of light.

If one draws near to it, approaches it closely, and diligently practices and trains in it, this is called the cultivation of the mind associated with the perception of light, which is the cultivation of the mind possessing light.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, whether under one tree, two, three, or even ten trees, with a pure mind, practices the pervasive liberation and possesses a superior mind of clear knowledge (*vidyā*). This is called cultivating the mind associated with the perception of clear knowledge, and cultivating the mind possessing clear knowledge.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu, with a pure mind, practices universal liberation within a single grove, this is called cultivating a mind associated with the perception of light, a mind that possesses light.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu, with a pure mind, practices universal liberation in one garden, or two, or three, up to ten gardens, this is called cultivating the mind associated with the perception of light, and cultivating a mind possessed of light.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, regarding one village, or two, or three, up to ten villages, practices with a pure mind through universal understanding and application; this is called cultivating the mind associated with the perception of light, and cultivating a mind possessed of light.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, extending even to the waters and the land on all sides, practices with a pure mind through universal application; this is called cultivating the mind associated with the perception of light, and cultivating the mind possessed of light.
What is meant by stabilizing the mind with the body and stabilizing the body with the mind?
It is when a bhikṣu, with his mind, holds the body up, raises it up, and fully uplifts it—
just as a person carrying a bowl for almsfood holds the bowl in a carrying-net, holding it up, raising it up, and fully uplifting it.
In this way, a bhikṣu uplifts and thoroughly uplifts the body with the mind.
How does a bhikṣu stabilize the mind by means of the body?

If a bhikṣu contemplates the body as impermanent—knowing it as impermanent, understanding it as impermanent, and accepting it as impermanent—and through such vigilant observation attains a concentrated mind that dwells and remains correctly established, characterized by bodily bliss, bodily composure, bodily lightness, bodily pliancy, and bodily tranquility, this is called stabilizing the mind by means of the body.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu contemplates the body as being afflicted by the suffering of a boil and an arrow, as a source of vexation, as subject to conditions, as subject to disintegration, as impermanent, as unsatisfactory, as fragile, as suffering, empty, and non-self; and when he contemplates its conditions, knows its conditions, understands its conditions, and accepts its conditions—namely, that ignorance is the condition for volitional formations, and so on up to name-and-form being the condition for the six sense bases—and thus, through such heedful observation, attains concentration, with the mind abiding and rightly established, resulting in bodily pleasure, bodily composure, bodily lightness, bodily pliancy, and bodily tranquility; this is called "stabilizing the mind by means of the body."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the cessation of the body, knows its cessation, understands its cessation, and accepts its cessation: namely, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease. Thus, through diligent observation he attains concentration; his mind becomes settled and rightly established, and his body becomes blissful, pliant, light, supple, and free from hindrance. This is called "stabilizing the mind by means of the body."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows the pleasure of walking when walking, knows the pleasure of standing when standing, knows the pleasure of sitting when sitting, and knows the pleasure of reclining when reclining. Thus, he knows as it truly is that the body dwells in pleasure and that he dwells in pleasure. By observing thus with heedfulness, he attains concentration; his mind becomes settled and rightly established. His body becomes blissful, composed, light, supple, and free from affliction. This is called "stabilizing the mind by means of the body."

Furthermore, monks, when a monk sees a corpse being burned on a pyre of fire, with its hair, body hair, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, and marrow gradually consumed until nothing remains, he contemplates this phenomenon as not going to the east, west, south, north, the four intermediate directions, or above or below, nor does it go to any other place to abide; this phenomenon was originally non-existent and has arisen, and having existed, it returns to extinction.

Contemplating the body as having such a nature, one attains concentration through heedful contemplation; the mind abides and is rightly established, thereby attaining bodily bliss, bodily composure, bodily lightness, bodily pliancy, and bodily tranquility. This is called "stabilizing the mind by means of the body. This section contains thirty-four items; furthermore, because the explanation of stabilizing the mind by means of the body is no different from what is taught in the *Ekāṅga-mārga* (The Single-Limb Path), it is abbreviated here.
How does a bhikṣu stabilize the body by means of the mind?

It is when a bhikṣu contemplates the mind as impermanent, knows the mind as impermanent, understands the mind as impermanent, and experiences the mind as impermanent; thus, through diligent observation, he attains concentration, and his mind dwells in right abiding, attaining mental joy, mental composure, mental lightness, mental pliancy, and mental tranquility. This is called stabilizing the body by means of the mind.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the mind as suffering, affliction, a boil, an arrow, a malady, a danger, dependent on conditions, subject to disintegration, unstable, insatiable, perishable, and characterized by suffering, emptiness, and non-self; he reflects upon conditions, knows conditions, understands conditions, and accepts conditions: namely, with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations, and with volitional formations as condition there is consciousness.

Thus, through heedful contemplation, one attains concentration; the mind abides and dwells rightly, attaining mental joy, pliancy, lightness, flexibility, and tranquility. This is called "stabilizing the body by means of the mind."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the cessation of the mind, knows its cessation, understands its cessation, and experiences its cessation: namely, with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases.

Thus, through heedfulness, one attains concentration; the mind abides and remains rightly settled, attaining mental joy, pliancy, lightness, flexibility, and tranquility. This is called "stabilizing the body by means of the mind."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu truly knows a mind with desire as a mind with desire, and truly knows a mind without desire as a mind without desire; he likewise truly knows a mind that is excelled by another as a mind excelled by another, and a mind that is not excelled by another as a mind not excelled by another.

Thus, through heedful contemplation, one attains concentration; the mind abides and is rightly established, attaining mental joy, pliancy, lightness, flexibility, and tranquility. This is called "stabilizing the body by means of the mind."
What is the perception of pleasure and the mental application regarding the practice of the higher body?
What is the perception of pleasure?

It is when a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and happiness.
If the body is suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, it becomes moistened and saturated;
this entire body is suffused with the rapture and happiness born of seclusion, becoming moistened and saturated without any part remaining unsuffused.

It is like a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice who places fine bath-powder in a vessel, sprinkles it with water, and kneads it into a ball; this ball is moistened and saturated throughout, neither too dry nor too wet, being perfectly supple both inside and out.

In this way, the bhikṣu’s body is completely saturated with the moisture of the joy and happiness born of seclusion; this entire body is thoroughly suffused with the moisture of the joy and happiness born of seclusion, without any part remaining unsuffused.
Whatever perception, recollection, or cognition a person of suchness may have is called the perception of pleasure.
This perception is a subtle experience of the body, a direct subtle experience, and an objective subtle experience.
By means of which body is it experienced?

Experiencing this with the mind and body, this is called the attainment of the second dhyāna, characterized by joy and bliss born of concentration, free from directed thought and evaluation, with internal purity and confidence.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu, with the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, and with internal clarity and confidence, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from directed thought and evaluation, born of concentration, and filled with joy and bliss. This is called the practice of the second dhyāna.
If this body is filled with the joy and bliss born of concentration, such that a moisture of joy and bliss pervades the entire body without exception, leaving no part unfulfilled—

just as a great lake surrounded by mountains has water gushing up from its own depths, with no water coming from the east, west, south, or north, and the lake’s water flows forth from within, so that the moisture of the lake pervades it entirely without decrease.

In this way, monks, this body is completely saturated with the moisture of rapture born of concentration; the entire body is suffused with the moisture of rapture born of concentration, such that there is no part of it that is not fully pervaded.
Whatever perception or recollection a person of suchness has is called the perception of pleasure.
This perception is a subtle sensation of the body, a direct subtle sensation, and a subtle sensation conditioned by the object.
By means of which body is it experienced?
Experiencing it with the mind and body—this is called the practice of the higher body characterized by the perception of pleasure.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, detached from joy, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing pleasure with the body; he attains and abides in the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and pleasure."

If this body is filled with the moisture of joyless bliss, and this body is entirely filled with that joyless bliss without any decrease—just as in a pond of *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, or *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, where the *utpala* flowers up to the *puṇḍarīka* flowers have emerged from the mud but have not yet risen above the water; whether it be the roots or the tips of these flowers, they are entirely filled with the moisture of the water, from root to tip and from tip to root, entirely filled without any decrease.
In this way, when a bhikṣu’s body is completely suffused with the moisture of joy and bliss, his entire body is thoroughly suffused with this moisture without any diminution.
Whatever perception, recollective perception, or cognitive perception a person of such reality possesses is called the perception of bliss.
If one wishes to contemplate the subtle feelings of the body, the correct subtle feelings, and the conditioned subtle feelings:
by means of which body are they experienced? They are experienced by the mental body.
This is called the practice of the higher body with the perception of pleasure.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, having abandoned pleasure and pain and previously extinguished sorrow and joy, attains the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.
If one practices universal understanding with a pure mind regarding this body, there will be no part of this body that is not purified.
It is like a man or a woman wearing clean white garments, complete from top to bottom; from head to foot and from foot to head, there is no place that is not covered.
Just as when a bhikṣu thoroughly practices the contemplation of this body with a pure mind, there is no part of this body that is not pervaded by purity.
Whatever perception, recollection, or cognitive perception a person of such reality has, this is called the perception of pleasure.
This perception of the body is a subtle feeling, a truly subtle feeling, and a feeling conditioned by subtlety.
By what body is it experienced?
It is experienced by the mental body.
This is called the practice of the perception of lightness in the upper body.
What is the perception of lightness?

It is when a bhikṣu contemplates the body as light, knows it as light, understands it as light, and experiences it as light—just as cotton wool is light, or as a karpāsa cloth is light; if it were laid upon level ground, even a slight breeze would cause it to rise off the earth.

In this way, the bhikṣu contemplates the lightness of the body, knows its lightness, understands its lightness, and experiences its lightness. Thus, through diligent observation, he attains concentration; his mind abides and remains rightly established. Having attained concentration, he rises into the air at a height of four inches above the ground.
Whatever perception, recollection, or cognition a person of suchness may have, this is called a subtle perception.
This perception is a subtle bodily feeling, a truly subtle feeling, and a condition-based subtle feeling.
By means of which body does one experience it?
One experiences it with the body through the mind;
this is called the perception of lightness associated with the upper part of the body.

If a bhikṣu becomes intimate with and frequently cultivates this concentration, he may rise one foot above the ground or two feet above the ground. Whatever a person of true realization perceives, recollects, or cognizes in this regard is called the perception of lightness.
This perception of the body is a subtle feeling, a truly subtle feeling, and a feeling conditioned by subtlety.
By what body does one experience it? One experiences it by the mental body (*manomaya-kāya*).
This is called the perception of lightness leading to upward movement of the body.
If a bhikṣu closely approaches and frequently cultivates this concentration, he can move upward to the height of half a person, one person, two persons, and so on, up to seven persons.
Whatever perception, ideation, or cognition a person of suchness has, this is called light perception.
If this perception is experienced subtly by the body, correctly experienced subtly, or perceived as a subtle object-condition.
By what body does one experience it?
One experiences it by the mental body.
This is called the light perception arising in the upper body.
If a bhikṣu closely approaches and frequently cultivates this concentration, he may rise up to a height of half a *tāla* tree, or one *tāla* tree, and even as far as seven *tāla* trees.
Whatever perception, recollection, or cognition a person of suchness may have, this is called a subtle perception.
This perception is a subtle bodily feeling, a truly subtle feeling, and a condition-based subtle feeling.
By what body does one experience it?
With mind and body experiencing [lightness], this is called the minor perception that ascends through the body.

If a bhikṣu closely approaches and frequently cultivates this concentration, he can, according to his wish, travel above the ground without limit; whether near or far, he is able to abide wherever he desires.
Whatever perception, ideation, or cognition a person of suchness may have is called a subtle perception.
If this perception is experienced subtly by the body, correctly experienced subtly, or perceived as a subtle object-condition, it is so designated.
By which body is it experienced?
It is experienced by the mental body.
This is called the perception of lightness arising in the upper part of the body.

If a bhikṣu closely approaches, thoroughly attends to, and frequently cultivates the perception of light and the perception of joy, desiring to bring his mind under control, to make it tranquil, and to attain mastery through power, he will accomplish various bases of supernormal power according to his wish.

If, having cultivated, closely approached, and extensively practiced those perceptions of pleasure and perceptions of lightness, his mind becomes pliant and tranquil; then, through the mastery of power, he achieves various supernormal powers (ṛddhi) according to his wishes.

He attains various and immeasurable supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), by which he can shake the great earth; he can make one into many and many into one; whether near or far, he rises above walls and passes through them without obstruction, as if walking through empty space.

Seated in the full lotus posture, he travels through the air like a bird; he appears and disappears from the earth as if entering and emerging from water; he treads upon water as if it were solid ground; his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire; and with hands possessing great majesty and power, he can even touch the sun and moon, attaining mastery of his body up to the Brahma-heaven, as described in detail in the "Chapter on Samādhi."
This is called the basis of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) consisting in the cultivation of concentration of desire and the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment.

The bases of psychic power consisting in the cultivation of concentration of energy, concentration of mind, and concentration of wisdom, accompanied by the accomplishment of the formations of abandonment, are also to be explained in detail in the same way.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Thirteen;
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Fourteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated by Dharmagupta and others.

Chapter Nine: Dhyāna, Part on Non-Questioning. Section Nine: Dhyāna. When the requisite conditions are complete, one can attain concentration; when the requisite conditions are incomplete, one cannot attain concentration.

The cultivation of meditative concentration has such causes and conditions: namely, that a bhikṣu protects the precepts of liberation, accomplishes dignified conduct, guards even the minor rules regarding his sphere of activity as if they were diamonds, upholds the precepts, abandons wrong livelihood and practices right livelihood, associates with virtuous friends, virtuous intimates, and virtuous assemblies, restrains the gates of the sensory faculties, is moderate in eating, exerts himself with diligent effort without sleeping at the beginning [of the night], and remains free from obstructive states.

In this way, a bhikṣu knows how to abandon the five hindrances—the defilements of the mind that impair wisdom—and, free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss; continuing in this manner until, having abandoned pleasure and pain and previously extinguished sorrow and joy, he attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is purified by equanimity and mindfulness.
What is meant by guarding the precepts of liberation?

It is to accord with the precepts and not practice negligence, taking the precepts as one's gate, one's feet, and one's cause, thereby being able to give rise to and fully accomplish wholesome dharmas; because of these precepts, it is called "upholding the precepts."
Following this with heedfulness is called maintaining the observance of dignified conduct; this is what is meant by cherishing and protecting the precepts of liberation.
How does one accomplish the practice of dignified conduct?
All unwholesome conduct of body, all unwholesome conduct of speech, and all unwholesome conduct of mind—these are called non-observance of decorum (*anairyāpathika*).
All wholesome conduct of body, all wholesome conduct of speech, and all wholesome conduct of mind—these are called accomplishment of observance of decorum (*airyāpathika-sampanna*).

Furthermore, to show reverence toward one’s preceptor (*upādhyāya*) and the preceptor’s fellow students, to show reverence toward one’s *ācārya* and the *ācārya*’s fellow students, and to show reverence toward those of superior and inferior seating rank—this is called the practice of dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*).
What are the improper places to frequent?

There are six improper places to frequent: the quarters of courtesans, the quarters of widows, the quarters of unmarried maidens, the quarters of eunuchs, the quarters of bhikṣuṇīs, and taverns; these are called the six improper places to frequent.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:
"O bhikṣus!
Do not go to other countries that are not places you have previously traveled."
If one goes to another country that is not a place where one has previously traveled, Māra will find an opportunity.
Bhikṣus! What is meant by "another country that is not a place where one has previously traveled"?
This refers to the five objects of desire.
This is called "reaching the five objects of desire but not yet having traversed their domain.
What is meant by "having traversed their domain"?

If that is not proper conduct and this is not a place where one has previously practiced, to abandon it, to rightly abandon it, to abandon it by way of its conditions; to not associate with it, to rightly not associate with it, to not associate with it by way of its conditions—this is called a place where one has already practiced.
Furthermore, as the Buddha said:

"If one walks upon the ground where one has already walked in one's own country, and if a bhikṣu walks upon the ground where he has already walked in his own country, Māra will find no opportunity. Bhikṣus!
What is meant by "one's own domain as a place already traversed"?
It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness;
these are one's own domain as a place already traversed.
If one practices with such deportment, arising correctly and experiencing correctly, this is called the accomplishment of practiced deportment.
What is meant by "guarding the subtle precepts with fear as if they were a vajra"?

If, regarding even the most subtle precepts—whether through mental recollection, the arousal of intention, or the desire for collective action—one frequently gives rise to a sense of dread toward them, thinking, "May I not transgress," this is called fearing even the subtlest precepts as one would a vajra.
What is meant by upholding the precepts?

If a bhikṣu does not depart from any precept, constantly maintains all precepts, always abides in all precepts, and remains close to the precepts; if he upholds the precepts without flaw, without defilement, without stain, without laxity, and without deficiency, thus upholding all precepts—this is called upholding the precepts.
How does one abandon wrong livelihood and practice right livelihood? What is wrong livelihood?

It refers to when śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas sustain themselves through wrong livelihood, namely: by flattery and deceitful boasting; by divining good or bad fortune; by acting as a messenger for others; by using gestures to incite others; and by seeking profit from profit. By these unlawful means, they obtain robes, bowls, medicine, bedding, and other necessities for their use and sustenance. Through this, they become bound by defilement and attachment, treating others with contempt, enduring what is unlawful, failing to see its faults, and lacking knowledge of the transcendence of the world.

If a bhikṣu is free from such wrong livelihoods, obtaining robes, bowls, medicine, bedding, and other necessary requisites in accordance with the Dharma, and consuming food without being bound by or attached to them through craving, nor disparaging others; if he cannot tolerate what is contrary to the Dharma, deeply perceives its faults and dangers, and understands the transcendence of the world—this is called abandoning wrong livelihood and practicing right livelihood.

What is a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*)? It refers to a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who upholds the precepts and is virtuous; who has severed arrogance and negligence; who is accomplished in patience; who has trained himself, extinguished himself, and entered *nirvāṇa* by himself; who desires to leave desire behind and exhausts desire, and so on, up to desiring to leave delusion behind and exhausting delusion; who is not stained where he ought to be stained, and so on, up to not being deluded where he ought to be deluded, not ceasing where he ought to cease, and not grasping where he ought to grasp; whose actions of body, speech, and mind are pure, and whose livelihood is pure; who practices faith, shame, and remorse; who is learned and diligent; who cultivates mindfulness and wisdom; who is fully endowed with the eightfold path; and who possesses morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; who is content with food and clothing. This is called a spiritual friend.
What is meant by "knowledge"?

If one knows and recognizes those who practice loving-kindness together, practice loving-kindness with earnestness, and practice loving-kindness to its ultimate extent—those who are ever-reverent and never depart from it—these are called "good friends" (kalyāṇamitra).
What is meant by being a virtuous and close friend?

A worldling who observes the precepts is a virtuous and close friend to a worldling who observes the precepts; one of firm faith is a virtuous and close friend to one of firm faith; one of firm Dharma is a virtuous and close friend to one of firm Dharma; and so on, up to an Arhat being a virtuous and close friend to an Arhat.
Those who are thus personally and mutually intimate are called "intimate.

Whether they be spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) or those who are virtuous intimates, if one follows them without separation and remains close to them, these are called "spiritual friends" and "virtuous intimates."
What is a virtuous assembly?

It is when one who relies on a person of ethical discipline learns ethical discipline, directing the mind toward them, honoring them, inclining toward them, and understanding them; or when one who relies on a person of meditative concentration learns concentration, and so on up to a person of liberation-knowledge-and-vision learning liberation-knowledge-and-vision, directing the mind toward them, honoring them, inclining toward them, and understanding them—this is called a virtuous assembly.
What is the restraint of the sense-faculties?

If a bhikṣu, seeing forms with the eye, does not grasp at their signs, he is able to exercise restraint over the eye-faculty so that it does not become heedless; he abandons evil and unwholesome states as well as worldly craving, maintains his precepts accordingly, guards the eye-faculty, and attains the discipline of the eye-faculty.

Furthermore, regarding the mental consciousness and mental phenomena, one does not grasp at the characteristics of phenomena; one restrains that which gives rise to the mind-faculty so as to prevent negligence, abandons evil and unwholesome states as well as worldly craving, accords with the precepts, and guards the mind-faculty.

Regarding these six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), one guards them with subtle mindfulness, accomplishes the practice of well-understood and directed mindfulness, and constantly protects the mind by seeing the faults and perils of sensual desire; this is called the restraint of the sense-faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*).
What is contentment with food and drink?

It is eating with moderation, without agitation, without giving rise to arrogance, not for the sake of nourishing the body, and not for the sake of adorning the body; it is solely for the purpose of sustaining the body, without giving rise to anger, desiring to cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and—by severing old sensations and not producing new ones—for the sake of maintaining life.
Abandoning the vajra of hatred and attachment, one should always abide in the Middle Way, not seeking profit, but diligently and joyfully practicing.
It is like a person suffering from a sore who applies medicine to it, desiring only its healing.
The bhikṣu is likewise: eating with moderation, he does not give rise to agitation nor produce arrogance, and so on, up to not seeking gain, but instead exerts himself and delights in practice.
What is agitation regarding food?
It is when one thinks:
"Having eaten this food, I shall engage in agitation of body, speech, and mind."
This is called the nutriment of restlessness.
What is the nutriment of arrogance?
It is when one forms this thought:
"Having eaten this food, I shall increase in negligence;
this is called 'food for pride.
What is 'food for nourishing the body'?"
If one thinks:
"Having eaten this food, it shall benefit my body," this is called food for nourishing the body.
What is food for the adornment of the body?
It is when one thinks:
"By eating this food, I shall become upright, beautiful, and endowed with excellent physical marks."
This is called food for adorning the body.
If a bhikṣu does not form such thoughts as:
"By eating this food, I shall cause agitation of body, speech, and mind; I shall become arrogant; I shall nourish my body; I shall adorn my body."
This is called eating without being fickle, without arrogance, without nourishing the body, and without adorning the body.
How does one eat merely for the purpose of maintaining the body?
One should form this thought:
"I eat this food only with the desire to maintain the body so that it does not perish or dissolve.
This is called "only desiring to maintain the body.
What is meant by "not giving rise to anger"?
If one is hungry, because of that hunger, painful feelings arise in body and mind.
If one eats to excess, because of that excess, painful feelings arise in body and mind.
If a bhikṣu eats with contentment and reflects well upon his food, then ill will is extinguished; it does not arise or manifest.
This is called not giving rise to ill will.
How should one cultivate the holy life?
The holy life refers to the Eightfold Noble Path.
One should reflect thus:
"Having eaten this food, I shall be able to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), so that the holy life may endure for a long time, for the sake of bringing an end to suffering.
This is called the desire to cultivate the holy life.
How does one abandon old feelings so that new feelings do not arise?
