Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not self; the self is not consciousness. If consciousness were the self, consciousness would not be subject to suffering and affliction, and consciousness would possess mastery. Such is its existence, and such is its non-existence.
Because consciousness is not-self, consciousness undergoes suffering and affliction; consciousness does not attain mastery; thus it exists in such a way, or does not exist in such a way.
Therefore, one should know that this phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, and subject to cessation.
"What belongs to me" is not "I," and "I" am not "what belongs to me"; in both "I" and "what belongs to me," there is no self at all—this is called the contemplation of right wisdom.
Thus, by practicing with diligence, mindfulness, right knowledge, and tranquility without negligence, one abandons craving and deluded conceptualization.

Having abandoned [these], one dwells with the mind rightly established and rightly stilled, alone in meditative concentration; a person of true reality recollects and bears this in mind—this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By approaching and frequently practicing this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); this is called the single limb of the path leading toward Nirvāṇa that constitutes the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"Regarding the various kinds of suffering in the world, what is the cause of this suffering? What is its continuity? What is its accumulation? What is its origin? What is its sovereign condition?"

Thus he contemplates the various aggregates of suffering in the world—the aggregates as causes, the aggregates as continuations, the aggregates as accumulations, the aggregates as births, and the aggregates as supreme conditions—which involve the suffering of losing one's father, mother, brothers, sisters, wife, children, and kinsmen, as well as the suffering of decline, loss, and manifold diseases.

There are various disagreeable contacts, such as the contact of hands or fists, the contact of whips or staves, the contact of tiles or stones, the contact of swords or clubs, the contact of cold or heat, the contact of hunger or thirst, the contact of wind or sun, and the contact of mosquitoes or gadflies.

There are kings and ministers who are bound with shackles and fetters, their flesh torn away until the bones protrude like conch shells; they are impaled on sharp wooden stakes, their feet struck with stone hammers, split apart by five chariots, bound with ropes, their bodies scorched by garlands of fire, their bodies turned into flaming torches, their flesh scraped off with knives, their flesh hooked out with iron hooks, their skin flayed and smeared with honey so that insects may devour it, wrapped in straw and burned, blown to pieces by fans and machines, their bodies encased in iron plates, their hands, feet, ears, and noses severed, driven onto the tops of flagpoles and shot with arrows, and finally executed by beheading—such are the sufferings they endure.
As the Blessed One said:
"There is no fire like desire; there is no poison like hatred;
there is no net like delusion; there is no suffering like the aggregates."
"Having known this as it truly is, Nirvana is the supreme bliss.

Therefore, one should know that these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to separation, and subject to cessation. "What belongs to me is not my self; I am not the owner of what belongs to me. In both "I" and "mine," there is no self at all. This is called the contemplation with right wisdom.
Thus, through heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right knowledge, and tranquil conduct, one abandons the delusory imaginings based on craving.

Having abandoned them, the mind dwells rightly and is stilled; dwelling alone in concentration, the person who acts according to reality recollects and remains mindful—this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By cultivating and frequently practicing this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single factor of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to Nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus: "The body has much suffering, much loss, much affliction, much sorrow, and much manifold misery.
He contemplates the body as being born, truly born; arising, truly arising; emerging, truly emerging;
and as it fully accomplishes and possesses the arising of various diseases—whether diseases born from heat, born from the humors, or born from...
Diseases arising from wind, diseases arising from one's own exertion, diseases arising from the affliction of others, diseases arising from seasonal changes,
diseases arising from the disharmony of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), diseases arising from undigested food, diseases arising from karmic retribution,
and diseases arising from the accumulation [of humors]; these include eye diseases, ear, nose, tongue, and body diseases, as well as headaches and shoulder pains.
Toothache, sore throat, neck pain, headaches, and skin eruptions; upward-moving qi with gasping and sobbing, throat obstruction, coughing, vomiting, diarrhea, and cramping pain;
feverish illness with abdominal pain; sores, scabs, itch, and ringworm; a pricking sensation in the skin as if insects are crawling;
invasive venereal sores, leprosy, carbuncles, and white leprosy with parched skin; insanity, madness, and hemorrhoids.
Regarding the disease of red swelling: externally, one is devoured by various kinds of insects, fleas, lice, bedbugs, mosquitoes, gadflies, and larvae;
internally, there is not even a single pore where no insect dwells.
As the Blessed One has said:

"Form arises, abides, originates, becomes ill, dwells in suffering, and issues forth in aging and death; so too do feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise, abide, originate, become ill, dwell in suffering, and issue forth in aging and death."
Furthermore, as the Blessed One has said:
there are three kinds of suffering—suffering due to conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), suffering due to pain (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and suffering due to change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).

Therefore, one should know that these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to separation, and subject to cessation. "What belongs to me is not I; I am not my own. Both "I" and "mine" are entirely devoid of a self. This is called the contemplation with right wisdom.
Thus, through heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right knowledge, and tranquil conduct, one abandons the deluded thoughts of craving.

Having abandoned them, the mind dwells correctly and is stilled within, as one who abides alone in concentration recollects with mindfulness according to reality; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By recollecting and frequently practicing this cultivation, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single limb of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to Nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"What is the cause? What is the basis? What is not the cause?
What is not the basis? Reflecting thus:

The foot bone depends on the shin bone; the shin bone depends on the thigh bone; the thigh bone depends on the hip bone; the hip bone depends on the spine; the spine depends on the ribs; the hand bone depends on the forearm bone; the forearm bone depends on the shoulder bone; the shoulder bone depends on the neck bone; the neck bone depends on the skull bone. The marrow depends on the bone; the bone depends on the sinews; the sinews depend on the flesh; the flesh depends on the blood; the blood depends on the skin; the skin depends on the thin outer skin; and the thin outer skin depends on the body hair.

Just as wind abides because of space, water abides because of wind, earth abides because of water, and all activities, the multitude of seeds, the multitude of sentient beings, and the thickets of medicinal herbs and forests abide because of earth.
The bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"Depending on the foot-bone, the shin-bone is situated; depending on the shin-bone, and so on up to the skull-bone; depending on the marrow, the bone is situated; depending on the bone, and so on up to the hair."

If there were no foot bones, the shin bones would not abide; if there were no shin bones, the thigh bones would not abide; if there were no thigh bones, the hip bones would not abide; if there were no hip bones, the spinal column would not abide; if there were no spinal column, the ribs would not abide; if there were no hand bones, the arm bones would not abide; if there were no arm bones, the shoulder bones would not abide; if there were no shoulder bones, the neck bones would not abide; if there were no neck bones, the skull bones would not abide. Without marrow, the bones would not abide; without bone-tendons, the muscles would not abide; without muscle, the flesh would not abide; without flesh, the blood would not abide; without blood, the skin would not abide; without skin, the thin outer skin would not abide; and without thin outer skin, the body hair would not abide.

Just as wind does not abide without space, just as water does not abide without wind, just as earth does not abide without water, so too, without earth, no activities, seeds, fields, sentient beings, villages, medicinal herbs, or forests can abide.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"If there were no foot bones, the shin bones would not remain; if there were no shin bones, up to the skull bones would not remain; without marrow, the bones would not remain; without bones, up to the hair would not remain. For the marrow is contained within the bones, the sinews bind the bones, the flesh covers the sinews, the blood coats the flesh, the skin envelops the blood, the thin skin and membranes cover the thick skin, and the hair covers the thin skin."
As the Blessed One has said:
"If a phenomenon arises and ceases, it does so by way of its activity and its persistence.

Therefore, one should know that this phenomenon is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to separation, and subject to cessation. It is not mine, nor do I belong to it, nor does it belong to me; both "I" and "mine" are entirely devoid of self. This is called the contemplation with right wisdom.
Thus, through heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, correct wisdom, and tranquil conduct, one abandons the deluded conceptualizations based on craving.

Having abandoned them, the mind dwells correctly and is stilled within, as one who abides alone in concentration recollects and remains mindful according to reality; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By frequently approaching and extensively cultivating this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single factor of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"What is the cause? What is the condition? What is not the cause? What is not the condition?
Reflecting in this manner:

Due to the body, there is conventional bodily action; where there is no body, there is no conventional bodily action. Due to speech, there is conventional verbal action; where there is no speech, there is no conventional verbal action. Due to the mind, there is conventional mental action; where there is no mind, there is no conventional mental action.

Whether it be action performed by the body or speech uttered by the mouth—namely, bodily instruction consisting of contact, movement, coming and going, bending and stretching, and turning about; or vocal instruction consisting of the collection of sounds, syllables, and language; or action performed through the mind—there is no mind without action, and no action without the mind.
It is like a skilled craftsman or his apprentice who carves a wooden figure with mechanical joints, enabling it to come and go, sit, and lie down.

In the same way, whether it be action performed by the body or speech uttered by the mouth, the bodily teaching consists of the movement of coming and going, bending and stretching, and turning about through the contact of karma; the verbal teaching consists of the collection of sounds, syllables, and words; and if action is performed due to the mind, there is no action without the mind.
As the Blessed One said:
"The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is supreme, the mind is the driver. If one harbors evil thoughts within the mind, they immediately manifest in speech and action;
suffering follows as a consequence of one's transgressions, like a chariot following its tracks."
The mind is the foundation of all phenomena; the mind is sovereign, the mind is the driver.
When one thinks of goodness within the heart, it is immediately expressed in speech and action; happiness and merit then follow of their own accord, like a shadow following a form.

Therefore, you should know that these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to separation, and subject to cessation. They are not "mine," nor do I belong to them, nor do they belong to me; in both "I" and "mine," there is no self. This is called right observation through wisdom.
Thus, through non-negligence, diligent mindfulness, right clear comprehension, and tranquil conduct, one abandons the deluded thoughts of craving.

Having abandoned them, the mind dwells correctly and is stilled within; dwelling alone in concentration, the person of true reality recollects and remains mindful. This is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By recollecting and frequently practicing this cultivation, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single factor of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"If the final formations cease while still unknown, or if after the immediate formations have ceased, consciousness continues to arise in another realm, those formations are the condition for that consciousness; this is called the 'immediately preceding condition' (samanantara-pratyaya)."

If that consciousness continues into another path due to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), those formations are the condition for that consciousness; this is called the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

If that consciousness continues into another path through the mental engagement (*manasikāra*) of volitional formations, those formations are the condition for that consciousness; this is called the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

If consciousness conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) continues to arise in another realm of existence, those formative forces are the condition for that consciousness; this is called the "condition as support" (*niśraya-pratyaya*).

If consciousness resulting from maturation (*vipāka*) continues to arise in another realm of existence, those formative forces are the condition for that consciousness; this is called the "condition as maturation" (*vipāka-pratyaya*).
If the formations that give rise to consciousness continue into another realm of existence, those formations condition that consciousness; this is called "conditioning by arising.
If the formations associated with consciousness continue into another realm of existence, those formations condition that consciousness; this is called "conditioning by difference."

If that consciousness, being predominant, continues to arise in another path through its predominance, then those formations are conditions for that consciousness, termed the "predominant condition" (adhipati-pratyaya).
When this final consciousness ceases, the initial consciousness arises continuing in the other path.
Once the final consciousness has ceased, the initial consciousness arises immediately; there is no interval between them.
It is like the movement of a shadow followed by the succession of the sun, or the movement of the sun followed by the succession of a shadow: between the shadow and the sun, there is no interval.
In this way, when the final consciousness ceases, the initial consciousness continues and arises in another state.
Once the final consciousness has ceased, the initial consciousness arises immediately; there is no interval between them.
Thus, the final consciousness, or the factors associated with that final consciousness, does not reach the initial consciousness.
If the initial consciousness and the mental factors associated with that initial consciousness do not reach the subsequent consciousness—

just as when the visual consciousness has ceased and the auditory consciousness arises, or when the auditory consciousness has ceased and the visual consciousness arises— the mental factors associated with the visual consciousness do not reach the auditory consciousness, nor do the mental factors associated with the auditory consciousness reach the visual consciousness.

In this way, the subsequent consciousness and its associated mental factors do not reach the initial consciousness, nor do the initial consciousness and its associated mental factors reach the subsequent consciousness. Yet, as soon as the subsequent consciousness has ceased, the initial consciousness arises; that is to say, "this time has passed," "having ceased, this is born," and "this ends while that begins."

Life is not the body, nor is the body life; life is not different from the body, nor is the body different from life; life is not annihilated, nor does it arise, nor does it abide, nor does it undergo transformation, nor is it without cause, nor is it created by a god, nor is it that one acts and another experiences the result, nor is it that one acts and another experiences the result. One knows there is going and coming, one knows there is birth and death, one knows there is the continuity of karma, one knows there is the teaching of the Dharma, and one knows there are conditions. There is no one who goes from here to there, nor anyone who comes from there to here; it is only the continuity of formations that arises through the condition of karma.
As the Blessed One said:

"The self is empty; one should not harbor doubt regarding the self or what belongs to the self, nor should one speak of 'self' or 'what belongs to the self'; one should not harbor doubt regarding any phenomena."

Therefore, one should know that these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, subject to change, subject to cessation, and subject to separation; they are not "mine," nor do I belong to them, nor do they belong to me; in both "mine" and "I," there is no self at all—this is called right wisdom contemplation.
Thus, through this practice of heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right clear comprehension, and tranquility, one abandons the deluded thoughts of craving.

Having abandoned them, the mind dwells correctly and is stilled within, abiding alone in concentration; one who is a person of suchness maintains recollection and mindfulness—this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By recollecting [the body], drawing near to it, and practicing it extensively, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single factor of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, seeing an infant whose mind is ignorant and without discernment, lying asleep in a filthy place, reflects thus:
"I too am of such a nature, such a characteristic; I have not yet escaped this condition."
My own body is likewise a phenomenon subject to birth and possesses the perils inherent in birth.
When a person of true reality reflects and recollects this, it is called the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By cultivating and frequently practicing this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*) up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single limb of the path leading toward Nirvana that consists of the application of mindfulness to the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see men or women who are aged and decrepit, with white hair and fallen teeth, loose skin and wrinkled faces, bodies bent and stooped, walking weakly with a staff, and breaths that are uneven.
He reflects thus:
"My own body is also of such a nature, such a character, and has not escaped this condition.
My body, too, is subject to the law of aging and possesses these defects."
When a person of true reality recollects and brings to mind [the body], this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By cultivating and frequently practicing this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single branch of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, if he sees a man or a woman afflicted by physical illness, lying in a defiled place, weak and powerless, requiring assistance for every movement, reflects thus:
"My own body is also of such a nature, such a character; it has not escaped this condition."
My own body also has illness; it possesses the affliction of disease.
When a person of true reality recollects and attends to this, it is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By attending to it, drawing near to it, and practicing it extensively, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body as a single branch of the path leading toward Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see when the bodies of men or women have passed away—whether they were relatives or non-relatives—their corpses cast aside like grass, dung, or soil.
He reflects thus:
"My body is of such a nature and such a character; it has not yet escaped this nature.
My body is likewise subject to disintegration and possesses the peril of death."
When a person of true reality recollects and attends to this, it is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By attending to it, cultivating it closely, and training extensively in it, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); this is called the single limb of the path leading toward nirvāṇa that consists of the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse abandoned in a cemetery, one day up to three days old.
He contemplates his own body: "It is of such a nature, such a character; it has not escaped this fate."
When a person of true reality recollects and brings to mind [the body], this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By cultivating and frequently practicing this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the branch of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse abandoned in a cemetery, one to three days old, bloated and discolored with lividity.
He contemplates his own body: "Such is its nature, such are its characteristics; it has not escaped this condition."
When a person of true reality recollects and attends to this, it is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By attending to it, cultivating it closely, and training in it extensively, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the limb of the path leading toward nirvāṇa that consists in the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse abandoned in a cemetery for one to three days, being devoured by crows, birds, tigers, wolves, and various other beasts of prey.
Observing one's own body as having such qualities and such characteristics, and not being free from these qualities—
when a person of true reality recollects and keeps this in mind, it is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna).

By recollecting and frequently practicing this cultivation, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single factor of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse with its bones and joints still connected, bluish-red and putrefied, with impure pus and blood, foul-smelling, filthy, and loathsome.
He contemplates his own body: "It is of such a nature, such a character, and has not yet escaped this condition."
When a person of true reality recollects and attends to [the body], this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By attending to it, cultivating it closely, and training extensively in it, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); this is called the branch of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints are still connected, covered with flesh and blood, and whose sinews and veins have not yet severed.
He contemplates his own body: "It is of such a nature, of such a character, and has not yet escaped this condition."
When a person of true reality recollects and attends to this, it is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By attending to it, cultivating it closely, and training extensively in it, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); this is called the limb of the path toward Nirvāṇa consisting of the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints are still connected but from which the flesh and blood have already detached, though the sinews and veins have not yet been severed.
He contemplates his own body: "Such is its nature, such is its characteristic; it has not yet departed from this nature."
When a person of true reality recollects and brings to mind [the body], this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By cultivating and frequently practicing this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*); this is called the single branch of the path leading toward nirvāṇa that consists in the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints have already fallen apart but have not yet left their original positions.
He contemplates his own body: "Such is its nature, such is its characteristic; it has not yet departed from this nature."
When a person of true reality recollects and attends to this, it is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By attending to it, cultivating it closely, and training in it extensively, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single limb of the path leading toward nirvāṇa that constitutes the foundation of mindfulness of the body.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints have already disintegrated and been moved from their original positions; the feet, calves, thighs, shoulders, hips, spine, ribs, hands, feet, upper arms, neck, and skull each lie in a different place.
Observing one's own body as having such qualities and such characteristics, and not being separated from these qualities—
when a person of true reality recollects and keeps this in mind, this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By recollecting and frequently practicing this cultivation, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single factor of the foundation of mindfulness of the body that leads toward the path to Nirvana.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints, being long-standing, are white in color like a conch shell or blue in color like a pigeon, decayed and shattered.
He contemplates his own body: "Such is its nature, such are its characteristics; it has not transcended this condition."
When a person of true reality recollects and keeps in mind [the body], this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By cultivating and frequently practicing this mindfulness, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); this is called the single limb of the path toward Nirvāṇa that consists in the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu sees a corpse upon a mass of fire; all its hair, fur, skin, flesh, blood, sinews, veins, and marrow—all from the hair down to the marrow—gradually dissolve and vanish.

Contemplate this body and its phenomena: they do not abide in the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, or above and below; these bodily phenomena are originally non-existent yet arise, and having existed, they return to extinction.
When a person of true reality recollects and brings to mind [the body], this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).

By attending to this mindfulness, cultivating it frequently, and training extensively therein, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the single limb of the path leading toward nirvāṇa that consists of the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
What is called mindfulness of the body?
The arising of the body is called mindfulness of the body.
Contemplating the arising of the body is called mindfulness of the body.
That which arises from the domain of the body is called mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛti*).
That which arises in dependence upon the body is called mindfulness of the body.
That which arises from the discernment of the body is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*).
What are called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to Nirvana?
What is concentration?
The mind abiding and dwelling rightly—this is called concentration.
What is wisdom? The discernment of knowledge is called wisdom.
Such concentration and such wisdom are called concentration and wisdom.

Having approached and extensively practiced these, one attains the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship; this is called the twofold path toward nirvana consisting of concentration and wisdom.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all conditioned phenomena, or conditioned phenomena in a single instance, as impermanent; he knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent.
Thus, through this heedful contemplation, one attains concentration (*samādhi*) such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called concentration.
When a person of reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called insight (*prajñā*).
Such concentration and such wisdom are called concentration and wisdom.

By drawing near to and extensively cultivating concentration and wisdom, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; these are called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to Nirvana.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, whether regarding all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) or conditioned phenomena in a single location, contemplates them as suffering, as a calamity, as a boil, as an arrow, as attachment to flavor, as dependent on conditions, as subject to decay, as unstable, as incomplete, as subject to transformation and destruction, as perishable, and as suffering, empty, and non-self. He contemplates their conditions, knows their conditions, understands their conditions, and accepts their conditions: namely, ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—the entire mass of pure suffering arises.
Thus, through heedful contemplation, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called concentration (*samādhi*).
When a person of true reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called insight (*prajñā*).
Such concentration and such wisdom are called concentration and wisdom.

By cultivating and frequently practicing concentration and wisdom, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; these are called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to nirvana.

Furthermore, monks, if a monk contemplates the cessation of all conditioned phenomena—or the cessation of conditioned phenomena in a single instance—and knows their cessation, understands their cessation, and accepts their cessation, then ignorance ceases; with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until the entire mass of suffering ceases.
Thus, through this heedful contemplation, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called concentration (*samādhi*).
When a person of reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called insight (*prajñā*).
Such concentration and such wisdom are called concentration and wisdom.

By drawing near to and extensively practicing these two—concentration and wisdom—one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to Nirvana.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows the pleasure of walking when walking, knows the pleasure of standing when standing, knows the pleasure of sitting when sitting, and knows the pleasure of lying down when lying down.

Just as he truly knows the pleasure of the body’s walking, standing, sitting, and lying down through heedful contemplation, he attains concentration, and his mind abides and remains rightly established; this is called concentration.
When a person of true reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called *prajñā*.
Such concentration and such wisdom are called "concentration and wisdom" (*samādhi-prajñā*).

By drawing near to and extensively cultivating concentration and wisdom, one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; these are called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to *nirvāṇa*.
...up to and including if he sees a corpse upon a pyre of fire, it is as described above. Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"When there is lustful defilement within me, I know as it truly is that there is lustful defilement within; when there is no lustful defilement within me, I know as it truly is that there is no lustful defilement within. As for lustful defilement not yet arisen, I know as it truly is that it has not arisen; as for lustful defilement having arisen, I know as it truly is that it has arisen; as for lustful defilement having arisen and been abandoned, I know as it truly is that it has been abandoned; and as for lustful defilement having been abandoned, I know as it truly is that it will not arise again."
The same applies to internal ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
When one observes with such heedfulness, attaining a concentrated mind that abides and dwells correctly, this is called concentration (*samādhi*).
When a person of true reality discriminates with knowledge, this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
Such concentration and such wisdom are called concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*).

By drawing near to and extensively practicing concentration and wisdom, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); these are called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way: "When there is lustful attachment and anger toward internal visual consciousness and its objects, he knows as it truly is that there is lustful attachment and anger toward internal visual consciousness and its objects; when there is no lustful attachment or anger toward internal visual consciousness and its objects, he knows as it truly is that there is no lustful attachment or anger toward internal visual consciousness and its objects. He knows as it truly is the non-arising of lustful attachment and anger toward visual consciousness and its objects when they have not yet arisen; he knows as it truly is the arising of lustful attachment and anger toward visual consciousness and its objects when they have not yet arisen. He knows as it truly is the abandonment of lustful attachment and anger toward visual consciousness and its objects once they have arisen; and he knows as it truly is that once lustful attachment and anger toward visual consciousness and its objects have been abandoned, they will not arise again."

The same applies to the ear-consciousness of sounds, the nose-consciousness of odors, the tongue-consciousness of tastes, the body-consciousness of tangibles, and the mind-consciousness of mental phenomena.
When one observes with heedfulness, attaining concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established, this is called concentration (*samādhi*).
When a person of true reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called *prajñā*.
Such concentration and such wisdom are called "concentration and wisdom" (*samādhi-prajñā*).

By drawing near to and extensively practicing concentration and wisdom, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up to the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*); this is called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way: "When there is mindfulness-enlightenment-factor within me, I know as it truly is that there is mindfulness-enlightenment-factor within me; when there is no mindfulness-enlightenment-factor within me, I know as it truly is that there is no mindfulness-enlightenment-factor within me. When the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor has not yet arisen, I know as it truly is that it has not yet arisen; when the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor has not yet arisen but is arising, I know as it truly is that it is arising; when the mindfulness-enlightenment-factor has already arisen and is being fully cultivated, I know as it truly is that it is being fully cultivated."

The same applies to the right awakening of the investigation of phenomena, the right awakening of energy, the right awakening of tranquility, the right awakening of concentration, and the right awakening of equanimity.
When one observes with such heedfulness, attaining concentration so that the mind dwells and remains rightly established, this is called concentration.
When a person of true reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called *prajñā*.
Such concentration and such wisdom are called *samādhi* and *prajñā*.

By drawing near to and extensively cultivating these two—concentration and wisdom—one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*; these are called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to *nirvāṇa*.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows as it really is suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering; he knows as it really is the outflows, the origin of the outflows, the cessation of the outflows, and the path leading to the cessation of the outflows.
Such non-negligent contemplation, which results in the attainment of concentration and the mind’s abiding and right abiding, is called *samādhi*.
When a person of true reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called *prajñā*.
Such concentration and such wisdom are called concentration and wisdom.

By drawing near to and extensively practicing these two—concentration and wisdom—one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; these are called the two factors of concentration and wisdom that lead toward the path to nirvana.
Furthermore, because the bhikṣu’s mind is filled with fear and dread, he emerges from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and enters the realm of ambrosia (*amṛta*).
This is the sublime tranquility: free from all conditioned phenomena, the exhaustion of craving, and nirvāṇa.
Thus, through this heedful contemplation, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called concentration (*samādhi*).
When a person of reality discriminates with wisdom, this is called insight (*prajñā*).
Such concentration and such wisdom are called concentration and wisdom.

By drawing near to and extensively practicing these two—concentration and wisdom—one attains the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship; this is called the twofold limb of concentration and wisdom leading toward the path to Nirvana.
What is concentration?
For one whose afflictions have not yet been abandoned, it is the abandonment, the right abandonment, and the pacification of lustful defilement;
the cessation, the right cessation, and the pacification of ill will, delusion, afflictions, hindrances, obscurations, all fetters, and unwholesome conduct.

Just as when dust, clouds, and mist arise in great abundance during autumn, and immediately rain falls, extinguishing the dust, clouds, and mist—extinguished, being extinguished, and stilled—in the same way, for one whose defilements have not yet been abandoned, the desire-taint is extinguished, being extinguished, and stilled;
hatred, delusion, hindrances, obscurations, all fetters, and evil conduct are extinguished, being extinguished, and stilled. This is called concentration (*samādhi*).
What is wisdom?
It is when a person of true reality discriminates with knowledge: they discriminate form as it truly is, and likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
It is like a person with clear vision standing on the peak of a high mountain; if they look toward the east, they discriminate it as it truly is.
If one discriminates the south, west, and north as they truly are,
such wisdom— which discriminates form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness as they truly are— is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
What is concentration with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*)?

If a concentration is associated with initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), arising, abiding, and ceasing together with them, this is called concentration with initial application and sustained application.

Furthermore, concentration with initial application and sustained application refers to a concentration that is attained, rightly attained, or acquired through the object of focus of initial application and sustained application; this is called concentration with initial application and sustained application.

Furthermore, there is the concentration with directed thought and evaluation: a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is accompanied by directed thought and evaluation, and possesses the joy and happiness born of seclusion.

When a bhikkhu possesses applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra), and with joy (pīti), bliss (sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (cittass'ekaggatā), enters this meditative absorption, he attains the five factors—attaining them correctly and attaining them as objects—namely, applied thought, sustained thought, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the first dhyāna with applied and sustained thought.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu attains a meditative concentration with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), a concentration accompanied by joy (*prīti*) and its associated relish (*āsvāda*), he contemplates that joy as coarse.
His mind possesses compassion (*karuṇā*) and is devoid of joy; he finds excellence in the tranquility of bliss (*sukha*).
When the bhikṣu has observed that joy is coarse, he brings joy to rest, perfectly stills it, extinguishes it, makes it vanish, and eliminates it.

Because he has brought joy to rest, perfectly stilled it, extinguished it, made it vanish, and eliminated it, there is directed thought and evaluation, along with raptureless bliss and one-pointedness of mind.

If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains its four factors through correct attainment and objective attainment: applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joyless bliss (*prīti-virahita-sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*). This is called the concentration with applied and sustained thought that is neither dhyāna nor an intermediate stage of dhyāna.

For example, when a bhikṣu—whether through practice, instruction, the characteristics of dharmas, skillful means, single-minded concentration, reflection, or contact—attains the concentration associated with vitarka, vicāra, and prīti, which is accompanied by relish.

Just as a bhikṣu, practicing the method of receiving the teachings, contemplates with focused attention, touches upon them, draws near to them, and trains extensively; once the bhikṣu has practiced in this way until he has touched upon, drawn near to, and trained extensively, his mind inclines toward tranquility.
Having inclined the mind toward tranquility, one honors tranquility.
Honoring tranquility, one leans toward tranquility.
Having leaned toward tranquility, one delights in tranquility.
Delighting in tranquility, one attains right tranquility.
With right tranquility, there is cessation, subsiding, and elimination.
Once cessation, subsiding, and elimination have occurred, there is initial and sustained application of mind, free from rapture and pleasure, with one-pointedness of mind.

If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains its four factors through direct attainment and conditional attainment: applied thought (vitarka), sustained thought (vicāra), joyless bliss (prīti-rahita-sukha), and one-pointedness of mind (citta-ekāgratā).
This is called the concentration with applied and sustained thought that is neither dhyāna nor intermediate dhyāna.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu attains a concentration accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, associated with the relish of joyless pleasure, that bhikṣu contemplates that joyless pleasure as coarse; he perceives that the mind’s equanimity (upekṣā), which is neither painful nor pleasant, is peaceful and superior.

Having observed that the joyless happiness is coarse, this bhikṣu finds the joyless happiness to be tranquil; it is tranquil, perfectly tranquil, and through perfect tranquility, it ceases, subsides, and is eliminated.

Because it has ceased, subsided, and been eliminated, there remains initial application (vitarka) and sustained application (vicāra), along with equanimity (upekṣā), one-pointedness of mind, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure.

If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains the four factors through direct attainment and objective attainment: vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the concentration with vitarka and vicāra that is neither dhyāna nor intermediate to dhyāna.

For example, when a bhikṣu—whether through practice, instruction, the characteristics of the Dharma, skillful means, single-mindedness, reflection, or contact—attains the concentration that is accompanied by initial and sustained application, devoid of rapture and pleasure, and characterized by relish.
Just as when a bhikkhu has practiced, even unto touching, and has cultivated it extensively, his mind inclines toward tranquility.

His mind inclines toward tranquility; it is elevated toward tranquility, directed toward tranquility. Having been directed toward tranquility, he experiences the joy and happiness of tranquility; through tranquility, there is perfect tranquility; through perfect tranquility, there is cessation, disappearance, and elimination.

Once [applied thought] has ceased, subsided, and been eliminated, there is applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind (*citta-ekāgratā*).

For one who enters this meditative absorption, these four factors—applied thought, sustained thought, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind—are correctly attained, fully attained, and acquired as objects; this is called the concentration with applied and sustained thought that is neither dhyāna nor the intermediate stage.
What is the concentration with applied thought and sustained thought (avitarko vicāramātraḥ samādhiḥ)?

If a concentration is dissociated from applied thought, yet is not produced, does not abide, and does not cease together with applied thought, while it is produced, abides, and ceases together with sustained thought, this is called the concentration with applied thought and sustained thought.

Furthermore, regarding the concentration with applied thought but without sustained thought (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ samādhiḥ*): if, within this concentration, one does not obtain applied thought—neither obtaining it correctly nor obtaining it through an object—but obtains sustained thought, obtaining it correctly and obtaining it through an object, this is called the concentration with applied thought but without sustained thought.

Furthermore, regarding the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), if a bhikṣu attains a concentration accompanied by directed thought, sustained thought, and joy (*prīti*) that is associated with relishing (*āsvādita*), this bhikṣu contemplates directed thought as coarse, seeing that the concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought is peaceful and superior.

Having observed that perceptions are coarse, this bhikṣu perceives tranquility; he perceives tranquility, attains right tranquility, and through right tranquility, they are extinguished, vanish, and are eliminated.
Once extinguished, vanished, and eliminated, there arises the perception of joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.

If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains the four factors—equanimity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness—through direct attainment and through objective attainment; this is called the intermediate dhyāna concentration that is without vitarka but with vicāra.

Suppose a bhikṣu, whether through his conduct, his receiving of instruction, his understanding of the characteristics of phenomena, his skillful means, his focused application of mind, his reflection, or his contact, attains a concentration accompanied by initial and sustained thought, rapture, and a sense of relish. If this bhikṣu closely approaches and frequently cultivates that conduct, up to and including that contact, [he will attain further progress].
Just as when a bhikkhu has practiced, even unto touching, and has cultivated this closely, his mind inclines toward tranquility, tends toward tranquility, and leans toward tranquility.
When his mind inclines toward, tends toward, and leans toward tranquility, he experiences tranquility, perfect tranquility, cessation, subsiding, and relinquishment.
Having awakened from vitarka, and having attained tranquility, perfect tranquility, cessation, disappearance, and removal, there exists vicāra, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.

For one who enters this meditative absorption, these four factors—vicāra, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness—are correctly attained, fully attained, and acquired as objects; this is called the intermediate dhyāna concentration that is without vitarka but with vicāra.
What is meant by the interval between dhyānas?
It is the interval between the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna, at the time when one proceeds from the first dhyāna toward the second.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains a concentration accompanied by the relish of joy, characterized by the absence of vitarka and the presence of vicāra.
The bhikṣu contemplates joy as coarse; although there is still compassion within the joyful mind, it lacks joy, and thus the bliss of tranquility is superior.
Having contemplated joy as coarse, the bhikṣu causes joy to become tranquil, perfectly tranquil, ceased, subsided, and eliminated.

Having delighted in, become tranquil in, rightly stilled, ceased, and eliminated joy (*pīti*), there remains equanimity (*upekkhā*), happiness (*sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittassekaggatā*).

For one who enters this meditative attainment, these three factors—equanimity, happiness, and one-pointedness of mind—are attained, correctly attained, and acquired as objects; this is called the concentration that is neither *dhyāna* nor the intermediate state, which is without initial application (*vitakka*) but with sustained application (*vicāra*).

For example, when a bhikṣu—whether through practice, instruction, the characteristics of dharmas, skillful means, single-mindedness, reflection, or contact—attains a concentration accompanied by relish, which is without applied thought but with sustained thought and joy.
Just as a bhikṣu practices up to the point of contact, he draws near to it and trains extensively in it.
Having drawn near and trained extensively, his mind inclines toward tranquility.
His mind having inclined toward tranquility, he holds tranquility in high esteem.
The Venerable One is inclined toward tranquility and leans toward tranquility.

Having leaned toward tranquility, and with the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly comprehending, experiencing a bliss that is described by the Noble Ones as "dwelling in equanimity, mindful, and blissful. This is the third jhāna.

If one enters this concentration, one attains the three factors through correct attainment and objective attainment: contemplation (*vitarka*), joyless bliss (*avītarāga-sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*ekāgratā*). This is called the concentration that is neither dhyāna nor intermediate dhyāna, characterized by applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains the concentration that is without vitarka, with vicāra, and accompanied by the relish of joy.

The bhikṣu contemplates that the joy without rapture is coarse; when the mind of joy without rapture still involves mental activity, there is the tranquility of equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant.
When the bhikṣu has observed that joyless bliss is coarse, then joyless bliss becomes tranquil, serene, and perfectly serene; through perfect serenity, it ceases, subsides, and is eliminated.
Once it has ceased, subsided, and been eliminated, there remains the observation of equanimity and one-pointedness of mind, which are neither painful nor pleasant.

If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains two factors through direct attainment and through objective attainment: equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind. This is called the concentration that is neither dhyāna nor intermediate dhyāna, and which is without vitarka but with vicāra.

For example, when a bhikṣu—whether through practice, instruction, the characteristics of dharmas, skillful means, single-mindedness, reflection, or contact—attains a concentration that is without vitarka but with vicāra, devoid of joy and pleasure, yet accompanied by their relish.
Just as a bhikkhu practices and cultivates with frequent application up to the point of contact;
having practiced and cultivated with frequent application up to the point of contact, his mind inclines toward tranquility, tends toward tranquility, and leans toward tranquility.
Having inclined toward tranquility, there is the tranquility of joyless bliss, right tranquility, cessation, disappearance, and elimination.
Because of this cessation, disappearance, and elimination, there is equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, accompanied by mindfulness and one-pointedness of mind.

If one enters this concentration, one attains the three factors through direct attainment and objective attainment: equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the concentration that is neither dhyāna nor intermediate dhyāna, which is without vitarka but with vicāra.

This is called the concentration with no initial application but with sustained investigation (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ samādhiḥ*). What is meant by the concentration with neither initial application nor sustained investigation (*avitarko ’vicāraḥ samādhiḥ*)?

If, in a state of concentration, one is free from initial application and sustained investigation, such that initial application and sustained investigation do not arise together, do not abide together, and do not cease together, this is called the concentration with neither initial application nor sustained investigation.

Furthermore, regarding the concentration without directed thought and sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ samādhiḥ*): if, in that concentration, one does not obtain, does not correctly obtain, and does not take as an object directed thought and sustained thought, it is called the concentration without directed thought and sustained thought.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Fifteen.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others, *The Non-Questioned Section*, Chapter Ten:

On the Path, Part Two. Furthermore, regarding the concentration without directed thought and sustained evaluation: as a bhikṣu, having stilled directed thought and sustained evaluation, with internal clarity and faith and one-pointedness of mind, attains the joy and happiness born of concentration without directed thought and sustained evaluation, and thus accomplishes the practice of the second dhyāna.
If this bhikṣu, possessing internal clarity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind, enters this concentration, he attains, correctly attains, and fully realizes its four factors:
internal clarity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the second dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought and sustained thought.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu may attain the concentration accompanied by vitarka, vicāra, and prīti, which is associated with relishing. Just as the bhikṣu contemplates that vitarka and vicāra are coarse, he perceives that the concentration without vitarka and vicāra is peaceful and superior.

When a bhikkhu has observed that initial and sustained application of mind (vitakka-vicāra) is coarse, and these have become tranquil, perfectly tranquil, ceased, subsided, and eliminated—because they have ceased, subsided, and been eliminated—there arises internal serenity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains the four factors—attainment through right attainment and attainment through conditions:
internal clarity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the second dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought.

For example, when a bhikṣu is practicing, receiving instruction, contemplating the characteristics of dharmas, applying skillful means, concentrating the mind, reflecting, or making contact, he attains the concentration accompanied by vitarka, vicāra, and prīti, which is associated with relishing.

Just as when a bhikkhu, having practiced up to the point of contact, approaches and trains extensively, once he has so trained, his mind inclines toward tranquility, tends toward tranquility, and leans toward tranquility; and having leaned toward tranquility, his applied and sustained thought become tranquil, perfectly stilled, ceased, and vanished; and with their cessation, there arises within him internal confidence, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind.
If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains the four factors through right attainment and proper acquisition:
internal clarity and purity, joy, bliss, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the second dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains the concentration accompanied by rapture, which is without directed thought and evaluation; the bhikṣu contemplates that rapture is coarse, for while the mind still possesses rapture, there is sorrow, and the bliss of being without rapture is more peaceful and superior.

When the bhikṣu has observed that joy is coarse, he brings about the stilling, perfect stilling, cessation, disappearance, and elimination of joy; because joy has been ceased, disappeared, eliminated, and removed, there arises internal clarity, a pleasure free from joy, and one-pointedness of mind.
The state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) upon entering this first dhyāna does not equal the state of equanimity upon entering the third dhyāna-concentration.
One who enters this concentration attains three factors correctly, through attainment and through objectification:

internal serenity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*), joyless bliss (*nirpīti-sukha*), and one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*). This is called the intermediate dhyāna concentration, which is without directed thought (*avitarka*) and without sustained thought (*avicāra*).
Between the second and third dhyānas, one proceeds from the second dhyāna toward the third.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains a concentration characterized by the relish of joyless bliss that is without vitarka and vicāra. The bhikṣu contemplates that this joyless bliss is coarse; because the mind still possesses volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*), the equanimity of neither-pain-nor-pleasure is more peaceful and superior.

When the bhikṣu has observed that joyless happiness is coarse, that joyless happiness becomes tranquil, perfectly tranquil, ceases, subsides, and is eliminated; because it has ceased, subsided, and been eliminated, there arises internal purity, equanimity characterized by neither suffering nor pleasure, and one-pointedness of mind.
If one enters this concentration, one attains three factors through right attainment and through acquisition:

internal serenity, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the concentration that is neither dhyāna nor intermediate, and is without vitarka and vicāra.

For example, if a bhikṣu—whether through practice, receiving instruction, the characteristics of dharmas, skillful means, single-minded concentration, reflection, or contact—attains the meditative absorption accompanied by the savoring of joy and bliss that is without applied thought and sustained thought.

When a bhikṣu practices up to the point of contact, approaching it and training extensively, having trained extensively, his mind inclines toward tranquility; his mind inclines toward tranquility, is directed toward supreme tranquility, and tends toward tranquility. Having tended toward tranquility, he delights in tranquility, attains right tranquility, and experiences cessation and disappearance. Having experienced cessation and disappearance, there arises within him internal clarity, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind. This is called the concentration that is neither dhyāna nor intermediate, being without vitarka and vicāra.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the fading away of joy, dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and abides in the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness."

A bhikṣu still possesses the concentration associated with relishing, equanimity, mindfulness and clear comprehension, joyless happiness, and one-pointedness of mind. If he enters this concentration, he attains, correctly attains, and gains the five factors:

association with relishing, equanimity, mindfulness and clear comprehension, joyless happiness, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the third dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought and sustained thought.

For example, when a bhikṣu—whether walking, receiving instruction, regarding the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), applying skillful means, concentrating the mind, reflecting, or experiencing contact—attains the absorption accompanied by joy and bliss that is without applied thought and sustained thought (avitarko 'vicāraḥ prītisukhasahagataḥ samādhiḥ).

Just as when a bhikkhu practices up to the point of contact, having approached and cultivated these extensively, once he has so cultivated them, his mind inclines toward tranquility, tends toward tranquility, and leans toward tranquility. Having leaned toward tranquility, there is joy in tranquility, perfect tranquility, cessation, and subsiding. Once there is cessation and subsiding, there arise, accordingly, zest, equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, happiness without rapture, and one-pointedness of mind.
If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains five factors:

zest accompanied by relish, equanimity, mindfulness, right knowledge, joyless bliss, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the third dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought and sustained investigation.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains the concentration associated with the flavoring of equanimity, which is without directed thought (vitarka), without sustained thought (vicāra), and without rapture (prīti). Just as the bhikṣu contemplates that this equanimity is coarse and that the mind still possesses mental activity, he perceives that the state of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (aduḥkhāsukha) characterized by equanimity is peaceful and superior.

When a bhikkhu has observed that joyless pleasure is coarse, and that joyless pleasure is peaceful, perfectly peaceful, ceased, subsided, and eliminated—once it has ceased, subsided, and been eliminated—he dwells with equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and one-pointedness of mind; for this person, inhalation and exhalation cease.

Regarding those who have not yet reached the fourth dhyāna: if one enters this concentration, one attains the four factors—neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, mindfulness and clear comprehension, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the intermediate dhyāna concentration, which is without vitarka and without vicāra.
Between the third and fourth dhyānas, one proceeds from the third dhyāna toward the fourth dhyāna.

For instance, if a bhikṣu—whether through practice, receiving instruction, the characteristics of dharmas, skillful means, single-minded concentration, reflection, or contact—attains the absorption that is free from vitarka and vicāra, devoid of joy, and characterized by the relish of bliss.

When a bhikkhu practices up to the point of contact, and having approached and cultivated this practice extensively, his mind inclines toward stillness, tends toward stillness, and leans toward stillness; once it leans toward stillness, there is no joy or pleasure, only stillness, perfect stillness, cessation, and disappearance; with that cessation and disappearance, there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and one-pointedness of mind, and for such a person, inhalation and exhalation cease.

Regarding those who have not yet entered the fourth dhyāna: if one enters this concentration, one attains the four factors—neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, mindfulness and clear comprehension, and one-pointedness of mind—and this is called the intermediate dhyāna concentration without applied thought and sustained thought.
Between the third and fourth dhyānas, he proceeds from the third dhyāna to the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu, having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of joy and grief, dwells in the attainment of the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness.

For example, when a bhikṣu possesses joyless, neither-painful-nor-pleasant, equanimity, pure mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind—if he enters this concentration, he attains, correctly attains, and gains the four factors:

neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, equanimity, pure mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the fourth dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought and sustained examination.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu attains the concentration associated with the relish of equanimity, which is without applied thought, without sustained thought, and without rapture. The bhikṣu contemplates that this equanimity is coarse; because the mind still possesses volitional activity, the tranquility and excellence of the equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant are superior.

When a bhikkhu has observed that joyless rapture is coarse, that joyless rapture becomes stilled, perfectly stilled, ceased, and eliminated; because it has ceased and been eliminated, there arises neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, purity of mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind.
If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains the four factors:
neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, purity of mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the fourth dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought or sustained evaluation.

For example, when a bhikṣu—whether walking, receiving instruction, regarding the characteristics of phenomena, applying skillful means, concentrating the mind, reflecting, or making contact—attains the concentration associated with the relish of meditative absorption that is without applied thought, without sustained thought, and without rapture and pleasure.

Just as when a bhikkhu practices up to the point of contact, having approached and trained extensively, once he has so trained, his mind inclines toward tranquility, tends toward tranquility, and leans toward tranquility; having leaned toward tranquility, there is the cessation, subsiding, disappearance, and elimination of rapture and pleasure; with their cessation, disappearance, and elimination, there is neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, purity of mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind.
If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains its four factors:
neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, purity of mindfulness, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the fourth dhyāna, the concentration without directed thought and sustained thought.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory impingement, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.

Just as when a bhikṣu possesses the perception of the sphere of infinite space, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind—if he enters this meditative absorption, he correctly attains, acquires, and gains three factors:
the perception of the sphere of infinite space, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space, without directed thought or sustained evaluation.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, transcending all perceptions of the sphere of infinite space, dwells having achieved the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Just as a bhikṣu possesses the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind.
If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains three factors through right attainment and through objective support:

the perception of the sphere of consciousness, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, equanimity, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the concentration of the sphere of consciousness without directed thought and without sustained thought.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, transcending all perceptions of the sphere of infinite consciousness, attains and dwells in the sphere of nothingness.
Just as a bhikṣu possesses the perception of the sphere of nothingness, he is characterized by neither-pain-nor-pleasure, equanimity, and one-pointedness of mind.

If one enters this meditative absorption, one attains its three factors through right attainment and through acquisition: the perception of the sphere of nothingness, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind; this is called the absorption of the sphere of nothingness, which is without directed thought and without sustained evaluation.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu, transcending the sphere of nothingness, attains and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, the bhikṣu possesses the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, equanimity that is neither painful nor pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind.
One who enters this meditative absorption attains three factors through right attainment, objective attainment, and mental attainment:
the perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, equanimity that is neither-painful-nor-pleasant, and one-pointedness of mind.
This is called the concentration of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, without applied thought and without sustained thought.
What is the concentration of emptiness?
It is when a bhikṣu contemplates all phenomena—or the phenomena of any single location—as empty, knows them as empty, understands them as empty, and realizes them as empty.
By what meaning is it empty?
It is empty of self, and that which belongs to the self is also empty.
Observing in this way with heedfulness, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells rightly; this is called the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Furthermore, there are six kinds of emptiness within the concentration on emptiness:
internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, the emptiness of emptiness, great emptiness, and the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
What is meant by internal emptiness?
For example, a bhikṣu contemplates all internal phenomena, or internal phenomena in a single location, as empty—he knows them as empty, understands them as empty, and accepts them as empty.
In what sense are they empty?
Because the self is empty, that which belongs to the self is also empty; it is empty of permanence and empty of immutability.
Observing thus with heedfulness, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells rightly; this is called internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*).
What is called "emptiness of the external"?
It is when a bhikṣu contemplates all external phenomena—or external phenomena in a single location—as empty, knows them as empty, understands them as empty, and realizes them as empty.
In what sense is it empty?
It is empty of self, and that which belongs to the self is also empty.
Contemplating thus with heedfulness, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called external emptiness.
What is internal-external emptiness?

It is as when a bhikṣu contemplates all internal and external phenomena—or internal and external phenomena in a single location—as empty, knows them as empty, understands them as empty, and accepts them as empty.
In what sense is it empty?
It is empty of self, and that which belongs to the self is also empty.
Observing in this way with heedfulness, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established; this is called internal and external emptiness (*adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā*).
What is meant by the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*)?

It is when a bhikṣu accomplishes the practice of the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), and the bhikṣu contemplates emptiness, knows emptiness, understands emptiness, and realizes emptiness.
In what sense is it empty?
Because the self is empty, that which belongs to the self is also empty; it is empty of permanence and empty of immutability.
When one observes thus with heedfulness, attaining the concentration on emptiness such that the mind abides and is rightly established, this is called "emptiness of emptiness."
What is called "great emptiness"?
It is as when a bhikṣu contemplates all phenomena as empty, knows them as empty, understands them as empty, and accepts them as empty.
In what sense are they empty?
Because the self is empty, that which belongs to the self is also empty.
Observing in this way with heedfulness, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells correctly; this is called the "Great Emptiness" (mahā-śūnyatā).
What is meant by the "Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha-śūnyatā)?
The first refers to nirvāṇa.
For example, a bhikṣu contemplates nirvāṇa as empty, knows it as empty, understands it as empty, and accepts it as empty.
In what sense is it empty?
Because the self is empty, that which belongs to the self is also empty; it is empty of permanence and empty of immutability.

Observing in this way with heedfulness, one attains concentration such that the mind abides and remains rightly established; this is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
These six kinds of emptiness are called the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
What is meant by the concentration of signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*)?
Any other concentration besides the concentration of emptiness that takes noble *nirvāṇa* as its object is called the concentration of signlessness.
Furthermore, regarding the concentration on the signless (*animitta-samādhi*): conditioned phenomena possess signs, whereas nirvāṇa is signless.
Conditioned phenomena have three characteristics—arising, abiding, and ceasing;
nirvāṇa lacks these three characteristics, being without arising, without abiding, and without ceasing.

Thus, conditioned existence has characteristics, while nirvāṇa is without characteristics; nirvāṇa is cessation, it is a dwelling, it is protection, it is illumination, it is a refuge, it is non-perishing, it is the destination, it is without feverish distress, it is without sorrow and affliction, and it is free from grief, lamentation, suffering, and all other conditioned formations.
