Contemplating nirvāṇa so that the concentrated mind attains stability and right abiding is called the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*).
What is the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*)?
Excluding the emptiness concentration, any other concentration that takes the noble conditioned phenomena as its object is called the wishless concentration.
Furthermore, regarding the concentration of wishlessness (*apranihita-samādhi*), there are two kinds of wishing:
attachment through craving (*tṛṣṇā-abhiniveśa*) and attachment through views (*dṛṣṭi-abhiniveśa*).

A bhikṣu contemplates conditioned phenomena as suffering, as a calamity, as an ulcer, as an arrow, as an attachment, and as a relish; he contemplates them as dependent on conditions, as perishable, as unstable, as insatiable, as subject to destruction, and as consisting of manifold sufferings. Without contemplating them as empty or selfless, he attains concentration such that his mind abides and remains rightly established.
A bhikṣu abandons craving and abandons views; this concentration can sever both craving and views, and is thus called the concentration of wishlessness (apraṇihita-samādhi).
What are the four foundations of mindfulness?
For example, a bhikṣu contemplates the body within the body, practicing with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, subduing longing and dejection regarding the world.
Contemplating the body externally while observing the activities of the body, he dwells with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, having stilled worldly hopes and anxieties;

contemplating the body internally and externally while observing the activities of the body, he dwells with diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, having stilled worldly hopes and anxieties.
Feeling, mind, and phenomena are also like this.
These are called the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four right endeavors?

Just as a bhikṣu, when unwholesome and unskillful states have not yet arisen, desires that they not arise, and thus arouses desire, exerts himself, strives for excellence, and applies right effort to restrain the mind;
when unwholesome states have already arisen, desires that they be abandoned, and thus arouses desire, exerts himself, strives for excellence, and applies right effort to restrain the mind;
when wholesome states have not yet arisen, desires that they arise, and thus arouses desire, exerts himself, strives for excellence, and applies right effort to restrain the mind;

When wholesome states have arisen, one desires them to remain, cultivating them fully so they are not forgotten but rather expand and increase; one arouses desire, exerts oneself, strives for excellence, and applies right effort to restrain the mind.
These are called the four right efforts.
What are the four bases of psychic power?

They are as follows: a bhikṣu cultivates the base of psychic power endowed with the cultivation of volitional formations, namely the base of psychic power endowed with the cultivation of volitional formations consisting of concentration of energy, concentration of mind, concentration of mindfulness, and concentration of wisdom. These are called the four bases of psychic power.
The four dhyānas are as explained in the Dhyāna Chapter.
What are the four immeasurables?
They are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
What is loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
It is when a bhikṣu contemplates the happiness of sentient beings, knows their happiness, understands their happiness, and experiences their happiness.
Suppose there are sentient beings who have previously harmed or troubled the bhikṣu; toward these beings, the bhikṣu’s mind remains obstructed, impure, unapproachable, and uncomprehending.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"Sentient beings have already harmed me.
Although sentient beings have injured me, it is not the dharma for me to retaliate; if I were to harbor anger or resentment toward sentient beings, I would only be harming myself."
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices patience toward sentient beings, extinguishing anger and affliction. With his mind, he reflects on the desire for sentient beings to be happy, to know happiness, to understand happiness, and to experience happiness.
There may be beings who have never before harmed or troubled a bhikṣu, yet now do so.
Toward these beings, the bhikṣu’s mind becomes obstructed and impure; he does not draw near to them nor understand them.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"Sentient beings have never previously harmed me, yet now they are harming me.

Although sentient beings are currently harming me, it may be the retribution for my own past karma and cannot be prevented by me; if I respond with anger and resentment toward these beings, I shall only bring harm upon myself."
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has harmed me.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices forbearance toward sentient beings, extinguishing the mind of anger and affliction, and contemplates wishing for sentient beings to have happiness, to know happiness, to understand happiness, and to experience happiness.
There may be sentient beings who have never previously harmed or troubled a bhikṣu, do not harm him now, but intend to harm him in the future.
Toward such beings, the bhikṣu’s mind is obstructed and impure; he does not associate with them and does not understand them.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"Sentient beings have never previously harmed me; they do not harm me now; yet they intend to harm me in the future.

Even though sentient beings may intend to harm me, perhaps they will not act upon it, or perhaps the necessary conditions will not converge. If I become angry and resentful toward these sentient beings, I shall only bring harm upon myself."
"Though he wishes to harm me, if I were to retaliate, I would injure myself far more than him.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices patience toward sentient beings, eliminates the mind of anger and affliction, and contemplates bringing happiness to sentient beings—making them know happiness, understand happiness, and experience happiness.

There may be sentient beings who have never previously harmed a bhikṣu, do not harm one now, and will not harm one in the future; yet, they have never previously harmed those whom I love, cherish, and find pleasing, but now they are currently harming those whom I love, cherish, and find pleasing.
A bhikṣu has mental obstacles toward sentient beings; his mind is impure, he does not associate with them, and he does not understand them.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Sentient beings have never previously harmed me, they do not harm me now, and they will not harm me in the future; yet those whom I hold dear, who are pleasing and agreeable to me, have harmed me."

Although sentient beings may harm those who are dear to me, pleasing to me, and agreeable to me, I should not harm them; for if I were to become angry and harm sentient beings, I would only bring harm upon myself.
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, my own harm would be even greater than his.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices forbearance toward sentient beings, eliminating the mind of malice and resentment, and contemplates wishing for sentient beings to find happiness, to know happiness, to understand happiness, and to experience happiness.

There may be sentient beings who have never previously harmed a bhikṣu, do not harm one now, and will not harm one in the future; yet who have never previously harmed those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing, but who now currently harm those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing.
A bhikṣu finds his mind obstructed toward sentient beings, unpurified, unapproachable, and uncomprehending.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:

"Sentient beings have never previously harmed me, they do not harm me now, and they will not harm me; those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing have never previously harmed me, yet those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing are harming me now."

Although sentient beings may harm those who are dear to me, pleasing, or agreeable to me, this is likely the retribution of past karma; I cannot obstruct the past karma of others, and if I respond with anger or vexation toward sentient beings, I only cause myself harm.
"If he harms me, and I retaliate in return, my own loss will be even greater than his.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices forbearance toward sentient beings, eliminates the mind of anger and affliction, and contemplates how to cause sentient beings to find happiness, to know happiness, to understand happiness, and to experience happiness.

There may be sentient beings who have never previously harmed a bhikṣu, do not harm one now, and will not harm one in the future; or those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing, who have never previously harmed me, do not harm me now, and will not harm me in the future; or those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing, who have never previously harmed me, do not harm me now, but will desire to harm me in the future.
A bhikṣu has a mind that is obstructed toward sentient beings, impure, unapproachable, and unintelligent.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Sentient beings have never harmed me in the past, they do not harm me now, and they will not harm me in the future."
Those whom I love, cherish, and find pleasing have never previously harmed me, nor do they harm me now;
yet those whom I love, cherish, and find pleasing might wish to harm me in the future.

Although sentient beings may wish to harm those whom I love, cherish, and find pleasing, they may fail to do so or the necessary conditions may not converge; yet, if I were to become angry and resentful toward these sentient beings, I would only bring harm upon myself.
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices forbearance toward sentient beings, eliminates his mind of malice and resentment, and contemplates how to bring happiness to sentient beings—making them know happiness, understand happiness, and experience happiness."
There may be sentient beings who have never previously harmed a bhikṣu, do not harm one now, and will not harm one in the future.
Or those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing, who have never previously harmed one, do not harm one now, and will not harm one in the future.
If I have not previously benefited those whom I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing,
then, O bhikṣu, my mind toward sentient beings is obstructed, impure, unapproachable, and unintelligent.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"Sentient beings have never harmed me in the past, do not harm me now, and will not harm me in the future.
Those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing have never harmed me in the past, do not harm me now, and will not harm me in the future."
Even if those whom I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing have already benefited me, I should not harm or afflict them;
for if I harbor anger or resentment toward sentient beings, I only bring about my own ruin.
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices forbearance toward sentient beings, eliminates the mind of malice and affliction, and contemplates how to cause sentient beings to find happiness, recognize happiness, understand happiness, and experience happiness."
There may be sentient beings who have never previously harmed bhikṣus, do not harm them now, and will not harm them in the future;
or those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing, who have never previously harmed them, do not harm them now, and will not harm them in the future.
If those whom I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing have never previously benefited me;
yet if those whom I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing now benefit me— then, monks,
my mind toward these beings is obstructed, impure, unapproachable, and unintegrated.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"Sentient beings have never previously harmed me, do not harm me now, and will not harm me in the future.
Those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing have never previously harmed me, do not harm me now, and will not harm me in the future."

If those whom I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing have never previously benefited me, yet they now benefit me—though these beings benefit me despite my lack of affection or pleasure—it may be due to the retribution of past karma;
I cannot obstruct the retribution of another's past karma. If I were to feel anger or distress toward these beings, it would only bring harm upon myself.
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu exercises patience toward sentient beings, eliminates his mind of malice and affliction, and contemplates how to cause sentient beings to find happiness, to recognize happiness, to understand happiness, and to experience happiness."
There may be sentient beings who have never before harmed or troubled a bhikṣu, do not harm him now, and will not harm him in the future;
and those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing, who likewise have never before harmed him, do not harm him now, and will not harm him in the future.
If that which I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing has never benefited me in the past and does not benefit me now,
yet if that which I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing should seek to benefit me— [then it would be a contradiction].
A bhikṣu has an obstructed, impure, unapproachable, and unintelligent mind toward sentient beings.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Sentient beings have never harmed me in the past, they do not harm me now, and they will not harm me in the future."
If there is one whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing, whom I have never harmed in the past, do not harm now, and shall not harm in the future;
and if there is one whom I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing, whom I have never benefited in the past, do not benefit now, and whom I intend to benefit [in the future].
If there are those whom I do not love, delight in, or find pleasing, yet whom I wish to benefit—

should they wish to benefit me but fail to do so due to lack of effort or the non-convergence of conditions— if I were to feel anger or resentment toward these beings, it would only bring harm upon myself.
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has harmed me.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu exercises patience toward sentient beings, eliminates his mind of anger and affliction, and contemplates how to cause sentient beings to find happiness, recognize happiness, understand happiness, and experience happiness.
There may be sentient beings who have never previously harmed a bhikṣu, do not harm one now, and will not harm one in the future.
Or, those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing have never previously harmed one, do not harm one now, and will not harm one in the future.
If I do not love, delight in, or find pleasure in someone, they have not benefited me in the past, do not benefit me now, and will not benefit me in the future.
In this way, a bhikṣu, without cause or condition, becomes cross with sentient beings; his mind toward those beings is obstructed, impure, unapproachable, and lacks understanding.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Sentient beings have never harmed me in the past, do not harm me now, and will not harm me in the future.
Those whom I love, delight in, and find pleasing have never harmed me in the past, do not harm me now, and will not harm me in the future."
If I do not love, delight in, or find pleasure in someone, they have not benefited me in the past, do not benefit me now, and will not benefit me in the future.
Without any cause or reason, I then become cross with sentient beings; my mind toward them becomes obstructed, impure, distant, and ignorant.
"If I harbor anger and vexation toward sentient beings, I only bring harm upon myself.
Since they have already harmed me, if I retaliate, my self-inflicted harm will be even greater than theirs.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices forbearance toward sentient beings, removes the mind of anger and vexation, and contemplates how to cause sentient beings to find happiness, recognize happiness, understand happiness, and experience happiness.

Just as a bhikṣu, regarding sentient beings in the eastern direction, eliminates a mind of hatred and affliction, and contemplates with the desire to cause those beings to find joy, know joy, understand joy, and experience joy;

and likewise, regarding sentient beings in the southern, western, and northern directions, he eliminates a mind of hatred and affliction, contemplating with the desire to cause those beings to find joy, know joy, understand joy, and experience joy.

Just as a bhikṣu practices by pervading one direction with a mind of loving-kindness, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—pervading the entire world with a mind of loving-kindness that is vast, sublime, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—this is called loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
What is compassion? It is as follows:
a bhikṣu does not contemplate the pleasure of sentient beings, does not know their pleasure, does not understand their pleasure, and does not experience their pleasure.

When a bhikṣu sees sentient beings suffering and undergoing suffering—whether they be parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, relatives, kinsmen, friends, ministers, or those in the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; or whether they be among humans who are poor and lowly, or among spirits who are poor and lowly—he feels pity for those sentient beings and gives rise to a heart of compassion.
There may be sentient beings who have already harmed or provoked a bhikṣu; toward such beings, the bhikṣu’s mind is obstructed, impure, unapproachable, and lacks understanding.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"Sentient beings have previously harmed me; although sentient beings harm me, I should not harm them in return. If I were to harbor anger and resentment toward sentient beings, it would only bring me self-injury."
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has harmed me.
Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu exercises forbearance toward sentient beings, eliminates his mind of anger and affliction, and gives rise to compassion through sympathy for sentient beings.
There may be sentient beings who have never before harmed or provoked a bhikṣu, yet they harbor groundless and unjust anger as described above.
Just as with a bhikṣu, if one extinguishes the mind of hatred and affliction toward sentient beings in the eastern direction and gives rise to compassion through a heart of pity for those beings;

and likewise extinguishes the mind of hatred and affliction toward sentient beings in the southern, western, and northern directions, giving rise to compassion through a heart of pity for those beings.

A bhikṣu practices by pervading one direction with a mind of compassion; then the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—all directions—pervading the entire world with a mind of compassion that is vast, sublime, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will. This is called compassion (*karuṇā*).
What is called joy (*muditā*)?
It is when a bhikṣu does not contemplate the happiness of sentient beings, does not know their happiness, does not understand their happiness, and does not experience their happiness.
Toward sentient beings, such a bhikṣu fails to attain compassion and does not give rise to a heart of pity (*karuṇā*).

Suppose, for example, a bhikṣu sees sentient beings experiencing happiness and joy—whether they be parents, brothers, sisters, wives, children, relatives, friends, ministers, or deities, sons of gods, Buddhas, or disciples of the Buddha—and he feels gladness toward those beings without relying on perceptions tainted by sensual desire.
There may be sentient beings who have previously harmed or provoked a bhikṣu; toward such beings, the bhikṣu’s mind becomes obstructed, impure, and lacks understanding.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"These beings have already harmed me. Although these beings have harmed me, I ought not to harm them in return. If I were to harm these beings, it would only bring about my own ruin."
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, I would harm myself even more than he has harmed me.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu practices forbearance toward sentient beings, eliminates the mind of anger and affliction, attains joy toward sentient beings, and does not rely on perceptions of sensual defilement.
There may be sentient beings who have never before harmed or provoked a bhikṣu, yet they harbor groundless and unjust anger toward him as described above.
If a bhikṣu eliminates his heart of anger and affliction toward sentient beings in the eastern direction and attains a heart of joy toward them, without relying on perceptions of sensual desire;

and if he eliminates his heart of anger and affliction toward sentient beings in the southern, western, and northern directions and attains a heart of joy toward them, without relying on perceptions of sensual desire.

A bhikṣu dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with joy; likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below. Pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with joy—vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity and free from ill will—he dwells. This is called joy.
What is meant by equanimity (*upekṣā*)?

It is when a bhikṣu does not contemplate the pleasure of sentient beings, does not know their pleasure, does not understand their pleasure, and does not experience their pleasure; he does not obtain compassion, does not give rise to a mind of pity, does not attain sympathetic joy, and does not rely on perceptions of sensual passion.

Just as a bhikṣu attains equanimity by taking only sentient beings as his object—just as when a person enters a forest, he does not discriminate, thinking, "This is a *pāṭala* tree, a *nyagrodha* tree, a *vīrakṣa* tree, an *udumbara* tree, a *kapiñjala* tree, a *kapittha* tree, a *nīpa* tree, a *mṛda* tree, or an *etagha* tree," but sees only the forest without discriminating among the various trees.

In this way, a bhikṣu does not contemplate the pleasure of sentient beings, does not know their pleasure, does not understand their pleasure, and does not experience their pleasure; he does not obtain compassion, does not give rise to a mind of pity, and does not attain sympathetic joy; he does not rely on perceptions of sensual desire, but attains equanimity solely by taking sentient beings as his object.
There may be sentient beings who have previously harmed or provoked a bhikṣu; toward such beings, the bhikṣu’s mind is obstructed, impure, unreflective, and ignorant.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"Sentient beings have already harmed me; although sentient beings harm me, I should not harm them in return. If I were to harbor anger and resentment toward sentient beings, I would only bring harm upon myself."
"He has already harmed me; if I were to retaliate, my own harm would be far greater than his.

Having reflected thus, the bhikṣu exercises patience toward sentient beings, eliminates the mind of anger and affliction, and attains equanimity solely by taking sentient beings as the object of focus.
There may be sentient beings who have never before harmed or provoked a bhikṣu, yet they harbor groundless and unjust anger as described above.
Just as with a bhikṣu, if one eliminates the mind of anger and affliction toward sentient beings in the eastern direction, one attains equanimity solely by taking those sentient beings as the object;

likewise, if one eliminates the mind of anger and affliction toward sentient beings in the southern, western, and northern directions, one attains equanimity solely by taking those sentient beings as the object.

Just as a bhikṣu dwells pervading one direction with a mind of equanimity, and likewise the second, third, and fourth directions, the four intermediate points, and above and below—in all cases, by means of a mind of equanimity that is vast, sublime, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—he dwells pervading the entire world; this is called equanimity.
These are called the four immeasurables.
What are the four formless attainments?

They are as follows: a bhikṣu, having transcended all perceptions of form, having extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, achieves and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
Detaching from all the sphere of infinite space, one accomplishes the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness;
detaching from all the sphere of infinite consciousness, one accomplishes the practice of the sphere of nothingness;
detaching from all the sphere of nothingness, one accomplishes the practice of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
These are called the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
What are the four paths of progress? They are:

the path of progress toward suffering that is difficult to practice, the path of progress toward suffering that is swift to practice, the path of progress toward happiness that is difficult to practice, and the path of progress toward happiness that is swift to practice.
What is the difficult-to-practice path leading toward suffering? It is as follows:
suppose there is a bhikṣu whose nature is full of greed, whose nature is full of hatred, and whose nature is full of delusion.

As this bhikṣu practices the path, he repeatedly experiences sorrow and suffering because he must guard against the defilement of desire; he repeatedly experiences sorrow and suffering because he must guard against hatred; and he repeatedly experiences sorrow and suffering because he must guard against delusion. This bhikṣu possesses dull practice regarding the five noble faculties.
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Because a bhikṣu possesses dull faculties, he realizes immediate concentration and exhausts all outflows; this is called the difficult path toward the cessation of suffering.
What is the swift practice of the path leading toward suffering? It is as follows:
suppose a bhikṣu is by nature full of greed, by nature full of hatred, and by nature full of delusion.

As this bhikṣu practices the path, because he restrains the defilement of desire, he repeatedly experiences sorrow and suffering; because he restrains hatred, he repeatedly experiences sorrow and suffering; because he restrains delusion, he repeatedly experiences sorrow and suffering. This bhikṣu’s noble practice consists of the sharp application of the five faculties.
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

When a bhikṣu practices with these five faculties sharpened, he swiftly realizes the uninterrupted concentration that exhausts all outflows; this is called the "swift path leading toward the end of suffering."
What is meant by the difficult practice of the path leading to pleasure? It is as follows:
A bhikṣu is one whose nature has little lustful passion, little ill will, and little delusion.

Because this bhikṣu has little lustful passion, he does not frequently experience sorrow and suffering; because he has little ill will, he does not frequently experience sorrow and suffering; because he has little delusion, he does not frequently experience sorrow and suffering. This bhikṣu possesses the five noble faculties, yet his practice is dull.
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

When a bhikṣu possesses dull faculties yet realizes the immediate concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) to exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*), this is called the path leading toward happiness that is difficult to practice.
What is meant by "swift progress toward the path of pleasure"? It is as follows:
suppose there is a bhikṣu who, by nature, has little greed, little ill-will, and little delusion.

As this bhikṣu practices the path, because his defilement of desire is slight, he does not frequently experience sorrow and suffering; because his ill-will is slight, he does not frequently experience sorrow and suffering; and because his delusion is slight, he does not frequently experience sorrow and suffering. This bhikṣu practices with the sharpest of the noble five faculties.
What are the five?
They are the faculty of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
When a bhikṣu practices with these five faculties sharpened, he realizes the immediate concentration that exhausts all outflows; this is called "swift progress on the path leading to bliss."
These are called the four paths of progress.
What are the four cultivations of concentration?
They are the four cultivations of concentration as taught by the Blessed One.
What are the four?

There is the cultivation of concentration through frequent practice and extensive training that results in the attainment of happiness in the present life; there is the cultivation of concentration through frequent practice and extensive training that results in the attainment of knowledge and vision; there is the cultivation of concentration through frequent practice and extensive training that results in the attainment of wisdom and discernment; and there is the cultivation of concentration through frequent practice and extensive training that results in the attainment of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
What is meant by cultivating concentration, approaching it, and training in it extensively so as to attain the practice of happiness in the present life?
It is, for example, when a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and happiness.

With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation (*vitarka-vicāra*), possessing internal clarity and confidence, and with one-pointed mind, he enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from directed thought and evaluation and possesses the joy and bliss born of concentration.

With the fading away of joy, he dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing bliss with the body; he enters and dwells in the third dhyāna, of which the noble ones declare: "He dwells in bliss who possesses equanimity and mindfulness."

Having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, one dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly conscious, experiencing the bliss of which the noble ones say, "One who is equanimous and mindful dwells in bliss"; thus one accomplishes the practice of the fourth dhyāna.
By thus cultivating concentration, approaching it, and training in it extensively, one attains the practice of happiness in the present life.
What is meant by cultivating concentration, approaching it, and training extensively therein so as to attain knowledge and vision?
It is as follows: a bhikṣu properly grasps the perception of light and properly maintains the perception of day.
Just as the bhikṣu cultivates the perception of light during the day, he does likewise at night.
Just as one cultivates the perception of light at night, so too during the day.
Through the awakening of the mind, the mind is not shrouded; the mind cultivated with light—this concentration, when approached and practiced extensively, leads to knowledge and vision.
What is meant by cultivating concentration, attending to it, and training in it extensively so as to attain the analytical wisdom of discernment?

It is as follows: when a bhikṣu knows the arising of feeling, knows the persistence of feeling, and knows the cessation of feeling; knows the arising of perception, knows the persistence of perception, and knows the cessation of perception; knows the arising of volitional formations, knows the persistence of volitional formations, and knows the cessation of volitional formations—this is cultivating concentration, attending to it, and training in it extensively so as to attain the analytical wisdom of discernment.
What is meant by practicing concentration, approaching it, and training in it extensively so as to attain the destruction of the outflows?

It is like a bhikṣu who knows the arising and passing away of the five aggregates of clinging; he knows form, he knows the origin of form, he knows the cessation of form; he knows feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; he knows the origin of consciousness, and he knows the cessation of consciousness. By practicing this concentration, approaching it, and training in it extensively, one attains the destruction of the outflows.

As asked in the *Pārāyaṇa Sūtra*: "One cuts off all perceptions of desire, extinguishes sorrow and affliction, abandons sloth and torpor, restrains restlessness and remorse, abandons mindfulness and purity, first extinguishes applied and sustained thought, realizes awakening and liberation, and severs ignorance."
These are called the four cultivations of concentration.
What are the four abandonments? They are:
abandonment through precepts, abandonment through subtle guarding, abandonment through cultivation, and abandonment through the object of wisdom.
What is meant by the restraint of the precepts?

It is when a bhikṣu, seeing forms with the eye, does not grasp at their signs nor engage in conceptualization that would agitate the faculty of the eye; he constantly maintains self-restraint in his conduct, does not rely on worldly hopes or anxieties, and avoids evil and unwholesome states, carefully guarding the faculty of the eye and attaining the precept of the faculty of the eye.

The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind: when the mind cognizes dharmas, do not grasp at signs or engage in discrimination that causes the mind-faculty to arise. Constantly restrain your conduct; do not rely on worldly hopes, anxieties, or unwholesome dharmas. Carefully guard the mind-faculty and attain the precept of the mind-faculty.
This is called abandonment through restraint (*śīla-prahāṇa*).
What is meant by abandonment through careful guarding (*susaṃvṛta-prahāṇa*)?

It is when a bhikṣu, taking up the signs of the wholesome, practices careful guarding [of the mind] toward [the corpse], whether it be the bones and joints, or a swelling and blister, or bloatedness, or lividity, or a dark-red or blackish discoloration, or putrefaction and disintegration.
Observing the arising of wholesome states in this way, one maintains subtle protection; this is called abandonment through subtle protection (*sūkṣmasaṃvara-prahāṇa*).
What is abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*)?

It is when a bhikṣu cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, relying on cessation, and culminating in relinquishment; he cultivates the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, and concentration, as well as the awakening factor of equanimity, relying on seclusion, relying on dispassion, and relying on cessation. This is called abandonment through cultivation.
What is meant by "abandonment through the condition of wisdom"?
It is as when a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, reflects thus:
"The retribution for unwholesome and evil bodily conduct occurs both in this life and in future lives."
Just as a bhikṣu endures and abandons bodily misconduct and cultivates good bodily conduct;
and just as a bhikṣu endures and abandons verbal misconduct and cultivates good verbal conduct, [thereby avoiding] the retribution for such unwholesome conduct in both this life and future lives.
Unwholesome mental conduct brings about evil retribution in both this life and future lives.
Just as a bhikṣu endures and abandons unwholesome mental conduct and cultivates wholesome mental conduct,
this is called "abandonment through the condition of wisdom."
The Tathāgata has taught that the abandonment through cultivation is guarded by the restraint of the precepts;
when a bhikṣu practices this Dharma, all suffering reaches its end—
this is called the fourfold knowledge of abandonment.
What are the five faculties?
The faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom—these are called the five faculties.
The five powers are likewise.
What are the five bases of liberation? They are as follows:

a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligence, mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility; thus, his mind that was not yet liberated becomes liberated, his outflows that were not yet exhausted become exhausted, and he attains the unsurpassed peace and security that he had not yet attained.
What are the five?

If the Blessed One teaches the Dharma to the bhikṣus, or if the Teacher teaches, or if wise brahmins and pure practitioners teach—teachings that accord with what the Tathāgata, the Teacher, or wise brahmins and pure practitioners have taught—one listens and then receives both the Dharma and its meaning.

Having received the Dharma and its meaning, joy arises; from joy, rapture arises; from rapture, tranquility of body is attained; from tranquility of body, one experiences pleasure; from experiencing pleasure, the mind becomes concentrated; and with the mind concentrated, one knows and sees according to reality.

If a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, and dwells in tranquility, he attains liberation where his mind was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains the unsurpassed peace where it was not yet attained. This is called the first ground of liberation.
Furthermore, monks, when it is not spoken by the Blessed One, nor by a teacher, nor by one who is wise and pure in holy life, one extensively recites and masters the Dharma as previously heard.
Just as a bhikṣu who has previously heard the Dharma extensively recites and masters it, receiving both the teachings and their meaning;

and just as that bhikṣu, having received the teachings and their meaning, gives rise to joy; having given rise to joy, he gives rise to rapture; having given rise to rapture, he attains tranquility of body; having attained tranquility of body, he experiences bliss; having experienced bliss, his mind becomes concentrated; and with his mind concentrated, he knows and sees according to reality.

In this way, a bhikṣu who practices with diligence, mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility—having attained liberation where the mind was not yet liberated, having attained the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted, and having attained supreme peace where it was not yet attained—is said to have reached the second basis of liberation.

Furthermore, monks, it is not when the Blessed One, the Teacher, or wise fellow practitioners of the holy life are speaking; nor is it when one is extensively reciting, chanting, and mastering a Dharma that was previously heard, but rather when a monk, having mastered a Dharma previously heard, explains it extensively to others.
Just as a bhikṣu, having mastered the Dharma he has heard, explains it extensively to others, receiving both the teachings and their meaning.

Having received the teachings and their meaning, the bhikṣu gives rise to joy; from joy, rapture arises; from rapture, the body becomes tranquil; with the body tranquil, he experiences bliss; experiencing bliss, his mind becomes concentrated; and with the mind concentrated, he knows and sees things as they truly are.

When a bhikṣu thus practices with diligence, mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, he attains liberation where his mind was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all outflows where they were not yet exhausted; he attains supreme peace where it was not yet attained. This is called the third basis of liberation.

Furthermore, it is as when a bhikṣu does not speak at a time when the Blessed One, his teacher, or wise companions in the holy life have spoken; nor at a time when he has extensively read, recited, and mastered a Dharma he had previously heard; nor at a time when he has extensively mastered a Dharma he had previously heard and analyzed it for others; rather, it is as when a bhikṣu analyzes within his own mind a Dharma he has previously heard and mastered.
Just as a bhikṣu, having mastered the Dharma as he has heard it and having analyzed it with his own mind, receives the teachings and their meaning;

once the bhikṣu has received the teachings and their meaning, joy arises; from joy, rapture arises; from rapture, tranquility of body is attained; from tranquility of body, he experiences bliss; from experiencing bliss, the mind becomes concentrated; and with the mind concentrated, he knows and sees things as they truly are.

When a bhikṣu thus practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, he attains liberation where the mind was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains the unsurpassed peace and security where it was not yet attained. This is called the fourth basis of liberation.

Furthermore, monks, it is not when the Blessed One, the Teacher, or a wise fellow practitioner of the holy life speaks; nor when one is extensively reciting and mastering a Dharma one has previously heard; nor when one is extensively mastering a Dharma one has previously heard and analyzing it for others; nor when one is mastering a Dharma one has previously heard and analyzing it within one's own mind. Rather, it is like a monk who has properly grasped the signs of concentration, who reflects well, and who is skilled in discernment.
When a bhikṣu has properly grasped the perception of concentration, properly reflected upon it, and properly mastered its application, he receives the Dharma and its meaning.

Having received the Dharma and its meaning, joy arises; from joy, rapture arises; from rapture, tranquility of body is attained; from tranquility of body, he experiences bliss; from experiencing bliss, the mind becomes concentrated; and with a concentrated mind, he knows and sees according to reality.

In this way, when a bhikkhu practices with diligence, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and tranquility, he attains liberation where his mind was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; he attains supreme peace where it was not yet attained. This is called the fifth ground for liberation.
These are called the five bases of liberation.
The five elements of transcendence are as explained in the "Chapter on Elements.
What are the five meditative concentrations of contemplation?
As stated in the *Saddhā-sutta*, Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
There is yet another unsurpassed Dharma, namely, the World-Honored One’s teaching on entering meditative concentration for contemplation."
World-Honored One!

There is this meditative absorption; there may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through diligent effort, heroic vigor, right reflection, extensive cultivation of the mind, and reflection in accordance with the Dharma, enter into meditative absorption.

Having entered meditative concentration, one contemplates the body from the crown of the head to the feet, and from the feet to the crown of the head, even down to the thin skin; all of it is impure. This is called the initial contemplation within meditative concentration.

Furthermore, there may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, being diligent, energetic, and resolute, with right reflection and a mind cultivated through extensive learning and practice, enter meditative concentration by reflecting in accordance with the Dharma.

Having entered meditative concentration, one does not observe the skin, flesh, or blood, but observes only human bones; that within this body there are bones, teeth, and nails is called the second stage of meditative observation.

Furthermore, there may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, being diligent, energetic, and resolute, with right reflection and a mind cultivated through extensive learning and practice, enter meditative concentration by reflecting in accordance with the Dharma.
Having entered meditative concentration, one does not observe skin, blood, flesh, or bone, but observes consciousness alone.

Consciousness dwells in this world and dwells in other worlds; as long as consciousness is not severed, it does not depart from these two worlds. This is called the third entry into meditative observation.

Furthermore, there may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are diligent, energetic, and resolute; who possess right reflection and a mind of extensive learning and practice; and who, reflecting in accordance with the Dharma, enter meditative absorption.
Having entered absorption, they do not contemplate skin, blood, flesh, or bone, but instead contemplate human consciousness.

Consciousness does not abide in this world, nor does it abide in another world; consciousness is severed from this world, yet not yet severed from another world—this is called the fourth meditative absorption.

Furthermore, there may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, being diligent, energetic, and resolute, with right reflection and a mind cultivated through extensive learning and practice, enter meditative concentration by reflecting in accordance with the Dharma.
Having entered concentration, they do not contemplate the internal blood, flesh, skin, or bones, but instead contemplate human consciousness.

Consciousness does not abide in this world, nor does it abide in another world; consciousness is well-severed and detached from both worlds. This is called the fifth absorption of meditative observation.
Such is the unsurpassed absorption of meditative observation, which the Blessed One knows well; the Blessed One has thoroughly penetrated it, and there is none who can surpass him.
As I understand it, it is impossible for any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa to claim that they know what the World-Honored One knows;
this is called the fifth entry into meditative observation.
What are the five factors for the arising of liberation?
As the Blessed One said:
"Having approached and frequently practiced these five dharmas, one attains liberation."
What are the five? They are as follows:

a bhikṣu contemplates the perception of the impurity of the body, contemplates the perception of the impurity of food, contemplates the perception of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena, contemplates the perception of the lack of delight in the world, and contemplates the perception of death.
If one approaches, frequently practices, and trains in these five dharmas, one can attain liberation; these are called the five dharmas that give rise to liberation.
What are the six recollections?
They are the recollection of the Buddha, up to and including the recollection of the devas.
What is meant by mindfulness of the Buddha?
Taking the Buddha as one's object of focus, recollecting his virtues with harmony and without opposition—this is called mindfulness of the Buddha.
What is meant by mindfulness of the Dharma?
Taking the Dharma as one's object, recollecting it with goodness, in accordance with it and not in opposition to it—this is called mindfulness of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*).
What is meant by mindfulness of the Sangha?
Taking the Sangha as one's object, recollecting it with goodness, in accordance with it and not in opposition to it—this is called mindfulness of the Sangha (*saṃghānusmṛti*).
What is meant by mindfulness of precepts?
Precepts refer to the precepts of body and speech.
Taking these precepts as one's object, to mindfully recollect them with goodness, in accordance with them and without opposition—this is called mindfulness of precepts.
What is meant by mindfulness of giving?
There are two kinds of giving:
the gift of material wealth and the gift of the Dharma.
Taking generosity as one's object, being mindful of its goodness, compliant with it, and not contrary to it—this is called "mindfulness of generosity.
What is meant by "mindfulness of the devas"?
It refers to those devas who have transcended material food and are born through transformation; those devas do not contemplate past karma, nor do they discriminate regarding past karma.
Taking the devas as one's object of focus, recollecting them with thoughts that are wholesome, compliant, and non-oppositional—this is called "recollection of the devas.
These are the six recollections.
The six emptinesses are as explained in the *Śūnyatā-samādhi*.
The six transcendences are as explained in the "Chapter on Elements" (*Dhātuvarga*).
What are the six factors conducive to clear knowledge (*vidyā-bhāgīya-dharma*)?
As the Blessed One said:
If one approaches and frequently cultivates these six dharmas, they will give rise to clear knowledge and its constituent parts, and enable that clear knowledge to become vast.
What are the six? They are:

the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of the impurity of food, the perception of non-delight in all worlds, and the perception of death.
What are the factors conducive to enlightenment that consist of the perception of impermanence?
It is as when a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, reflects thus:
"Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent."
If one thus contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as impermanent, according to what the Blessed One has said regarding the three characteristics of conditioned phenomena—
arising, abiding, and ceasing— the bhikṣu contemplates arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Having thus tamed the mind through contemplation and cultivated it until it is pliant, and once it is pliant, he contemplates the impermanence of form and the impermanence of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If a practitioner contemplates and reflects upon this, it is called the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*).

By drawing near to it and practicing it extensively, having so drawn near and practiced it extensively, one gives rise to clarity, attains clarity, and acquires the factors conducive to clarity, thereby enabling that clarity to become vast; this is called the factor conducive to clarity regarding the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā-ālokapaṭilābhī dhammo*).
What is the light-factor of the perception of impermanence and suffering?
It is as when a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, reflects thus: "Form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering."
Thus, one contemplates these five aggregates of clinging as suffering.
As the Blessed One has said: "If form arises and persists, that itself is the arising of suffering; it is subject to illness, aging, and death.
If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness arise and persist, that itself is the arising of suffering; they are subject to illness, aging, and death."
Furthermore, as the Blessed One has taught the three types of suffering:
the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkha*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
What is meant by the suffering of conditioned existence?

The five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are suffering by their very nature, suffering in their form, and suffering in their specific characteristics; this is called the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
What is meant by the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*)?
The five aggregates of clinging are suffering by their very nature; they involve birth and further birth, arising and further arising, and manifestation and further manifestation.

Fully endowed with these, various diseases arise: diseases arising from heat, from phlegm, from wind, from excessive force, from the affliction of others, from seasonal changes, from the disharmony of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), from undigested food and drink, from the retribution of past karma, and from the imbalance of the primary elements; thus, eye-disease arises.
There arise diseases of the ears, nose, tongue, and body; there arise headaches, facial pains, ailments of the mouth, teeth, and throat, and ailments of the chest;
there arise snake-like body ailments, hiccups, coughing, vomiting, constricting pains, fevers, and abdominal pains;
there arise ringworm, scabs, eczema, and sores, as well as afflictions caused by the invasion of subtle winds.
Ulcers, carbuncles, maggots, white leprosy, emaciation, insanity, hemorrhoids, dysentery, red swellings, diseases of worms, and so forth; from fleas, lice, nits,
mosquitoes, gadflies, ants, and the like— there is not even a single pore on this body that does not harbor insects.

Just as when a carbuncle forms upon a person’s existing abscess, so too is the nature of suffering in the activity of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*): through birth and further birth, arising and further arising, and emerging and further emerging, they fully bring about various diseases. From illnesses born of heat, there is not even a single pore that does not harbor worms; this is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
What is the suffering of change?

It refers to the five aggregates of clinging undergoing transformation, decay, and maturation; their disintegration, exhaustion, and cessation; and their final disappearance and extinction. This is called the suffering of change.

Just as a bhikṣu, regarding those sufferings of conditioned existence, suffering as suffering, and the suffering of change, disciplines his mind and cultivates it until it becomes supple; once it has become supple, he contemplates the suffering of form, and contemplates the suffering of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
If a practitioner contemplates or reflects in this way, it is called the perception of impermanence and suffering (*anicca-dukkha-saññā*).

By drawing near to it, practicing it extensively, and training in it, one gives rise to knowledge, attains knowledge, and attains the factors conducive to knowledge; it can cause knowledge to become vast. This is called the factor conducive to knowledge regarding the perception of impermanence and suffering (*anicca-dukkha-saññā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi-nibbedhika-bhāgiya-dhamma*).
What are the factors conducive to enlightenment known as the perception of suffering and non-self?
It is when a bhikṣu, staying beneath a tree or in the open air, reflects thus:
"Form is impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; that which is suffering is non-self."
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent; that which is impermanent is suffering; and that which is suffering is non-self.
Thus, one contemplates these five aggregates of clinging as non-self, just as the Blessed One said: "Form is non-self."
If form were the self, form would not be subject to suffering and affliction, and form would attain mastery;
such would be its existence, and such its non-existence.
Because form is not the self, form is subject to suffering and affliction, and form does not attain mastery.
In this way, it exists; in this way, it does not exist.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without self.
If feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness were the self, then consciousness would not be subject to suffering and affliction, and consciousness would possess mastery over itself.
In this way it exists, and in this way it does not exist.
Just as a bhikṣu thus disciplines his mind and cultivates it until it becomes supple, once it has become supple, he contemplates:
"Form is non-self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are non-self."
If a practitioner forms a reflection or a mental recollection [of this], it is called the perception of suffering as being without self.

By drawing near to and frequently practicing this, one gives rise to knowledge, attains knowledge, and acquires the factors conducive to knowledge; it can cause knowledge to become vast. This is called the factor conducive to knowledge regarding the perception of suffering as being without self.
What is the factor conducive to enlightenment known as the perception of the impurity of food?
What is food? There are four kinds of food:
namely, edible food (kabalīkāra-āhāra), contact-food (sparśa-āhāra), volition-food (manaḥsañcetanā-āhāra), and consciousness-food (vijñāna-āhāra).
As the Blessed One has said:
"Sentient beings have four kinds of nutriment.
By consuming this nutriment, sentient beings are able to subsist, the aggregates are able to coalesce, and they are able to derive benefit."
What are the four?
First is edible food; second is contact as food; [the third is mental volition as food; the fourth is consciousness as food].
Third, the food of volition;
fourth, the food of consciousness.
What is meant by "edible food" (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra)?
There are two kinds of solid food:
coarse and subtle.
What is meant by "coarse"?
Excluding the pure food of the devas and the fragrant food of the devas, and excluding the food for clothing, bathing, and bodily grooming, any other solid food is called coarse solid food.
What is meant by subtle solid food?
Food? Celestial pure food, celestial fragrant food, and food consisting of clothing and bathing for the regulation of the body—these are called subtle edible morsels (*sūkṣma-kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Furthermore, coarse edible morsels—excluding celestial fragrant food and excluding food consisting of clothing and bathing—if there is any other edible morsel, this is called coarse edible morsels (*audārika-kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
Furthermore, there is subtle edible food: celestial fragrant food, clothing, bathing, and food that conditions the body—these are called subtle edible food.
What is contact as nutriment?
It consists of the six contacts:
Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—these are called the nutriment of contact.
What is the nutriment of volition?
It is the six groups of volition:
Volition regarding forms, volition regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six groups of volition; this is called the nutriment of volition.
What is the nutriment of consciousness?
It is the six groups of consciousness.
Visual consciousness, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness—these are called the six groups of consciousness, and these are called the nutriment of consciousness.
As for the nutriment of physical food, it may be either sustenance or non-sustenance.
The nutriment of contact, the nutriment of volition, and the nutriment of consciousness may be either nutriment or non-nutriment.
What is meant by "edible food as nutriment"?
If, by depending on edible food, the sense faculties increase, do not deteriorate, and life is not diminished, this is called edible food as nutriment.
What is edible food that is not food?
If, conditioned by edible food, the sense faculties do not increase, but rather deteriorate and life is diminished, this is called edible food that is not food.
What is meant by contact, volition, and consciousness as nutriment?
If, conditioned by the nutriment of consciousness, the sense faculties increase, do not deteriorate, and life is not diminished, this is called the nutriment of consciousness as nutriment.
What is meant by nutriment for consciousness and non-nutriment for consciousness?
If, conditioned by the nutriment of consciousness, the sense-faculties do not increase, but rather deteriorate and life is diminished, this is called non-nutriment for the nutriment of consciousness.
When a bhikṣu receives morsel food, he contemplates it as impure, as if eating the flesh of his own son.

Regarding the food of contact, volition, and consciousness, he maintains the perception of being pierced by arrows; through contemplation, he eliminates their basis and becomes free from the defilement of desire.
If a practitioner forms a thought or a mental recollection of this, it is called the perception of the impurity of food.

Having approached and extensively practiced it, one gives rise to clarity, attains clarity, and acquires the factors conducive to clarity, thereby enabling clarity to become vast; this is called the factor conducive to clarity within the perception of the impurity of food.
What are the factors conducive to enlightenment consisting of the perception of non-delight in all worlds? It is as follows:

a bhikṣu feels weary of and finds no delight in all worlds—the world of hell-beings, the world of animals, the world of hungry ghosts, the world of humans, the world of gods, the world of sentient beings, and the world of conditioned formations—and he is weary of them and finds no delight in them.
Just as a bhikṣu who possesses a mind of grasping in this world will inevitably cling to what he sees,
so too, a bhikṣu should sever, detach from, and not accept such views.
If a practitioner forms a thought or a mental recollection such as this, it is called the perception of non-delight in all the world.

Having approached and extensively practiced it, one gives rise to clarity, attains clarity, and develops the factors conducive to clarity, thereby enabling clarity to become vast; this is called the factor conducive to enlightenment consisting of the perception of non-delight in all the world.
What are the factors conducive to enlightenment known as the perception of death?
It is when a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, reflects thus:
"I am subject to the nature of death; there is the peril of death."
If other sentient beings also possess the nature of death and the calamity of death—

whether they be those in the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, devas, or all sentient beings who come and go within birth and death and are thus designated as "sentient beings"— they all possess the nature of death and the calamity of death.
A bhikṣu contemplates the disintegration of the aggregates, relinquishes the body, and maintains mindfulness of death.
The bhikṣu contemplates death, knows death, understands death, and awakens to death.
Whatever conceptualization or recollective thought a practitioner has regarding this is called the perception of death (maraṇasaṃjñā).

Having approached and practiced these extensively, one gives rise to clear knowledge, attains clear knowledge, and develops the factors conducive to clear knowledge, thereby enabling clear knowledge to become vast. This is called the perception of death as a factor conducive to clear knowledge.
These are known as the six factors conducive to clear knowledge.
What are the six factors that cause joy? They are as follows:

when a bhikṣu is joyful, rapture arises; from rapture, he attains physical pliancy; from physical pliancy, he experiences bliss; from experiencing bliss, his mind becomes concentrated; and with a concentrated mind, he knows and sees things as they truly are. These are called the six factors that cause joy.
What are the six factors of enlightenment without rapture?
They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity; these are called the six factors of enlightenment without rapture.
What are the seven factors of enlightenment?
From mindfulness of the Perfectly Awakened One up to relinquishing the Perfectly Awakened One—these are called the seven perfect awakenings.
What are the seven perceptions?
As the Blessed One has said:
If one draws near to, frequently cultivates, and trains extensively in seven perceptions, one will attain great merit and reach the Deathless.
What are the seven perceptions of impurity?

They are: the perception of repulsiveness in food, the perception of non-delight in all the world, the perception of death, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in what is impermanent, and the perception of non-self in what is suffering—these are called the perceptions of impurity.
By approaching and practicing these extensively, having practiced them extensively, one attains great fruit and reward, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless.
For what reason is this said?

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, recognizes the perception of impurity, causing the mind of desire to recede and not expand; he should gradually eliminate it until it is exhausted, and having turned away from it with renunciation, he dwells in right stability.
Just as sinew, bird feathers, or *tṛṇa* grass, when cast into a fire, curl up and shrivel without unfolding, and subsequently are consumed by the flames;

so too, a bhikṣu who understands and discerns the perception of impurity with his mind causes the lustful mind to retreat and shrink without unfolding, until it is subsequently consumed. Having turned away from it, become weary of it, and detached from it, he dwells in right stability.

For example, there may be a bhikṣu who, though his mind knows and discriminates the perception of impurity, still experiences the arising of outflows regarding perceptions of desire, no different from before; his mind does not turn away, does not feel weary detachment, and does not abide correctly.

A bhikṣu knows for himself as it truly is: "I have not yet cultivated the perception of impurity; I have not yet increased my understanding of name-and-form (nāmarūpa); I have not yet attained the fruit of cultivation. In this way, the bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.

Just as when a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, recognizes the perception of impurity, no fluxes arise in his mind regarding the perception of desire; he turns away from what was previously present, becomes disenchanted with it, and dwells in right equipoise.

When a bhikṣu knows correctly and in accordance with reality: "I have cultivated the perception of impurity; I possess an increase in the diversity of name-and-form; I have attained the fruit of cultivation"—this bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.
Having cultivated and frequently practiced the perception of impurity, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless nectar (*amṛta*).

For this reason, it is said that by cultivating and frequently practicing the perception of impurity as if it were food, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless nectar.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Sixteen *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*,
Fascicle Seventeen Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others.
Non-Question Section, Chapter on the Path, Part Ten, Section Three. For what reason is this said?

For example, when a bhikṣu, through mental cognition, discerns the perception of the impurity of food, his mind recedes from the thought of physical nutriment (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra), does not advance toward it, and gradually eliminates it until it is exhausted; having turned away from it, abandoned it, and become weary of it, he dwells in right stability.
Just as sinew, bird feathers, or *tūla* grass, when thrown into a fire, curl up and shrivel without unrolling, and are subsequently consumed;

so too, a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, contemplates the impurity of edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*). He causes the perception of purity regarding edible food to recede and not advance, gradually eliminating it until it is exhausted. Having turned away from it, become disenchanted with it, and detached from it, he dwells in right stability.

For example, suppose a bhikṣu has a mind that understands and discriminates the perception of the impurity of edible food, yet his mind still produces a flow of craving toward edible food, no different from before; his mind does not turn away from it, does not feel revulsion for it, and does not dwell correctly.

A bhikṣu knows for himself as it truly is: "I have not yet cultivated the perception of the impurity of physical food; I have not increased my knowledge of name-and-form through its various synonyms; I have not attained the fruit of cultivation. In this way, the bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, contemplates the impurity of edible food; his mind does not give rise to craving or outflows regarding edible food, and he dwells correctly in detachment, revulsion, and renunciation toward what was previously present.

When a bhikṣu knows correctly and in accordance with reality: "I have cultivated the perception of the impurity of physical food; I have gained increase in name-and-form; I have attained the fruit of cultivation"—this bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.
Having cultivated and frequently practiced the perception of the impurity of edible food, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless (amṛta).
It is for this reason that it is so said.
Just as when one has approached, cultivated, and frequently practiced the perception of non-delight in all worldly things, one obtains great fruit, obtains great merit, and attains the deathless.
For what reason is this said?

It is as with a bhikṣu who, through mental cognition, discerns all perceptions of the world as unpleasurable; his mind recedes from and does not advance toward the various perceptions of the world, gradually eliminating them until they are exhausted, and having turned away from them, become disenchanted and detached, he abides correctly.
Just as sinew, bird feathers, or *tṛṇa* grass, when thrown into a fire, curl up and shrivel without unfolding, and are subsequently consumed;

so too, a bhikṣu, through mental awareness and discernment, cultivates the perception of the lack of delight in all the world, causing various worldly perceptions to subside and not arise, gradually eliminating them until they are exhausted, and having turned away from them with revulsion, he dwells in right stability.

For example, a bhikṣu may have a mind that cognizes and discriminates the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds; yet, because of various perceptions regarding the world, his mind still gives rise to taints and outflows, remaining no different from before, neither turning away nor renouncing, neither becoming weary of nor detached from them, and not abiding correctly.

A bhikṣu knows for himself as it truly is: "I have not yet cultivated the perception of non-delight in all the world; I have not increased my mastery over name-and-form; I have not attained the fruit of cultivation. Thus, this bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, perceives all worldly perceptions as unpleasurable; his mind does not give rise to taints regarding the various perceptions of the world; he turns away from what was previously present, becomes disenchanted with it, and dwells in right liberation.

When a bhikṣu knows correctly and in accordance with reality: "I have cultivated the perception of non-delight in all the world; I have increased my name-and-form; I have attained the fruit of cultivation"—this bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.

One should cultivate and frequently practice the perception of non-delight in all worldly things; having cultivated it extensively, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the Deathless. It is for this reason that it is so taught.
Having approached, cultivated, and frequently practiced the perception of death, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the Deathless.
For what reason is this said?

Just as a bhikṣu who, through mental discernment, recognizes the perception of death, yet relies upon and takes pride in the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), believing that the life-faculty is fixed, enduring, and permanent, and thus becomes greedily attached to the life-faculty—all such [attachments] are completely severed without remainder.

For example, there may be a bhikṣu who, through mental cognition, discriminates the perception of death, yet relies upon the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) to become self-conceited, considering the life-faculty to be determinate, enduring, and permanent; thus, his mind is greedily attached to the life-faculty, and in this way, [the defilements] are not yet severed.

A bhikkhu knows for himself as it truly is: "I have not yet cultivated the perception of death; I have not increased my understanding of name-and-form; I have not cultivated the fruit of retribution. In this way, a bhikkhu possesses right knowledge.

Just as a bhikṣu who, through mental discernment, recognizes the perception of death, yet relies upon the life-faculty to become arrogant, believing that the life-faculty is certain, enduring, and permanent, and thus becomes greedily attached to the life-faculty—such [attachments] he completely cuts off without remainder.

Just as a bhikṣu knows for himself in accordance with reality: "I have cultivated the perception of death, I have increased name-and-form, and I have attained the fruit of retribution"—in this way, a bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.
Having approached, cultivated, and frequently practiced the perception of death, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless; it is for this reason that it is so taught.
Just as with the perception of impermanence, having approached it, cultivated it extensively, and trained in it, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless.
For what reason is this said?

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, recognizes the perception of impermanence, his mind recedes from gain, fame, and honor rather than advancing toward them; these shall gradually be eliminated until they are exhausted, and having turned away, renounced, and become weary of them, he dwells in right stability.
Just as sinew, bird feathers, or *tūla* grass, when thrown into a fire, curl and shrivel without expanding, and are subsequently consumed, so it is with the bhikṣu:

when he understands and discerns the perception of impermanence with his mind, his heart recedes from gain, fame, and honor rather than advancing toward them; these shall gradually be eliminated until they are exhausted, and having turned away from them, become disenchanted and detached, he dwells in right stability.

For example, suppose a bhikṣu has a mind that understands and discerns the perception of impermanence, yet toward gain, fame, and honor, his mind still gives rise to taints (*āsrava*), remaining no different from before; he does not relinquish them, does not feel weary of them, and does not dwell correctly.

A bhikṣu knows for himself as it truly is: "I have not yet cultivated the perception of impermanence; I have not increased my mastery over name-and-form under its various names; I have not attained the fruit of cultivation. In this way, a bhikṣu knows for himself as it truly is.

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, recognizes the perception of impermanence; his mind does not give rise to outflows regarding gain, fame, or honor; he turns away from what was previously present, abandons it, feels weary of it, and dwells correctly in detachment.

"A bhikṣu knows things as they truly are: 'I have cultivated the perception of impermanence; I possess an increase of various names and forms; I have attained the fruit of cultivation. Thus, a bhikṣu possesses right knowledge."

If one draws near to the perception of impermanence and practices it extensively, having practiced it extensively, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless; for this reason, it is so taught.
Just as with the perception of impermanence and suffering, once one has approached, cultivated, and practiced it extensively, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless.
For what reason is this said?

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, perceives the notions of impermanence and suffering, he gives rise to a sense of terror, great dread, and urgent compulsion toward indolence, laziness, lack of faith, negligence, lack of diligence, and lack of contemplation—just as one facing death views the notion of impermanence and suffering with a raised sword.

A bhikṣu may possess the mental awareness and discernment of the perceptions of impermanence and suffering, yet toward indolence, laziness, lack of faith, negligence, lack of diligence, and lack of contemplation, he does not give rise to the perception of terror, great fear, or urgent distress, as if facing death with a raised sword.

Just as a bhikṣu knows for himself according to reality: "I have not yet cultivated the perception of impermanence and suffering; I have not increased my mastery over name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); I have not attained the fruit of cultivation"—in this way, the bhikṣu knows for himself according to reality.

Just as a bhikṣu who discerns with his mind the perceptions of impermanence and suffering develops a sense of terror, great dread, and urgent pressure toward indolence, laziness, lack of faith, negligence, lack of diligence, and lack of contemplation—just like one facing death who perceives impermanence and suffering while looking at a raised sword.

If a bhikṣu knows correctly and in accordance with reality: "I have cultivated the perception of impermanence and suffering; I have increased my name-and-form; I have obtained the fruit of retribution"—this bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.

Having approached and extensively practiced the perception of impermanence and suffering, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless; it is for this reason that it is so taught.

Just as with the perception of suffering and the perception of non-self, once one has drawn near to them and practiced them extensively, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless.
For what reason is this said?

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental cognition and discernment, realizes the selflessness of suffering; regarding all conscious bodies and external objects, he abandons all notions of "I" and "mine," along with pride and the like, and attains peaceful, perfect liberation.

For example, a bhikṣu may have a mind that discriminates the notion of suffering and non-self; yet, regarding all conscious bodies and external objects, he still conceives of "I" and "mine," giving rise to pride and other such states, so that his mind remains undivided from them, unpacified, and unliberated.
