Just as a bhikṣu knows for himself according to reality: "I have not yet cultivated the perception of suffering and non-self, I have not increased the various designations of name-and-form, and I have not attained the fruit of cultivation"—in this way, a bhikṣu knows for himself according to reality.

Just as a bhikṣu, through mental discernment, knows and realizes the selflessness of suffering; regarding all conscious bodies and external objects, he abandons the conceiving of "I" and "mine," and with a mind free from pride and the like, attains peaceful and correct liberation.

When a bhikṣu knows in accordance with reality: "I have cultivated the perception of non-self in suffering; I have increased my cultivation of the fruit of retribution through the various names and forms of self"—this bhikṣu possesses right knowledge.

Having approached and extensively practiced the perception of suffering as being without self, one attains great fruit, attains great merit, and reaches the deathless; it is for this reason that it is so taught.
These are called the seven perceptions.
What are the seven factors conducive to concentration?
Right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, and right mindfulness; these are called the seven factors conducive to concentration.
What is the Eightfold Noble Path?
Right View through to Right Concentration—this is called the Eightfold Noble Path.
What are the eight liberations?
Perceiving forms while observing forms is called the first liberation.
Having no perception of form internally while observing forms externally is called the second liberation.
The liberation of purity is called the third liberation.

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory impingement, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, one achieves the sphere of infinite space; this is called the fourth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one achieves the practice of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is called the fifth liberation.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness, one achieves the sphere of nothingness; this is called the sixth liberation.
Transcending all spheres of nothingness, one achieves the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the seventh liberation.
Transcending all spheres of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one achieves the cessation of feeling, perception, and mental formations; this is called the eighth liberation.
What is the first liberation, which consists of observing forms while possessing the perception of form?
It is as follows: a bhikṣu, without extinguishing the internal perception of form, takes up the perception of external forms.
By means of these external forms, the bhikṣu disciplines the mind, cultivating it until it becomes pliant; having cultivated it until it is pliant, he attains liberation from form.
It is as when a bhikṣu, with his mind cognizant and discerning external perceptions of form, directs his mind toward them, honors them, inclines toward them, and through them attains liberation.
What is meant by "form"?
For example, when a bhikṣu has not yet analyzed internal form, and has not yet extinguished, suppressed, or eliminated it, this is called "form.
What is meant by "contemplation"?

If external form has been previously seen by the eye-consciousness, seeing it as it truly is, seeing it subtly, and seeing it through its conditions; and if it is subsequently analyzed by the mental consciousness, analyzing it as it truly is, analyzing it subtly, and analyzing it through its conditions—this is called "contemplation."
What is meant by "the first"?

It refers to the eight liberations followed in their proper sequence, neither out of order nor inverted, entering meditative absorption according to that sequence; this is the beginning, the start, and the precursor—this is called "the first.
What is meant by "attaining liberation"?
The mind is directed toward that, honors that, inclines toward that, and takes that as liberation; this is called liberation.
What is the second liberation: internal non-perception of form, perceiving forms externally?

For example, a bhikṣu, having extinguished the perception of internal forms, takes up the signs of external forms; he trains his mind with these external forms to make it supple, and having made it supple, he attains liberation.
Just as a bhikṣu, with his mind cognizant of and discriminating external forms, directs his mind toward them, honors them, inclines toward them, and through them attains liberation.
What is meant by "the perception of internal formlessness"?
For example, when a bhikṣu has extinguished, eliminated, and removed the internal perception of form, this is called "the absence of internal perception of form.
What is meant by "contemplation" (vīmaṃsā)?

If one contemplates external forms that have been previously seen by the eye-consciousness—seeing them as they truly are, seeing them subtly, and seeing them through their conditions—and then discriminates them with the mind-consciousness, discriminating them as they truly are, discriminating them subtly, and discriminating them through their conditions, this is called "contemplation."
What is called the second of the eight liberations?
Proceeding in sequence and not in reverse, entering meditative absorption in order such that there is no interval between the second and the first—this is called the second.
What is called liberation?
When the mind is directed toward that, honors that, and inclines toward that, attaining liberation by means of that, it is called liberation.
What is the third pure liberation?

For example, a bhikṣu takes up a single pure form, such as the form of fire, the sun, moon, or stars; a mani-jewel; a palace made of the seven treasures; garments of variegated colors; flowers and fruits; rings of gold, silver, or copper; lapis lazuli, pearls, conch shells, coral, jade, and other precious substances.
Having grasped these various pure forms, the bhikṣu attains the liberation of purity.
The bhikṣu’s mind knows and discerns these pure forms; his mind inclines toward them, honors them, and leans toward them, taking them as liberation.
What is meant by "purity" (śubha)?
It refers to various beautiful forms that reflect one another, which are pleasing to behold and never wearying to look upon; this is called purity.
What is meant by "liberation" (vimokṣa)?
The mind being directed toward that is called liberation.
What is the third of the eight liberations?
Proceeding in sequence without reversal, entering meditative concentration in order such that there is no interval between the third and the second, this is called the third.
What is called liberation?
When the mind is directed toward that, honors that, inclines toward that, and is liberated by means of that, it is called liberation.

What is the fourth liberation: transcending all perceptions of form, extinguishing perceptions of sensory resistance, not attending to perceptions of diversity, and attaining the sphere of infinite space?
What is the perception of form?
Any perception associated with visual consciousness is called the perception of form.
What is the perception of ill will?
If it is a perception associated with anger, this is called the perception of ill will (*vyāpāda-saṃjñā*).
What is the perception of diversity (*nānātva-saṃjñā*)?
If it is an external perception that is defiled, turbid, and not conducive to the wholesome, this is called the perception of diversity.

Furthermore, regarding the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*): if it is a perception that does not dissociate from the perception of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and is associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), this is called the perception of form.

Furthermore, regarding the perception of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃjñā*): if it is a perception associated with the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*) and associated with anger (*krodha*), this is called the perception of ill-will.

Furthermore, as for various perceptions (*nānātva-saṃjñā*): whether they pertain to sentient beings, material things, objective spheres, states of purity, or afflictions—these are called various perceptions.
Just as a bhikṣu, having departed from all perceptions of form, having extinguished perceptions of ill-will,

and not attending to perceptions of diversity, contemplates, knows, understands, and accepts the emptiness of the cavities within the body— such as the ear canals, the nostrils, the mouth, the place where food enters, the place where food dwells, and the place where food exits.

Just as a bhikṣu knows that there is a husk upon the body, like the skin of a garlic bulb, he contemplates making it thin, knowing it is thin, resolving it to be thin, and experiencing it as thin; he contemplates gradually breaking it apart, knowing it is broken apart, resolving it to be broken apart, and experiencing it as broken apart.

In this way, a bhikṣu, having understood the perception of internal forms, contemplates, knows, understands, and experiences emptiness regarding the hollows of external objects, as well as the holes, pits, wells, jars, ravines, ditches, and caves within the earth.

Just as a bhikṣu, having analyzed internal and external perceptions of form, contemplates the tranquility of the sphere of infinite space; he reflects upon infinite space, knows infinite space, understands infinite space, and experiences infinite space—whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of infinite space.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with meditative concentration; this is called "entering the concentration of the base of infinite space. Furthermore, a bhikṣu forms the perception of the great earth and Mount Sumeru as a mass of fire.

He contemplates the smoke, knows the smoke, understands the smoke, and experiences the smoke; he contemplates the burning, knows the burning, understands the burning, and experiences the burning; having contemplated the combustion, known the combustion, understood the combustion, and experienced the combustion, the bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the base of infinite space. Contemplating the base of infinite space, knowing, understanding, and experiencing the tranquility and excellence of the base of infinite space—whatever perceptions or recollections the practitioner may have, these are called the "perception of the base of infinite space."

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the meditative absorption; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"The perceptions of sensual desire in the present life and the future, and the perceptions of form in the present life and the future, are coarse; the perception of the sphere of infinite space is peaceful, superior, subtle, virtuous, and pure."
A bhikṣu contemplates the peaceful and superior state of the base of infinite space, knowing, understanding, and experiencing the peaceful and superior state of the base of infinite space.
Whatever mental image or recollection the practitioner has regarding this is called the perception of the base of infinite space.
This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the meditative absorption; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"The perception of sensual desires in the present and the perception of sensual desires in the future, as well as the perception of forms in the present and the perception of forms in the future—these perceptions are coarse. Only the sphere of infinite space is eternally extinguished without remainder, tranquil, and superior."

A bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility of the sphere of infinite space; he knows, understands, and experiences the sphere of infinite space. Whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of space.
This perception arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the meditative concentration; this is called entering the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
What is the fourth of the eight liberations?

Proceeding in regular order and not in reverse order, one enters the meditative practice of the fourth [liberation] immediately after the third without any interval between them; this is called the fourth.
What is called liberation?
When the mind is directed toward that, honors that, inclines toward that, and is liberated by means of that, it is called liberation.
What is the fifth liberation: being detached from the sphere of infinite space, one accomplishes and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness?
Just as a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I have already accomplished the practice of the sphere of infinite space; is there any dharma that surpasses the sphere of infinite space?
The bhikṣu then forms this thought:
He dwells only in the sphere of emptiness, like a person covering a small vessel with a large one,
reflecting thus:
"This vessel is superior to that vessel."
"For what reason is this vessel superior?
It is because I have covered that vessel with this one.
Thus does a bhikṣu reflect:
"I have fully mastered the practice of the base of infinite space; is there perhaps any phenomenon superior to the base of infinite space?
Then the bhikṣu thought:
"Only the base of consciousness is superior to the practice of the base of infinite space."
For what reason is consciousness superior?
It is because I have fully understood the sphere of infinite space through consciousness.

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility of the sphere of infinite consciousness, knowing, understanding, and experiencing that tranquility, whatever mental image or recollection the practitioner has is called the perception of the sphere of consciousness.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"Whether it be perceptions of desire in the present or future, or perceptions of form in the present or future, or perceptions of the sphere of infinite space and so forth—they are coarse; the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness is peaceful and superior."

The bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness; he knows, understands, and experiences the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
This perception arises, abides, and ceases together with the meditative absorption; this is called "entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"Whether it be perceptions of desire in the present or future, perceptions of form in the present or future, or perceptions of the sphere of infinite space and so forth—these are all utterly extinguished without remainder in the sphere of infinite consciousness alone; only the sphere of infinite consciousness is tranquil and supreme."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and through knowledge and understanding experiences the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness—whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of consciousness.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"The sphere of infinite space is coarse; the sphere of infinite consciousness is peaceful, sublime, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and through knowledge, understanding, and experience realizes the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness—whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatanasaṃjñā*).
This perception arises, abides, and ceases together with the concentration; this is called the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"If the attainment of the sphere of infinite space is coarse, then the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness is tranquil, superior, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and through knowing, understanding, and experiencing it, realizes the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of infinite consciousness—whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
This perception arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the meditative concentration; this is called the attainment of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
What is the fifth of the eight liberations?
Proceeding in regular order and not in reverse, one enters the meditative practice of the fifth immediately after the fourth without any interval; this is called the fifth.
What is called liberation?
When the mind is directed toward that, honors that, inclines toward that, and is liberated by means of that, it is called liberation.
What is the sixth liberation: being detached from the sphere of infinite consciousness and accomplishing the practice of the sphere of nothingness?
Just as a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I have fully mastered the practice of the base of infinite consciousness; is there perhaps any state that surpasses the base of infinite consciousness?
The bhikṣu then forms this thought:
There is only consciousness, which is superior to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness, knowing, understanding, and experiencing that tranquility and excellence, whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"I am not mine, and what belongs to me is not mine."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness, and through knowledge, understanding, and experience, realizes the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness—whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
This perception arises, abides, and ceases together with the meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates all worlds as empty; having contemplated all worlds as empty, his perception finds no basis for support.
Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness, he knows, understands, and experiences the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness.
Whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has is called the perception of the sphere of nothingness.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Furthermore, O bhikṣu, one forms the perception of the great earth and Mount Sumeru as a mass of fire; one contemplates the smoke, understands and experiences the smoke; one contemplates the burning, understands and experiences the burning; and having contemplated the combustion, one understands and experiences the combustion once it has ceased.

A bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness; he understands, comprehends, and experiences the tranquility and excellence of the perception of the sphere of nothingness. Whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of nothingness.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"Whether it be the perception of desire in the present or the future, the perception of form in the present or the future, the perception of the sphere of infinite space, or the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness—these perceptions are coarse. The perception of the sphere of nothingness is tranquil, superior, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness, and through knowledge, understanding, and experience realizes the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness—whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of nothingness.

This perception arises together with the concentration, abides together with it, and ceases together with it; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"The perception of desire in the present and the perception of desire in the future, the perception of form in the present and the perception of form in the future, as well as the perception of the sphere of infinite space and the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness—these are all surpassed by the excellence of complete tranquility."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness, and through knowledge, understanding, and acceptance, realizes the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness—just as the practitioner’s perception or mental recollection arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with that concentration—this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"The sphere of infinite space is coarse; the sphere of consciousness is coarse; the sphere of nothingness is peaceful, superior, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), knowing, understanding, and experiencing the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness—whatever perceptions or mental recollections the practitioner has therein are called the perception of the sphere of nothingness.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the meditative absorption; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Furthermore, monks, one reflects thus:

"The meditative absorptions of the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness are coarse, whereas entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness is tranquil, supreme, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and through knowledge, understanding, and experience realizes the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of nothingness—whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of nothingness.
This perception arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
What is the sixth of the eight liberations?
Proceeding in regular order and not in reverse, one enters the meditative absorptions in sequence such that there is no interval between the sixth and the fifth; this is called the sixth.
What is called liberation?
When the mind is directed toward that, honors that, inclines toward that, and is liberated by means of that, it is called liberation.
What is the seventh liberation: transcending the sphere of nothingness, one achieves and dwells in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Just as a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Perception is my affliction; perception is a festering sore; perception is an arrow; the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful and sublime."

A bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he knows, understands, and experiences the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with meditative concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"The perception of desire in the present and the perception of desire in the future, the perception of form in the present and the perception of form in the future, the perception of the sphere of infinite space, the perception of the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the perception of the sphere of nothingness are coarse; the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is tranquil, supreme, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

A bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he knows, understands, and experiences the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the meditative absorption; this is called entering the absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"Whether it be the perception of desire in the present or the future, the perception of form in the present or the future, the perception of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness—compared to these, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is eternally extinguished without remainder, quiescent, and supreme."

A bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; knowing, understanding, and experiencing the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the meditative absorption; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"The entry into the sphere of infinite space, the entry into the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the entry into the sphere of nothingness are coarse; the entry into the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful, sublime, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

A bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he understands, realizes, and experiences the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Whatever thought or recollective thought the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

This perception arises together with the concentration, abides together with it, and ceases together with it; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"The meditative absorptions of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness are coarse, whereas the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is peaceful, sublime, subtle, virtuous, and pure."

A bhikṣu contemplates the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; he knows, understands, and experiences the tranquility and excellence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Whatever perception or mental recollection the practitioner has therein is called the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
This perception arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the concentration; this is called entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What are the seventh and eighth liberations?
Proceeding in sequence without inversion, entering meditative absorption in order, there is no interval between the seventh and the sixth; this is called "seven.
What is meant by "liberation"?
The mind inclines toward that, honors that, and leans toward that; through that, one is liberated—this is called liberation.
What is called the eighth liberation: transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one achieves the cessation of perception and feeling?

It is when a bhikṣu, relying on the precepts and abiding in the precepts, further cultivates the two dharmas of concentration and wisdom, and through concentration and wisdom, brings about the cessation of perception and feeling.
If one extinguishes feeling and perception, this is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Furthermore, monks, a bhikṣu dwells having touched and realized superior perception; while dwelling having touched and realized superior perception, he reflects thus:
"Volition is still evil for me; the absence of volition is good."
When I have volition, there is activity; when there is activity, the perception of pleasure arises; when the perception of pleasure arises, the coarse perceptions of other stages arise.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:

"If I were without volition and without activity, then once activity has ceased, the perception of pleasure would not arise; and if the perception of pleasure does not arise, the coarse perceptions of other stages would likewise not arise."

Just as when a bhikṣu is without volition and without activity, once there is no activity, the perception of pleasure ceases; with the cessation of the perception of pleasure, the coarse perceptions of the remaining stages also cease, and he attains the realization of the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
What is called the eighth liberation?
Following the sequence without reversal, one enters meditative absorption in successive order; because there is no interval between the eighth and the seventh, it is called the eighth.
What is called liberation?
When the mind is directed toward that, honors that, inclines toward that, and is liberated by means of that, it is called liberation.
These are called the eight liberations.
What are the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)?

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or unattractive, with mastery of knowledge and mastery of vision. One maintains such a perception.

Having the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are immeasurable, whether beautiful or unattractive, with mastery of knowledge and mastery of vision. One maintains such a perception.
Having such a perception, with no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly, with superior knowledge and superior vision.
Having such a perception, with no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are immeasurable, whether beautiful or ugly, with superior knowledge and superior vision.

Having such a perception, while being internally percipient of formlessness, one perceives external forms as blue—blue in color, with a blue luster—just like an *umaka* flower, which is blue in color and has a blue luster, or like a Benares cloth, well-dyed, which is blue in color and has a blue luster.
One contemplates such a sublime form—green, with green color and green light—with superior knowledge and superior vision.

Having such a perception, while being internally percipient of no forms, one contemplates external forms that are yellow, with yellow color and yellow light, like the *kaṇikāra* flower which is yellow, with yellow color and yellow light, or like a Benares cloth well-dyed which is yellow, with yellow color and yellow light.
One contemplates such exquisite form as yellowish-yellow in color and yellowish-yellow in luster, with superior knowledge and superior vision.

Having such a perception, while being internally percipient of no form, one contemplates external forms that are red, red in color and red in luster—like the *pāṇḍu* flower, which is red in color and red in luster, or like a robe from Vārāṇasī well-dyed in red, which is red in color and red in luster.
One contemplates such exquisite forms—red, red-colored, with a red luster—with superior knowledge and superior vision.

Having such a perception, being internally percipient of no form, one perceives external forms that are white, white-colored, with a white luster; like the whiteness of the star Śukra (the planet Venus), or like a Benares cloth well-washed, which is white, white-colored, with a white luster.
One contemplates such exquisite forms—white, white-colored, and white-light—with superior knowledge and superior vision, maintaining such a perception.

What is meant by "possessing the perception of internal forms while contemplating external forms that are few, whether beautiful or unattractive, with superior knowledge and superior vision, maintaining such a perception"?

That is to say, a bhikṣu who has not yet extinguished the internal perception of forms perceives external forms that are few—whether beautiful or ugly, pleasing or unpleasing, loathsome or not loathsome.
Other than a bhikṣu, one cultivates the mind with regard to a small amount of external form to make it pliant; having cultivated it to be pliant, one attains the liberation through mastery over form.
The bhikṣu knows, sees, and discerns that small amount of external form; his mind inclines toward it, honors it, and tends toward it, resolving upon it with mastery.
What is meant by "perception of internal forms"?
It refers to when a bhikṣu has not yet extinguished the perception of internal forms—when it is not extinguished, not submerged, and not removed; this is called the perception of internal forms.
What is meant by "contemplating external forms"?

If there is a small amount of external form that has been seen by the eye-consciousness, seen as it truly is, and seen as its object; and which is conceptually distinguished by the mental consciousness, distinguished as it truly is, and distinguished as its object—this is called observing external form.
What is meant by "few"?
That which can be calculated in number, which is not infinite or immeasurable, not asaṃkhyeya, and not boundless or limitless—this is called "few."
What is meant by "attractive form" and "unattractive form"?
Purity and impurity—these are called attractive and unattractive forms.
What is meant by "superior knowledge and superior vision"?
That resolute conviction is called superior knowledge and superior vision.
What is meant by "having such a perception"?
If there is a perception of limited form that is undispersed, inseparable, and entirely uniform, this is called having such a perception.

What is meant by having the perception of internal forms while contemplating external forms that are immeasurable, whether beautiful or ugly, with superior knowledge and superior vision, and possessing such a conception?

It means that a bhikṣu, without having extinguished the perception of limited forms, takes up the perception of immeasurable external forms—whether beautiful or ugly, pleasing or unpleasing, loathsome or not loathsome.

A bhikṣu, by means of those external immeasurable forms, disciplines the mind and cultivates it until it becomes pliant; having cultivated it until it is pliant, he attains resolute conviction regarding form.
The bhikṣu knows, sees, and discerns external immeasurable forms; his mind inclines toward them, honors them, leans toward them, and is resolved upon them.
What is meant by "perception of internal forms"?
When a bhikṣu has not yet extinguished, submerged, or eliminated the perception of internal forms, this is called "the absence of perception of internal forms.
What is meant by "contemplating external forms"?

If there are external immeasurable forms that have been seen by the eye-consciousness, seen as they truly are, and seen as objects of perception; and which are discriminated by the mental consciousness, discriminated as they truly are, and discriminated as objects of perception—this is called contemplating external forms.
What is meant by "immeasurable"?
It is that which is not slight, not measurable, boundless and immeasurable, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), and without limit; this is called "immeasurable."
What is meant by "agreeable form" and "disagreeable form"?
That which is pure or impure is called agreeable form and disagreeable form.
What is meant by "superior knowledge and superior vision"?
If, having attained superior reception regarding those phenomena, one knows, sees, and discerns them, this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision.
What is meant by "possessing such a perception"?
If a perception is undispersed, inseparable, fixed, and immeasurable—a perception of form—this is called "possessing such a perception."
What is meant by "internally perceiving no form, one contemplates external forms that are blue, blue in color and blue in luster"?
It refers to having such a perception regarding these forms through superior knowledge and vision.
For example, when a bhikṣu has extinguished the perception of internal form, he takes up the perception of external blue form.
Apart from the monk, he cultivates the mind by means of external blue so that it becomes pliant; having become pliant, he attains resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding form.
The monk knows, sees, and discerns the external blue; his mind inclines toward it, honors it, leans toward it, and resolves upon it.
What is meant by "internal perception of formlessness"?
It refers to the cessation, disappearance, and elimination of internal perceptions of form; this is called "internal perception of formlessness.
What is meant by "contemplating external forms"?

If there is an external blue form that has been seen by the eye-consciousness, seen as it truly is, and seen as its object; and which is conceptually differentiated by the mental consciousness, differentiated as it truly is, and differentiated as its object—this is called contemplating external forms.
What is meant by "blue"?
There are two kinds of blue: natural blue and dyed blue; this is what is called blue.
What is meant by "superior knowledge and vision"?

If, having excelled in regard to that form, one knows, sees, and discerns it, such that the mind inclines toward it, honors it, leans toward it, and resolves upon it—that is called "excellence of knowledge and vision."
What is meant by "possessing such a perception"?
If there is a perception that is not dispersed, not separated, and is exclusively the perception of blue, this is called "possessing such a perception."

What is meant by "having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as yellow, with a yellow luster; having mastered these forms, one knows and sees them, and possesses such a perception"?
It is like a bhikṣu who, having eliminated the perception of internal forms, takes up the perception of external yellow forms.
Apart from the monk, he cultivates the mind toward external yellow tones until it becomes pliant; having become pliant, he attains resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding yellow.
The monk discerns external yellow through knowledge and vision; his mind inclines toward it, honors it, leans toward it, and resolves upon it.
What is meant by "internally being without the perception of form"?
When a bhikṣu has extinguished, eliminated, and removed the perception of internal forms, this is called "the perception of being internally without form.
What is meant by "contemplating external forms"?

If there is an external yellow color, which has been seen by the eye-consciousness, seen as it truly is, and seen as its object; and which is conceptualized by the mental consciousness, conceptualized as it truly is, and conceptualized as its object—this is called contemplating external forms.
What is meant by yellow?
There are two kinds of yellow: natural yellow and dyed yellow; this is what is meant by yellow.
What is meant by superior knowledge and vision?

If, having excelled in the perception of those forms, one knows, sees, and discriminates them, such that the mind inclines toward them, honors them, leans toward them, and resolves upon them—that is called "excellence of knowledge and vision."
What is meant by having such a perception?
If there is a perception that is not dispersed, a perception that is not dissociated, and which is fixedly yellow—this is called having such a perception.

What is meant by "having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as red, with a red luster; if one has superior knowledge and vision regarding these forms, one has such a perception"?
It is like a bhikṣu who, having eliminated the perception of internal forms, takes up the perception of external red forms.
Apart from the monk, he cultivates the mind by means of the color red until it becomes pliant; once it is pliant, the monk attains resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) regarding the color red.
The monk knows, sees, and discerns the color red; his mind inclines toward it, honors it, leans toward it, and resolves upon it.
What is meant by "having no perception of internal form"?
When a bhikṣu has extinguished, eliminated, and removed the perception of internal form, this is called "having no perception of internal form.
What is meant by "contemplating external forms"?

If there is an external red color that has been seen by the eye-consciousness—seen as it truly is, seen through its conditions—and is conceptualized by the mental consciousness—conceptualized as it truly is, conceptualized through its conditions—this is called contemplating external forms.
What is meant by "red"?
There are two kinds of red: natural red and dyed red; this is what is called red.
What is meant by "superior knowledge and vision"?

If, having excelled in the perception of that form, one knows, sees, and discerns it, such that the mind inclines toward it, honors it, leans toward it, and resolves upon it—that is called "superior knowledge and vision."
What is meant by "having such a perception"?
If there is a perception that is not dispersed, not separated, and fixedly red, this is called "having such a perception.

What is meant by "internally having no perception of form, one perceives external forms as white with white light, and regarding these forms, one possesses superior knowledge and vision, having such a perception"?
Just as when a bhikṣu, having extinguished the perception of internal forms, takes up the perception of external white forms;
the bhikṣu, taking up the external white forms, disciplines the mind and cultivates it until it becomes supple, and once it is supple, he attains resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) in white.
The bhikṣu perceives, sees, and discerns white color; his mind inclines toward it, honors it, leans toward it, and resolves upon it.
What is meant by "the perception of internal formlessness"?
When a bhikṣu has internally eliminated and removed the perception of form, this is called "the internal non-perception of form.
What is meant by "contemplating external forms"?

If there are external white forms that have been seen by the eye-consciousness—seen as they truly are, seen through their conditions—and are conceptualized by the mental consciousness—conceptualized as they truly are, conceptualized through their conditions—this is called "contemplating external forms."
What is meant by "white"?
There are two kinds of white: natural white and dyed white; these are called white.
What is meant by "superior knowledge and vision"?

If, having excelled in regard to those forms, one knows, sees, and discerns them, such that the mind inclines toward them, honors them, leans toward them, and resolves upon them—that is called "excellent knowledge and vision."
What is meant by having such a perception?
If there is a perception that is not dispersed, not separated, and is exclusively white, this is called having such a perception.
These are called the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What are the nine cessations?
If one enters the first dhyāna concentration, the thorn of speech ceases.
If one enters the second dhyāna, the thorns of vitarka and vicāra are extinguished.
If one enters the third dhyāna, the thorn of prīti is extinguished.
If one enters the fourth dhyāna, the thorns of out-breath and in-breath are extinguished.
If one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space, the thorn of perception of form is extinguished.
If one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the thorn of the sphere of infinite space is extinguished.
If one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, the thorn of the sphere of infinite consciousness is extinguished.
If one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the thorn of nothingness is extinguished.
If one enters the attainment of cessation, the thorns of feeling and perception are extinguished.
These are called the nine cessations.
What are the nine successive attainments?

They are as follows: a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

Up to and including the transcendence of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one achieves the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling; these are called the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
What are the nine perceptions?

The perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of non-delight in all worlds, the perception of death, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of non-self in suffering, the perception of abandonment, and the perception of dispassion—these are called the nine perceptions.
What are the ten perceptions? They are:

the perception of impurity, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of non-delight in all worlds, the perception of death, the perception of impermanence and suffering, the perception of suffering and non-self, the perception of cessation, the perception of dispassion, and the perception of extinction. These are called the ten perceptions.
What are the ten rectitudes?
Right view, right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, right liberation, and right knowledge.
These are called the ten rectitudes.
What are the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
The earth universal base: by means of a single perception, [one contemplates] above, below, and across, without duality and immeasurably.

The totalities of water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, space, and consciousness; through a single perception, one knows them above, below, across, and in all directions, as non-dual and immeasurable.
What is meant by the "earth-kasina" (pathavī-kasiṇa), wherein one contemplates it as a single mental image—above, below, across, and in all directions—as non-dual and immeasurable?
What is meant by "earth"?
"Earth" refers to the earth-element (pathavī-dhātu) and the earth-magnitude (pathavī-mahābhūta); this is called "earth."
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted without any further means remaining, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If one is alone and not accompanied by other realms—just as when a person enters the earth-kasina—this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (*saṃjñā*)?
If perception is not dispersed, not separated, and is exclusively the perception of earth, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, and in all directions"?
"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; and "in all directions" refers to the four quarters.
If a person contemplates the earth, understands it, and experiences it throughout the above, the below, and all directions, this is called "above, below, and in all directions."
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

It is non-dual above, non-dual below, and non-dual across; immeasurable above, immeasurable below, and immeasurable across. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of earth—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless, and without end. Having no other perception regarding the earth, this is called "immeasurable."
What is called the "totality of water" (āpokasiṇa), which is a single perception extending upward, downward, and across?
What is meant by "water"?
The water element (abdhātu) and the water constituent (abhamahābhūta)—this is called water.
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted such that no further means remain, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If one is alone and not with others in a realm, such as when a person enters water and perceives it entirely as water, this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (saṃjñā)?
If perception is not dispersed, not separated, and is consistently the perception of water, this is called perception.
What is meant by "above, below, and across"?
"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; and "across" refers to the four directions.
If a person contemplates water, understands, perceives, and accepts water throughout the above, below, and across, this is called "above, below, and across."
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

There is no duality above, no duality below, and no duality across; there is immeasurability above, immeasurability below, and immeasurability across. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of water—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless, and shoreless. Having no other perception than that of water, this is called "non-dual and immeasurable."
What is meant by the "totality of fire" (tejokasina), which is perceived as a single mental image extending above, below, and across?
What is meant by "fire"?
The fire element (tejo-dhātu) and the fire constituent (tejo-mahābhūta); this is called fire.
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted without any further means remaining, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If one contemplates only this realm and not others, as when a person enters the fire-kasina, this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception"?
If the perception is not dispersed, not separated, and is exclusively the perception of fire, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, length, and breadth"?
"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; "length and breadth" refers to the four directions, just as one speaks of a person's height, depth, length, and breadth.
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

There is no duality above, no duality below, and no duality across; there is immeasurability above, immeasurability below, and immeasurability across. One has no perception of duality, but only the perception of fire—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless, and without end. Having no other thought than that of fire, this is called "non-dual and immeasurable."
What is meant by the "totality of wind" (vāyukasiṇa), which is perceived as a single mental image extending upward, downward, and across?
What is meant by "wind"?
The wind element (vāyudhātu) and the wind great-element (vāyomahābhūta)—this is called "wind."
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted such that no further means remain, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If one contemplates only this [element] and not the other elements, as when a person enters the wind-kasina, this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception"?
If the perception is undispersed, inseparable, and consistently the perception of wind, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, and across"?

"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; and "across" refers to the four directions. Just as when a person contemplates wind, understands wind, and experiences wind throughout the above, below, and across, this is called "above, below, and across."
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

There is no duality above, no duality below, and no duality across; there is immeasurability above, immeasurability below, and immeasurability across. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of wind—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless, and without end. Having no other perception regarding the wind, this is called "non-dual and immeasurable."
What is the blue universal base (*kasiṇa*), which is a single perception of above, below, and across, without duality and immeasurable?
What is meant by "blue"?
There are two kinds of blue: natural blue and dyed blue; this is what is called "blue."
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted such that no further means remain, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If it is exclusively blue and nothing else—just as when a person enters the universal base of blue (nīla-kṛtsnāyatana)—this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (saṃjñā)?
If the perception is not dispersed, not separated, and is consistently the perception of blue, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, and across"?

"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; and "across" refers to the four directions. Just as when a person contemplates blue, understands blue, and perceives blue throughout all that is above, below, and across, this is called "above, below, and across."
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

It is non-dual above, non-dual below, and non-dual across and in breadth; it is immeasurable above, immeasurable below, and immeasurable across and in breadth. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of blue—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless, and without end. Within this blue there is no divergent perception; this is called "non-dual and immeasurable."
What is called the yellow universal base (*pīta-kasiṇa*), which is a single perception of above, below, and across, without duality and immeasurable?
What is meant by "yellow"?
There are two kinds of yellow: natural yellow and dyed yellow; this is what is called "yellow."
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted without any remaining means, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If it is exclusively one thing and not others—such as when a person enters the yellow universal base (kasiṇa)—this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (saññā)?
If perception is undispersed, inseparable, and consistently the perception of yellow, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, and across"?

"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; and "across" refers to the four directions. Just as when a person contemplates yellow throughout the above, below, and across, and knows, understands, and experiences yellow therein—this is called "above, below, and across."
What is meant by “non-dual and immeasurable”?

It is non-dual above, non-dual below, and non-dual across and throughout; it is immeasurable above, immeasurable below, and immeasurable across and throughout. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of yellow—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless and shoreless. Within this yellow, there is no perception of difference; this is called “non-dual and immeasurable.”
What is meant by the "red universal base" (*lohitakṛtsnāyatana*), which is a single perception of above, below, and across, without duality and immeasurable?
What is meant by "red"?
There are two kinds of red: natural red and dyed red; this is what is called "red."
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted and there are no further means remaining, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If it is exclusively that and not anything else—just as when a person enters the all-encompassing meditation on red (*lohitakṛtsnāyatana*)—this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (*saṃjñā*)?
If perception is undispersed, inseparable, and consistently directed toward the perception of red, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise"?

"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; "lengthwise and crosswise" refers to the four directions. Just as when a person contemplates, understands, and perceives redness throughout the above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise, this is called "above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise."
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

There is no duality above, no duality below, and no duality across; there is immeasurability above, immeasurability below, and immeasurability across. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of redness—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), limitless, and shoreless. Within this redness, there is no divergent perception; this is called "non-dual and immeasurable."
What is meant by the "white universal base" (*śukla-kṛtsnāyatana*), which is a single perception of above, below, and across, non-dual and immeasurable?
What is meant by "white"?
There are two kinds of white: natural white and dyed white; this is what is called "white."
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted such that no further means remain, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If it is exclusively one and not others—such as when a person enters the all-white *kṛtsnāyatana* (totality sphere)—this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (*saṃjñā*)?
If perception is undispersed, inseparable, and consistently a perception of white, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, and across"?

"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; and "across" refers to the four directions. Just as when a person contemplates, understands, and experiences whiteness throughout the above, below, and across, this is called "above, below, and across."
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

It is non-duality above, non-duality below, and non-duality across and in breadth; it is immeasurability above, immeasurability below, and immeasurability across and in breadth. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of white, which is immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), and limitless. Within this whiteness there is no divergent perception; this is called "non-dual and immeasurable."
What is meant by the "sphere of universal space" (ākāsakasiṇa), which is a single perception of above, below, and across, without duality and immeasurable?
What is meant by "space"?
There are two kinds of space: the internal space-element and the external space-element; these are called space.
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted such that no further means remain, this is called "all.
What is meant by "one"?
If it is exclusively one and not the others—just as when a person enters the empty *kasiṇa*—this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (*saññā*)?
If perception is undispersed, inseparable, and consistently the perception of emptiness, this is called "perception."
What is meant by "above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise"?

"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; "lengthwise and crosswise" refers to the four directions. Just as a person contemplates space above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise, and thus knows, understands, and experiences space—this is called "above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise."
What is meant by "non-dual and immeasurable"?

There is no duality above, no duality below, and no duality in length or breadth; there is immeasurability above, immeasurability below, and immeasurability in length and breadth. There is no perception of duality, but only the perception of emptiness—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), and limitless. Within this emptiness, there is no divergent perception; this is called non-dual and immeasurable.
What is meant by the "totality of consciousness" (vijñāna-kṛtsnāyatana), which is a single perception above, below, and across, undivided and immeasurable?
What is meant by "consciousness"? It refers to the six groups of consciousness (ṣad-vijñāna-kāya):
The body of visual consciousness, and the bodies of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness—these are called "consciousness.
What is meant by "all"?
If it is exhausted without remainder through skillful means, this is called "all."
What is meant by "one"?
If one is alone and not accompanied by others—just as when a person enters the *kasiṇa* of consciousness—this is called "one.
What is meant by "perception" (*saṃjñā*)?
If one wishes for perception to be undispersed, inseparable, and consistently characterized by the ideation of perception, this is called "perception" (*saṃjñā*).
What is meant by "above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise"?

"Above" refers to space; "below" refers to the earth; "lengthwise and crosswise" refers to the four directions. Just as a person contemplates, cognizes, understands, and experiences perception regarding what is above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise—this is called "above, below, lengthwise, and crosswise."
What is meant by non-dual and immeasurable?

There is no duality above, no duality below, and no duality in length and breadth; there is no dualistic perception of the immeasurability above, the immeasurability below, and the immeasurability in length and breadth. There is only the perception of consciousness—immeasurable, boundless, incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*), and without limit. Within this consciousness, there is no differentiating perception; this is called non-dual and immeasurable.
These are called the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
What are the eleven liberations (*vimokṣāyatana*)?
For example, when the householder Dhaśa approached the Venerable Ānanda, prostrated himself, and sat to one side, he asked the Venerable Ānanda:

Is there any single dharma by which a bhikkhu, through heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquil conduct, might attain liberation for a mind not yet liberated, the exhaustion of all taints for those not yet exhausted, or supreme peace and security where it has not yet been attained?
The Venerable Ānanda replied to the householder Dāsaka, saying: "There is.
The householder asked:
"What is it? Ānanda said to the householder:

"It is like a bhikṣu who, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna."
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"This concentration is rightly practiced and rightly produced.
Once it has been rightly practiced and rightly produced in its entirety, he fully knows that it is a phenomenon subject to impermanence and cessation.
A bhikṣu knows and sees things as they truly are, thereby severing all outflows (āsrava) and attaining liberation of mind.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn by transformation in that realm, and attains parinirvāṇa there, never returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind attains liberation where it was not yet liberated; he attains the destruction of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains supreme peace where it was not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu, having stilled applied and sustained thought, with internal confidence and one-pointedness of mind, attains and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"This concentration is rightly practiced and rightly produced.
Once it has been rightly practiced and rightly produced in its entirety, he fully knows that all things are impermanent and subject to cessation.
A bhikṣu knows and sees things as they truly are, thereby severing all outflows (āsrava) and attaining liberation of mind.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn there by transformation, and attains parinirvāṇa, never again returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind that was not yet liberated becomes liberated; his outflows that were not yet exhausted become exhausted; and he attains the unsurpassed peace that he had not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu, detached from joy, dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body—attaining that which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness"—he accomplishes the practice of the third dhyāna.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"This concentration is correctly practiced and correctly generated.
When it has been correctly practiced and correctly generated in its entirety, he fully knows it to be impermanent and subject to cessation.
A bhikṣu knows and sees according to reality, severing all outflows (āsrava) so that his mind attains liberation.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn by transformation there, and attains parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world again.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind attains liberation where it was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains the unsurpassed peace where it was not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu, having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the prior disappearance of sorrow and joy, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"This concentration is being rightly practiced and rightly generated.
Once it has been rightly practiced and rightly generated in its entirety, he fully knows that it is a phenomenon subject to impermanence and cessation.
A bhikṣu knows and sees things as they truly are, severing all outflows (āsrava) so that his mind attains liberation.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn by transformation in that realm, and attains parinirvāṇa there, never returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind attains liberation where it was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains unsurpassed peace where it was not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu dwells with a mind of loving-kindness, pervading one direction, and likewise the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below—pervading all worlds with a mind of loving-kindness that is vast, sublime, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"This mind of loving-kindness is being rightly trained and rightly generated.
Once it has been rightly trained and rightly generated in its entirety, he knows that all these are phenomena subject to impermanence and cessation."
A bhikṣu knows and sees things as they truly are, thereby severing all outflows (āsrava) and attaining liberation of mind.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn by transformation in that realm, and attains parinirvāṇa there, never returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: namely, when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind attains liberation where it was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all outflows where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains the unsurpassed peace where it was not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu pervades one direction with a heart of compassion, and likewise the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—with a heart of compassion that is vast, sublime, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will—pervading all the worlds in this manner.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"This mind of compassionate liberation is being rightly trained and rightly generated.
Once it has been rightly trained and rightly generated in its entirety, he fully knows that all things are impermanent and subject to cessation."
A bhikṣu knows and sees things as they truly are, thereby severing all outflows (āsrava) and attaining liberation of mind.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn there by transformation, and attains parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: namely, when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind attains liberation where it was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains the unsurpassed peace where it was not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu dwells pervading one direction with a mind of loving-kindness, and likewise the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir—pervading the entire world with a mind of loving-kindness that is vast, exalted, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"This mind of joyful liberation is rightly trained and rightly generated.
Once it has been entirely rightly trained and rightly generated, he fully knows it to be a phenomenon that is impermanent and subject to cessation."
A bhikṣu knows and sees things as they truly are, thereby severing all outflows (āsrava) and attaining liberation of mind.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn by transformation in that realm, and attains parinirvāṇa there, never returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind attains liberation where it was not yet liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all outflows where they were not yet exhausted; and he attains supreme peace where it was not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu dwells with a mind of equanimity that pervades one direction—south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, above, and below—so too does he dwell pervading the entire world with a mind of equanimity that is vast, sublime, non-dual, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I cultivate and correctly generate the mind of equanimity.
Once he has cultivated and correctly generated all [these states], he fully knows them to be impermanent and subject to cessation.
The bhikṣu knows and sees according to reality, severing all outflows (āsrava) so that his mind attains liberation.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, he severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn by transformation in that realm, and attains parinirvāṇa there, never returning to this world again.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: namely, when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind attains liberation where it had not yet been liberated; he attains the exhaustion of all outflows where they had not yet been exhausted; and he attains supreme peace where it had not yet been attained."
Furthermore, householder!

Just as a bhikṣu, having transcended all perceptions of form, having extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, and not attending to perceptions of diversity, attains and dwells in the sphere of infinite space.
The bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I am entering this meditative absorption, correctly training and correctly generating it.
Once he has completely trained and correctly generated it all, he fully knows that these are phenomena subject to impermanence and cessation.
A bhikṣu knows and sees things as they truly are, thereby severing all outflows (āsrava) and attaining liberation of mind.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni), is reborn by transformation in that realm, and there attains parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: when a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind—which had not yet attained liberation—attains liberation; his outflows—which had not yet been exhausted—become exhausted; and he attains the unsurpassed peace that he had not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!
Just as a bhikṣu, having transcended all spheres of emptiness, accomplishes and dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness,
that bhikṣu reflects in this way:
Entering this concentration, one trains correctly and gives rise to it correctly.
Once all have been trained correctly and given rise to correctly, one fully knows them to be impermanent and subject to cessation.
The bhikṣu, knowing and seeing according to reality, severs all outflows, and his mind attains liberation.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, the bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters; he is reborn by transformation there and attains parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world.
"Householder!

This is one dharma: if a bhikṣu practices with heedfulness, diligent mindfulness, right wisdom, and tranquility, his mind will attain liberation where it was not yet liberated; he will attain the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted; and he will attain the unsurpassed peace where it was not yet attained."
Furthermore, householder!
Just as a bhikṣu, having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, achieves and dwells in the sphere of nothingness,
that bhikṣu reflects thus:
Entering this concentration, one trains correctly and is born correctly.
Once all have been trained correctly and born correctly, one fully knows that these are phenomena subject to impermanence and cessation.
The bhikṣu, knowing and seeing according to reality, severs all outflows, and his mind attains liberation.

Although he has not yet severed all outflows, because of his desire for the Dharma and delight in the Dharma, this bhikṣu severs the five lower fetters; he is reborn by transformation there and attains parinirvāṇa, never returning to this world.

This is one dharma: as when a bhikkhu practices with heedfulness, diligence, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, living in tranquility; he attains liberation where his mind was not yet liberated, he attains the exhaustion of all taints where they were not yet exhausted, and he attains supreme peace where it was not yet attained.
After Ānanda had finished speaking, the householder Dhaśa said:
"It is as if a person seeking one treasure-trove has obtained eleven treasure-troves.
Venerable Ānanda!"
I am also like this: seeking one entrance to liberation, I have attained eleven entrances to liberation.
Venerable Ānanda!
It is as if there were a house belonging to a householder’s son with eleven doors that has been set ablaze by fire, its fierce flames burning intensely.
"O Householder, when you wish to exit through any of the gates, you can do so with ease.
Venerable Ānanda, it is the same for me:
among these eleven gateways of Dharma, I can exit through whichever one I desire, according to my will."
Venerable Ānanda!
Even a brahmin of wrong views still seeks wealth for the sake of making offerings to his teacher; how much more so should one hear the right view and yet fail to make offerings?

At that time, the elder Dhaśa invited the community of monks from Vaiśālī and the community of monks from Pāṭaliputra; having invited them, he prepared various kinds of delicacies and fed the community of monks.
Once they had eaten their fill, he offered sandals or ten thousand pieces of white cotton cloth to the assembly of monks, and separately presented the three robes and an excellent dwelling to Ānanda.
These are called the eleven liberative entrances (*vimokṣamukha*).
