Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on Defilements (Kleśavarga), Part One of the Non-Question Section. There is one person who appears in the world: the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. He has severed evil and unwholesome dharmas and produced all wholesome dharmas; he has severed the dharmas of suffering and attained the dharmas of happiness; he has stilled all outflows (āsrava) and extinguished all outflows; he has eliminated all karmic activities and is able to attain the tranquility of the ultimate truth, the supreme coolness, the final end, the ultimate holy life, the ultimate peace and happiness, and the final limit of suffering—attaining Nirvāṇa.
For these reasons, I shall now collect the various gateways of unwholesome dharmas:
relying on birth, relying on lineage, relying on physical appearance, relying on wealth, relying on nobility, relying on high status, relying on a prestigious clan,
relying on freedom from illness, relying on youth, relying on longevity, relying on skillful craftsmanship, and relying on abundance.
Relying on learning; relying on eloquence; relying on obtaining gains and offerings; relying on receiving respect; relying on being honored; relying on being fully provided for;
relying on being a teacher or model; relying on precepts; relying on a following of disciples; relying on a faction or companions;
relying on seniority; relying on physical strength; relying on supernormal powers; relying on meditative concentration; relying on being free from desire; and relying on contentment.
Relying on dwelling alone; relying on staying in an araṇya; relying on begging for food; relying on wearing rag-robes from refuse heaps;
relying on my ability to abstain from cultivated food; relying on eating at a single sitting; relying on staying among burial mounds; relying on staying in the open air;
relying on staying at the foot of a tree; relying on always sitting upright; relying on sitting wherever a seat is spread; and relying on possessing only the three robes.

Flattery, crooked reverence, seeking profit by hinting at one’s needs, dependence on messengers, soliciting through praise, seeking profit with profit, the conceit of superiority, relishing flavors, failing to guard the precepts, the transformation of aversion into signs, resentment toward the Teacher’s instruction, contravening the Teacher’s instruction, defying the Teacher’s instruction, deception and contempt, and physical assault.

Deceiving with measures, deceiving with scales, deceiving with wealth and goods; inflicting injury, imprisonment, beating, plundering, acting with malice, speaking excessively, and speaking perversely.
They slander others, use intimidation, deceive the virtuous, conceal [their faults], and live in common with [the laity].

They take pleasure in discussing matters of government, worldly affairs, military conflicts, battles, high officials, chariots and vehicles, women, flower garlands, wine and meat, sexual desire, bedding and furniture, clothing, food and drink, taverns, and relatives.
Engaging in various kinds of talk, contemplating worldly affairs, and discussing maritime matters;

they do not know the Dharma, they do not know the meaning, they do not know the proper time, they do not know contentment, they do not know themselves, they do not know sentient beings, they do not know others, and they do not know the superior or inferior among men.
Such as wrong view, extreme view, inverted view, seeking view, seeking precepts, and seeking the path of precepts;

the agitation of the view of a self, self-praise, lack of faith, lack of awakening, stinginess, flattery, concealment and parsimony, disbelief in the retribution of karma, disparagement of giving, disparagement of training, self-exaltation, praising enemies, empty praise, lack of self-mastery, dependence on others, and serving others.
Being without resentment or hatred;
being submerged; having a sorrowful mind; lacking contentment; lacking diligent progress; lacking patience; lacking dignified deportment; and not receiving instruction.

Distraction of mind, delighting in strife, laxity in the prohibitions and precepts, reverence for false teachings, regression from wholesome dharmas, restlessness, preoccupation with physical adornment, treachery, impudence, incoherent speech, lack of mindfulness, outward-directed attention, following after sorrow and joy, self-exaltation, disparaging others, lack of respect, lack of humility, insincere reverence, being difficult to satisfy, being difficult to support, indolence, laziness, middling regression, and subsequent goodness.

Desire-exertion, suffering-exertion, greed, greedy-exertion, entanglement, vexation, sorrow, pain, anxious thought, manifold sufferings, fear, a weak countenance, a harsh countenance, doubt, lack of kinship, obstruction of the wholesome, lack of harmony, obstruction of the wholesome, extreme reality, non-approach, avoidance of approach, inferiority, self-aggrandizement, endurance of humiliation, following after greed, self-exaltation, self-indulgence, lack of support, departure from dhyāna, lack of remorse, harboring anger, stinginess, false teaching, litigation, lack of humility, loss of respect, calamitous joy, seeking loss, improper conduct, seeking dhyāna, and unbeneficial dhyāna.

Not recognizing kindness, not recognizing one's own kindness; disparaging and slandering; being prone to anger; having a naturally evil disposition; being stubborn and headstrong; severing the practice of study; responding with reproach when admonished; speaking in confusion and giving rise to groundless anger after being rebuked; failing to achieve what was intended by the rebuke; and lacking clarity in one's own rebukes.

Grasping at the view of a self-body, hungering for the view of a self-body, raising the banner of the view of a self-body, grieving over the view of a self-body, seeking the view of a self-body, associating with the view of a self-body, the prideful view of a self-body, sporting with the view of a self-body, cherishing the view of a self-body, and the view of a self-body as "I."
Sensual lust, coarseness of sensual lust, grief, lack of affection, and increased desire for pleasure;
longing, insatiability, and excessive longing; and ultimate longing.

It is insufficient, unsatisfying, obstructive, and dissipating; it flows like water through a channel, causing one to sink; it is a branch of craving, the root that gives rise to suffering, the pursuit of gain, and attachment; it is a dwelling place of parching thirst, capable of enduring the itch of the wound of desire for dharmas.
Lapse of mindfulness, lack of right knowledge, failure to guard the doors of the sense faculties, and lack of moderation in eating;

ignorance, craving for existence, views of existence, views of non-existence, the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence, the pursuit of desire, the pursuit of existence, violation of precepts, violation of views, decline of morality, decline of views, decline of life, decline of conduct, decline of practice, performing evil, and failing to perform good.

These two factors combine internally, combine externally, and combine both internally and externally.
Hope, great hope, and evil hope;
greed, evil greed, and unlawful desire-taint;
the three unwholesome roots, the three difficult-to-subdue states, the three darknesses, the three wastelands, the three fetters, and the three agitations.

and again another three powers, the three cravings, the three non-restraints, the three types of misconduct, and the three types of bodily misconduct.

the three desires, the three perceptions, the three thoughts, the three seekings, the three fires,

The three [types of] non-disparagement, the three [types of] non-weakness, and the three [types of] non-removal—these three sets of three dharmas are completed.

The four floods (*ogha*), the four yokes (*yoga*), the four graspings (*upādāna*), the four defilements (*saṃkleśa*), the four evil verbal actions, the four fetters (*saṃyojana*), the four arrows, the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the four conditions that give rise to craving, the four unions of craving, the four practices leading to the evil destinies, the four karmic afflictions, the four inversions (*viparyāsa*), the four fears, and furthermore another four fears, and furthermore another four types of retrogression—these four sets of four dharmas are completed.

The five desires, the five hindrances, the five lower-tier fetters, the five upper-tier fetters, the five destinies, the five mental derangements, the five mental entanglements, the five fears, the five enmities, the five immediate transgressions, the five violations of precepts, the five unrighteous discourses, the five forms of dissatisfaction, the five modes of mutual hatred, the five states of resentment, the five factors associated with the faculty of grief, the five types of envy, the five conditions for birth, and the five faults associated with sleep and the violation of precepts.
Furthermore, there are five faults: disrespecting one’s parents, disrespecting śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, and disrespecting elders—this concludes the five dharmas.

There are six based on greed for joy, six based on greed for sorrow, six based on greed for equanimity; six defilements, six pleasures, another six pleasures, six cravings, six angers, six hooks, six non-protections, and six roots of dispute—this concludes the six dharmas.

The seven things common to defilement; the seven things common to sensual defilement; the seven stations of consciousness; the seven types of pride; the seven types of disrespect; the seven outflows; the seven factors of weakness; the seven tremblings; the seven forms of self-reliance; the seven searches; the seven touches; the seven activities; and the seven births. Thus ends the section on the seven dharmas.

The eight worldly dharmas, the eight non-noble expressions, the eight grounds of indolence, and the eight unfavorable conditions that obstruct the practice of the holy life—these eight sets of dharmas are concluded.
The nine diverse dharmas, the nine roots of craving, the nine abodes of sentient beings, and the nine faults of transgressing the precepts—these nine sets of dharmas are concluded.

The ten latent defilements (*anuśaya*), the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*), the ten perceptions, the ten thoughts, the ten perversions, the ten bases of affliction, the ten unwholesome paths of action, and the ten dharmas by the accomplishment of which one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear—this concludes the section on the ten dharmas.
Eleven types of mental envy;
twenty kinds of views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); twenty dharmas that, when accomplished, lead to falling into hell as swiftly as a sharp spear;
and twenty-one stains of the mind.
One who accomplishes thirty factors falls into hell as swiftly as a whirling spear.
There are thirty-six modes of craving.
One who accomplishes these thirty factors falls into hell.
One who fails to accomplish forty qualities falls into hell as swiftly as a whirling spear.
Regarding the sixty-two views,
what is meant by "relying on birth"?
Sentient beings cherish life; they exalt themselves because of life and take life as their objective domain.
If the mind recollects it, deeming life to be wonderful and thereby exalting oneself, this is called "relying on birth."
Furthermore, regarding pride in birth (*jāti-māna*): one thinks, "My birth is superior to that of others; their birth is inferior; among all births in the world, my birth is the most excellent.
Sentient beings value birth and always revere it; if, with a mind that recollects the excellence of various births, one exalts oneself, this is called pride in birth.
Relying on one’s lineage; relying on one’s physical appearance; relying on wealth and nobility; relying on high status and excellence;
relying on belonging to a prestigious clan; relying on being free from illness; relying on youth; relying on the vigor of life; relying on skill and craftsmanship;
relying on extensive learning; relying on eloquence; relying on obtaining gains and offerings; relying on receiving respect; relying on being honored; relying on being fully provided for.
Relying on one's teacher, relying on one's assembly of disciples, relying on one's faction, relying on seniority, relying on physical strength, relying on supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*),
relying on meditative absorption (*dhyāna*), relying on being free from desire, relying on contentment, relying on solitary dwelling, relying on staying in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*),
relying on begging for food, relying on wearing rag-robes (*pāṃśukūla*), and relying on my ability to abstain from fine foods.

The first is relying on eating at a single sitting; relying on dwelling in cemeteries; relying on dwelling in the open air; relying on dwelling at the foot of trees; relying on always sitting upright;
relying on sitting wherever a seat is spread; and relying on possessing only the three robes—these are also explained in detail as above.
What is meant by flattery?
If one seeks profit by depending on others, altering one's proper conduct and feigning the restraint of the sense faculties, this is called flattery.
What is meant by perverse respect?

If one seeks profit from others by using embellished phrases and pleasant words, conforming to their intentions and feigning skillful means, and thereby practices such forms of respect, this is called wrong respect (*mithyā-gaurava*).
What is meant by seeking gain through hinting?

If one seeks gain by depending on others, and upon seeing clothing, food, bedding, medicine, or other such items, desires them with a covetous mind and manifests a pleasing appearance to attract them—this is called seeking gain through hinting.
What is meant by "being driven by servitude"?
To be employed as a servant, following after one’s master without ceasing for the sake of profit, even if treated with contempt and disdain—this is called being driven by servitude.
What is meant by "begging and seeking"?

If, in seeking profit from others, one sees clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicinal requisites, or other articles, and with a mind desiring to obtain them, first praises their excellence and then says, "I have need of these," this is called "praising to solicit."
What is meant by seeking profit through profit?
It is when the mind covets gain such that, if one obtains profit from a certain person, one shows it to another;
or if one obtains profit from a certain person, one shows it to the former.
If one praises this donor to those who have received benefits from him,
or praises that donor to those who have received benefits from him,
such that profit is gained in this manner, it is called "seeking profit through profit."
What is meant by "I am superior"?
If one exalts oneself through pride, claiming that one's own person is superior, this is called "I am superior.
What is meant by "craving for flavors"?
To crave food and seek out various flavors is called "indulgence in taste.
What is meant by "not guarding the precepts"?
If one abandons the dignified deportment of a renunciant, this is called "not guarding the precepts."
What is meant by the transformation of the signs of anger?
If an unwholesome mind arises, it causes the sense faculties to undergo transformation;
if each of the ten forms of affliction is provoked, it causes the sense faculties to undergo transformation—this is called the transformation of the signs of anger.
What is meant by being resentful toward the teachings of the Honored One?
The "Honored One" refers to the Buddha and his disciples. If one rejects and opposes their instructions with anger and resentment, or speaks excessively, or frowns to manifest indignation;

or if, when instructed to guard against the heavy prohibitions, one resists and rebels with anger and resentment, or speaks much, or again frowns to manifest indignation—this is called being resentful toward the teachings of the Honored One.
What is meant by "contravening the instructions of the Honored One"?

The "Honored One" refers to the Buddha and his disciples. If one is instructed to comply with and guard the weighty prohibitions, yet acts in opposition to them, this is called contravening the instructions of the Honored One.
What is meant by "contravening the Venerable One’s teaching"?

If the Venerable One has prescribed: "Do not speak thus; do not act thus; do not say thus; do not discriminate thus," yet one speaks because one does not [follow] that instruction to speak, acts because one does not [follow] that instruction to act, says because one does not [follow] that instruction to say, and discriminates because one does not [follow] that instruction to discriminate—this is called contravening the Venerable One’s teaching.
What is meant by "insulting and humiliating"?
If one touches upon, vexes, or treats sentient beings with contempt, yet does not intend to sever or harm their lives, this is called insulting and humiliating.
What is meant by "beating"?
If one strikes with the hand or fist lightly or recklessly, this is called "beating.
What is meant by "cheating with measures"?
If one receives or gives out unequal amounts due to a lack of impartiality, this is called "cheating with measures."
What is meant by deception regarding weights?
If one receives or dispenses with unequal intent, making light or heavy as desired, this is called deception regarding weights.
What is meant by deception regarding goods?

If one mixes inferior items with superior goods, or divides various kinds of objects, or moves them from their original location by means of boundary markers such as ropes, this is called "deception regarding property.
What is meant by "injury"?
If one violates or destroys another's body, this is called "wounding.
What is meant by "injury"?
If one treats sentient beings with contempt, harbors malice and a desire to harm, and seeks to terminate their life, this is called "injury."
What is meant by "being bound and confined"?
If sentient beings are entangled and fettered by birth and death, constantly dwelling in profound darkness, this is called being bound and confined.
What is meant by "grasping and groping"?
If one gives rise to an unwholesome mind and searches with the hands, this is called "palpation.
What is meant by "seizure"?
If one gives rise to an unwholesome mind and defrauds, robs, or plunders the wealth and property of others, this is called "seizure."
What is meant by "intentional action" (*saṃcetanika*)?
If the mind gives rise to unpeaceful conduct and one acts with full awareness of it, this is called intentional action.
What is meant by "prolonged speech"?
If one speaks perversely or slanders, this is called "prolix speech.
What is meant by perverse speech?
If it is speech that is devoid of meaning, this is called perverse speech.
What is meant by "slandering without basis"?
To deceive others with what is untrue is called slandering without basis.
What is meant by "coercion and intimidation"?
If a king, a royal minister, or a royal official uses force or inflicts suffering to seize the wealth of others, this is called extortion.
What is meant by feigning virtue?
To feign intimacy for the purpose of deceiving others or seizing their property is called "feigned goodness.
What is meant by "concealment"?
If, when people have shared goods that have not yet been divided, one privately takes the better portion and hides it away, this is called concealment.
What is meant by "storing together"?
If a person has already participated in the counting of tally-sticks to divide property, yet forcibly selects the better items because the goods are of poor quality, this is called "storing together.
What is meant by "speaking well of official matters"?

Constantly speaking of official laws—whether discussing administrative calculations, or matters of length and brevity—and taking pleasure in such affairs is called "fondness for talking of official business.

It is the same with worldly affairs, military affairs, battles, chariots, women, flower garlands, wine and meat, sexual desire, bedding, clothing, food and drink, the selling of liquor, and matters concerning relatives; likewise, if one takes pleasure in such affairs, it is the same.
What is meant by "various expressions"?

Excluding the aforementioned matters of eloquent exposition, if there are other matters—such as differences among sentient beings, differences among things, differences among objects, or differences among natures—these are called various expressions.
What is meant by "contemplating worldly matters"?
If one takes recollection as the primary focus and contemplates the formation and destruction of the world, this is called contemplating worldly matters.
What is meant by "speaking of maritime affairs"?

If one takes the ocean as the primary subject, whether speaking of its various jewels or of their authenticity and falsity, and becomes stained by attachment to such matters, this is called "discussing maritime affairs.
What is meant by "not knowing the Dharma"?

If, regarding wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, one does not know their specific characteristics, does not contemplate their characteristics, and does not discern their characteristics, this is called "not knowing phenomena."
What is meant by not knowing the meaning?

If, regarding the meaning of all phenomena in this life and future lives, one does not know their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), does not contemplate their characteristics, and does not discern their characteristics, this is called not knowing the meaning.
What is meant by "not knowing the time"?

It refers to not knowing the proper occasion for entering a village or leaving a village, for reciting, for receiving instruction, or for contemplation; at such times, one does not know their own characteristics, does not observe their characteristics, and does not discern their characteristics—this is called not knowing the time.
What is meant by not knowing contentment with one's food?

Not knowing contentment, yet claiming not to know contentment; not knowing its own characteristic, not observing its characteristic, and not discerning its characteristic—this is called not knowing contentment.
What is meant by not knowing oneself? It means not knowing:

"I should have such faith, such ethical discipline, such learning, such generosity, such wisdom, and such a manner of response. If, regarding these qualities, one does not know their own characteristics, does not contemplate their characteristics, and does not discern their characteristics, this is called not knowing oneself.
What is meant by not knowing sentient beings?

Regarding the assemblies of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, and śramaṇas—how they should come and go, how they should sit and rise, and how they should speak and remain silent—if, within these assemblies, one does not know their individual characteristics, does not observe their characteristics, and does not know how to distinguish their characteristics, this is called not knowing the assembly.
What is meant by not knowing persons?

Whether it be a person who maintains the precepts or one who violates them, or a person who is worthy of observation—if regarding such a person one does not know their own characteristics, does not observe their characteristics, and does not discern their characteristics, this is called not knowing persons.
What is meant by not knowing those who are superior or inferior?

If, among persons of high or low status, one does not know their own characteristics, does not observe their characteristics, and does not discern their characteristics, this is called not knowing those who are superior or inferior.
What is wrong view? It is when someone gives rise to such a view:

"There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice; there is no fruit or retribution for good or evil deeds; there is no this world or the next world; there are no parents and no devas; there are no spontaneously born beings; and there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world who have correctly proceeded and correctly attained, who have realized for themselves through direct knowledge in this world or the next and explain it to others. This is called wrong view.
What is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?

If one views all things as existent, views all things as non-existent, views all things as identical, views all things as distinct, or views all things as manifold—this is called the view of extremes.
What is meant by inverted views?

It is to see the Truly Awakened One as not truly awakened, or to see that which is not truly awakened as truly awakened; to see wholesome phenomena as unwholesome, or to see unwholesome phenomena as wholesome; and to see those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have entered the right path as not having entered the right path, or to see those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who have not entered the right path as having entered the right path.
If one holds such a view as this:
"I am happy, the world is happy, and my future rebirth shall be happy; it is eternal, uninterrupted, an unchanging phenomenon, and shall remain fixed forever"—this is called a perverted view.
What is meant by the view of seeking?
If, among various views, one repeatedly discriminates and selects for oneself, this is called the view of seeking.
What is meant by the precept of seeking?
If one regards precepts as purification and greedily seeks after them with grasping and attachment, this is called seeking after precepts.
What is meant by seeking after the path?
If one regards the path as purification and greedily seeks after it with grasping and attachment, this is called seeking after the path.
What is meant by the pursuit of the path of precepts?
If one regards [worldly things] as pure and greedily seeks after them with grasping, this is called the pursuit of the path of precepts.
What is meant by the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)?
Regarding the view of self:
what is meant by the view of self?

Some may say that form is the self, that the self is within form, that form belongs to the self, or that the self possesses form; the same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. This is called the view of a personal body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
What is meant by "restlessness"?
If one’s movements and stops are light, quick, and rapid, this is called restlessness.
What is meant by "self-praise"?
If one praises one's own superior abilities, this is called self-proclamation.
What is meant by lack of faith?
If one does not believe, does not enter into faith, does not excel in faith, and does not have true faith—if the mind lacks faith—this is called lack of faith.
What is meant by "lack of awakening"?
If there is no wisdom, this is called lack of awakening.
What is meant by "miserliness"?
If one’s greed is not relinquished, this is called stinginess.
Furthermore, stinginess is the harboring of resentment toward others’ giving of gifts, offerings, and necessities; this is called stinginess.
What is meant by "praising in one's presence"?
Not seeking wealth or profit from others, but acting in accordance with their intentions to correspond to their goodness—this is called "praise in one's presence.
What is meant by "concealment and stinginess"?
If one is miserly regarding material goods and causes others to guard the doors and gates, fearing that śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas might enter to beg for alms—this is called "concealment and stinginess."
What is meant by non-faithful karma?
If, regarding wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral karma, one does not understand it, repeatedly fails to understand it, or ultimately fails to understand it, this is called non-faithful karma.
What is meant by not believing in the retribution of karma?

There is retribution for wholesome and unwholesome karma; if one does not understand this retribution, does not deeply understand it, and does not ultimately understand it, this is called not believing in the retribution of karma.
What is meant by "corrupt giving"?
If one practices giving in an unrighteous manner, this is called corrupt giving.
What is meant by "corrupt training"?
If one is not a learner, this is called disparaging the learner.
What is meant by self-exaltation?
If one exalts oneself, thinking, "I possess faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, and eloquence," this is called self-exaltation.
What is meant by praising an enemy?

If a person has an enemy and, wishing to manifest that enemy's faults, instead praises their virtues—claiming they possess faith, ethical discipline, generosity, learning, wisdom, and eloquence—this is called praising an enemy.
What is meant by "vain praise"?
When the mind harbors false regret, yet one lacks faith, precepts, generosity, learning, wisdom, or eloquence, yet speaks in praise as if possessing them—this is called vain praise.
What is meant by "lack of mastery"?
If afflictive states of mind arise, one’s various wholesome deeds cannot be carried out according to one's will; this is called lack of sovereignty (*asvatantra*).
What is meant by "being subject to others" (*parādhīna*)?
If one’s karma is impure, such that one must appear as a relative, or act as a slave or attendant, this is called being subject to others.
What is meant by "serving others"?
If one associates with those of noble and superior status, frolicking and laughing together, relying upon them for protection and influence, this is called serving others.
What is meant by "not feeling resentment or hatred"?
If one feels love and joy, this is called being without enmity or hatred.
What is meant by enmity and hatred?
If one feels anger and resentment, this is called enmity and hatred.
What is meant by "sinking"?
If wholesome dharmas decline and fall away, this is called sinking.
What is meant by "mental sorrow"?
If the mind is not characterized by compassion, this is called "compassion of the mind.
What is meant by "insatiability"?
If one has excessive desire for the requisites of life and does not cease from it, this is called insatiability.
What is meant by lack of diligent exertion?
If one’s mind does not take singular delight in wholesome dharmas, this is called lack of diligent exertion.
What is meant by lack of forbearance?
If one is unable to endure or accept wholesome dharmas, this is called "lack of forbearance.

Furthermore, lack of forbearance may consist in being unable to tolerate hunger and thirst, cold and heat, wind and rain, mosquitoes, gadflies, and horseflies; unpleasant speech; or physical and mental suffering and anguish, including the final moment when the winds of death dismember the body—being unable to endure or accept these is called "lack of forbearance."
What is meant by "non-decorum"?
If one violates the precepts established by the Buddha, this is called non-decorum.
What is meant by "not accepting instruction"?
If one does not respect or comply with the instruction when it is given according to the Dharma, this is called "not receiving the teaching.
What is meant by "associating with evil friends"?

If one associates with those who kill, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsely, or indulge in intoxicants and negligence—treating such persons as friends, close friends, or ultimate friends, and regarding them with respect and mindfulness—this is called "associating with evil friends."
What is meant by associating with evil companions?

If one associates with, closely associates with, or thoroughly associates with those who kill living beings, steal, engage in sexual misconduct, speak falsehoods, or indulge in intoxicants and negligence—respecting them and never parting from them—this is called associating with evil companions.
What is called the undertaking of unwholesome conduct?
It is when one who relies on killing trains in killing, directing the mind toward it, honoring it, inclining toward it, and regarding it as liberation.

Following those who steal, one learns to steal; following those who engage in sexual misconduct, one learns to engage in sexual misconduct; following those who speak falsehoods, one learns to speak falsehoods; following those who indulge in intoxicants and heedlessness, one learns to indulge in intoxicants and heedlessness. With the mind directed toward them, held in high esteem by them, leaning toward them, and regarding them as the standard—this is called adopting unwholesome conduct.
What is meant by "unwholesome conduct"?
Any conduct directed toward unwholesome objects is called unwholesome conduct.
What is meant by "associating with those who are timid and weak"?

If one associates with, reveres, and serves those who lack faith, those who are without shame or remorse, those who do not study, those who are indolent, those who have lost mindfulness, or those who lack wisdom, this is called associating with the timid and weak.
What is meant by "accepting the dharma of the timid"?
If one respectfully accepts and practices the teachings spoken by those who are timid, this is called accepting the dharma of the timid.
What is meant by "knowing the timid"?

If one is able to listen well to and receive the teachings and unwholesome dharmas spoken by those who are timid and weak, and can discern them with the mind, this is called knowing the timid and weak dharmas.
What is meant by upholding the timid and weak dharmas?

If one upholds, correctly maintains, dwells in, does not forget, continuously recollects, and does not lose that which is the Dharma taught for those who are timid and weak, this is called "upholding the Dharma for the timid and weak."
What is meant by improper reflection?
If one reflects improperly rather than reflecting skillfully, this is called improper reflection.
What is meant by associating with the timid path?
This refers to wrong view up to wrong concentration; if one associates with and frequently cultivates these, it is called associating with the path of the timid.
What is meant by an inferior mind?
If the mind is indolent, it is called an inferior mind.
What is meant by a distracted mind?
If the mind is scattered among the five desires—forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—it is called a distracted mind.
What is meant by delighting in contention?
If there is litigation, imprisonment, or constant mutual opposition and conflict, this is called "delighting in dispute.
What is meant by "slackening the precepts"?
If they are deficient, neglected, defiled, or abandoned, this is called "slackening the precepts."
What is meant by "revering wrong dharmas"?
If one regards evil and unwholesome dharmas as supreme and thereby attains concentration, this is called revering wrong dharmas.
What is meant by "retreating from wholesome dharmas"?
If one falls away from or regresses from supramundane dharmas, this is called the regression of wholesome dharmas.
What is restlessness?
If the mind is agitated and distracted, lacking tranquility and not being rightly tranquilized, this is called restlessness.
What is meant by "adorning the body"?
If one personally applies ointments and ornaments, this is called adorning the body.
What is meant by "perilous"?
If the actions of body, speech, and mind arise and proceed in a contrary manner, this is called "perilous.
What is meant by "enduring shame"?
If one is in a multitude and speaks falsely when not questioned, this is called "enduring shame."
What is meant by "frivolous speech"?
If one speaks at random without restraint, this is called frivolous speech.
What is meant by "not answering"?
If one loses mindfulness of what is wholesome, this is called the mind not being mindful.
What is meant by external mindfulness?
If mindfulness dwells upon the five desires—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—this is called external mindfulness.

Furthermore, regarding external mindfulness (*bahirdhā-smṛti*): if one recollects non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or pays respectful homage to non-Buddhists, and the mind dwells upon their teachings, this is called external mindfulness.
What is meant by "conforming to sorrow and joy" (*anuvitarka-anuprīti*)?

If there are various joys and pleasures or various sorrows and sufferings in the mundane world, and the mind harbors aspirations that accord with and conform to them, this is called "conforming to sorrow and joy.
What is meant by "self-exaltation"?
If one praises one's own physical marks as being possessed of many abilities, this is called self-exaltation.
What is meant by disparaging others?
If one speaks of another’s shortcomings, this is called disparaging others.
What is meant by lack of respect?
To treat one's elders and superiors with contempt and to be devoid of reverence is called lack of respect.
What is meant by not being humble?
If one does not lower oneself, this is called "lack of humility.
What is meant by "insincere respect"?
If one praises various qualities of a pure practitioner with falsehood and unreality, this is called "insincere respect."
What is meant by "difficult to satisfy"?
If one is never satiated with food and drink, this is called difficult to satisfy.
What is meant by "difficult to sustain"?
Seeking delicious flavors is called being difficult to support.
What is meant by indolence?
If one is lax and remiss, this is called indolence.
What is called indolence?
If one is lazy and remiss, this is called indolence.
What is called desisting midway?
If one seeks superior benefit, the conditions for practice are easy; yet because of indolence, one ceases, which is called "stopping midway.
What is meant by "good at the end"?
If, within the midst of wholesome dharmas, one loses them, extinguishes them, and sinks away, this is called "good at the end."
What is meant by "exertion through desire"?
If one takes pleasure in and becomes attached to sensual desires, this is called exertion through desire.
What is meant by "painful exertion"?
If various forms of bodily suffering are not in accordance with the noble Dharma, being without decorum, without benefit, and without purpose, this is called "exertion in toil.
What is meant by "craving"?
If love is vast and extends to the furthest limit, this is called "craving."
What is called the fetter of greed?
If craving is vast and extends to its furthest limit, this is called the fetter of greed.
What is called vexation?

If sentient beings are oppressed by various sufferings—whether it be affliction, intense affliction, or ultimate affliction—and experience internal burning heat and mental confusion, this is called "affliction" (daurmanasya).
What is called compassion?

If sentient beings are oppressed by suffering and affliction, and the arrow of distress enters their hearts, such that they weep, speak aloud, and remember [the pain] without letting go—this is called compassion.
What is called suffering?
If the body does not tolerate the painful feelings arising from contact with the eye, or the painful feelings arising from contact with the ear, nose, tongue, or body, this is called suffering.
What is called grief?
If the mind does not tolerate suffering, this is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
What is meant by manifold suffering (*bahudukkha*)?
When one is oppressed by various kinds of suffering and the mind finds no rest, this is called manifold suffering.
What is meant by "terror"?
If the mind is agitated and alarmed, this is called terror.
What is meant by "pale countenance"?
If one performs wholesome dharmas with attachment, delusion, and delight, this is called "weak countenance.
What is meant by "bold countenance"?
It is like the speech of a small child, which knows no restraint or difficulty; this is called "bold countenance."
What is meant by doubt?
To have two minds, to waver, and to be unable to sever the fetters—this is called doubt.
What is meant by lack of kinship?
If one distances oneself from wholesome dharmas, this is called having no kinsman.
What is meant by "obstacles to the wholesome"?
If one turns one's back on wholesome dharmas, this is called an obstacle.
What is meant by "mutual disapproval"?
If one delights in strife, entanglement, and mutual verbal disputes, this is called mutual disapproval.
What is meant by "obstructing what is wholesome"?
If one performs wholesome dharmas and, because of this, gives rise to self-exaltation, this is called "obstruction by the wholesome.
What is meant by "extreme reality"?
If one with extreme views clings to what they perceive as being firm and real, this is called "extreme reality."
What is meant by "not associating"?
If one does not associate with the Buddha or the disciples of the Buddha, and does not offer them support, respect, or prostrations, this is called "not associating."
What is meant by "abandoning through proximity"?

If one has previously associated with the Buddha or the disciples of the Buddha, making offerings, honoring, and prostrating to them, but later withdraws from this practice and no longer associates with, makes offerings to, honors, or prostrates to them, this is called abandoning through proximity.
What is meant by "base"?
To perform acts of body, speech, and mind that are deceitful, unreal, and inferior—this is called base.
What is meant by "self-exertion"?
If one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts and manifests them through body, speech, and mind, this is called "self-exertion.
What is meant by "enduring humiliation"?
If one is greedily attached to worldly dharmas and seeks after them with ceaseless coming and going, this is called "enduring humiliation."
What is meant by "following greed"?
If one pursues gain and offerings with insatiable greed, thereby losing the marks of a virtuous person, this is called following greed.
What is meant by "self-exaltation"?
If the actions of body, speech, and mind are collectively restless, this is called self-exaltation.
What is meant by self-indulgence?
If the mind is agitated and scattered without being restrained, this is called self-indulgence.
What is meant by "lack of restraint"?
If one's afflictions regarding the hands and feet have no fixed discipline, such that they roam hither and thither, scratching the ground, this is called lack of restraint.
Furthermore, lack of restraint refers to being fond of coming and going; this is called lack of restraint.
What is meant by "leaving meditation"?
If one does not draw near to a place of tranquility, this is called leaving meditation.
What is meant by "no regret"?
If one gives rise to unwholesome thoughts yet remains joyful and exultant without any change or loss [of that state], this is called "absence of regret" (*a-vipratisāra*).
What is meant by "harboring resentment" (*upanāha*)?
If there is an irrepressible cause for constant affliction that increases further defilements, this is called "harboring resentment."
What is meant by stinginess?
If one guards and clings to wealth or the Dharma and does not relinquish them, this is called mental stinginess.
What is meant by false teaching?
If one speaks of false teachings, this is called a false teaching.
If those with wrong views assemble sounds, syllables, and speech as oral instruction, this is called a false teaching.
What is meant by dispute?
To seek out the faults of others and fail to give rise to harmony and compliance is called contention.
What is meant by "lack of deference"?
If, in performing one's actions, the mind is haughty and devoid of respect and compliance, this is called lack of deference.
What is meant by "the failure of respect"?
If one respects that which is inferior and contrary to the Dharma, this is called the failure of respect.
What is meant by "delighting in calamity"?
If one sees the decline or loss of others and instead gives rise to joy and pleasure, this is called "joy in calamity" (*āpad-rati*).
What is meant by "seeking loss"?
If one harbors resentment or aversion toward another and constantly watches for their flaws or failings, this is called "seeking loss."
What is meant by non-practice?
If a bhikṣu violates the rules of decorum and engages in improper conduct, this is called non-practice.
What is meant by seeking dhyāna?
If a person, while in a gathering, seeks fame and profit with their mind and then manifests the appearance of sitting in meditation, this is called "seeking meditation.
What is meant by "unbeneficial meditation"?
If a person practices sitting meditation without proper decorum, this is called unbeneficial meditation.
What is meant by not knowing gratitude?

If one receives from another the gift of material wealth or the gift of the Dharma, yet fails to discern it correctly, fails to discern it through right discernment, and fails to engage with it through discernment, this is called not knowing gratitude.
What is meant by not recognizing one's own kindness?
If one has previously received from another the gift of material wealth or the gift of the Dharma, yet does not acknowledge that kindness, this is called not recognizing one's own kindness.
What is meant by disparagement?
To speak of another's faults without any sense of hesitation or restraint is called disparagement.
What is meant by malice?
If one is angry and does not protect the minds of others, this is called hatred (*dveṣa*).
What is meant by innate wickedness?
If one’s body, speech, and mind are impetuous and violent, this is called innate wickedness.
What is meant by "stiffness"?
If one lacks the practice of patience, this is called stiffness.
What is meant by "abandoning cultivation and study"?
If one obstructs another from performing wholesome deeds, this is called "interrupting training.
What is meant by "reproving and admonishing, yet being met with derision"?
If a person commits evil and does not accept wholesome admonition, this is called "reproving and admonishing, yet being met with derision."

What is meant by rebuking and admonishing one who speaks in confusion and gives rise to anger? What is meant by rebuking and admonishing one who is unsuccessful? What is meant by rebuking and admonishing one who is not clear-headed? All these are as explained above.
What is meant by grasping at the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)?
Because of the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), one clings to the view of a self-body; because the view of a self-body is evil, one clings to the view of a self-body.
It is like a perilous path covered above by grasses, shrubs, and forests, such that those traveling upon it do not know its elevations and depressions, or its depths and shallows.
Thus, one who clings to the view of a self-body fails to recognize right from wrong or good from evil; this is called clinging to the view of a self-body.
What is meant by "hunger for the view of a self-body"?
It is hunger for the view of a self-body because one takes that view as a condition.
Because the view of a self is evil, one is famished by the view of a self, which causes sentient beings to dwell amidst various sufferings and difficulties.
Likewise, there is thirst and hunger among birds, beasts, and malevolent insects; there is hunger among humans and non-humans.
Thus, those who proceed along that path undergo immeasurable and manifold sufferings.
Likewise, by grasping at the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one undergoes various pains and fails to reach the further shore; this is called "hunger of the view of a self-identity."
What is meant by "establishing the banner of the view of a self" (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
If one delights in giving rise to the view of a self, this is called establishing the banner of the view of a self.
What is meant by "anxiety regarding the view of a self"?

If, by taking the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as an object, one gives rise to distress and affliction, or gives rise to them repeatedly and ultimately, this is called "distress regarding the view of a self-body.
What is meant by "seeking the view of a self-body"?
If, by reason of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one wrongly seeks form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, this is called "seeking the view of a self-body.
What is meant by "associating with the view of a self-body"?
If, by reason of the view of a self-body, one associates with form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, this is called "associating with the view of a self-body."
What is called the view of bodily conceit?
If, due to the view of a self in the body, one uses bodily conceit to adorn and embellish oneself, this is called the view of bodily conceit.
What is called the playfulness of the view of a self in the body?

If one takes as an object the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), or because of taking the view of a self-identity as an object, one grasps at craving for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is called "cherishing the view of a self-identity.

If, because of taking the view of a self-identity as an object, one grasps at a self within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, this is called "the view of a self in the body" (*ātmakāyadṛṣṭi*).
What is called "desire-taint" (*kāmarāga*)?
Whatever desire there is in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), and whatever desire there is in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is termed desire-taint.
The same applies to "concomitant desire-taint," "compassion," "lack of intimacy," and "increased longing for pleasure."
What is called "expectation"?
If there is craving upon the initial contact, this is called expectation.
What is called "intense expectation"?
If craving is vast but has not reached the further shore, it is called "heavy longing.
What is meant by "ultimate longing"?
If craving is vast and has reached the further shore, it is called "ultimate longing."
What is meant by "difficult to satisfy"?
If there is dissatisfaction with the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and dissatisfaction with the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*), this is called "difficult to satisfy.

It is also difficult to fulfill; it is attachment, a discharge of moisture, a flowing and sinking, the growth of branches and nets, rooted in longing and craving, a dwelling of parching thirst, and the acceptance of the sores of dust—all as previously explained for the single dharma. Thus ends the first dharma.
What is called loss of mindfulness?
If one abandons wholesome mindfulness, this is called loss of mindfulness.
What is called lack of clear comprehension?

There may be a bhikṣu who, lacking clear comprehension, goes out or comes in, bends or stretches, turns around, puts on his saṃghāṭī robe, takes up his robes and bowl, eats, drinks, defecates, urinates, exhales, inhales, sleeps, walks, stands, sits, or lies down; who, while sleeping, waking, or remaining silent, does not guard his conduct—this is called lack of clear comprehension.
What is meant by not guarding the sense-doors?
If one perceives forms and grasps at them, this is called not guarding the sense-doors.
What is meant by not knowing moderation in eating?
If one does not measure one's food intake, this is called being ignorant of satiety in eating.
What is ignorance? If it is the unwholesome root of delusion, this is called ignorance.
What is craving for existence (*bhavarāga*)?
Craving for the realm of form and the formless realm is called craving for existence.
What is the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*)?
If one holds the view of eternalism, this is called the view of existence.
What is meant by the view of non-existence?
If one holds the view of annihilationism, this is called the view of non-existence.
What is called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*)?
If one is greedily attached to the phenomena of the desire realm, this is called the outflow of desire.
What is called the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*)?
If one is greedily attached to the dharmas of the form and formless realms, this is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
What is meant by "seeking through desire" (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*)?

If one has not transcended the desire realm, has not known the desire realm, and has not abandoned the desire realm—seeking, searching for, and accumulating the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the desire realm, namely forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects—this is called seeking through desire.
What is meant by "seeking existence" (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*)?

If one has not transcended the realm of form and the formless realm, has not known the realm of form and the formless realm, and has not abandoned the realm of form and the formless realm; and if, regarding the aggregates, elements, sense-bases, meditative absorptions, liberations, concentrations, and attainments of the realm of form and the formless realm, one seeks, searches for, or accumulates them—this is called seeking existence.
What is meant by not upholding the precepts?
Whether one violates the precepts or fails to uphold them, this is called not upholding the precepts.
What is meant by harmful views?
If one holds the sixty-two views or false views, this is called "corrupt view" (*dṛṣṭi-vipatti*).
What is meant by "corruption of morality" (*śīla-vipatti*)?
If one violates the precepts and fails to maintain them, this is called "corruption of morality."
What is meant by the decline of views?
If one holds the sixty-two views as well as false views, this is called the decline of views.
What is meant by the decline of life?
If one’s livelihood is wrong, this is called the decline of livelihood.
What is meant by the decline of conduct?
If one’s actions do not accord with proper decorum, this is called the decline of conduct.
What is meant by "declining conduct"?
If a bhikṣu engages in conduct that is not his own proper domain, this is called declining conduct.
What is meant by "committing evil"?
The accomplishment of unwholesome dharmas is called "committing evil.
What is meant by "not performing good"?
If one does not perform or accomplish supramundane wholesome dharmas, this is called "not performing good."
What is meant by associating with householders?
If one conforms to worldly ways and deviates from right practice, this is called associating with householders.
What is meant by associating with those who have gone forth?
If one does not conform to the ways of householders and acts contrary to worldly conduct, this is called associating with those who have gone forth.
What are the two conditions for the arising of sensual desire?
If sensual desire arises by taking pure forms as an object or by taking improper mental attention as an object, these are called the two conditions for the arising of sensual desire.
What are the two conditions for the arising of ill-will?
Taking an enemy as an object and engaging in improper reflection—these are called the two conditions that give rise to ill-will, which permeates one like smoke in a field of weeds.
What are the two conditions that give rise to wrong view?
Wrong view arises conditioned by another’s false teaching and conditioned by improper reflection; these are called the two conditions that give rise to wrong view.
What is called ill-will (*vyāpāda*)?
If there is anger and intense anger, this is called ill-will.
What is called harboring resentment (*upanāha*)?

If one wishes to take revenge, being bound by entanglements and ultimate entanglements, performing deluded actions with the mind, and reaching the culmination of fury or hatred—this is called harboring resentment.
What is meant by "bearing a grudge"?
If the mind is defiled and stained by afflictions, this is called harboring resentment.
What is meant by "burning heat"?
If one gives rise to distress because things do not accord with one's wishes, this is called burning heat.
What is envy? If one gives rise to envy, intense envy, and ultimate envy toward others who obtain gain, offerings, honor, respect, and veneration, this is called envy.
What is meant by stinginess?
If one is greedy and parsimonious regarding material gifts or the gift of Dharma, failing to relinquish them, amassing them, and taking pleasure in attachment to them—this is called stinginess.
What is meant by illusion and transformation?
If, in the presence of those who are venerable and superior, or others, one conceals one's own faults and deceives others for the sake of fame and hollow reputation—what is this called?
It is called crafty deception.
If the mind is crooked and not upright, this is called deceitful fraud.
What is meant by lack of shame?
If one commits evil oneself and does not feel regret in one's inner heart, this is called lack of shame.

Furthermore, regarding lack of shame (*ahrīkya*): if a person lacks shame, feeling no shame for that which is shameful, and feeling no shame for evil and unwholesome states, this is called lack of shame.
What is called "lack of shame" (*anottappa*)?
If one commits evil oneself and does not feel shame before others, this is called lack of shame.
Furthermore, as for lack of shame: if a person feels no shame regarding that which is shameful, and feels no shame regarding evil and unwholesome states, this is called lack of shame.
What is meant by arrogance?
To be conceited toward others and to praise oneself—this is called arrogance.
What is meant by contention?
If one gives rise to unwholesome states of body, speech, and mind—such as agitation, coarse words, and resentment—this is called contention.
What is meant by arrogance?
If one gives rise to an unwholesome mind, adorning one’s own person and praising one’s own virtues while the mind remains closed and unyielding, this is called arrogance.
What is called negligence?
If one does not restrain distracted thoughts, this is called negligence.
What is called pride?
If one says, "I am superior," this is called pride (*māna*).
What is overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?
To say, "I am equal to those who are superior," is called overweening pride. These two dharmas are concluded.
*Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle 18. *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle 19.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others, *The Non-Questioned Section*, Chapter Eleven: Defilements, Part Two. What is internal origination (*ādhyātmika-samudaya*)?

It refers to desire and passion (*rāga*), along with the accompaniments of desire and passion, within internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*). This includes not being without increased longing, hoping, intensely hoping, and ultimately hoping; being difficult to satisfy and difficult to fulfill; greed, flow, and leakage; sinking into the net of branches; the root of birth and hope; the dwelling of craving and parching thirst; and the wound of attachment to the dust of existence. This is called internal origination.
What is meant by external accumulation?
If one has desire-taints regarding phenomena, co-arising with desire-taints, up to and including the craving for the sores of sensory objects—this is called external accumulation.
What is meant by internal-and-external accumulation?

If there is desire-taint (*rāga-āsava*), the taint of co-desire, and even the craving for the sores of sensory objects (*raja-kṣata-tṛṣṇā*) regarding internal and external phenomena, this is called the accumulation of the internal and external.
What is meant by "expectation" (*ākāṅkṣā*)?
If, because one possesses wholesome qualities, one desires that others know of them, this is called expectation.
What is meant by "great longing"?
If one has much longing, this is called great longing.
What is meant by "evil longing"?
If, because one lacks wholesome qualities oneself, one desires that others know one possesses them, this is called "evil longing" (pāpicchā).
What is greed (lobha)?
If one feels covetous desire, defiled attachment, and clinging toward one's own possessions, wealth, wife, children, and so forth, this is called greed.
What is called "evil greed"?
If, regarding the property, wealth, wife, children, or other possessions of another, one desires them for oneself, being defiled by craving and attached through greed—this is called evil greed.
What is meant by unrighteous lustful attachment?
If one engages in lustful acts with one’s mother, the wife of a teacher, or others such as these, this is called unrighteous lustful attachment.
What are the three unwholesome roots?
The unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion—these are called the three unwholesome roots.
What are the three that are difficult to subdue?
The difficulty of subduing desire, the difficulty of subduing hatred, and the difficulty of subduing delusion—these are called the three that are difficult to subdue.
What are the three darknesses?
The darkness of greed, the darkness of hatred, and the darkness of delusion; these are called the three darknesses.
What are the three deserts?
The wilderness of desire, the wilderness of hatred, and the wilderness of delusion—these are called the three wildernesses.
What are the three entanglements?
The entanglement of desire, the entanglement of hatred, and the entanglement of delusion—these are called the three entanglements.
What are the three agitations?
The agitation of desire, the agitation of hatred, and the agitation of delusion; these are called the three agitations.
What are the three internal stains?
The stain of desire, the stain of hatred, and the stain of delusion—these are called the three internal stains.
What are the three internal rivalries?
The rivalry of desire, the rivalry of hatred, and the rivalry of delusion—these are called the three internal rivalries.
What are the three internal enemies?
The enemy of desire, the enemy of hatred, and the enemy of delusion—these are called the three internal enemies.
What are the three internal snares?
The net of desire, the net of hatred, and the net of delusion—these are called the three internal nets.
What are the three internal harms?
The harm of desire, the harm of hatred, and the harm of delusion—these are called the three internal harms.
What are the three internal aversions?
Aversion born of desire, aversion born of hatred, and aversion born of delusion; these are called the three internal aversions.
What are the three internal poisons?
The poison of desire, the poison of hatred, and the poison of delusion—these are called the three internal poisons.
What are the three haughtinesses?
The conceit of "I am," the conceit of inferiority, and the conceit of superiority—these are called the three haughtinesses.
What are the three clusters of darkness?
They are doubt concerning whether the self existed in the past or did not exist in the past; what lineage one had in the past; and what causes one had in the past.
One harbors doubt as to whether the self will exist in the future or not, what lineage one will have in the future, and by what causes one will exist in the future.
One harbors doubt as to whether the self exists in the present or not, what lineage one has in the present, and by what causes one exists in the present.
These are called the three masses of darkness.
What are the three swords?
The sword of desire, the sword of hatred, and the sword of delusion; these are called the three swords.
What are the three further swords?
The sword of body, the sword of speech, and the sword of mind; these are called the three further swords.
What are the three cravings?
Sensual craving, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence—these are called the three cravings.
What are the three non-restraints?
Non-restraint of body, non-restraint of speech, and non-restraint of mind—these are called the three non-restraints.
What are the three types of unwholesome conduct?
Unwholesome conduct of body, unwholesome conduct of speech, and unwholesome conduct of mind—these are called the three types of unwholesome conduct.
What are the three types of unwholesome conduct of body?
Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these are called the three unwholesome actions of the body.
What are the three unwholesome actions of the mind?
Greed, malice, and wrong view—these are called the three unwholesome actions of the mind.
What are the three impurities?
Impurity of body, speech, and mind—these are called the three impurities.
What are the three non-awakenings?
When body, speech, and mind are not awakened, these are called the three non-awakenings.
What are the three crookednesses?
When body, speech, and mind are not upright, these are called the three crookednesses.
What are the three phlegms?
The phlegm of desire, the phlegm of hatred, and the phlegm of delusion; these are called the three phlegms.
What are the three desires?
Sensual desire, ill will, and harmful intent—these are called the three desires.
What are the three perceptions?
The perception of sensuality, the perception of ill will, and the perception of delusion—these are called the three perceptions.
What are the three thoughts?
The thought of sensual desire, the thought of ill will, and the thought of harmfulness—these are called the three thoughts.
What are the three searches?
Seeking through the body, seeking through speech, and seeking through the mind—these are called the three seekings.
What are the three fires?
The fire of desire, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion—these are called the three fires.
What are the three heats?
The heat of desire, the heat of hatred, and the heat of delusion; these are called the three heats.
What are the three warmth-qualities?
The warmth of desire, the warmth of hatred, and the warmth of delusion—these are called the three warmths.
What are the three burnings?
The burning of desire, the burning of hatred, and the burning of delusion—these are called the three burnings.
What are the three fevers?
The fever of desire, the fever of hatred, and the fever of delusion; these are called the three fevers.
What are the three humors?
The burning of desire, the burning of hatred, and the burning of delusion—these are called the three burnings.
What are the three evils?
Evil of body, evil of speech, and evil of mind—these are called the three evils.
What are the three realms of existence?
They are the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; these are called the three realms of existence.
What are the three outflows?
The outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*); these are called the three outflows.
What are the three turbidities?
The turbidity of body, the turbidity of speech, and the turbidity of mind; these are called the three turbidities.
What are the three types of non-pliancy?
Non-pliancy of body, non-pliancy of speech, and non-pliancy of mind; these are called the three types of non-pliancy.
What are the three things that are not eliminated?
The non-removal of body, the non-removal of speech, and the non-removal of mind—these are called the three dharmas of non-removal.
What are the four floods?
The flood of desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance—these are called the four floods.
What are the four yokes?
The yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance—these are called the four yokes.
What are the four clingings?
Sensual clinging, clinging to existence, clinging to precepts and rituals, and clinging to a self—these are called the four clingings.
What are the four defilements?
Sensual defilement, defilement of form, defilement of the formless, and defilement of views—these are called the four defilements.
What are the four types of verbal misconduct?
False speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech—these are called the four types of verbal misconduct.
What are the four fetters?
The bodily tie of longing, the bodily tie of ill will, the bodily tie of attachment to precepts and observances, and the bodily tie of dogmatic views—these are called the four ties.
What are the four arrows?
The arrow of desire, the arrow of hatred, the arrow of pride, and the arrow of views—these are called the four arrows.
What are the four stations of consciousness?
A bhikṣu’s consciousness is conditioned by form; form is its object, and within form, craving arises and continues, whereby it attains growth and expansion.
Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise; these are called the four stations of consciousness.
What are the four conditions that give rise to craving?

If a bhikṣu gives rise to craving conditioned by robes, craving conditioned by food, craving conditioned by bedding and seats, and craving conditioned by medicine for illness—these are called the four conditions that give rise to craving.
What are the four conditions for the arising of craving?

If, conditioned by craving, craving arises; conditioned by craving, aversion arises; conditioned by aversion, aversion arises; and conditioned by aversion, craving arises—these are called the four conditions for the arising of craving.
What are the four modes of conduct leading to the evil realms?

They are conduct leading to the evil realms through desire, conduct leading to the evil realms through hatred, conduct leading to the evil realms through fear, and conduct leading to the evil realms through delusion. These are called the four modes of conduct leading to the evil realms.
What are the four karmic afflictions?

They are the karmic affliction of killing, the karmic affliction of stealing, the karmic affliction of sexual misconduct, and the karmic affliction of false speech; these are called the four karmic afflictions.
What are the four inversions?
Taking the impermanent to be permanent is an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view;
taking suffering to be pleasure is an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view.
To perceive what is non-self as self is an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view;
to perceive what is impure as pure is an inversion of perception, an inversion of mind, and an inversion of view. These are called the four inversions.
What are the four fears?
Fear of royal law, fear of thieves and robbers, fear of fire, and fear of water—these are called the four fears.
What are the further four fears?
The fear of old age, the fear of illness, the fear of death, and the fear of the evil realms.
What are the four further fears?
The fear of waves, the fear of surging billows, the fear of whirlpools, and the fear of the *śiśumāra*—in the language of Qin, the "crocodile."
What are the four further fears?
They are the fear of one's own decline, the fear of slander, the fear of being left alone and destitute, and the fear of having no son; these are called the four further fears.
What are the four factors of decline?
As the Blessed One has said:
there are four factors of decline.
What are the four?

A bhikṣu honors anger and does not honor the True Dharma; he honors malice and envy and does not honor the True Dharma; he honors gain and offerings and does not honor the True Dharma; he honors veneration and does not honor the True Dharma.
"Anger, malice, and envy; gain, offerings, and honor—when a bhikṣu respects such things, he loses the Path.
Like a ruined seed in fertile soil, the wholesome dharmas will not grow."
These are called the four factors of retrogression; the four factors are concluded.
What are the five desires?
They are the eye-consciousness of forms, which is characterized by craving, delight, and pleasure; it is the attachment to forms that continues as a succession of defilements.
The same applies to the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and their respective contacts; these are called the five desires (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
What are the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*)?
They are the hindrance of sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt; these are called the five hindrances.
What are the five lower fetters?
They are the view of a self-identity, doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill will; these are called the five lower fetters.
What are the five higher fetters?
Attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness—these are called the five higher-tier afflictions (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-kleśa*).
What are the five destinies?
Hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas—these are called the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
What are the five types of mental derangement?
Suppose a bhikṣu harbors doubt regarding the Blessed One, lacking faith, lacking resolution, and lacking understanding.

When a bhikṣu’s mind harbors doubt regarding the Blessed One, and his mind lacks faith, resolution, and understanding, the bhikṣu’s mind does not turn toward the Blessed One; lacking faith, lacking intimacy, and lacking understanding, this is called the first type of mental derangement.
The same applies to the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, there may be a bhikṣu whose observance of the precepts is deficient, negligent, or defiled.

Once a bhikṣu’s observance of the precepts has become deficient, negligent, or defiled, his mind does not incline toward the precepts; he lacks faith in them, does not draw near to them, and does not understand them.
When a bhikṣu does not turn toward the precepts, lacks faith, does not draw near to them, and lacks understanding, this is called the fourfold desolation of the mind.

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu’s mind causes harm to those pure practitioners of the holy life, his mind becomes desolate and he lacks faith; he reviles them with harsh words and slanders those pure practitioners of the holy life.

A bhikṣu who harasses those of pure and holy conduct, whose harassing mind is wild with lack of faith, and who, having reviled others with evil words and slandered those of pure and holy conduct, finds his mind no longer directed toward those of pure and holy conduct—lacking faith, not associating with them, and failing to understand them.

When a bhikṣu’s mind does not incline toward those who practice the holy life with purity, and having failed to have faith in them, to associate with them, or to understand them, this is called the five kinds of mental desolation.
What are the five kinds of mental entanglements?
Just as a bhikkhu’s body is not free from passion, not free from desire, not free from craving, not free from thirst, and not free from fever;

when a bhikkhu is thus not free from passion, not free from desire, not free from craving, not free from thirst, and not free from fever, his mind does not incline toward exertion, faith, tranquility, or the abandoning of fetters.
When a bhikṣu does not apply himself to diligent exertion, faith, tranquility, and the severing of fetters, this is called the first entanglement of the mind.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu applies himself to the pleasure of sensual desires such as form, and applies himself to the pleasure of bedding and sleep.

When a bhikṣu is devoted to the pleasures of sensual desires and the like, and is devoted to bedding and sleep, his mind does not incline toward diligent effort, right faith, peaceful conduct, or the severing of the fetters.

When a bhikṣu’s mind does not incline toward diligent effort, right faith, and the practice of tranquility, and having abandoned them, this is called the second and third mental entanglements (*cittopakleśa*).

Furthermore, when a bhikṣu attains a small measure of progress and remains stationary there, he does not strive upward for what has not yet been attained—desiring to attain it, what has not yet been understood—desiring to understand it, or what has not yet been realized—desiring to realize it.

If a bhikkhu, having attained a slight degree of progress, remains stationary and does not strive upward for what has not yet been attained—seeking to attain it, seeking to understand what has not yet been understood, and seeking to realize what has not yet been realized—then that bhikkhu does not incline toward diligent effort, right faith, tranquil conduct, or the severance of the fetters.
When a bhikkhu’s mind does not incline toward diligent effort, right faith, peaceful conduct, and the abandoning of the fetters, this is called the fourth mental entanglement (*cittānusaṃsagga*).

Furthermore, a bhikkhu practices the holy life with the hope of being reborn in various heavenly realms, thinking: "By means of these precepts, the path, asceticism, and the holy life, may I become a king of gods or a minister."

A bhikkhu practices the holy life with the hope of being born in various heavenly realms, thinking: "By means of this morality, path, austerity, and holy life, may I become a king of gods or a minister. Such a bhikkhu’s mind does not incline toward diligent effort, right faith, peaceful conduct, or the severing of fetters.
When a bhikṣu’s mind does not incline toward diligent effort, right faith, tranquil conduct, or the severing of fetters, these are called the five mental entanglements (*cittasaṃyojana*).
What are the five fears?
If one kills living beings, because of killing, there is fear in the present life and fear in future lives;
the same applies to stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, and the fear arising from intoxication through drinking liquor and negligence—these are called the five fears.
The five enemies are likewise. What are the five acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*)?

Killing one’s father is an act of immediate retribution; killing one’s mother is an act of immediate retribution; killing an Arhat is an act of immediate retribution; causing a schism in the Saṃgha is an act of immediate retribution; and with a malicious mind shedding the blood of a Buddha is an act of immediate retribution. These are called the five acts of immediate retribution.
What are the five transgressions of the precepts?
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, and drinking intoxicants with negligence—these are called the five transgressions of the precepts.
What are the five types of unrighteous speech?
Untimely speech, untruthful speech, meaningless speech, unrighteous speech, and undisciplined speech—these are called the five types of unrighteous speech.
What are the five things that are not to be delighted in?

Not delighting in dwelling alone, not delighting in transcending the world, not delighting in tranquility, not delighting in the holy life, and not delighting in all wholesome dharmas—these are called the five non-delights.
What are the five things that are loathed?

Not associating with those one should associate with; rebuking those who should not be rebuked; frequently visiting the homes of laypeople; always delighting in excessive speech; and being fond of wandering for alms—these are called the five loathsome things.
What are the five fundamental dharmas of anger?
Obstruction, provocation, resentment, contention, and dogmatic adherence—these are called the five fundamental dharmas of anger.
What are the five fundamental dharmas of sorrow?
Sorrow, lamentation, suffering, distress, and manifold suffering—these are called the five fundamental dharmas of sorrow.
What are the five types of envy?
Envy regarding dwellings, envy regarding noble lineage, envy regarding gain and offerings, and envy regarding fame—these are called the five types of envy.
What are the five conditions for sleep?
Yawning, drowsiness, lack of joy, heaviness of body, and mental depression—these are called the five conditions for sleep.
What are the five faults of violating the precepts?
