Bringing about one's own decline, being censured by others, the spread of an evil reputation, regret at the time of death, and falling into the miserable realms after death—these are called the five faults of violating the precepts.
What are the five further disadvantages of violating the precepts?
Because of violating the precepts, one does not obtain wealth not yet possessed, and one is cheated of or robbed of wealth already obtained;
furthermore, when entering among the assemblies of kṣatriyas, brahmins, householders, or śramaṇas, one harbors fear in one’s heart.
To speak of the faults and transgressions of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas far and wide;
when the body breaks up and life ends, one falls into an evil destination—this is called the fifth fault of violating the precepts.
What are the five things that are not respected or obeyed?
Lacking respect and obedience toward one’s parents, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and elders—this concludes the five dharmas of lacking respect and obedience.
What are the six bases of delight based on craving?

When the eye perceives forms, there arises love, delight, and pleasure; there is attachment to the desire for forms that continues in succession, obtaining them in the present and hoping to obtain them in the future.
Having previously experienced them, one recollects their past transformation and cessation, thereby giving rise to joy; this is called the first basis for joy based on craving.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are termed the six bases for joy based on craving.
What are the six bases for sorrow rooted in craving?

When the eye-consciousness perceives a form, there arises a craving, a delight, and a satisfaction that is agreeable; one becomes stained by desire for that form and continues in that state. Not obtaining it in the present, one fears not obtaining it in the future;
having previously obtained it, one recalls its past transformation and cessation and gives rise to sorrow. This is called the first basis for sorrow rooted in craving.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six bases of craving and grief.
What are the six bases of equanimity based on craving?
When an ordinary person sees a form with the eye, they give rise to equanimity; like a small child, they are deluded, failing to contemplate its faults and not knowing its karmic retribution.
Thus, not knowing and not discriminating, one abandons form; this is called the first abandonment based on craving.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; these are called the six abandonments based on craving.
What are the six defilements?
Defilement regarding forms, and defilement regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six defilements.
What are the six pleasures?
Delighting in forms, and delighting in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six delights.
What are the further six delights?

Delighting in various activities, delighting in speech, delighting in sleep, delighting in social gatherings, delighting in dwellings, and delighting in frivolous play—these are called the further six delights.
What are the six cravings?
Craving for forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six cravings.
What are the six angers?
Anger toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six types of anger.
What are the six hooks?
Hooks toward forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six hooks.
What are the six things that do not need guarding?
Not guarding against forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena—these are called the six things that do not need guarding.
What are the six roots of dispute?
As the Blessed One said:
"O bhikṣus!
There are six roots of dispute which should be understood; having understood them, one should practice diligently to bring them to an end."
What are the six?
A bhikṣu harbors anger and constantly dwells on resentment and malice; he does not revere, respect, or praise the World-Honored One, nor does he make offerings of incense and flowers to him;
he treats the Dharma and the Saṃgha in the same manner.
Regarding deficient conduct, desolate conduct, and defiled conduct in the precepts, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"If a bhikṣu is full of anger and constantly harbors resentment and malice, and gives rise to anger and contention within the Saṃgha, such contention will cause the decline of many sentient beings, cause many sentient beings to suffer, and lead to the decay of devas and humans."
He addressed the bhikṣus:

"Regarding such unwholesome roots of contention, as long as you perceive that they have not been severed in yourselves or others, you should dwell together in harmony and exert yourselves with diligence; you must courageously sever these unwholesome roots of contention."
He addressed the bhikṣus:

"When one has thus observed these unwholesome roots of contention and severed them—both in oneself and in others—and focuses the mind with single-minded attention so that they do not arise again, one then knows that the unwholesome roots of contention have been severed."
Furthermore, bhikṣu!

Whether it be harboring resentment and burning with feverish distress, or being envious and stingy, or practicing deceit, fraud, and misconduct, or seeking various views while slandering others—constantly recollecting these without letting them go; whether it be wrong views or extreme views, it is likewise so.
This concludes the six dharmas regarding the six roots of dispute.
What are the seven things associated with defilement?

If a woman reflects upon herself—her female body, her female form, her female characteristics, her female attire, her female desires, her female voice, and her female ornaments—the woman takes pleasure in being defiled by these things.

Having become attached to these things, she contemplates the external male body, the male form, the male characteristics, male attire, male desires, male voices, and male ornaments; likewise, women become attached to these things.
Having become stained by delighting in these things, they contemplate union.
Because of the condition of union, they give rise to joy, pleasure, and greedy attachment, taking delight in the female body.
Having delighted in union, for this reason, they constantly do not wish to transform their female bodies.
A man reflects to himself: "If this male body were to persist until the end of my life, I would never wish to change it"—this is also the case [for the others].
These are called the seven common defilements.
What is meant by the defilement of desire?
There was a brahmin of noble lineage who went to where the Tathāgata was; having arrived, he exchanged greetings and sat to one side.
He asked the World-Honored One, saying:
"O Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Are you, then, one who practices pure Brahma-conduct?
The World-Honored One answered the brahmin:
"If one may be called a practitioner of true Brahma-conduct, it is I."
For what reason? O Brahmin!
My holy life is unimpaired, unbroken, and undefiled.
The brahmin asked again:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Is the Brahma-faring way wild, deficient, and defiled?"
The Blessed One replied:
"The holy life of the brahmins is wild, deficient, and defiled.
The brahmin asked again:
"What constitutes the wilderness, the deficiency, and the defilement of the pure Brahma-faring?
The Blessed One replied:
"Some person might say:"
"I am a practitioner of pure conduct.
Although I do not engage in sexual intercourse with women, I nevertheless take pleasure and find delight in receiving from women baths, clothing, massages, and bodily adjustments."
He addressed the brahmin, saying:

"This is what is called being defiled by desire; it is not the pure holy life (*brahmacarya*). It is wild, deficient, and stained; it has not escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—the mass of suffering that is the accumulation of all these sufferings. I say that this has not escaped from suffering."
Furthermore, O Brahmin!
There may be someone who says:

"I am a practitioner of the Brahma-faring; I do not engage in sexual intercourse with women, nor do I accept their bathing, clothing, or massages for the sake of bodily care; yet I associate with women, conversing, joking, and playing with them, taking this as my delight and my gratification."
He addressed the brahmin, saying:

"This is called being defiled by desire; it is not the pure holy life. It is wild, deficient, and stained; one has not yet escaped from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—the mass of suffering that gathers together. I say that this has not yet escaped from suffering."
Furthermore, O Brahmin! There may be someone who says: "I am a practitioner of the Brahma-faring;

I do not engage in sexual intercourse with women; I do not accept from women bathing, clothing, or massage for the sake of bodily comfort; I do not associate with women through speech, laughter, or flirtation; yet, I gaze directly into the eyes of women, taking this as my pleasure and my delight."
He addressed the brahmin, saying: "This is called being defiled by desire;

it is not the pure practice of the holy life (brahmacarya). It is characterized by wildness, deficiency, and impurity; one has not yet escaped from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—the mass of suffering that is the accumulation of all these. I say that such a person has not yet escaped from suffering."
Furthermore, O Brahmin! Suppose there is someone who says:

"I am a pure practitioner of the Brahma-life; I do not engage in sexual intercourse with women; I do not accept from women baths, clothing, or massages for the body; I do not associate with women through speech, jesting, or flirtation; nor do I gaze directly into their eyes. Yet, when I hear from outside the enclosure the sounds of women—singing, dancing, speaking, laughing, or weeping—I take them as my delight and as my flavor."
He addressed the brahmin, saying: "This is called being defiled by desire;

it is not the pure holy life (brahmacarya). It is wild, deficient, and stained; it has not escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair—the mass of all these sufferings. I say that this has not escaped from suffering."
Furthermore, O Brahmin! There may be someone who says:

"I am a practitioner of the Brahma-faring; I do not engage in sexual intercourse with women; I do not accept from women baths, clothing, or massages for the sake of bodily comfort; I do not associate with women through speech, jesting, or flirtation; I do not gaze directly into the eyes of women; nor do I hear from behind a screen the sounds of women singing, dancing, speaking, laughing, or weeping. Nevertheless, when I recollect women with whom I have previously engaged in such activities—jesting, talking, and enjoying each other’s company—I take that as pleasure and as a source of gratification."
He addressed the brahmin, saying: "This is called being defiled by desire;

it is not the pure practice of the holy life. It is characterized by wildness, deficiency, and impurity; one has not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair—the massing of all these sufferings. I say that such a person has not yet escaped from suffering."
Furthermore, brahmin! Suppose someone says: "I am a pure practitioner of the Brahma-faring;

I do not engage in sexual intercourse with women; I do not accept women's bathing, clothing, or massage for the sake of bodily refinement; I do not associate with women through speech, jesting, or flirtation; I do not gaze directly into a woman's eyes; I do not hear sounds, singing, dancing, speech, laughter, or weeping from beyond a partition; nor do I recall women with whom I formerly engaged in dalliance, jesting, conversation, or mutual pleasure. Yet, when he sees an elder or an elder’s son enjoying themselves, fully endowed with the five objects of sensual desire, he regards that as joy and regards it as a flavor.
He addressed the brahmin, saying: "This is called being defiled by desire;

it is not the practice of pure brahmacarya. It is characterized by wildness, deficiency, and impurity; one has not yet escaped from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair—the mass of suffering that has gathered. I say that such a person has not yet escaped from suffering."
Furthermore, O Brahmin!
Some people say:

"I am a practitioner of pure celibacy (*brahmacarya*); I do not engage in sexual intercourse with women; I do not accept from women baths, clothing, or massages for the sake of physical comfort; nor do I associate with women through conversation, jesting, or flirtation; I do not gaze intimately at women face-to-face; I do not hear the sounds of women singing, dancing, or weeping beyond a partition; I do not dwell upon memories of times when I engaged in play, laughter, or speech with them for mutual enjoyment; nor do I see elders or their sons enjoying themselves with the five objects of desire. Nevertheless, it is with the wish to be reborn in the heavens that I practice this pure celibacy. By means of these precepts, this path, and this ascetic practice of pure celibacy, may I become a celestial king or a minister, taking this as my joy and my flavor."
He addressed the brahmins, saying: "This is called being defiled by desire;

it is not the practice of pure brahmacarya. It is characterized by wildness, deficiency, and impurity; one has not yet escaped birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair—the massing of all these sufferings. I say that such a person has not yet escaped from suffering."
Furthermore, Brahmin!

Regarding these seven types of common sensual defilements, when I examine my own inner mind, even if these seven common sensual defilements have not been abandoned, I do not claim to possess pure and holy conduct.
"O Brahmin! Because I have abandoned these seven things associated with the defilement of sensual desire, I declare that I possess the true, pure Brahma-faring and have attained fearlessness.
These are called the seven things associated with the defilement of sensual desire."
What are the seven stations of consciousness?
There are sentient beings who possess various bodies and various perceptions—namely, humans or devas of the desire realm; this is called the first station of consciousness.
If there are sentient beings who have multiple bodies but a single perception, such as those first born in the Brahma-heaven, this is called the second station of consciousness.
If there are sentient beings who have a single body but diverse perceptions, such as those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, this is called the third station of consciousness.
There are some sentient beings who possess a single body and a single perception, as in the Heaven of Universal Purity; this is called the fourth station of consciousness.
There are some sentient beings in the sphere of infinite space; this is called the fifth station of consciousness.
If there are sentient beings in the sphere of infinite consciousness, this is called the sixth station of consciousness.
If there are sentient beings in the sphere of nothingness, this is called the seventh station of consciousness.
These are called the seven stations of consciousness.
What are the seven types of conceit?
They are: conceit, inferiority-conceit, superiority-conceit, overweening conceit, self-conceit, false conceit, and conceit among conceits.
What is pride (*māna*)?
If one thinks, "I am superior," and the mind becomes haughty toward others, this is called pride.
What is the pride of inferiority (*ūnamāna*)?
When one is inferior yet the mind harbors arrogance toward that person, this is called *anavamanyanā-māna* (the pride of being not inferior).
What is called *śreyān-māna* (the pride of being superior)?
When one is equal to those who are superior, yet the mind harbors arrogance toward them, this is called *śreyān-māna*.
What is called overweening pride (*adhimāna*)?
To conceive the thought that one has attained what has not been attained, and for the mind to be haughty on account of that—this is called overweening pride.
What is called pride of self (*asmimāna*)?
When one possesses wholesome qualities and the mind becomes conceited on account of them, this is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").
What is called *mithyāmāna* (false pride)?
When one lacks wholesome qualities and the mind becomes conceited on account of them, this is called *mithyāmāna*.
What is called "pride within pride"?
If one sees another who is proud and gives rise to a mind of pride toward that person's arrogance, this is called "pride within pride.
Furthermore, as for "ego-pride" (*asmimāna*): if there is a sense of self, and the mind gives rise to arrogance toward that [self], this is called "ego-pride."
Furthermore, as for false pride (*mithyāmāna*): if one who possesses wrong views gives rise to arrogance toward them in the mind, this is called false pride.

Furthermore, as for pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*): thinking "I am superior among the superior" or "noble among the noble," and giving rise to arrogance toward them in the mind, this is called pride beyond pride.
These are called the seven types of conceit.
What are the seven forms of disrespect?

If one does not respect the Buddha, does not respect the Dharma, does not respect the Saṅgha, does not respect the precepts, does not respect meditative concentration, does not respect wisdom, and does not respect wholesome dharmas—these are called the seven forms of disrespect.
What are the seven outflows? They are:

the outflow to be abandoned by vision, the outflow to be abandoned by patience, the outflow to be abandoned by association, the outflow to be abandoned by separation, the outflow to be abandoned by subduing, the outflow to be abandoned by precepts, and the outflow to be abandoned by cultivation. These are called the seven outflows.
What are the seven dharmas of timidity?
Killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech—these are called the seven dharmas of timidity.
What are the seven perturbations?

They are: "I shall exist," "I shall not exist," "My form shall exist," "My form shall not exist," "The perception of self shall exist," "The perception of self shall not exist," and "The perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception shall exist. These are called the seven perturbations.
The seven types of self-reliance, the seven types of seeking, the seven types of transgression, the seven types of action, and the seven types of birth are likewise explained;
thus ends the section on these seven dharmas.
What are the eight worldly dharmas? Gain, loss, defamation, praise, fame, insignificance, suffering, and pleasure—these are called the eight worldly dharmas.
What are the eight non-noble statements? To say one has seen when one has not seen;

to say one has not seen when one has seen; to say one has heard when one has not heard; to say one has not heard when one has heard; to say one has sensed when one has not sensed; to say one has not sensed when one has sensed; to say one has cognized when one has not cognized; and to say one has cognized when one has not cognized—these are called the eight non-noble statements.
What are the eight matters of indolence?
If there is an indolent bhikṣu who thinks to himself:

"Today, having entered the village for alms, I have not obtained sufficient coarse or fine food. Because of this insufficiency, I have become emaciated; I take no pleasure in walking meditation or sitting in dhyāna, and I wish only to sleep."

A lazy bhikṣu then lies down to sleep and is unable to exert himself diligently to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, and to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the first matter of laziness.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:

"Today I entered the village for alms and obtained sufficient food, both coarse and fine; my body is heavy and cumbersome, like a money-bag filled with meat. I have no desire for walking meditation or seated dhyāna; I wish to lie down and sleep."

A lazy bhikṣu then falls asleep and lies down; he is unable to apply himself with diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, and to realize what has not yet been realized. This is called the second matter of indolence.
Furthermore, a lazy bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Today I am exhausted from my labors; I have no desire for walking meditation or seated dhyāna, and I wish to sleep."

The indolent bhikṣu then falls asleep and lies down; he is unable to exert himself diligently to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, and to realize what has not yet been realized. This is called the third matter of indolence.
Furthermore, a lazy bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Tomorrow I must perform my duties and my body will become weary; therefore, I have no desire for walking meditation or sitting in dhyāna. I shall go to sleep early tonight."

A lazy bhikṣu then falls asleep and lies down, unable to apply himself with diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, or to realize what has not yet been realized; this is called the fourth matter of laziness.
Furthermore, a lazy bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Today I have traveled back and forth until my body is utterly exhausted; I have no desire for walking meditation or seated dhyāna, and wish only to sleep."

A lazy bhikṣu immediately falls asleep and lies down; he is unable to apply himself with diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, and to realize what has not yet been realized. This is called the fifth matter of laziness.
Furthermore, a lazy bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Tomorrow I must travel, and my body will surely become utterly exhausted; therefore, I have no desire for walking meditation or sitting in dhyāna, I wish only to sleep."

A lazy bhikṣu then falls asleep and lies down, unable to apply diligent effort toward that which is not yet attained, desiring to attain it; that which is not yet understood, desiring to understand it; or that which is not yet realized, desiring to realize it. This is called the sixth matter of laziness.
Furthermore, a lazy bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I am currently afflicted by illness and suffering; I have no desire for walking meditation or seated dhyāna; I wish to sleep.

This lazy bhikṣu then immediately sleeps and does not exert himself with diligence to attain what has not yet been attained, to understand what has not yet been understood, or to realize what has not yet been realized. This is called the seventh matter of laziness.
Furthermore, a lazy bhikṣu reflects thus:
"My illness has not been long cured; my body is weak and frail. I have no desire for walking meditation or sitting in dhyāna; I wish to sleep and lie down."

A lazy bhikṣu then falls asleep and lies down, unable to apply diligent effort toward what has not yet been attained, what has not yet been understood, or what has not yet been realized; this is called the eighth matter of laziness.
What are the eight unfavorable conditions that obstruct the practice of the holy life?

When a Buddha appears in the world—one who is a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān—who proclaims the Dharma of tranquility, cessation, and dispassion, the path leading directly to Nirvāṇa; yet there are sentient beings dwelling in the realms of hell. This is called the first unfavorable condition that obstructs the practice of the holy life.

Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, up to the Buddha, the World-Honored One—who teaches the Dharma of tranquility, cessation, and detachment from desire, the path leading directly to Nirvāṇa; yet there may be sentient beings dwelling in the realm of animals, the realm of hungry ghosts, or among the long-lived gods; or those who are ignorant people living in remote borderlands; or those places not frequented by monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen. These are called the fifth difficult circumstances that obstruct the cultivation of the holy life.

Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world—the Tathāgata, the Arhat, up to the Buddha, the World-Honored One—he teaches the Dharma of tranquility and detachment from desire, the path leading directly to Nirvāṇa. Yet there may be sentient beings born within that same realm who possess wrong views and inverted views.

Because the retribution for wrong views and perverted views has fully ripened, one is inevitably born in hell; this is called the sixth difficult circumstance that hinders the practice of the holy life (*brahmacarya*).

Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, and so forth, up to a Buddha, a World-Honored One—who proclaims the Dharma of tranquility, cessation, and dispassion, the path leading directly to Nirvāṇa, there may be sentient beings born within that same land who are deaf, blind, or mute like sheep, communicating only through hand gestures; they do not know how to speak of the karmic retribution of good and evil deeds. This is called the seventh difficult circumstance that hinders the practice of the holy life.

Furthermore, when a Buddha does not appear in the world, one is not called a Tathāgata, nor even a Buddha-Bhagavān; the Dharma of tranquility, cessation, and detachment from desire, as well as the path leading rightly to Nirvāṇa, is not taught. There may be sentient beings within the realm who are neither deaf, blind, nor mute, and who are also capable of discerning the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma, yet they do not encounter the era of a Buddha.
These are called the eight difficult conditions that obstruct the cultivation of the holy life;

the eight factors are now concluded. What are the nine "various" phenomena? Because of various elements (*dhātu*), various contacts (*sparśa*) arise; because of various contacts, various feelings (*vedanā*) arise; because of various feelings, various perceptions (*saṃjñā*) arise; because of various perceptions, various thoughts (*vitarka*) arise; because of various thoughts, various desires (*chanda*) arise; because of various desires, various gains (*lābha*) arise; because of various gains, various quests (*paryeṣaṇā*) arise; because of various quests, various fevers (*paridāha*) arise. These are called the nine "various" phenomena.

What are the nine fundamental dharmas of craving? Conditioned by craving, seeking arises; conditioned by seeking, gain and support arise; conditioned by gain and support, activity arises; conditioned by activity, sensual passion arises; conditioned by sensual passion, endurance arises; conditioned by endurance, stinginess and attachment arise; conditioned by stinginess and attachment, accumulation arises; conditioned by accumulation, there arise guarding, injury, striking, binding, confinement, and mutual strife. These are called the nine fundamental dharmas of craving.
What are the nine abodes of sentient beings?
There are some sentient beings who possess diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, such as humans and devas in the desire realm; this is called the first abode of sentient beings.
There are some sentient beings who have multiple bodies but a single perception; these are the beings born in the Brahma-world, and this is called the second abode of sentient beings.
There are some sentient beings who have a single body but multiple perceptions; these are the beings in the Ābhāsvara Heaven, and this is called the third abode of sentient beings.
There are sentient beings who possess a single body and a single perception; these are the Śubhakṛtsna devas, and this is called the fourth abode of sentient beings.
There are sentient beings who are without sensation and without perception; these are the Āsaṃjñika devas, and this is called the fifth abode of sentient beings.
There are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of infinite space; this is called the sixth abode of sentient beings.
There are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is called the seventh abode of sentient beings.
There are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of nothingness; this is called the eighth abode of sentient beings.
There are sentient beings who dwell in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is named the ninth abode of sentient beings.
What are the nine disadvantages of violating the precepts?

Remorse, lack of gladness, lack of joy, lack of tranquility, mental suffering, distraction, lack of knowledge and vision according to reality, lack of understanding, and lack of skillful means—these are called the nine disadvantages of violating the precepts. This concludes the nine dharmas.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Nineteen *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*,
Fascicle Twenty Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others.
Non-Question Section, Chapter Eleven: The Afflictions, Part Three. What are the ten latent afflictions (*anuśaya*)? They are:

the latent affliction of views, the latent affliction of doubt, the latent affliction of attachment to rules and rituals, the latent affliction of craving, the latent affliction of hostility, the latent affliction of envy, the latent affliction of avarice, the latent affliction of ignorance, the latent affliction of pride, and the latent affliction of restlessness. These are called the ten latent afflictions.
What are the ten fetters of affliction? They are:

the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of attachment to precepts and rituals, the fetter of sensual desire, the fetter of ill will, the fetter of desire for the realm of form, the fetter of desire for the formless realm, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of conceit, and the fetter of restlessness. These are called the ten fetters of affliction.
What are the ten perceptions? They are:

the perception of sensual desire, the perception of ill will, the perception of cruelty, the perception of greed, the perception of disparagement, the perception of this and that (internal and external), the perception of the country, the perception of inferiority, the perception of unwholesomeness, the perception of diversity, and the perception based on craving. These are called the ten perceptions.
What are the ten thoughts? They are:

thoughts of ill will, thoughts of harm, thoughts of kin, thoughts of one’s country, thoughts of immortality, thoughts of others’ gain, thoughts associated with consciousness, thoughts associated with lack of loving-kindness, thoughts based on gain, and thoughts based on craving.
These are called the ten right thoughts.
What are the ten wrong dharmas?

Wrong view, wrong thought, wrong speech, wrong action, wrong livelihood, wrong effort, wrong concentration, wrong wisdom, wrong liberation, and wrong knowledge; these are called the ten wrong dharmas.

What are the ten types of vexation? They are: the arising of a vexed mind when someone has already wronged one; the arising of a vexed mind when someone is currently wronging one; the arising of a vexed mind when someone intends to wrong one; the arising of a vexed mind when someone has already benefited one whom one does not love, approve of, or find pleasing; the arising of a vexed mind when someone is currently benefiting such a person; the arising of a vexed mind when someone intends to benefit such a person; and the arising of a vexed mind through groundless anger. These are called the ten vexations.
What are the ten unwholesome courses of action? They are:
killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, harsh speech, divisive speech, frivolous speech, covetousness, malice, and wrong view. These are called the ten unwholesome courses of action.
What are the ten dharmas whose accomplishment leads to falling into hell as swiftly as a whirling spear?
Killing, up to and including wrong view—these ten dharmas, when accomplished, lead to falling into hell as swiftly as a whirling spear. This concludes the ten dharmas.
What are the eleven defilements of the mind? Doubt is a defilement of the mind;

lack of reflection is a defilement of the mind; fear is a defilement of the mind; sorrow is a defilement of the mind; malice is a defilement of the mind; sleepiness is a defilement of the mind; excessive exertion is a defilement of the mind; feeble exertion is a defilement of the mind; incapacity is a defilement of the mind; manifold perceptions are a defilement of the mind; and attachment to form is a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by doubt being a defilement of the mind?

There may be someone who, taking the past as an object, is deluded, wondering: "Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? What was my lineage in the past? By what cause did I exist in the past?"
If one harbors doubt regarding the future, thinking: "Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? What will my name be in the future? By what cause will I exist in the future?"

If one harbors doubt regarding the present, wondering: "Do I exist now? Do I not exist now? What lineage do I have now? By what cause do I exist now? From where do all sentient beings come? To where do they go?"

If one harbors doubt concerning the present, thinking, "Do I exist now? Do I not exist now? What clan do I belong to now? By what cause do I exist now? From where have all sentient beings come, and to where do they go?"
If one has doubt regarding the Buddha, the World-Honored One—whether he is the Buddha or not the Buddha;
whether the World-Honored One has well-expounded the Dharma or not; whether the World-Honored One’s assembly of śrāvakas follows the path to a good destination or not;
whether [the teachings] are eternal or non-eternal; and whether they are suffering or not suffering.
The dharma of non-self and the dharma that is not non-self; quiescent nirvāṇa and that which is not quiescent nirvāṇa;
existence and non-existence; giving and non-giving; sacrifice and non-sacrifice;
the existence and non-existence of the retribution for good and evil karma; and the existence and non-existence of this present life.
There is an afterlife, or there is no afterlife; there are parents, or there are no parents;
there are devas, or there are no devas; beings are born by transformation, or beings are not born by transformation;
there are recluses and brahmins who, having attained the right path and reached the right goal, personally realize and declare this world and the next, or there are no such recluses and brahmins.

When a Brahmin who is rightly directed and rightly attained speaks from his own direct realization regarding this world and the world beyond, if one harbors doubt, repeated doubt, or ultimate doubt toward those teachings;

if the mind is not settled, but is wavering, double-minded, uncertain, possessed of immeasurable doubt, and fails to reach exhaustion through non-liberation; if there is hesitation, repeated hesitation, or ultimate hesitation—this is called doubt, which is a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by "non-attention" as a defilement of the mind?

If one does not correctly deliberate, discriminate, calculate, or recollect regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, or regarding sentient beings and phenomena, this is called non-attention as a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by "fear" as a defilement of the mind?

It refers to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects, or sentient beings and phenomena; when one is conditioned by these, there arises fear, ultimate dread, alarm, horripilation, and a change in complexion—this is called "fear" as a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by compassion being a defilement of the mind?
If unwholesome thoughts arise while practicing compassion, this is called compassion being a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by malice being a defilement of the mind?
Evilness of body, speech, and mind—this is called evil; it is the defilement of the mind.
What is meant by "sleep" as a defilement of the mind?

If afflictions have not been severed and one sinks into sleep, such that the body lacks joy, the body lacks composure, the body lacks lightness, the body lacks flexibility, and the body lacks purification—this is called sleep.
Whether it be sleep or the failure to sever afflictions, being submerged in sleep, or when one desires to sleep and the mind is oppressed by drowsiness and torpor—this is called *middha*.
Such sleep is called "sleepiness," which is a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by excessive diligence being a defilement of the mind?
If diligence is agitated, this is called excessive diligence being a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by lax diligence being a defilement of the mind?
If diligence falters, this is called weak diligence, which is a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by incapacity being a defilement of the mind?
If the mind is timid and weak, this is called incapacity, which is a defilement of the mind.
What is meant by "diverse perceptions are defilements of the mind"?

If sentient beings are diverse, their objects are diverse, their spheres of experience are diverse, and their initial births are diverse, these are called diverse perceptions that are defilements of the mind.
What is meant by "attachment to forms is a defilement of the mind"?
If one perceives forms with exclusive attachment, this is called "attachment to forms is a defilement of the mind.
These are known as the eleven defilements of the mind.
What are the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity)?
Some may say: "Form is the self," "the self is within form," "the self possesses form," or "form belongs to the self.
The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. These are called the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
What are the twenty dharmas by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a discharged arrow? They are:

committing killing oneself and inciting others to kill, up to and including holding wrong views oneself and inciting others to hold wrong views. These twenty dharmas, when accomplished, cause one to fall into hell as swiftly as a discharged arrow.
What are the twenty-one stains of the mind?

Longing is a stain of the mind; ill will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, doubt, vexation, harmfulness, constant recollection of resentment and aversion, harboring hatred, burning fever, envy, stinginess, guile, deceit, lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, self-exaltation, contention, self-aggrandizement, heedlessness, pride, and overweening pride—these are called the twenty-one stains of the mind.
What are the thirty factors by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear?

They are: committing killing oneself, inciting others to kill, and praising killing; and so on, up to: holding wrong views oneself, inciting others to hold wrong views, and praising wrong views. These are called the thirty factors by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a hurled spear.
What are the thirty-six modes of craving?
There are eighteen modes of craving arising internally and eighteen modes of craving arising externally.
What are the eighteen modes of craving arising internally?
As the Blessed One has said:

"Because of this, that exists; because of that, this exists. Thus there is existence through a cause, existence through a different cause, existence through a future cause, and non-existence through a future cause; "I shall exist," and "that I shall exist."

"Thus I shall exist," "I shall exist otherwise," "by means of this I shall obtain that," "thus I shall obtain otherwise," "longing for existence," "longing for that existence," "longing for such existence," and "longing for existence otherwise"—these are called the eighteen modes of craving arising internally.
What are the eighteen modes of craving pertaining to the external? As the Blessed One has said: "Because of this, that exists; because of that, this exists.

There is existence through such a cause, existence through another cause, existence through a future cause, and existence through no cause. There is "I shall exist," "that I shall exist," "thus I shall exist," and "otherwise I shall exist. There is attainment through this, attainment through thus, attainment through otherwise, and attainment through another. There is the hope for existence, the hope for that existence, the hope for existence thus, and the hope for existence otherwise. These are called the eighteen modes of craving pertaining to the external.
Thus, eighteen modes of craving arise internally, and eighteen modes of craving arise externally; these are called the thirty-six modes of craving.
What are the forty factors by whose accomplishment one falls into hell as swiftly as a whirling spear?

To kill living beings oneself, to incite others to kill, to praise killing, or to rejoice upon seeing others kill; and likewise, to hold wrong views oneself, to incite others to hold wrong views, to praise wrong views, or to rejoice upon seeing others hold wrong views—these forty factors, when fully accomplished, lead one to fall into hell as swiftly as a whirling spear.
What are the sixty-two views?
As stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There is yet another dharma, a profound, subtle, and great dharma-light, which only the noble and holy disciples are able to praise the Tathāgata by means of."
What is this profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light, by which the noble disciples can praise the Tathāgata?

Whatever various and countless things the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas speak according to their own inclinations—whether concerning the past eons and past views, or the future eons and future views—they all fall within the sixty-two views.

Regarding views concerning the past eons and views concerning the future eons—whatever various and innumerable things they may say according to their own inclinations, none can transcend these sixty-two views.

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through whatever various and innumerable things they each say according to their own inclinations regarding views of the past eons and views of the future eons, all fall within these sixty-two views and none are able to surpass them?

Whatever various and countless views concerning the past eons and the origin of the world that the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas may propound according to their own inclinations, they all fall within the eighteen views.
Whatever various and countless views concerning the past eons and the origin of the world they may propound according to their own inclinations, none of them can transcend these eighteen views.

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on various and countless views concerning the past eons, each speak according to their own inclinations, yet all fall within the eighteen views and none can transcend them?
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on their views regarding the past eons, give rise to eternalist doctrines, asserting:
"The self and the world are eternal.
All such views are included within these four [extreme] views.
Regarding the views concerning the past and the origin of the world, they declare: "I and the world are eternal.
These are all included within four views; none can transcend them.
For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past and the origin of the eon, give rise to eternalist doctrines, claiming:
"The self and the world are eternal"?
Are these not all included within four views, such that none can transcend them?

There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind, and with that concentrated mind, recollect twenty eons of formation and twenty eons of destruction.
He speaks thus:
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Why is that?

By means of various skillful means, I enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; with this samādhi-mind, I recollect twenty eons of formation and destruction, during which the sentient beings therein neither increase nor decrease, remaining constantly gathered and never dispersing.
"By this I know that the self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
This is the first view.
On account of this, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eons and past views, reckon that the self and the world are eternal; among these four views, none can surpass them.
There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind, and with a mind in samādhi, recollect forty eons of formation and destruction.
He speaks thus:
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Why is that?

By means of various skillful means, I entered the samādhi of concentrated mind; with this mind of samādhi, I recollected forty eons of formation and destruction, during which the sentient beings therein neither increased nor decreased, always gathering together and never dispersing.
"By this I know that the self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
These are two views.

Based on these, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, through their views concerning the past eons (*pūrvakalpa*), speculate that the self and the world are eternal; among the four views, none can surpass these.

There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind, and with that concentrated mind, recollect eighty eons of formation and destruction.
He speaks thus:
"I and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false. Why is that?

By means of various skillful methods, I entered the samādhi of concentrated mind; with this concentrated mind, I recollected eighty eons of formation and destruction, during which the sentient beings therein neither increased nor decreased, always gathering together without dispersing.
"By means of this knowledge, I and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false.
These are the three views.
Based on these, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eon and their views of the past, reckon that "I and the world are eternal," and among the four views, none can surpass them.
There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess swift and penetrating wisdom and are skilled in discernment.

Using the skillful means of their swift and penetrating wisdom to investigate, they consider themselves to have attained definitive certainty. Based on what they have seen and their own eloquence, they proclaim:
"The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, all else is false."
These are the four views.

Based on these, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas maintain that the self and the world are eternal through their theories concerning the past and the origin of the aeon; among these four views, none can surpass them.
These śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eons and past views, reckon that the self and the world are eternal; all such cases are entirely included within these four views.
"The self and the world are eternal"—among these four views, none can surpass them.
Only the Tathāgata knows the basis of these views, how they are maintained, how they are grasped, and he also knows their karmic retribution.
What the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this. Although he knows, he does not cling;

because he does not cling, he attains tranquility. He knows the origin, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding craving. Through the contemplation of equality, he attains liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is called another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light, which enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is yet another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light, which enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
What are those teachings?
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the past eons and past views, put forward this doctrine:
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal."

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on this fundamental view regarding the past eon, speculate that both the self and the world are partly eternal and partly non-eternal; among these four views, none can surpass them.

There may be a time when this kalpa first begins to form, and there are certain sentient beings whose merit, lifespan, and karma have been exhausted; they pass away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and are reborn in the empty Brahma palace. There, they immediately give rise to a mind of attachment and further wish for other sentient beings to be born together with them in this place.

Once this being had conceived such attachment and aspiration, there were others whose life-span and merit were exhausted; they passed away from the Ābhāsvara Heaven and were reborn here in this empty Brahma palace.
When he first produced sentient beings, he thought to himself:
"In this place, I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā.
I exist of my own accord; there is no one who can create me."
I fully know all meanings and govern a thousand worlds; therein I am sovereign and most honored, capable of performing transformations that are subtle and unsurpassed.
I am the father of sentient beings; I alone existed first, while other sentient beings came later, and those later beings were transformed and brought forth by me.
Thereafter, sentient beings again had this thought:
"He is Mahābrahmā.
He is able to create himself; there is no one who creates him."
He fully knows all meanings and governs a thousand worlds; therein he is sovereign and most noble, capable of transformations that are the foremost in subtlety.
He is the father and mother of sentient beings; he alone existed first, and only later did we come to be.
"We sentient beings were emanated by him.

When the life-span of that Brahmā’s existence came to an end, he was reborn here; as he gradually grew up, he shaved off his hair and beard, left the household life to don the dharma-robes, practiced the conduct of a brahmacārī, and entered the samādhi of concentrated mind."
Following his samādhi-mind, he recalled his own past lives and spoke these words:

"That Great Brahmā is able to create himself; there is no creator of him. He fully knows all meanings and presides over a thousand worlds. Within them, he is sovereign and most noble, capable of manifesting transformations that are subtle and supreme."
He is the father of all sentient beings, eternally abiding and unchanging.
Yet that Brahmā has created us; we are impermanent and subject to transformation, unable to abide for long.
Therefore, you should know that both the self and the world are both eternal and impermanent; this is the truth, and all else is false.
This is called the first view.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the past eon, raise the argument that [the world] is both eternal and non-eternal, none can transcend these four views.
There may be sentient beings who delight in jesting and indolence, repeatedly engaging in jesting and amusement for their own entertainment.
While thus amusing themselves, their bodies become utterly exhausted, and they consequently lose their mindfulness.
Because he lost his mind, he passed away and was reborn in this world.
As he gradually grew up, he shaved off his hair and beard, left the household life to don the dharma robes, practiced the conduct of a brahmacārin, and entered the samādhi of concentrated mind.
By the power of samādhi, he recollected his own past lives and spoke these words:
"Those other sentient beings do not engage in frequent play, laughter, or entertainment; they always remain in that place, eternally abiding and unchanging."
"Because I repeatedly engaged in jesting, this law of impermanence and change has come to pass.
Therefore, know that both I and the world are both eternal and impermanent; this alone is true, and all else is false."
This is called the second view.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eon, give rise to this doctrine:
"Both the self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal."
Among these four views, there is none that can surpass them.
There are sentient beings who gaze at one another; having gazed, they lose their mental composure, and as a result, they pass away and are reborn in this realm.
Having gradually grown up, he shaved off his hair and beard, left the household life to don the dharma robes, and practiced the conduct of a brahmacārin, entering the samādhi of concentrated mind.
By the power of that samādhi, he recognized his original place of birth and spoke these words:
"Just as those sentient beings do not look at one another and do not lose their mindfulness, they remain eternally constant and unchanging."
"Because we looked at one another repeatedly, we lost our mindfulness, which led to this state of impermanence and change.
By this I know that both the self and the world are both eternal and impermanent; this alone is true, and all else is false."
This is called the third view.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on their views regarding the past eon, give rise to this doctrine:
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal."
Among these four views, there is none that can surpass them.
There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess swift wisdom of marks and are well able to investigate.
Having observed with the wisdom of swift discernment, he declared:
"Both I and the world are both eternal and non-eternal; this alone is the truth, and all else is false."
This is called the fourth view.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eon, formulate this theory:
"Both the self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal."
Among these four views, there is none that can surpass them.
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, regarding the past eons and past views, propound the theory:
"The self and the world are both eternal and non-eternal," all fall within these four views; there is none that can surpass them.
Only the Buddha can know this locus of views—how they are maintained and how they are grasped—and he also knows their karmic retribution.
What the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this.

Although he knows [these things], he does not cling; because he does not cling, he attains nirvana. He understands the arising, cessation, gratification, danger, and the escape regarding craving, and through equal contemplation, he achieves liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is called another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that causes the noble disciples to praise the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that causes the noble disciples to praise the Tathāgata with true equanimity.
What is this teaching?
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the views concerning the past and the origin of the world, put forward the thesis:
"The self and the world are finite, or they are infinite."
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on their views regarding the past eons, propound the thesis:
"The self and the world are finite, or infinite.
Among these four views, none can surpass them.

There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; by the power of that samādhi, they contemplate the world and conceive the notion of its finitude, asserting:
"This world is finite; this alone is the truth, and all else is false."

Why is this so? By means of various skillful means, I enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; through the power of that samādhi, I contemplate that the world has limits, and therefore I know that the world has limits—this alone is true, and all else is false.
This is called the first view.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on their views concerning the past eon, give rise to the thesis:
"The self and the world are finite. Among these four views, none can surpass them.

There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; by the power of that samādhi, they contemplate the world and give rise to the perception of it being boundless.
He speaks thus:
"The world is infinite; this alone is true, and all else is false. Why is that?"

By means of various skillful means, I enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; through the power of this samādhi, I observe that the world is infinite. Therefore, I know that the world is infinite: this alone is true, and all else is false.
This is called the second view.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eon (*pūrvakalpa*), give rise to the thesis:
"The self and the world are infinite. Among these four views, none can surpass them.

There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who, through various skillful means, enter the samādhi of concentrated mind; by the power of that samādhi, they contemplate the world and perceive that it is finite above but infinite in the four directions.
He speaks thus:
"The world is both finite and infinite; this alone is true, and all else is false. Why is that?

By means of various skillful methods, I entered the samādhi of concentrated mind; through the power of this samādhi, I observed that the zenith has a limit while the four cardinal directions are limitless.
Therefore, I know that the world is both finite and infinite—this alone is true, and all else is false.
This is called the third view.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eon, give rise to the thesis:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite. Among these four views, none can surpass them.
There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess swift analytical wisdom and are skilled in observation.
Having observed with their swift analytical wisdom, they declare:
"Both myself and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, and all else is false."
This is called the fourth view.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on their views regarding the past eon, propound the following theory:
"The self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; this alone is true, and all else is false."
Among these four views, there is none that can surpass them.

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas propound theories regarding the past eons and past views—such as "the self and the world are finite," "infinite," or other such positions—all fall within these four views; there is none that can surpass them.
Only the Buddha can know this locus of views—how they are maintained and how they are clung to—and he also knows their karmic retribution.

What the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this; though he knows it, he does not cling to it. Because he does not cling, he attains tranquility. He knows the origin, cessation, gratification, danger, and the escape regarding craving; through the contemplation of equality, he attains liberation without remainder, and is therefore called the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are other profound, subtle, and great Dharma-lights that cause the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
What are these other profound, subtle, and great Dharma-lights that cause the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata?
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the views concerning the past eon, ask different questions and give different answers.
Because these various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas ask different questions and give different answers based on their views concerning the past eon, none among them is able to surpass these four views.
There may be some śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and such a view as this:
"Do I not know whether there is the retribution for good and evil karma,
or whether there is no retribution for good and evil karma?"
Because I neither see nor know [the ultimate nature of things], whether one says that there is retribution for good and evil karma, or that there is no retribution for good and evil karma.

In this world, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who are erudite and widely learned, intelligent and wise, who always delight in seclusion and tranquility, whose eloquence is subtle and refined, and who are respected by the world.
One who is able to skillfully discern various views through wisdom would feel shame and remorse if,
when asked about the profound and subtle meaning of those views, they were unable to provide an answer.
With a heart full of fear, I shall answer them thus: "This is to be taken as a refuge, as an island, as a shelter, and as the ultimate path.
If they should ask further, I shall answer:
"This matter is not so; this matter is truly not so; this matter is otherwise than so; this matter is neither otherwise than so nor not otherwise than so."
This is called the first view.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, none are able to surpass these four views, as they provide different answers to this question.
Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and maintain such a view:
I neither see nor know whether there is another world or whether there is no other world.
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who, by means of the divine eye and the knowledge of others' minds, can see me from afar, yet they cannot see me even when I am near.
Such a person might know whether there is a future world or no future world, yet I neither know nor see whether there is a future world or no future world.
If I were to speak on this matter, it would be a falsehood.
Out of fear of false speech, I take this as my refuge, my island, my shelter, and my ultimate path.
Should anyone question me, I shall answer thus:
"This matter is not so; this matter is not true; this matter is otherwise than it is; this matter is neither otherwise nor not otherwise."
This is called the second view.
Among these four views, no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa can surpass them by giving a different answer to this question.
Furthermore, there are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:
I do not know and do not see what is wholesome and what is unwholesome.
Because I do not know and do not see, if someone says, "This is wholesome" or "This is unwholesome," I then give rise to attachment.
From craving arises aversion; when there is craving and aversion, there is the arising of feeling.
Because I desire to extinguish feeling and because I dread feeling, I take it as my refuge, as my island, as my shelter, and as the ultimate path.
If someone were to raise such a question, one should answer thus:
"This matter is not so; this matter is truly not so; this matter is otherwise than not so; this matter is neither otherwise nor not otherwise."
This is called the third view.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, none are able to surpass these four views, wherein their questions differ and their answers differ.
There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are ignorant, deluded, and dull-witted.
Because they are ignorant, deluded, and dull-witted, when others question them, they answer merely by echoing those others:

"This matter is thus; it is not otherwise. This matter is real; it is not unreal. This matter is different; it is not otherwise. This matter is neither different nor not-different; it is not otherwise."
These are called the four views.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who provide various answers to various questions based on these [views], none can surpass these four views.
All those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who provide various answers to various questions concerning the past eons and past views are entirely included within these four views; none can surpass them.
Only the Buddha can know this locus of views—how they are maintained and how they are clung to—and he also knows their retribution.

What the Tathāgata knows exceeds even this; though he knows it, he does not cling to it. Because he does not cling, he attains tranquility. He knows the arising, the cessation, the gratification, the peril, and the escape regarding feeling. Through impartial contemplation, he attains liberation without remainder; therefore, he is called the Tathāgata.
This is the profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is another profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata.
What is this other profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light that enables the noble disciples to truly and impartially praise the Tathāgata?
As for those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, regarding the past eons and past views, claim that this world exists without cause—they all fall into two types of views.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eon (*pūrvakalpa*), maintain that this world exists without cause; among these two views, there is none that can surpass them.

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, regarding the views on the past and the beginning of the eon, maintain that things exist without a cause, such that no one can surpass these two views?
There are some sentient beings who are without perception and without sensation.
If those sentient beings give rise to perception, they immediately pass away and are reborn in this world.
As they gradually grow up, they shave off their hair and beards, leave the household life to don the dharma robes, practice the conduct of a brahmacārin, and enter the samādhi of concentrated mind.
Through the power of samādhi, he perceives the arising of original ideation and thinks:
"I originally did not exist; ideation arose spontaneously. This is how the world comes to be without a cause; this alone is real, and all else is false."
This is called the first view.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the past eon, maintain that things exist without a cause—within these two views, there is none who can surpass them.
There may be certain śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess swift analytical knowledge and are skilled in observation.
Having observed with their swift analytical knowledge, they declare:
"This world exists without a cause; this alone is true, and all else is false."
This is called the second view.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the past eon, maintain that this world exists without cause—within these two views, none can surpass them.
Regarding those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, concerning the past eons and past views, maintain that things exist without cause—they all fall within two views and none can transcend them.
Only the Buddha can know the basis of these views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.
Whatever various things those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas have spoken according to their own inclinations within their views concerning the past eons, they are all included within these eighteen views.
Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eon, speak in countless various ways according to their own inclinations,
they cannot surpass these eighteen views.
Only the Buddha can know this basis for views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.
Furthermore, there are other profound, subtle, and great dharmas of light, which only the noble disciples are able to praise the Tathāgata with.
What is this profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light, by which the noble disciples can praise the Tathāgata?

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas may say according to their own inclinations during the final age and with regard to final views—those countless and diverse assertions are all included within the forty-four views.
Regarding the various and countless assertions made at will concerning the final eon and final views, none can surpass these forty-four views.
For what reason do the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, in their various and countless assertions made at will concerning the final eon and final views, fail to surpass these forty-four views?

Whatever śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, during this final age, hold views regarding existence after death that maintain the doctrine of having perceptions—claiming that perception is the self and the world—all of them are included within these sixteen views.
Regarding the doctrine of existence after death held during the final age—the view that "perception is the self and the world"—among the sixteen views, there is none that surpasses it.

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, during the final age, hold this view of existence after death—that perception is the self and the world—and how is it that they all fall within these sixteen views with none able to transcend them?
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who maintain this doctrine:
"Form is the self; perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is the truth; all else is false."
This is called the first view.

Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on the views of the final age, maintain the doctrine of having perception—claiming that perception is the self and the world—none among these sixteen views can surpass it.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
"Form is not the self; perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is true; all else is false.
These are called the two views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Form and formlessness are the self; perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is the truth, and all else is false.
These are called the three views.
Again, there are those who say:
"Neither form nor formlessness is the self; perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is the truth, and all else is false."
These are called the four views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"The self is finite; perception is the world; after death I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, all else is false."
These are called the five views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
"The self is infinite; perception is the world; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the six views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The self is finite or infinite; perception is the world; after death I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, all else is false."
These are called the seven views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"The self is neither finite nor infinite; perception is the world; after death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the eight views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"I am exclusively happy; this is my world; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is the truth, and all else is false."
These are called the nine views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"I am exclusively suffering; this is the world; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, all else is false."
These are called the ten views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
"Pleasure and pain are the self; perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the eleven views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
"Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the self; perception is the world; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, all else is false."
These are called the twelve views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
"The perception [of self] is the self; the perception [of self] is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is true; all else is false."
These are called the thirteen views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"A certain perception is the self, and that perception is the world; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is the truth, and all else is false."
These are called the fourteen views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
"Limited perception is the self; perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the fifteen views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Infinite perception is the self; perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is the truth; all else is false."
These are called the sixteen views.

Among the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, during the final age, hold views regarding existence with perception, asserting "This is the self; this perception is the world," none can surpass these sixteen views.
Only the Buddha can know these bases of views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.
Furthermore, there are other profound, subtle, and great dharmas of light, which only the noble disciples can use to praise the Tathāgata.
What is this profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light by which the noble disciples can praise the Tathāgata?

Regarding the various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, in this final age and with final views, hold the doctrine of non-perception—claiming that non-perception is the self and is the world—they all fall within eight views.

In the final age, there will be those who hold views concerning non-perception (*asaṃjñika*), asserting that "non-perception is the self and this world. They are all included within the eight views and none can transcend them.
Furthermore, there may be śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who propound such a doctrine:
"Form is the self; non-perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is true; all else is false."
This is called the first view.

Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, due to views concerning the final eon, hold the doctrine of non-perception—claiming that this non-perception is the self and the world—none can surpass these eight views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Form is not the self; the state of non-perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is true; all else is false.
These are called the two views.
Again, there are those who say:
"Form and formlessness are the self; non-perception is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist. This alone is the truth; all else is false."
These are called the three views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The self is neither material nor immaterial; the world is non-perceptual; after death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the four views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"The self is finite; non-perception is the world; after death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, all else is false."
These are called the five views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
"The self is finite; this world is non-perceptual; after death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the six views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The self is finite or infinite; the world is non-perceptive; after death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the seven views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"The self is neither finite nor infinite; the world is non-perceptual; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the eight views.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on the views of the final age regarding non-perception, claim that non-perception is the self and the world; they are all included within these eight views.
Only a Buddha can know these bases of views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.
Furthermore, there are other profound, subtle, and great dharmas of light, which only the noble disciples are able to praise the Tathāgata with.
What is this profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light by which the noble disciples can praise the Tathāgata?

As for those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, due to views concerning the final age, maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—claiming that neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the self and the world—they are all included within the eight views.

Due to the views of the final age, there are those who hold the doctrine of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception," asserting that neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the self and the world; all such views are included within the eight [wrong] views and none can transcend them.
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine:
"Form is the self; the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the world; after death, I shall no longer exist. This alone is the truth, all else is false."
This is called the first view.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the final age and the final view, maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, asserting that "neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the self and the world. Among the eight views, there is none that can surpass this.
Again, there are those who say:
"Form is not the self; neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the world; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is the truth, and all else is false."
These are called the two views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"Form and formlessness are the self; the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the world. After death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the three views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:

"It is neither material nor immaterial that is the self; it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception that is the world. After the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the four views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"The self is finite; non-perception and non-non-perception is the world; after death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the five views.
Furthermore, there is one who says:
"I am neither finite nor infinite; non-perception and non-non-perception is the world; after the end of life, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, all else is false."
These are called the six views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
"The self is finite or infinite; non-perception and non-non-perception constitute the world; after death, I shall no longer exist; this alone is true, and all else is false."
These are called the seven views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:
