"The self is neither finite nor infinite; it is neither percipient nor non-percipient; this is the world. After death, I shall no longer exist. This alone is true, all else is false."
These are called the eight views.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on the views of the final age and the views of the final period, maintain the doctrine of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, asserting that "neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the self and the world. They all fall within these eight views; none can transcend them.
Only the Buddha can know this basis for views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.
Furthermore, there are other profound, subtle, and great dharmas of light, which only the noble disciples are able to praise the Tathāgata with.
What is this profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light by which the noble disciples can praise the Tathāgata?

There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the final age and the end of existence, maintain an annihilationist doctrine, asserting that sentient beings are utterly annihilated without remainder; they all fall within seven types of views.

Regarding the annihilationist view held during the final age and the final period of views, which asserts that sentient beings cease to exist without remainder—among the seven types of views, there is none that surpasses this.

For what reason do these śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, during the final age and the final period of views, hold the annihilationist view and assert that sentient beings are annihilated without remainder, such that among the seven views, there is none that can surpass it?
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a doctrine and maintain such a view:

"This body, composed of the four great elements, born of father and mother, nourished by milk, food, and clothing, and sustained by being massaged, rubbed, and protected—is impermanent and must inevitably return to destruction; this constitutes my annihilation."
This is called the first view.

Among the various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the final age, hold the doctrine of annihilationism and assert that sentient beings are annihilated, none can surpass these seven views.
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold this doctrine:
"This cannot be called annihilation; for me, the gods of the desire realm are annihilated without remainder—this is the limit of my annihilation."
These are called the two views.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who propound this theory:

"This is not called annihilation; rather, it is the annihilation of the form-body in the realm of form, wherein the sense faculties are complete. Up to this point, we say that the self is annihilated without remainder."
These are called the three views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:

"This is not called annihilation; rather, it is the annihilation in the sphere of infinite space within the formless realm. Up to this point, I declare that my annihilation is complete and without remainder."
These are called the four views.
Furthermore, there is another who says:

"This is not called annihilation; rather, it is the cessation of the sphere of infinite consciousness within the formless realm. Up to this point, I declare that my self is annihilated without remainder."
These are called the five views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:

"This is not called annihilation; it is the annihilation at the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception among the formless realms. Up to this point, I declare that my self is annihilated without remainder."
These are called the six views.
Furthermore, there are those who say:

"This is not called annihilation; rather, it is the cessation at the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception within the formless realm. Up to this point, I declare that my self is annihilated without remainder."
These are called the seven views.

On account of these, various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, during the final age and regarding final views, declare that this class of sentient beings will be annihilated without remainder; among these seven views, none can surpass them.
Only the Buddha can know these bases of views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.
Furthermore, there are other profound, subtle, and great dharmas of light, which only the noble disciples are able to praise in the Tathāgata by means of these dharmas.
What is this profound, subtle, and great Dharma-light, by which the noble disciples can praise the Tathāgata?

There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the final age and the final period, maintain a discourse on the existence of nirvāṇa in the present, asserting that sentient beings attain nirvāṇa while still existing in the present; they all fall within the five types of views.
Regarding the claim made during the final age and based on the final view that there is *nirvāṇa* in the present, among the five views there is none that can surpass it.

For what reason do those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, during the final age and based on the final view, claim that sentient beings have *nirvāṇa* in the present, such that among the five views there is none that can surpass it?
There are some śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold such a view and maintain such a doctrine:
"I shall exhaust myself in the indulgence of the five present sensual pleasures; by this alone I shall attain nirvāṇa in the present life."
This is called the first view.

Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on views concerning the final eon, claim that they attain nirvāṇa in the present life—namely, those who maintain the doctrine that sentient beings attain nirvāṇa in the present existence—none can surpass these five views.
Furthermore, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
"This is not called present nirvāṇa; there is another present nirvāṇa, subtle and supreme, which you do not know, but which I alone know."

"Just as one who, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna—up to this point, I say that I have attained nirvāṇa in the present life."
These are called the two views.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who speak as follows:
"This is not what is called nirvāṇa in the present; there is another nirvāṇa in the present that is subtle and supreme, which you do not know, but which I alone know."

Just as when one extinguishes directed thought and evaluation, with internal purity, confidence, and one-pointedness of mind, attaining the joy and happiness born of concentration that is without directed thought or evaluation, and accomplishing the practice of the second dhyāna—at this point, I declare that I have attained nirvana in the present.
These are called the three views.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
"This is not called nirvāṇa in the present life; there is another nirvāṇa in the present life that is subtle and supreme, which you do not know, but which I alone know."

Just as one, being detached from joy, dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body—just as the noble ones describe "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness"—one accomplishes the practice of the third dhyāna; up to this point, one attains nirvāṇa in the present life.
These are called the four views.
Furthermore, there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who say:
"This is not called nirvāṇa in the present life; there is another nirvāṇa in the present life that is subtle and supreme, which you do not know, but which I alone know."

When one is able to abandon pleasure and abandon pain, and first extinguishes sorrow and joy, attaining a state that is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity, and thus accomplishing the practice of the fourth dhyāna—up to this point, I say that I have attained nirvāṇa in the present life.
These are called the five views.
Among all śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on the final age and final views, maintain the doctrine that there is nirvāṇa in the present life, none can surpass these five views.
Only the Buddha can know these bases for views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.
All those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, based on the final age and final views, give rise to various opinions and speak according to their own inclinations, cannot surpass these forty-four views.
Only the Buddha can know these bases for views, up to and including liberation without remainder; therefore he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.

All śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eons and the past, and views concerning the future eons and the future, give rise to various views and speak according to their own inclinations—all of them are entirely contained within these sixty-two views.

Based on views concerning the past eons and the past, and views concerning the future eons and the future, various views arise and are expressed according to one's own inclinations; among these sixty-two views, there is none that can surpass them.
Only the Buddha can know the basis of these views, and because he has attained liberation without remainder, he is called the Tathāgata, as explained above.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on their views regarding the past eon, maintain the doctrine of eternalism, asserting that the self and the world are eternal. Regarding this, those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas produce various forms of knowledge, namely: different faiths, different desires, different learning, different conditions, different insights, different views, different concentrations, and different tolerances.
From this, knowledge arises: that through giving one receives a name, and so on up to the present nirvāṇa, it is likewise.

As for those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who hold the doctrine of eternalism, claiming that the world is eternal—they receive sensation, and conditioned by sensation, craving arises; yet they do not realize their own defiled attachment. Subjugated by craving, they are overcome by craving, and so on up to the present nirvāṇa, it is likewise.

Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eon, claim that the world is eternal; because they rely on contact as their condition, it is impossible for them to establish such a thesis apart from the condition of contact, and this remains the case even regarding present nirvāṇa.
All śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, based on views concerning the past eons and the future eons, each speak according to their own perspectives; all of these are included within the sixty-two views.
Each speaks according to what they perceive, and all rely upon these [views], with none able to transcend them.
It is like a fisherman who covers a small pond with a fine net; you should know that all aquatic creatures within the pond will enter the net, leaving no place to escape.

The various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are also like this; based on views concerning the past eons and the past, and views concerning the future eons and the future, all their various teachings are entirely contained within the sixty-two views and none can transcend them. These are called the sixty-two views.

These are the afflictions and fetters that bind sentient beings, causing them to undergo birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress—the accumulation of all sufferings—and preventing them from attaining liberation; thus ends the section on "That Which Is Not Subject to Inquiry."
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty; *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-one.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśa during the Yao Qin dynasty.

Translated by Dharmagupta and others. Section on Compendium and Correspondence (Saṃgraha-saṃprayukta-varga), Part One: Chapter on Compendium (Saṃgraha-paṭala). One should know that regarding all phenomena—those that are included and those that are not included—if one establishes the categories of inclusion (saṃgraha-mukha), it becomes clear:

the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana) include all phenomena; the aggregates, elements, and bases do not include all phenomena; the aggregates, elements, and bases include a portion of all phenomena as they actually exist; and the aggregates, elements, and bases do not include a portion of all phenomena as they actually exist. Furthermore, a nature includes itself, while a nature does not include other natures; a nature is bound to itself, while a nature is not bound to other natures. Thus, there is inclusion and non-inclusion, and there is neither inclusion nor non-inclusion.

Regarding the categories of inclusion (*saṃgraha-mukha*): these refer to phenomena associated with the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and those not associated with the truth of suffering; likewise, up to phenomena associated with the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*) and those not associated with the truth of the path; phenomena associated with the noble truths (*ārya-satya*) and those not associated with the noble truths; phenomena that are faculties (*indriya*) and those that are not faculties; phenomena that are faculties associated with the truth of suffering and those that are not faculties associated with the truth of suffering; likewise, up to phenomena that are faculties associated with the truth of the path and those that are not faculties associated with the truth of the path; phenomena that are faculties associated with the noble truths and those that are not faculties associated with the noble truths; phenomena that are non-faculties associated with the truth of suffering and those that are non-faculties not associated with the truth of suffering; likewise, up to phenomena that are non-faculties associated with the truth of the path and those that are non-faculties not associated with the truth of the path; and phenomena that are non-faculties associated with the noble truths and those that are non-faculties not associated with the noble truths.

The dharma of the eye-base and the dharma that is not the eye-base, up to the dharma of the mind-base and the dharma that is not the mind-base; the dharma of the form-base and the dharma that is not the form-base, up to the dharma of the mental-object-base and the dharma that is not the mental-object-base;

the dharma of feeling and the dharma that is not feeling, the dharma of perception and the dharma that is not perception, the dharma of volition and the dharma that is not volition, the dharma of contact and the dharma that is not contact, the dharma of attention and the dharma that is not attention, the dharma of applied thought and the dharma that is not applied thought, the dharma of sustained thought and the dharma that is not sustained thought, the dharma of view and the dharma that is not view, the dharma of wisdom and the dharma that is not wisdom, and the dharma of liberation and the dharma that is not liberation.

The dharma of non-greed is not the dharma of non-greed; the dharma of non-hatred is not the dharma of non-hatred; the dharma of non-delusion is not the dharma of non-delusion; the dharma of confidence is not the dharma of confidence; the dharma of remorse is not the dharma of remorse; the dharma of non-remorse is not the dharma of non-remorse; the dharma of gladness is not the dharma of gladness; the dharma of joy is not the dharma of joy; the dharma of mental exertion is not the dharma of mental exertion; the dharma of mental tranquility is not the dharma of mental tranquility; the dharma of faith is not the dharma of faith; the dharma of desire is not the dharma of desire; the dharma of heedfulness is not the dharma of heedfulness; the dharma of mindfulness is not the dharma of mindfulness; the dharma of concentration is not the dharma of concentration; the dharma of equanimity of mind is not the dharma of equanimity of mind; the dharma of doubt is not the dharma of doubt; the dharma of fear is not the dharma of fear.

Dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of affliction and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of affliction; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of views and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of views; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of doubt and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of doubt; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of attachment to rules and observances and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of attachment to rules and observances; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of craving and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of craving; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of malice and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of malice; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of envy and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of envy; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of avarice and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of avarice; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of ignorance and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of ignorance; dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of pride and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of pride;

dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of restlessness and dharmas not associated with the underlying tendency of restlessness; dharmas of birth and dharmas not of birth; dharmas of aging and dharmas not of aging; dharmas of death and dharmas not of death; dharmas of life and dharmas not of life; dharmas of affliction and dharmas not of affliction.

The dharma of the attainment of non-perception is not the dharma of the attainment of non-perception; the dharma of the attainment of cessation is not the dharma of the attainment of cessation; the dharma of attaining the fruits is not the dharma of attaining the fruits; the dharma of morality is not the dharma of morality; the dharma of non-morality is not the dharma of non-morality; the dharma of the exertion of the tainted body is not the dharma of the exertion of the tainted body; the dharma of the removal of the tainted body is not the dharma of the removal of the tainted body.

The dharma of right speech and the dharma of non-right speech; the dharma of right action and the dharma of non-right action; the dharma of right livelihood and the dharma of non-right livelihood; the dharma of right bodily effort and the dharma of non-right bodily effort; the dharma of right bodily removal and the dharma of non-right bodily removal; the dharma of the cessation through wisdom and the dharma of non-cessation through wisdom; the dharma of non-cessation through wisdom and the dharma of non-non-cessation through wisdom; the determinate dharma and the indeterminate dharma; the dharma of the stability of dharmas and the dharma of the instability of dharmas; the dharma of conditions and the dharma of non-conditions; the dharma of the sphere of infinite space and the dharma of non-infinite space, up to the dharma of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the dharma of non-neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The dharma of the eye-element and the non-dharma of the eye-element, up to the dharma of the dharma-element and the non-dharma of the dharma-element;
the dharma of the aggregate of form and the non-dharma of the aggregate of form, up to the dharma of the aggregate of consciousness and the non-dharma of the aggregate of consciousness.

The phenomenon of the noble truth of suffering is not the phenomenon of the noble truth of suffering; likewise, up to the phenomenon of the noble truth of the path is not the phenomenon of the noble truth of the path.

The phenomenon of the faculty of the eye is not the phenomenon of the faculty of the eye; likewise, up to the phenomenon of the faculty of one who has already known is not the phenomenon of the faculty of one who has already known.

The factor of the awakening-factor of mindfulness and the factor that is not the awakening-factor of mindfulness, up to the factor of the awakening-factor of equanimity and the factor that is not the awakening-factor of equanimity.

The factor of the unwholesome root of greed and the factor that is not the unwholesome root of greed, up to the factor of the unwholesome root of delusion and the factor that is not the unwholesome root of delusion.

The wholesome root of non-attachment is not a phenomenon that is not the wholesome root of non-attachment; this extends up to the wholesome root of non-delusion being not a phenomenon that is not the wholesome root of non-delusion.
The great element of earth is not a phenomenon that is not the great element of earth; this extends up to the great element of wind being not a phenomenon that is not the great element of wind.

The dharma of the precept against taking life is not the dharma of the precept against taking life; likewise, up to the dharma of abstaining from intoxicants and heedlessness is not the dharma of abstaining from intoxicants and heedlessness.
Form-dharmas are not non-form-dharmas, and so on, up to past, future, and present dharmas are not past, future, and present dharmas.
What are called the dharmas bound to the Truth of Suffering?
Excluding craving, all other conditioned dharmas that are not noble are called dharmas bound to the truth of suffering.
What are called dharmas not bound to the truth of suffering?
Craving, as well as noble and non-noble unconditioned dharmas, are called dharmas not bound to the truth of suffering.
What are the phenomena associated with the truth of origination?
Craving is called the phenomenon associated with the truth of origination.
What are the phenomena not associated with the truth of origination?
Excluding craving, if there are other phenomena, these are called phenomena not bound to the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
What are phenomena bound to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*)?
The extinction through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is called a phenomenon bound to the truth of cessation.
What are the phenomena not bound by the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*)?
With the exception of the cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), all other phenomena are called phenomena not bound by the truth of cessation.
What are the phenomena bound by the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*)?
The Eightfold Noble Path is called the dharma bound to the Truth of the Path.
What is meant by dharmas not bound to the Truth of the Path?
With the exception of the Eightfold Noble Path, whatever other dharmas there may be, these are called dharmas not bound to the Truth of the Path.
What are the phenomena associated with the Noble Truths?
Non-noble conditioned phenomena—namely, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—are called phenomena associated with the Noble Truths.
What are the phenomena not associated with the Noble Truths?

Excluding the truths of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, whatever other noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) or non-noble unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena there may be, these are called the dharmas not bound to the noble truths.
What are called the faculty dharmas (*indriyadharma*)?
Those that are neither noble faculties nor noble conditioned phenomena are called faculty phenomena (*indriya-dharma*).
What are called non-faculty phenomena?
Those that are neither noble nor faculties, as well as noble unconditioned phenomena, are called non-faculty phenomena (*anindriya-dharma*).
What are the faculties bound to the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya-saṃyukta-indriya*)?
If a faculty is non-noble (*anārya*), it is called a faculty bound to the truth of suffering.
What are the faculties not bound to the truth of suffering?
If the faculties are noble, these are called the faculties that are not bound by the truth of suffering.
What are the faculties bound by the truth of origination?
There are no faculties bound by the truth of origination.
What are the faculties bound by the truth of origination?
All faculties are called the faculties not bound by the truth of origination.
What are the faculties bound by the truth of cessation?
There are no faculties bound to the truth of cessation.
What are the faculties not bound to the truth of cessation?
All faculties are called the faculties not bound to the truth of cessation.
What are the factors associated with the truth of the path that are faculties?
The Noble Eightfold Path; these are called the factors associated with the truth of the path that are faculties.
What are the factors not associated with the truth of the path that are faculties?
Excluding the Eightfold Noble Path, any other faculties are called the factors of the faculties not bound to the Truth of the Path.
What are the factors of the faculties bound to the Noble Truths?
Those faculties that are not non-bound, as well as the remaining eightfold Noble Path, are called the factors of the faculties bound to the Noble Truths.
What are the faculties not bound by the Noble Truths?
With the exception of the Eightfold Noble Path, any other noble faculties are called the faculties not bound by the Noble Truths.
What are the non-faculty phenomena associated with the truth of suffering?
Excluding craving, any other non-faculty phenomena that are conditioned non-faculties are called non-faculty phenomena associated with the truth of suffering.
What is meant by phenomena that are neither bound to the Truth of Suffering nor are faculties?
Craving and all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)—these are called phenomena that are neither bound to the Truth of Suffering nor are faculties.
What is meant by phenomena that are bound to the Truth of Origination but are not faculties?
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is called a non-root dharma associated with the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
What is meant by a non-root dharma not associated with the truth of origination?
With the exception of craving, whatever other non-roots there may be—these are called non-root dharmas not associated with the truth of origination.
What is meant by "dharmas associated with the truth of cessation that are not faculties"?
The extinction through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is called dharmas associated with the truth of cessation that are not faculties.
What is meant by "dharmas not associated with the truth of cessation that are not faculties"?

Excluding the cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), if there are other factors that are not faculties (*indriya*), these are called non-faculty factors bound to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
What are non-faculty factors bound to the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*)?
There are no such non-faculty factors bound to the truth of the path.
What is meant by "dharmas not bound to the Truth of the Path and not being faculties"?
All that are not faculties are called dharmas not bound to the Truth of the Path and not being faculties.
What is meant by "dharmas bound to the Noble Truths and not being faculties"?
If they are neither noble nor faculties, yet are suffering, its origin, or its cessation, these are called the noble truths that are bound to non-faculty phenomena.
What are the phenomena that are neither bound to the noble truths nor are faculties?
Excluding the Noble Truths of Suffering, Origin, and Cessation, if there are other factors that are not faculties (*indriya*), these are called non-faculty factors bound by the Noble Truths.
What is the eye-base factor (*cakṣur-āyatana-dharma*)? The eye-base is called the eye-base factor.
What is meant by "dharmas that are not the eye-base"?
With the exception of the eye-faculty, any other dharmas are called "dharmas that are not the eye-base.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
What is the dharma of the form base (rūpāyatana)?
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is called the dharma of the form base.
What is the dharma that is not the form base?
Excluding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), if there are other phenomena (*dharma*), these are called non-form entrance phenomena (*arūpāyatana-dharma*).
It is the same for the sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental-object entrances (*śabda-, gandha-, rasa-, spraṣṭavya-, dharmāyatana*).
What are called feeling phenomena (*vedanā-dharma*)?
If it is that which is experienced by the mind, this is called "dharma experienced.
What is meant by "dharma not experienced"?
With the exception of what is experienced, if there are other dharmas, these are called "dharmas not experienced."
What is meant by the perception of phenomena?
If there is conceptualization and recollective conceptualization, this is called the perception of phenomena.
What is meant by the non-perception of phenomena?
Excluding perception, if there are other dharmas, these are called non-perception dharmas.
What are called volition dharmas?
If there is volition or right volition, these are called volition dharmas.
What is meant by "non-thought phenomena" (*acetanadharma*)?
With the exception of thought (*cetanā*), any other phenomena are called non-thought phenomena.
What is meant by "contact phenomena" (*sparśadharma*)?
The six contacts are called contact-dharmas.
What are non-contact dharmas?
With the exception of contact, whatever other dharmas there are are called non-contact dharmas.
What is meant by "contemplating phenomena" (*dharma*)?
If one calculates, discriminates, deliberates, and recollects, this is called contemplating phenomena.
What is meant by "not contemplating phenomena"?
Excluding volition, any other phenomena are called non-volitional phenomena.
What are called awakening phenomena?
If there is awakening through recollective conceptualization, these are called awakening phenomena.
What are called non-consciousness factors?
With the exception of consciousness, whatever other factors there are—these are called non-consciousness factors.
What are called contemplation factors?
If the mind’s activities, subtle activities, and conforming activities are present, this is called the contemplation of dharmas (*dharmānupaśyanā*).
What is meant by that which is not the contemplation of dharmas?
With the exception of contemplation, if there are other dharmas, these are called that which is not the contemplation of dharmas.
What is meant by "seeing the Dharma"?
Seeing wisdom free from delusion, seeing the latent tendencies of views and the latent tendencies of the path of precepts—this is called seeing the Dharma.
What is meant by "not seeing the Dharma"?
Excluding views, if there are other dharmas, these are called non-view dharmas.
The same applies to wisdom dharmas.
What are called liberation dharmas?
If there is liberation, further liberation, and ultimate liberation, these are called the factors of liberation (*vimokṣa-dharma*).
What are the non-factors of liberation?
With the exception of the factors of liberation, whatever other phenomena (*dharma*) there may be, these are called the non-factors of liberation.
What is meant by the dharma of non-attachment?
If a dharma is not characterized by longing, it is called the dharma of non-attachment.
What is meant by that which is not the dharma of non-attachment?
Excluding non-attachment, any other phenomena are called phenomena that are not non-attachment.
What are called phenomena of non-ill will?
If there is no malice, these are called phenomena of non-ill will.
What is meant by "states that are not non-ill-will"?
With the exception of non-ill-will, any other states are called "states that are not non-ill-will.
What is meant by "states that are non-delusion"?
Wholesome view, wholesome wisdom, and non-delusion—these are called the factors of non-delusion (*amoha-dharma*).
What are the factors that are not non-delusion?
With the exception of non-delusion, whatever other factors there may be—these are called the factors that are not non-delusion.
What is meant by the factors conducive to faith (*śraddhānulomika-dharma*)?
Right faith, the faculty of faith, and conformity with faith—these are called the factors conducive to faith.
What is meant by the factors not conducive to faith?
Apart from the factors conducive to faith (*śraddhā*), whatever other dharmas there are, these are called non-conducive-to-faith dharmas.
What are called dharmas of remorse (*kaukṛtya*)?
Having performed what should not be done or failed to do what should be done, if there is a mind of regret characterized by burning distress, these are called dharmas of remorse.
What is meant by the state of being without remorse?
With the exception of remorse, any other phenomena are called the state of being without remorse.
What is meant by the state of not being remorse?

Having performed what should not be done and failed to perform what should have been done, if one feels no remorse and the mind is not consumed by feverish distress, this is called a state that is not subject to regret.
What is meant by a state that is not "without regret"?
Except for remorse, if it is any other dharma, this is called a dharma that is not "without remorse.
What is meant by the "dharma of joy"?
If the mind is joyful and glad, this is called the dharma of joy.
What is meant by "non-delighting dharmas"?
With the exception of delighting dharmas, whatever other dharmas there may be are called non-delighting dharmas.
What is meant by "joyful dharmas"?
If there is joy, exultation, intense exultation, and gladness of mind, this is called the dharma of joy (*prāmodya-dharma*).
What is meant by the non-dharma of joy?
Any other dharmas apart from the dharma of joy are called the non-dharma of joy.
What is the mental factor of exertion?
If the mind is initiated, manifested, and transcends [its state], this is called the mental factor of exertion.
What is not the mental factor of exertion?
Excluding mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), any other phenomena are called non-mental-exertion phenomena (*na-cittavīrya-dharma*).
What are called mind-purifying phenomena (*citta-vodāniya-dharma*)?
If there is mental joy, mental pliancy, mental lightness, and mental flexibility, these are called mind-purifying phenomena.
What is meant by "dharmas not to be abandoned by the mind"?
Any dharma other than those to be abandoned by the mind is called a dharma not to be abandoned by the mind.
What is meant by "dharma of faith"?
If one enters into faith with conviction, this is called "dharmas of faith.
What are called "non-dharmas of faith"?
Apart from the dharmas of faith, whatever other dharmas there may be, these are called "non-dharmas of faith."
What is meant by "dharmas of desire"?
If one hopes to act out of desire, these are called dharmas of desire.
What is meant by "non-dharmas of desire"?
Excluding desire, any other phenomena are called non-desire phenomena.
What are called non-negligence phenomena?
If the mind is guarded, these are called non-negligence phenomena.
What is meant by the factors that are not non-heedfulness?
With the exception of non-heedfulness, any other factors are called the factors that are not non-heedfulness.
What is meant by the factor of mindfulness?
If one recollects and keeps in mind, this is called mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmānusmṛti*).
What is meant by non-mindfulness of phenomena?
Apart from mindfulness, whatever other phenomena there may be, these are called non-mindfulness of phenomena.
What is meant by the dharma of concentration?
If the mind is single-pointed, this is called the dharma of concentration.
What is meant by the dharma that is not concentration?
Excluding concentration (*samādhi*), any other phenomena are called non-concentrated phenomena (*asamāhita-dharma*).
What are called mental phenomena of equanimity (*upekṣā-dharma*)?
If there is equanimity, superior equanimity, conformable equanimity, mental non-action (*akriyā*), and non-acceptance (*anupādāna*), these are called mental phenomena of equanimity.
What are the factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktadharma*)?
With the exception of those factors associated with mind, all other factors are called factors dissociated from mind.
What are the factors associated with doubt (*vicikitsādharmas*)?
If one does not reach the state where the afflictions to be abandoned are eliminated, this is called "doubt regarding phenomena" (*vicikitsā-dharma*).
What is meant by "not doubt regarding phenomena"?
With the exception of doubt, any other phenomena are called "not doubt regarding phenomena."
What is called the "fearful dharma"?
That which is startled and terrified is called the fearful dharma.
What is called the "non-fearful dharma"?
Excluding fear, if it is any other dharma, this is called a non-fear-inducing dharma.
What are the dharmas that are the underlying tendencies of affliction?
If they are the ten underlying tendencies, these are called the dharmas that are the underlying tendencies of affliction.
What are the factors that are not the underlying tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*)?
With the exception of the ten underlying tendencies, all other factors are called the factors that are not the underlying tendencies of affliction.
What are the factors of the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*)?
Unwholesome views and unwholesome wisdom—specifically those that are part of the proclivity of views—are called the phenomena of the proclivity of views (*dṛṣṭy-āsrava*).
What are the phenomena that are not the proclivity of views?
With the exception of the proclivity of views, all other phenomena are called the phenomena that are not the proclivity of views.
What are the phenomena associated with the latent tendency of doubt?
As explained above.
What are the phenomena not associated with the latent tendency of doubt?
The fetter of doubt and any other phenomena are called non-fetter-of-doubt phenomena.
What are called fetters of the path of precepts?
Unwholesome views and unwholesome wisdom, as well as the precepts that constitute the path of precepts, are called fetters of the path of precepts.
What are the phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of non-virtuous conduct?

With the exception of the phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of virtuous conduct, all other phenomena are called phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of non-virtuous conduct.
What are the phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of craving?
Sensual desire is called the underlying tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇā-anuśaya*).
What are the phenomena that are not the underlying tendency of craving?
With the exception of the underlying tendency of craving, whatever other phenomena there may be are called the phenomena that are not the underlying tendency of craving.
What are the phenomena associated with the latent tendency of aversion?
Harmfulness is called the phenomenon associated with the latent tendency of aversion.
What are the phenomena not associated with the latent tendency of aversion?
Those factors other than the underlying tendency of aversion are called factors that are not the underlying tendency of aversion.
What are the factors of the underlying tendency of envy?

When another person obtains gain, offerings, honor, or respect, one feels resentment toward them, intense resentment, and ultimate resentment; these are called the factors of the underlying tendency of envy.
What are phenomena not associated with the underlying tendency of envy?
With the exception of the underlying tendency of envy, any other phenomena are called phenomena not associated with the underlying tendency of envy.
What are phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of stinginess?
If one does not give or bestow material wealth, and the mind is stingy and refuses to let go, this is called the dharma of the latent tendency of stinginess (*mātsarya-anuśaya*).
What is meant by the dharma that is not the latent tendency of stinginess?
With the exception of the latent tendency of stinginess, all other dharmas are called the dharma that is not the latent tendency of stinginess.
What is meant by the phenomena of the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*)?
Delusion, the unwholesome root—this is called the phenomenon of the underlying tendency of ignorance.
What is meant by the phenomena that are not the underlying tendency of ignorance?
Those phenomena that exclude the underlying tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) are called non-ignorance-underlying-tendency phenomena.
What are called pride-underlying-tendency phenomena?
Those by which one exalts oneself through conceit are called pride-underlying-tendency phenomena.
What are the factors not associated with the underlying tendency of pride?
With the exception of the underlying tendency of pride, any other factors are called the factors not associated with the underlying tendency of pride.
What are the factors associated with restlessness?

If there is restlessness, excessive restlessness, ultimate restlessness, agitation, lack of stability, flightiness, and lack of mental tranquility, these are called the phenomena of the underlying tendency toward restlessness (*uddhacca-anuśaya-dharma*).
What are the phenomena that are not the underlying tendency toward restlessness?
Excluding the underlying tendency of restlessness, any other phenomena are called non-restless-underlying-tendency phenomena.
What are called phenomena of arising?
Any aggregates that emerge are called phenomena of arising.
What are non-arising phenomena?
With the exception of arising, whatever other phenomena there are are called non-arising phenomena.
What are aging phenomena?
If the aggregates (skandhas) decay, this is called the phenomenon of aging.
What is meant by the phenomenon that is not aging?
With the exception of aging, if there are other phenomena, these are called the phenomena that are not aging.
What is called the nature of death?
The disintegration of the aggregates (skandhas) is called the nature of death.
What is called the nature that is not death?
Excluding death, any other phenomena are called non-death phenomena.
What are called life-phenomena?
The dwelling of sentient beings is called life-phenomena.
What is meant by "phenomena that are not life" (*ajīvadharma*)?
With the exception of life, if there are other phenomena, these are called phenomena that are not life.
What is meant by "phenomena that are fetters of affliction" (*kleśasaṃyojanadharma*)?
The ten fetters (saṃyojana) are called the phenomena of the fetters of affliction (kleśa-saṃyojana-dharma). What are the phenomena that are not the fetters of affliction?
With the exception of the fetters, any other phenomena are called the phenomena that are not the fetters of affliction.
What is the state of non-conceptual absorption (asaṃjñi-samāpatti)?

It is the entry into meditative concentration wherein the mind and mental factors are stilled, occurring apart from the Heaven of the Fruitful (bṛhatphala). This is called the state of non-conceptual absorption.
What is meant by "dharmas that are not the attainment of non-conceptualization" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*)?
With the exception of the attainment of non-conceptualization, all other dharmas are called "dharmas that are not the attainment of non-conceptualization.
What is meant by "dharmas of attaining the fruit"?
If one realizes the fruit, this is called the dharma of attaining the fruit.
What is meant by the dharma of not attaining the fruit?
With the exception of the attainment of the fruit, whatever other dharmas there may be are called the dharma of not attaining the fruit.
What is the dharma of the attainment of cessation?

It is the supramundane dharma in which the mind and mental factors are stilled after one has transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the dharma of the attainment of cessation.
What is meant by "dharmas other than the attainment of cessation"?
With the exception of the attainment of cessation, any other dharmas are called "dharmas other than the attainment of cessation.
What is meant by "non-precept dharmas"?
The seven kinds of non-precepts are called the dharma of non-precepts.
What is meant by the dharma of absence of precepts?
Any other dharma, excluding the dharma of non-precepts, is called the dharma of absence of precepts.
What is meant by the dharma of precepts?
The seven types of precepts are called the dharma of precepts.
What is meant by the absence of the dharma of precepts?
Excluding the precepts, if there are other dharmas, these are called the dharma of non-precept.
What is meant by the dharma of exertion of the tainted body?
If one initiates, manifests, and transcends by means of the tainted body, this is called the dharma of exertion of the tainted body.
What is meant by "factors of progress for the body that are not with-outflows" (anāsrava)?
With the exception of the factors of progress for the body that are with-outflows, any other factors are called "factors of progress for the body that are not with-outflows.
What is meant by "factors of removal for the body that are with-outflows"?

If there is bodily pleasure, bodily composure, bodily lightness, bodily pliancy, and bodily tranquility that are with outflows (*sāsrava*), these are called the factors for the removal of the body with outflows.
What are the factors for the removal of the body that are not with outflows?

Excluding those phenomena that are to be abandoned by the removal of the outflows from the body, any remaining phenomena are called "phenomena not to be abandoned by the removal of the outflows from the body.
What are the phenomena of right speech?

Those phenomena which involve distancing oneself from and taking no pleasure in the four faults of speech, and which consist of guarding and practicing restraint—these are called the phenomena of right speech.
What is meant by the factor of wrong speech?
With the exception of right speech, any other factors are called the factor of wrong speech.
What is meant by the factor of right action?
If one distances oneself from the three evils of the body, takes no pleasure in them, and practices their guarding and restraint, this is called the dharma of right action (*samyak-karmānta*).
What is meant by the dharma of non-right action?
Any other dharmas apart from right action are called the dharma of non-right action.
What is the dharma of right livelihood?

It is the abstention from evil conduct of body and speech; furthermore, not engaging in nor taking pleasure in other forms of wrong livelihood, but rather guarding and maintaining one's conduct—this is called the dharma of right livelihood.
What is meant by the dharma of non-right livelihood?
Any dharma other than right livelihood is called the dharma of non-right livelihood.
What is meant by the dharma of right bodily exertion?
If the untainted body initiates, manifests, and transcends, this is called the factor of right bodily exertion (*samyak-kāya-vyāyāma*).
What is meant by the factor that is not right bodily exertion?
With the exception of right bodily exertion, any other factors are called the factor that is not right bodily exertion.
What is called the method for rectifying the body and removing afflictions?
It is the untainted bodily pleasure, bodily composure, bodily lightness, bodily pliancy, and bodily removal of afflictions; this is called the method for rectifying the body and removing afflictions.
What is meant by "dharmas that are not the right abandonment of the body"?
Any dharmas other than the right abandonment of the body are called "dharmas that are not the right abandonment of the body.
What is meant by "dharmas whose cessation is through wisdom"?
If all causes are exhausted without remainder, this is called the dharma of the extinction through wisdom as condition (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What is meant by the dharma of extinction not through wisdom as condition (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
Any other dharmas, excluding those that are extinction through wisdom as condition, are called the dharma of extinction not through wisdom as condition.
What is meant by the phenomenon of cessation not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)?
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) do not arise because their various conditions do not converge, this is called the phenomenon of cessation not through wisdom.
What is meant by the phenomenon that is not cessation not through wisdom?
Except for those phenomena conditioned by the exhaustion of wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), all other phenomena are called non-non-phenomena-conditioned-by-the-exhaustion-of-wisdom.
What are called determined phenomena?
Those phenomena that are fixed are called determined phenomena.
What is meant by "non-determined phenomena"?
With the exception of determined phenomena, all other phenomena are called non-determined phenomena.
What is meant by "the stability of phenomena" (dharma-sthititā)?

Excluding the conditionality of suchness, if there are other phenomena that are such, unchanging, immutable, not different [from themselves], permanent phenomena, real phenomena, the stability of phenomena, and the fixed nature of phenomena that are not conditions—this is called the "dharma-stability dharma" (dhammaṭṭhiti-dhamma).
What is meant by "dharmas that do not abide in dharmas"?
With the exception of dharmas that abide in dharmas, any other dharmas are called "dharmas that do not abide in dharmas.
What is meant by "conditioned dharmas"?
If something takes suchness as its object, it is called a "conditioned dharma" (pratyayadharma).
What is meant by a "non-conditioned dharma" (apratyayadharma)?
Any dharma other than that which is conditioned is called a non-conditioned dharma.
What is the dharma of the sphere of empty space?
The sphere of empty space is of two kinds: either conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is the conditioned sphere of empty space?
Regarding the concentration of the sphere of infinite space and birth in the sphere of infinite space:
what is meant by the concentration of the sphere of infinite space?

If a bhikṣu, having transcended all perceptions of form, extinguished perceptions of sensory resistance, and does not attend to perceptions of diversity, accomplishes the practice of the sphere of infinite space, this is called the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
What is birth in the sphere of infinite space?

If, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, one receives the fourfold aggregates of self—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—in the celestial realm of the sphere of infinite space, this is called birth in the sphere of infinite space.
Thus, the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space and birth in the sphere of infinite space are called the conditioned sphere of infinite space.
What is the unconditioned sphere of infinite space?
If one abandons the sphere of infinite space through wisdom, this is called the unconditioned sphere of infinite space.
The same applies to the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is called the dharma of the eye-element?
The eye-base; this is termed the dharma of the eye-element.
What is meant by "dharmas that are not the eye-element"?
With the exception of the eye-element, any other dharmas are called "dharmas that are not the eye-element.
This applies likewise up to the consciousness-element.
What are the phenomena of the aggregate of form?
Those which are the ten bases of form and the form included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)—these are called the phenomena of the aggregate of form.
What are the phenomena that are not the aggregate of form?
Excluding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), whatever other phenomena (*dharma*) there may be, these are called non-form-aggregate phenomena.
What are called the phenomena of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*)?
The six types of feeling—these are called the phenomena of the aggregate of feeling.
What are the phenomena that are not the aggregate of feeling?
With the exception of the aggregate of feeling, any other phenomena are called phenomena that are not the aggregate of feeling.
What are the phenomena that are the aggregate of perception?
If there are six types of perception, these are called the phenomena of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
What are the phenomena that are not the aggregate of perception?
With the exception of the phenomena of the aggregate of perception, whatever other phenomena there may be, these are called the phenomena that are not the aggregate of perception.
What are the phenomena of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)?
The six types of volition (*cetanā*); these are called the phenomena of the aggregate of formations.
What are the phenomena that are not the aggregate of formations?
Excluding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), any other phenomena are called non-formations-aggregate phenomena.
What are called consciousness-aggregate phenomena?
The six consciousnesses are called consciousness-aggregate phenomena.
What are the phenomena that are not the aggregate of consciousness?
With the exception of the aggregate of consciousness, whatever other phenomena there are—these are called the phenomena that are not the aggregate of consciousness.
What are the phenomena of the Noble Truth of Suffering?
The eight kinds of suffering are called the noble truth of suffering.
What is meant by that which is not the noble truth of suffering?
Any phenomena other than the noble truth of suffering are called that which is not the noble truth of suffering.
What is the Dharma of the Noble Truth of Origination?
It refers to craving, which is accompanied by further desire, passion, delight, and attachment; this is called the Dharma of the Noble Truth of Origination.
What is the Dharma that is not the Noble Truth of Origination?
Excluding the noble truth of the origin, any other phenomena are called non-origin-noble-truth phenomena.
What are called cessation-noble-truth phenomena?
The departure from craving, relinquishment, renunciation, liberation, and its cessation without remainder—these are called cessation-noble-truth phenomena.
What is meant by the phenomena that are not the noble truth of cessation?
With the exception of the noble truth of cessation, any other phenomena are called phenomena that are not the noble truth of cessation.
What is meant by the phenomena that are the noble truth of the path?
The Noble Eightfold Path is called the Dharma of the Noble Truth of the Path.
What is meant by the Dharma that is not the Noble Truth of the Path?
Any other dharmas besides the Noble Eightfold Path are called the Dharma that is not the Noble Truth of the Path.
What is meant by the phenomena of the eye-faculty?
The eye-base; this is called the phenomena of the eye-faculty.
What is meant by phenomena that are not the eye-faculty?
Excluding the eye faculty, any other phenomena are called non-eye-faculty phenomena.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body faculties.
What are called female-faculty phenomena?
The female body, femininity, female characteristics, and female form—these are called the phenomena of the female faculty (*strīndriya*).
What are called the phenomena that are not the female faculty?
With the exception of the female faculty, any other phenomena are called the phenomena that are not the female faculty.
What is the phenomenon of the male faculty?
The male body, male nature, male characteristics, and male form—these are called the phenomenon of the male faculty.
What is the phenomenon that is not the male faculty?
Excluding the male faculty, if it is any other dharma, this is called a non-male-faculty dharma.
What is meant by the life-faculty dharma?
If it is vitality (*āyus*), this is called the life-faculty dharma.
What is meant by dharmas that are not the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
With the exception of the life-faculty, whatever other dharmas there may be—these are called dharmas that are not the life-faculty.
What is meant by the dharma of the pleasure-faculty (*sukhendriya*)?
The faculty of pleasure within the aggregate of feeling is called the dharma of the faculty of pleasure.
What is meant by the dharma that is not the faculty of pleasure?
Any other dharmas, excluding the faculty of pleasure, are called the dharma that is not the faculty of pleasure.
The faculty of suffering, the faculty of grief, the faculty of joy, and the faculty of equanimity are also like this.
What is called the mental faculty (manendriya)?
The sphere of mind (manāyatana); this is called the mental faculty.
What are the factors that are not the faculty of mind?
With the exception of the faculty of mind, whatever other factors there are—these are called the factors that are not the faculty of mind.
What are the factors of the faculty of faith?
Noble faith, noble compliant faith, and the faculty of faith—these are called the phenomena of the faculty of faith.
What are the phenomena that are not the faculty of faith?
With the exception of the faculty of faith, whatever other phenomena there may be—these are called the phenomena that are not the faculty of faith.
What are the factors of the faculty of energy?
The noble mind’s energy, right bodily energy, and the faculty of energy—these are called the factors of the faculty of energy.
What are the factors that are not the faculty of energy?
Excluding the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), any other phenomena are called non-faculties of energy.
What are the phenomena of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)?
The noble one’s mindfulness and the faculty of mindfulness—these are called the phenomena of the faculty of mindfulness.
What are the factors that are not the faculty of mindfulness?
With the exception of the faculty of mindfulness, any other factors are called the factors that are not the faculty of mindfulness.
What are the factors that are the faculty of concentration?
The noble faculty of concentration (samādhindriya) is called the faculty of concentration.
What is meant by the non-faculty of concentration?
Any other phenomena (dharma) apart from the faculty of concentration are called the non-faculty of concentration.
What is the dharma of the faculty of wisdom?
The noble vision, the noble wisdom, and the noble faculty of non-delusion—this is called the dharma of the faculty of wisdom.
What is the dharma that is not the faculty of wisdom?
Excluding the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), any other phenomena are called non-wisdom-faculty phenomena.
What are called phenomena of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?

For those who possess firm faith and firm realization, the noble, untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena—which are not faculties but are designated as faculties because they share the same factors as perception (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*)—are called phenomena of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What are the phenomena that are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
With the exception of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," all other phenomena are called phenomena that are not the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
The faculty of knowing and the faculty of having known are also like this.
What is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness?
Noble mindfulness is what is called the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
What is meant by factors that are not the awakening factor of mindfulness?
With the exception of the awakening factor of mindfulness, any other factors are called factors that are not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
What is meant by the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena?

Noble vision, noble wisdom, and noble non-delusion regarding the discernment of phenomena as factors of enlightenment—this is called the factor of enlightenment of the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is meant by the factor that is not the discernment of phenomena?
With the exception of the discernment of phenomena as a factor of enlightenment, whatever other factors there may be—these are called the factors that are not the discernment of phenomena.
What is the factor of enlightenment of energy?
It is the noble mind’s application of energy, the right bodily application of energy; this is called the factor of enlightenment of energy.
What is that which is not the factor of enlightenment of energy?
Excluding the awakening factor of energy, any other dharmas are called non-energy-awakening-factor dharmas.
What are called joy-awakening-factor dharmas?
The noble joy and the awakening factor of joy—these are called joy-awakening-factor dharmas.
What are the factors not associated with the awakening factor of joy?
With the exception of the awakening factor of joy, any other factors are called the factors not associated with the awakening factor of joy.
What are the factors excluding the awakening factors?
The noble mind’s discernment of relinquishment is called the factor of the awakening-factor of relinquishment.
What is meant by the factors that are not the awakening-factor of relinquishment?
The discernment of relinquishment and whatever other factors there may be are called the factors that are not the awakening-factor of relinquishment.
What is the factor of enlightenment that is concentration?
Noble concentration and the awakening to concentration—this is called the factor of enlightenment that is concentration.
What is the factor of enlightenment that is not concentration?
Excluding the factor of concentration, any other factors are called non-concentration factors.
What are the factors of equanimity?
The noble mind’s relinquishment of the factor of equanimity is called the factor of equanimity.
What are the factors that are not the awakening-factor of equanimity?
With the exception of the awakening-factor of equanimity, any other factors are called the factors that are not the awakening-factor of equanimity.
What are the factors of the unwholesome root of greed?
If there is longing, this is called the unwholesome root of greed.
What is meant by the factor that is not the unwholesome root of greed?
With the exception of the unwholesome root of greed, whatever other factors there are, these are called the factors that are not the unwholesome root of greed.
Hatred and delusion are also like this.
What is called the wholesome root of non-attachment?
If there is no longing or desire, this is called the wholesome root of non-attachment.
What are the factors that are not the wholesome root of non-attachment?
With the exception of the wholesome root of non-attachment, any other factors are called factors that are not the wholesome root of non-attachment.
The same applies to non-hatred and non-delusion.
What is called the earth-element factor?
That which is the earth element within the sphere of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana) is called the earth-element factor.
What is called the non-earth-element factor?
Excluding the earth element, any other phenomena are called non-earth-element phenomena.
The same applies to the water, fire, and wind elements.
What is meant by the precept of abstaining from taking life?
The precept of non-killing is called the dharma of the precept of non-killing.
What is meant by that which is not the dharma of the precept of non-killing?
Any other dharma apart from the precept of non-killing is called that which is not the dharma of the precept of non-killing.
The same applies up to not drinking alcohol and being heedful.
What are called material phenomena (*rūpadharma*)?
Any phenomenon that is material is termed a material phenomenon.
What are non-material phenomena (*arūpadharma*)?
With the exception of matter, whatever other phenomena there are are called non-material phenomena.
What are visible phenomena (*sanidarśanadharma*)?
The sense-base of form (rūpāyatana) is called the visible dharma.
What is the invisible dharma?
With the exception of the sense-base of form, whatever other dharmas there are are called the invisible dharmas.
What are the dharmas with resistance?
The ten bases of form; these are called the dharmas with resistance.
What are the dharmas without resistance?
The sense-base of mind (manāyatana) and the sense-base of mental objects (dharmāyatana) are called non-obstructive phenomena (apratigha-dharma).
What are noble phenomena (āryadharma)?
Those phenomena that are untainted (anāsrava) are called noble phenomena.
What are called non-noble dharmas?
Any dharma that is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is called a non-noble dharma.

The same applies to those with outflows and those without outflows (*anāsrava*), those with defilement and those without defilement, those with seeking and those without seeking, those to be grasped and those not to be grasped, those with grasping and those without grasping, and those with superiority and those without superiority.
What is meant by "appropriated phenomena" (*upātta-dharma*)?
Any phenomenon that is internal is called an appropriated phenomenon.
What is meant by "non-appropriated phenomena" (*anupātta-dharma*)?
If a phenomenon is external, it is called a non-appropriated phenomenon (*anupātta-dharma*).
What is meant by internal phenomena?
If a phenomenon is appropriated, it is called an internal phenomenon (*ādhyātmika-dharma*).
What are called external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*)?
Any phenomenon that is not felt (*anupātta*) is termed an external phenomenon.
What are called phenomena with retribution (*savipākadharmas*)?
If a dharma is a resultant dharma, it is called a dharma with retribution.
What is a dharma without retribution?
If a dharma is neither a resultant nor a dharma that is not a resultant, it is called a dharma without retribution.
What are the mental factors?
The sphere of mind (manāyatana); these are called mental factors.
What are the non-mental factors?
Excluding the mind, if there are other dharmas, these are called non-mental dharmas (*acittadharma*).
What are called mental concomitants (*cittasaṃprayuktadharma*)?
If a dharma is a mental factor (*caitasika*), it is called a mental concomitant.
What are the factors dissociated from mind?
Those factors which are neither mental concomitants nor mind itself are called factors dissociated from mind.
What are the factors not associated with mind?
If a dharma is not a mental concomitant (citta-saṃprayukta), it is called a dharma that is not associated with the mind.
What is meant by a dharma that is not "not associated with the mind"?
If a dharma is a mental concomitant, it is called a dharma that is not "not associated with the mind."
What are the phenomena that are neither associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind?
The sense-sphere of the mind (*manāyatana*), this is called the phenomenon that is neither associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind.
What are the phenomena that are neither non-associated with the mind nor non-dissociated from the mind?
If a dharma is both a mental concomitant and not a mental concomitant, it is called a dharma that is neither non-associated with mind nor non-non-associated with mind.
What are mental concomitants?
With the exception of mind itself, whatever other dharmas have an object are called mental concomitants.
What are the non-mental factors (*acaitasika-dharma*)?
Those phenomena that are without objects (*anālambana*) and are not associated with the mind (*citta-viprayukta*) are called non-mental factors.
What are the phenomena with objects (*sālambana-dharma*)?
If a dharma is either a mental factor (*caitasika*) or the mind (*citta*), it is called a dharma with an object (*sālambana*).
What is meant by a dharma without an object (*anālambana*)?
With the exception of the mind, if there are other dharmas that are not mental factors, these are called dharmas without an object.
What are the mental concomitants (*cittasahaja-dharma*)?
Those phenomena that follow the mind, arising together with the mind, abiding together with the mind, and ceasing together with the mind—these are called mental concomitants.
What are the non-mental-concomitant phenomena (*acittasahaja-dharma*)?

If a dharma does not turn in accordance with the mind, does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind, it is called a non-associated mental dharma (citta-viprayukta-dharma).
The same applies to those that turn in accordance with the mind (cittānuvartin).
What are called the phenomena of action (*karmadharma*)?
The actions of body, speech, and mind—these are called the phenomena of action.
What are called the non-phenomena of action?
Excluding the actions of body, speech, and mind, any other phenomena are called non-action phenomena (*akarmadharma*).
What are phenomena associated with action (*karmasamprayuktadharma*)?
Any phenomenon that is associated with volition (*cetanā*) is called a phenomenon associated with action.
What are phenomena not associated with karma?
Those that are neither associated with volition (*cetanā*) nor are volition itself are called phenomena not associated with karma.
What are phenomena not associated with action?
If a dharma is not associated with volition (*cetanā*), it is called a dharma not associated with karma.
What is meant by "not a dharma that is not associated with karma"?
If a dharma is associated with volition, it is called a dharma that is not non-associated with karma.
What is meant by phenomena that are neither associated with karma nor dissociated from karma?
Volition (*cetanā*)—this is called a phenomenon that is neither associated with karma nor dissociated from karma.
What is meant by phenomena that are neither non-associated with karma nor non-dissociated from karma?
Whether associated with volition or not associated with volition, these are called phenomena that are neither non-associated with karma nor non-non-associated with karma.
What are phenomena common to karma?

If a phenomenon evolves in accordance with karma, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called a phenomenon that shares in karma (*sādhāraṇa-karmika-dharma*).
What is meant by a phenomenon that does not share in karma?

If a phenomenon does not evolve in accordance with karma, nor arises together with it, nor abides together with it, nor ceases together with it, this is called a phenomenon that does not share in karma (*asādhāraṇa-karmika-dharma*).
The same applies to those that follow karma and those that do not follow karma.
What are called "conditioned phenomena" (*hetu-dharma*)?

Any phenomenon that has an object-condition (*sālambana*), or any phenomenon that lacks an object-condition but possesses retribution (*savipāka*), with the exception of the attainment of fruition (*phala-prāpti*), as well as wholesome retribution and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—these are called conditioned phenomena.
What is meant by "dharmas without cause"?
If a dharma has no object-condition, no retribution, is not a shared karma, and yet attains its fruit, this is called a dharma without cause.
What is meant by "dharmas with cause"?
If a phenomenon has a continuity, it is called a phenomenon with a cause.
What is a phenomenon without a cause?
If a phenomenon lacks continuity, it is called a phenomenon without a cause.
The same applies to having a causal thread or being without a causal thread, having conditions or being without conditions, and being conditioned or unconditioned.
What is meant by "knowing phenomena"?
To know all phenomena as they truly are, through their characteristics, and to perceive and see them—this is called knowing phenomena.
What is meant by "dharmas that are not known"?
There are no such dharmas.
Furthermore, because all dharmas are not perceived in accordance with their characteristics, they are called "dharmas that are not known."
It is the same for consciousness being non-consciousness, comprehension being non-comprehension, and understanding being non-understanding.
What is meant by the knowledge of abandonment that knows phenomena?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome, this is called the knowledge of abandonment that knows phenomena.
What are the phenomena known through knowledge that does not involve abandonment (*aprahāṇajñānajñeya-dharma*)?
If a phenomenon is wholesome or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is called a phenomenon known through knowledge that does not involve abandonment.
The same applies to what is to be abandoned and what is not to be abandoned.
What is meant by "cultivating the Dharma"?
If a phenomenon is wholesome, it is called cultivating the Dharma.
What is meant by "not cultivating the Dharma"?
If a dharma is unwholesome or indeterminate, it is called a non-cultivated dharma.
What is meant by realized dharmas?
All dharmas realized through the knowledge and vision of suchness (tathatā) are called realized dharmas.
What is meant by "non-realization-dharmas"?
There are no such things as non-realization-dharmas.
Furthermore, because all dharmas are not realized through a cognition that accords with their true nature, they are called non-realization-dharmas.
What are called wholesome dharmas?
If a dharma is cultivated, it is named a wholesome dharma.
What are called unwholesome dharmas?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome or indeterminate, it is called a non-virtuous phenomenon (*asaddharma*).
What is meant by an unwholesome phenomenon?
If a phenomenon is to be abandoned, it is called an unwholesome phenomenon.
What is meant by "the absence of unwholesome dharmas"?
If a dharma is wholesome or indeterminate, this is called the absence of unwholesome dharmas.
What is meant by "indeterminate dharmas"?
If a dharma is either acquired (*upātta*) or is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor of the nature to produce a result (*avipākadharman*), it is called an indeterminate dharma (*avyākṛtadharma*).
What is meant by "not non-indeterminate"?
If a dharma is either wholesome (*kuśala*) or unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is called not non-indeterminate.
What are the dharmas of training (*śaikṣa*)?
Those dharmas that are noble (*ārya*) but not those of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are called the dharmas of training.
What are the non-training dharmas?
If a dharma is neither noble nor of one beyond training, it is called a non-learner dharma (*aśaikṣadharma*).
What is meant by a dharma of one beyond training?
If a dharma is noble and not of one in training, it is called a dharma of one beyond training.
What are the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
Those dharmas which are not noble or are learner-dharmas are called non-non-learner dharmas.
What are the dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
If a dharma is non-noble, it is called a dharma that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is meant by a dharma that is not "neither-learner-nor-non-learner"?
If a dharma is noble, it is called a dharma that is not "neither-learner-nor-non-learner."
What is meant by "dharma as retribution" (*vipāka-dharma*)?
That which is either feeling (*vedanā*) or a wholesome retribution—this is called dharma as retribution.
What is meant by "dharma that is not retribution" (*avipāka-dharma*)?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome, or wholesome with retribution, or neither retribution nor a phenomenon subject to retribution, it is called a non-retribution phenomenon (*avipāka-dharma*).
What is a phenomenon that is a retribution phenomenon (*vipāka-dharma*)? If a phenomenon has retribution, it is called a retribution phenomenon.
What is meant by phenomena that are not of the nature of retribution (*avipāka-dharma*)?
Whether they are retribution, or non-retribution, or phenomena that are neither retribution nor non-retribution—these are called phenomena that are not of the nature of retribution.
What is meant by phenomena that are neither retribution nor of the nature of retribution?
If a dharma is indeterminate, not included within one's own sphere, and is a noble unconditioned phenomenon, this is called a dharma that is neither a result nor a dharma that produces a result.
What is meant by a dharma that is neither non-result nor non-dharma-that-produces-a-result?
If it is a result or a dharma that is a result, this is called "neither non-result nor non-result-dharma.
What are dharmas abandoned by vision?
If a dharma is unwholesome and not abandoned by cultivation, this is called a dharma abandoned by vision.
What are the factors not abandoned by insight (*na-darśana-prahātavya*)?
Those factors that are wholesome (*kuśala*), indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), or abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*); these are called the factors not abandoned by insight.
What are the factors abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome and not abandoned through vision, it is called a phenomenon to be abandoned through cultivation.
What is meant by phenomena not to be abandoned through cultivation?
If a phenomenon is wholesome or indeterminate and is abandoned through vision, it is called a phenomenon not to be abandoned through cultivation.
What are the phenomena that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
Any phenomena that are wholesome or indeterminate are called phenomena that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What are the phenomena that are neither not-abandoned-by-vision nor not-not-abandoned-by-cultivation?
If a phenomenon is unwholesome, it is called a phenomenon that is neither non-seeing-abandoned nor non-reflection-abandoned.
What is meant by phenomena whose cause is seeing-abandonment?
If a phenomenon is seeing-abandoned, or is the retribution of a phenomenon that is seeing-abandoned, this is called a phenomenon whose cause is seeing-abandonment.
What is meant by "dharmas that do not have views as their cause" (*na-dṛṣṭi-heya-hetu-dharma*)?

If a dharma is wholesome, or the retribution of a wholesome dharma; or if it is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), or the retribution of a dharma abandoned through cultivation; or if it is neither retribution nor a dharma that produces retribution—these are called dharmas that do not have views as their cause.
What are the factors whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation?
Any factor that is to be abandoned by cultivation, or the retribution of a factor to be abandoned by cultivation—these are called factors whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation.
What are the factors whose cause is not to be abandoned by cultivation?

If a dharma is wholesome, or the fruition of a wholesome dharma, or the fruition of a dharma abandoned by vision, or neither fruition nor a dharma leading to fruition—these are called dharmas whose cause is not to be abandoned by contemplation.
What is meant by phenomena that have neither the faculty of vision nor the faculty of reflection as their cause?

If a phenomenon is wholesome, or is the fruition of a wholesome phenomenon, or is a phenomenon that is neither fruition nor the cause of fruition, these are called phenomena that have neither the faculty of vision nor the faculty of reflection as their cause.
What is meant by "dharmas that are neither caused by what is not abandoned through insight nor by what is not abandoned through cultivation"?
