What dharmas are excluded?
Dharmas other than the eye-faculty (cakṣur-indriya) are excluded.
This applies likewise up to the faculty of having known (ājñātāvīndriya).
Regarding the mental factor of the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), how many are not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or bases (*āyatana*)?
What dharma is being asked about? It is asking about that which is not the mental factor of the awakening factor of mindfulness.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
The dharma of the awakening factor of mindfulness is excluded.

Regarding those factors that are not associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), how many are not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
What factors are being asked about? The factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness are being asked about.
Excluding other factors.
Which factors are excluded?
Excluding those factors that are not the awakening factor of mindfulness.
The same applies up to the factors of the awakening-factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Regarding the factors of the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha-akuśalamūla*):
how many are not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
Question: What dharma is being asked about?
It is the dharma that is not the unwholesome root of greed;
all other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
The unwholesome root of greed is excluded.
Regarding those dharmas that are not the unwholesome root of greed, how many are not subsumed within the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?
Question: What dharma is being asked about?
Answer: The unwholesome root of greed;
other dharmas are excluded.
What dharmas are excluded?
Dharmas that are not the unwholesome root of greed are excluded.
The same applies to the unwholesome roots of hatred and delusion.
Regarding the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*), how many are not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
What dharmas are being asked about?
They are the dharmas that are not the wholesome root of non-attachment.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
The dharma of the wholesome root of non-attachment is excluded.
Regarding those factors that are not the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*), how many are not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
What kind of factors are being asked about?
They are the factors that are the wholesome root of non-attachment.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas that are not the wholesome root of non-attachment.
The same applies to non-hatred and non-delusion.
Regarding the great element of earth, how many are not included within the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?
What dharmas are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the great dharma that is not earth,
setting aside other dharmas—
what dharmas are being set aside?
Excluding the great element of earth,
as for those things that are not the great element of earth, how many are not subsumed within the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?
What kind of dharmas are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the great element of earth,
setting aside other phenomena—
what phenomena are set aside?
Except for the earth element,
the same applies to the water, fire, and wind elements.
Regarding the dharma of the precept against killing, how many are not subsumed within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
What dharma is being asked about?
It is not the dharma of the precept against killing;
it excludes all other dharmas.
What dharmas are excluded?
The dharma of the precept against taking life is excluded.
As for that which is not the dharma of the precept against taking life, how many are not subsumed within the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and bases (āyatana)?
What dharma is being asked about?
It is the dharma of the precept of non-killing;
other dharmas are excluded.
What dharmas are excluded?
The dharma of the precept against taking life is excluded.
This applies likewise, up to and including the state of non-negligence regarding the abstention from intoxicants.
Regarding material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), how many are not subsumed under the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
What kind of phenomena are being asked about?
They are non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*).
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding material dharmas (*rūpadharma*).
What are non-form phenomena (*arūpadharma*)?
How many are not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)?
What kind of phenomena are being asked about?
Question: Regarding material phenomena (*rūpadharma*),
with the exception of other phenomena— what phenomena are excluded?
Except for form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*).
This applies likewise to [the past, future, and present].
*Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle 22.
The Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra, Scroll Twenty-three.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī and Dharmagupta et al. during the Yao Qin dynasty.

Chapter Two: On Correspondence (Saṃprayoga), Part One: The Section on the Compendium of Correspondence. Regarding mental states and mental factors, one should know their correspondence, one should know their non-correspondence, one should know that there is no correspondence, and one should know that it is not the case that there is no correspondence.
Regarding association (*saṃprayukta*), one should know that there is also association, non-association, absence of association, and non-absence of association.
Regarding non-association (*viprayukta*), one should know that there is also association, non-association, absence of association, and non-absence of association.
Regarding non-association, one should know that there is also association, non-association, non-association, and not non-association.
Regarding non-association, one should know that there is also association, non-association, non-association, and not non-association.

Regarding association (*saṃprayoga*): it means that the mind is associated with mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), mental factors are associated with the mind, and mental factors are associated with one another, excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The intrinsic nature is not associated with itself, yet it is not the case that there is no association.
Regarding the correct inquiry into the association of mind and mental factors, it shall now be explained. From the eye-consciousness element up to the mind-element and mind-consciousness element;

the contact of the body, the contact of the mind—namely, contact, opposition-contact, contact of craving, contact of aversion, contact of clarity, contact of ignorance, contact of the portion of clarity, and contact of the portion of ignorance; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, patience, view, knowledge, liberation; non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; faith, remorse, absence of remorse, gladness, joy, mental exertion, and mental tranquility.

Faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, equanimity, and fear; the latent tendency of afflictions, the latent tendency of views, the latent tendency of doubt, the latent tendency of attachment to precepts and rituals, the latent tendency of craving, the latent tendency of aversion, the latent tendency of envy, the latent tendency of stinginess, the latent tendency of ignorance, the latent tendency of pride, and the latent tendency of restlessness; the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, the concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought, the concentration without directed thought and without sustained thought; the concentration on emptiness, the concentration on signlessness, and the concentration on wishlessness; and the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom—these are called association.
Question:
What is the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)? Answer:
If a consciousness arises, has arisen, will arise, or is indeterminate, depending on the eye faculty and having visible form as its object, this is called the visual consciousness element.
The ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness elements are also like this.
What is the mind element (*manodhātu*)?
If the mind cognizes mental objects (*dharma*) and attends to them—whether that initial mind has already arisen, is currently arising, will arise, or is indeterminate—this is called the mind element.
What is the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)?

It is that which does not depart from its respective object; whether it is another mind similar to it that has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate, this is called the mental consciousness element.
What is called body-contact?
Any contact associated with body-consciousness is termed body-contact. Furthermore, regarding body-contact:
any contact associated with the group of five consciousnesses—namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and body-consciousness—is termed body-contact.
What is meant by mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*)?
If a contact is associated with the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), it is called mental contact.
What is meant by name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*)?
If it is mental contact, this is called "contact of the name" (*nāma-saṃsparśa*).
What is "contact of the resistant" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*)? If it is bodily contact, this is called "contact of the resistant."
What is called "contact of craving" (*tṛṣṇā-sparśa*)?
If contact is associated with desire and defilement, this is called contact of craving.
What is called "contact of aversion" (*pratigha-sparśa*)?
If contact is associated with hatred, it is called the contact of hatred.
What is the contact of clarity?
If contact is associated with noble wisdom, it is called the contact of clarity.
What is called contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*)?
If a contact is unwholesome and not associated with knowledge, this is called contact with ignorance.
What is called contact belonging to the side of knowledge (*vidyā-bhāgīya-saṃsparśa*)?
If contact gives rise to clarity, produces clarity, attains clarity, and can cause clarity to expand, this is called contact pertaining to the side of clarity (*vidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*).
What is meant by the side of ignorance?
Contact that gives rise to ignorance, produces ignorance, attains ignorance, and can cause ignorance to expand—this is called contact pertaining to the side of ignorance (*avidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*).

Furthermore, regarding the contact of the portion of clarity (*vidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*): if contact is associated with noble patience (*ārya-kṣānti*), it is called the contact of the portion of clarity.

Furthermore, regarding the contact of the portion of ignorance (*avidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*): if contact is neither noble nor associated with afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called the contact of the portion of ignorance.

Furthermore, regarding the contact of the portion of clarity (*vidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*): if a contact is noble and capable of attaining the fruit of knowledge, it is called the contact of the portion of clarity.

Furthermore, regarding the contact of the portion of ignorance (*avidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*): if a contact is non-noble, whether wholesome or neutral, it is called the contact of the portion of ignorance.
What is the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?

If the body experiences pleasant sensation, or if there is pleasant sensation arising from eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, or body-contact—that is, the element of pleasure—this is called the faculty of pleasure.
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?

If the body does not tolerate suffering—the painful feeling arising from eye-contact, and the painful feelings arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-contact, as well as the element of suffering—this is called the faculty of suffering.
What is the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*)?
If the mind experiences the pleasant sensation born of mental contact and the element of joy, this is called the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of grief (*domanassindriya*)?
If the mind does not tolerate suffering, nor the mental contact with the sensation of suffering or the element of grief, this is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?

If the body and mind do not tolerate either suffering or pleasure, and there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation arising from eye-contact, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation arising from ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, or mind-contact, as well as the element of equanimity, this is called the faculty of equanimity.
What is feeling? Whatever is mental feeling is called feeling.
Furthermore, there are six types of feeling: feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
What is meant by "feeling born of eye-contact"?
Any feeling associated with eye-consciousness is called feeling born of eye-contact.
This applies likewise up to the feeling of the mind.

Furthermore, regarding eye-contact-feeling (*cakṣuḥ-saṃsparśajā-vedanā*): conditioned by the eye and conditioned by visible forms, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors is contact, and conditioned by that contact is feeling. This is called eye-contact-feeling.
This applies likewise up to mental feeling (*manovedanā*).
What is perception (*saṃjñā*)?
If there is perceiving, recollecting, and superior perceiving, this is called perception.
Furthermore, there are six perceptions: the perception of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
What is the perception of form?
If a perception is associated with visual consciousness, it is called the perception of form.
The same applies to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the perception of forms (*rūpa-saṃjñā*): when one contemplates forms within the objective sphere of form, whatever perception, recollection, or superior perception arises, this is called the perception of forms.
The same applies to the perceptions of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
What is volition (*cetanā*)?
If there is thinking, right thinking, or mental engagement with an object, and if the mind exerts itself, this is called volition.
Furthermore, there are six types of volition: volition regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
What is volition regarding form?
If volition is associated with visual consciousness, it is called volition regarding form.
Volition regarding sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena is likewise.

Furthermore, regarding the volition of form (*rūpa-saṃskāra*): one contemplates form as the object of form; if there is volition, right volition, or conditional volition, and if the mind exerts itself, this is called the volition of form.
The same applies to the volitions of sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
What is contact? If there is correct contact, this is called contact.
Furthermore, there are six types of contact: eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact.
What is eye-contact? If contact is associated with visual consciousness, it is called eye-contact.
Ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact are likewise.
Furthermore, regarding eye-contact: conditioned by the eye and conditioned by forms, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors is called eye-contact.
Ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact are likewise.
What is meant by reflection (*vitarka*)?
If the mind discriminates, calculates, deliberates, and recollects, this is called reflection.
Furthermore, there are six types of reflection: reflection on forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
What is the contemplation of form?
If one contemplates that which is associated with eye-consciousness, this is called the contemplation of form.
The same applies to the contemplations of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena.

Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of form (*rūpa-vitarka*): when one contemplates form as an object and the mind discriminates, calculates, deliberates, and recollects it, this is called the contemplation of form.
The same applies to the mental applications regarding sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (*dharma*).
What is called *vitarka* (applied thought)?
If there is an initial application of thought, repeated application of thought, conceptualization, and mental speech directed toward an object, this is called *vitarka*.
Furthermore, there are six types of perception: perception of forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
What is perception of forms?

If one contemplates forms by means of the objective field of form, such that there is perception, repeated perception, recollection, conceptualization, and mental discourse directed toward the objective field—this is called perception of forms.
The same applies to the perceptions of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
What is meant by "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*)?
If the mind moves subtly, acts subtly, flows subtly, and discriminates subtly such that the mind follows these subtle movements, this is called contemplation.
Furthermore, there are six contemplations: the contemplation of form, sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharma*).
What is meant by the contemplation of form?

If one contemplates form by means of the objective sphere of form, and if the mind’s activity, subtle activity, subtle flow, and subtle discrimination cause the mind to follow that subtlety and turn accordingly, this is called the contemplation of form.
The contemplation of sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena is also like this.
What is meant by "patience" (kṣānti)?
It is the state of being able to endure and remain patient toward both favorable and unfavorable phenomena, despite having a craving for and desire to obtain them; this is called patience.
What is meant by "view"?
There are two kinds of view:
either the view of patience or the view of wisdom.
What is called patience through vision (*dṛṣṭi-kṣānti*)?
If one is free from craving for gain, and is capable of enduring and remaining patient toward both favorable and unfavorable phenomena, this is called patience through vision.
What is called knowledge through vision (*dṛṣṭi-jñāna*)?
If one is necessarily attached to phenomena, this is called "view-knowledge.
What is meant by "knowledge"?
If one is necessarily attached to wholesome phenomena, this is called "knowledge."
Furthermore, there are four kinds of knowledge:

the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna); these are called "knowledge.
What is meant by "liberation" (vimukti)?

If one has understanding, profound understanding, and ultimate understanding; if the mind is directed toward that, honors that, and inclines toward that, and is liberated by means of that—this is called liberation.
Furthermore, regarding liberation, there are six liberations:
liberation from form, and liberation from sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena.
What is liberation from form?
If liberation is associated with eye-consciousness, this is called liberation from form (*rūpa-vimokṣa*).
Liberation from sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental phenomena (*dharma*) is likewise.

Furthermore, regarding liberation from form: if one contemplates form by means of the objective field of form, and there is liberation, repeated liberation, and ultimate liberation, such that the mind inclines toward it, honors it, and leans toward it—being liberated by means of that—it is called liberation from form.
The same applies to liberation from sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
What is meant by non-attachment?
If one has no longing, this is called non-attachment.
Furthermore, if one possesses forbearance and is free from a mind of greed, this is called non-greed.

Furthermore, if within the five objects of desire there is a continuous succession of attachment, delight, and mental satisfaction toward desirable forms, and a continuous succession of attachment, delight, and mental satisfaction toward desirable forms through the eye-consciousness perceiving forms; and a continuous succession of attachment, delight, and mental satisfaction toward desirable forms through the ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousnesses perceiving their respective objects; [this is called greed].

If one does not desire to greedily take what belongs to others—be it their desires, their wealth, their necessities, or their wives—and if one is without greed, is intensely without greed, and is ultimately without greed; if the mind is not attached, does not long for, does not crave, and is not stained by them; and if, regarding other things that may be objects of greed, one is without greed, is intensely without greed, and is ultimately without greed; if the mind is not greedily attached, does not long for, does not crave, and is not stained by them—this is called non-greed (*alobha*).
What is meant by non-ill will?
If there is no contention or dispute, this is called non-ill will.
Furthermore, if one is patient and free from a mind of ill will, this is called non-ill will.

Furthermore, if toward a few beings or many beings, one desires that these beings be neither bound, nor confined, nor harmed; that they not be subjected to various forms of suffering; and if one is without anger, deeply without anger, and ultimately without anger; with a mind free from anger, without contention, without malice, and without causes for affliction; with a mind that harbors no resentment, and with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), deep loving-kindness, and ultimate loving-kindness; out of compassion and the desire to benefit beings, as well as toward other factors that might provoke anger, being without anger, deeply without anger, and ultimately without anger; with a mind free from anger, without contention, without malice, and without causes for affliction; with a mind that harbors no resentment, and with loving-kindness, deep loving-kindness, and ultimate loving-kindness; out of compassion and the desire to benefit those factors—this is called "absence of anger" (*avyāpāda*).
What is non-delusion? Clarity is called non-delusion.
Furthermore, non-delusion is the capacity to endure and the mind’s freedom from delusion; this is called non-delusion.

Furthermore, if one knows suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; if one knows the past limit, the future limit, and both the past and future limits; if one knows the internal and the external; if one knows the arising, cessation, great peril, and the escape regarding the six bases of contact; if one knows dependent origination; if one knows karmic retribution; and if one knows what is conditioned and unconditioned, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; black and white; with cause and without cause; with clarity and without clarity; what is to be done and what is not to be done; and what is to be cultivated and what is not to be cultivated.

Regarding those phenomena, there is no delusion, no darkness, no forgetfulness, and no loss; there is right mindfulness, free from obstruction, free from covering, free from obscuration, free from wildness, free from entanglement, and free from turbidity. It is the illumination, the flame, the skillful art, the light, the knowing, the seeing, the penetration, and the application; it is the eye of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, and right view.

Furthermore, among other states of delusion, there is no delusion, no darkness, no forgetfulness, and no loss; there is right mindfulness, absence of obstruction, absence of covering, absence of obscuration, absence of wildness, absence of entanglement, and absence of turbidity; it is the illumination, flame, skill, light, clarity, knowledge, vision, understanding, penetration, and expedient means; it is the eye of wisdom, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, and right view—this is called non-delusion.
What is meant by "conformable faith" (*anulomikī śraddhā*)?
If one has faith that is wholesome, conformable, and non-opposing, this is called conformable faith.
What is meant by "remorse" (*kaukṛtya*)?

If, regarding what should or should not have been done, one has already acted or failed to act, and as a result the mind experiences distress, intense distress, and ultimate distress, this is called remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
What is meant by "absence of regret"?

Whether regarding what should or should not be done, or having already done what should or should not be done, if one is not tormented or distressed therein, is not repeatedly tormented or distressed, and is ultimately not tormented or distressed, this is called absence of regret.
What is meant by "satisfaction" (saumanasya)?
If the mind is pleased, joyful, delighted, and finds delight in what has not yet been gladdened, this is called satisfaction.
What is meant by "joy" (prīti)?
If one is joyful and exultant, truly exultant, free from ill will and tranquil, this is called joy (*prīti*).
What is mental exertion?
If the mind initiates, manifests, and transcends, this is called mental exertion (*citta-pragraha*).
What is meant by "mental pliancy" (*citta-praśrabdhi*)?
If the mind is joyful, well-tamed, light, and supple, this is called mental pliancy.
What is meant by "faith" (*śraddhā*)?
If there is faith, entry into faith, and superior faith, this is called "faith" (*śraddhā*).
What is "desire" (*chanda*)?

If there is desire, intense desire, longing, the wish to act, the impulse to initiate, the wish to manifest, the wish to transcend, the wish to attain, the wish to touch, the wish to penetrate, the wish to realize, and the wish to witness, this is called "desire."
What is called heedfulness?

It is the guarding of mental attention so that my mind may not become defiled by defiling dharmas, not become angry toward anger-inducing dharmas, not become deluded by deluding dharmas, not become attached to impure dharmas, not follow after the dharmas of sensual desire for form, not be arrogant toward arrogance-inducing dharmas, and not be heedless regarding heedlessness-inducing dharmas; this is called heedfulness.
What is mindfulness? If there is recollection and mindful attention, this is called mindfulness.
What is equanimity of mind?
If one relinquishes superior relinquishment—such that the mind is equanimous, balanced, pure, free from volitional effort, and non-receptive—this is called relinquishment.
What is meant by fear?

If, regarding forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, or regarding sentient beings, one experiences fear, intense fear, or ultimate fear, such that the heart is startled and the hair stands on end—this is called fear.
What are the latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*)?
There are ten latent tendencies:

the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*), the latent tendency of attachment to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśānuśaya*), the latent tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*), the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), the latent tendency of envy (*īrṣyānuśaya*), the latent tendency of avarice (*mātsaryānuśaya*), the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), the latent tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*), and the latent tendency of restlessness (*auddhatyānuśaya*). These are called the latent tendencies of affliction.
What is the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*)?
With the exception of the view of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), any other views are called the latent tendency of views.
Furthermore, the sixty-two views and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) are called the latent tendency of views.
What is the latent tendency of doubt?

It is when a person, with respect to the past, entertains uncertainty: "Did I exist in the past? Did I not exist in the past? By what nature did I exist in the past? What was the cause of my existence in the past?"

Due to doubt concerning the future, one wonders: "Will I exist in the future? Will I not exist in the future? By what nature will I exist in the future? What is the cause for my existence in the future? What is the condition for my existence in the future?"
Now I am in doubt: "Do I exist now? Do I not exist now? By what nature do I exist now? What is the cause for my existence now, and what is that which is called my place of birth?"
"From where do these sentient beings come, and to where do they go?
If the World-Honored One has doubts—whether this is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, or not a Buddha, a World-Honored One;
whether the World-Honored One teaches the Dharma well, or the World-Honored One does not teach the Dharma well?"
Is the community of the Blessed One’s disciples on the path to a good destination, or is the community of the Blessed One’s disciples not on the path to a good destination?

They hold that what is conditioned is permanent, or that what is conditioned is impermanent; that what is conditioned is suffering, or that what is conditioned is not suffering; that the dharma of non-self is not the dharma of non-self; that peaceful nirvana is not peaceful nirvana; that there is giving and there is no giving; that there is sacrifice and there is no sacrifice; that there is the fruit of retribution for good and evil karma and there is no fruit of retribution for good and evil karma; that there is this world and there is no this world; that there is a future world and there is no future world; that there are parents and there are no parents; that there are devas and there are no devas; that there are spontaneously born beings and there are no spontaneously born beings; that there are śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who have attained the right path and reached the right goal, and who, having personally realized this world and the future world, proclaim it, or that there are no such śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas in the world who have attained the right path and reached the right goal, and who, having personally realized this world and the future world, proclaim it.

If one harbors doubt, deep doubt, or ultimate doubt regarding those phenomena; if the mind is not resolved, but is hesitant, double-minded, skeptical, and lacks clarity; if immeasurable doubt remains inexhaustible and one is not liberated from it; and if there is vacillation, deep vacillation, or ultimate vacillation—this is called the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).

What is the underlying tendency toward the path of precepts (*sīlabbataparāmāsa-anuśaya*)? If one views the path of precepts as such, this is called the underlying tendency toward the path of precepts.

Furthermore, it is the conviction that purification comes through precepts and the path of precepts, leading to liberation, non-reliance, and the exhaustion of the limits of all suffering; it is the acceptance of, desire for, the awakening to, contact with, and realization of precepts, which are said to protect body and speech.

The Way consists of seeking auspiciousness through heterodox means, such as grooming the hair and reverently serving water, fire, the sun, and the moon; observing precepts such as abstaining from eating beef, venison, or dog meat, and maintaining silence; and seeking to become a powerful being honored among humans and devas as a reward for these practices.
Thus, they diligently practice asceticism and wrong practices;

this is what they call the Path. Whether it be precepts or the Path, they seek them out; having sought them, they regard them as purity; having attained purity, they regard it as liberation; and having attained liberation, they regard themselves as noble ones, as Arhats, and as having reached Nirvana.

If one is patient toward, desirous of, capable of enduring, and takes pleasure in attachment to those [objects], this is called the underlying tendency of precepts and practices (*śīlavrataparāmarśānuśaya*).
What is the underlying tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇānuśaya*)?
If there is defilement by desire, this is called the underlying tendency of craving.
What is the latent tendency of ill will?
If one feels hatred and resentment, this is called the latent tendency of ill will.
What is the latent tendency of envy?

If, when others obtain gain, offerings, honor, respect, praise, or prostrations, one feels resentment, malice, anger, and a jealous mind, this is called the underlying tendency of envy (*īrṣyānuśaya*).
What is the underlying tendency of stinginess (*mātsaryānuśaya*)?
If one is stingy with material wealth and possesses a mind of craving that refuses to relinquish it, this is called the underlying tendency of stinginess (*mātsarya-anuśaya*).
What is the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*)?
Delusion, which is an unwholesome root, is called the underlying tendency of ignorance.
What is the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*)?
If one exalts oneself through conceit, this is called the latent tendency of pride.
What is the latent tendency of restlessness (*auddhatya-anuśaya*)?
If the mind is restless, unsettled, flighty, unpeaceful, not rightly stilled, and does not come to rest, this is called the underlying tendency of restlessness (*uddhacca-anuśaya*).

The concentrations with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), without directed thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), and without directed thought or sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*); as well as the concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), are explained in detail within the threefold path of the *mārga-varga*.
What is the faculty of faith?

It is when a trainee, having abandoned the afflictions, with a noble mind enters the noble path; whether it be one who possesses firm faith and firm Dharma, or others who have seen the faults and perils of conditioned existence, who contemplate the tranquility of Nirvana, and who contemplate suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path according to reality—desiring to attain what has not yet been attained, desiring to understand what has not yet been understood, and desiring to realize what has not yet been realized.

Those training for the sake of abandoning afflictions through the path of cultivation—namely, stream-enterers, once-returners, and non-returners—who are fully endowed with contemplative practice, whether on the stage of knowledge or through the liberation of the mind by means of contemplation, immediately attain the fruits of śramaṇaship: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, and the fruit of non-returning.

An Arahant who is a person beyond training (asekha), desiring to attain the noble dharmas not yet attained, fulfills the practice of the path through cultivation; whether it be the stage of knowledge or the liberation of mind through insight, he immediately attains the fruit of Arhatship.

When a person who accords with reality and accords with the destination possesses faith—faith that enters, surpassing faith, true faith, and purity of mind—this is called the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
The faculties of energy (*vīryendriya*), mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and wisdom (*prajñendriya*) are likewise.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-three.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.

The Section on Correspondence (*Saṃprayoga-vibhaṅga*), Part Two of the Chapter on Correspondence (*Saṃprayoga-pāda*), Seventy-second: The Section on the Divisions of Correspondence Gates shall now be explained.
There are twelve for each of the five consciousness-elements (*vijñāna-dhātu*).
The two consciousness elements each have sixty [types].
The body-contact has thirteen;
the mind-contact and the name-contact each have fifty-three.
Contact with regard to the object (*ālambana-sparśa*) is also thirteenfold.

Contact of the body (*kāya-sparśa*) is twenty-five; contact of craving (*tṛṣṇā-sparśa*) is twenty-three; contact of aversion (*pratigha-sparśa*) is twenty-three; contact of clarity (*vidyā-sparśa*) is thirty-five; contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*) is thirty-four; contact associated with clarity (*vidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*) is thirty-five; and contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa*) is thirty.

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) consists of thirteen; the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) is likewise. The faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) consists of fifty-one; the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) consists of thirty-seven; the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) consists of fifty-six. Feeling (*vedanā*) consists of sixty-five.

For perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*), the respective numbers are obtained by excluding their own intrinsic natures. Initial inquiry (*vitarka*) consists of fifty-nine; sustained investigation (*vicāra*) consists of sixty; patience (*kṣānti*) consists of fifty-three; vision (*dṛṣṭi*) consists of fifty-four; knowledge (*jñāna*) consists of thirty-five; and liberation (*vimukti*) consists of sixty-nine.

Non-greed: twenty-nine; non-ill will: likewise; non-delusion: forty-two; confidence: forty-four; remorse: thirty-four; non-remorse: thirty-six; gladness: fifty-two; joy: likewise; mental energy: sixty; mental tranquility: forty-one; faith: fifty-eight; desire-to-act: sixty-one; heedfulness: forty-six; mindfulness: fifty-nine; equanimity: forty-one; fear: twenty-seven.

There are forty-nine latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*): twenty-eight latent tendencies of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), nineteen latent tendencies of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*), twenty-eight latent tendencies regarding precepts and rules (*śīlavrataparāmarśānuśaya*), twenty-nine latent tendencies of craving (*rāgānuśaya*), twenty-seven latent tendencies of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), twenty-four latent tendencies of envy (*īrṣyānuśaya*), and the same number for the latent tendencies of stinginess (*mātsaryānuśaya*). There are thirty-nine latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), and the same applies to the latent tendencies of pride (*māna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).

There are thirty-five concentrations with both vitarka and vicāra; thirty-four concentrations with no vitarka but with vicāra; thirty-three concentrations with neither vitarka nor vicāra; thirty-four concentrations of emptiness; and the same applies to the signless and the wishless concentrations.

The faculty of faith consists of thirty-eight; the faculty of vigor, thirty-nine; the faculty of mindfulness is likewise; the faculty of concentration, thirty-four; and the faculty of wisdom, thirty-six.
What is the category of the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?

Those phenomena associated with the eye-consciousness element—namely, contact of the body, contact of resistance, contact of the portion of ignorance; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, and liberation—these are called the category of the eye-consciousness element.
The divisions of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and consciousness elements are also like this.
What are the divisions of the mind element?

Those phenomena associated with the mind element—namely, mental contact, name-contact, contact of affection, contact of aversion, contact of clarity, contact of ignorance, contact belonging to the side of clarity, and contact belonging to the side of ignorance; as well as the faculty of joy up to the faculty of wisdom—these are called the divisions of the mind element.
The division of the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) is likewise.
What is the division of body-contact (*kāyasparśabhāga*)?

Those phenomena associated with body-contact—namely, the eye-consciousness element, ear-consciousness element, nose-consciousness element, tongue-consciousness element, and body-consciousness element; the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); as well as feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and liberation (*vimukti*)—these are called the division of body-contact.
What is the mental-contact constituent?

Those factors associated with mental contact—namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), excluding contact itself, as well as the faculty of joy up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)—are called the mental-contact constituent.
The category of contact by designation (*nāma-saṃsparśāṅga*) is also like this.
What is the category of contact through opposition (*pratigha-saṃsparśāṅga*)?

If a phenomenon is associated with contact through opposition—namely, the visual consciousness element, the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness elements; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, and the faculty of equanimity; as well as feeling, perception, volition, attention, and resolve—this is called the category of contact through opposition.
What is the factor of craving-contact (*tṛṣṇā-saṃsparśāṅga*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with craving-contact, namely:

the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), acceptance (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-regret (*avipratisāra*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittapragraha*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*); the latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*), the latent tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇānuśaya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and the latent tendency of restlessness (*auddhatyānuśaya*). These are called the factor of craving-contact.

What is the category of contact associated with aversion (*pratigha-saṃsparśa-varga*)? Those phenomena that are associated with contact associated with aversion, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial mental application (*vitarka*), sustained mental application (*vicāra*), acceptance (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); remorse (*kaukṛtya*), mental energy (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), fear (*bhaya*); the underlying tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and the underlying tendency of restlessness (*auddhatyānuśaya*). These are called the category of contact associated with aversion.
What is the factor of contact with clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśāṅga*)?

It refers to those phenomena associated with contact with clarity: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), feeling, perception, volition, attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), view, knowledge, liberation, non-delusion, pliancy of faith (*śraddhā-prasāda*), serenity (*prīti*), joy (*prāmodya*), mental exertion (*citta-vīrya*), mental tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, mental equanimity, concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation, concentration without initial inquiry but with sustained investigation, concentration without initial inquiry or sustained investigation, the concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, the concentration of wishlessness, the faculty of faith up to the faculty of wisdom—these are called the factor of contact with clarity.

What is the constituent of contact associated with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśāṅga*)? Those factors that are associated with contact associated with ignorance—namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial mental application (*vitarka*), sustained mental application (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); remorse (*kaukṛtya*), lack of remorse (*akaukṛtya*), contentment (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), fear (*bhaya*); the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), including the ten latent tendencies—these are called the constituent of contact associated with ignorance.

What is contact pertaining to the factors of enlightenment (*vidyāṅga-saṃsparśa*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with contact pertaining to the factors of enlightenment, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy of faith (*śraddhāprasrabdhi*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittapragraha*), mental tranquility (*cittaprasrabdhi*); faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and equanimity of mind (*cittopekṣā*); concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*), up to and including the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). This is called contact pertaining to the factors of enlightenment.
What is contact associated with the division of ignorance (*avidyāṅga-saṃsparśa*)? Those phenomena that are associated with contact associated with the division of ignorance are:

the element of eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, the mind-element, and the mind-consciousness-element; the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, attention, initial application, sustained application, patience, view, and liberation; non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion; confidence, remorse, absence of remorse, gladness, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, and the removal of fear; the concentration with initial and sustained application, the concentration without initial but with sustained application, and the concentration without initial or sustained application—these are called contact associated with the division of ignorance.
What is the category of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?

Any phenomena associated with the faculty of pleasure—namely, the element of eye-consciousness, the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; the contact of the body, the contact of opposition, and the contact of ignorance; as well as perception, volition, contact, attention, and liberation—these are called the category of the faculty of pleasure.
What is the category of the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?

Those phenomena associated with the faculty of suffering, namely: the sphere of visual consciousness, the spheres of auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness; contact of the body, contact through opposition, and contact associated with the portion of ignorance; as well as perception, volition, contact, attention, and liberation—these are called the category of the faculty of suffering.

What is the category of the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the faculty of joy, namely: the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); mental contact (*manosamphassa*), name-contact (*nāmasamphassa*), craving-contact (*taṇhāsamphassa*), clear-knowledge-contact (*ñāṇasamphassa*), ignorance-contact (*avijjāsamphassa*), clear-knowledge-portion-contact (*ñāṇa-bhāgasamphassa*), and ignorance-portion-contact (*avijjā-bhāgasamphassa*); perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*phassa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), patience (*khanti*), view (*diṭṭhi*), knowledge (*ñāṇa*), liberation (*vimutti*); non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), non-delusion (*amoha*); confidence (*saddhā*), non-regret (*avippaṭisāra*), gladness (*pāmojja*), joy (*somanassa*), mental exertion (*cittassa paggaha*), mental tranquility (*passaddhi*); faith (*saddhā*), desire-to-act (*chanda*), heedfulness (*appamāda*), mindfulness (*sati*), equanimity of mind (*cetaso upekkhā*); the underlying tendencies of affliction (*kilesānusaya*), the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhānusaya*), the underlying tendency of attachment to rules and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsānusaya*), the underlying tendency of craving (*taṇhānusaya*), ignorance (*avijjā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*uddhaccānusaya*); concentration with initial and sustained application (*savitakka-savicāra-samādhi*), and so forth, up to the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*). This is called the category of the faculty of joy.

What is the category of the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the faculty of grief, namely: the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāmasaṃsparśa*), contact of aversion (*pratighasaṃsparśa*), contact of ignorance (*avidyāsaṃsparśa*), and contact associated with the portion of ignorance (*avidyābhāgīyasaṃsparśa*); perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained examination (*vicāra*), acceptance (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-greed (*alobha*), non-aversion (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*), confidence (*prasāda*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*), energy (*vīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and fear (*bhaya*); the latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*), the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*), the latent tendency of attachment to precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśānuśaya*), the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), the latent tendencies of envy (*īrṣyā*) and stinginess (*mātsarya*), as well as ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*). These are called the category of the faculty of grief.
What is the category of the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the faculty of equanimity:

namely, the element of eye-consciousness, the elements of ear-, nose-, tongue-, and body-consciousness; the element of mind and the element of mental consciousness; the contacts of eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body; mental contact; nominal contact; impingement-contact; contact of craving; contact of clarity; contact of ignorance; contact belonging to the side of clarity; contact belonging to the side of ignorance; non-delusion; pliancy; serenity of mind; faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, and equanimity; the latent tendencies of affliction, views, doubt, attachment to rules and rituals, craving, ignorance, pride, and restlessness; the meditative concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation, up to the faculty of wisdom—these are called the category of the faculty of equanimity.
What is meant by "associated with feeling" (*vedanā-saṃprayukta*)? It refers to those phenomena that are associated with feeling. What is meant by "not associated"?
It refers to those phenomena that are not so associated.
That is to say, all intrinsic natures (svabhāva) are called the non-feeling constituent (a-vedanā-aṅga).
What is the perception constituent (saṃjñā-aṅga)? It refers to those phenomena (dharma) that are associated with perception (saṃjñā-samprayukta).
What is meant by "non-portion" (*aprakāra*)?
It refers to all intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); this is called the non-perception portion.
What is meant by the "volition portion" (*cetanā-prakāra*)?
If a phenomenon is associated with volition (*cetanā*), what is meant by "not part of it" (*aprakāra*)?
It refers to all intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); these are called the non-volitional portion (*acetanā-prakāra*).
What is meant by the "contact factor" (sparśāṅga)?
It refers to those phenomena that are associated with contact. What is meant by the "non-factor"? [It refers to those phenomena that are not associated with contact.]
That is to say, the various intrinsic natures (svabhāva) are called the non-contact factor.
The contemplation factor is as explained for perception (saṃjñā).
What is the awakening factor (bodhyaṅga)?
If a dharma is associated with awakening (*vitarka*), what is meant by "not being a constituent" (*aprakāra*)?

It refers to the five consciousness-elements (*pañca-vijñāna-dhātu*), body-contact (*kāya-saṃsparśa*), contact through opposition (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), the nature of concentration with no applied thought but sustained thought (*avitarko vicāramātraḥ samādhiḥ*), and concentration with neither applied nor sustained thought (*avitarko 'vicāraḥ samādhiḥ*). These are called the non-constituents of awakening (*avitarka-bhāga*).
What is meant by "the analytical portion" (*vibhaṅga-bhāgīya*)?

It refers to those phenomena that are associated with analytical insight (*vipaśyanā*). What is meant by "the non-analytical portion" (*avibhaṅga-bhāgīya*)? It refers to those phenomena that are not so associated.

That is to say, the five consciousness-elements, the body-contact, the contact of resistance, the faculty of pleasure, and the faculty of pain, which by their very nature are without vitarka and without vicāra in meditative concentration—this is called the non-vicāra portion.
What is meant by the "factor of patience"?
It refers to those phenomena associated with patience (*kṣānti*). What is meant by the "non-factor"? [It refers to those not so associated.]

This refers to the contact of the body with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), which consists of fifteen intrinsic natures: patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), non-delusion (*amoha*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*); as well as the three afflictions to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya-kleśa*): the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and the attachment to rites and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). These are called the factors not included in patience (*akṣāntibhāga*).
What is meant by the "seeing portion" (darśana-bhāga)?
It refers to those dharmas that are associated with seeing. What is meant by the "non-portion" (a-bhāga)? [It refers to those not so associated.]

Nine are exclusively faculties of the body; five are of their own nature: the faculties of patience, wisdom, non-delusion, and discernment. The three afflictions abandoned through vision—namely, the view of a self-identity, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals—are called the non-view portion.

What is the wisdom-factor (paññā-bhāga)? It refers to those phenomena associated with wisdom: namely, the mind-element (manodhātu) and the mind-consciousness-element (manoviññāṇadhātu); mental contact, name-contact, and contact through clear knowledge; the faculty of joy (somanassindriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekkhindriya); feeling, perception, contact, volition, initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), and liberation; confidence, gladness, joy, mental exertion, and mental tranquility; faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, and mental equanimity; and the concentration with both initial and sustained application up to the faculty of concentration—this is called the wisdom-factor.
What is meant by the "factors conducive to liberation"?
It refers to those phenomena that are associated with liberation. What is meant by the "non-factors"? [It refers to those not so associated.]
That which consists of the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) by its very nature is called the "non-liberative portion" (*amokṣabhāgīya*).

What is the "portion of non-attachment"? Any dharma associated with non-attachment, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), and the contact of the portion of ignorance (*avidyābhāga-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), confidence (*śraddhā*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), lack of regret (*akaukṛtya*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*). These are called the portion of non-attachment.
What is called the non-ill-will constituent? Those factors associated with non-ill-will, namely:

the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, and the contact of the constituent of ignorance; the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, patience, view, and liberation; non-delusion, confidence, regret, lack of regret, serenity, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, heedfulness, and mindfulness—these are called the non-ill-will constituent.

What is called the factor of non-delusion? It refers to those phenomena associated with non-delusion: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), contact of clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), contact belonging to the side of clarity (*vidyāpakṣya-saṃsparśa*), and contact belonging to the side of ignorance (*avidyāpakṣya-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), confidence (*prasāda*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), absence of regret (*akaukṛtya*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittapragraha*), mental tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*); concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*) up to the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*). These are called the factors of non-delusion.

What is the factor of conformity with faith (*saddhānusāri-bhāga*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with conformity to faith, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, contact with knowledge (*viddāsamsa-samphassa*), contact belonging to the portion of knowledge, and contact belonging to the portion of ignorance; the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), patience, view, wisdom, liberation; non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion; remorse, absence of remorse, serenity, joy, mental exertion, mental tranquility, desire-to-act, heedfulness, mindfulness, and mental equanimity—excluding the faculty of faith; as well as concentration accompanied by initial and sustained application up to the faculty of wisdom. These are called the factor of conformity with faith.

What is the faculty of remorse (*kaukṛtya*)? Any phenomena associated with remorse, namely: the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, anger-contact, ignorance-contact, and contact associated with the portion of ignorance; the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*); confidence (*prasāda*), mental energy (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*); the latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*), the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), the latent tendency of attachment to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśānuśaya*), the latent tendency of hatred (*pratighānuśaya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), arrogance (*mada*), conceit (*māna*), and the latent tendency of restlessness (*auddhatyānuśaya*). These are called the faculty of remorse.

What is meant by "not partaking of remorse" (*avippaṭisāra-bhāgiya*)? It refers to those phenomena that are not associated with remorse: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); mental contact (*manosamphassa*); the contact of names (*nāmasamphassa*); the contact of craving (*taṇhāsamphassa*); the contact of ignorance (*avijjāsamphassa*); the contact belonging to the category of ignorance (*avijjābhāgiyasamphassa*); the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*phassa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial application (*vitakka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), patience (*khanti*), view (*diṭṭhi*), liberation (*vimokkha*); non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adosa*), non-delusion (*amoha*); confidence (*saddhā*), gladness (*pasāda*), joy (*pāmojja*), mental energy (*cittappaggaha*), faith (*saddhā*), desire-to-act (*chanda*), heedfulness (*appamāda*), mindfulness (*sati*); the underlying tendencies of defilement (*āsava-anusaya*), the underlying tendency of views (*diṭṭhi-anusaya*), the underlying tendency of attachment to rules and observances (*sīlabbata-parāmāsa-anusaya*); craving (*taṇhā*), ignorance (*avijjā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*). These are called the factors not partaking of remorse.
What is meant by the "factor of gratification"?
It refers to those phenomena that are associated with gratification. What is meant by the "non-factor"? [It refers to those phenomena that are not so associated.]

That is to say: the nine contacts associated with aversion of the body, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity, the intrinsic nature of regret, fear, doubt, aversion, envy, and parsimony—these are called the non-pleasurable factors.
What is meant by the "factor of joy"?
It refers to any phenomenon associated with joy. What is meant by the "non-factor"? [It refers to phenomena not associated with joy.]

That is to say: the nine bodily contacts associated with aversion, the faculty of grief, the faculty of equanimity, the intrinsic nature of regret, joy, fear, doubt, aversion, envy, and parsimony—these are called the factors incompatible with joy.
What is meant by the factor of mental exertion?
It refers to those dharmas associated with mental exertion. What is meant by the non-factor?
It refers to those not so associated.

The nine factors of the body that are of the nature of the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*) are called the non-mental factor of energy. What is the mental factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi*)? Those factors associated with mental tranquility, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*);

mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāmasaṃsparśa*), contact of clarity (*vidyāsaṃsparśa*), contact belonging to the portion of clarity (*vidyābhāgīyasaṃsparśa*), and contact belonging to the portion of ignorance (*avidyābhāgīyasaṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental energy (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*); concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation (*savitarkasavicārasamādhi*) up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). These are called the mental factor of tranquility.
What is meant by the factor of faith?
It refers to those phenomena associated with faith. What is meant by the non-factor? [It refers to those phenomena not so associated.]
That is to say: the nine factors associated with the body, faith (*śraddhā*), the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*)—these are called the non-factors of faith.
What are the factors of desire?
They are those dharmas that are associated with desire (*chanda*).
What is meant by "non-appropriate" (*aprakṛta*)?
It refers to the ninefold nature of doubt regarding the body; this is called the non-desire-portion (*akāma-bhāga*).
What is meant by the "heedfulness-portion" (*apramāda-bhāga*)?

If a dharma is associated with heedfulness—namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), contact with clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), contact belonging to the portion of clarity (*vidyā-bhāgīya-saṃsparśa*), and contact belonging to the portion of ignorance (*avidyā-bhāgīya-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-greed (*alobha*), non-hatred (*adveṣa*), non-delusion (*amoha*); faith (*śraddhā*), remorse (*kaukṛtya*), absence of remorse (*akaukṛtya*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*citta-vīrya*), mental tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); from the concentration accompanied by initial inquiry and sustained investigation up to the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*)—these are called the factors of heedfulness (*apramāda-bhāga*).
What is meant by "the factor of mindfulness"?
It refers to those phenomena associated with mindfulness. What is meant by "non-factors"? It refers to those not so associated.

That is to say, the nine factors of the body, self-nature, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and doubt—these are called the non-mindfulness factors (*a-smṛty-aṅga*). What are the mental equanimity factors (*citta-upekṣā-aṅga*)? Those factors associated with mental equanimity: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*);

mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāmasaṃsparśa*), clear contact (*vidyāsaṃsparśa*), contact belonging to the side of clarity (*vidyāpakṣasaṃsparśa*), and contact belonging to the side of ignorance (*avidyāpakṣasaṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), faith (*śraddhā*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), mental tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*); concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)—these are called the mental equanimity factors.

What is the division of fear (*bhaya-bhāgīya*)? Those phenomena associated with fear, namely: the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), contact of aversion (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), contact of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), and contact associated with the portion of ignorance; the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); mental energy (*citta-vīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*); the latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*), the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and the latent tendency of restlessness (*auddhatyānuśaya*). These are called the division of fear.
What is the category of the underlying tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya-varga*)?

Those phenomena associated with the underlying tendencies of the afflictions, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, craving-contact, hatred-contact, and ignorance-contact; the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, patience, view, liberation; regret, non-regret, elation, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, mindfulness, and fear; and the underlying tendency of views up to the underlying tendency of restlessness—this is called the category of the underlying tendencies of the afflictions.

What is the category of views (*diṭṭhi-āsava*)? It refers to those factors associated with the proclivity of views, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, and contact accompanied by ignorance; the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, and liberation; remorse, lack of remorse, elation, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire, and mindfulness; as well as the proclivities of afflictions, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness. These are called the category of the proclivity of views.

What is the category of the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of doubt: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), and contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), and mental exertion (*cittapragraha*); as well as the underlying tendencies of afflictions, ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*). This is called the category of the underlying tendency of doubt.

What is the category of the fetters associated with the path of virtue (*śīlamārga-nivaraṇa-bhāga*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the fetters of the path of virtue: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), and contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), and liberation (*vimukti*); remorse (*kaukṛtya*), lack of remorse (*akaukṛtya*), elation (*prīti*), joy (*prāmodya*), mental exertion (*cittapragraha*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*); and the fetters of affliction (*kleśa-nivaraṇa*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*). These are called the category of the fetters associated with the path of virtue.

What is the category of the underlying tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇā-anuśaya*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of craving: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, craving-contact, and contact of ignorance; the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), receptivity (*kṣānti*), view, and liberation; non-regret, gladness, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire-to-act, and mindfulness; as well as the underlying tendencies of afflictions, ignorance, pride, and restlessness. This is called the category of the underlying tendency of craving.

What is the category of the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya-varga*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of aversion: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), contact of aversion (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), and contact of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), acceptance (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); remorse (*kaukṛtya*), mental energy (*cittavīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), fear (*bhaya*); the underlying tendencies of affliction (*kleśānuśaya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*). These are called the category of the underlying tendency of aversion.
What is the category of the underlying tendency of envy (*īrṣyānuśaya*)? Those factors associated with the underlying tendency of envy, namely:

the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, and contact accompanied by ignorance; the faculty of grief; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, patience, view, liberation; mental energy, faith, desire, and mindfulness; as well as the underlying tendencies of affliction, ignorance, pride, and restlessness—these are called the category of the underlying tendency of envy.
What is the category of the underlying tendency of stinginess (*mātsarya-anuśaya*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of stinginess, namely:

the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), and contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), liberation (*vimukti*); mental energy (*citta-vīrya*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*); and the underlying tendencies of affliction (*kleśa-anuśaya*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya-anuśaya*). This is called the category of the underlying tendency of stinginess.
What is the category of the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya-varga*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of ignorance:

namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, craving-contact, aversion-contact, and ignorance-contact; the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial inquiry, sustained investigation, patience, view, liberation; remorse, lack of remorse, elation, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire-to-act, mindfulness, and fear; as well as the underlying tendencies of affliction, views, doubt, attachment to rules and rituals, craving, aversion, envy, parsimony, pride, and restlessness. These are called the category of the underlying tendency of ignorance.

What is the category of the underlying tendency of conceit (*mānānusaya*)?
