It refers to those phenomena associated with the underlying tendency of conceit: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, craving-contact, aversion-contact, and ignorance-contact; the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application, sustained application, patience, view, liberation; remorse, lack of remorse, elation, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire-to-act, mindfulness, fear; and the underlying tendencies of affliction, views, doubt, precepts-and-rituals, craving, aversion, envy, parsimony, ignorance, and restlessness. These are called the category of the underlying tendency of conceit.

What is the category of restlessness (*uddhacca-nīvaraṇa*)? It refers to those phenomena associated with restlessness: namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, craving-contact, aversion-contact, and ignorance-contact; the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity; feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, initial application (*vitarka*), sustained application (*vicāra*), patience, view, liberation; remorse, lack of remorse, elation, joy, mental exertion, faith, desire-to-act, mindfulness, fear; the underlying tendency of afflictions, the underlying tendency of views, the underlying tendency of doubt, the underlying tendency of rules and observances, the underlying tendency of craving, the underlying tendency of aversion, the underlying tendency of envy, the underlying tendency of avarice, the underlying tendency of ignorance, and the underlying tendency of pride—these are called the category of restlessness.
What is the factor of concentration with vitarka and vicāra? It refers to those factors associated with concentration that possess vitarka and vicāra, namely:

the mind element (manodhātu), the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu); mental contact, name-contact, contact of knowledge, contact belonging to the category of knowledge, and contact belonging to the category of ignorance; the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya); feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), vitarka, vicāra, patience (kṣānti), view (dṛṣṭi), wisdom (jñāna), liberation (vimukti); non-delusion (amoha), pliancy (prasrabdhi), gladness (prāmodya), joy (prīti), mental exertion (cittapragraha), mental tranquility (cittaprasāda), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), mental equanimity (cittopekṣā); the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya), the faculty of exertion (vīryendriya), the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya), and the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya). These are called the factors of concentration with vitarka and vicāra.

What is the factor of concentration with vitarka and without vicāra? It refers to those factors associated with concentration with vitarka and without vicāra, namely: the mind-element (manodhātu), the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu); mental contact (manas-saṃsparśa), name-contact (nāma-saṃsparśa), contact of clarity (vidyā-saṃsparśa), contact belonging to the portion of clarity (vidyā-bhāgīya-saṃsparśa), contact belonging to the portion of ignorance (avidyā-bhāgīya-saṃsparśa); the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya), and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya); feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), vitarka, vicāra, patience (kṣānti), view (dṛṣṭi), knowledge (jñāna), liberation (vimukti); non-delusion (amoha), pliancy (prasrabdhi), gladness (prāmodya), joy (prīti), mental exertion (citta-vīrya), mental tranquility (citta-praśrabdhi), faith (śraddhā), desire (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), mental equanimity (citta-upekṣā); the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya), the faculty of energy (vīryendriya), the faculty of mindfulness (smṛtīndriya), and the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya). These are called the factor of concentration with vitarka and without vicāra.
What are the factors of concentration without vitarka and without vicāra? They are those phenomena associated with concentration without vitarka and without vicāra:

namely, the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact, name-contact, contact of clarity, contact belonging to the portion of clarity, and contact belonging to the portion of ignorance; the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling, perception, volition, contact, attention, vitarka, vicāra, patience, view, knowledge, liberation; non-delusion, pliancy, serenity, joy, mental exertion, mental tranquility, faith, desire, heedfulness, mindfulness, mental equanimity; and the faculty of faith, the faculty of mindfulness, and the faculty of wisdom. These are called the factors of concentration without vitarka and without vicāra.

What are the factors associated with the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*)? Those phenomena associated with the concentration of emptiness are: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāmasaṃsparśa*), contact with clarity (*vidyāsaṃsparśa*), and contact that is a factor of clarity (*vidyāṅgasaṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittapragraha*), mental tranquility (*cittaprasāda*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*); the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of exertion (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). These are called the factors of the concentration of emptiness.

What are the factors associated with the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*)? Those factors that are associated with the signless concentration are: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāmasaṃsparśa*), and contact pertaining to clear knowledge (*vidyāṅgasaṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittotsāha*), mental tranquility (*cittaprasāda*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*); the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). These are called the factors associated with the signless concentration.

What are the factors associated with the concentration of wishlessness (*appaṇihita-samādhi*)? Those phenomena associated with the concentration of wishlessness are: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), contact of clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), and contact associated with the factor of clarity (*vidyāṅga-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittapragraha*), mental tranquility (*cittaprasāda*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*); the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). These are called the factors associated with the concentration of wishlessness.

What is the constituent of the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*)? Those factors associated with the faculty of faith, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāmasaṃsparśa*), contact with clarity (*vidyāsaṃsparśa*), contact belonging to the category of clarity (*vidyābhāgīyasaṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittavīrya*), mental pliancy (*cittakarmaṇyatā*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*). Excluding the faculty of faith itself, from the concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*), these are called the constituent of the faculty of faith.
What is the faculty of energy (vīryendriya) category?

It refers to those phenomena associated with the faculty of energy: namely, the mind-element (manodhātu), the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu), mental contact (cittasparśa), designation-contact (adhivacanasparśa), contact pertaining to the factor of clear knowledge (vidyāṅgasparśa), the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), initial application (vitarka), sustained application (vicāra), patience (kṣānti), view (dṛṣṭi), knowledge (jñāna), liberation (vimukti), non-delusion (amoha), pliancy (praśrabdhi), serenity (prasāda), gladness (prāmodya), joy (prīti), tranquility of mind (cittapraśrabdhi), faith (śraddhā), desire-to-act (chanda), heedfulness (apramāda), mindfulness (smṛti), equanimity of mind (cittopekṣā)—excluding the faculty of energy itself—and from the concentration with initial and sustained application up to the faculty of wisdom (prajñendriya). These are called the faculty of energy category.

What is the factor of the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*)? Those phenomena associated with the faculty of mindfulness, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), contact of clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), contact associated with the portion of clarity (*vidyā-bhāgīya-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy of faith (*śraddhā-prasāda*), serenity (*praśrabdhi*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*citta-vīrya*), mental tranquility (*citta-praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and mental equanimity (*citta-upekṣā*). Excluding the faculty of mindfulness itself, [it includes] from the concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation up to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). This is called the factor of the faculty of mindfulness.

What is the constituent of the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)? Any dharma associated with the faculty of concentration, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manaḥsaṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāmasaṃsparśa*), contact of clarity (*vidyāsaṃsparśa*), contact belonging to the category of clarity (*vidyābhāgīyasaṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), patience (*kṣānti*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), knowledge (*jñāna*), liberation (*vimukti*); non-delusion (*amoha*), pliancy (*prasrabdhi*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*cittapragraha*), mental tranquility (*cittaprasāda*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), mental equanimity (*cittopekṣā*); the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), the faculty of exertion (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*). These are called the constituent of the faculty of concentration.

What is the factor of the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*)? Those phenomena associated with the faculty of wisdom, namely: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*); mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa*), name-contact (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), contact of clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), contact belonging to the category of clarity (*vidyā-bhāgīya-saṃsparśa*); the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), initial inquiry (*vitarka*), sustained investigation (*vicāra*), liberation (*vimukti*); pliancy of faith (*śraddhā-prasāda*), gladness (*prāmodya*), joy (*prīti*), mental exertion (*citta-vīrya*), mental tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), faith (*śraddhā*), desire (*chanda*), heedfulness (*apramāda*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), and mental equanimity (*citta-upekṣā*); from the concentration with initial inquiry and sustained investigation up to the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*). These are called the factor of the faculty of wisdom.
Regarding the eye-consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns the factors associated with the eye-consciousness element.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the visual consciousness element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) are excluded.
The visual consciousness element refers to the portion of mental consciousness that lacks an objective condition (*anālambana*).
The four consciousness elements of the body—namely, the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousness elements—are likewise.
As for the mind element (*manodhātu*), with how many factors is it associated?
Question: What dharmas? Answer:
Dharmas associated with the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
Exclude all other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas not associated with the mind-element (*manodhātu*) are excluded.
As for the mind-element, it refers to the portion of the mind-element that consists of non-objective (*anālambana*) dharmas.
Regarding the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
It is asking about the factors associated with the mental consciousness element.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the mental consciousness element (manovijñānadhātu) are excluded.
The consciousness element refers to that which lacks the factors of the basis of cognition (*āśraya*).
Regarding bodily contact (*kāyasparśa*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the factors associated with body-contact,
setting aside other factors—
what factors are being set aside?
Except for those phenomena associated with body-contact.
Body-contact refers to the mental consciousness-element that is without an object.
With how many phenomena is mind-contact associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with mind-contact;
all other dharmas are excluded.
What dharmas are excluded?
Non-associated-with-mind-contact dharmas are excluded.
Mind-contact refers to those factors that lack an objective referent (anālambana).
Regarding "contact" (sparśa), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
It is asking about the factors associated with contact.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas that are not associated with contact and are not termed "contact."
Regarding "contact by designation" (*nāma-saṃsparśa*), it refers to that which lacks the constituent parts of a dharma-base.
Regarding "contact by opposition" (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the dharmas associated with contact (sparśa-samprayukta),
setting aside other dharmas—
what dharmas are excluded?
Except for those phenomena associated with contact.
Regarding contact, this refers to the mental consciousness element that has no object.
With how many phenomena is the contact of craving associated?
Question: What dharmas?
Question: Dharmas associated with contact of craving;
excluding all other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas not associated with the contact of craving (*tṛṣṇā-sparśa*) are excluded.

Regarding the contact of craving: this refers to the portion of the bases of consciousness that are without objects, the wholesome and neutral portions of the mental consciousness, and the portions associated with the various afflictions that are unwholesome and not associated with the contact of craving.
With how many factors is the contact of aversion associated?
What factors are asked about?
It asks about the factors associated with the contact of aversion.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with contact accompanied by ill-will (*vyāpāda*).

Contact of aversion refers to those factors of the aggregate of mental objects that are not associated with aversion, as well as those factors of the aggregate of consciousness that are wholesome or neutral, or those factors associated with unwholesome defilements that are not associated with contact of aversion.
Regarding "clear contact" (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns the factors associated with the constituent parts of clear contact.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with contact that is not accompanied by ignorance (avidyā-saṃsparśa) are excluded.
The division of contact with clarity consists of: the portion of factors dissociated from mind, the portion of non-noble mental consciousness, and the portion of noble wisdom.
With how many factors is contact with ignorance associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with contact conditioned by ignorance;
all other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with contact that is not associated with ignorance are excluded.

"Contact associated with ignorance" refers to the portions of the factors of existence (dharmas) that lack an object-condition, as well as the wholesome and indeterminate portions of mental consciousness.
Regarding the contact of the bright portion (*ālokabhāgīya-sparśa*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
It is asking about the factors associated with the contact of the bright portion.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with contact that is not part of the division of non-illumination (avidyā-bhāga) are excluded.

Regarding the contact of the bright side (*vidyāpakṣa-sparśa*), this refers to the non-noble portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that lacks the factors of the bright side, as well as the noble wisdom portion.
With how many factors is the contact of the ignorance side (*avidyāpakṣa-sparśa*) associated?
Question: What dharmas are asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with contact that is a portion of ignorance;
all other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those associated with contact that is not part of ignorance (avidyā-bhāgīya-sparśa) are excluded.
Contact that is part of ignorance refers to the wholesome and indeterminate portions of mental consciousness that lack an object, as well as those belonging to the noble portion (ārya-bhāga).
Regarding the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns those factors associated with the faculty of pleasure.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas not associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).

The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) refers to the portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that is without an object, as well as the portions of the bodily faculties of pain (*duḥkhendriya*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
With how many factors is the faculty of pain associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the phenomena associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),
setting aside other phenomena—
what phenomena are being set aside?
Excluding those factors associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*),

the faculty of suffering consists of the portion of mental consciousness that is without an object (*anālambana*) and the portions of the faculties of bodily pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
With how many factors is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) associated?
Question: What dharmas? Answer:
Dharmas associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*);
exclude all other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) are excluded.

As for the faculty of joy, it refers to that portion of the factors of the body which lack an object (*anālambana*), as well as the portions of the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
With how many factors is the faculty of grief associated?
What factors are being asked about?
It is the factors associated with the faculty of grief that are being asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*)?

It refers to the portions of the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) that are dissociated from the body and the portions of the faculties of mental joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
With how many factors is the faculty of equanimity associated (*samprayukta*)?
Question: What dharmas? Question:
Dharmas associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Exclude all other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya) are excluded.

As for the faculty of equanimity, it refers to the portion of the dharma-body that is without objects, the portions of the faculties of pleasure (sukhendriya) and pain (duḥkhendriya), and the portions of the mental consciousness associated with the faculties of joy (saumanasyendriya) and grief (daurmanasyendriya).
Regarding the dharma of feeling (*vedanā*), with how many dharmas is it associated?
What kind of dharmas are being asked about?
It is asking about the dharmas associated with feeling.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas not associated with feeling are excluded.
Feeling (vedanā) is that which has no object-condition (anālambana-dharma).
The same applies to perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), and attention (manasikāra).
With how many factors is awareness (bodha) associated?
Question: What dharmas? Question: Dharmas associated with enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*).
With the exception of other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Non-associated-with-vitarka dharmas are excluded.
"Vitarka" refers to the portion of the dharma-body that lacks both vitarka and vicāra, and the portion of the mental consciousness that possesses vicāra but lacks vitarka.
Regarding "contemplation" (vipaśyanā): with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
It is asking about the factors associated with contemplation.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those not associated with the contemplation of impermanence are excluded.

Regarding "observation" (*vitarka*): it refers to the factor of the dharma-body that lacks observation, and the factor of mental consciousness that lacks both initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*).
Regarding "patience" (*kṣānti*): with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being inquired about?
Question: Regarding the phenomena associated with patience (*kṣānti*),
setting aside other phenomena—
what phenomena are set aside?
Excluding the factors associated with patience (*kṣānti*).
Patience refers to the factors of the absence of objects, the portion of mental consciousness, and the portions of knowledge and doubt.
How many factors are associated with vision (*dṛṣṭi*)?
Question: What dharmas?
Question: Dharmas associated with views.
Excluding all other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those not associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*) are excluded.
"View" refers here to the portion of the dharma-body that lacks an object and the portion of consciousness characterized by doubt.
With how many factors is wisdom associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Wisdom-associated factors are being asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas that are not associated with non-wisdom (*ajñāna*).

Regarding "wisdom" (*jñāna*): it refers to the portion of the factors of a dharma that is without an object (*anālambana*), the portion of consciousness that is non-noble (*anārya*), and the portion of noble patience (*āryakṣānti*).
Regarding "liberation" (*vimukti*): with how many factors is it associated?
What kind of factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the factors associated with liberation,
setting aside other factors—
what factors are set aside?
Except for those factors associated with liberation.
Liberation refers to the portion of consciousness and doubt that are without objects.
With how many factors is non-attachment associated?
Question: What dharmas? Answer:
Dharmas associated with non-greed;
excluding all other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Dharmas associated with non-greed (*alobha*) are excluded.

Non-greed refers to those parts of the dharma-body that lack an object, those parts of the mental consciousness that are unwholesome or neutral, those wholesome parts that do not belong to the desire realm, or those parts of the desire realm that are free from ill-will (*avyāpāda*).
Furthermore, there is a portion of the desire realm that is not associated with non-greed, yet is associated with non-hatred and non-delusion.
Regarding non-hatred: with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the factors associated with non-ill will,
setting aside other factors—
what factors are set aside?
Except for those factors associated with non-ill-will (*avyāpāda*).

Non-ill-will refers to: factors that lack an object; the unwholesome and indeterminate portions of the mental constituent (*manodhātu*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); wholesome portions that do not belong to the desire realm; and the portion of non-greed (*alobha*) within the desire realm.
Furthermore, there is a portion of the desire realm that is not associated with non-hatred, yet is associated with non-greed and non-delusion.
Regarding non-delusion, with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Dharmas associated with non-delusion,
excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those factors associated with non-delusion (*amoha*).
Non-delusion refers to the factorless portion of the mental constituents (*dharmāyatana*) and the unwholesome and neutral portions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
With how many factors is confidence (*śraddhā*) associated?
Question: What dharmas? Question:
Dharmas associated with compliant faith (*anulomikī śraddhā*).
Exclude all other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with non-conformity to faith are excluded.
What is conformity to faith?
That is to say, regarding the factors of the dharma-base that are without an object, as well as the unwholesome or neutral portions of the mental consciousness:
with how many factors is remorse associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the factors associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*),
with the exception of other factors,
which factors are excluded?
Except for those factors associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*).

Remorse refers to that which is not associated with the factors of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), nor with the factors of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) or the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), but rather with the factor of the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) that is not associated with remorse.
With how many factors is non-regret associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns the factors associated with non-regret.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas that are not associated with non-regret.

Non-remorse (*avippaṭisāra*) means it does not have the factors of the aggregate of mental objects (*dhammakkhandha*), nor the factors of the faculty of mental grief (*domanassindriya*) or the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*) within the aggregate of consciousness; rather, it is not associated with non-remorse, but is associated with the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*).
With how many factors is "gladness" (*pāmojja*) associated?
Question: Which phenomena?
Answer: Phenomena associated with joy;
other phenomena are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas not associated with joy (*saumanasya*) are excluded.

"Joy" refers to the portion of the factors of the dharma-body that are without objects, the portion of the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the portion associated with the faculty of gladness (*prīti*) that is not associated with joy.
With how many factors is joy associated?
What factors are being asked about?
It is the factors associated with joy that are being asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas that are not associated with joy (*prīti*).

Regarding *pīti* (joy): it refers to that which is not associated with the factors of the dharma-body, nor with the mental consciousness, nor with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasya*), nor with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*), nor with the factors associated with dissatisfaction (*arati*) but rather associated with gladness (*saumanasya*).
With how many factors is *cittapragraha* (mental exertion) associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with mental exertion (*cittapragraha*).
All other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those not associated with mental exertion (*cittavīrya*) are excluded.
Mental exertion refers to those factors of the body that lack an object of perception (*anālambana*).
Regarding the mental factor of "absence of ill-will" (*abyāpāda*): with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns the factors associated with the mental factor of absence of ill-will.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding non-mental dharmas and excluding associated dharmas.

Regarding the exclusion of the mind (*citta-vivarjana*): this refers to those factors that lack the constituent parts of the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*) and the indeterminate portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As for faith (*śraddhā*), with how many factors is it associated?
What kind of factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding phenomena associated with faith,
setting aside other phenomena—
what phenomena are set aside?
Except for the factors associated with faith (*śraddhā*).
Faith refers to that which is not associated with the factors of the body (*kāyabhāga*) or the factors of doubt (*vicikitsābhāga*) within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
With how many factors is desire (*chanda*) associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with desire;
other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Dharmas not associated with desire are excluded.
"Desire" refers to those factors of the dharma-body that lack an object, as well as the portion of consciousness consisting of doubt.
With how many factors is heedfulness associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The factors associated with heedfulness are being asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas that are not associated with heedfulness (apramāda) are excluded.

Regarding heedfulness (*apramāda*): it refers to the absence of factors associated with the mental body (*kāyavijñānakāya*) and the unwholesome or indeterminate portions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As for mindfulness (*smṛti*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
Question: Regarding the factors associated with mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃprayukta-dharma*),
setting aside other factors,
what factors are set aside?
Excluding the factors associated with mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃprayukta-dharma*).
Mindfulness refers to the factor of the body (*kāya-bhāga*) that is without an object (*anālambana*) and the factor of doubt (*vicikitsā-bhāga*) within the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).
With how many factors is the equanimity of mind (*citta-upekṣā*) associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with equanimity of mind;
all other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas not associated with equanimity of mind (*citta-upekṣā*) are excluded.
Equanimity of mind refers to those factors of the body that lack an object (*anālambana*) and the indeterminate portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding "fear" (*bhaya*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
One is asking about the factors associated with fear.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with fear.

Regarding fear (*bhaya*): it refers to the factors of the aggregate of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), the factors of the consciousness aggregate, the joy faculty (*sukhendriya*), and the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*), excluding the factors associated with fear and those associated with the grief faculty (*daurmanasyendriya*).
As for the latent proclivities of the afflictions (*kleśānuśaya*), with how many factors are they associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with the latent tendencies of affliction;
other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions are excluded.

Regarding the underlying tendencies of the afflictions, this refers to the portions of the factors of existence that are without objects (*anālambana*), as well as the wholesome and indeterminate portions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Regarding the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns the factors associated with the latent tendency of views.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya) are excluded.

The latent tendency of views (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya) refers to those factors that are dissociated from the latent tendencies of views, namely: the category of the mind-base (manāyatana), the category of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) that is wholesome or neutral, and the category of afflictions associated with unwholesome factors that are not themselves associated with the latent tendencies of views.
With how many factors is the latent tendency of doubt associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The factors associated with the latent tendency of doubt are being asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of doubt (vicikitsā-anuśaya).

The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) refers to those factors that do not have [doubt] as their object, namely: the wholesome and indeterminate portions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and those portions associated with afflictions other than the latent tendency of doubt.
With how many factors is the fetter of the path of morality associated?
What factors are asked about?
The factors associated with the fetter of the path of morality are asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the path of non-precept.

The fetters of the path of morality (*śīlamārga-nīvaraṇa*) refer to those factors dissociated from the constituents of the body, the wholesome and indeterminate portions of mental consciousness, and those portions associated with afflictions that are not associated with the fetters of the path of morality.
With how many factors is the latent tendency of craving associated?
What factors are asked about?
The factors associated with the latent tendency of craving are asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of craving are excluded.

The latent tendency of craving (*rāgānuśaya*) refers to those factors that are dissociated from objects, the indeterminate portion of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the portion associated with afflictions that are not associated with the latent tendencies of craving or aversion.
With how many factors is the latent tendency of aversion associated?
What factors are asked about?
It is asked about the factors associated with the latent tendency of aversion.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the latent tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*).

The latent tendency of aversion refers to those factors that are dissociated from the constituents of the dharma-body, the wholesome and indeterminate constituents of the mental consciousness, and those factors associated with afflictions that are not associated with the latent tendency of aversion.
With how many factors is the latent tendency of envy associated?
What factors are asked about?
The factors associated with the latent tendency of envy are asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of envy (īrṣyānuśaya).

The latent tendency of envy (īrṣyānuśaya) refers to those factors that are dissociated from the latent tendencies, namely: the portion of the factors of the dissociated aggregates; the portion of consciousness that is wholesome or indeterminate; and the portion associated with afflictions that are unwholesome but not associated with the latent tendency of envy.
With how many factors is the underlying tendency of stinginess associated?
What factors are inquired about?
The factors associated with the underlying tendency of stinginess are inquired about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the underlying tendency of stinginess (*mātsarya-anuśaya*).

The latent tendency of stinginess (mātsarya-anuśaya) refers to those factors that are dissociated from the latent tendencies, namely: the portion of the mental consciousness that is wholesome or neutral, and the portion of unwholesome factors that are not associated with the latent tendency of stinginess but are associated with other latent afflictions.
With how many factors is the latent tendency of ignorance associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The factors associated with the latent tendency of ignorance are being asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya).

Regarding the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*), it refers to the factors of the category of non-objective phenomena (*anālambana-dharma*) and the wholesome and neutral portions of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The same applies to conceit (*māna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
With how many factors is the concentration with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*) associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with concentration that possesses both vitarka and vicāra;
all other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the concentration with vitarka and vicāra (savitarka-savicāra-samādhi) are excluded.

Concentration with vitarka and vicāra refers to the portion of the factors of enlightenment that lack an object, the portion of the mental consciousness that is not fixed, and the portion associated with the two concentrations.
In the concentration with no vitarka but with vicāra, how many factors are associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns the factors associated with the concentration with no vitarka but with vicāra.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the concentration that is without vitarka but with vicāra.
The concentration with no vitarka but with vicāra consists of the factors of the dharma-body, the indeterminate mental consciousness, and the factors associated with the two concentrations.
How many factors are associated with the concentration with neither vitarka nor vicāra?
Question: What are the phenomena?
Answer: The phenomena associated with concentration that is without vitarka and without vicāra;
all other phenomena are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the concentration that is without vitarka and without vicāra (avitarkāvicārā samādhi) are excluded.

This concentration without vitarka and vicāra refers to the category of factors dissociated from objects (anālambana-dharmāṅga), the category of indeterminate mental consciousness (manovijñāna-aniyata-bhāga), and the category associated with the two concentrations (dvaya-samādhi-saṃprayukta-bhāga).
Regarding the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), with how many factors is it associated?
What factors are being asked about?
The question concerns the factors associated with the concentration on emptiness.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas associated with the concentration of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi).

Regarding the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*): it refers to the factors of the non-objective dharma-body, the non-noble portion of mental consciousness, and the portions associated with signlessness (*animitta*) and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
As for the concentration on signlessness (*animitta-samādhi*), with how many factors is it associated?
Question: What dharmas are being asked about?
Answer: Dharmas associated with the signless concentration (animitta-samādhi);
all other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those dharmas associated with the concentration of signlessness (animitta-samādhi) are excluded.

"Concentration of signlessness" refers to the factors of the body that lack an object, the non-noble portion of mental consciousness, and the noble portions associated with emptiness (śūnyatā) and wishlessness (apraṇihita).
With how many factors is the concentration of wishlessness associated?
What factors are being asked about?
It is the factors associated with the concentration of wishlessness that are being asked about.
Excluding other dharmas.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Excluding those dharmas not associated with the concentration of wishlessness (apraṇihita-samādhi).

Regarding the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), it consists of the factors of the dharma-body that are without objects, the non-noble portion of mental consciousness, and the noble portions associated with emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and signlessness (*animitta*).
With how many factors is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) associated?
Question: What dharmas? Answer:
Dharmas associated with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*);
all other dharmas are excluded.
Which dharmas are excluded?
Those not associated with the faculty of faith are excluded.
The faculty of faith refers to those factors of the body that lack an object and those factors of the mental consciousness that are not noble.
The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) are also like this.
In the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, the character "shè" (射) in this sutra is "tuójiě" (脫解) in other editions.
Examining the nineteenth and twenty-first fascicles, it is explained that "shooting" refers to untainted contemplation (*anāsrava-vipaśyanā*).
The meaning is that the fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*) are like arrows being shot, for they cause injury.
The observation of the untainted (anāsrava) understands that [the object] is without harm; therefore, this name is established.
Fearing that later generations might see that many ancient editions all use the character "liberation" (vimukti) and consequently give rise to doubt, I have pointed this out.
Presented and pointed out.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others.

Preface to the Section on Pervasiveness. Chapter One: The Section on Pervasiveness. The Ten Conditions of the True Dharma Gate; the sevenfold revolution and ten practices of pervasiveness, which explain the equal entry into all dharmas.

The ten conditions are: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the support condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*), the karmic action condition (*karma-pratyaya*), the retribution condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*), the origination condition (*jāti-pratyaya*), the diversity condition (*vicitra-pratyaya*), the continuity condition (*santati-pratyaya*), and the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
What is meant by "conditioned cause" (*hetu-pratyaya*)? If a phenomenon is a cause, it is called a conditioned cause.
Furthermore, regarding the conditioned cause: if a phenomenon is common [to many] yet does not share a common maturation (*vipāka*), it is called a conditioned cause.

Furthermore, regarding causal conditions (*nidāna*): if a dharma has an object-condition (*sālambana*) or if a dharma lacks an object-condition but possesses retribution (*savipāka*), with the exception of the attainment of fruition (*phala-prāpti*), as well as other dharmas that lack an object-condition but are wholesome and possess retribution, and the four great elements—these are called causal conditions.
What is the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon arises and ceases, this is called the immediate condition.

Furthermore, regarding the immediate condition: whether a phenomenon has already ceased or has not yet ceased, if the phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*) arise according to their own intrinsic nature, or if that which previously ceased now exists in the present, this is called the immediate condition.
What is the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
All phenomena serve as object-conditions; when they give rise to mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) in accordance with their characteristics, this is called the object-condition.
What is the support-condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*)?

If a phenomenon has dependence, it is called a condition by way of dependence (*niśraya-pratyaya*). Furthermore, regarding the condition by way of dependence: if a phenomenon arises depending upon another phenomenon, that [latter] phenomenon is the condition by way of dependence for the former.

Depending on the body, there is bodily action; depending on speech, there is vocal action; depending on the mind, there is mental action. Depending on the four great elements, there are actions of body, speech, and mind. Depending on the earth, there are the activities of cultivation, the accumulation of seeds, and the populations of sentient beings, as well as medicinal herbs and forests. Depending on an evil friend, unwholesome and evil phenomena arise; depending on a virtuous friend, wholesome phenomena arise. Depending on the eye and depending on forms, visual consciousness and the phenomena associated with visual consciousness arise; the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.

Based on the internal great elements, the internal great elements arise; based on the internal great elements, the external great elements arise; based on the internal great elements, both internal and external great elements arise.

Based on the external great elements, the internal great elements arise; based on the external great elements, the external great elements arise; based on the external great elements, both internal and external great elements arise.

Based on the internal and external great elements, the internal great elements arise; based on the internal and external great elements, the external great elements arise; based on the internal and external great elements, both internal and external great elements arise.
Cessation is likewise so; this is called dependence on conditions.
What is meant by the condition of karma?
Karma is the condition of karma.
Whether it be non-karma that serves as the condition for karma, or whether karma arises from a cause distinct from karma—this is called the condition of karma.
What is called the condition of retribution (*vipāka-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon possesses retribution, this is termed the condition of retribution.
What is called the condition of origination (*samutthāna-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon can give rise to that which is to be produced, it is called the "condition of origination" (*jāti-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, regarding the condition of origination: if a phenomenon arises by itself and can cause others to flow forth, increase, and flourish—namely, the fetters of killing, the roots of goodness, the roots of unwholesomeness, mental consciousness, perception, volition, thought, and the four great elements—it is called the condition of origination.
What is meant by "distinct condition" (*anyathā-pratyaya*)?
If dharmas arise together, this is called a distinct condition.
What is meant by "successive condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon increases without interruption, this is called the condition of continuity (*saṃtati-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, regarding the condition of continuity: if a phenomenon is weak when first arising, middling when arising next, and superior when arising later.
When inferior dharmas serve as the condition for superior dharmas in their continuity, this is called the condition of continuity (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
What is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?
If a dharma is predominant, it is called the dominant condition.

Furthermore, regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is that by which a phenomenon is dominated, toward which it is directed, to which it returns, or toward which it inclines as it arises. This includes:

being dominated by desire (*chanda*), being dominated by diligence (*vīrya*), being dominated by the mind (*citta*), being dominated by reflection (*mīmāṃsā*); being dominated by greed (*lobha*), being dominated by hatred (*dveṣa*), being dominated by delusion (*moha*); being dominated by non-greed (*alobha*), being dominated by non-hatred (*adveṣa*), being dominated by non-delusion (*amoha*); being dominated by ethical discipline (*śīla*), being dominated by concentration (*samādhi*), being dominated by wisdom (*prajñā*); being dominated by the self (*ātman*), being dominated by the world (*loka*), being dominated by phenomena (*dharma*); being dominated by the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*), being dominated by the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; being dominated by the dominant itself; being dominated by the object (*viṣaya*); and being dominated by the basis (*āśraya*).
What is meant by "predominance through desire"?
If a phenomenon arises with desire as its superior factor, that desire serves as the predominant condition for that phenomenon.
It is the same for the predominance of energy, of the mind, of volition, of greed, of hatred, of delusion, of non-greed, of non-hatred, of non-delusion, and of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
What is meant by "self-mastery" (ātma-adhipateya)?
As the Buddha taught in the sūtras, there are three kinds of mastery.
What are these three?
There is supremacy of self, supremacy of the world, and supremacy of the Dharma.
What is meant by supremacy of self?
It is as when a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, gives rise to thoughts of evil and unwholesome dharmas within his mind.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Suppose I were to commit an evil and unwholesome deed in a secluded place;
having committed that evil and unwholesome deed, my own mind would feel regret and self-reproach."
A bhikṣu reflects in this way:

"I wish to uphold the prohibitive precepts and perfect my dignified deportment; even regarding minor transgressions, I shall fear them as if they were a vajra, and I shall train myself in accordance with the practice of the precepts."
This is called "having oneself as the authority.
Because a bhikṣu has himself as the authority, he abandons evil and unwholesome dharmas and cultivates wholesome dharmas; therefore, it is called "having oneself as the authority."
What is meant by "worldly predominance"?
It is when a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, gives rise to thoughts of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
The bhikṣu reflects in this way:
There are devas dwelling in all places throughout the world who possess the divine eye and know the minds of others.
From afar, these devas see me, yet from nearby, I do not see them.
They say to one another:
Observe this son of good family: having left the household life out of faith, he has abandoned the practice of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess the divine eye and know the minds of others; they see me from afar, yet do not see me when I am near.
Various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas said to one another:
"Observe this son of good family; having gone forth out of faith, he has abandoned the practice of evil and unwholesome dharmas.
The bhikṣu reflected thus:
"I wish to uphold the prohibitive precepts and perfect my dignified deportment.
If I should violate even a minor precept, I shall fear it as if it were a vajra, and I shall train myself in accordance with the practice of the precepts.
This is called mundane supremacy.
Because the bhikṣu acts as a preeminent influence for the world, he abandons evil and unwholesome dharmas and cultivates wholesome dharmas; therefore, he is called "preeminent in the world.
What is meant by being "preeminent in the Dharma"?
Just as a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, reflects thus:
"The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma according to the proper occasion; those possessed of wisdom can receive it and proceed toward Nirvāṇa."
This Dharma cannot be received by one who is covetous, one who is angry, one who is drowsy, one who is restless and regretful, or one who is full of doubt.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I desire to guard and uphold the prohibitive precepts and to perfect my dignified deportment."

If one fears even the slightest transgression of the precepts as if they were a vajra, and trains accordingly in the practice of the precepts, this is called "the predominance of the Dharma" (*dhammādhipateyya*).
Because the bhikṣu takes the Dharma as his predominance, he abandons evil and unwholesome states and cultivates wholesome states; therefore, it is called the predominance of the Dharma.
As a verse says:
"In this world there is no place, shielded from view, where one may commit evil deeds;
for it is only the person themselves who knows, whether [the act] was empty or real."
One who speaks without falsehood is superior; thus they do not bring ruin upon themselves.
If there should be a transgression, they know it and do not conceal it.
When the wise and the devas see one committing evil in this world, [they take note].
By means of this supreme practice of mine, I am the supreme bhikṣu in the world;
following the supreme Dharma, I do not regress from the true Dharma.
Having conquered Māra through the power of my excellence, I have personally realized the supreme nirvāṇa.

"Far removed, having abandoned the six sense-faculties, extinguishing suffering and no longer undergoing existence, having already sunk [into nirvana], one does not return; forever free from birth and death.
This is called the threefold supremacy.
What is meant by the predominance of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?

When the eye sees forms and contemplates forms, whether the eye-faculty gives rise to the objective sphere of form or to mental factors (*caitasika*), this phenomenon is superior due to the eye-faculty; this is called the predominance of the eye-faculty.
The predominance of the faculties of the ear, nose, tongue, and body is likewise.
What is meant by the predominance of the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*)?

The mind cognizes phenomena and contemplates phenomena; the mental faculty is sovereign, taking phenomena as its object. When mental concomitants arise in relation to these phenomena, this mental faculty is preeminent; this is called the predominance of the mental faculty.
What is meant by "predominance as predominance"?
If a dharma first arises and subsequently other dharmas follow its function, this is called "predominance as predominance.
What is meant by "predominance of the object"?
If all objects of perception are superior to their respective entities, this is called the predominance of the object (*ālambanādhipati*).
What is meant by the predominance of the basis (*āśrayādhipati*)?
If all phenomena are superior to their respective bases, this is called the predominance of the basis.
How many conditions are there?
Four. What are the four?
Concomitance, arising, increase, and retribution—these are called the four conditions of causes.
This refers to the sense of "causing birth," like that of a mother and her child.
"Immediate" refers to the sense of "succession," like taking one's place in a seat.
"Object" (*viṣaya*) has the meaning of "that which is shot at," like an arrow.
"Basis" (*āśraya*) has the meaning of "that upon which something rests," like a house.
"Action" (*karma*) has the meaning of "doing," like commanding someone to work.
"Result" (*vipāka*) has the meaning of "outflow," like a tree producing fruit.
"Arising" (*utpatti*) has the meaning of "origination," like a sprout from a seed.
"Dissociation" (*visaṃyoga*) has the meaning of "inseparability," like members of a retinue.
"Continuity" (saṃtati) has the meaning of growth, as in the growth of wealth.
"Predominance" (adhipati) has the meaning of sovereignty, as in a king of men.

Regarding the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) and the immediate condition (anantara-pratyaya): either the causal condition is the immediate condition, or the causal condition is not the immediate condition.
What is meant by "the causal condition that is also the immediately preceding condition"?
If a phenomenon arises through a cause and subsequently ceases, this is called the causal condition that is also the immediately preceding condition.
What is meant by "the causal condition that is not the immediately preceding condition"?

If a phenomenon arises from a cause that is not subject to cessation, or if it has not yet ceased, this is called a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) but not an immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*).
Regarding those that are neither causal nor immediate conditions: they may be non-causal conditions that are indeed immediate conditions, or they may be neither causal nor immediate conditions.
What is meant by that which is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) but is an immediately preceding condition (*anantara-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon does not arise and cease through a cause, it is not a causal condition but is an immediately preceding condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a causal condition nor an immediately preceding condition?
If a dharma is neither a cause nor subject to arising and ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, this is called being neither a causal condition nor an immediate condition.
Regarding the causal condition and the object-condition: either the causal condition is the object-condition, or the causal condition is not the object-condition.
What is meant by "the causal condition that is simultaneously the objective condition"?
If a phenomenon has an object as its cause, this is called the causal condition that is simultaneously the objective condition.
What is meant by "the causal condition that is not the objective condition"?
If a dharma has a cause but lacks an object, this is called a causal condition that is not an object-condition.

Regarding those that are neither causal conditions nor object-conditions, there are cases where something is a causal condition but not an object-condition, or cases where it is neither a causal condition nor an object-condition.
What is meant by "not a causal condition, but rather a condition as an object"?
If a phenomenon does not exist as a cause but exists as an object, this is called "not a causal condition, but rather a condition as an object.
What is meant by "neither a causal condition nor a condition as an object"?
If a dharma is neither a cause nor an object, it is called "neither a causal condition nor an object-condition.
Regarding the causal condition and the supporting condition: all causal conditions are supporting conditions;
however, there are no non-causal conditions that are supporting conditions.

Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*): either the causal condition is itself the karmic condition, or the causal condition is not the karmic condition.
What is meant by "the causal condition is itself the karmic condition"?
If a phenomenon has karma as its cause and is capable of producing karma, this is called the causal condition being itself the karmic condition.
What is meant by "conditioned by cause, but not conditioned by karma"?
If a phenomenon has a cause that is not karma, or if karma cannot produce further karma, this is called being conditioned by cause but not conditioned by karma.
There is no case where something is not conditioned by cause yet is conditioned by karma.

Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the retributive condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*): either the causal condition is itself the retributive condition, or the causal condition is not the retributive condition.
What is meant by the causal condition being itself the retributive condition?
If a phenomenon has a retribution because it arises from this [cause], this is called the causal condition being itself the retributive condition.

What is meant by being a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) but not a retributive condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*)? If a dharma has a cause but no retribution, this is called being a causal condition but not a retributive condition.
There is no case of being a non-causal condition that is simultaneously a retributive condition.
The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is the condition for arising; alternatively, the causal condition is itself the condition for arising, or the causal condition is not the condition for arising.
What is meant by "the causal condition is itself the condition for arising"?
If a phenomenon arises because of a cause, this is called "the causal condition is itself the condition for arising."
What is meant by "condition as cause but not condition as origination"?
If a phenomenon is a cause but not an origination, this is called "condition as cause but not condition as origination.
There is no such thing as being a condition as origination without being a condition as cause.

Regarding causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and specific conditions (*viśeṣa-pratyaya*): either the causal condition is itself a specific condition, or the causal condition is not a specific condition.
What is meant by "the causal condition is itself a specific condition"?
If a phenomenon has a common cause, this is called "the causal condition is itself a specific condition."
What is meant by "condition as cause, not as a distinct condition"?
If a phenomenon is a cause but not a concomitant [condition], this is called "condition as cause, not as a distinct condition.
There is no such thing as being a non-condition as cause while being a distinct condition.
There are conditions that are both causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and continuous conditions (*santati-pratyaya*), or there are causal conditions that are not continuous conditions.
What is meant by a causal condition that is also a continuous condition?
If a cause increases and continues until it produces a third [moment], this causal condition is a continuous condition (*santati-pratyaya*).
What is meant by a causal condition that is not a continuous condition?
If a cause lacks the conditions for increase, or even if it increases, it is unable to produce a third [moment], this is called a causal condition that is not a continuous condition.
That which is not a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is a continuous condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); such a thing does not exist.
Regarding the causal condition and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), either the causal condition is itself the dominant condition, or the causal condition is not the dominant condition.
What is meant by "the causal condition is itself the dominant condition"?
If a phenomenon is both a cause and a dominant factor, then that causal condition is also a dominant condition.
What is meant by "a causal condition that is not a dominant condition"?
If a phenomenon is a causal condition but not a dominant condition, it is called a "causal condition that is not a dominant condition.
Regarding conditions that are neither causal nor dominant: they may be non-causal conditions that are dominant conditions, or they may be neither causal nor dominant conditions.
What is meant by that which is not a causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) but is a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)?
If a dharma is not a cause but is a dominant factor, this is called "not a causal condition but a dominant condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a causal condition nor a dominant condition?
If a phenomenon is neither a cause-condition nor a predominance-condition, it is called "neither cause-condition nor predominance-condition.
Regarding the immediate-condition and the object-condition: either the immediate-condition is the object-condition, or the immediate-condition is not the object-condition.
What is meant by an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) that is also an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon arises and ceases while having an object, this is called an immediately preceding condition that is also an object-condition.
What is meant by an immediately preceding condition that is not an object-condition?
If a phenomenon arises and ceases without an objective field (*ālambana*), this is called an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but not an objective-field condition.

There are cases that are neither immediately preceding conditions nor objective-field conditions; or cases that are immediately preceding conditions but not objective-field conditions; or cases that are neither immediately preceding conditions nor objective-field conditions.
What is meant by that which is not an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) but is an object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not ceased and possesses an object, this is called being not an immediate condition but an object condition.
What is meant by that which is neither an immediate condition nor an object-condition?
If a dharma is not subject to arising and ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, it lacks an object-condition; this is called being neither an immediate condition nor an object-condition.
Regarding the immediate condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) and the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*): the immediate condition is the support condition.
There is no case where something is not an immediate condition but is a support condition.
Regarding the immediate condition and the kamma condition (*kamma-paccaya*): either the immediate condition is the kamma condition, or the immediate condition is not the kamma condition.
What is meant by the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) being the karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon arises and ceases as karma, or if karma is capable of producing further karma, this is called the immediate condition being the karmic condition.
What is meant by "proximate condition but not karmic condition"?
If a dharma arises and ceases and it is not karma, or if karma cannot produce karma, this is called "proximate condition but not karmic condition."

There are [factors] that are neither immediate conditions nor karmic conditions; or those that are immediate conditions but not karmic conditions; or those that are neither immediate conditions nor karmic conditions.
What are those that are immediate conditions and are karmic conditions?

If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, this karma can produce karma; this is called being a non-immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) but not a karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*).
What is meant by being neither an immediate condition nor a karmic condition?
If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, it is not karma; or if karma cannot produce karma—this is called being neither an immediate condition nor a karmic condition.

Regarding the immediate condition (*samanantara-paccaya*) and the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*): either the immediate condition is the resultant condition, or the immediate condition is not the resultant condition.
What is meant by the immediate condition being the resultant condition?
If a phenomenon arises and ceases and possesses retribution, this is called the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which is also the retribution condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*).
What is meant by an immediate condition that is not a retribution condition?
If a phenomenon arises and ceases and lacks retribution, this is called an immediate condition that is not a retribution condition.
Regarding the non-immediate condition and the retribution condition: either the non-immediate condition is the retribution condition, or the non-immediate condition is not the retribution condition.
What is meant by "the non-immediate condition is the retribution condition"?
If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not ceased yet possesses retribution, this is called being a non-immediate condition but a retribution condition.
What is meant by being neither an immediate condition nor a retribution condition?

If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, it has no retribution; this is called being neither a condition of immediate succession (*anantara-pratyaya*) nor a condition of retribution (*vipāka-pratyaya*).
There is no such thing as an immediate succession condition that is also an arising condition (*jāti-pratyaya*).

There are cases where the immediate condition is not the arising condition; cases where the immediate condition is the arising condition; and cases where the immediate condition is neither the immediate condition nor the arising condition.
What is meant by "the immediate condition is the arising condition"?

If a phenomenon is neither arising nor ceasing, and it can arise while not yet ceased, this is called being a non-immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) but not an arising condition (*utthāna-pratyaya*).
What is meant by being neither a non-immediate condition nor an arising condition?

If a phenomenon is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not ceased and does not arise, this is called being neither a condition of immediate succession (anantara-pratyaya) nor a condition of arising (utpatti-pratyaya).
There is no such thing as a condition of immediate succession that is a distinct condition (anya-pratyaya).

That which is not an immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is a distinct condition (anyathā-pratyaya); or, that which is not an immediately preceding condition may be a distinct condition, or it may be neither an immediately preceding condition nor a distinct condition.
What is meant by "that which is not an immediately preceding condition is a distinct condition"?

If a phenomenon is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, and these are simultaneous, this is called being a non-immediate condition (*na-anantara-pratyaya*) and a different condition (*anya-pratyaya*).
What is meant by being neither a non-immediate condition nor a different condition?

If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, it is not common; this is called being neither an immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) nor a homogeneous condition (*sabhāga-pratyaya*).
Since an immediate condition is a continuous condition (*santati-pratyaya*), it does not exist [in such cases].

There are those that are not immediate conditions but are continuity conditions; those that are immediate conditions and are also continuity conditions; and those that are neither immediate conditions nor continuity conditions.
What is meant by "not an immediate condition but a continuity condition"?
If a phenomenon is neither arising nor ceasing,

and while it has not yet ceased, this growth continues until it can produce a third [moment], this is called a non-immediate condition (*asamanantara-pratyaya*) that is a continuity condition (*santati-pratyaya*).
What is meant by that which is neither an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) nor a continuity condition (*santati-pratyaya*)?

If a dharma is not subject to arising and ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, or if it does not increase, or if it increases but cannot lead to the production of a third [moment], this is called being neither an immediate condition nor a continuity condition.
There is no case where the immediately preceding condition (anantara-pratyaya) is also the dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Alternatively, something may be an immediately preceding condition but not a dominant condition, or it may be neither an immediately preceding condition nor a dominant condition.
What is meant by that which is not an immediate condition (anantara-pratyaya) but is a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)?
If a phenomenon is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, and thus acts as a dominant factor, this is called being not an immediate condition but rather a dominant condition.
What is meant by that which is neither an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) nor a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?

If a phenomenon is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, it is not a predominant condition; this is what is meant by being neither an immediate condition nor a predominant condition.

Regarding the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): either the immediate condition is the causal condition, or the immediate condition is not the causal condition.
What is meant by the immediate condition being the causal condition?
If a phenomenon’s arising and ceasing is a cause, this is called the immediately preceding condition as a causal condition.
What is meant by the immediately preceding condition not being a causal condition?
If a phenomenon’s arising and ceasing occurs, yet it is not a cause, this is called the immediately preceding condition not being a causal condition.

Regarding that which is neither an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) nor a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), or that which is an immediate condition but not a causal condition, or that which is neither an immediate condition nor a causal condition:
what is meant by "neither an immediate condition nor a causal condition"?
If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, this is called "not being a contiguous condition but being a causal condition.
What is meant by "neither being a contiguous condition nor being a causal condition"?
If a dharma is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, it is not a cause; this is called being neither an immediate condition nor a causal condition.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the support-condition (*nissaya-pratyaya*): the object-condition is the support-condition; there is no [case where] the object-condition is not the support-condition.
There is no case where an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is an objective support-condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*).
Regarding the object-condition and the karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*): either the object-condition is the karmic condition, or the object-condition is not the karmic condition.
What is meant by "having an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and being a karmic condition (karma-pratyaya)"?
