If a phenomenon has an object, is itself karma, or if karma can produce karma, this is called having an object-condition and being a karmic condition.
What is meant by being an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not an action-condition (*karma-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon possesses an object but is not an action, or if an action cannot produce another action, this is called being an object-condition but not an action-condition.

Regarding non-object-condition (anālambana-pratyaya) and karmic-condition (karma-pratyaya): either it is a non-object-condition that is a karmic-condition, or it is a non-object-condition that is not a karmic-condition.
What is meant by "a non-object-condition that is a karmic-condition"?

If a dharma has no objective sphere (*ālambana*), yet is karma, or if karma can produce karma, this is called "non-sphere-condition" (*anālambana-pratyaya*) which is also "karma-condition" (*karmapratyaya*).
What is meant by that which is neither "non-sphere-condition" nor "karma-condition"?
If a dharma has no object, it is not karma; if karma cannot produce karma, this is called the "non-object-condition and non-karma-condition" city.
Regarding the object-condition and the retribution-condition: either the object-condition is the retribution-condition, or the object-condition is not the retribution-condition.
What is meant by an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) that is also a retribution-condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon possesses both an object and retribution, it is called an object-condition that is also a retribution-condition.
What is meant by an object-condition that is not a retribution-condition?
If a dharma has an object but lacks retribution, it is called an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) but not a retribution-condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*).

Regarding that which is neither an object-condition nor a retribution-condition: either it is not an object-condition but is a retribution-condition, or it is neither an object-condition nor a retribution-condition.
What is meant by "not being an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) while being a retribution-condition (vipāka-pratyaya)"?
If a dharma lacks an object yet its condition possesses retribution, this is called "not being an object-condition while being a retribution-condition."
What is meant by "neither object-condition nor retribution-condition"?
If a dharma has no object and possesses no retribution, this is called neither object-condition nor retribution-condition.
Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) as a condition for arising: either the object-condition is a condition for arising, or the object-condition is not a condition for arising.
What is meant by the object-condition being a condition for arising?
If a phenomenon possesses an object and is an arising, this is called the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) which is also the "arising-condition" (samutthāna-pratyaya).
What is meant by an object-condition that is not an arising-condition?
If a phenomenon possesses an object but is not an arising, this is called the "object-condition" that is not the "arising-condition."
There are conditions that are not object-conditions but are arising-conditions; there are conditions that are not object-conditions and are not arising-conditions.
What are those that are not object-conditions but are arising-conditions?
If a phenomenon lacks an object and yet arises, this is called "having non-object as its condition" and "arising as its condition.
What is meant by "having non-object as its condition" and "not arising as its condition"?
If a phenomenon lacks an object and does not arise, this is called "having non-object as its condition" and "not arising as its condition."
The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the distinct condition (anya-pratyaya): either the object-condition is the distinct condition, or the object-condition is not the distinct condition.
What is meant by the object-condition being the distinct condition?
If a dharma has an object and is shared, this is called the object-condition as a distinct condition.
What is meant by the object-condition that is not a distinct condition?
If a dharma has an object and it is not shared, this is called the object-condition that is not a distinct condition.

There are conditions that are not object-conditions but are other-conditions; or, there are those that are not object-conditions yet are other-conditions, and those that are neither object-conditions nor other-conditions.
What is meant by being a condition that is not an object-condition but is an other-condition?
If a phenomenon has no objective sphere (*gocara*) and is common, this is called "having no objective sphere as its condition" and "having a different condition.
What is meant by "having no objective sphere as its condition" and "not having a different condition"?
If a phenomenon has no objective sphere and is not common, this is called "having no objective sphere as its condition" and "not having a different condition."

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the continuity-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): either the object-condition is the continuity-condition, or the object-condition is not the continuity-condition.
What is meant by the object-condition being the continuity-condition?

If a phenomenon has an object, is an increase, and can even give rise to a third [moment], this is called the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) which is also the continuity-condition (samanantara-pratyaya).
What is meant by an object-condition that is not a continuity-condition?

If a dharma has an object but does not increase, or if it increases but cannot continue until the third moment arises, this is called an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and not a continuity-condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

There are conditions that are not object-conditions but are continuity-conditions; or there are those that are not object-conditions yet are continuity-conditions; or there are those that are neither object-conditions nor continuity-conditions.
What is meant by "not an object-condition but a continuity-condition"?

If a dharma has no objective sphere (*ālambana*), yet it increases and can even give rise to a third [moment], this is called a non-sphere condition that is a continuity condition (*saṃtati-pratyaya*).
What is meant by a non-sphere condition that is not a continuity condition?

If a dharma has no objective sphere (*ālambana*), it does not increase; if it increases, it cannot even give rise to a third [moment]. This is called being a non-sphere condition (*anālambana-pratyaya*) and a non-continuity condition (*asamtāna-pratyaya*).
Object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya): either an object-condition is a predominant condition, or an object-condition is not a predominant condition.
What is meant by an object-condition that is a predominant condition?
If a dharma possesses an object and is predominant, this is called an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) that is also a predominance-condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
What is meant by an object-condition that is not a predominance-condition?
If a dharma has an object but is not a predominant condition, this is called an object-condition that is not a predominant condition.

Regarding non-object-conditions and predominant conditions: either they are non-object-conditions that are predominant conditions, or they are non-object-conditions that are not predominant conditions.
What is meant by "that which is not an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)"?
If a phenomenon lacks an object yet serves as a dominant condition, this is called "that which is not an object-condition is a dominant condition."
What is meant by being neither an object-condition nor a predominant condition?
If a dharma has no object and is not a predominant factor, this is called being neither an object-condition nor a predominant condition.

Regarding the object-condition (ālambanapratyaya) as the causal condition (hetupratyaya): sometimes the object-condition is the causal condition, and sometimes the object-condition is not the causal condition.
What is meant by the object-condition being the causal condition?
If a phenomenon possesses an object and is a cause, this is called "object-condition as causal condition.
What is meant by "object-condition that is not a causal condition"?
If a phenomenon possesses an object but is not a cause, this is called "object-condition that is not a causal condition."
Regarding non-object-condition (anālambana-pratyaya), it may be a causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), or it may not be a causal condition.
What is meant by a non-object-condition that is a causal condition?
If a dharma has no objective sphere (*ālambana*), this is called "non-sphere-condition" (*anālambana-pratyaya*) which is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
What is meant by "non-sphere-condition" that is not a causal condition?
If a dharma has no objective sphere and it is not a cause, this is called "non-sphere-condition" that is not a causal condition.

Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the immediate-condition (anantara-pratyaya): either the object-condition is the immediate-condition, or the object-condition is not the immediate-condition.
What is meant by the object-condition being the immediate-condition?
If a phenomenon possesses an object and is subject to arising and ceasing, this is called the "object-condition" (ālambana-pratyaya) and the "immediately preceding condition" (samanantara-pratyaya).
What is meant by being an object-condition but not an immediately preceding condition?
If a phenomenon possesses an object but is not subject to arising and ceasing, or has not yet ceased, this is called being an object-condition but not an immediately preceding condition.

Regarding the non-object-condition (anālambana-pratyaya) and the immediate-condition (samanantara-pratyaya): either it is a non-object-condition that is an immediate-condition, or it is a non-object-condition that is not an immediate-condition.
What is meant by a non-object-condition that is an immediate-condition?
If a dharma has no object and is subject to arising and ceasing, this is called "non-object-condition" (agocara-pratyaya) which is also "immediate-condition" (anantara-pratyaya).
What is meant by that which is a non-object-condition but not an immediate-condition?

If a dharma has no object of perception (*ālambana*), it is neither arising nor ceasing; if it has not yet ceased, this is called being a non-object-condition (*anālambana-pratyaya*) and a non-immediate-condition (*anantara-pratyaya*).

Regarding the dependence-condition (*niśraya-pratyaya*) and the karmic-condition (*karma-pratyaya*): either the dependence-condition is the karmic-condition, or the dependence-condition is not the karmic-condition.
What is meant by "conditioned by dependence" being "conditioned by karma"?
If a phenomenon is dependent, is karma, or if karma can produce karma, this is called "conditioned by dependence" being "conditioned by karma.
What is meant by "conditioned by dependence" not being "conditioned by karma"?
If a phenomenon is a basis-condition but is not karma, or if it is karma that cannot produce karma, this is called being a basis-condition but not a karma-condition.
There is no case where something is a non-basis-condition but a karma-condition.

Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the retribution-condition (vipāka-pratyaya): either the object-condition is the retribution-condition, or the object-condition is not the retribution-condition.
What is meant by the object-condition being the retribution-condition?
If a phenomenon is both an object-condition and possesses retribution, this is called the object-condition being the retribution-condition.
What is meant by being a dependence condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) but not a result-of-kamma condition (*vipāka-paccaya*)?
If a phenomenon is a dependence condition but not a result-of-kamma, this is called being a dependence condition but not a result-of-kamma condition.
There is no case of being a dependence condition that is not a result-of-kamma condition.
Regarding the condition of dependence (*nissaya-paccaya*), the condition of dependence may be a condition of origination (*upaniṣad-paccaya*) or it may not be a condition of origination.
What is meant by the condition of dependence being a condition of origination?
If a phenomenon is both a condition of dependence and a condition of origination, this is called the condition of dependence being a condition of origination.
What is meant by "condition as support but not condition as origination"?
If a phenomenon is a support but not an origination, this is called "condition as support but not condition as origination.
There is no case where something is a condition as origination but not a condition as support.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the support-condition (*nissaya-pratyaya*), the support-condition may be the object-condition, or the support-condition may not be the object-condition.
What is meant by the support-condition being the object-condition?
If a phenomenon is both a support and a concomitant, this is called the support-condition being the object-condition.
What is meant by "condition as support but not condition as distinct"?
If a phenomenon is a support but is not common [to others], this is called "condition as support but not condition as distinct.
There is no case where it is not a condition as support but is a condition as distinct.
Regarding the dependence condition as a continuity condition: either the dependence condition is a continuity condition, or the dependence condition is not a continuity condition.
What is meant by the dependence condition being a continuity condition?

If a phenomenon serves as a basis, increases, and even gives rise to a third [phenomenon], this is called the condition as basis (nissaya-paccaya) which is also the condition as continuity (anantara-paccaya).
What is meant by the condition as basis that is not the condition as continuity?

If a phenomenon depends on something else for its arising but does not increase, or if it increases but cannot continue until a third moment arises, this is called a condition by way of dependence (*āśraya-pratyaya*) and not a condition by way of continuity (*sambandha-pratyaya*).
There are no cases where the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) is a continuity-condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

Regarding the support-condition (niśraya-pratyaya) and the predominant-condition (adhipati-pratyaya): either the support-condition is a predominant-condition, or the support-condition is not a predominant-condition.
What is meant by "the condition of dependence being the predominant condition"?
If a phenomenon is both a condition of dependence and a predominant condition, this is called "the condition of dependence being the predominant condition.
What is meant by "the condition of dependence not being the predominant condition"?
If a dharma is a support-condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*) but not a predominant-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), this is called a support-condition that is not a predominant-condition.
There is no case where something is not a support-condition but is a predominant-condition.
A support-condition may be a causal-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); that is, a support-condition may either be a causal-condition or not a causal-condition.
What is meant by "conditioned by dependence" being a "causal condition"?
If a phenomenon is both dependent and a cause, this is called "conditioned by dependence" being a "causal condition.
What is meant by "conditioned by dependence" not being a "causal condition"?
If a dharma is a support-condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*) but not a cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is called a support-condition that is not a cause-condition.
There is no such thing as a support-condition that is a cause-condition.
Regarding the support-condition and the immediate-condition (*anantara-pratyaya*): a support-condition may be an immediate-condition, or a support-condition may not be an immediate-condition.
What is meant by "conditioned by dependence and being an immediate condition"?
If a phenomenon is dependent and undergoes arising and ceasing, this is called "conditioned by dependence and being an immediate condition.
What is meant by "conditioned by dependence but not an immediate condition"?

If a phenomenon is a supporting condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*) but is neither arising nor ceasing, or has not yet ceased, it is called a supporting condition that is not an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
There is no case where something that is not a supporting condition is an immediately preceding condition.
Regarding the object-condition as a dependence-condition: either the dependence-condition is the object-condition, or the dependence-condition is not the object-condition.
What is meant by the dependence-condition being the object-condition?
If a phenomenon has both a basis and an object, it is called a condition as basis and a condition as object.
What is meant by a condition as basis but not a condition as object?
If a phenomenon has a basis but no object, it is called a condition as basis but not a condition as object.
There is no case where an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is not an objective-condition (*viṣaya-pratyaya*).

Regarding the karma-condition (*karma-pratyaya*) and the retribution-condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*), either the karma-condition is the retribution-condition, or the karma-condition is not the retribution-condition.
What is meant by "karmic condition that is also a retribution condition"?
If a phenomenon is karma, capable of producing karma, and possesses retribution, this is called a karmic condition that is also a retribution condition.
What is meant by "karmic condition that is not a retribution condition"?
If a dharma is karma, capable of producing karma, and without retribution, this is called being a condition by way of karma but not a condition by way of retribution.

Regarding that which is neither a condition by way of karma nor a condition by way of retribution: it may be a condition by way of retribution despite not being a condition by way of karma, or it may be neither a condition by way of karma nor a condition by way of retribution.
What is meant by that which is not a karmic condition but is a retribution condition?
If it is not karma, or if karma is unable to produce further karma that has retribution, this is called that which is not a karmic condition but is a retribution condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a karmic condition nor a retributive condition?
If a phenomenon is not karma, or if karma is unable to produce further karma and lacks retribution, this is called being neither a karmic condition nor a retributive condition.
The kamma-condition (kamma-paccaya) may be a productive condition (janaka-paccaya), or the kamma-condition may not be a productive condition.
What is meant by the kamma-condition being a productive condition?
If a dharma is kamma and is capable of producing kamma, this is called the kamma-condition being a productive condition.
What is meant by "karma-condition that is not an origination-condition"?
If karma cannot produce karma and it is not an origination-condition, this is called a karma-condition that is not an origination-condition.

Regarding non-karma-conditions that are origination-conditions: either they are non-karma-conditions that are origination-conditions, or they are non-karma-conditions that are not origination-conditions.
What is meant by that which is not a karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*) but is a productive condition (*samutthāna-pratyaya*)?
If a dharma is not karma, or if karma cannot produce karma, this is called that which is not a karmic condition but is a productive condition.

What is meant by that which is neither a karmic condition nor a productive condition? If a dharma is not karma, or if karma cannot produce the arising of karma, this is called that which is neither a karmic condition nor a productive condition.
Karmic conditions and distinct conditions: either karmic conditions are distinct conditions, or karmic conditions are not distinct conditions.
What is meant by "karmic conditions that are distinct conditions"?
If a phenomenon is karma, capable of producing karma, and is common [to both], this is called a karmic condition that is a distinct condition.
What is meant by "karmic condition that is not a non-distinct condition"?
If a phenomenon is karma, capable of producing karma, and not shared [with others], this is called a karmic condition that is not a non-distinct condition.

Regarding conditions that are neither karmic nor non-distinct: either they are not karmic conditions but are non-distinct conditions, or they are neither karmic conditions nor non-distinct conditions.
What is meant by "not being a karmic condition but being a distinct condition"?
If a phenomenon is not karma, or if karma cannot produce karma, this is called "not being a karmic condition but being a distinct condition."
What is meant by "neither a karmic condition nor a distinct condition"?
If a phenomenon is not karma, or if karma cannot produce either karma or non-karma, this is called "neither a karmic condition nor a distinct condition."
Karmic conditions are either continuous conditions or karmic conditions that are not continuous conditions.
What is meant by a karmic condition that is a continuous condition?

If a dharma is karma and is capable of producing karma, this is called "growth" (*vṛddhi*); even up to being capable of producing a third [karma], this is termed the "karmic condition" (*karmapratyaya*), which is the "condition of continuity" (*saṃtānapratyaya*).
What is meant by a karmic condition that is not a condition of continuity?

If a dharma is an action (karma) or a birth-action that does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is called being an action-condition (karmapratyaya) but not a continuity-condition (saṃtānapratyaya).

Regarding what is neither an action-condition nor a continuity-condition: either it is not an action-condition but is a continuity-condition, or it is neither an action-condition nor a continuity-condition.
What is meant by that which is not a karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*) but is a continuity condition (*saṃtati-pratyaya*)?

If a phenomenon is not karma, or if karma gives rise to that which is not karma as its growth, continuing even to the third [moment], this is called that which is not a karmic condition but is a continuity condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a karmic condition nor a continuity condition?

If a phenomenon is not karma; or if, though it gives rise to karma, that karma does not increase; or if, though it increases, it does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is called being neither a karmic condition nor a continuity condition.

Regarding the karmic condition (*kamma-paccaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-paccaya*): either the karmic condition is the dominant condition, or the karmic condition is not the dominant condition.
What is meant by "the karmic condition is the dominant condition"?

If a phenomenon is an action (*karman*) or a productive action (*janaka-karman*) that is predominant (*adhipati*), it is called an action-condition (*karma-pratyaya*) that is also a predominance-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
What is meant by an action-condition that is not a predominance-condition?
If a phenomenon is an action or a productive action that is not predominant, it is called an action-condition that is not a predominance-condition.

Regarding non-karmic conditions and predominant conditions: either they are non-karmic conditions that are predominant conditions, or they are non-karmic conditions that are not predominant conditions.
What is meant by "non-karmic conditions that are predominant conditions"?
If a dharma is not karma, or if it is karma that produces what is not karma, this is predominance; this is called "non-karma condition as predominance condition.
What is meant by "non-karma condition as non-predominance condition"?

If a dharma is karma, or if that which is born from karma is neither karma nor the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), this is called being neither a karma-condition (*karma-pratyaya*) nor a dominant condition.
A karma-condition is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); a karma-condition is a causal condition.
Regarding non-karmic conditions, there are those that are causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), those that are not causal conditions, or those that are neither karmic conditions nor causal conditions.
What is meant by a non-karmic condition that is a causal condition?
If a phenomenon is not karma, or if karma arises with that which is not karma as its cause, this is called "non-karma-condition as causal condition.
What is meant by "non-karma-condition as non-causal condition"?
If a phenomenon is not karma, or if it is karma that arises as something not karma and not a cause, this is called "not being a karma-condition and not being a cause-condition.
Regarding the karma-condition and the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*): either the karma-condition is the immediate condition, or the karma-condition is not the immediate condition.
What is meant by "karmic condition as immediate condition"?
If a phenomenon arises from karma and that [karma] ceases immediately upon arising, this is called "karmic condition as immediate condition.
What is meant by "karmic condition not as immediate condition"?
If a dharma is produced by karma, is not subject to cessation, and has not yet ceased, this is called a karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*) that is not an immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*).
That which is not a karmic condition may be an immediate condition, or it may be neither a karmic condition nor an immediate condition.
What is meant by that which is not a karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*) but is an immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*)?
If a dharma is not karma, or if karma gives rise to what is not karma, and this [latter] arises and ceases, this is called that which is not a karmic condition but is an immediate condition.
What is meant by being neither a kamma-condition nor an immediate-condition?

If a dhamma is not kamma; or if kamma gives rise to what is not kamma; or if it is not subject to arising and ceasing; or if it has not yet ceased—this is called being neither a kamma-condition nor an immediate-condition.

There are the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the karmic-condition (*karma-pratyaya*). Either the karmic-condition is the object-condition, or the karmic-condition is not the object-condition.
What is meant by the karmic-condition being the object-condition?
If a phenomenon is produced by karma and possesses an object, it is called a karmic condition and an objective condition.
What is meant by being a karmic condition but not an objective condition?
If a phenomenon is produced by karma and lacks an object, it is called a karmic condition but not an objective condition.

Regarding that which is not a karmic condition (karma-pratyaya) but a condition of objective sphere (viṣaya-pratyaya), or that which is not a karmic condition yet is a condition of objective sphere, or that which is neither a karmic condition nor a condition of objective sphere:
what is meant by "not a karmic condition but a condition of objective sphere"?

If a dharma is not karma, or if karma gives rise to that which is not karma, and it possesses an objective sphere (*ālambana*), this is called "non-karma-condition" being an "objective-sphere condition.
What is meant by "neither non-karma-condition nor objective-sphere condition"?
If a dharma is not karma, or if it is karma that produces what is not karma, and it lacks an objective sphere (ālambana), this is called "neither karma-condition nor objective-sphere-condition.
Regarding the karma-condition and the dependence-condition (niśraya-pratyaya): the karma-condition is the dependence-condition, and what is not a karma-condition is also the dependence-condition.
There is no case where a retribution condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*) is simultaneously an arising condition (*samutthāna-pratyaya*).
Regarding what is not a retribution condition: it may be an arising condition, or it may be neither a retribution condition nor an arising condition.
What is meant by "non-resultant condition that is an origination condition"?
If a phenomenon is non-resultant and is an origination, this is called a non-resultant condition that is an origination condition.
What is meant by "non-resultant condition that is not an origination condition"?
If a dharma is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor an arising (*samutthāna*), it is called a non-result condition (*avipāka-paccaya*) and a non-arising condition (*asamutthāna-paccaya*).
There is no such thing as a result condition that is also a different condition (*nānā-paccaya*).
Regarding a non-result condition that is a different condition: either a non-result condition is a different condition, or a non-result condition is not a different condition.
What is meant by "non-retribution condition" (avipāka-pratyaya) being "distinct condition" (visabhāga-pratyaya)?
If a dharma is non-retribution and is common, this is called "non-retribution condition" being "distinct condition.
What is meant by "non-retribution condition" not being "distinct condition"?
If a dharma is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor shared (*sabhāga*), it is called a non-result condition (*avipāka-pratyaya*) and a non-different condition (*avisabhāga-pratyaya*).
There is no such thing as a result condition that is also a continuity condition (*santati-pratyaya*).
Regarding non-result conditions that are continuity conditions: either a non-result condition is a continuity condition, or a non-result condition is not a continuity condition.
What is meant by being a non-retribution condition (*avipāka-pratyaya*) and a continuity condition (*saṃtati-pratyaya*)?
If a dharma is non-retribution, is an increase (*upacaya*), and reaches the third stage of arising, this is called being a non-retribution condition and a continuity condition.
What is meant by being neither a resultant condition nor a continuity condition?

If a dharma is not a result, is not an increase, or if it is an increase that does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is called being neither a resultant condition nor a continuity condition.
There is no case where a retribution-condition (vipāka-pratyaya) is also a dominant-condition (adhipati-pratyaya).
Regarding what is not a retribution-condition, it is either a dominant-condition or it is neither a retribution-condition nor a dominant-condition.
What is meant by that which is a non-retribution condition (avipāka-pratyaya) and a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya)?
If a phenomenon is non-retribution and is a dominant condition, this is called being a non-retribution condition and a dominant condition.
What is meant by that which is a non-retribution condition and not a dominant condition?
If a dharma is neither a resultant condition nor a predominance condition, it is called a non-resultant condition and a non-predominance condition.
Regarding the resultant condition and the causal condition: the resultant condition is a causal condition.

Regarding non-retribution conditions (avipāka-pratyaya) and causal conditions (hetu-pratyaya): either non-retribution conditions are causal conditions, or non-retribution conditions are not causal conditions.
What is meant by "non-retribution conditions that are causal conditions"?
If a dharma is not a result of retribution (*avipāka*) but is a cause, this is called "non-retribution condition as causal condition.
What is meant by "non-retribution condition that is not a causal condition"?
If a dharma is neither a result of retribution nor a cause, this is called "non-retribution condition that is not a causal condition."

Regarding the retributive condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*) and the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*): either the retributive condition is the immediate condition, or the retributive condition is not the immediate condition.
What is meant by the retributive condition being the immediate condition?
If a phenomenon has retribution and is subject to arising and ceasing, this is called the condition of retribution (vipāka-pratyaya) which is also the immediate condition (anantara-pratyaya).
What is meant by a condition of retribution that is not an immediate condition?
If a phenomenon has retribution but is not subject to arising and ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased, this is called a condition of retribution that is not an immediate condition.

Regarding non-retribution conditions (avipāka-pratyaya) and immediate conditions (anantara-pratyaya): either a condition is a non-retribution condition and is an immediate condition, or it is a non-retribution condition but not an immediate condition.
What is meant by a non-retribution condition that is an immediate condition?

If a dharma is not a result of retribution (*vipāka*) and is subject to arising and ceasing, this is called "non-retribution condition" (*avipāka-pratyaya*) and "immediate condition" (*anantara-pratyaya*).
What is meant by "non-retribution condition" that is not an "immediate condition"?
If a dharma is not a result of retribution and is neither subject to arising and ceasing nor has already ceased, this is called "non-retribution condition" that is not an "immediate condition."

Regarding the condition of retribution (*vipāka-pratyaya*) and the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*): either the condition of retribution is the condition of object, or the condition of retribution is not the condition of object.
What is meant by the condition of retribution being the condition of object?
If a dharma has both retribution and an object, it is called a condition of retribution and a condition of object.
What is meant by a condition of retribution that is not a condition of object?
If a dharma has retribution but no object, it is called a condition of retribution that is not a condition of object.

Regarding non-retribution conditions (avipāka-pratyaya) and object conditions (ālambana-pratyaya): either something is a non-retribution condition and is an object condition, or it is a non-retribution condition but not an object condition.
What is meant by being a non-retribution condition and an object condition?

If a phenomenon is not a result of retribution (*avipāka*) and possesses an object (*sālambana*), this is called being a non-retribution condition (*avipāka-pratyaya*) and an object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
What is meant by being neither a non-retribution condition nor an object condition?
If a phenomenon is not a result of retribution and lacks an object, this is called being neither a non-retribution condition nor an object condition.

Regarding the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*) and the support condition (*nissaya-paccaya*): the resultant condition is the support condition. There is no case where something is a support condition but not a resultant condition.
Regarding the resultant condition and the kamma condition (*kamma-paccaya*): either the resultant condition is the kamma condition, or the resultant condition is not the kamma condition.
What is meant by "having the condition of retribution and the condition of karma"?
If a phenomenon has retribution, is karma, or arises from karma, this is called having the condition of retribution and the condition of karma.
What is meant by "having the condition of retribution but not the condition of karma"?
If a dharma has fruition but is not karma, or if it is born of karma but is not karma itself, this is called "conditioned by fruition, but not conditioned by karma.

Regarding "not conditioned by fruition but conditioned by karma," it refers either to that which is not conditioned by fruition but is karma, or to that which is neither conditioned by fruition nor conditioned by karma.
What is meant by that which is a non-retribution condition (*avipāka-pratyaya*) and a karma condition (*karma-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon is not a retribution, is karma, or if karma produces karma, this is called being a non-retribution condition and a karma condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a resultant condition nor a karmic condition?
If a phenomenon is neither a result nor karma, or if it is karma that gives rise to what is not karma—this is called being neither a resultant condition nor a karmic condition.

Regarding the arising condition (*samudaya-paccaya*) and the diversity condition (*nānatta-paccaya*): either the arising condition is the diversity condition, or the arising condition is not the diversity condition.
What is meant by the arising condition being the diversity condition?
If a phenomenon arises and is common [to others], this is called the arising condition being the diversity condition.
What is meant by "arising condition that is not a distinct condition"?
If a phenomenon arises and is not shared [with others], this is called an arising condition that is not a distinct condition.
Regarding conditions that are neither arising nor distinct: they may be non-arising conditions that are distinct conditions, or they may be non-arising conditions that are not distinct conditions.
What is meant by "not a condition for arising, but a condition of difference"?
If a phenomenon is not a condition for arising but is a common condition, this is called "not a condition for arising, but a condition of difference.
What is meant by "neither a condition for arising nor a condition of difference"?
If a dharma is neither arising nor co-arising, it is called a non-arising condition and a non-different condition.
There is no such thing as an arising condition that is a continuity condition.

Regarding non-arising conditions and continuity conditions, there are four possibilities: either a non-arising condition is a continuity condition, or a non-arising condition is not a continuity condition.
What is meant by that which is not a condition for origination but is a condition for continuity?
If a dharma is not an origination [condition], but is an increase and reaches the third stage of arising, this is called being a condition for continuity but not a condition for origination.
What is meant by being neither a condition for arising nor a condition for continuity?
If a phenomenon does not increase and does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is called being neither a condition for arising nor a condition for continuity.

Regarding the arising condition (*samutthāna-paccaya*) and the predominance condition (*adhipati-paccaya*): either the arising condition is the predominance condition, or the arising condition is not the predominance condition.
What is meant by the arising condition being the predominance condition?
If a phenomenon arises and is predominant, this is called the arising condition as the predominance condition.
What is meant by the arising condition that is not the predominance condition?
If a phenomenon arises and is not predominant, this is called the arising condition that is not the predominance condition.

There are cases that are neither arising conditions nor dominant conditions; or cases that are arising conditions but are dominant conditions; or cases that are neither arising conditions nor dominant conditions.
What is meant by "neither arising conditions but dominant conditions"?
If a phenomenon is neither an arising condition nor a dominant condition, this is called a non-arising condition that is not a dominant condition.
What is meant by a non-arising condition that is not a non-dominant condition?
If a phenomenon is neither an arising condition nor a non-dominant condition, this is called a non-arising condition that is not a non-dominant condition.
That which arises conditioned by causes and conditions is a cause and condition that arises as a condition.

That which does not arise conditioned by causes and conditions is either a cause and condition that does not arise as a condition, or it is neither a cause and condition nor does it arise as a condition.
What is meant by "that which is not a condition of arising is a causal condition"?
If a phenomenon is not a condition of arising and yet is a cause, this is called "that which is not a condition of arising is a causal condition.
What is meant by "that which is not a condition of arising is not a causal condition"?
If a dharma is neither an arising nor a cause, it is called "neither an arising-condition nor a causal-condition.
Regarding arising-conditions—which are equivalent to immediate-conditions—there are none.
As for non-arising-conditions and immediate-conditions, either a non-arising-condition is an immediate-condition, or a non-arising-condition is not an immediate-condition.
What is meant by that which is not an origination-condition (*anuppāda-paccaya*) but is an immediate-condition (*anantara-paccaya*)?
If a dharma is not an origination but is subject to arising and ceasing, this is called being not an origination-condition but an immediate-condition.
What is meant by that which is neither an origination-condition nor an immediate-condition?
If a dharma neither arises nor undergoes birth and cessation, or if it has not yet ceased, this is called the non-arising condition and the non-immediate condition.
Regarding the arising condition and the object condition: either the arising condition is the object condition, or the arising condition is not the object condition.
What is meant by "the condition of arising being the condition of the object"?
If a phenomenon arises and there is an object, this is called "the condition of arising being the condition of the object.
What is meant by "the condition of arising not being the condition of the object"?
If a dharma arises without an object, this is called an arising-condition but not an object-condition.

Regarding non-arising-conditions and object-conditions, there are cases where it is a non-arising-condition that is an object-condition, and cases where it is neither a non-arising-condition nor an object-condition.
What is meant by "the condition of non-arising being the condition of the object"?
If a phenomenon does not arise but possesses an object, this is called "the condition of non-arising being the condition of the object.
What is meant by "neither the condition of non-arising nor the condition of the object"?
If a phenomenon is neither arising nor possesses an objective sphere, it is called a non-arising condition and a non-sphere condition.
The arising condition is the dependence condition; the non-arising condition is the dependence condition.

Regarding the origination condition (*samudaya-paccaya*) and the kamma condition (*kamma-paccaya*): either the origination condition is the kamma condition, or the origination condition is not the kamma condition.
What is meant by "the origination condition is the kamma condition"?
If a phenomenon arises such that it is kamma producing kamma, this is called "the origination condition is the kamma condition."
What is meant by "arising condition but not kamma condition"?
If a phenomenon arises and is not kamma, or if kamma gives rise to what is not kamma, this is called "arising condition but not kamma condition.

Regarding "not arising condition but kamma condition," it refers either to that which is not an arising condition but is a kamma condition, or to that which is neither an arising condition nor a kamma condition.
What is meant by "not a condition of origination, but a condition of karma"?
If a dharma is not an origination, yet is karma and produces karma, this is called "not a condition of origination, but a condition of karma.
What is meant by "neither a condition of origination nor a condition of karma"?
If a phenomenon is neither arising nor karma, or if it is karma that gives rise to non-karma, this is called the non-arising condition and the non-karma condition.
There is no such thing as an arising condition that is simultaneously a retribution condition.
Regarding the non-arising condition and the retribution condition: either the non-arising condition is the retribution condition, or the non-arising condition is not the retribution condition.
What is meant by "the non-arising condition is the retribution condition"?
If a phenomenon is not an arising [condition] but possesses retribution, this is called a non-arising condition that is a retribution condition.
What is meant by a non-arising condition that is not a retribution condition?
If a phenomenon is neither an arising [condition] nor possesses retribution, this is called a non-arising condition that is not a retribution condition.
There is no case where the condition of difference (anyathā-pratyaya) is the condition of continuity (samanantara-pratyaya).

It is not that the condition of difference is the condition of continuity; rather, either the condition of difference is the condition of continuity, or the condition of difference is not the condition of continuity.
What is meant by "not a condition through difference" (*na-anyathā-pratyaya*) being a "condition through continuity" (*santati-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon is not shared, is an increase, and reaches the third [moment] of arising, this is called "not a condition through difference" being a "condition through continuity."
What is meant by "neither a condition of difference nor a condition of continuity"?

If a dharma is not shared, does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is called "neither a condition of difference nor a condition of continuity."
Regarding the object-condition and the dominant condition: either the object-condition is the dominant condition, or the object-condition is not the dominant condition.
What is meant by the object-condition being the dominant condition?
If a phenomenon is both concomitant and predominant, this is called "other-condition as predominant condition.
What is meant by "other-condition that is not a predominant condition"?
If a phenomenon is concomitant but not predominant, this is called "other-condition that is not a predominant condition."

There are conditions that are neither other-conditions nor dominant conditions; there are those that are other-conditions and are dominant conditions; and there are those that are neither other-conditions nor dominant conditions.
What is meant by "being an other-condition and being a dominant condition"?
If a dharma is not common but is predominant, this is called "not a different-condition but a predominant-condition.
What is meant by "neither a different-condition nor a predominant-condition"?
If a dharma is neither common nor predominant, this is called "neither a different-condition nor a predominant-condition."
Regarding different conditions as causes and conditions: different conditions may be causes and conditions;
or different conditions may not be causes and conditions; or it may be that different conditions are causes and conditions, or that different conditions are neither causes nor conditions.
What is meant by "non-different condition as cause-condition"?
If a phenomenon is not shared [with others] and yet is a cause, this is called "non-different condition as cause-condition.
What is meant by "neither non-different condition nor cause-condition"?
If a dharma is neither common nor a cause, it is called "neither a condition of difference nor a causal condition.
Regarding the condition of difference, which is the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), there is none [that is not a causal condition].

As for the non-condition of difference and the immediately preceding condition: either the non-condition of difference is the immediately preceding condition, or the non-condition of difference is not the immediately preceding condition.
What is meant by being a non-different-condition (anantara-pratyaya) but not a contiguity-condition (samanantara-pratyaya)?
If a dharma is not common [to others] and is subject to arising and ceasing, this is called being a non-different-condition but not a contiguity-condition.
What is meant by being neither a non-different-condition nor a contiguity-condition?
If a dharma is not common, does not arise or cease, or has not yet ceased, it is called a non-object-condition and a non-immediate-condition.
Regarding the object-condition and the object-condition as a distinct condition: either the distinct condition is the object-condition, or the distinct condition is not the object-condition.
What is meant by "a different condition that is an object-condition"?
If a phenomenon is both common [to others] and possesses an object, this is called "a different condition that is an object-condition.
What is meant by "a different condition that is not an object-condition"?
If a dharma is concomitant yet lacks an object, it is called "having a different object-condition but not an object-condition.

Regarding that which is neither a different object-condition nor an object-condition, it is either a different object-condition that is an object-condition, or a different object-condition that is not an object-condition.
What is meant by "not a different-condition but a condition as object"?
If a dharma is not common [to others] and possesses an object, this is called "not a different-condition but a condition as object.
What is meant by "neither a different-condition nor a condition as object"?
If a phenomenon is not shared and lacks an object, it is called "neither an object-condition nor a condition by way of an object.

Regarding the condition by way of another and the supporting condition: the condition by way of another is itself the supporting condition; that which is not a condition by way of another is the supporting condition.
Regarding the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) and the karmic condition (karma-pratyaya): either the object-condition is the karmic condition, or the object-condition is not the karmic condition.
What is meant by "the object-condition is the karmic condition"?
If a phenomenon is concomitant, is karma, and gives rise to karma, this is called "the object-condition is the karmic condition."
What is meant by "conditioned by the dissimilar (nānatta-paccaya) but not by kamma (kamma-paccaya)"?
If a phenomenon is conditioned by the dissimilar but not by kamma, or if that which is born from kamma is not itself kamma—this is called "conditioned by the dissimilar but not by kamma.

Regarding "not conditioned by the dissimilar but conditioned by kamma," it refers either to that which is not conditioned by the dissimilar but is conditioned by kamma, or to that which is neither conditioned by the dissimilar nor conditioned by kamma.
What is meant by "not being a different-condition (na-anyathā-pratyaya) but being a karmic-condition (karma-pratyaya)"?
If a dharma is not shared [with others], is karma, and produces karma, this is called "not being a different-condition but being a karmic-condition.
What is meant by "not being a different-condition and not being a karmic-condition"?
If a dharma is non-common and non-karmic, or if it is karmic-born yet non-karmic, this is called "neither different-object condition nor karmic condition.
There is no such thing as a different-object condition that is a retribution condition.

There are conditions that are neither non-different conditions nor retribution conditions; or there are those that are non-different conditions and are retribution conditions; or there are those that are non-different conditions and are not retribution conditions.
What is meant by being a non-different condition and a retribution condition?
If a phenomenon is not shared and possesses retribution, this is called "not a condition by way of difference, but a condition by way of retribution.
What is meant by "neither a condition by way of difference nor a condition by way of retribution"?
If a phenomenon is not shared and does not possess retribution, this is called "neither a condition by way of difference nor a condition by way of retribution."
Regarding the condition of difference and the condition of arising: either the condition of difference is the condition of arising, or the condition of difference is not the condition of arising.
What is meant by "the condition of difference is the condition of arising"?
If a phenomenon is both concomitant and an arising, this is called "the condition of difference is the condition of arising."
What is meant by "conditioned by difference but not by arising"?

If a phenomenon is conditioned by difference but not by arising, this is called "conditioned by difference but not by arising. Regarding that which is neither conditioned by difference nor by arising:

it may be neither conditioned by difference nor an arising condition; or it may be conditioned by difference but not an arising condition; or it may be neither conditioned by difference nor an arising condition.
What is meant by "not a condition through difference, but a condition through arising"?
If a dharma is not shared [with others] and is an arising, this is called "not a condition through difference, but a condition through arising.
What is meant by "neither a condition through difference nor a condition through arising"?
If a phenomenon is neither common nor arising, it is called neither a different-condition nor an arising-condition.
There is no such thing as a continuity-condition that is also a dominant-condition.
Regarding non-continuity-conditions and dominant-conditions: either a non-continuity-condition is a dominant-condition, or a non-continuity-condition is not a dominant-condition.
What is meant by a non-continuous condition that is a dominant condition?

If a dharma does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], it is a dominant condition; this is called a non-continuous condition that is a dominant condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a contiguous condition nor a dominant condition?

If a phenomenon does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], and is thus not dominant, this is called being neither a contiguous condition nor a dominant condition.
There is no such thing as a "conditioned by continuity" that is also a "causal condition.
That which is conditioned by continuity is not a causal condition; or, that which is conditioned by continuity may be a causal condition, or it may not be a causal condition.
What is meant by "a non-continuous condition that is a causal condition"?
If a dharma does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is a cause; this is called "a non-continuous condition that is a causal condition."
What is meant by that which is neither a condition of continuity nor a causal condition?

If a phenomenon is not an increase, or if it is an increase that does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], and is not a cause—this is called that which is neither a condition of continuity nor a causal condition.
That which is a continuity condition (*saṃtati-pratyaya*) is not a contiguity condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

It is not the case that what is not a continuity condition is a contiguity condition; rather, either something is a continuity condition and is also a contiguity condition, or it is neither a continuity condition nor a contiguity condition.
What is meant by that which is a non-continuous condition (*asaṃtati-pratyaya*) and is also an immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*)?

If a dharma does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], yet there is this arising and ceasing, this is called being a non-continuous condition and an immediate condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a condition of continuity (*samanantara-pratyaya*) nor a condition of immediate succession (*anantara-pratyaya*)?

If a phenomenon is not increasing, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], or if it is neither arising nor ceasing, or if it has not yet ceased—this is called being neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of immediate succession.
There are conditions of continuity and conditions of the object; that is, either a condition of continuity is a condition of the object, or a condition of continuity is not a condition of the object.
What is meant by a condition of continuity being a condition of the object?
If a phenomenon increases until it reaches the third stage and possesses an objective sphere, this is called a condition of continuity and a condition of objective sphere.
What is meant by a condition of continuity that is not a condition of objective sphere?

If a dharma increases until it reaches the production of a third [moment] and lacks an objective field (*ālambana*), this is called a condition of continuity (*santati-pratyaya*) and not a condition of objective field.
It is either not a condition of continuity but a condition of objective field, or it is neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of objective field.
What is meant by that which is not a condition of continuity (*anubandha-pratyaya*) but is a condition of objective sphere (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?

If a phenomenon is not increasing, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], yet there is an objective sphere, this is called that which is not a condition of continuity but is a condition of objective sphere.
What is meant by "neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of object"?

If a phenomenon is not increasing, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], and there is no object, this is called "neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of object."
Continuity-condition is dependence-condition; non-continuity-condition is dependence-condition.
*Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle 25; *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Fascicle 26.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kaśmīra, together with Dharmagupta and others, during the Yao Qin dynasty.

From the second part of the *Sarvavastuka-vibhaṅga*, "The Chapter on Pervasive Factors": Regarding the conditions of continuity and the conditions of karma—either the condition of continuity is the condition of karma, or the condition of continuity is not the condition of karma.
What is meant by "conditioning by continuity" being "conditioning by karma"?
If a phenomenon increases to the point of producing a third [moment], and that is karma, or produces karma—this is called "conditioning by continuity" being "conditioning by karma."
What is meant by "condition as continuity" (santati-paccaya) that is not "condition as kamma" (kamma-paccaya)?

If a phenomenon increases until it reaches the production of a third [moment], being non-kamma; or if kamma produces what is non-kamma—this is called "condition as continuity" that is not "condition as kamma."
There are non-continuous conditions that are karmic conditions, or non-continuous conditions that are karmic conditions, or non-continuous conditions that are not karmic conditions.
What is meant by a non-continuous condition that is a karmic condition?

If a phenomenon does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the production of a third [moment], that is karma; or if karma produces karma, this is called a non-continuous condition, which is a karmic condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of karma?

If a dharma is not an increase, or if it is an increase but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], or if it is not karma, or if it is karma that produces what is not karma—this is called being neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of karma.
There is no case where the condition of continuity (*saṃtati-pratyaya*) is the condition of retribution (*vipāka-pratyaya*).

Regarding the relationship between the condition of continuity and the condition of retribution: either the condition of continuity is the condition of retribution, or the condition of continuity is not the condition of retribution.
What is meant by "not a condition of continuity, but a condition of retribution"?

If a dharma is not an increase, or if it is an increase that does not reach the production of a third [moment], yet possesses retribution—this is called "not a condition of continuity, but a condition of retribution."
What is meant by being neither a condition of continuity (*na-anvaya-pratyaya*) nor a condition of retribution (*na-vipāka-pratyaya*)?

If a dharma is not an increase, or if it is an increase that does not reach the production of a third [moment], and is not retribution—this is called being neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of retribution.
The condition of continuity is not the condition of origination.

It is not the case that the condition of continuity is the condition of origination; rather, either the condition of continuity is the condition of origination, or the condition of continuity is not the condition of origination.
What is meant by "not being a continuity-condition (anvaya-pratyaya) but being an arising-condition (utpāda-pratyaya)"?
If a dharma is not an increase, or if it is an increase that does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is called "not being a continuity-condition but being an arising-condition."
What is meant by that which is neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of arising?

If a dharma does not increase, or even if it increases, it does not reach a third stage of birth and thus does not arise; this is called being neither a condition of continuity nor a condition of arising.
There is no such thing as a continuous condition that is simultaneously a distinct condition.
It is not the case that a continuous condition is a distinct condition; rather, either a continuous condition is a distinct condition, or a continuous condition is not a distinct condition.
What is meant by "non-sequential condition" being "distinct condition"?

If a phenomenon does not increase, or if it increases but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], this is a common [condition]; this is called "non-sequential condition" being "distinct condition."
What is that which is neither a continuous condition nor a distinct condition?

If a dharma is not augmented, or if it is augmented but does not reach the point of producing a third [moment], or if it is not common, this is called neither a continuous condition nor a distinct condition.

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): either the dominant condition is the causal condition, or the dominant condition is not the causal condition.
What is meant by the dominant condition being the causal condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant and is a cause, it is called a dominant condition that is also a causal condition.
What is a dominant condition that is not a causal condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant but not a cause, it is called a dominant condition that is not a causal condition.

Regarding that which is not a dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) but is a causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), or that which is not a dominant condition yet is a causal condition, or that which is neither a dominant condition nor a causal condition:
what is meant by "not a dominant condition but a causal condition"?
If a phenomenon is not predominant but is a cause, this is called "not a predominating condition, but a causal condition.
What is meant by "neither a predominating condition nor a causal condition"?
If a phenomenon is neither predominant nor a cause, this is called "neither a predominating condition nor a causal condition."
The predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is not the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*).

There is no such thing as a predominant condition that is also an immediate condition; rather, there are cases where it is a predominant condition but not an immediate condition, and cases where it is neither a predominant condition nor an immediate condition.
What is meant by that which is not a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but is an immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon is not predominant yet is subject to arising and ceasing, this is called being not a dominant condition but an immediate condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a dominant condition nor an immediate condition?
If a dharma is not predominant, does not arise or cease, or has not yet ceased, this is called being neither a dominant condition nor an immediate condition.

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): either the dominant condition is the object-condition, or the dominant condition is not the object-condition.
What is meant by the dominant condition being the object-condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant and possesses an object, it is called a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and an object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
What is meant by a dominant condition that is not an object condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant but lacks an object, it is called a dominant condition that is not an object condition.

There are cases that are not dominant conditions (adhipati-pratyaya) but are object conditions (ālambana-pratyaya); or cases that are not dominant conditions yet are object conditions; or cases that are neither dominant conditions nor object conditions.
What is meant by "not being a dominant condition but being an object condition"?
If a phenomenon is not predominant yet possesses an object, it is called a non-predominant condition that is an object-condition.
What is meant by a condition that is neither a predominant condition nor an object-condition?
If a dharma is neither predominant nor has an object, it is called neither a predominant condition nor an object condition.
Regarding the predominant condition as a supporting condition: a predominant condition is a supporting condition, and that which is not a predominant condition is also a supporting condition.

Regarding the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the karmic condition (*karma-pratyaya*): either the dominant condition is the karmic condition, or the dominant condition is not the karmic condition.
What is meant by the dominant condition being the karmic condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant, and it is karma or gives rise to karma, this is called the predominance condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) which is also the karma condition (*karma-pratyaya*).
What is the predominance condition that is not the karma condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant, but it is not karma, or if it gives rise to what is not karma, this is called the predominance condition that is not the karma condition.

There are cases that are neither dominant conditions nor karmic conditions; or cases that are dominant conditions but are karmic conditions; or cases that are neither dominant conditions nor karmic conditions.
What is meant by "neither a dominant condition nor a karmic condition"? What is meant by "a dominant condition that is a karmic condition"?
If a dharma is not predominant, yet is karma and gives rise to karma, this is called being a non-predominant condition and a karmic condition.
What is meant by being neither a non-predominant condition nor a karmic condition?
If a dharma is neither predominant nor karmic, or if it is karmic but produces what is non-karmic, this is called being neither a predominance condition nor a karma condition.
There is no case where a predominance condition is a retribution condition.

Regarding that which is neither a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) nor a retribution condition (*vipāka-pratyaya*), or that which is a dominant condition but not a retribution condition, or that which is neither a dominant condition nor a retribution condition:
what is meant by "that which is a dominant condition but not a retribution condition"?
If a phenomenon is not predominant (*adhipati*) but has retribution (*vipāka*), this is called "not a predominating condition, but a retribution condition.
What is meant by "neither a predominating condition nor a retribution condition"?
If a phenomenon is neither predominant nor has retribution, this is called "neither a predominating condition nor a retribution condition."
Regarding the predominance condition as the arising condition: either the predominance condition is the arising condition, or the predominance condition is not the arising condition.
What is meant by the predominance condition being the arising condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant and is an arising, it is called a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) that is an arising condition.
What is meant by a dominant condition that is not an arising condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant but is not an arising, it is called a dominant condition that is not an arising condition.

There are cases where that which is not a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is an arising condition (*samutthāna-pratyaya*), cases where what is a dominant condition is an arising condition, and cases where what is not a dominant condition is not an arising condition.
What is meant by "that which is not a dominant condition is an arising condition"?
If a phenomenon is not predominant but is productive, this is called being a non-predominant condition but a productive condition.
What is meant by being neither a predominant condition nor a productive condition?
If a phenomenon is neither predominant nor productive, this is called being neither a predominant condition nor a productive condition.

Regarding the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the distinct condition (*anya-pratyaya*): either the predominant condition is the distinct condition, or the predominant condition is not the distinct condition.
What is meant by the predominant condition being the distinct condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant and shared, it is called a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and a distinct condition (*anya-pratyaya*).
What is meant by a dominant condition that is not a distinct condition?
If a phenomenon is predominant and not shared, it is called a dominant condition that is not a distinct condition.

There are conditions that are neither dominant conditions nor specific conditions; or those that are dominant conditions but not specific conditions; or those that are neither dominant conditions nor specific conditions.
What is meant by "neither a dominant condition nor a specific condition"?
If a phenomenon is neither predominant nor common, it is called a non-predominant condition and a distinct condition.
What is meant by being neither a non-predominant condition nor a distinct condition?
If a phenomenon is neither predominant nor common, it is called neither a non-predominant condition nor a distinct condition.
There is no case where the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is the continuity condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Regarding the non-dominant condition, it may be the continuity condition, or it may be neither the dominant condition nor the continuity condition.
What is meant by that which is not a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) but is a continuity condition (*santati-pratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon is not predominant, yet is an increase that leads to the arising of a third [moment], this is called being not a dominant condition but a continuity condition.
What is meant by that which is neither a dominant condition nor a continuity condition?
If a dharma is not predominant, does not increase, or if it increases but does not continue up to the third moment, this is called being neither a dominant condition nor a continuity condition.

Wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena; wholesome-unwholesome phenomena; wholesome-indeterminate phenomena; unwholesome-indeterminate phenomena; and wholesome-unwholesome-indeterminate phenomena.

Conditioned by wholesome phenomena, there arise wholesome phenomena; unwholesome phenomena; indeterminate phenomena; wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; wholesome and indeterminate phenomena; unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena; and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.

Conditioned by unwholesome states, there arise wholesome states, unwholesome states, indeterminate states, wholesome and unwholesome states, wholesome and indeterminate states, unwholesome and indeterminate states, and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate states.

Conditioned by indeterminate phenomena, there arise wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, wholesome and indeterminate phenomena, unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena, and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.

Conditioned by wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, there arise wholesome dharmas, unwholesome dharmas, indeterminate dharmas, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, wholesome and indeterminate dharmas, unwholesome and indeterminate dharmas, and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas.

Conditioned by wholesome and indeterminate phenomena, there arise wholesome phenomena; unwholesome phenomena; indeterminate phenomena; wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; wholesome and indeterminate phenomena; unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena; and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.

Conditioned by unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena, there arise wholesome phenomena; unwholesome phenomena; indeterminate phenomena; wholesome and unwholesome phenomena; wholesome and indeterminate phenomena; unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena; and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.

Conditioned by wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena, there arise wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, wholesome and indeterminate phenomena, unwholesome and indeterminate phenomena, and wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena.

Chapter Two: The Chapter on Causes (Hetu-varga) from the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Section on the Introduction. Regarding causes: that which exists by way of cause, proceeds by way of cause, and arises by way of cause—this is the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*).
There are four matters by which one should know that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) possess the sense of having causes.
This is the primary gateway for the collection of various causes.

These are: the cause of cause (*hetu-hetu*), the immediate cause (*anantara-hetu*), the objective-field cause (*ālambana-hetu*), the support cause (*niśraya-hetu*), the action cause (*karma-hetu*), the retribution cause (*vipāka-hetu*), the origination cause (*utthāna-hetu*), the differentiation cause (*viśeṣa-hetu*), the continuity cause (*prabandha-hetu*), the sovereign cause (*adhipati-hetu*), the name cause (*nāma-hetu*), the form cause (*rūpa-hetu*), the ignorance cause (*avidyā-hetu*), the formations cause (*saṃskāra-hetu*), the consciousness cause (*vijñāna-hetu*), the name-and-form cause (*nāmarūpa-hetu*), the six sense-bases cause (*ṣaḍāyatana-hetu*), the contact cause (*sparśa-hetu*), the feeling cause (*vedanā-hetu*), the craving cause (*tṛṣṇā-hetu*), the grasping cause (*upādāna-hetu*), the existence cause (*bhava-hetu*), the birth cause (*jāti-hetu*), the aging cause (*jarā-hetu*), the death cause (*maraṇa-hetu*), the sorrow cause (*śoka-hetu*), the lamentation cause (*parideva-hetu*), the suffering cause (*duḥkha-hetu*), the affliction cause (*daurmanasya-hetu*), the cause of manifold sufferings (*sambhāra-duḥkha-hetu*), the nutriment cause (*āhāra-hetu*), the outflow cause (*āsrava-hetu*), and furthermore, the cause of renewed existence (*punarbhava-hetu*).

It is not a cause of causes, nor an immediate cause, nor an objective cause, nor a supporting cause, nor a karmic cause, nor a retributive cause, nor a productive cause, nor a divergent cause, nor a continuous cause, nor a dominant cause; it is not a cause of name, nor a cause of form, nor a cause of ignorance, nor a cause of volitional formations, nor a cause of consciousness, nor a cause of name-and-form, nor a cause of the six sense bases, nor a cause of contact, nor a cause of sensation, nor a cause of craving, nor a cause of grasping, nor a cause of existence, nor a cause of birth, nor a cause of aging, nor a cause of death, nor a cause of sorrow, nor a cause of lamentation, nor a cause of suffering, nor a cause of affliction, nor a cause of manifold sufferings; it is not a cause of nutriment, nor a cause of outflows, nor a cause of renewed existence.
What is the cause of causes?
If a phenomenon is the cause of another phenomenon, that is called the cause of causes.
What is the immediate cause?
If a dharma is the cause of past and present [dharmas], it is called the immediate cause (*samanantara-hetu*).
What is the objective-field cause (*ālambana-hetu*)?
All dharmas as objective fields are like the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*); if there is a cause that serves as the basis for dharmas, this is called the objective-field cause.
What is meant by the cause of dependence?
All phenomena are causes; if they are the causes of conditioned phenomena, these are called the cause of dependence.
What is meant by the cause of karma?
If a phenomenon is the cause for the actions of body, speech, and mind, it is called a causal factor of karma (*karmahetu*).
What is meant by a causal factor of retribution (*vipākahetu*)? If a phenomenon is a feeling or a wholesome causal factor of retribution, it is called a causal factor of retribution.
What is called the "cause of arising"?
If a phenomenon has a cause for its arising, this is termed the "cause of arising.
What is called the "cause of difference"?
If a dharma shares a cause [with another], this is called a "different cause" (anyahetu).
What is meant by a "successive cause" (prabandhahetu)?
If a dharma is a cause for growth, this is called a successive cause.
What is the dominant cause (*adhipatipratyaya*)?
If a phenomenon is a predominant cause, it is called the dominant cause.
What is the naming cause (*nāmapratyaya*)?
All conceptualizations that are provisionally designated by names are called the cause of name (*nāma-hetu*).

Furthermore, from these conceptualizations and provisional designations, there arise feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), contact (*sparśa*), and attention (*manasikāra*); these are called name.
Furthermore, the five factors headed by contact—namely, feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), volition (cetanā), contact (sparśa), and attention (manasikāra)—are called "name" (nāma).
Furthermore, any phenomenon that is non-material and conditioned is called "name."
If such a phenomenon is a cause, it is called the "cause of name" (*nāma-hetu*).
What is the "cause of form" (*rūpa-hetu*)?
If a phenomenon is form, that is called form.
Furthermore, the ten bases of form and the form included within the base of mental objects—these are called form.
