Furthermore, the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements—these are called form.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of form:
That which is visible and resistant, that which is invisible and resistant, and that which is invisible and non-resistant—this is called form (*rūpa*).
If such factors are the cause, this is termed the cause of form (*rūpa-hetu*).
What is the cause of ignorance?
If it is the cause of the unwholesome root of delusion, this is called the cause of ignorance.
What is the cause of volitional formations?
Bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations—these are called formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and imperturbable formations—these are called formations.
Furthermore, the five aggregates of clinging are called formations (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, the aggregate of formations is called formations.
If such dharmas are the cause, this is termed the cause of formations.
What is the cause of consciousness?
The eye-consciousness, body, ear, nose, tongue, and mind-consciousness aggregates are the causes; these are called the cause of consciousness.
What is the cause of name-and-form?
If one designates a conventional name through conceptualization and mental construction, this is called "name" (nāma).
If it is a phenomenon that is material, this is called "form" (rūpa).
Furthermore, if, by means of conceptualization and mental construction, there arise feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention, these are called "name."
The ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), these are called "form" (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, the five factors beginning with tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*), these are called "name" (*nāman*).
The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the form derived from the four great elements (*upādāyarūpa*), these are called "form."
Furthermore, those phenomena that are non-material and conditioned are called "name" (nāma).
There are three kinds of matter (rūpa):
visible and resistant, invisible and resistant, and invisible and non-resistant.
If such phenomena as name-and-form (nāmarūpa) exist, these are called the cause of name-and-form.
What is the cause of the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana)?
If the eye-base and the bases of ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind exist as the causes of phenomena, these are called the cause of the six sense bases.
What is the cause of contact?
Eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact—contact with mental objects; these are called the causes of contact.
What is the cause of feeling?
If the causes for painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are factors, these are called the causes of feeling (*vedanā-hetu*).
What are the causes of craving (*tṛṣṇā-hetu*)?
If the causes for craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for cessation are factors, these are called the causes of craving.
What is the cause of grasping (*upādāna*)?
If there are the causes for the dharma of grasping at sensual desires, grasping at views, grasping at precepts and rituals, and grasping at a self, these are called the cause of grasping.
What is the cause of existence (*bhava*)?

If the causes for the phenomena of existence in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are present, these are called "having causes.
What is the cause of birth?

If, among sentient beings, there is the process of being born, being truly born, entering the womb, emerging from the aggregates (*skandha*), and the causal factors for the accomplishment of the aggregates and sense bases (*āyatana*), these are called the "cause of birth."
What is the cause of old age?

When, among sentient beings, there is the whitening of hair, the falling out of teeth, the wrinkling of skin, the trembling of the body, the maturation and decay of the sense faculties, the exhaustion of vitality, and the shortening of life—all such factors are called the cause of old age.
What is the cause of death?

When sentient beings reach their end, pass away, and die; when the aggregates are relinquished and the physical form undergoes transformation and separation from its constituent factors, this is called the cause of death.
What is the cause of sorrow?

If sentient beings are oppressed by various sufferings—whether it be sorrow, profound sorrow, ultimate sorrow, or internal burning heat and distress—this dharma is the cause; this is called the cause of sorrow.
What is the cause of compassion?

When sentient beings experience manifold sufferings and are distressed, being oppressed by grief so that the arrow of sorrow pierces their hearts; when they recall these with lamentation and wail, and when there is the verbal teaching as a causal factor—this is called the cause of compassion.
What is the cause of suffering?

If the body does not endure suffering, and the factors that cause painful feelings arising from eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, and body-contact arise, this is called the cause of suffering.
What is the cause of vexation?
If the mind does not endure suffering, and the mental contact with the factors of painful feeling is the cause, this is called the cause of vexation.
What is the cause of manifold suffering?
If there is suffering of body and mind, heavy suffering, and ultimate suffering, which are the causes of mental affliction and confusion, these are called the causes of manifold suffering.
What are the causes of sustenance?
There are four kinds of sustenance:
Edible food, contact as food, mental volition as food, and consciousness as food—such factors as these are called the cause of nutriment.
What is the cause of the outflows?

The factors that are the causes for the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) are called the cause of the outflows (*āsrava-hetu*).
What, then, is the cause of renewed existence (*punarbhava-hetu*)?
Those factors that are the causes for the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) at the initial stage are called the cause of renewed existence.
What is a non-cause that functions as a cause?
If a phenomenon is not a cause, it is called a non-cause that functions as a cause.
What is a non-immediate cause?
If a dharma is not an immediate cause (*samanantara-hetu*), it is called a non-immediate cause.
What is a non-object-cause (*ālambana-hetu*)?
There is no such thing as a non-object-cause.
There is nothing that is not a cause based on conditions. What is not a karmic cause?
If a phenomenon is not a karmic cause, it is called "not a karmic cause."
What is a non-retribution cause?
If a dharma is not a retribution cause, it is called a non-retribution cause.
What is a non-arising cause?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of arising, it is called "not a cause of arising.
What is "not a different cause"?
If a phenomenon is not a common cause, it is called "not a different cause."
What is a non-continuity cause?
If a dharma is not a cause of increase, it is called a non-continuity cause.
What is a non-predominant cause?
If a dharma is not a predominant cause, it is called a non-predominant cause.
What is a non-name-cause?
If a dharma is not a name-cause, it is called a non-name-cause.
What is the non-cause of form?
If a dharma is not the cause of form, it is called the non-cause of form.
What is the non-cause of ignorance?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of ignorance, it is called "not a cause of ignorance.
What is "not a cause of volitional formations"?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of volitional formations, it is called "not a cause of volitional formations."
What is not the cause of consciousness?
If a phenomenon is not the cause of consciousness, it is called "not the cause of consciousness.
What is not the cause of name-and-form?
If a phenomenon is not a cause for name-and-form, it is called "not a cause for name-and-form.
What is not a cause for the six sense bases?
If a phenomenon is not a cause for the six sense bases, it is called "not a cause for the six sense bases."
What is the cause that is not contact?
If a dharma is not the cause of contact, it is called the cause that is not contact.
What is the cause that is not feeling?
If a phenomenon is not a cause for feeling, it is called "not a cause for feeling.
What is not a cause for craving?
If a phenomenon is not a cause for craving, it is called "not a cause for craving."
What is the non-grasping cause?
If a phenomenon is not a grasping cause, it is called the non-grasping cause.
What is the non-existence cause?
If a phenomenon does not have a cause, it is called "that which lacks a cause.
What is meant by "not being a cause of arising"?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of arising, it is called "not being a cause of arising."
What is not a cause of aging?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of aging, it is called "not a cause of aging.
What is not a cause of death?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of death, it is called "not a cause of death.
What is not a cause of sorrow?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of sorrow, it is called "not a cause of sorrow."
What is the non-cause of compassion?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of compassion, it is called the non-cause of compassion.
What is the non-cause of suffering?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of suffering, it is called "not a cause of suffering.
What is not a cause of affliction?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of affliction, it is called "not a cause of affliction."
What is not a cause of manifold suffering?
If a phenomenon is not a cause of manifold suffering, it is called "not a cause of manifold suffering.
What is not a cause of nutriment?
If a phenomenon is not a cause for nutriment, it is called "not a cause for nutriment.
What is "not a cause for outflows"?
If a phenomenon is not a cause for outflows, it is called "not a cause for outflows."
What is meant by "not having further causes"?
If a dharma is not the cause for the initial aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), or bases (*āyatana*), it is called "not having further causes.

There are: dharmas that are causes but do not have causes; dharmas that have causes but are not causes; dharmas that are both causes and have causes; dharmas that are neither causes nor have causes; dharmas that are causes but not conjoined causes; dharmas that are conjoined causes but are not causes; dharmas that are both causes and conjoined causes; and dharmas that are neither causes nor conjoined causes.
What is a causal phenomenon that is not itself a cause?
A causal phenomenon has no non-cause.
Furthermore, the roots of goodness, the roots of unwholesomeness, and the fetters of devotion—these are called causal phenomena that are not themselves causes.
What is a conditioned phenomenon that has a cause but is not itself a cause?
If a phenomenon is conditioned and does not function as a cause, it is called a conditioned phenomenon that has a cause but is not itself a cause.
What is a phenomenon that is both a cause and has a cause?
Excluding the roots of goodness, the roots of unwholesomeness, and the fetter of devotion, any other phenomena are called "phenomena that have causes and possess causes.
What are phenomena that neither have causes nor possess causes?
Excluding causal factors and factors possessing causes, any other factors are termed non-causal factors and factors not possessing causes.

This applies likewise to causal factors that are not conjoined causes, conjoined causes that are not causal factors, factors that are both causal and conjoined, and factors that are neither causal nor conjoined causes.

Dharmas that are prior causes are not common causes; dharmas that are common causes are not prior causes; there are dharmas that are both prior and common causes; and there are also dharmas that are neither prior nor common causes.

Dharmas that are prior causes are not subsequent causes; dharmas that are subsequent causes are not prior causes; there are dharmas that are both prior and subsequent causes; and there are also dharmas that are neither prior nor subsequent causes.

There are dharmas that are common causes but not subsequent causes; dharmas that are subsequent causes but not common causes; dharmas that are both common and subsequent causes; and dharmas that are neither common nor subsequent causes.
What are dharmas that are prior causes but not common causes?
If a dharma arises such that it is a prior cause but not a simultaneous cause, this is called a "prior cause dharma that is not a simultaneous cause.
What is a "simultaneous cause dharma that is not a prior cause"?
If a dharma arises such that it has a co-existent cause but not a preceding cause, this is called a dharma with a co-existent cause but not a preceding cause.
What is a dharma with both a preceding cause and a co-existent cause?
If a dharma arises such that it has both a preceding cause and a co-existent cause, this is called a dharma with both a preceding cause and a co-existent cause.
What are phenomena that are neither antecedent causes nor common causes?
With the exception of phenomena that are antecedent and common causes, any remaining phenomena are called phenomena that are neither antecedent nor common causes.

Furthermore, regarding "dharmas that are prior causes but not common causes": if a dharma, when first arising, is not a result of maturation (*vipāka*), it is called a dharma that is a prior cause but not a common cause.
What is a dharma that is a common cause but not a prior cause?
If a dharma is not a cause for conditioned phenomena, it is called a "common cause" (sādhāraṇa-hetu) but not a "prior cause" (pūrva-hetu).
What are prior causes that are also common causes?
With the exception of the first moment of birth that is not a result of maturation (avipāka), all other common dharmas are called prior causes that are also common causes.
What are phenomena that are neither antecedent causes nor common causes?
With the exception of phenomena that are antecedent causes or common causes, any remaining phenomena are called phenomena that are neither antecedent causes nor common causes.

The dharma of the prior cause is not the posterior cause; the dharma of the posterior cause is not the prior cause; the dharma of both the prior and posterior causes, as well as the dharma of neither the prior nor the posterior cause, are likewise so.
What is a dharma that is a co-existent cause but not a subsequent cause?
If a dharma arises such that it is a co-existent cause and not a subsequent cause, this is called a dharma that is a co-existent cause but not a subsequent cause.
How is it that the subsequent causal dharma is not a common cause?
The dharma produced by a subsequent cause is indeed a common cause.

Furthermore, having attained the first *dhyāna*, one attains the second *dhyāna*; through this subsequent cause, one attains the purity of the first *dhyāna* and exercises power, mastery, and sovereignty.
Having attained the second dhyāna, he attains the third dhyāna; subsequently, by reason of the purity of the second dhyāna, he dwells with power, mastery, and sovereignty.
Having attained the third dhyāna, he attains the fourth dhyāna; subsequently, by reason of the purity of the third dhyāna, he dwells with power, mastery, and sovereignty.

If a bodhisattva has attained the supernormal powers and clear knowledges (*abhijñā*), at the moment of awakening to those powers and knowledges, there arises a subsequent cause through contemplation that penetrates the infinite;

upon attaining the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and the stability of life-span, there likewise arises a subsequent cause, whether abiding for an eon or the remainder of an eon—this is called the dharma of subsequent causes, not of common causes.
What are phenomena that are both co-existent causes and subsequent causes?
If a phenomenon arises such that it is both a co-existent cause and a subsequent cause, these are called phenomena that are both co-existent causes and subsequent causes.
What are phenomena that are neither co-existent causes nor subsequent causes?

Excluding those factors that are both common causes and subsequent causes, if there are other factors, these are called "factors that are neither common nor subsequent causes. Regarding the analysis of causes and non-causes, there are thirty-two phrases for each; these last two constitute four sets of four phrases.

Chapter Three: On Name-and-Form (*nāmarūpa*) In the *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Part One: Introduction, Chapter Three: On Name-and-Form. There is one who has appeared in the world, called the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; he teaches name-and-form, the analysis of name-and-form, and the abandonment of name-and-form.
What is name-and-form?
That which is designated through conceptualization and conventionally established as a name is called "name. What is "form"?
If a phenomenon is form, this is called "form.
Furthermore, that which arises through conceptual designation—namely, feeling, perception, volition, contact, and attention—is called "name."
The ten bases of form and the form included within the base of mental objects—this is called "form.
Furthermore, the five factors beginning with tangibility—this is called "name.
The four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements—this is called "form."
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is non-material and conditioned, this is called "name" (nāma).
Matter (rūpa) is of three kinds:
visible and resistant, invisible and resistant, and invisible and non-resistant; this is called "matter."
Such as these are name-and-form; this is what is called "name-and-form.
For what reason is "name-and-form" spoken of?
It is because one wishes to cause this name-and-form to be correctly explained, understood, analyzed, manifested, and conventionally designated; therefore, "name-and-form" is spoken of.
What is meant by "understanding the penetration of name-and-form"?
If one knows and sees the skillful means for penetrating name-and-form, this is called understanding the penetration of name-and-form.
What is meant by "abandoning name-and-form"?
If one subdues desire and passion for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and severs desire and passion for it, this is called the severance of name-and-form.
Now, the primary gateways for the collection of name-and-form shall be presented:
cause, origination, retribution, concomitance, predominance, dependence, and nutriment.
Nourishment, maintenance, subtle gathering, support, necessity;
the initial conception in the womb, the place of abiding, birth, the path, the destination, the crossing, the fluid, the pervasion, and the fulfillment.
Not disciplined, not firm, not guarded, not restrained, and not cultivated; yet [it is] disciplined, firm, guarded, restrained, and cultivated.
Not understood, not realized, not abandoned, not exhausted, and not extinguished.
Understanding, realization, abandonment, exhaustion, and cessation;
the basis of joy, the basis of sorrow, and the basis of equanimity;
the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
Trainee, non-trainee, and neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee;
fruition, dharma subject to fruition, and neither-fruition-nor-dharma-subject-to-fruition;
abandoned by vision, abandoned by cultivation, and neither-abandoned-by-vision-nor-abandoned-by-cultivation.
Causes abandoned by vision, causes abandoned by cultivation, and causes neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation;
those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm, and those that are unbound.
Past, future, and present— this is called the primary gateway of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
"Cause" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Arising" refers to causes and conditions;
"retribution" refers to causes and conditions;
"conjunction" refers to causes and conditions.
"Predominance" refers to the condition as support (*āśraya-pratyaya*).
"Support" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
"Nutriment" refers to the condition as support.
The same applies to nourishment, maintenance, grasping, the basis, and what is required.
"Initial conception" refers to the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*);
"abiding place" refers to the supporting condition (*āśraya-pratyaya*).
Birth refers to causes and conditions;
the path refers to causes and conditions;
seeking and proceeding refer to causes and conditions.
"Channel" (*tīra*) refers to the basis and condition.
"Fluid," "pervasion," and "filling" are also like this.
"Dysregulation" (*avyūha*) means not knowing the world and not abandoning the world.
The same applies to being unfirm, unprotected, uncultivated, and unpracticed.
"Discipline" (dama) means knowing the world and abandoning the world.
The same applies to being firm, protected, cultivated, and practiced.
"Not understanding" means not yet knowing through wisdom, nor knowing through the knowledge of abandonment.
"Not realizing" means not yet having realized through knowledge and vision.
"Not abandoning" means not yet having severed the fetters.
"Not exhausted" means not yet ultimately exhausted.
"Not extinguished" means not yet extinguished through the condition of wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) or not extinguished through the non-condition of wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
"Understanding" means knowing through wisdom and knowing through the wisdom of abandonment.
Realization refers to knowledge, vision, and abandonment.
Abandonment refers to temporary abandonment.
Exhaustion refers to ultimate exhaustion.
Cessation refers to cessation through wisdom (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through wisdom (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The basis for joy refers to the causes that give rise to joy and the experience of its retribution.
The basis for sorrow refers to the causes that give rise to sorrow and the experience of its retribution.
The locus of relinquishment refers to the causes for relinquishment and the experience of retribution.
"Wholesome" refers to the name-and-form that is cultivated;
"unwholesome" refers to the name-and-form that is abandoned.
Indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) refers to the name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) that is experienced as well as those factors that are not retribution (*avipāka*).
Learner (*śaikṣa*) refers to the noble (*ārya*) name-and-form that is not of one who has completed the training (*aśaikṣa*).
One beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*) refers to the noble name-and-form that is not of a learner.
Neither-learner-nor-non-learner refers to non-noble name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Resultant refers to the experience of name-and-form as well as wholesome results.
Dharma of result refers to name-and-form that is of the nature to produce a result.
Neither-result-nor-dharma-of-result refers to name-and-form that is neutral (*avyākṛta*) and not included within one's own portion.
Abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) refers to name-and-form that is unwholesome (*akuśala*) and not abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Abandoned by cultivation refers to name-and-form that is unwholesome and not abandoned by insight.
That which is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation refers to name-and-form that is either wholesome or indeterminate.
That which has as its cause what is abandoned by vision refers to name-and-form that is either abandoned by vision or is the fruition of factors abandoned by vision.
The cause that is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) which is either abandoned by cultivation or is the retribution of what is abandoned by cultivation.

The cause that is neither abandoned by vision (*darśana-heya*) nor abandoned by cultivation refers to name-and-form which is either wholesome (*kuśala*), the retribution of wholesome dharmas, or that which is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution (*na-vipāka-na-vipākadharma*).
Bound to the desire realm refers to name-and-form that is either outflow-tainted (*āsrava*) or defiled (*sāsrava*) by the outflows of the desire realm.
Bound to the form realm refers to name-and-form that is either outflow-tainted or defiled by the outflows of the form realm.
Bound to the formless realm refers to name-and-form that is either outflow-tainted or defiled by the outflows of the formless realm.
"Unbound" refers to name-and-form that is noble and untainted (*anāsrava*).
"Past" refers to name-and-form that has already arisen and already ceased.
"Future" refers to name-and-form that has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged.
The present refers to the arising of name-and-form that has not yet ceased.
Name is the cause of name, the cause of form, and the cause of name-and-form.
Form is the cause of name, the cause of form, and the cause of name-and-form.
Name-and-form is the cause of name; name-and-form is the cause of form; name-and-form is the cause of name-and-form.
Name gives rise to name; name gives rise to form; name gives rise to name-and-form.
Form gives rise to name; form gives rise to form; form gives rise to name-and-form.
Name-and-form gives rise to name; name-and-form gives rise to form; name-and-form gives rise to name-and-form.
Name is the result of name, name-and-form is the result of name-and-form, and name-and-form is the result of both name and name-and-form.
Form is the result of name, form is the result of form, and form is the result of both name and name-and-form.
Name-and-form is called the retribution of name, the retribution of form, and the retribution of both name and form.
Name is associated with name, name is associated with form, and name is associated with both name and form.
Form is associated with name, form is associated with form, and form is associated with both name and form.
Name-and-form together with name, name-and-form together with form, and name-and-form together with both name-and-form.
Name is predominant over name, name-and-form is predominant over name-and-form, and both name-and-form are predominant over both name-and-form.
Matter is called the predominance of matter; matter is the predominance of matter; matter is called the predominance of name-and-matter.
Name-and-matter is called the predominance of name-and-matter; name-and-matter is the predominance of matter; name-and-matter is called the predominance of name-and-matter.
Name depends on name, name depends on form, and name depends on name-and-form.
Form depends on name, form depends on form, and form depends on name-and-form.
Name-and-form depends on name, name-and-form depends on form, and name-and-form depends on name-and-form.
The nutriment of name by name, the nutriment of name-and-form by name, and the nutriment of name-and-form by name-and-form;
the nutriment of form by name, the nutriment of form by form, and the nutriment of form by name-and-form;
the nutriment of name-and-form by name, the nutriment of name-and-form by form, and the nutriment of name-and-form by name-and-form.
The same applies to nourishment, maintenance, grasping, support, and requisites.
It is called the initial embryo of name, the initial embryo of form, and the initial embryo of name-and-form.
Form is called the initial embryo; form-form is the initial embryo; form-name-and-form is the initial embryo.
Name-and-form is called the initial embryo; name-and-form-form is the initial embryo; name-and-form-name-and-form is the initial embryo.
The dwelling place is also like this:
it is called name arising from name, name arising from form, and name-and-form arising from name;
it is called form arising from name, form arising from form, and name-and-form arising from form.
Name-and-form gives rise to name; name-and-form gives rise to form; name-and-form gives rise to name-and-form.
Name is the path of name, name is the path of name-and-form, name is the path of name-and-form.
Form is the path of name, form is the path of form, form is the path of name-and-form.
Name-and-form is called the path of name, name-and-form is called the path of form, and name-and-form is called the path of name-and-form.
The same applies to where they lead.
Name is called the ford of name, name-and-form is called the ford of name-and-form, and name-and-form is called the ford of name-and-form.
Form is called a drop; form is a drop of form; form is a drop of name-and-form.
Name is called a drop; name is a drop of name; name is a drop of name-and-form.
It is the same for moistening, pervading, and filling.
Name is undisciplined, name is undisciplined; name is undisciplined, form is undisciplined; name is undisciplined, both name and form are undisciplined.
Form is undisciplined, form is undisciplined; form is undisciplined, form is undisciplined; form is undisciplined, both name and form are undisciplined.

When name-and-form are undisciplined, they are called "undisciplined"; when name-and-form are undisciplined, form is undisciplined; when name-and-form are undisciplined, both name-and-form are undisciplined.
The same applies to being unfirm, unprotected, uncollected, and uncultivated.
Name is called "name-conditioning," name is called "form-conditioning," and name is called "name-and-form-conditioning.
Form is called "form-conditioning," form is called "form-conditioning," and form is called "name-and-form-conditioning."
The taming of name-and-form is the taming of name, the taming of form, and the taming of both name-and-form.
The same applies to firmness, guarding, gathering, and cultivation.
Name is not understood, name is not understood; name is not understood, form is not understood; name is not understood, name-and-form are not understood.
Form is not understood, name is not understood; form is not understood, form is not understood; form is not understood, name-and-form are not understood.

When name-and-form are not understood, name is not understood; when name-and-form are not understood, form is not understood; when name-and-form are not understood, both name-and-form are not understood.
It is the same for that which has not been realized, not abandoned, not exhausted, and not extinguished.
It is called the understanding of name, the understanding of name, the understanding of name and form.
It is the understanding of form as name, the understanding of form as form, and the understanding of form as name and form.
The liberation from name-and-form is the liberation from name, the liberation from form, and the liberation from both name-and-form.
The same applies to realization, abandonment, exhaustion, and cessation.
Conditioned by the name of the sphere of joy, there arise the name of the sphere of joy, the form of the sphere of joy, and the name-and-form of the sphere of joy.
Conditioned by the form of the sphere of joy, there arise the name of the sphere of joy, the form of the sphere of joy, and the name-and-form of the sphere of joy.
Conditioned by name-and-form that is a basis for joy, there arise name, form, and name-and-form that are bases for joy.
It is the same for the bases of grief and the bases of equanimity.

Chapter Four: The Chapter on Designated Bonds (*Prajñapti-saṃyojana-varga*) from the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Section on the Introduction. Regarding bonds, the various proclivities (*anuśaya*), the faculties, the courses of all afflictions, and the subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsana*): as long as these bonds have not been extinguished and have not been exhausted, one continues to undergo birth, old age, death, and the accumulation of all manner of suffering.
Now, we shall collect the provisional gates for the rectification [of the teachings]:

the ten fetters (saṃyojana), the twelve bases (āyatana), the eighteen elements (dhātu), the five aggregates (skandha), the four truths (satya), the twenty-two faculties (indriya), the five destinies (gati), the three realms (dhātu), and the phenomena pertaining to persons and the phenomena pertaining to persons themselves.
What are the ten fetters?

The fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of attachment to rules and rituals, the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill will, the fetter of lust for the realm of form, the fetter of lust for the formless realm, the fetter of ignorance, the fetter of conceit, and the fetter of restlessness.
What is the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?

If there are afflictions of view that are not associated with the mind, which do not arise together with the mind, do not abide together with it, and do not cease together with it—by reason of these causes and conditions, the proclivity of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) arises; this is called the fetter of views.

Furthermore, if the affliction of restlessness is not associated with the mind, does not arise together with the mind, does not abide together with the mind, and does not cease together with the mind, yet by reason of these conditions gives rise to the latent tendency of restlessness, this is called the fetter of restlessness.

Furthermore, wherever there is a subtle, firm attachment that lies dormant and submerged, by reason of this cause and condition, the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) arises; this is called the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

This continues until: wherever there is a subtle, firm attachment that lies dormant and submerged, by reason of this cause and condition, the latent tendency of restlessness (*auddhatya-anuśaya*) arises; this is called the fetter of restlessness (*auddhatya-saṃyojana*).
The twelve bases (*āyatana*), eighteen elements (*dhātu*), five aggregates (*skandha*), four truths (*satya*), twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), and three realms (*dhātu*) are as explained above.
What are the five destinies (*gati*)?
Hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.
What is hell? The uninterrupted and the intermittent; these are called hells.
What are animals?
Those that move in water, on land, or through the air are called animals.
What are hungry ghosts?
Those who eat little or do not eat at all are called hungry ghosts (*preta*).
What are humans?
The inhabitants of the four continents are called humans.
What is "deva"?
The devas of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—these are called devas.
What is "dharma"?
Form-dharmas and non-form-dharmas, up to past dharmas, future dharmas, present dharmas, and those that are neither past, nor future, nor present—these are called dharmas.
What kind of person is this?
It is one who has not yet produced wisdom and has not yet finished with the realm of desire, has not yet finished with the realm of form, and has not yet finished with the formless realm.
It is also one who has already produced wisdom but has not yet finished with the realm of desire, and has not yet finished with the realms of form and the formless.

Furthermore, there is a person who has already produced wisdom and has completed [the transcendence of] the desire realm, but has not yet completed [the transcendence of] the form and formless realms.
This is called a "person.
Such phenomena and such a person are called "phenomena of persons and the person of phenomena."
Of the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Three are abandoned by vision; seven are of two parts, being either abandoned by vision or abandoned by cultivation.
What are the three abandoned by vision?
View, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—these are called the three that are abandoned through vision (*dṛṣṭi-prahātavya*).
What are the seven that are twofold, being either abandoned through vision or abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?

Sensual lust, ill-will, lust for the realm of form, lust for the formless realm, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness—these are called the seven that are twofold, being either abandoned through vision or abandoned through cultivation.
Of the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
All are abandoned by insight.
How many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Seven [fetters] are abandoned through cultivation, excluding those abandoned through vision, doubt, and the attachment to rites and rituals.
Among the ten fetters, how many are bound to the desire realm, how many are bound to the form realm, and how many are bound to the formless realm?

Two are bound to the desire realm, one is bound to the form realm, one is bound to the formless realm, one is twofold—either bound to the desire realm or the form realm—and five are threefold—either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
What are the two bound to the desire realm?
Attachment to sensual desire and ill will—these two are bound to the desire realm.
What is the one bound to the form realm?
Regarding the defilement of form (*rūpa-rāga*), this one is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is the one bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
Regarding the defilement of the formless (*ārūpya-rāga*), this one is bound to the formless realm.
What are the two parts that are either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm?
The path of ethical discipline (*śīlamārga*); these two parts are either bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm.
What are the five factors that belong to three parts—either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm?
They are view, doubt, ignorance, pride, and restlessness; these five belong to three parts, being either bound to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
Of the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are bound to the desire realm?
Eight, excluding those bound to the form realm and the formless realm.
Of the ten fetters, how many are bound to the form realm?
Seven [fetters] exclude desire-taint, ill-will, and formless-taint.
Among the ten fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are bound to the formless realm?
Six: namely, views, doubt, formless-taint, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
Regarding the fetters bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-saṃyojana*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Three are abandoned by insight; five are of two kinds, being either abandoned by insight or abandoned by cultivation.
Which three are abandoned through vision?
Views, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals—these three are abandoned through vision.
Which five are of two parts, being either abandoned through vision or abandoned through cultivation?
Sensual desire, ill will, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness—these five are of two parts, being either abandoned by vision or abandoned by cultivation.
Among the eight fetters bound to the desire realm, how many are abandoned by vision?
All are abandoned through insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
How many are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Five are abandoned through cultivation, excluding views, doubt, and the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Regarding the seven fetters bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Three are abandoned by insight; four are of two parts, being either abandoned by insight or abandoned by cultivation.
What are the three that are abandoned through vision?
Views, doubt, and attachment to rites and rituals—these three are abandoned through vision.
What are the four that are of two parts, being either abandoned through vision or abandoned through cultivation?

Regarding the four—attachment to form (*rūparāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—these four are of two types: either abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Among the seven fetters bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-saṃyojana*), how many are abandoned by insight?
All are abandoned through insight.
How many are abandoned through cultivation?
Four are abandoned through cultivation, excluding views, doubt, and the attachment to precepts and rituals.

Regarding the six fetters associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-saṃyojana*), how many are abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) and how many are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Two are abandoned by insight; four are of two kinds, being either abandoned by insight or abandoned by cultivation.
Which two are abandoned through vision?
Views and doubt—these two are abandoned through vision.
Which four are of both kinds, being either abandoned through vision or abandoned through cultivation?

The four—stain of the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—are of two parts: they are either abandoned by seeing (*darśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Among the six fetters (*saṃyojana*) bound to the formless realm, how many are abandoned by seeing?
All are abandoned through vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
How many are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Four are abandoned through cultivation, namely: the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*), ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
In how many fetters does the underlying tendency of the view-fetter (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana-anuśaya) reside?
It resides in eight fetters, excluding its own nature and doubt.
It resides in nine fetters, excluding its own nature.
The fetter of attachment to precepts and observances (*sīlabbataparāmāsa*) underlies five fetters:
views, attachment to precepts and observances, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The fetter of ill will (*vyāpāda*) underlies six fetters: views, doubt, attachment to precepts and observances, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.

The fetter of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga-saṃyojana*) subsides within five fetters: views, adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
The fetter of attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga-saṃyojana*) subsides within four fetters: views, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) and the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) submerge within nine fetters, excluding its own nature.
The fetters of conceit (*māna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) likewise submerge within nine fetters, excluding their own natures.
How many fetters submerge within the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
Eight [factors] are excluded from the self-nature and the fetter of morality (śīla-vrata-parāmarśa).
Within the fetter of doubt (vicikitsā), four underlying tendencies (anuśaya)—hostility, ignorance, pride, and restlessness—are included.
Within the fetter of morality, eight underlying tendencies are included, excluding the self-nature and the defilements of the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).
The five fetters lie latent within the fetter of sensual lust (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*): namely, views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The five fetters lie latent within the fetter of ill will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*): namely, the fetter of views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The five fetters that underlie the defilements of the form realm consist of the fetter of views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The five fetters that underlie the defilements of the formless realm consist of the fetter of views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.

The eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) are submerged within the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), excluding their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the fetter of morality and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
The eight fetters are also submerged within the fetters of conceit (*māna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*), excluding their own intrinsic nature and the fetter of morality and observances.

The eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) lie dormant within the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the ear-base (*śrotra-āyatana*), excluding those associated with the path of morality (*śīlamārga*) and the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

The seven fetters lie dormant within the nose-base (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*) and the tongue-base (*jihvā-āyatana*), excluding those associated with the path of morality, the defilements of the form realm (*rūparāga*), and the defilements of the formless realm.

The eight fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant within the sense-base of the body (kāyāyatana), excluding those associated with the path of morality (śīlamārga) and the defilements of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The nine fetters lie dormant within the sense-base of the mind (manāyatana), excluding those associated with the path of morality.
The nine fetters lie dormant within the sense-bases of form (rūpāyatana) and sound (śabdāyatana), excluding the defilements of the formless realm.

The seven fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent within the sense-sphere of odors and tastes (*gandha-āyatana* and *rasa-āyatana*), with the exception of the path of morality (*śīlamārga*), the defilements of the form realm (*rūparāga*), and the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

The eight fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent within the sense-sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya-āyatana*), with the exception of the path of morality and the defilements of the formless realm.
The ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) subside within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

Eight fetters and underlying tendencies subside within the eye-sphere (*cakṣur-dhātu*) and ear-sphere (*śrotra-dhātu*), excluding those associated with the path of morality (*śīlamārga*) and the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

Seven fetters and underlying tendencies subside within the nose-sphere (*ghrāṇa-dhātu*) and tongue-sphere (*jihvā-dhātu*), excluding those associated with the path of morality, the defilements of the form realm (*rūparāga*), and the defilements of the formless realm.
The eight fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant within the body-element (kāyadhātu), excluding the defilements of the path of morality (śīlamārga) and the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The nine fetters lie dormant within the form-element (rūpadhātu) and the sound-element (śabdadhātu), excluding the defilements of the formless realm.

The seven fetters and latent tendencies (anuśaya) lie dormant within the fragrance realm (*gandha-dhātu*) and the taste realm (*rasa-dhātu*), excluding the path of morality (*śīla-mārga*), the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*), and the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).
The eight fetters and latent tendencies lie dormant within the tangible realm (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*), excluding the path of morality and the defilements of the formless realm.
Eight fetters underlie the eye-consciousness element and the ear-consciousness element, excluding the taints of morality, the path, and the formless realm.
Seven fetters underlie the nose-consciousness element and the tongue-consciousness element, excluding the taints of morality, the path, the form realm, and the formless realm.

The eight fetters (saṃyojana) lie latent within the element of the body (kāyadhātu), excluding those pertaining to the path of morality (śīlamārga) and the defilements of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The nine fetters lie latent within the element of the mind (manodhātu) and the element of mental consciousness (manovijñānadhātu), excluding those pertaining to the path of morality.
The ten fetters lie latent within the element of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Ten fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged within the aggregate of form; nine fetters and underlying tendencies—excluding the fetter of attachment to precepts and observances—are submerged within the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Ten fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged within the truth of suffering.

The five fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) subside within the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*): namely, views (*dṛṣṭi*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
They do not exist within the Truths of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) or the Path (*mārgasatya*).

Eight fetters and underlying tendencies subside within the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) and the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*), excluding the path of precepts (*śīlamārga*) and the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

The seven fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) reside in the nose-faculty and the tongue-faculty, excluding the path of morality (śīlamārga), the defilements of the form realm (rūparāga), and the defilements of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The eight fetters and underlying tendencies reside in the body-faculty, excluding the path of morality and the defilements of the formless realm.

The seven fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent in the male faculty (puruṣendriya) and female faculty (strīndriya), excluding the path of morality (śīlamārga), the defilement of the realm of form (rūparāga), and the defilement of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
Nine fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent in the life-faculty (jīvitendriya), excluding the path of morality.

Seven fetters (saṃyojana) have their latent tendencies (anuśaya) submerged in the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), excluding the precept-delusion (śīlavrataparāmarśa), ill-will (vyāpāda), and the defilement of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).

Six fetters have their latent tendencies submerged in the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya): views (dṛṣṭi), doubt (vicikitsā), ill-will (vyāpāda), ignorance (avidyā), pride (māna), and restlessness (auddhatya).
Seven fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are submerged in the faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*), excluding the precept-delusion, ill-will, and the defilements of the formless realm.
Six fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*): doubt, ill-will, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
The eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) lie dormant within the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), excluding the faculty of morality and the path, as well as ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
The nine fetters lie dormant within the mental faculty (*manendriya*), excluding the faculty of morality and the path.
They do not exist within the noble faculties (*āryendriya*).
The hells are either six or seven.
The six underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell are: views, doubt, hatred, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
The seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that lead to rebirth in the Avīci Hell are: views, doubt, sensual desire, ill-will, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.

The eight underlying tendencies that lead to rebirth among animals are the same as those for the hells, with the exception of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*) and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
The eight fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant within the hungry ghosts (preta), excluding the defilements of the form realm (rūpārāga) and the formless realm (ārūpyārāga).
The eight fetters lie dormant within humans, excluding the defilements of the form realm and the formless realm.
The ten fetters lie dormant within the various devas.
Eight fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant in the heavens of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), excluding attachment to the form realm (rūparāga) and attachment to the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
Seven fetters lie dormant in the heavens of the form realm (rūpadhātu), excluding attachment to the desire realm, ill will (vyāpāda), and attachment to the formless realm.
The six fetters have their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) submerged in the formless realm heavens: views, doubt, formless-taint (*ārūpya-rāga*), ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The eight fetters have their latent tendencies submerged in the desire realm, excluding form-taint and formless-taint.
Seven fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) have their latent presence in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding sensual desire, ill will, and the defilement of the formless realm.
Six fetters and underlying tendencies have their latent presence in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*): views, doubt, the defilement of the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
Ten fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent in material phenomena (rūpadharma).
Nine fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent in non-material phenomena (arūpadharma), excluding those associated with the path of morality (śīlamārga).
Nine fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent in visible phenomena (sanidarśanadharma), excluding those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The ten fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are latent in phenomena that are not visible (anidarśana).
Nine fetters and underlying tendencies are latent in phenomena that possess resistance (sapratigha), excluding those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).
Ten fetters and underlying tendencies are latent in phenomena that lack resistance (apratigha).
The noble dharmas are not [the objects of] these.
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies pertain to non-noble dharmas.
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies pertain to dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava*).
There are no untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
There are ten tainted (sāsrava) dharmas; there are no untainted dharmas.
There are ten dharmas associated with seeking (paryeṣaṇā); there are no dharmas not associated with seeking.
There are ten dharmas that should be grasped; there are no dharmas that should not be grasped.
There are ten dharmas that are to be taken up; there are no dharmas that are not to be taken up.
There are ten superior dharmas; there are no dharmas that are not superior.
The nine fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant within the phenomena of grasping (upādāna-dharma), excluding the path of morality (śīla-mārga).
The ten fetters lie dormant within non-grasping phenomena (anupādāna-dharma).
The nine fetters lie dormant within internal phenomena (ādhyātma-dharma), excluding the path of morality.
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) submerge into external phenomena (*bāhyadharma*).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies submerge into phenomena with retribution (*savipākadharmā*).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies submerge into phenomena without retribution (*avipākadharmā*).
The nine fetters (saṃyojana) lie latent in mental factors (citta-dharma), excluding the path of precepts (śīla-mārga).
The ten fetters lie latent in non-mental factors (acitta-dharma).
The nine fetters lie latent in factors associated with the mind (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma), excluding the path of precepts.
The ten fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant in non-mental-associated dharmas.
Nine fetters lie dormant in mental concomitants (caitasika-dharma), excluding the path of morality (śīla-mārga).
Ten fetters lie dormant in non-mental-concomitant dharmas.
The nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) that cease through the cessation of objects (*ālambana-nirodha*) are factors with objects (*sālambana*), excluding the path of morality (*śīlamārga*).
The ten fetters that cease through the cessation of objects are factors without objects (*anālambana*).
The ten fetters that cease through the cessation of the mind (*citta-nirodha*) are factors associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*).
The ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) subside in relation to phenomena not associated with the mind (*cittaviprayukta-dharma*).
The same applies to phenomena that arise in accordance with the mind (*cittānuparivartin*) and phenomena that do not arise in accordance with the mind (*acittānuparivartin*).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies also subside in relation to karmic phenomena (*karma-dharma*).
The same applies to non-karmic dharmas (*akarmadharmas*).
Nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) lie dormant within karmically associated dharmas (*karmasaṃprayuktadharma*), with the exception of the path of morality (*śīlamārga*).
Ten fetters and latent tendencies lie dormant within dharmas not associated with karma (*akarmasaṃprayuktadharma*).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) involve immersion in both shared and unshared dharmas.
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies involve immersion in non-shared dharmas.
It is the same for dharmas that follow the transformation of karma and dharmas that do not follow the transformation of karma.
The ten fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that subside in things that are not causes;
the ten fetters and underlying tendencies that subside in things that are not causes;
the ten fetters and underlying tendencies that subside in things that have causes.
There is no such thing as a phenomenon without a cause.
The same applies to phenomena with a causal sequence and those without, phenomena with conditions and those without, and conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.
The ten fetters (saṃyojana) involve the sinking into the knowable-dharmas;
the ten fetters do not involve the sinking into the non-knowable-dharmas.
It is the same for the cognizable-dharmas and the non-cognizable-dharmas, the resolvable-dharmas and the non-resolvable-dharmas, and the comprehensible-dharmas and the non-comprehensible-dharmas.

The nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that subside through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) are dharmas known by that knowledge, with the exception of the path of morality (*śīlamārga*).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies that do not subside through the knowledge of abandonment are dharmas not known by that knowledge.
The same applies to dharmas that are subject to abandonment and dharmas that are not subject to abandonment.
The ten fetters (saṃyojana) as objects of submergence for the cultivation of the Dharma;
the ten fetters as objects of submergence not for the cultivation of the Dharma;
the ten fetters as objects of submergence for the realization of the Dharma.
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) do not subside in the non-realized dharmas.
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies subside in wholesome dharmas.
Nine fetters and underlying tendencies subside in unwholesome dharmas, with the exception of the path of morality (śīlamārga).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) subside in indeterminate dharmas;
they do not exist in dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies subside in dharmas that are neither of those in training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa).

The ten fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) subside into the phenomena that are results of maturation (vipāka-dharma). The ten fetters and underlying tendencies subside into the phenomena that are both results of maturation and the causes of further maturation (vipāka-vipāka-dharma).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies subside into the phenomena that are neither results of maturation nor the causes of further maturation (na-vipāka-na-vipāka-dharma).
The nine fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant and submerge within those phenomena abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), excluding the path of morality (*śīla-mārga*).
The nine fetters lie dormant and submerge within those phenomena abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), excluding the path of morality.
The ten fetters lie dormant and submerge within those phenomena abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation (*na-darśana-na-bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The nine fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant with respect to those phenomena whose causes are to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), excluding the factors of morality and the path.
The nine fetters lie dormant with respect to those phenomena whose causes are to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), excluding the factors of morality and the path.
The ten fetters lie dormant with respect to those phenomena whose causes are neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the eight fetters (*saṃyojana*) lie dormant within phenomena bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding those associated with attachment to the form realm (*rūparāga*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).

The latent dispositions of the seven fetters lie dormant within phenomena bound to the form realm, excluding those associated with attachment to the desire realm (*kāmarāga*), ill will (*vyāpāda*), and attachment to the formless realm.

The six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) that subside in the factors associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) are: views, doubt, formless-taint (*ārūpyarāga*), ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
There are none that subside in the unconditioned factors (*apratisaṃyukta*).
The ten fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie dormant in past phenomena;
the ten fetters and underlying tendencies lie dormant in future phenomena;
the ten fetters and underlying tendencies lie dormant in present phenomena.
There is no dharma that is not past, not future, and not present.

For a person whose wisdom has not yet arisen, who has not yet transcended the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm—how many fetters and latent tendencies (anuśaya) remain submerged?
10. In the desire realm there are eight, excluding attachment to form and attachment to the formless.
In the form realm there are seven, excluding attachment to desire, ill-will, and attachment to the formless.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are six: views, doubt, attachment to the formless, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.

For a person who has already produced knowledge but whose [defilements] in the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm are not yet exhausted, how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) remain?
Seven:
five in the desire realm, excluding attachment to form and attachment to the formless;
four in the form realm: attachment to form, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
In the formless realm, there are four: the defilement of the formless, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.

Furthermore, regarding a person who has attained the knowledge of birth, for whom the desire realm is finished but the form and formless realms are not yet finished—how many fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) remain?
Five: doubt of the desire realm;
four of the form realm—namely, attachment to form, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
Regarding the four [defilements] of the formless realm— namely, attachment to the formless, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness—

for a person who has not yet produced knowledge and for whom the desire realm is not yet exhausted, the form realm is not yet exhausted, and the formless realm is not yet exhausted, how many fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are present?
Within the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), eight [latent tendencies] are included, excluding its own nature and that of the precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Within the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*), four fetters are included: ill-will (*vyāpāda*), ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
Within the latent tendency of the precepts and observances, eight fetters are included, excluding its own nature and those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).
The five fetters (saṃyojana) that lie latent within the fetter of sensual desire (kāmarāga) are: views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The five fetters that lie latent within the fetter of ill will (vyāpāda) are: views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The five fetters that lie dormant within the fetter of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga-saṃyojana*) are: views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The five fetters that lie dormant within the fetter of attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga-saṃyojana*) are: views, doubt, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The eight fetters (saṃyojana) are submerged within the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana), excluding their own nature and the fetter of morality and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa).
The eight fetters are also submerged within the fetters of conceit (māna) and restlessness (auddhatya), excluding their own nature and the fetter of morality and observances.
The eight fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are submerged within the eye-base and ear-base, excluding the taints of the path of morality and the formless realm.
From the nose-base and tongue-base, up to the past, future, and present, it is also as explained above.
It is not past, not future, and not present; it does not exist.

For a person of wisdom who has been born, while the realm of desire is not yet finished, the realm of form is not yet finished, and the formless realm is not yet finished—how many fetters and latent tendencies (anuśaya) have subsided?
They are not included within the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Doubt (*vicikitsā*) and the attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are also not included.

Among the three fetters, the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are subsumed within the fetter of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*), as are ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
The three fetters lie latent within the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*): namely, ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
The three fetters lie latent within the fetter of attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga-saṃyojana*): namely, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The three fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant within the fetter of attachment to the formless realm (ārūpyarāga): namely, ignorance (avidyā), pride (māna), and restlessness (auddhatya).
Six fetters lie dormant within the fetter of ignorance: namely, all except for its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
The six fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) subside in the fetter of conceit (*māna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*), excluding their own intrinsic nature.

The six fetters and underlying tendencies subside in the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and the sense-base of the ear (*śrotra-āyatana*), excluding the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*).

Five fetters and underlying tendencies subside in the sense-base of the nose (*ghrāṇa-āyatana*) and the sense-base of the tongue (*jihvā-āyatana*), excluding the defilements of the form realm (*rūpa-rāga*) and the formless realm.
Six fetters (saṃyojana) have their latent tendencies (anuśaya) submerged in the sense-base of body (kāyāyatana), excluding those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).
Seven fetters have their latent tendencies submerged in the sense-base of mind (manāyatana).
Six fetters have their latent tendencies submerged in the sense-bases of visible form (rūpāyatana) and sound (śabdāyatana), excluding those defiled by the formless realm.

The five fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are submerged in the sense-sphere of odors (*gandhāyatana*) and the sense-sphere of tastes (*rasāyatana*), excluding the defilements of the form realm (*rūparāga*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
The six fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the sense-sphere of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), excluding the defilements of the formless realm.
The seven fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the sense-sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The six fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are submerged in the eye-element and ear-element, excluding those associated with the defilement of the formless realm.
The five fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the nose-element and tongue-element, excluding those associated with the defilement of the form realm and the formless realm.
Six fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are submerged in the element of the body (kāyadhātu), excluding those associated with the taints of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
Six fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the elements of visible forms (rūpadhātu) and sounds (śabdadhātu), excluding those associated with the taints of the formless realm.
Five fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the elements of odors (gandhadhātu) and tastes (rasadhātu), excluding those associated with the taints of the form and formless realms.
Six fetters and latent tendencies (anuśaya) subside within the sphere of tangibles (spraṣṭavyadhātu), excluding those associated with formless-taint (ārūpyarāga).

Six fetters and latent tendencies subside within the spheres of visual-consciousness (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) and auditory-consciousness (śrotravijñānadhātu), excluding those associated with formless-taint.

Five fetters and latent tendencies subside within the spheres of olfactory-consciousness (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu) and gustatory-consciousness (jihvāvijñānadhātu), excluding those associated with form-taint (rūparāga) and formless-taint.
The six fetters (saṃyojana) lie latent within the body-consciousness element (kāyavijñānadhātu), excluding those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The seven fetters lie latent within the mind-element (manodhātu), the mind-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu), and the mental-object-element (dharmadhātu).
The seven fetters lie latent within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
The aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this.
Seven fetters lie latent within the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Three fetters—ignorance (*avidyā*), conceit (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—lie latent within the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
The truth of cessation and the truth of the path do not exist [as objects of these fetters].
Six fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent in the eye-faculty and the ear-faculty, excluding those associated with the defilement of the formless realm.
Five fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent in the nose-faculty and the tongue-faculty, excluding those associated with the defilement of the form realm and the formless realm.
The six fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent within the body-faculty (kāyendriya), with the exception of those associated with the defilement of the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).

The five fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent within the male-faculty (puruṣendriya) and female-faculty (strīndriya), with the exception of those associated with the defilement of the form realm (rūpa-rāga) and the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).
The seven fetters (saṃyojana) lie latent in the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Five fetters lie latent in the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), excluding the fetter of ill-will (pratigha) and the defilement of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
Four fetters lie latent in the faculty of pain (duḥkhendriya): ill-will, ignorance (avidyā), pride (māna), and restlessness (auddhatya).
The five fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are submerged in the faculty of joy (sukhendriya), excluding those associated with hatred and the defilements of the formless realm.
Four fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya): namely, hatred, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
The six fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) subside in the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya), with the exception of ill-will (vyāpāda).
The seven fetters and underlying tendencies subside in the mental faculty (manendriya).
They do not exist in the noble faculties (āryendriya).
In the hells, among animals, and among hungry ghosts, these do not exist.
Among humans, five fetters and latent tendencies remain, excluding the defilements of the form realm and the formless realm.
In the heavens, all seven fetters are present.
The five fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) are submerged in the heavens of the desire realm, excluding the defilements of form and the formless realm.
The four fetters and underlying tendencies are submerged in the heavens of the form realm: the defilement of form, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
The four fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that subside in the formless realm heavens are: attachment to the formless, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
The five fetters and underlying tendencies that subside in the desire realm are those same factors, excluding attachment to the form realm and attachment to the formless realm.
The four fetters that lie dormant in the realm of form are: passion for form, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The four fetters that lie dormant in the formless realm are: passion for the formless, ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The seven fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) pervade both material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) and non-material phenomena (arūpa-dharma). It is the same for non-material phenomena.
Six fetters and underlying tendencies pervade visible phenomena (sanidarśana-dharma), with the exception of those associated with formless defilement (ārūpya-rāga).
Seven fetters (saṃyojana) have their underlying tendencies (anuśaya) latent in dharmas that are invisible (anidarśana).
Six fetters have their underlying tendencies latent in dharmas that possess resistance (sapratigha), excluding those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).
Seven fetters have their underlying tendencies latent in dharmas that lack resistance (apratigha).
There are none among the noble dharmas.
The seven fetters and latent tendencies do not submerge non-noble dharmas.
There are seven [types] among the tainted (sāsrava) dharmas; there are none among the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
There are seven phenomena associated with defilement; there are none that are not associated with defilement.
There are seven phenomena associated with seeking; there are none that are not associated with seeking.
There are seven phenomena subject to appropriation; there are none that are not subject to appropriation.
There are seven factors with grasping; there are none without grasping.
There are seven superior factors; there are none that are not superior.
There are seven factors associated with feeling; there are seven factors not associated with feeling.
There are seven internal phenomena and seven external phenomena.
There are seven phenomena that have retribution and seven phenomena that are without retribution.
There are seven mental phenomena and seven non-mental phenomena.
Seven factors are associated with the mind; seven factors are not associated with the mind.
Seven factors are mental concomitants; seven factors are not mental concomitants.
Seven factors have an object; seven factors have no object.
Seven factors are concomitant with the mind; seven factors are not concomitant with the mind.
Seven factors follow the movement of the mind; seven factors do not follow the movement of the mind.
Seven factors are karma; seven factors are not karma.
Seven factors are associated with karma; seven factors are not associated with karma.
Seven factors are common to karma; seven factors are not common to karma.
Seven factors follow the transformation of karma; seven factors do not follow the transformation of karma.
Seven with causes, seven without causes;
seven with causal conditions, seven without causal conditions;
seven with continuities, seven without continuities.
There are seven factors with objects and seven factors without objects.
There are seven conditioned factors and seven unconditioned factors.
There are seven factors that are cognizable and seven factors that are not cognizable.
Seven factors are cognizable by consciousness; seven factors are not cognizable by consciousness.
Seven factors are resolvable; seven factors are not resolvable.
Seven factors are fully understood; seven factors are not fully understood.
There are seven factors known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), and seven factors not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
There are likewise seven factors that are subject to abandonment (*prahātavya*) and seven factors not subject to abandonment.
There are seven factors to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) and seven factors not to be cultivated.
Seven are factors realized through direct knowledge (*abhisamaya-dharma*), and seven are factors not realized through direct knowledge.
Seven are wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*), seven are unwholesome factors (*akuśala-dharma*), and seven are indeterminate factors (*avyākṛta-dharma*).
There are no factors of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); seven are factors of neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa-dharma*).

There are seven [factors] that are resultant phenomena; seven that are both resultant phenomena and the nature of producing results; and seven that are neither resultant phenomena nor the nature of producing results.
There are none that are abandoned by vision; seven that are abandoned by cultivation; and seven that are neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.

There are no factors with causes abandoned through seeing; there are seven factors with causes abandoned through cultivation; and there are seven factors with causes neither abandoned through seeing nor abandoned through cultivation.
There are five factors bound to the desire realm, excluding those stained by the form realm and the formless realm.
There are four factors bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*): attachment to form, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
There are four factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-dharma*): attachment to the formless, ignorance, pride, and restlessness.
There are no unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta) dharmas.
There are seven past dharmas, seven future dharmas, and seven present dharmas; there are none that are neither past, nor future, nor present.

When a person of wisdom is born, having already transcended the desire realm but not yet transcended the form realm and not yet transcended the formless realm, how many fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) remain?
Among the fetters of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana), there are none.
Doubt, attachment to precepts and rituals, sensual desire, and ill-will are absent [from the fetter of attachment to existence].
Regarding the latent tendencies of the three fetters, they subside within the fetter of attachment to form: ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
Regarding the latent tendencies of the three fetters, they subside within attachment to the formless: ignorance, conceit, and restlessness.
The four fetters (saṃyojana) lie dormant within the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana), excluding its own nature.
The four fetters lie dormant within the fetters of conceit (māna) and restlessness (auddhatya), excluding their own natures.
