The four fetters lie dormant within the sense-base of the eye (cakṣur-āyatana) and the sense-base of the ear (śrotra-āyatana), excluding those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).
The nose-base and tongue-base have none.
The four fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) subside in the body-base, excluding those associated with the taints of the formless realm.
The five fetters and underlying tendencies subside in the mind-base.

The four fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) descend into the sphere of visible form (rūpāyatana) and the sphere of sound (śabdāyatana), excluding those associated with the defilement of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
They do not descend into the spheres of odor (gandhāyatana) or taste (rasāyatana).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies descend into the sphere of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana), excluding those associated with the defilement of the formless realm.
The five fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) subside within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Four fetters and underlying tendencies subside within the eye-sphere (cakṣur-dhātu) and ear-sphere (śrotra-dhātu), excluding those associated with the defilement of the formless realm (ārūpya-rāga).
There are none for the nose-sphere (ghrāṇa-dhātu) or the tongue-sphere (jihvā-dhātu).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie dormant within the body element (*kāyadhātu*), excluding the defilements of the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies lie dormant within the visible-form element (*rūpadhātu*) and the sound element (*śabdadhātu*), excluding the defilements of the formless realm.
They do not exist within the nose element (*ghrāṇadhātu*) or the tongue element (*jihvādhātu*).
The four fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent within the sphere of tangibles (spraṣṭavyadhātu), excluding those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).

The four fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent within the spheres of visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñānadhātu) and auditory consciousness (śrotravijñānadhātu), excluding those defiled by the formless realm.
They do not exist within the spheres of olfactory consciousness (ghrāṇavijñānadhātu) and gustatory consciousness (jihvāvijñānadhātu).

The four fetters (saṃyojana) and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) lie latent within the sphere of body-consciousness (kāyavijñānadhātu), excluding those associated with the taints of the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The five fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent within the mind-sphere (manodhātu), the mind-consciousness-sphere (manovijñānadhātu), and the dharma-sphere (dharmadhātu).

The five fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha); the same applies to the aggregates of feeling (vedanā), perception (saṃjñā), formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).
The five fetters (saṃyojana) have their latent tendencies (anuśaya) submerged within the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya).
Three fetters have their latent tendencies submerged within the Truth of Origination (samudayasatya): ignorance (avidyā), conceit (māna), and restlessness (auddhatya).
They do not exist within the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya) or the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) reside in the eye-faculty and the ear-faculty, excluding those associated with the defilements of the formless realm.
They do not exist in the nose-faculty or the tongue-faculty.
The four fetters and underlying tendencies reside in the body-faculty, excluding those associated with the defilements of the formless realm.
The male faculty and female faculty have no underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
The five fetters (*saṃyojana*) have their underlying tendencies submerged in the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).

Four fetters have their underlying tendencies submerged in the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), with the exception of those associated with the defilements of the formless realm.
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) do not exist [therein].
The five fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) subside within the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) and the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
All untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*) do not exist [therein].
They do not exist among hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or humans.
The five fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) pervade the heavens;
they do not exist among the gods of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that subside in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) exclude those associated with the taints of the formless (ārūpya-rāga).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies that subside in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) exclude those associated with the taints of form (rūpa-rāga).
There are none in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that subside in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) exclude those defiled by the formless realm (ārūpyarāga).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies that subside in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) exclude those defiled by the realm of form.
The same applies to the four fetters and underlying tendencies that subside in phenomena of the realm of form; it is likewise for phenomena of the formless realm.
The four fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) lie latent in visible phenomena (*dṛśya-dharma*), excluding those associated with formless-taint (*ārūpya-rāga*).
The five fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent in invisible phenomena (*adṛśya-dharma*).
The four fetters and underlying tendencies lie latent in phenomena with resistance (*sapratigha-dharma*), excluding those associated with formless-taint.

Regarding the five fetters (*saṃyojana*), their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) subside within the category of non-reactive phenomena (*appaṭigha-dhamma*). They do not exist in noble phenomena (*ariya-dhamma*); they exist in five types of non-noble, contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*), and do not exist in uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*).
They exist in five types of defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*), and do not exist in undefiled phenomena (*akliṣṭa-dharma*).
There are five [factors] that seek the Dharma; there are none that do not seek the Dharma.
There are five [factors] that should be grasped as the Dharma; there are none that should not be grasped as the Dharma.
There are five [factors] that grasp the Dharma; there are none that do not grasp the Dharma.
There are five superior dharmas; there are none that are non-superior dharmas.
Five are acquired dharmas; five are non-acquired dharmas.
Five are internal dharmas; five are external dharmas.
There are five factors with retribution and five factors without retribution.
Five are mental factors and five are non-mental factors.
Five are factors associated with the mind and five are factors dissociated from the mind.
There are five mental concomitants and five non-mental concomitants.
There are five objects with conditions and five objects without conditions.
There are five factors associated with the mind and five factors dissociated from the mind.
There are five factors that follow the mind and five factors that do not follow the mind.
There are five factors that are karma and five factors that are not karma.
There are five factors associated with karma and five factors not associated with karma.
There are five factors that are common karma and five factors that are not common karma.
There are five factors that evolve according to karma and five factors that do not evolve according to karma.
There are five factors that are causes and five factors that are not causes.
There are five factors with causes and five factors without causes.
There are five factors with a continuity and five factors without a continuity.
There are five conditioned factors and five unconditioned factors.
There are five types of knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), but there is no absence of knowledge of phenomena.

It is the same for the cognition of phenomena and non-cognition of phenomena, the understanding of phenomena and non-understanding of phenomena, and the realization of phenomena and non-realization of phenomena.
There are five factors known through the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), and five factors not known through the knowledge of abandonment.
The same applies to factors of abandonment and factors not of abandonment.
There are five factors to be cultivated (*bhāvanīya*), and five factors not to be cultivated.
Five realized dharmas and five non-realized dharmas.
Five wholesome dharmas and five unwholesome dharmas.
Five dharmas of those beyond training, five dharmas of those in training, and five dharmas of those who are neither in training nor beyond training.

There are five [factors] that are resultant (*vipāka-dharma*), five that are both resultant and productive of result (*vipāka-vipāka-dharma*), and five that are neither resultant nor productive of result (*naiva-vipāka-na-vipāka-dharma*).

There are none that are abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya-dharma*); there are five that are abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-dharma*), and five that are abandoned neither by vision nor by cultivation (*naiva-darśana-na-bhāvanā-prahātavya-dharma*).

There are no factors with causes abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*). There are five factors with causes abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). There are five factors with causes neither abandoned by insight nor by cultivation.
There are four factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and four factors bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), excluding those defiled by the formless realm.
There are four factors bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), excluding those defiled by attachment to form (*rūparāga*). There are none that are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
There are five past factors, five future factors, and five present factors; there are none that are neither past, nor future, nor present.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-six;
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle Twenty-seven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others.

Section on the Exposition of the Fictitious Bonds, Part Two. If a person is submerged in the bonds of views, doubt, and attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), how many bonds does this person possess?
There are ten.
If a person is submerged in sleep within the fetters of sensual desire and ill-will, how many fetters does this person possess?
Either ten or seven.

If a person is submerged in sleep within the fetters of attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, ignorance, pride, and restlessness, how many fetters does this person possess?
Either ten or five.
If the fetter of views and the fetter of doubt are latent within a given dharma, how many fetters are present in that dharma?
They may be ten, nine, eight, seven, six, or five.
If the fetters of the path of morality (*śīlamārga*) lie dormant within a given dharma, how many fetters are there within that dharma?
They may be ten, nine, eight, or seven.
If the fetters of sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) lie dormant within a given dharma, how many fetters are there within that dharma?
Whether there be ten, nine, eight, seven, or six:
if the fetter of ill will is submerged within a given phenomenon, how many fetters are present within that phenomenon?
There may be ten, nine, eight, seven, six, or five.
If a phenomenon is subject to the latent tendencies of attachment to the realm of form or the formless realm, how many fetters are present within that phenomenon?
There may be ten, nine, eight, seven, or six.
If the fetters of ignorance (*avidyā*), pride (*māna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*) are latent within a given phenomenon, how many fetters are present in that phenomenon?
[The answer is] ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, or four; thus it concludes for each person.
If one sees that the fetters of views and doubt have submerged a person within the factors of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*), how many fetters does this person possess?
They may have ten, nine, eight, seven, six, or five.
If the fetter of the path of precepts (*śīlamārga-saṃyojana*) lies dormant within a person’s human factors (*pudgala-dharma*), how many fetters does that person possess?
There may be ten, nine, eight, or seven.
If the fetter of sensual passion (*kāmarāga-saṃyojana*) lies dormant within a person’s human factors, how many fetters does that person possess?
Whether there be ten, nine, eight, seven, or six:
if the fetter of ill-will lies dormant within a person regarding these phenomena (dharma), how many fetters does that person possess with respect to those phenomena?
There may be ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, or four.

If the fetters of attachment to the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*) and the realm of formlessness (*arūpa-rāga*) lie dormant within a person's phenomena (*dharma*), how many fetters does that person possess?
They may have ten, nine, eight, seven, or six.
If the fetters of ignorance, conceit, and restlessness lie dormant within a person’s mental states (dharma), how many fetters does that person possess?
They may have ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, or four.

Whether it be the desire for cessation, the absence of the desire for cessation, or neither the desire nor the absence of the desire for cessation; whether it be the desire for birth, the absence of the desire for birth, or neither the desire nor the absence of the desire for birth.
"The desire for cessation" refers to the final moment of consciousness.
"Non-termination" refers to excluding the final moment of consciousness;
"termination" refers to the final moment of consciousness;
"non-termination" refers to remaining within these aggregates.
"Desiring birth" refers to the initial moment of mind.
"Not desiring birth" refers to [moments] excluding the initial moment of mind.
"Birth" refers to being within these aggregates (*skandha*).
"Not born" means not yet existing within these aggregates (*skandha*).
This applies likewise to the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; and to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If sentient beings are about to die within the hells, in how many fetters do they sink and perish?
If sentient beings are not about to die within the hells, in how many fetters do they sink and perish?
If sentient beings pass away within the hells, in how many fetters do they sink and perish?
If sentient beings do not pass away within the hells, in how many fetters do they sink and perish?
If sentient beings are born for the first time within the hells, in how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) are they submerged?
If sentient beings are not born for the first time within the hells, in how many fetters are they submerged?
If sentient beings are born in the hells, how many fetters (saṃyojana) do they sleep within and submerge in?
If sentient beings are not born in the hells, how many fetters do they sleep within and submerge in?
It is the same for animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas, as well as for the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
If a sentient being is about to die in hell and is reborn for the first time among animals, how many fetters (saṃyojana) does he sink into during the intermediate state?
If a sentient being is about to die in hell but is not reborn for the first time among animals, how many fetters does he sink into during the intermediate state?
If a sentient being is about to die within the hells and is reborn among animals, how many fetters (*saṃyojana*) does he remain submerged in?
If a sentient being is about to die within the hells and is not reborn among animals, in how many fetters is he submerged?
If sentient beings, while not yet desiring their end in hell, are first born among animals, how many fetters do they sink into during sleep?
If sentient beings, while not yet desiring their end in hell and not yet first born among animals, [pass away], how many fetters do they sink into during sleep?
If sentient beings in the hells do not die there intentionally but are reborn among animals, how many fetters (saṃyojana) must they pass through while submerged in the intermediate state?
If sentient beings in the hells do not die there intentionally and do not initially take birth among animals, how many fetters must they pass through while submerged in the intermediate state?
If sentient beings die in the hells and are born for the first time among animals, how many fetters (saṃyojana) do they fall asleep into and sink into?
If sentient beings die in the hells and are not born for the first time among animals, how many fetters do they fall asleep into and sink into?
If sentient beings die in the hells and are reborn among animals, how many fetters do they remain submerged in?
If sentient beings die in the hells and are not reborn among animals, how many fetters do they remain submerged in?
If sentient beings do not end their existence in hell and are not yet born among animals, how many fetters (saṃyojana) do they remain submerged in?
If sentient beings do not end their existence in hell and are not yet born among animals, how many fetters do they remain submerged in?
If sentient beings do not die within the hells, nor are they reborn among animals, how many fetters (saṃyojana) must they sleep through and submerge themselves in?
It is the same for those who go from the hells to the hungry ghosts, from the hells to the human realm, and from the hells to the heavens.
From the animal realm to the hungry ghost realm; from the animal realm to the human realm; from the animal realm to the heavenly realms;
from the animal realm to the hell realms; from the hungry ghost realm to the human realm; from the hungry ghost realm to the heavenly realms;
from the hungry ghost realm to the hell realms; from the hungry ghost realm to the animal realm; from the human realm to...

Chapter Five: The Section on the Analysis of Conduct (*Caryā-vibhaṅga*) from the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*. The stages of bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct.
What is bodily conduct?
In-and-out breathing is called bodily formation (*kāyasaṃskāra*).
What is verbal formation (*vāksaṃskāra*)?
Initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) are called verbal formation.
What are mental formations?
They are perception and volition; these are called mental formations.
The sphere of bodily formations extends from the body possessing inhalation and exhalation up to the fourth dhyāna; this is called the sphere of bodily formations.
What is the stage that is not the sphere of bodily formations?
That which transcends the body of non-inhalation and exhalation and the fourth dhyāna is called the stage that is not the sphere of bodily formations.
What is the stage of verbal formations?

The mental consciousness of the desire realm, or that which is indeterminate in the form realm, or that which belongs to the first dhyāna and the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna—these are called the ground of verbal formation (*vāk-saṃskāra-bhūmi*).
What is the ground that is not the ground of verbal formation?
If the five bodies of consciousness are in the second dhyāna or above, this is called the stage that is not the ground of vocal formation (*vāk-saṃskāra-bhūmi*).
What is the stage of mental formation (*manas-saṃskāra-bhūmi*)?
Excluding the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and one birth (*upapatti*), if it is in any other place, this is called the stage of mental formation.
What is the stage that is not the sphere of mental activity?
The two meditative attainments and one birth—these are called the stage that is not the sphere of mental activity.
In what place does bodily activity arise and not cease?
From the body without inhalation and exhalation up to the body with inhalation and exhalation, if one arises from the fourth dhyāna, bodily formations arise here and do not cease.
Where do bodily formations cease and fail to arise?
From the body with inhalation and exhalation to the body without inhalation and exhalation—should one enter the fourth dhyāna, it is in this state that bodily formations cease and do not arise.
Where do bodily formations arise and cease?
Wherever there is the place of inhalation and exhalation, there the bodily formations arise and cease.
Where do the bodily formations move such that they neither arise nor cease?
Within a body that is without inhalation and exhalation, or in the fourth dhyāna, or beyond it—this is called the non-arising and non-ceasing of bodily formations.
In what place do verbal formations arise and cease?
From the point of departing from the fivefold body of consciousness up to the mental consciousness, and from the second dhyāna onward—in this place, verbal formations arise and cease.
In what place do verbal formations cease and fail to arise?

From the point of transcending the mental consciousness up to the fivefold body of sensory consciousness, or upon entering the second dhyāna—in these places, verbal formations cease and fail to arise.
In what place do verbal formations arise and cease?
Wherever there is vitarka and vicāra, in that place verbal formations arise and cease.
In what place do verbal formations neither arise nor cease?
Within the five groups of consciousness, from the second dhyāna upward, there is neither the arising nor the cessation of verbal formations (*vāksaṃskāra*).
Where, then, do mental formations (*manaḥsaṃskāra*) arise and cease?
When arising from the two meditative attainments, or when passing away at the end of a lifetime in a particular birth-place, the mental formations (*saṃskāra*) arise here and do not cease.
Where do the mental formations cease and fail to arise?
If one enters the two meditative attainments or is born in a certain realm of existence, there, mental formations (*saṃskāra*) cease and do not arise.
Where do mental formations arise and cease?
Wherever mental formations arise, therein they cease.
In what place does the mental formation (manas-karma) neither arise nor cease?
If it is within the two meditative attainments (samāpatti) or up to the single birth-place (upapatti-sthāna), it is there that the mental formation neither arises nor ceases.

Chapter Six: Contact (Phassa-vagga). Introduction to the Śāriputra Abhidharma Treatise, Chapter Six: Contact. The fool is shrouded by ignorance; through the conjunction of craving and the afflictions, and by means of these factors, the body is formed as an accumulation. Conditioned by that name-and-form, contact arises from these two factors.
Now, we shall collect the primary gate of the conventional nature of contact (*saṃvṛti-sparśa*).
Body-contact, mind-contact, and so forth up to the eighteen types of contact—these are called the phenomena of contact (*sparśa-dharma*).
What is body-contact?
If contact is associated with body-consciousness, it is called body-contact (*kāyasparśa*).
What is mental contact?
If contact is associated with mind-consciousness, it is called mental contact (*manasparśa*).
Furthermore, if it is associated with the five consciousnesses—namely, the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses—it is called "bodily contact" (*kāyasamsparśa*).
If it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), it is called "mental contact" (*manaḥsamsparśa*).
What is called "contact" (*sparśa*)?
If it is contact that touches the mind, this is called "mental contact" (*nāma-sparśa*).
What is "objective contact" (*pratigha-sparśa*)?
If it is contact with the body, this is called impingement-contact (*pratigha-sparśa*).
What is craving-contact (*tṛṣṇā-sparśa*)?
If it is contact associated with sensual passion, this is called craving-contact.
What is contact associated with aversion?
Contact that is associated with irritation is called contact associated with aversion.
What is contact associated with clarity?
If contact is associated with noble wisdom, it is called "contact of clarity" (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*).
What is "contact of ignorance" (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*)?
If contact is unwholesome and not associated with wisdom, it is called "contact of ignorance."
What is contact belonging to the side of clarity (*vidyāpakṣa-sparśa*)?
If contact arises from the side of clarity and clarity can cause it to expand, this is called contact belonging to the side of clarity.
What is contact belonging to the side of ignorance (*avidyāpakṣa-sparśa*)?
If contact arises from the portion of ignorance and ignorance causes it to expand, this is called contact belonging to the portion of ignorance (*avidyāṃśika-sparśa*).
Furthermore, if contact is associated with noble receptivity (*āryakṣānti*), this is called contact belonging to the portion of knowledge (*vidyāṃśika-sparśa*).
If contact is associated with non-noble afflictions, it is called contact belonging to the category of ignorance (*avidyāṅga-sparśa*).
Furthermore, if contact is attained by the noble ones as the fruit of knowledge, it is called contact belonging to the category of clear knowledge (*vidyāṅga-sparśa*).
If contact is non-noble, or is wholesome or neutral, it is called contact associated with ignorance (*avidyāṅga-sparśa*).
What is noble contact?
If contact is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called noble contact.
What is non-noble contact?
If contact is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called non-noble contact.
What is contact with outflows?
If contact is associated with defilement, it is called tainted contact (*sāsrava-sparśa*).
What is untainted contact?
If contact is free from defilement, it is called untainted contact (*anāsrava-sparśa*).
What is contact with attachment?
If contact involves seeking, it is called contact with attachment.
What is contact without attachment?
If contact is without seeking, it is called untainted contact (*asaṃkliṣṭa-sparśa*).
What is contact with seeking?
If contact is to be grasped, it is called contact with seeking (*sopādāna-sparśa*).
What is contact without seeking?
If contact is not to be grasped, it is called contact without seeking.
What is contact to be grasped?
If contact is accompanied by grasping, it is called "contact pertaining to what is to be grasped.
What is contact not pertaining to what is to be grasped?
If contact is without grasping, it is called "contact not pertaining to what is to be grasped."
What is contact with grasping (*sopādāna-sparśa*)?
If contact is accompanied by excellence (*viśeṣa*), it is called contact with grasping.
What is contact without grasping (*anupādāna-sparśa*)?
If contact is without superiority, it is called contact without grasping (*anupādāna-sparśa*).
What is contact with superiority?
If contact is accompanied by grasping, it is called contact with superiority (*sopādāna-sparśa*).
What is contact without superiority?
If contact is without grasping, it is called contact without superiority.
Furthermore, if this contact possesses other superior or sublime qualities, it is called contact with superiority.
If this contact has no other superior or sublime quality, it is called "unsurpassed contact" (*anuttara-sparśa*).
Furthermore, if the contact produced by a Tathāgata possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena, up to and including the accomplishment of mastery.
Apart from this contact, any other contact is called "contact with superiority.
The contacts excluded above are called "contact without superiority.
What is "feeling-contact"?
If contact is internal, it is called "contact that is felt.
What is contact that is not felt?
If contact is external, it is called "contact that is not felt."
What is internal contact?
If contact is associated with feeling, it is called internal contact.
What is external contact?
If contact is not feeling, it is called external contact.
What is contact with retribution?
If contact is of a nature that entails retribution, it is called contact with retribution.
What is contact that is without retribution (*avipāka*)?
If contact is either retribution itself, or neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution, this is called contact without retribution.
What is contact shared with ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)?

If a contact is not acquired by birth by non-ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and is also acquired by birth by ordinary beings, this is called "contact shared with ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjanasādhāraṇa-sparśa*).
What is "contact not shared with ordinary beings"?

If a contact is not acquired by birth by non-ordinary beings and cannot be acquired by birth by ordinary beings, this is called "contact not shared with ordinary beings. What is "contact shared with non-ordinary beings"?
If contact is acquired by ordinary persons and also acquired by those who are not ordinary persons, it is called contact shared with those who are not ordinary persons.
What is contact not shared with those who are not ordinary persons?
If contact arises for ordinary persons and does not arise for those who are not ordinary persons, this is called the "contact exclusive to those who are not ordinary persons.
What is the "contact shared by śrāvakas"?
If a contact is not acquired by birth by non-Śrāvakas, yet is acquired by birth by Śrāvakas as well, this is called a contact common to Śrāvakas.
What is a contact uncommon to Śrāvakas?
If a contact is not acquired by birth by non-Śrāvakas, and is not acquired by birth by Śrāvakas either, this is called a contact uncommon to Śrāvakas.
What is contact not shared with śrāvakas?
If a contact is acquired by birth by both śrāvakas and non-śrāvakas, this is called contact not shared with śrāvakas.
What is the contact not shared with śrāvakas?
If a contact arises for a śrāvaka but does not arise or is not attained by one who is not a śrāvaka, this is called the contact not shared with śrāvakas.
What is contact like lightning?
It is contact that abides for only a very brief duration, remaining for a short time.
Just as lightning abides for only a very brief duration, remaining for a short time, so too is this contact; this is called contact like lightning.
What is the diamond-like touch?
If a touch abides immeasurably and remains for immeasurable time—just as a diamond abides immeasurably and remains for immeasurable time, so too is this touch; this is called the diamond-like touch.

Furthermore, if, once contact has arisen, it severs a small portion of the afflictions—just as lightning emerging from the clouds illuminates a small portion of darkness and quickly vanishes—contact is likewise; this is called "lightning-like contact."
If, once contact has arisen, all afflictions are severed and no afflictions remain—whether coarse or subtle—none fail to be extinguished.
Just as when a diamond is cast against a bead or stone, it breaks and shatters them without exception, so too is this contact; this is called "diamond-like contact."
Furthermore, if upon the arising of contact one attains the fruit of a *srotāpanna* up to that of an *anāgāmin*, this is called "contact like lightning.
If upon the arising of contact one attains the fruit of an *arhat*, this is called "diamond-like contact."

Furthermore, if, once contact has arisen, one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer up to that of a non-returner, or attains the fruits of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or an arhat, this is called "contact like lightning."

If, once contact has arisen, one attains unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena—even up to the accomplishment of mastery—with respect to the contact produced by a Tathāgata, this is called "vajra-like contact."
What is contact that is not definitely attained?
If contact is attained, but is not definitely attained, is difficult to attain, and difficult to maintain, this is called contact that is not definitely attained.
What is contact that is definitely attained?
If a contact is obtained, definitely obtained, not difficult to obtain, and easy to maintain, this is called "contact definitely obtained.
What is "contact with effort that is difficult to maintain"?

It is a contact that, when obtained, is not definitely obtained, is difficult to obtain, and difficult to maintain; it lacks the power of mastery and sovereignty, and is not as desired, does not follow what is desired, and does not fulfill what is desired; it arises with effort and is difficult to obtain.
Just as a boat going against the current is difficult to move, so too is contact [that is difficult to maintain]; this is called "contact that is difficult to maintain due to effort.
What is "contact that is easy to maintain without effort"?
It is contact that is attained, definitely attained, not difficult to attain, and easily attained.
Just as a boat travels easily with the current, so too is contact; this is called "contact that is easy to maintain without effort.
What is "contact cultivated in one part"?
If, after contact has arisen, there is the perception of light but no seeing of forms, or if forms are seen but there is no perception of light, this is called "contact cultivated in one part."
What is contact cultivated as two parts?
If, once contact has arisen, there is perception of light and one also sees forms, this is called contact cultivated as two parts.

Furthermore, if contact has arisen and knowledge is produced but defilements are not abandoned, or if defilements are abandoned but knowledge is not produced, this is called contact cultivated as one part.
If, once contact has arisen, the arising of knowledge is able to sever the afflictions, this is called the cultivation of contact with two parts.
Furthermore, if, once contact has arisen, the arising of the knowledge of exhaustion occurs rather than the knowledge of non-arising, this is called the cultivation of contact with one part.
If, once contact has arisen, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arise, this is called the cultivation of contact that belongs to both parts.
What is contact with desire?
If contact belongs to one who possesses desire and is associated with the defilement of desire, this is called contact with desire.
What is contact free from desire?
If contact belongs to one who is free from desire and is not associated with the defilement of desire, this is called contact free from desire.
What is contact of ill-will?
If contact is associated with one who possesses hatred and is conjoined with aversion, it is called "contact with hatred.
What is "contact without hatred"?
If contact is dissociated from one who is free from hatred and is not conjoined with aversion, it is called "contact without hatred."
What is contact accompanied by delusion?
If contact belongs to a person with delusion and is associated with delusion, this is called contact accompanied by delusion.
What is contact free from delusion?
If contact is dissociated from delusion and not associated with delusion, this is called contact free from delusion (*amoha-sparśa*).
What is submerged contact (*līna-sparśa*)?

If contact is associated with sleep, not associated with internal mindfulness of cessation, wisdom is unaccomplished, and one is unable to discern wholesome phenomena, this is called submerged contact.
What is distracted contact (*vikṣipta-sparśa*)?

If one contacts thoughts of desire and passion, being accompanied by passion and associated with passion, and seeing much impurity as pure, becoming stained and attached to the five external sense-objects—this is called distracted contact.
What is slight contact?
If contact is indeterminate, it is called slight contact.
What is abundant contact?
If contact is fixed, it is called "fixed contact.
What is "unfixed contact"?
If contact belongs to an unfixed person and is not associated with fixedness, it is called "unfixed contact."
What is concentration-contact (*samādhi-sparśa*)?
If contact belongs to one who is concentrated and is associated with concentration, this is called concentration-contact.
What is non-liberation-contact (*avimukti-sparśa*)?
If contact is with one who is not liberated and is not associated with liberation, this is called "contact of non-liberation.
What is contact of liberation?
If contact is with one who is liberated and is associated with liberation, this is called "contact of liberation."
What is contact with excellence?
If contact is associated with excellent persons or excellent dharmas, it is called contact with excellence.
What is contact without excellence?
If contact is associated with no superior person and no superior dharma, it is called "contact without superiority.
What is contact with applied thought (*savitarka*)?
If contact is associated with applied thought, arising together with, coexisting with, and ceasing together with applied thought, it is called "contact with applied thought."
What is contact without vitarka?
If contact is not associated with vitarka, and does not arise, abide, or cease together with vitarka, this is called contact without vitarka.
What is contact with observation (*savitarka-sparśa*)?
If contact is associated with observation, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called contact with observation.
What is contact without observation (*avitarka-sparśa*)?

If contact is not associated with contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), does not arise together with contemplation, does not abide together with contemplation, and does not cease together with contemplation, this is called "contact without contemplation" (*avipaśyanā-sparśa*).
What is "contact accompanied by joy" (*prītisaha-gata-sparśa*)?
If contact is associated with joy, arising together with joy, abiding together with joy, and ceasing together with joy, this is called "contact accompanied by joy.
What is contact without joy?
If contact is not associated with joy, not arising together with joy, not abiding together with joy, and not ceasing together with joy, this is called "contact without joy."
What is contact associated with attachment (*sāsvāda-sparśa*)?
If contact is associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), this is called contact associated with attachment.
What is contact associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-sparśa*)?
If contact is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is called contact associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is contact associated with patience (*kṣānti*)?
If contact arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with patience, it is called contact associated with patience.
What is contact not associated with patience (*kṣānti*)?
If contact does not arise, abide, or cease together with patience, this is called contact not associated with patience.
What is contact associated with knowledge (*jñāna*)?
If contact arises, abides, and ceases together with wisdom, it is called contact associated with wisdom.
What is contact not associated with wisdom?
If contact does not arise, abide, and cease together with wisdom, it is called contact not associated with wisdom.
What is the contact of the first patience (*kṣānti*)?
If it is the contact cultivated by those who possess firm faith and those who possess the nature of firm dharma (*dharmakṣānti*), this is called the contact of the first patience.
What is the contact of the first knowledge (*jñāna*)?
If one experiences contact cultivated by those on the noble, untainted path of vision, this is called "contact of initial wisdom.
What is "contact at the end of desire"?
If one experiences contact associated with the final consciousness, this is called "contact at the end of desire."
What is initial contact?
If contact is associated with the first moment of consciousness, it is called initial contact.
What is wholesome contact?
If contact is cultivated, it is called wholesome contact.
What is unwholesome contact?
If contact is abandoned, it is called unwholesome contact.
What is indeterminate contact (*avyākṛta-sparśa*)?
If contact is feeling (*vedanā*), or is neither a result (*vipāka*) nor of the nature of producing a result (*avipākadharma*), this is called indeterminate contact.
What is the contact of one in training (*śaikṣa-sparśa*)?
If it is a noble contact that is not of one beyond training, this is called the contact of one in training (*śaikṣa-sparśa*).
What is the contact of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-sparśa*)?
If it is a noble contact that is not of one in training, this is called the contact of one beyond training.
What is contact that is neither of training nor beyond training?
If contact is not noble (ārya), it is called contact that is neither of training nor beyond training.
What is resultant contact (vipākaja-sparśa)?
If contact experiences a wholesome retribution, this is called "contact as retribution" (*vipāka-sparśa*).
What is "contact consisting of retribution-producing phenomena" (*vipākadharmaka-sparśa*)? If contact possesses retribution, this is called "contact consisting of retribution-producing phenomena."
What is contact that is neither resultant nor a factor leading to result?
If contact is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not comprised within one's own continuum (*asvaka*), this is called contact that is neither resultant nor a factor leading to result.
What is contact to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
If a contact is unwholesome and not abandoned by insight, it is called a contact abandoned by insight.
What is a contact abandoned by cultivation?
If a contact is unwholesome and not abandoned by insight, it is called a contact abandoned by cultivation.
What is contact that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?
If contact is wholesome or indeterminate, this is called contact that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is contact that has insight as its cause for abandonment?
If it is contact that is abandoned by vision, or the retribution of a dharma abandoned by vision, this is called contact caused by what is abandoned by vision.
What is contact caused by what is abandoned by cultivation?
If it is contact that is abandoned by cultivation, or the retribution of a dharma abandoned by cultivation, this is called contact caused by what is abandoned by cultivation.
What is contact that is neither caused by what is abandoned through vision nor caused by what is abandoned through cultivation?

It is contact that is wholesome, or the result of wholesome dharmas, or that which is neither a result nor a dharma leading to a result; this is called contact that is neither caused by what is abandoned through vision nor caused by what is abandoned through cultivation.
What is weak contact?
If contact is unwholesome, it is called weak contact.
What is middling contact?
If contact is neutral, it is called intermediate contact.
What is superior contact?
If contact is wholesome, it is called superior contact.
Furthermore, if contact is unwholesome or neutral, it is called weak contact.
If contact is non-noble and wholesome, it is called middling contact.
If contact is noble and untainted, it is called superior contact.
What is coarse contact?
If contact is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse contact.
What is subtle contact?
If contact is bound to the form realm or is unbound, it is called subtle contact.
What is minute contact?
If contact is bound to the formless realm, it is called minute contact.
Furthermore, that which is bound to the realm of form is called coarse contact.
That which is bound to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or that which is unbound, is called subtle contact.
That which is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called subtle contact (*sūkṣma-sparśa*).

Furthermore, if contact is bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, it is called coarse contact (*audārika-sparśa*).
If contact is unconditioned by the realms of existence, it is called subtle contact.
If contact is conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is called minute contact.
What is contact associated with pleasant feeling?
If contact is associated with pleasant feeling, it is called contact associated with pleasant feeling.
What is contact associated with painful feeling?
If contact is associated with painful feeling, it is called contact associated with painful feeling.
What is contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
If contact is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is called contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, if contact results in a pleasant retribution, it is called contact associated with pleasant feeling.
If contact results in the experience of a painful retribution, it is called contact associated with painful feeling.
If contact results in the experience of a neither-painful-nor-pleasant retribution, it is called contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, excluding the contact of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, if other contacts are wholesome and subject to retribution, they are called contacts of pleasant feeling;
if a contact is unwholesome, it is called a contact of painful feeling.

Excluding the contact associated with pleasant feeling, if there is any other contact that is wholesome and has a result, this is called the contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, if contact is wholesome and has a result, it is called the contact associated with pleasant feeling.
If contact is unwholesome, it is called contact associated with painful feeling.
Excluding contact associated with pleasant feeling and contact associated with painful feeling, any remaining contact is called contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is contact that is a basis for joy?
If contact, having first arisen, gives rise to joy, this is called contact that is a basis for joy.
What is contact that is a basis for sorrow?
If a contact arises that has already produced sorrow, this is called "contact associated with the sphere of sorrow. What is "contact associated with the sphere of equanimity"?
If a contact arises that has already produced equanimity, this is called "contact associated with the sphere of equanimity."

Furthermore, setting aside the contact associated with the neutral state (*upekṣā-sthānīya-sparśa*), if there is any other contact that is wholesome and has a karmic result (*savipāka*), it is called contact associated with the state of joy (*saumanasya-sthānīya-sparśa*).
If the contact is unwholesome, it is called contact associated with the state of grief (*daurmanasya-sthānīya-sparśa*).
Excluding contact that is a basis for joy, if there is any other wholesome contact with a result, this is called contact that is a basis for equanimity.
Furthermore, if contact is wholesome and has a result, it is called contact that is a basis for joy.
If contact is unwholesome, it is called contact associated with the sphere of sorrow (*daurmanasya-sthānīya*).

Excluding contact associated with the sphere of joy and contact associated with the sphere of sorrow, any other contact is called contact that is neither associated with the sphere of joy nor associated with the sphere of sorrow.
What is contact with vitarka and vicāra?
If contact is associated with meditative absorption that possesses vitarka and vicāra, this is called contact with vitarka and vicāra.
What is contact without vitarka but with vicāra?
If contact is associated with concentration that is without vitarka but with vicāra, this is called contact without vitarka but with vicāra.
What is contact without vitarka and without vicāra?
If contact is associated with concentration that is without vitarka and without vicāra, this is called contact without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is contact associated with emptiness?
If contact arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the meditative concentration on emptiness, this is called contact associated with emptiness.
What is contact associated with the signless?
If contact arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the signless concentration, this is called contact associated with the signless.
What is contact associated with the wishless?
If contact arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the wishless concentration, this is called contact associated with the wishless.
What is contact with immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-sparśa*)?

If a contact arises that is comprised within one's own continuum, or if the activity produced by a contact achieves fulfillment such that it is comprised within one's own continuum as a received retribution, this is called contact with immediate retribution.
What is contact that results in retribution upon rebirth?

If contact is comprised within one's own continuum, or if the action arising from that contact is accomplished such that the experience of its retribution arises immediately thereafter, this is called contact resulting in retribution upon rebirth.
What is contact with subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-sparśa*)?

If a contact arises that is included within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtānaparigṛhīta*), or if the action produced by that contact is destined to yield its retribution in the third or fourth birth, or even later, this is called contact with subsequent retribution.
What is contact associated with pleasure?
If a contact has a pleasant result, it is called contact associated with pleasure.
What is contact associated with suffering?
If one experiences a painful result through contact, this is called "contact associated with suffering.
What is "contact that is neither associated with pleasure nor associated with suffering"?

With the exception of contact associated with pleasure and contact associated with suffering, any other contact is called "contact that is neither associated with pleasure nor associated with suffering."
Furthermore, if contact is wholesome and associated with retribution, it is called "contact associated with pleasure.
If contact is unwholesome, it is called "contact associated with suffering.
Apart from contact associated with pleasure and contact associated with suffering, any other contact is called "contact that is neither associated with pleasure nor associated with suffering."
What is contact that has a pleasant result?
If contact has a pleasant retribution, it is called contact with a pleasant result.
What is contact that has a painful result?
If contact results in a painful retribution, it is called contact with a painful fruit.
What is contact that is neither a pleasant fruit nor a painful fruit?
Apart from contact with a pleasant fruit and contact with a painful fruit, any other contact is called contact that is neither a pleasant fruit nor a painful fruit.
Furthermore, if contact is wholesome and has a result, it is called contact with a pleasant result.
If contact is unwholesome and has a result, it is called contact with a painful result.
Apart from contact with a pleasant result and contact with a painful result, any other contact is called contact that is neither with a pleasant result nor with a painful result.
The same applies to contact resulting in pleasant retribution, contact resulting in painful retribution, and contact resulting in neither pleasant nor painful retribution.
What is past contact?
If contact has arisen and subsequently ceased, it is called past contact.
What is future contact?
If contact has not yet arisen and not yet occurred, this is called future contact.
What is present contact?
If contact has arisen and has not yet ceased, this is called present contact.
What is contact with past objects?
If contact arises through reflecting upon past phenomena, this is called contact with past objects.
What is contact with future objects?
If contact arises through reflecting upon future phenomena, this is called contact with future objects.
What is contact with present objects?
If, by reflecting on present phenomena, contact arises, this is called contact with a present object.
What is contact with an object that is neither past, nor future, nor present?
When contact arises through reflecting on phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present, this is called contact with an object that is neither past, future, nor present.
What is contact bound to the desire realm?
If contact is associated with the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) and is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called contact bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*).
What is contact bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)?
If contact is associated with the outflow of form (*rūpa-āsrava*) and is tainted, it is called contact bound to the form realm.
What is contact associated with the formless realm?
If contact is associated with outflows and is tainted by the formless realm, it is called contact associated with the formless realm.
What is unconditioned contact?
If one contacts that which is noble and untainted, this is called unconditioned contact (*asaṃyukta-sparśa*).
What is contact associated with loving-kindness (*maitrī-sahagata-sparśa*)?
If one contacts that which arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with a mind liberated by loving-kindness, this is called contact associated with loving-kindness.
The same applies to contact associated with sorrow, contact associated with joy, and contact associated with equanimity.
What is contact associated with the faculty of pleasure?
That which arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the faculty of pleasure is called contact associated with the faculty of pleasure.
The same applies to contact associated with the faculty of suffering, the faculty of joy, the faculty of grief, and the faculty of equanimity.
What is eye-contact?
If contact is associated with visual consciousness, it is called eye-contact.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, conditioned by visible forms, eye-consciousness arises; the conjunction of these three factors gives rise to contact, which is called "eye-contact."
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
What is contact associated with the eye-consciousness element?
If contact arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with the eye-consciousness element, this is called contact associated with the eye-consciousness element.
The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind-consciousness elements are also like this.
What is contact associated with the mind element?
If contact arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the mental consciousness, it is called contact associated with the mind element.
The contact associated with the consciousness element is also like this.
What are the eighteen contacts? They are:
eye-contact as pleasant feeling, eye-contact as painful feeling, and eye-contact as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These are called the eighteen contacts.

Chapter Seven: The Provisional Nature of Mind. In the *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, Part One: The Introduction, Chapter Seven: The Provisional Nature of Mind. The nature of the mind is intrinsically pure, yet it is defiled by adventitious dust.
Because ordinary persons have not heard [the teaching], they are unable to know and see things as they truly are, nor do they cultivate the mind.
Because noble ones have heard it, they know and see things as they truly are, and they also cultivate the mind.
The nature of the mind is pure, free from adventitious defilements.
Because ordinary beings have not heard [the teaching], they are unable to know and see it as it truly is, nor do they cultivate the mind.
Because noble ones have heard it, they are able to know and see it as it truly is, and they also cultivate the mind.
Now, we shall collect the primary gateways for the provisional mind.
Regarding the noble mind and the non-noble mind, up to the minds of the six consciousness-elements and the seventh consciousness-element:
what is the noble mind?
If the mind is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the noble mind (*ārya-citta*).
What is the non-noble mind?
If the mind is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called the non-noble mind.
What is the mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*)?
If the mind is defiled, it is called the mind with outflows.
What is the mind without outflows (*anāsrava-citta*)?
If the mind is without defilement, it is called the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
What is the defiled mind?
If the mind has seeking, it is called the defiled mind.
What is the mind free from defilement?
If the mind is without seeking, it is called the mind free from defilement.
What is the mind with seeking?
If the mind is about to grasp, it is called a mind with seeking.
What is a mind without seeking?
If the mind is not about to grasp, it is called a mind without seeking.
What is the mind that is subject to appropriation?
If the mind has appropriation, it is called the mind subject to appropriation.
What is the mind not subject to appropriation?
If the mind is without grasping, it is called the mind that is not to be grasped.
What is the mind with grasping?
If the mind has superiority, it is called the mind with grasping.
What is the mind without grasping?
If the mind is without excellence, it is called the mind without grasping.
What is the mind with excellence?
If the mind has grasping, it is called "mind with superiority.
What is "mind without superiority"?
If the mind is without grasping, it is called "mind without superiority."
Furthermore, if there exists another mind that surpasses this mind in excellence, it is called a "surpassable mind.
If there is no other mind that surpasses this mind in excellence, it is called an "unsurpassable mind."
Furthermore, if the mind produced by a Tathāgata possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena, up to and including the accomplishment of mastery—
any other mind besides this is called a "mind with superior qualities."
If there is no other mind remaining, this is called the unsurpassed mind.
What is the experiencing mind?
If the mind is internal, it is called the experiencing mind.
What is the mind that is not felt?
If the mind is external, it is called the mind that is not felt.
What is the internal mind?
If the mind is associated with feeling, this is called the internal mind.
What is the external mind?
If the mind is not associated with feeling, this is called the external mind.
What is a mind with retribution?
If a mind is of a nature to be retributed, it is called a mind with retribution.
What is a mind without retribution?
If a mind is neither resultant (*vipāka*) nor subject to resultancy (*vipākadharmatā*), it is called a mind without retribution (*avipāka*).
What is the mind shared by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana-sādhāraṇa-citta*)?
If a mind is acquired by an ordinary person and is also acquired by an ordinary person, it is called the mind shared by ordinary persons.
What is the mind not shared by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*)?
If a mind is not acquired at birth by ordinary persons, nor can it be acquired by ordinary persons, this is called the mind not shared by ordinary persons.
What is the mind not shared with ordinary persons?
If a mind is acquired by both ordinary persons and non-ordinary persons, this is called the mind not shared with ordinary persons.
What is the mind that is not shared with ordinary persons?
If a mind is acquired by an ordinary person but is neither produced nor acquired by one who is not an ordinary person, this is called the mind not shared with ordinary persons.
What is the mind shared by Śrāvakas?
If a mind is acquired by Śrāvakas and is also acquired by [other] Śrāvakas, this is called the mind shared by Śrāvakas.
What is the mind not shared by Śrāvakas?
If a mind is not acquired by birth by Śrāvakas, yet is not unacquired by Śrāvakas, this is called the uncommon mind of the Śrāvakas.
What is the mind common to those who are not Śrāvakas?
If a mind is acquired by birth both by śrāvakas and by those who are not śrāvakas, it is called a mind common to those who are not śrāvakas.
What is a mind uncommon to those who are not śrāvakas?
If a mind is acquired by Śrāvakas but not acquired by those who are not Śrāvakas, this is called the "mind not shared with those who are not Śrāvakas.
What is the "mind like lightning"?
If the mind abides for only a brief duration, abiding for only a short time—like lightning, which abides for only a brief duration and for only a short time—this is called the "mind like lightning.
What is the "mind like a diamond"?
If the mind dwells for immeasurable time in immeasurable abidings, dwelling like a vajra for immeasurable time in immeasurable abidings, this is called the "vajra-like mind.

Furthermore, if the mind, having arisen, severs a portion of minor afflictions—just as lightning emerging from the clouds illuminates a small portion of darkness and quickly vanishes—the mind is likewise; this is called the "lightning-like mind."

If, once the mind has arisen, all afflictions are severed without remainder—whether coarse or subtle—and none are left unextinguished, just as a vajra hurled at pearls or stones destroys and shatters them all, this is called the "vajra-like mind."
Furthermore, if upon the arising of the mind one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *anāgāmin*, this is called the "mind like lightning.
If upon the arising of the mind one attains the fruit of *arhat*, this is called the "mind like a diamond."

Furthermore, if, once the mind has arisen, one attains the fruit of a stream-enterer up to the fruit of a non-returner, or attains the fruits of a śrāvaka, a pratyekabuddha, or an arhat, this is called the lightning-like mind.

If, once the mind has arisen, the mind produced by the Tathāgata possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena, up to and including the accomplishment of mastery, this is called the adamantine mind.
What is the mind that is not attained with certainty?
If a mind is attained that is not certain, difficult to attain, and difficult to maintain, this is called the mind not attained with certainty.
What is the mind attained with certainty?
That which is the opposite of the above is called the mind that has attained concentration (*samāhita-citta*).
What is the mind that is difficult to maintain due to effortful application (*sābhisaṃskāra-duḥsthitam cittaṃ*)?

If the mind is attained, it is not attained with stability; it is difficult to attain and difficult to maintain. It lacks power, dignity, and mastery; it does not accord with one's wishes, does not follow one's wishes, and does not fulfill one's wishes. It is characterized by effortful application, being difficult to produce and difficult to practice, like a boat going against the current is difficult to move. The mind is also like this; this is called the mind that is difficult to maintain due to effortful application.
What is the mind that is effortless and easy to maintain?
That which is the opposite of the aforementioned is called the mind that is effortless and easy to maintain.
What is the mind cultivated in one part?

If, once the mind has arisen, one perceives that there is light but does not see forms, or if one sees forms but does not perceive that there is light, this is called "cultivating the mind in one part.
What is "cultivating the mind in two parts"?
If, once the mind has arisen, one perceives light and also sees forms, this is called the twofold cultivation of the mind.

Furthermore, if the mind has arisen and wisdom has been produced, yet afflictions are not severed; or if afflictions are severed but wisdom is not produced, this is called the singlefold cultivation of the mind.
If, once the mind has arisen, wisdom arises and is able to sever the afflictions, this is called the twofold cultivation of the mind.

Furthermore, if, once the mind has arisen, there is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) but not the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), this is called the singlefold cultivation of the mind.
If, once the mind has arisen, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arise, this is called the twofold cultivation of the mind.
What is the mind possessed of desire?
If the mind possesses desire and is associated with the defilement of human desire, this is called the mind possessed of desire.
What is the mind free from desire?
If the mind is detached from desire and is not associated with the defilement of desire, this is called the mind free from desire.
What is the mind possessed of ill will?
If the mind possesses anger and is associated with anger in others, it is called a mind with anger.
What is a mind without anger?
If the mind is free from anger and is not associated with anger in others, it is called a mind without anger.
What is a mind with delusion?
If a mind possesses delusion and is associated with the delusion of a person, this is called a mind with delusion.
What is a mind without delusion?
If a mind is free from delusion and is not associated with delusion, it is called a mind without delusion.
What is a sunken mind?

If a mind is associated with sleepiness and does not associate with internal mindfulness of cessation, and its wisdom is unaccomplished such that it cannot discern wholesome dharmas, this is called a sunken mind.
What is the distracted mind?

If the mind is stained by desire, associated with desire, and conjoined with desire; if it perceives much purity and becomes attached to this or that among the five external sense-objects—this is called the distracted mind.
What is the limited mind?
If the mind is not concentrated, it is called the limited mind.
What is the expansive mind?
If the mind is concentrated, this is called "many minds.
What is an unconcentrated mind?
If the mind is not concentrated and the person is not associated with concentration, this is called an unconcentrated mind.
What is the concentrated mind?
If the mind is concentrated and associated with concentration, this is called the concentrated mind.
What is the unliberated mind?
If a mind is not liberated and is not associated with liberation, it is called an unliberated mind.
What is a liberated mind?
If a mind is liberated and is associated with liberation, it is called a liberated mind.
What is the mind that possesses superiority?
If a mind is associated with superior persons or superior dharmas, it is called the mind that possesses superiority.
What is the mind that lacks superiority?
If the mind is associated with neither superior persons nor superior dharmas, it is called the "mind without superiority.
What is the "mind with applied thought"?
If the mind is associated with applied thought, arising, abiding, and ceasing together with applied thought, it is called the "mind with applied thought."
What is the mind without vitarka?
If a mind is not associated with vitarka, and does not arise, abide, or cease together with vitarka, it is called the mind without vitarka.
What is the mind with investigation (*savitarka*)?
If the mind is associated with investigation, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called the mind with investigation.
What is the mind without investigation (*avitarka*)?
If a mind is not associated with contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and does not arise, abide, or cease together with contemplation, this is called a mind without contemplation.
What is a mind accompanied by joy (*prīti*)?
If the mind is associated with joy (*prīti*), arising together with joy, abiding together with joy, and ceasing together with joy, this is called a mind with joy.
What is a mind without joy?
If the mind is not associated with joy, not arising together with joy, not abiding together with joy, and not ceasing together with joy, this is called a mind without joy.
What is the mind associated with attachment (*sāsvāda-citta*)?
If a mind is associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), it is called the mind associated with attachment.
What is the mind associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*)?
If the mind is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, this is called the mind associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is the mind associated with patience (*kṣānti*)?
If the mind arises, abides, and ceases together with patience, this is called the mind associated with patience.
What is the mind not associated with patience (*kṣānti*)?
If a mind does not arise, abide, or cease together with patience, it is called the mind not associated with patience.
What is the mind associated with knowledge (*jñāna*)?
If a mind arises, abides, and ceases together with wisdom, it is called a mind associated with wisdom.
What is a mind not associated with wisdom?
If a mind does not arise, abide, and cease together with wisdom, it is called a mind not associated with wisdom.
What is the mind that has patience as its beginning?
If a mind is noble, untainted, and cultivated through firm faith and firm dharma, this is called the mind that has patience as its beginning.
What is the mind that has knowledge as its beginning?
If a mind is noble, untainted, and cultivated by one on the path of vision, this is called the "mind of wisdom" and the "initial mind.
What is the "mind at the end of desire"?
If it is the final consciousness, this is termed the "mind at the end of desire."
What is the "initially arising mind"?
If the mind is the first consciousness, it is called the initially arising mind.
What is a wholesome mind?
If the mind is cultivated, it is called a wholesome mind.
What is an unwholesome mind?
If the mind is severed, it is called an unwholesome mind.
What is the indeterminate mind?
If a mind is a feeling, or if a mind is neither a result nor of a nature to produce results, this is called the indeterminate mind.
What is the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*)?
If a mind is noble but not that of one beyond training, it is called a mind of training (*śaikṣa*).
What is a mind beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
If a mind is noble but not that of one in training, it is called a mind beyond training.
What is the mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner?
If a mind is not noble (*ārya*), it is called the mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
What is the resultant mind (*vipākacitta*)?
If a mental feeling is a wholesome result, this is called a resultant mind (*vipākacitta*).
What is a mind characterized by result (*vipākadhammacitta*)?
If a mind possesses a result, this is called a mind characterized by result.
What is the mind that is neither resultant nor of the nature of being resultant?
If a mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not included within one's own continuum (*asvaka*), it is called the mind that is neither resultant nor of the nature of being resultant.
What is the mind to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*)?
If a mind is unwholesome and is not abandoned by insight, it is called a mind abandoned by insight.
What is a mind abandoned by cultivation?
If a mind is unwholesome and is not abandoned by insight, it is called a mind abandoned by cultivation.
What is the mind that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation?
If the mind is wholesome or indeterminate, this is called the mind that is neither abandoned by insight nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is the mind whose cause is to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya-hetuka-citta*)?
If a mind is itself to be abandoned by insight, or if it is the retribution (*vipāka*) of a dharma to be abandoned by insight, this is called the mind whose cause is to be abandoned by insight.
What is the mind whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya-hetuka-citta*)?

If the mind contemplates that which is abandoned through cultivation, or contemplates the retribution of that which is abandoned through cultivation, this is called the mind whose cause is abandoned through cultivation.
What is the mind whose cause is neither abandoned through vision nor abandoned through cultivation?

If a mind is a wholesome dharma that is a result (*vipāka*), or if a mind is neither a result nor a dharma subject to ripening (*avipākadharman*), this is called a mind whose cause is neither to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*) nor by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
What is a weak mind (*mṛdu-citta*)?
If the mind is unwholesome, it is called a weak mind.
What is a middling mind?
If the mind is indeterminate, it is called a middling mind.
What is the superior mind?
If the mind is wholesome, it is called the superior mind.
Furthermore, if the mind is unwholesome or neutral, it is called the inferior mind.
If the mind is not noble or wholesome, it is called the intermediate mind.
If the mind is noble and untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called the superior mind.
What is the coarse mind?
If the mind is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse mind.
What is subtle mind?
If the mind is bound to the form realm or is unbound, it is called subtle mind.
What is the subtle mind?
If the mind is not bound to the form realm, it is called the subtle mind.
Furthermore, if the mind is bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm, it is called the coarse mind.
If the mind is bound to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or is unbound, this is called the subtle mind.
If the mind is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this is called the minute mind.

Furthermore, if the mind is bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, this is called coarse mind.
If the mind is not bound, it is called a subtle mind (*sūkṣmacitta*).
If the mind is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is called a minute mind (*sūkṣmatamacitta*).
What is a mind associated with pleasant feeling (*sukhavedanīyacitta*)?
If the mind is associated with pleasant feeling, it is called a mind of pleasant feeling.
What is a mind of painful feeling?
If the mind is associated with painful feeling, it is called a mind of painful feeling.
What is the mind associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
If the mind is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is called the mind associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, if the mind experiences a pleasant retribution, it is called the mind associated with pleasant feeling.
If the mind experiences the retribution of suffering, it is called the mind of painful feeling.
If the mind experiences the retribution of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure, it is called the mind of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, setting aside the mind of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, if any other mind is wholesome and has a karmic result, it is called a mind of pleasant feeling;
if the mind is unwholesome, it is called a mind of painful feeling.
Excluding the mind associated with pleasant feeling, if there is any other wholesome mind that has a result, this is called the mind associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, if a mind is wholesome and has a result, it is called the mind associated with pleasant feeling.
If the mind is unwholesome, it is called a mind of painful feeling.
Excluding minds of painful and pleasant feeling, if there is any other mind, it is called a mind of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
What is the mind that has joy as its object?
If the mind, upon first arising, gives rise to joy, this is called the mind that has joy as its object.
What is the mind that has sorrow as its object?
If a state of mind first arises as sorrow, it is called a mind with the basis of sorrow.
What is a mind with the basis of equanimity?
If a state of mind first arises as equanimity, it is called a mind with the basis of equanimity.
Furthermore, setting aside the mind that is neutral (upekṣā), if other minds are wholesome and result in maturation, they are called "minds associated with joy" (saumanasya-sthānīya).
If the mind is unwholesome, it is called "a mind associated with grief" (daurmanasya-sthānīya).
A mind that is wholesome and possesses a result, excluding those states of mind associated with the basis of joy, is called a mind associated with the basis of equanimity (*upekṣā-sthānīya-citta*).
Furthermore, if a mind is wholesome and possesses a result, it is called a mind associated with the basis of joy (*prīti-sthānīya-citta*).
If the mind is unwholesome, it is called a mind associated with the sphere of sorrow (*daurmanasya-sthānīya*).

Excluding minds associated with the spheres of joy and sorrow, any remaining mind is called a mind that is neither associated with the sphere of joy nor the sphere of sorrow (*naiva-saumanasya-sthānīya-na-daurmanasya-sthānīya*).
What is the mind with vitarka and vicāra?
If a state of mind is associated with meditative concentration that possesses both vitarka and vicāra, this is called the mind with vitarka and vicāra.
What is the mind without vitarka but with vicāra?
If the mind is associated with concentration that is without vitarka but with vicāra, this is called the mind without vitarka but with vicāra.
What is the mind without vitarka and without vicāra?
If the mind is associated with concentration that is without vitarka and without vicāra, this is called the mind without vitarka and without vicāra.
What is the mind associated with emptiness?
If the mind arises, abides, and ceases together with the concentration of emptiness, this is called the mind associated with emptiness.
What is the mind associated with the signless?
If the mind arises, abides, and ceases together with the concentration on signlessness, this is called the mind associated with signlessness.
What is the mind associated with wishlessness?
If the mind arises, abides, and ceases together with the concentration on wishlessness, this is called the mind associated with wishlessness.
What is the mind that yields immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)?

If a mind is comprised within one's own continuum at the very moment it arises, or if a mind is comprised within one's own continuum at the very moment its activity is accomplished, and the retribution for that activity is experienced [in this life], this is called the mind that yields immediate retribution.
What is the mind that results in retribution in the next life?

If a mind arises that is categorized as my own portion and belongs to the class of retribution, or if what is produced and accomplished results in the experience of retribution arising immediately thereafter, this is called the mind that results in retribution in the next life.
What is the mind of subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*)?
