If a mind arises that is included within one's own continuum (*ātma-bhāva-parigṛhīta*), and the karma produced thereby is destined to yield its retribution in the first, second, third, or fourth birth, or even beyond, this is called the mind of subsequent retribution.
What is the mind that bestows happiness?
If the mind takes delight in its fruit, it is called the mind that bestows happiness.
What is the mind that bestows suffering?
If the mind has suffering as its fruit, this is called a mind associated with suffering.
What is a mind that is neither associated with pleasure nor associated with suffering?
Excluding the minds associated with pleasure and those associated with suffering, any remaining mind is called a mind that is neither associated with suffering nor associated with pleasure.
Furthermore, if a mind is wholesome and possesses retribution, it is called a mind that bestows happiness.
If a mind is unwholesome and possesses retribution, it is called a mind that bestows suffering.
Excluding those that bestow suffering or happiness, any remaining mind is called a mind that bestows neither suffering nor happiness.
What is a mind with pleasant fruition?
If a mind has a pleasant retribution, it is called a mind with pleasant fruition.
What is a mind with painful fruition?
If the mind has a painful retribution, it is called a mind with a bitter fruit (*duḥkhavipāka-citta*).
What is a mind that is neither a fruit of pleasure nor a fruit of suffering?
Excluding minds with a bitter fruit and minds with a pleasant fruit, any remaining mind is called a mind that is neither a fruit of pleasure nor a fruit of suffering (*naivāduḥkhasukhavipāka-citta*).
Furthermore, if a mind is wholesome and possesses retribution, it is called a mind with pleasant results.
If a mind is unwholesome and possesses retribution, it is called a mind with painful results.
Excluding minds with pleasant results and minds with painful results, any remaining minds are called minds that are neither with pleasant results nor with painful results.
The same applies to the mind with a pleasant retribution, the mind with a painful retribution, and the mind with a neither-pleasant-nor-painful retribution.
What is the past mind?
If a mind has arisen and ceased, it is called the past mind.
What is the future mind?
If a mind has not yet arisen and not yet emerged, it is called the future mind.
What is the present mind?
If a mind has arisen but not yet ceased, this is called the present mind.
What is the mind that takes the past as its object?
If a mind arises through reflecting upon past phenomena, this is called the mind that takes the past as its object.
What is the mind with future objects?
If a thought arises while contemplating future phenomena, this is called the mind with future objects.
What is the mind with present objects?
If one contemplates present phenomena and a mind arises, this is called the mind whose object is the present.
What is the mind whose object is neither past, nor future, nor present?
If one generates a thought while contemplating phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present, this is called a mind whose object is neither past, nor future, nor present.
What is the mind bound to the desire realm?
If the mind is characterized by the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) or is tainted (*sāsrava*), it is called the mind bound to the desire realm.
What is the mind bound to the form realm?
If the mind possesses the outflows of form (*rūpāsrava*) and is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*), this is called a mind bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-citta*).
What is a mind bound to the formless realm?
If the mind possesses the outflows of the formless (*ārūpyāsrava*) and is subject to outflows, this is called a mind bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-citta*).
What is the mind that is unbound?
If the mind is noble and untainted, this is called the unbound mind.
What is the mind associated with loving-kindness?
If the mind arises, abides, and ceases together with loving-kindness, this is called "the mind associated with loving-kindness.
The same applies to the mind associated with compassion, the mind associated with sympathetic joy, and the mind associated with equanimity.
What is the mind associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*)?
If a mind arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the faculty of pleasure, it is called a mind associated with the faculty of pleasure.

The same applies to minds associated with the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
What are the six groups of consciousness?
They are the group of eye-consciousness up to the group of mind-consciousness.
What is the group of eye-consciousness?

Conditioned by the eye, conditioned by forms, conditioned by light, and conditioned by attention—through the conjunction of these four conditions, consciousness has arisen, arises, will arise, or is indeterminate; this is called the aggregate of eye-consciousness.
The same applies to the groups of consciousness of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
These are called the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*).
What are the seven elements of consciousness (*sapta-vijñāna-dhātu*)?
The eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element.
What is the eye-consciousness element?

If consciousness arises from the eye-faculty with respect to the objective field of visible forms—whether it has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate—it is called the eye-consciousness element.
The ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness elements are also like this.
What is the mind element (*manodhātu*)?

It is the mind that arises in relation to mental phenomena and contemplates them—whether it be the initial moment of mind already arisen, currently arising, about to arise, or indeterminate. This is called the mind element.
What is the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*)?

It is that which does not depart from its respective object; whether it has arisen, is arising, will arise, or is indeterminate, provided it is a mind resembling that [object], it is called the mental consciousness element.
Chapter 8: The Ten Unwholesome Paths of Action. *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Introductory Section, Chapter Eight: The Ten Unwholesome Paths of Action. Question:
How many unwholesome paths of action are there?
Answer: Ten.
From killing up to wrong view.
What is killing?
If a person kills with an evil mind, lacking compassion and intent solely on slaughter, this is called killing.
What is stealing?
If a person steals another's property within a village or in the mountains and wilds, this is called theft.
What is sexual misconduct?

If a woman is protected by her parents, protected by her brothers and sisters, protected by herself, protected by the Dharma, protected by her clan, protected by her relatives and acquaintances, or even protected by the reception of a flower garland—if one violates any of these [protections], this is called sexual misconduct.
What is false speech?

If a person says they know what they do not know, says they do not know what they know, says they have seen what they have not seen, or says they have not seen what they have seen—whether for their own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of wealth—they deliberately utter such false speech; this is called false speech.
What is divisive speech?
It is when a person, having heard something here, goes and speaks of it there with the intent to cause dissension in this person;
or, having heard something there, comes and speaks of it here with the intent to cause dissension in that person.

To cause those who have not yet been divided to be divided, and to cause those already divided to be further dispersed; to delight in the separation of others—this is called double-tongued speech (*paiśunya*).
What is harsh speech (*pāruṣya*)?
If a person utters words that are coarse, violent, and cutting, such that others, having heard them, are displeased and unhappy—this is called harsh speech.
What is frivolous speech?

If a person utters words at an improper time, words that are meaningless, words that are contrary to the Dharma, words that are not conducive to discipline, or words that lack tranquility, this is called frivolous speech.
What is covetousness?
If a person conceives a longing for the wealth of others in another village or town, desiring that those things belonging to others become one's own, this is called covetousness.
What is ill will?
If a person, out of ill will, desires that other sentient beings be imprisoned, harmed, or subjected to various forms of suffering, this is called ill will.
What is wrong view? If a person holds wrong views, saying:

"There is no giving, no sacrifice; there is no retribution for good and evil deeds; there is no this world or another world; there are no parents; there are no devas or beings born by transformation; there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas"—this is called wrong view.
By what causes does one kill?
For whose sake does one kill?
One kills by reason of greed, by reason of hatred, by reason of delusion, and by reason of the mind and mental factors.

Taking life is the cause for rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; it is the cause for poverty and low status among gods and humans; and as a residual karmic result, it leads to a short lifespan if one is born among humans.
By what cause does theft arise?
For whom is theft the cause?
Theft arises by the cause of greed, and so on, up to the cause of mental states and mental factors.

Theft is the cause for rebirth in the hells, as an animal, or as a hungry ghost; it is the cause for poverty and low status among gods, humans, and spirits; or, if a remaining karmic retribution causes one to be born among humans, it results in the depletion of one's wealth and possessions.
By what cause does sexual misconduct arise?
For whom is sexual misconduct the cause?
Sexual misconduct arises with greed as its cause, and so on, up to mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as its cause.

Sexual misconduct is the cause for rebirth in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts; it is the cause for poverty and low status among gods, humans, and spirits; and if there is a remaining karmic retribution, one will be born among humans in a state of strife and contention.
What is the cause of false speech?
For whom is false speech the cause?
False speech has greed as its cause, and so on, up to having the mind and mental factors as its cause.

Lying is the cause for rebirth in the hells, as an animal, or as a hungry ghost; it is the cause for poverty and low status among gods, humans, and spirits; and if one is born among humans as a residual karmic result, one will constantly suffer slander.
What is the cause of divisive speech?
For whom is divisive speech the cause?
Divisive speech has greed as its cause, and so on, up to having the mind and mental factors as its cause.
What is the cause of divisive speech?

It is the cause for rebirth in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts; it is the cause for being poor and lowly among gods and humans. If there is a residual karmic retribution leading to birth among humans, one's relatives and close associates will harbor mutual hatred and jealousy, leading to their destruction.
By what cause does harsh speech arise?
For whom is harsh speech the cause?
Harsh speech arises with greed as its cause, and so on, up to having the mind and mental factors as its cause.
What is the cause of harsh speech?

Harsh speech is the cause for rebirth in the hells, the animal realm, and the realm of hungry ghosts; it is the cause for poverty and low status among gods, humans, and spirits; or, as a residual retribution, it results in hearing unpleasant sounds when born among humans.
What is the cause of frivolous speech?
For whom is frivolous speech the cause?
Frivolous speech has greed as its cause, and so on, up to having the mind and mental factors as its cause.
What is the cause of frivolous speech?

It is the cause for rebirth in the hells, as an animal, or as a hungry ghost; it is the cause for being poor and lowly among gods, humans, and spirits; or, if one is born among humans as a residual karmic result, one's words will not be held in high esteem.
By what cause does greed arise?
For whom is greed the cause?
Greed arises by means of the cause of fetters, the cause of bonds, and the cause of the mind and mental factors.
For whom is greed the cause?

It is the cause of rebirth in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts; it is the cause of poverty and low status among gods, humans, and spirits; and if one is born again among humans as a residual retribution, it results in many complications and entanglements.
By what cause does ill-will arise?
Of what is ill-will the cause?
Ill-will arises by way of the cause of fetters, by way of the cause of bonds, and by way of the cause of mind and mental factors.
What is the cause of ill will?

It is the cause for rebirth in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts; it is the cause for poverty and low status among gods, humans, and spirits; and if one is born again among humans as a residual result, one will have many enemies and much hatred.
By what causes does wrong view arise?
For whom is wrong view a cause?
Wrong view arises by means of the fetters as its cause, by means of the latent tendencies as its cause, and by means of the mind and mental factors as its cause.
What is the cause of wrong view?

It is the cause for rebirth in the hells, as animals, or as hungry ghosts; it is the cause for being poor and lowly among gods, humans, and spirits; and if one is born among humans due to other residual karmic retribution, it causes one to regard what is wrong as auspicious.
Chapter Nine: The Ten Paths of Wholesome Action. From the *Śāriputrābhidharmaśāstra*, Section on the Introduction, Chapter Nine: The Ten Paths of Wholesome Action. Question:
How many paths of wholesome action are there?
Answer: Ten. What are the ten?
From non-killing up to right view.
What is non-killing?
If a person abstains from killing, discards the sword and staff, and possesses a sense of shame, compassion, and pity for all sentient beings, this is called non-killing.
What is non-stealing?
If a person abstains from theft and does not steal the property of others, this is called non-stealing.
What is non-sexual misconduct?
If a person abstains from sexual misconduct, never committing adultery with women protected by others, this is called non-sexual misconduct.

What is non-false speech? If a person abstains from false speech, saying they do not know what they do not know, saying they know what they know, saying they have not seen what they have not seen, and saying they have seen what they have seen; and if they do not utter false speech for their own sake, for the sake of another, or for the sake of wealth, this is called non-false speech.
What is non-divisive speech?
If a person abandons divisive speech, having heard something here, they do not repeat it there with the intent to cause dissension among those people;

having heard something there, they do not repeat it here with the intent to cause dissension among these people. If there is discord, they desire to bring about reconciliation; if there is already harmony, they desire to increase their joy and mutual delight. This is called non-divisive speech.
What is non-malicious speech?
If a person abstains from malicious speech and refrains from harsh and coarse words, speaking with gentleness that is loved and cherished by all people—this is called non-malicious speech.
What is non-frivolous speech?

If one speaks at the proper time, speaks what is true, speaks what is meaningful, speaks with self-control, speaks with tranquility, and speaks words that are timely and virtuous, this is called non-frivolous speech.
What is non-attachment?
If a person is free from greed and does not desire the wealth and goods of other villages or towns to be their own, this is called non-attachment.
What is non-hatred?
If a person is free from a mind of ill-will and does not desire that these sentient beings be harmed, imprisoned, or made to undergo various sufferings, this is called non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
What is right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?

If a person possesses right view, believing that there is giving and there are sacrifices, and even that there are in this world śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who possess right view and right practice, and who have realized for themselves this world and the world beyond—this is called right view.
For what cause is there non-killing?
Of whom is non-killing the cause?
Non-killing has as its cause the absence of greed, the absence of hatred, the absence of delusion, and the mental states and mental factors.
For what reason does one refrain from taking life?
It is the cause for experiencing happiness among gods and humans; as for other karmic results, it leads to a long life if reborn among humans.
For what reason does one refrain from stealing?
What is the cause for not stealing?
Not stealing has non-attachment as its cause, and so on, up to having the mind and mental factors as its cause.
Not stealing is the cause for experiencing happiness among gods and humans; as for its remaining retribution, if one is born among humans, one's wealth and possessions will not be depleted.
For what cause is there no sexual misconduct?
Of what is non-sexual misconduct the cause?
Non-sexual misconduct has non-attachment as its cause, and so on, up to having the mind and mental factors as its cause.

Abstaining from sexual misconduct is the cause for experiencing happiness among gods and humans; as for its remaining retribution, if one is born among humans, one will not engage in strife or contention.
What is the cause of abstaining from false speech?
For whom is abstaining from false speech the cause?
Abstaining from false speech is caused by non-attachment, and so forth, up to being caused by the mind and mental factors.
Abstaining from false speech is the cause for experiencing happiness among gods and humans; as for its remaining retribution, if one is born among humans, one will not be subject to slander.
By what cause is there no divisive speech?
For whom is the absence of divisive speech the cause?
The absence of divisive speech has non-attachment as its cause, and so on, up to having the mind and mental factors as its cause.

Abstaining from divisive speech is the cause for experiencing happiness among devas and humans; as for other karmic results, if one is born among humans, one’s kin and associates will be harmonious and affectionate, and they will not harbor mutual hatred, jealousy, or discord.
For what cause is there no harsh speech? For whom is there no harsh speech?
There is no harsh speech because of the cause of non-attachment, and so on, up to the cause of the mind and mental factors.

Abstaining from harsh speech is a cause for experiencing happiness among gods and humans; as for its remaining retribution, if one is born among humans, one hears sounds that are pleasing to the mind.
For what reason does abstaining from frivolous speech [bring this result]?
For what cause does one refrain from frivolous speech?
One refrains from frivolous speech by means of the cause of non-attachment, and so on, up to the causes of the mind and mental factors.

Refraining from frivolous speech is the cause for experiencing happiness among gods and humans; if there is further retribution, one will be born among humans where one's words are held in high esteem.
What is the cause of non-attachment?
For whom is non-attachment the cause?
Non-attachment has single-minded reverence as its cause; single-minded reverence has the roots of goodness as its cause; and it has the mind and mental factors as its cause.
Non-attachment is the cause for experiencing happiness among gods and humans; if there were other [causes] for birth as a human, there would be no such conditions.
For what reason is non-hatred [a cause]?
Of what is non-hatred the cause?
Non-ill will is the cause for single-minded reverence, and so on, up to being the cause for the mind and mental factors.
Non-ill will is the cause for receiving happiness among devas and humans; as for other karmic results, even if one is born among humans, one will have few enemies or hatreds.
By what cause does right view arise?
For whom is right view a cause?
Right view arises by the cause of single-minded reverence, and so on, up to the cause of the mind and mental factors.
Right view is the cause for experiencing happiness among devas and humans; if one is born among humans through other karmic retribution, one does not regard what is wrong as auspicious.
*Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle 27; *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra*, Fascicle 28.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī and Dharmagupta et al. during the Yao Qin dynasty. Chapter Ten:

The Section on Concentration (Samādhi-varga), Part One. The Five-Limb Concentration, the Five-Knowledge Concentration, the Concentration with Mindfulness of Exhalation and Inhalation, the Concentration with the Contemplation of Impurity, and the Fire-Element Concentration.

They collectively realize the concentration of the bases of psychic power; they collectively realize the concentration of the divine ear; they collectively realize the concentration of knowing the minds of others; they collectively realize the concentration of recollecting past lives; and they clearly realize the concentration of the perception of light, the uninterrupted concentration, the concentration of the faculties, the concentration of the powers, and the concentration of perfect enlightenment.

Right concentration and wrong concentration; noble concentration and non-noble concentration; contaminated concentration and uncontaminated concentration; defiled concentration and undefiled concentration; concentration with seeking and concentration without seeking; concentration subject to appropriation and concentration not subject to appropriation; concentration with grasping and concentration without grasping; superior concentration and non-superior concentration.
There is concentration with sensation and concentration without sensation; internal concentration and external concentration;
concentration that is retributive and concentration that is non-retributive;

concentration shared by ordinary persons, concentration not shared by ordinary persons, concentration shared by those who are not ordinary persons, and concentration not shared by those who are not ordinary persons.
The shared concentration of śrāvakas, the unshared concentration of śrāvakas, the concentration shared with those who are not śrāvakas, and the concentration unshared with those who are not śrāvakas;
as well as the lightning-like concentration and the vajra-like concentration.
Concentration attained from the indeterminate, concentration attained from the determinate;
concentration difficult to maintain through effort, concentration easy to maintain without effort;
concentration cultivated in one part, concentration cultivated in two parts.
There is the attainment of perception (saṃjñā-samāpatti) and the attainment of non-perception (asaṃjñā-samāpatti).

There is the attainment according to the object (yathābhūta-samāpatti) and the attainment of recollecting perception (saṃjñā-anusmṛti-samāpatti). There is the attainment of detachment from form (rūpa-viveka-samāpatti) and the attainment of non-detachment from form (arūpa-viveka-samāpatti).
There is the attainment of the non-excellence entry (anabhibhava-praveśa-samāpatti) and the attainment of universal entry (sarvatraga-praveśa-samāpatti).
There is concentration with applied thought and concentration without applied thought;
concentration with sustained thought and concentration without sustained thought;
concentration with rapture and concentration without rapture.
The concentration associated with zest and the concentration associated with equanimity;
the concentration associated with patience and the concentration not associated with patience;
the concentration associated with knowledge and the concentration not associated with knowledge.
Patience is the initial concentration; wisdom is the initial concentration.
Desire is the final concentration; birth is the initial concentration.
There is wholesome concentration, unwholesome concentration, and neutral concentration.
The concentration of one in training (*śaikṣa*), the concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and the concentration of neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training.
The resultant concentration (*vipāka*), the concentration of the nature of result (*vipākadharmatā*), and the concentration of neither-result-nor-nature-of-result.

The concentration to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), the concentration to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and the concentration of neither-vision-nor-cultivation-abandonment.

The concentration whose cause is to be abandoned by vision, the concentration whose cause is to be abandoned by cultivation, and the concentration whose cause is neither to be abandoned by vision nor by cultivation;
the lower concentration, the middle concentration, and the superior concentration.
Coarse concentration, subtle concentration, and extremely subtle concentration.
Concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, concentration without directed thought but with sustained thought, and concentration without directed thought or sustained thought.
The concentration of emptiness, the concentration of signlessness, and the concentration of wishlessness.
The threefold concentration is attained through aspiration, not by means other than aspiration:

concentration through observing the internal body within the internal body, concentration through observing the external body within the external body, and concentration through observing both the internal and external body within the internal and external body.

One contemplates internal feelings while established in concentration on internal feelings; one contemplates external feelings while established in concentration on external feelings; and one contemplates both internal and external feelings while established in concentration on both internal and external feelings.

One contemplates the internal mind while established in concentration on the internal mind; one contemplates the external mind while established in concentration on the external mind; and one contemplates both internal and external minds while established in concentration on both internal and external minds.

Contemplating internal phenomena, one attains concentration on internal phenomena; contemplating external phenomena, one attains concentration on external phenomena; contemplating both internal and external phenomena, one attains concentration on both internal and external phenomena.
One attains concentration on internal objects, concentration on external objects, and concentration on both internal and external objects.
The concentration on internal objects, the concentration on external objects, and the concentration on sentient beings;
the concentration on the realm of form, the concentration on the formless realm, and the concentration on sentient beings.
The concentration on conditioned objects, the concentration on unconditioned objects, and the concentration on sentient beings;
the concentration on phenomena, the concentration on non-objects, and the concentration on sentient beings.
There is limited concentration, intermediate concentration, and immeasurable concentration.
There is concentration with a limited object, concentration with an intermediate object, and concentration with an immeasurable object.
There is limited concentration with a limited object, limited concentration with an intermediate object, and limited concentration with an immeasurable object.
The intermediate concentration with limited objects, the intermediate concentration with medium objects, and the intermediate concentration with immeasurable objects.
The immeasurable concentration with limited objects, the immeasurable concentration with medium objects, and the immeasurable concentration with immeasurable objects.
The concentration of limited duration, the concentration of intermediate duration, and the concentration of immeasurable duration.
Limited concentration with limited duration, limited concentration with intermediate duration, and limited concentration with immeasurable duration.
Intermediate concentration with limited duration, intermediate concentration with intermediate duration, and intermediate concentration with immeasurable duration.
Abiding briefly in immeasurable concentration, abiding for a long time in immeasurable concentration, and abiding immeasurably in immeasurable concentration.
Past concentration, future concentration, and present concentration.
Concentration on past objects, concentration on future objects, concentration on present objects, and concentration on objects that are neither past, nor future, nor present.
There are concentrations bound to the desire realm, concentrations bound to the form realm, concentrations bound to the formless realm, and unbound concentrations.

There is concentration that is practiced but not detached, concentration that is detached but not practiced, concentration that is both practiced and detached, and concentration that is neither practiced nor detached.

Entering meditative absorption is not emerging from it; emerging from meditative absorption is not entering it; there is both entering and emerging from meditative absorption; and there is neither entering nor emerging from meditative absorption.

There is meditative absorption with attachment that is not free from attachment; there is meditative absorption free from attachment that is not with attachment; there is meditative absorption both with and free from attachment; and there is meditative absorption neither with nor free from attachment.

There is concentration that possesses the yoke but is not free from the yoke; there is concentration that is free from the yoke but does not possess the yoke; there is concentration that both possesses the yoke and is free from the yoke; and there is concentration that neither possesses the yoke nor is free from the yoke.

There is concentration that is the fruit of knowledge but not the fruit of abandonment; there is concentration that is the fruit of abandonment but not the fruit of knowledge; there is concentration that is both the fruit of knowledge and the fruit of abandonment; and there is concentration that is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the fruit of abandonment.

The fruit of wisdom is certainly not the attainment of the fruit; the attainment of the fruit is certainly not the fruit of wisdom; the fruit of wisdom and the attainment of the fruit are certainly neither the fruit of wisdom nor the attainment of the fruit.
Cessation is certainly not awakening; awakening is certainly not cessation; the cessation and awakening are certainly neither the cessation nor the awakening.

Concentration of shooting is definitely not concentration of liberation; concentration of liberation is definitely not concentration of shooting; there is concentration that is both shooting and liberation; and there is concentration that is neither shooting nor liberation.
There is concentration of retrogression, concentration of maintenance, concentration of increase, and concentration of penetration.

The concentration of retrogression is not the concentration of maintenance; the concentration of maintenance is not the concentration of retrogression; there is the concentration of both retrogression and maintenance, and there is the concentration that is neither retrogression nor maintenance.

The concentration of retrogression is not the concentration of increase; the concentration of increase is not the concentration of retrogression; there is the concentration of increase, and there is the concentration that is neither retrogression nor increase.

The concentration of the stage of decline is not the concentration of the stage of progress; the concentration of the stage of progress is not the concentration of the stage of decline; there is a concentration of the stage of progress that is neither the concentration of the stage of decline nor the concentration of the stage of progress.

The concentration of the stage of maintenance is not the concentration of the stage of increase; the concentration of the stage of increase is not the concentration of the stage of maintenance; there is a concentration of the stage of maintenance and the stage of increase that is neither the concentration of the stage of maintenance nor the concentration of the stage of increase.

The concentration of the stage of abiding is not the concentration of the stage of progress; the concentration of the stage of progress is not the concentration of the stage of abiding; there is the concentration of both the stage of abiding and the stage of progress, as well as the concentration of neither the stage of abiding nor the stage of progress.

The concentration of the stage of increase is not the concentration of the stage of progress; the concentration of the stage of progress is not the concentration of the stage of increase; there is the concentration of both the stage of increase and the stage of progress, as well as the concentration of neither the stage of increase nor the stage of progress.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the four paths of the seekers, the four fruits, the four meditative cultivations, and the four abandonments.

The five faculties, the five powers, the five bases of liberation, the five elements of emergence, the five meditative concentrations of contemplation, and the five factors for the arising of liberation.
The six recollections, the six meditative concentrations.
Six factors for transcending the world;
six factors pertaining to the division of light;
six factors for gladdening the faculties.
Six are the factors of right awakening without joy;
seven are the factors of awakening;
seven are the perceptions.
Seven are required for meditative concentration:
the Noble Eightfold Path, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery,
the nine cessations, the nine successive attainments, and the nine perceptions of cessation.
The ten bases of wholesome qualities (*daśa kuśaladharma*), the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatana*),
and the eleven spheres of liberation (*ekādaśa vimokṣāyatana*).
What is the meditative concentration with five factors (*pañcāṅgasamādhi*)?
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain to you the noble five-factored concentration.
The bhikṣus said:
"Very well, we shall receive your instruction.
How does one cultivate the noble five-factored right concentration?

It is when a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and filled with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna."

With the body detached from [sensual desires], there arises joy and happiness; this moisture pervades the entire body, such that the joy and happiness born of detachment completely suffuse it without any diminution.
It is like a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice who places fine bathing powder in a vessel, sprinkles it with water, and kneads it into a ball.
This moisture pervades the entire body, neither too dry nor too wet, harmonizing both internally and externally.

In this way, the bhikṣu’s body is suffused with the joy and bliss born of seclusion; it is completely saturated with moisture, without any diminution. This is called the first limb of the noble five-limbed concentration.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, possessing internal confidence and mental unification, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.
This body is filled with the joy and bliss born of concentration;
it is saturated with moisture, completely pervaded by it, without any decrease.

It is like a pond or lake where water wells up from the bottom, not coming from the east, south, west, or north; this water welling up from the bottom causes the pool to be saturated with moisture, completely pervaded by it, without any decrease.
In this way, monks, this body is suffused with the joy and happiness born of concentration;
it is drenched, saturated, and filled with no part left untouched. This is called the cultivation of the second limb of the noble fivefold concentration.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the fading away of joy, dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and abides in the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness."
This body is completely filled with the moisture of joy and bliss; this body is completely filled with the moisture of joy and bliss, without any diminution.

It is like a pond of *utpala* flowers, a pond of *kumuda* flowers, a pond of *padma* flowers, or a pond of *puṇḍarīka* flowers, which have emerged from the mud but have not yet risen above the water; these flowers, from root to tip and from tip to root, are entirely filled with moisture and lack nothing.
In this way, monks, immeasurable joy and bliss permeate this body; they pervade the entire body without any deficiency. This is called the third limb of the noble fivefold concentration.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, having abandoned pleasure and pain and previously extinguished sorrow and joy, attains and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.
This body is practiced with a pure mind throughout its entirety; this body is practiced with a pure mind throughout its entirety without any diminution.
It is like a man or woman wearing clean white garments, from head to foot and from foot to head, with no part left uncovered.

In this way, a bhikṣu practices with a pure mind through pervasive analytical contemplation; because this body is practiced with pure pervasive analytical contemplation, there is no deficiency. This is called the cultivation of the fourth limb of the noble five-limbed concentration.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu properly grasps the signs for observation, reflects well, and understands well, just as a standing person observes one who is sitting, or as a sitting person observes one who is lying down.

In this way, a bhikṣu who has properly grasped the contemplation, properly reflected upon the signs, and properly understood them, is said to be practicing the fifth limb of the noble five-limbed concentration.

When a bhikṣu has thus practiced the noble five-limbed concentration and, having cultivated it extensively, desires to realize the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and aspires to their realization, he is able to realize them immediately according to his wish, knowing for himself that they are unimpeded.
Just as when a well-trained horse has been properly harnessed, a skilled charioteer who mounts it can travel wherever he desires with complete mastery;

so too, a bhikṣu who draws near to the noble fivefold concentration and has practiced it extensively, if he wishes to realize the supernormal powers and aspires to such realization, he will be able to realize them immediately according to his heart's desire, with mastery and without hindrance.
Just as a water jar that is sturdy and leak-proof, filled to the brim with pure water, can be tilted and used at will by a person according to their desire;

so too, a bhikṣu who has drawn near to and extensively cultivated the noble fivefold concentration can, when wishing to realize the supernormal powers, do so according to his heart's desire, with mastery and without obstruction.
Just as when a pond or spring is filled to the brim with water for drinking, a person may divert it at will and according to their desire, and the water flows out wherever they direct it;

so too, when a bhikṣu has drawn near to and extensively practiced the noble fivefold concentration, if he desires to realize the supernormal powers and yearns for such realization, he can realize them immediately according to his heart's desire, with mastery and without obstruction.

For example, a bhikṣu who wishes to attain immeasurable and manifold supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) that shake the earth—such as making one into many and many into one, and even attaining mastery over his body up to the Brahma-heaven, entering therein according to his ability—as described in the "Chapter on Knowledge" (*Jñānavarga*).
For example, a bhikṣu who wishes to attain the purified divine ear that transcends that of humans, by which he can hear the voices of both humans and non-humans, enters it according to his capacity.

For example, a bhikṣu who wishes to attain the knowledge of the minds of other sentient beings, being able to know them as they truly are: he knows a mind with desire as a mind with desire, and a mind without desire as a mind without desire, up to knowing a mind without supreme qualities as a mind without supreme qualities; he enters it according to his capacity, as described in the *Jñānavarga*.

For example, when a bhikṣu wishes to attain the recollection of immeasurable past lives, he can remember one birth, two births, three births, four births, five births, and so on, until he achieves this practice; he enters it according to his capacity, as explained in the "Chapter on Knowledge."

Just as a noble bhikṣu, desiring to attain the pure divine eye that surpasses that of humans, is able to see the birth and death of sentient beings, even unto their retribution according to their karma, entering therein as far as he is capable—just as it is explained in the "Chapter on Knowledge" (Jñānavarga).

Just as a noble bhikṣu, desiring to exhaust all outflows and realize the state of being without outflows, attains liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, personally realizes through his own knowledge in this very life the fulfillment of the practice, and enters accordingly into the realization: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence."
Having thus cultivated, approached, and frequently practiced the noble five-factored concentration, one attains such a fruit and reward.

How does a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, achieve and dwell in the first dhyāna?

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates all conditioned phenomena—or conditioned phenomena in a single instance—as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent.

Thus, through this vigilant contemplation, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

In this way, the bhikṣu, being detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.
In this manner, up to the contemplation of a corpse upon a pyre, as explained at length in the section on the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Within me there is the defilement of sensual desire."
One knows as it truly is when there is lustful defilement within;
one knows as it truly is when there is no lustful defilement within.
One knows as it truly is when lustful defilement has not yet arisen.
When sensual desire has not yet arisen, he knows as it truly is that it has not arisen;
when sensual desire has arisen, he knows as it truly is that it has arisen; when sensual desire has been abandoned, he knows as it truly is that it has been abandoned;
and when sensual desire has been abandoned, he knows as it truly is that it will not arise again.
The same applies to the presence of ill-will, sloth-and-torpor, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt within.

Thus, through such heedful contemplation, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

In this way, a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"Within me, there is desire-taint and ill-will regarding forms cognized by the internal eye-consciousness."
He knows, as it truly is, that there is desire-taint and ill-will regarding internal eye-consciousness and forms;

he knows, as it truly is, that there is no desire-taint or ill-will regarding internal eye-consciousness and forms. He knows, as it truly is, that when desire-taint and ill-will regarding eye-consciousness and forms have not yet arisen, they have not yet arisen.
When eye-consciousness has not yet arisen, and desire-taint or ill-will regarding forms arises, he knows as it truly is that they have arisen.
When desire-taint or ill-will regarding forms has already arisen and is abandoned, he knows as it truly is that they have been abandoned.
Just as when visual consciousness has abandoned desire-taint and anger regarding forms, one knows them as they truly are and they do not arise again;

so it is with auditory consciousness regarding sounds, olfactory consciousness regarding odors, gustatory consciousness regarding tastes, tactile consciousness regarding tangibles, and mental consciousness regarding phenomena.

With heedfulness as his object of contemplation, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

Thus, the bhikṣu, being detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I possess the right awakening of mindfulness within.
He knows, as it truly is, that he possesses the right awakening of mindfulness within.
When there is no mindfulness-enlightenment internally, he knows as it really is that there is no mindfulness-enlightenment internally.
When mindfulness-enlightenment has not yet arisen, he knows as it really is that it has not yet arisen.
When mindfulness-enlightenment has arisen where it had not previously arisen, he knows as it really is that it has arisen.
Just as one fully cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness once it has arisen, so too does one know, as they truly are, that it is fully cultivated.
It is the same for the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.

Thus, through this heedful contemplation, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

In this way, the bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, the bhikṣu knows as it really is suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering; he knows as they really are the taints, the origin of the taints, the cessation of the taints, and the path leading to the cessation of the taints.

Thus, through this practice of heedfulness, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

In this way, a bhikṣu, having detached from sensual desires and unwholesome, unskillful states, with directed thought and evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

Furthermore, because his mind is fearful, the bhikṣu emerges from all conditioned phenomena and enters the realm of the deathless—this which is peaceful, sublime, and transcendent, the cessation of all formations, the exhaustion of craving, nirvāṇa.

Thus, through this practice of heedfulness, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

In this way, a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and characterized by joy and bliss.
The second, third, and fourth dhyānas are also described in the same manner.
How does a bhikṣu properly grasp the sign of contemplation, properly reflect, and properly understand?

It is when a bhikṣu, regarding all conditioned phenomena—or conditioned phenomena in a single instance—contemplates them as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent.

Thus, through this practice of heedfulness, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of detachment, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

Just as a bhikṣu, whether walking or contemplating the characteristics of dharmas, becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, and, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna, which is born of seclusion and accompanied by joy and bliss.

If one well grasps the characteristics of phenomena, well reflects upon them, and well understands them—well cognizing, cognizing in accordance with, and cognizing as an object; discerning, discerning in accordance with, and discerning as an object.
In this way, the bhikṣu correctly grasps the signs for contemplation, correctly reflects, and correctly understands.

Furthermore, bhikṣu, if one contemplates a single conditioned phenomenon as suffering, as a calamity, as a boil, as an arrow, as a gratification, as a fault, as dependent on conditions, as subject to destruction, as unstable, as unsatisfactory, as perishable, as suffering, empty, and non-self; and if one contemplates its conditions, knows its conditions, and experiences its conditions—namely: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—the entire mass of suffering thus arises.

Thus, through this heedful contemplation, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

For example, a bhikṣu, regarding the nature of phenomena, being free from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and experiencing the joy and happiness born of seclusion, accomplishes the practice of the first dhyāna.

Whether it be formations or the characteristics of phenomena, one correctly grasps their characteristics, correctly contemplates them, and correctly understands them; one correctly cognizes them, cognizes them in accordance with reality, and cognizes them as conditions; one discriminates them, discriminates them in accordance with reality, and discriminates them as conditions.
In this way, the bhikṣu properly grasps the signs of contemplation, properly reflects, and properly understands.

Furthermore, bhikṣu, regarding all conditioned phenomena—or even a single instance of a conditioned phenomenon—he contemplates the cessation of phenomena, knows their cessation, understands their cessation, and accepts their cessation: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form cease; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; and with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair—the entire mass of suffering—cease.

Thus, through this practice of heedfulness, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

For example, a bhikṣu, whether walking or contemplating the characteristics of phenomena, becomes detached from desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he accomplishes and dwells in the first dhyāna.

Whether it be formations or the characteristics of phenomena, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them; one skillfully cognizes, cognizes in accordance with, and takes them as objects of cognition; one discriminates, discriminates in accordance with, and takes them as objects of discrimination.
In this way, a bhikṣu skillfully grasps the signs of observation, skillfully reflects, and skillfully understands.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows when walking that he is walking and delights in it; he knows when standing that he is standing and delights in it; he knows when sitting that he is sitting and delights in it; he knows when lying down that he is lying down and delights in it.
Thus, dwelling in bodily pleasure, he knows as it truly is that he dwells in pleasure.

With such heedful observation, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and abides in the first dhyāna.

For example, a bhikṣu, whether walking or contemplating the characteristics of phenomena, becomes detached from desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he accomplishes the practice of the first dhyāna.

Whether it be formations or the characteristics of phenomena, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them; one skillfully cognizes, cognizes in accordance with, and cognizes as an object; one discriminates, discriminates in accordance with, and discriminates as an object.
In this way, the bhikṣu correctly grasps the signs of contemplation, correctly reflects, and correctly understands.

Furthermore, bhikṣu, from the acts of going and coming, bending and stretching, up to the point of mental fear, he emerges from all conditioned phenomena and enters the realm of ambrosia; it is explained in this same manner.
The second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna are also explained in this same way.
What is meant by "skillfully grasping the signs of contemplation, skillfully reflecting, and skillfully understanding"?

Just as a bhikṣu contemplates all conditioned phenomena—or conditioned phenomena in a single instance—as impermanent, knows them as impermanent, understands them as impermanent, and accepts them as impermanent.

Thus, through this heedful contemplation, he becomes detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states; with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, he attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

Suppose, for instance, a bhikṣu, regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them; he skillfully cognizes them, cognizes them accordingly, and cognizes them as objects; he discriminates them, discriminates them accordingly, and discriminates them as objects.
In this way, a bhikṣu properly grasps the signs of contemplation, properly reflects, and properly understands.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu regards all conditioned phenomena—or even those in a single location—as suffering, as a calamity, as an abscess, and as an arrow; because his mind is thus filled with dread, he emerges from all conditioned things and enters the realm of the deathless (*amṛta*). This is tranquility, this is sublime excellence; it is the departure from all conditioned things, the exhaustion of craving, and *nirvāṇa*.

Thus, through this practice of heedfulness, he dwells having transcended sensual desires and unwholesome states, with applied thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, having attained the first dhyāna.

For example, a bhikṣu, regarding form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them; he skillfully cognizes, cognizes accordingly, and cognizes by way of conditions; he discriminates, discriminates accordingly, and discriminates by way of conditions.
In this way, the bhikṣu correctly grasps the signs of observation, correctly contemplates, and correctly understands.
Regarding the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna, it is also as explained above.
These five factors are called the five-factored concentration (*pañcāṅga-samādhi*).
What is the concentration of the five knowledges (*pañcajñāna-samādhi*)?
As the Blessed One has said:
The bhikṣus cultivate meditative concentration until it is immeasurable and clearly manifest.
Once the bhikṣus have cultivated meditative concentration until it is immeasurable and clearly manifest, they give rise to five kinds of knowledge based upon it.
What are these five?

If there is concentration that has the nature of yielding a reward of happiness both in the present and in the future, one generates knowledge conditioned by this; if there is concentration that is certainly noble and untainted, one generates knowledge conditioned by this; if there is concentration that is certainly not cowardly and can be approached with intimacy, one generates knowledge conditioned by this; if there is concentration that is certainly tranquil, sublime, and attained through solitary cultivation, one generates knowledge conditioned by this; if there is concentration characterized by mindfulness, entering with right mindfulness and arising with right mindfulness, one generates knowledge conditioned by this.
What is the concentration that has a ripening result of happiness both in the present and in the future, and by which one generates knowledge?
What is the certainty of happiness in the present?

It is as follows: a bhikṣu, detached from sensual desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained thought, and with the joy and happiness born of seclusion, attains and dwells in the first dhyāna.

If the body is suffused with the moisture of joy and happiness born of seclusion, this entire body is completely suffused with the moisture of joy and happiness born of seclusion, without any part being deficient.

It is like a skilled bath-attendant or his apprentice who places fine bathing powder in a vessel, sprinkles it with water, and kneads it into a ball; this ball is entirely suffused with moisture, neither dry nor wet, but moist and supple both inside and out.

In this way, the bhikṣu’s body is completely saturated with the moisture of joy and happiness born of seclusion; his entire body is thoroughly suffused with this moisture of joy and happiness born of seclusion, without any part remaining unsuffused.

Just as the bhikṣu increases and experiences the joy and happiness born of seclusion, supramundane happiness, the happiness of tranquility, the happiness of cessation, the happiness of perfect awakening, the happiness of the fruits of śrāmaṇya, and the happiness of nirvāṇa—this concentration is likewise characterized by present happiness.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the subsiding of applied and sustained thought, possessing internal clarity and mental unification, enters and dwells in the second dhyāna, which is free from applied and sustained thought and possesses the joy and happiness born of concentration.
If the body is completely filled with the moisture born of joy and bliss, this entire body is pervaded by the moisture born of joy and bliss without any diminution.
It is like a great lake surrounded by mountains, where water wells up from the bottom and does not come from the east, south, west, or north.
Just as this pond is completely filled with water and moisture, such that the entire pond is saturated with moisture and there is no decrease;
so too, a bhikṣu’s body is completely filled with the moisture and juice of joy and bliss born of concentration, such that his entire body is saturated with this moisture and there is no decrease.

Just as a bhikṣu increases and experiences the bliss of non-attachment, supramundane bliss, the bliss of tranquility, the bliss of cessation, the bliss of perfect awakening, the bliss of the fruits of śramaṇahood, and the bliss of nirvāṇa—this concentration is likewise called "bliss in the present."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, with the fading away of joy, dwells in equanimity, mindfulness, and clear comprehension, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters and abides in the third dhyāna, which the noble ones describe as "dwelling in equanimity, mindfulness, and happiness."

If the body is filled with the moisture of joy and bliss, and this moisture of joy and bliss pervades the entire body without any diminution—just as in a pond of *utpala* flowers, a pond of *padma* flowers, a pond of *kumuda* flowers, or a pond of *puṇḍarīka* flowers, where the flowers have just emerged from the mud and have not yet risen above the water; whether it be the roots or the tips of these flowers, they are completely saturated with the moisture of the water, from root to tip and from tip to root, entirely saturated without any diminution.
In this way, monks, if the body is completely suffused with the moisture of rapture and joy, this entire body is thoroughly suffused with that moisture, without any part remaining unsuffused.

Just as a monk increases his experience of rapture and joy, supramundane bliss, the bliss of tranquility, the bliss of cessation, the bliss of perfect awakening, the bliss of the fruits of the ascetic life, and the bliss of nirvana—this concentration is likewise called "bliss in the present."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu, having abandoned suffering and pleasure, and with the prior cessation of sorrow and joy, enters and dwells in the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant, characterized by equanimity, mindfulness, and purity.
If one practices with a body and a mind of universal purity, this body will be pure and there will be no place it does not pervade.
It is like a man or a woman wearing clean white garments, complete from top to bottom; from head to foot and from foot to head, there is nowhere that is not covered.
In this way, a bhikṣu, if he practices with a pure mind pervading the body, that body will be pure without any part not pervaded.

Just as a bhikṣu increases his experience of sublime peace, supramundane bliss, the bliss of tranquility, the bliss of cessation, the bliss of perfect awakening, the bliss of the fruits of the śramaṇa, and the bliss of nirvāṇa—such concentration is called "bliss in the present."
What is the pleasant retribution following meditative concentration?

It is as when a bhikṣu contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and contemplates the tranquility of nirvāṇa, thereby attaining concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established.
Just as when a bhikṣu has attained meditative concentration, he immediately attains the first noble five faculties;
having attained the first noble five faculties, he enters into right determination and abandons the stage of an ordinary person.
It is impossible that one would die midway without having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*).
It is impossible that, without having attained the fruit of stream-entry, one would commit evil deeds and, upon death, fall into the three miserable realms.

Just as a bhikṣu who approaches this concentration and trains in it extensively, having trained extensively, sees and abandons the three afflictions to be abandoned by insight and realizes the fruit of stream-entry.

Having realized this, they sever the sufferings of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; they undergo seven more births as humans or devas, thereby severing all remaining suffering within the realms of gods and men.
Such concentration is said to have a pleasant result in the future.

For example, a bhikṣu who draws near to this concentration and practices it extensively, having practiced it extensively, contemplates the abandonment of the afflictions consisting of sensual desire and ill will.

Having severed the portion of afflictions consisting of sensual desire and ill will, one attains and realizes the fruit of the Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*). Having realized it, one severs the suffering of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, and receives birth among devas and humans, thereby severing the remaining suffering of birth among devas and humans.
Such concentration is said to have a pleasant ripening in the future.

For example, if a bhikṣu draws near to this concentration and trains in it extensively, having trained extensively, he contemplates and abandons sensual desire and ill will until they are exhausted without remainder. Having abandoned them without remainder, he attains and realizes the fruit of *anāgāmin*. Having attained and realized it, he cuts off the suffering of the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, and among humans.
Whether one receives birth in a single heaven or five heavens, all suffering in the remaining heavens is severed.
Such concentration is called the fruition of future bliss.

If a bhikṣu draws near to this concentration and practices it extensively, having practiced it extensively, he contemplates the severance of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) until they are exhausted without remainder. Having exhausted them without remainder, he attains the realization of the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*). Having attained that realization, he severs the suffering of the hells, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas; all existence (*bhava*), all paths (*gati*), all births (*jāti*), all fetters (*bandhana*), and all afflictions of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are severed without remainder.
Such concentration refers to the subsequent fruit of blissful retribution.
What is meant by "arising of knowledge conditioned by this"?
Whether it be internal discrimination or external discrimination, that which is known, seen, awakened to, and realized—this is called the arising of knowledge conditioned by this.
What is meant by "noble concentration with an undefiled object from which knowledge arises"?
What is meant by "non-noble concentration"?
If concentration is with outflows (*sāsrava*), this is called non-noble concentration.

Furthermore, non-noble concentration (*anārya-samādhi*): if a concentration is neither that of a learner (*śaikṣa*) nor that of one beyond learning (*aśaikṣa*), this is called non-noble concentration.

Furthermore, non-noble concentration: excluding the concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), if it is any other concentration, this is called non-noble concentration.
What is called noble concentration (*ārya-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is named noble concentration.
Furthermore, regarding noble concentration: if a concentration belongs to those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), this is called noble concentration.
Furthermore, regarding noble concentration (*ārya-samādhi*): the concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) are called noble concentration.
In what sense are they called "noble"?
Because they sever and abandon desire, hatred, delusion, and all fetters and afflictions (*kleśa*), they are called noble concentration.
What is concentration with outflows (*sāsrava-samādhi*)?
If a concentration involves seeking, this is called concentration with outflows.
Furthermore, concentration with outflows refers to a concentration that is neither of the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) nor beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); this is called concentration with outflows.
Furthermore, there are defiled concentrations; excluding the concentrations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, any other concentration is called a defiled concentration.
In what sense are they "defiled"?
"Defilement" refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

When craving is acquired, correctly acquired, and conditionally acquired within this meditative absorption, and when the absorption is likewise acquired, correctly acquired, and conditionally acquired within craving, it is called "defiled absorption."
What is undefiled concentration?
If a concentration is without seeking, this is called undefiled concentration.
Furthermore, undefiled concentration refers to the concentration of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa); this is called undefiled concentration.
Furthermore, regarding the untainted concentrations—the concentration of emptiness, the signless concentration, and the wishless concentration—these are called the untainted concentrations.
In what sense are they untainted?
"Taint" refers to craving.

If one does not obtain, does not correctly obtain, and does not take as an object within craving for concentration, and does not obtain, does not correctly obtain, and does not take as an object within concentration that is craved, this is called undefiled concentration.
What is meant by "conditioned by this, knowledge arises"?
Whether it be internal discrimination or external discrimination, that which is known, seen, realized, and personally experienced—this is called "conditioned by this, knowledge arises.
How does one who possesses concentration and is not timid approach this "knowledge arising conditioned by this"?
What is meant by the "timid and weak"?
One who lacks faith, lacks a sense of shame and dread of blame, does not engage in study, is indolent, has lost mindfulness, and lacks wisdom—this is called the timid and weak.
Furthermore, the timid and weak are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
In what sense are they called "timid and weak"?
Because they have not yet understood the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and have not yet abandoned the view of a self-identity, for this reason they are called "timid and weak."
What is meant by "not being weak"?
Not being weak refers to possessing faith, a sense of shame and dread of blame, extensive learning, diligent effort, focused mindfulness, and abundant wisdom; this is what is meant by not being weak.
Furthermore, regarding "not being timid":
if it concerns the Buddha and his śrāvaka disciples,
in what sense are they called "not timid"?
Because one understands the view of a self-identity and because one has abandoned the view of a self-identity, for this reason one is called "one who is not timid.
Thus, the one who is not timid attains concentration and approaches it with frequent cultivation; for this reason, it is said that "the one who is not timid approaches [it]."
What is meant by "knowledge arises dependent on this"?
Whether it be internal discrimination or external discrimination, that which is known, seen, realized, and personally attained—this is called "knowledge arising dependent on this.
What is meant by "having attained knowledge arising dependent on this through the cultivation of concentration, tranquility, excellence, solitude, and renunciation"?
What is tranquility?
If it is the fruit of retribution associated with meditative concentration, this is called tranquility.
What is the sublime concentration?
If a concentration is noble, possesses fruition, and is able to sever the afflictions, it is called sublime concentration.
Furthermore, regarding tranquil concentration: if a concentration is noble, possesses fruition, and is able to sever the afflictions, it is called tranquil concentration.
Furthermore, regarding sublime concentration (*praṇīta-samādhi*): if a concentration is accompanied by its karmic fruit, it is called sublime concentration.
Furthermore, tranquility (*śānta*) is itself the sublime, and the sublime is itself tranquility; this is what is meant by "tranquility that is sublime."
What is meant by "practicing alone"?
If the mind is single-mindedly settled in right stillness while dwelling alone in concentration, this is called practicing alone.
What is meant by "attaining through elimination"?
What is meant by "attaining concentration without elimination"?
If concentration is attained without having eliminated [defilements], or if it is attained with difficulty, this is called attaining concentration without elimination.
What is meant by "attaining concentration through elimination"?
If it is attained with certainty, attained decisively, and not difficult to attain, this is called "attainment through the removal of obstacles.
What is meant by "arising of knowledge conditioned by this"?
Whether it be internal discrimination or external discrimination, knowing, seeing, awakening to, and realizing it—this is called "arising of knowledge conditioned by this."
What is meant by "entering with concentration and right mindfulness, arising with right mindfulness, and giving rise to knowledge conditioned by this"?

It is when one enters with right knowledge and arises with right knowledge; having entered with right knowledge and arisen with right knowledge, for that reason it is called "entering with right mindfulness and arising with right mindfulness."

One enters with exclusive mindfulness of the body and emerges with exclusive mindfulness of the body; having entered with exclusive mindfulness of the body and emerged with exclusive mindfulness of the body, this is called entering with right mindfulness and emerging with right mindfulness.
What is meant by "arising of knowledge conditioned by this"?
Whether it be internal discrimination or external discrimination, that which is known, seen, awakened to, and realized—this is called the arising of wisdom conditioned by this.
These five kinds of wisdom constitute the concentration of the five wisdoms.
What is the concentration on mindfulness of breathing out and breathing in?
As the Blessed One said:

"Monks, cultivate mindfulness of breathing out and breathing in; draw near to it and train in it extensively. Having trained extensively, one attains great fruit and reward, even up to the attainment of the Deathless."
How does one cultivate mindfulness of breathing out and breathing in, drawing near to it and training in it extensively, so as to attain great fruits and even attain the Deathless?

It is like a bhikṣu who dwells in a secluded place—within a forest, at the foot of a tree, or in an open space; in a mountain cave, in the open air upon a spread of grass, or among burial mounds, on a rocky bank.
Suppose a bhikṣu goes to a village for alms in the morning; having eaten and the day having passed its midday, he puts away his robes and bowl and washes his feet.

Having washed his feet, the bhikṣu sits cross-legged, straightens his body, and fixes his mindfulness, contemplating the abandonment of longing. With a mind free from longing and craving, he attains purity regarding longing and craving. He abandons ill will and practices a mind of loving-kindness; with a mind detached from ill will, he attains purity.
Having abandoned sloth and torpor, being free from sloth and torpor, with clear comprehension and mindful awareness, his mind is liberated from sloth and torpor and attains purity.
Having abandoned restlessness and remorse, being free from restlessness and remorse, with an inner tranquility, he is liberated from restlessness and remorse and attains purity.
Cutting off doubt and practicing without doubt, with a mind fixed upon wholesome qualities, one leaves behind doubt and attains purity.
Just as a bhikṣu cuts off the five hindrances—which are defilements of the mind that impair wisdom—he practices mindfulness while breathing out and mindfulness while breathing in.

Just as a bhikṣu, when breathing out long, knows he is breathing out long; when breathing in long, knows he is breathing in long; when breathing out short, knows he is breathing out short; and when breathing in short, knows he is breathing in short.
One trains in being aware of the entire body while breathing in; one trains in being aware of the entire body while breathing out.
One trains in breathing out calming the bodily formations; one trains in breathing in calming the bodily formations.

One trains in being aware of joy while breathing out; one trains in being aware of joy while breathing in. One trains in being aware of pleasure while breathing out; one trains in being aware of pleasure while breathing in.
He trains in being mindful of the mental formation while breathing out; he trains in being mindful of the mental formation while breathing in.
He trains in being mindful of the calming of the mental formation while breathing out; he trains in being mindful of the calming of the mental formation while breathing in.

He trains in being mindful of the mind while breathing out; he trains in being mindful of the mind while breathing in. He trains in breathing out gladdening the mind; he trains in breathing in gladdening the mind.
He trains in exhaling with a concentrated mind, he trains in inhaling with a concentrated mind;

he trains in exhaling with a liberated mind, he trains in inhaling with a liberated mind; he trains in exhaling while contemplating impermanence, he trains in inhaling while contemplating impermanence;
he trains in exhaling while contemplating dispassion, he trains in inhaling while contemplating dispassion; he trains in exhaling while contemplating cessation—
