One trains in observing the cessation while inhaling; one trains in observing the transcendental while exhaling; one trains in observing the transcendental while inhaling.
What is meant by mindful exhalation and mindful inhalation?

If one is clearly aware of the out-breath and clearly aware of the in-breath, having been clearly aware of the out-breath and clearly aware of the in-breath, this is called mindfulness of out-breathing and mindfulness of in-breathing.

One is mindful of the body while exhaling, and mindful of the body while inhaling; having been mindful of the body while exhaling and mindful of the body while inhaling, this is called right mindfulness of exhalation and right mindfulness of inhalation.
What is meant by a bhikṣu who, when breathing out long, knows he is breathing out long, and when breathing in long, knows he is breathing in long?

It is when a bhikṣu, while reflecting on the Dharma, produces long exhalations and inhalations, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflecting upon it, and skillfully understanding it.

If one contemplates phenomena that do not give rise to out-breaths and in-breaths, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to give rise to out-breaths and in-breaths, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, developing clear comprehension of the out-breath and in-breath, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflecting upon it, and skillfully understanding it.

Or, while contemplating the Dharma, he does not develop clear comprehension of the out-breath and in-breath, yet he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflects upon it, and skillfully understands it.

If there are dharmas, whether superior or non-superior, that can produce the awareness of out-breathing and in-breathing, one should skillfully grasp their characteristics, skillfully contemplate them, and skillfully understand them.
Just as a bhikṣu contemplates dharmas while producing out-breathing and in-breathing, he contemplates those dharmas;
if they do not arise, he does not contemplate those dharmas, but instead draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to non-superior dharmas.
A bhikṣu, while contemplating the Dharma, develops long out-breaths and in-breaths, being clearly aware that he is contemplating the Dharma;
if they do not arise, he does not contemplate the Dharma.

Associating with superior dharmas and not associating with inferior dharmas, the bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that ought to be cultivated; associating with superior dharmas and not associating with inferior dharmas, he develops long out-breaths and in-breaths.

Furthermore, when one is aware of long out-breaths and in-breaths and attains a mind of joy, this is called a bhikṣu who, breathing out long, knows he is breathing out long; breathing in long, knows he is breathing in long.
What is meant by long exhalation and inhalation?

If there is immeasurable exhalation and immeasurable inhalation, and having completed immeasurable exhalations and immeasurable inhalations, for this reason they are called long exhalation and long inhalation.
One does not exhale hurriedly, nor does one inhale hurriedly; having neither exhaled hurriedly nor inhaled hurriedly, it is therefore said that the exhalation is long and the inhalation is long.
He does not exhale or inhale hurriedly; having ceased hurrying in exhalation and inhalation, for this reason it is called long exhalation and inhalation.

He does not exert the body in exhaling, nor does he exert the body in inhaling; having ceased exerting the body in exhalation and inhalation, for this reason it is called long exhalation and inhalation.
One does not continue the out-breath and in-breath; having ceased the out-breath and in-breath, for this reason they are called long out-breaths and in-breaths.
This concludes the single section on long out-breaths and in-breaths.
What is meant by knowing the short out-breath as a short out-breath, and knowing the short in-breath as a short in-breath?

It is when a bhikṣu, while contemplating the Dharma, gives rise to short out-breaths and in-breaths, correctly grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, correctly reflecting upon them, and correctly understanding them.

If one contemplates the dharmas that do not give rise to short out-breaths and in-breaths, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If dharmas, whether superior or non-superior, can give rise to short out-breaths and in-breaths, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to the awareness of short out-breaths and in-breaths, he correctly grasps the characteristics of the phenomena, correctly contemplates them, and correctly understands them.

When he contemplates the Dharma and does not give rise to the awareness of short out-breaths and in-breaths, he still correctly grasps the characteristics of the phenomena, correctly contemplates them, and correctly understands them.

If a phenomenon is superior or non-superior that gives rise to the awareness of short out-breaths and in-breaths, one correctly grasps its characteristics, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates a phenomenon that gives rise to the awareness of short out-breaths and in-breaths, or does not contemplate a phenomenon that does not give rise to them, he draws near to superior phenomena and does not draw near to non-superior phenomena. Just as when a bhikṣu contemplates a phenomenon that gives rise to the awareness of short out-breaths and in-breaths, or does not contemplate a phenomenon that does not give rise to them, he draws near to superior phenomena and does not draw near to non-superior phenomena.

A bhikṣu does not contemplate those dharmas that should not be cultivated, but contemplates those dharmas that should be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas, and his exhalations and inhalations are short.

Furthermore, when one experiences joy through being aware of short exhalations and inhalations, this is called knowing the short exhalation as a short exhalation and knowing the short inhalation as a short inhalation.
What is meant by short exhalation and inhalation?
There is measured exhalation and measured inhalation; having exhaled and inhaled with measure, for this reason they are called short exhalations and inhalations.
When one exhales quickly, having exhaled quickly, for this reason it is called short exhalation and inhalation.
When one exhales continuously and rapidly, having exhaled continuously and rapidly, for this reason it is called short exhalation and inhalation.
One exhales and inhales with forceful exertion of the body; having exhale and inhaled with forceful exertion of the body, for this reason it is called short exhalation and inhalation.
One continues the exhalation and inhalation; having continued the exhalation and inhalation, for this reason it is called short exhalation and inhalation.
One does not physically eliminate the out-breath and in-breath; having not physically eliminated the out-breath and in-breath, for this reason it is said that the out-breath and in-breath are short.
This concludes the two matters concerning the shortness of the out-breath and in-breath.
What is meant by training in the awareness of exhaling with the entire body and training in the awareness of inhaling with the entire body?
It is as when a bhikṣu, having filled the entire body with the breath, exhales; or when, after the interior of the entire body has been made empty, he inhales.
It is like a skilled bellows-maker or his apprentice who, having filled the bellows bag, presses it to release the air;
or when the bellows bag is empty, he opens its mouth again so that it may be filled with air.
In this way, a bhikṣu, having caused the breath to fill his entire body, exhales; or, having made the interior of his entire body empty, inhales.
If he contemplates the Dharma, as he exhales and inhales throughout his entire body, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If one contemplates the dharmas such that no out-breath or in-breath arises within the entire body, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of the dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

Whether the dharmas are superior or non-superior, if out-breath and in-breath do arise within the entire body, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of the dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

Just as a bhikṣu, when contemplating the Dharma, gives rise to the awareness of all inhalations and exhalations within his body, skillfully grasping the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflecting upon them, and skillfully understanding them.

If one contemplates the Dharma, such that within the entire body there arises no perception of out-breath or in-breath, one will skillfully grasp the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplate them, and skillfully understand them.

Whether a phenomenon is superior or non-superior, it can give rise to the awareness of all exhalations and inhalations within the body; one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

Just as when a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he gives rise to the contemplation of all inhalations and exhalations within his body; if he does not give rise to it, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he gives rise to mindfulness of the inhalations and exhalations throughout his entire body; when he does not give rise to it, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. Within his entire body, as he exhales and inhales, he becomes aware of the exhalations and inhalations throughout the whole body and attains joy. This is called training in the awareness of exhaling the entire body and training in the awareness of inhaling the entire body; thus the three matters are concluded.
What is meant by training in exhaling while calming bodily formations and training in inhaling while calming bodily formations?
Bodily formations refer to exhalations and inhalations that are either coarse or subtle.
What are coarse bodily formations?
If there is agitation, this is called coarse bodily activity (*audārika-kāya-saṃskāra*).
What is subtle bodily activity?
If there is tranquility, this is called subtle bodily activity. Just as a bhikṣu, by means of subtle bodily activity, subdues, overcomes, eliminates, and transcends coarse bodily activity.
Just as a skilled carpenter or a carpenter’s apprentice uses a small wedge to extract a large wedge,
so too does a bhikṣu use subtle bodily conduct to subdue coarse bodily conduct.
It is like a person running who thinks to himself:
"For what reason am I running?
I should walk slowly and steadily."
He then proceeded with composure.
This person further reflected:
"Why am I proceeding with such composure?"
"I should abide; so I shall abide.
Then that person further reflects:
"Why do I stand?
I shall sit. And he sat down.
This person further reflects in this way:
"For what reason am I sitting?
I shall lie down."
He then lay down.
In this way, that person eliminates gross bodily activities and cultivates subtle bodily activities.
In the same way, a bhikṣu eliminates gross bodily activities and cultivates subtle bodily activities.
When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and coarse bodily formations arise, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of that Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
When he contemplates the Dharma and coarse bodily formations do not arise, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon is either superior or non-superior and can produce coarse bodily formations, one properly grasps its characteristics, properly contemplates it, and properly understands it.
When a bhikṣu contemplates a phenomenon that produces subtle bodily formations, he properly grasps its characteristics, properly contemplates it, and properly understands it.

If one contemplates dharmas that do not give rise to subtle bodily formations, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If dharmas—whether superior or non-superior—are able to give rise to subtle bodily formations, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.
If a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while eliminating coarse bodily formations, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma without eliminating coarse bodily formations, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a state, whether superior or non-superior, can eliminate coarse bodily formations, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the states that give rise to the elimination of bodily formations during exhalation and inhalation, he skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates the phenomena that do not give rise to the breaths that eliminate bodily formations, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—that can give rise to the breaths that eliminate bodily formations, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

A bhikṣu contemplates the phenomena that give rise to the awareness of the exhalation and inhalation which eliminate bodily formations; he skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If he contemplates the phenomena that do not give rise to the awareness of the exhalation and inhalation which eliminate bodily formations, he likewise skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of producing the awareness of the exhalation and inhalation that eliminates bodily formations, and if one correctly grasps its characteristics, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it, then when a bhikṣu contemplates such a phenomenon, coarse bodily formations arise;
yet when he does not contemplate such a phenomenon, they do not arise. When he contemplates such a phenomenon, he draws near to superior phenomena and does not draw near to non-superior phenomena.

When a bhikṣu contemplates dharmas that give rise to subtle bodily formations, he contemplates those dharmas; when they do not arise, he does not contemplate them. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma to eliminate gross bodily formations; he contemplates the Dharma when they are eliminated, and does not contemplate it when they are not. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, there arise the out-breaths and in-breaths that eliminate bodily formations; when he contemplates the Dharma or does not contemplate it, he should cultivate superior dharmas and not cultivate inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, there arises the awareness of exhalation and inhalation that removes bodily formations; he contemplates the Dharma when it arises, and does not contemplate it when it does not arise. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

The bhikṣu does not contemplate what is not to be cultivated, but contemplates what is to be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. Excluding the bodily formations of exhalation and inhalation, and through the awareness of excluding these bodily formations of exhalation and inhalation, he attains joy. This is called the completion of the four matters regarding the training in excluding the bodily formations of exhalation and inhalation.
What is meant by training in the awareness of exhaling with joy and training in the awareness of inhaling with joy?
What is joy (*prīti*)?
When the mind is gladdened and elated, this is called joy.
A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to joy, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplating it, and skillfully understanding it.
Or, he contemplates the Dharma and does not give rise to joy, yet still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon, whether superior or non-superior, can produce joy, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena and generates joy during exhalation and inhalation, he skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates phenomena that do not produce joy while exhaling and inhaling, one properly grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, properly contemplates them, and properly understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to produce joy while exhaling and inhaling, one properly grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, properly contemplates them, and properly understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to joy while being aware of the out-breath and in-breath, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When he contemplates the Dharma and does not give rise to joy while being aware of the out-breath and in-breath, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If there are dharmas, whether superior or non-superior, that can produce joyful out-breaths and in-breaths, he correctly grasps their characteristics, correctly contemplates them, and correctly understands them.

When the bhikṣu contemplates dharmas that produce joy, he contemplates those dharmas; when they do not produce it, he does not contemplate them. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to non-superior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while exhaling and inhaling, if joy arises, he should contemplate the Dharma; if it does not arise, he should not contemplate it. He should cultivate superior dharmas and not cultivate those that are not superior.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to joy while being mindful of the out-breath and in-breath, he contemplates the Dharma; if joy does not arise, he does not contemplate it. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to those that are not superior.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas; he takes joy in the exhalation and inhalation, and through the joyful awareness of the exhalation and inhalation, he attains gladness and rapture. This concludes the five matters concerning training in the joyful awareness of exhalation and training in the joyful awareness of inhalation.
What is meant by training in the mindful awareness of exhaling with pleasure and training in the mindful awareness of inhaling with pleasure?
What is pleasure?
If the mind endures pleasure, and there is a pleasant feeling born of mental contact, this is called pleasure.
Just as when a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to joy, he correctly grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it;
so too, when he contemplates it and does not give rise to joy, he still correctly grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it.
If a phenomenon is superior or non-superior and can produce pleasure, one properly grasps its characteristics, properly contemplates it, and properly understands it.
A bhikṣu, while contemplating phenomena that produce pleasure during exhalation and inhalation, properly grasps their characteristics, properly contemplates them, and properly understands them.
If one contemplates phenomena that do not produce pleasant out-breaths and in-breaths, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to produce pleasant out-breaths and in-breaths, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

A bhikṣu, while contemplating the Dharma, is mindful of the out-breath and in-breath that arise with joy; he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If, while contemplating the Dharma, there arises no mindfulness of the out-breath and in-breath accompanied by joy, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If a phenomenon, whether superior or non-superior, can produce the awareness of pleasant out-breaths and in-breaths, one should skillfully grasp its characteristics, skillfully contemplate it, and skillfully understand it.

A bhikṣu contemplates phenomena while breathing out and in pleasantly, or does not contemplate phenomena when such breathing does not arise; he draws near to superior phenomena and does not draw near to non-superior phenomena.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while exhaling and inhaling, he gives rise to joy; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, he does not give rise to it. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to joy while being mindful of the out-breath and in-breath, he contemplates that Dharma; if he does not give rise to it, he does not contemplate that Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas; he delights in the exhalation and inhalation of breath, and through delighting in the exhalation and inhalation of breath, he attains joy through clear comprehension. This is called training in the clear comprehension of joyful exhalation and training in the clear comprehension of joyful inhalation; thus ends the six matters.
What is meant by training in the awareness of the out-breath as a mental formation, and training in the awareness of the in-breath as a mental formation?
"Mental formation" refers to volition (*cetanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), which possess coarseness and subtlety.
What is coarse mental formation?
If the mental formations are restless and agitated, this is called coarse mental formation.
What is subtle mental formation?
If the mental formations are tranquil, this is called subtle mental formation.
Just as a bhikṣu, through subtle mental activity, subdues coarse mental activity— overcoming, excelling, eliminating, and emerging from it—
just as a skilled craftsman or his apprentice uses a small wedge to drive out a large wedge.
In this way, a bhikṣu uses subtle mental activity to subdue coarse mental activity.
When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and coarse mental activity arises, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflects upon it, and skillfully understands it.

If, when contemplating a phenomenon, one does not give rise to coarse mental activity, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of that phenomenon, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
Whether a phenomenon is superior or non-superior, if it can give rise to coarse mental activity, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and subtle mental activities arise, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
Even when contemplating the Dharma and no subtle mental activities arise, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon is superior or non-superior and can give rise to subtle mental formations, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena and gives rise to mental formations regarding the exhalation and inhalation of breath, he skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates phenomena that do not give rise to mental formations regarding the out-breath and in-breath, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to give rise to mental formations regarding the out-breath and in-breath, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas and gives rise to mental formations regarding the awareness of out-breathing and in-breathing, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of those dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When he contemplates the dharmas and does not give rise to mental formations regarding the awareness of out-breathing and in-breathing, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If a dharma—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of producing mental formations regarding the out-breath and in-breath, and one perceives them with skillfully grasped characteristics of phenomena, skillful reflection, and skillful understanding, then that bhikṣu, by reflecting on such dharmas, generates coarse mental formations;
yet when not reflecting on such dharmas, or when reflection does not arise, he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to non-superior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, subtle mental activities arise; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, such activities do not arise. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to those that are not superior.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he gives rise to mental formations and is aware of the exhalation and inhalation while contemplating the Dharma; if he does not give rise to them, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu does not contemplate dharmas that should not be cultivated, but contemplates dharmas that should be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. He is mindful of the mental activities during exhalation and inhalation, and through this awareness of the mental activities during exhalation and inhalation, he attains joy. This is called training in the awareness of mental activities during exhalation and training in the awareness of mental activities during inhalation. Thus ends the seventh [section].
The Śāriputra Abhidharma Śāstra, Volume Twenty-Eight.
The Śāriputra Abhidharma Śāstra, Volume Twenty-Nine.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmayaśas of Kapiśī during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Translated together with Dharmagupta and others.

Section on the Analysis of the Stages, Chapter on Concentration, Part Two. What is meant by "training in the exhalation that removes mental formations" and "training in the inhalation that removes mental formations"?
Mental formations refer to perception (*saṃjñā*) and volition (*cetanā*), which possess both coarse and subtle aspects.
What is coarse mental activity?
If there is agitation and restlessness, this is called coarse mental activity.
If mental activity is tranquil, this is called subtle mental activity.
Just as a bhikṣu uses subtle mental activity to subdue coarse mental activity— overcoming, removing, and eliminating it—
just as a master craftsman or his apprentice uses a small wedge to extract a large wedge, so too does a bhikṣu use subtle mental activity to subdue coarse mental activity.
It is like a person running who thinks to himself:
"For what reason am I running?
I should walk slowly and steadily."
He then walked slowly and steadily,
reflecting to himself:
"For what reason do I walk so slowly and steadily?"
"I shall abide; thus I abide.
Then he reflects within himself:
"Why do I stand?
I shall sit. And he sat down.
One reflects to oneself:
"For what reason am I sitting?
I shall lie down."
He then lies down.
In this way, he abandons coarse mental activities and cultivates subtle mental activities.
A bhikṣu, in this manner, abandons coarse mental activities and cultivates subtle mental activities.
When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and coarse mental activity arises, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
When he contemplates the Dharma and coarse mental activity does not arise, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon is either superior or non-superior and can give rise to coarse mental activity, a bhikṣu correctly grasps its characteristics, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it.
When the bhikṣu contemplates the phenomenon, subtle mental activity arises; he correctly grasps its characteristics, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it.
If one contemplates phenomena that do not give rise to subtle mental activity, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to give rise to subtle mental activity, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.
A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma to eliminate coarse mental activities, skillfully grasping the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflecting upon them, and skillfully understanding them.

Or, while contemplating the Dharma, he does not eliminate coarse mental activities, yet still skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.
If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is able to eliminate coarse mental formations, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena and knows that he is eliminating mental formations while exhaling and inhaling, he skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates phenomena that do not give rise to mental activity regarding the practice of exhaling and inhaling, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to give rise to mental activity regarding the practice of exhaling and inhaling, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, a mind arises that is aware of the mental formations of out-breathing and in-breathing; he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When he contemplates the Dharma, no such mind arises that is aware of the mental formations of out-breathing and in-breathing; yet he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If there are dharmas, whether superior or non-superior, that can give rise to the mental application of mindfulness of breathing—wherein one correctly apprehends the characteristics of dharmas, correctly contemplates them, and correctly understands them—a bhikṣu, by contemplating such dharmas, gives rise to coarse mental applications and does not contemplate other dharmas;
or if he does not give rise to [such] contemplation of dharmas, he approaches superior dharmas and does not approach non-superior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, subtle mental activities arise; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, such activities do not arise. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma to eliminate coarse mental activities; if he does not eliminate them, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, his mind gives rise to the practice of mindfulness of exhaling and inhaling; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, his mind does not give rise to it. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, giving rise to the mind that perceives the mindfulness of breathing out and in while contemplating the Dharma; or, if he does not give rise to such contemplation of the Dharma, he approaches superior dharmas and does not approach inferior dharmas.

The bhikṣu does not contemplate dharmas that should not be cultivated, but contemplates dharmas that should be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. With the mind’s purification, he breathes out and breathes in, and through the awareness of the mind’s purification while breathing out and breathing in, he attains joy. This is called training in the out-breath with the purification of mental formations and training in the in-breath with the purification of mental formations; thus ends the eight items.
What is meant by "training in the awareness of exhaling with a focused mind" and "training in the awareness of inhaling with a focused mind"?

By "mind" is meant the mind, intellect, and consciousness; the sixfold group of consciousnesses, and the sevenfold sphere of consciousness—this is called "mind. That mind possesses both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
For example, when a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and an unwholesome mind arises, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
When he contemplates the Dharma and no unwholesome mind arises, he likewise skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon, whether superior or non-superior, can give rise to an unwholesome mind, one should correctly grasp its characteristics, correctly contemplate it, and correctly understand it.
When a bhikṣu contemplates a phenomenon and gives rise to a wholesome mind, he should correctly grasp its characteristics, correctly contemplate it, and correctly understand it.
If one contemplates a phenomenon that does not give rise to a wholesome mind, yet skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it;

or if one contemplates a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—that can give rise to a wholesome mind, and skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while his mind is engaged with the out-breath and in-breath, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When he contemplates the Dharma without his mind being engaged with the out-breath and in-breath, he likewise skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of producing the mind that exhales and inhales, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
A bhikṣu, while contemplating phenomena, is aware of the mind that exhales and inhales, skillfully grasping their characteristics, skillfully contemplating them, and skillfully understanding them.

If one contemplates phenomena such that the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath does not arise in the mind, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to give rise to the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath in the mind, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, unwholesome thoughts arise; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, they do not arise. He should associate with superior dharmas and not associate with inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, wholesome thoughts arise; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, no such thoughts arise. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while generating the mental application of mindfulness toward the out-breath and in-breath, or when not generating it and thus not contemplating the Dharma, he should cultivate association with superior dharmas and avoid association with inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he is mindful of the arising of the mind and of the inhalation and exhalation while contemplating the Dharma; if they do not arise, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

The bhikṣu does not contemplate dharmas that should not be cultivated, but contemplates dharmas that should be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. As for the mind’s out-breath and in-breath, through the awareness of the mind’s out-breath and in-breath, he attains joy. This is called training in the awareness of the mind’s out-breath and training in the awareness of the mind’s in-breath; thus ends the nine matters.
What is meant by training in exhaling with a gladdened mind and training in inhaling with a gladdened mind?
"Gladdened mind" refers to gladness, profound gladness, and ultimate gladness; it is simply not joy (*prīti*), and this is called "gladness" (*saumanasya*).
When a bhikkhu contemplates the Dhamma and joy arises, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dhamma, skillfully reflects upon it, and skillfully understands it.
When he contemplates the Dhamma and joy does not arise, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dhamma, skillfully reflects upon it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon, whether superior or non-superior, can produce joy, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
When a bhikṣu contemplates a phenomenon and gives rise to a joyful mind, he skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If, when contemplating a phenomenon, joy does not arise in the mind, one should skillfully grasp its characteristics, skillfully contemplate it, and skillfully understand it.
If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is able to produce joy in the mind, one should skillfully grasp its characteristics, skillfully contemplate it, and skillfully understand it.

A bhikṣu, while contemplating the Dharma, breathes out and breathes in with a mind of joy, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflecting upon it, and skillfully understanding it;

or, while contemplating the Dharma, he breathes out and breathes in without a mind of joy, yet still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflects upon it, and skillfully understands it.

If, while breathing out and in with a mind gladdened by dharmas that are either superior or non-superior, this bhikṣu is well-grasping the characteristics of dharmas, well-reflecting, and well-understanding;
and if, while breathing out and in with a mind gladdened by reflecting on dharmas, he is aware of it, being well-grasping the characteristics of dharmas, well-reflecting, and well-understanding.

If, while contemplating phenomena that do not give rise to a joyful mind, one is aware of the out-breath and in-breath, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If, while contemplating phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—that can give rise to a joyful mind, one is aware of the out-breath and in-breath, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to joy; he contemplates the Dharma or, if it does not arise, he does not contemplate it. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while exhaling and inhaling, his mind gives rise to joy; if it does not arise, he should contemplate the Dharma. He should draw near to superior dharmas and not draw near to those that are not superior.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he is aware of the exhalation and inhalation that give rise to a joyful mind while contemplating the Dharma; if they do not arise, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

The bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. With a gladdened mind, he exhales and inhales, and through the awareness of exhaling and inhaling with a gladdened mind, he attains joy. This is called training in exhaling with a gladdened mind and training in inhaling with a gladdened mind. Thus ends the ten items.
What is meant by training in mindful exhalation and training in mindful inhalation?
"Concentration" (samādhi) refers to the mind abiding and dwelling rightly; this is called concentration.

For example, when a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to a concentrated mind, he correctly grasps the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), correctly contemplates them, and correctly understands them.
If one contemplates a phenomenon that does not produce a concentrated mind, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is able to produce a concentrated mind, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to a concentrated mind, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplating it, and skillfully understanding it.

Or, while contemplating the Dharma, he may not give rise to a concentrated mind, yet he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
If a phenomenon, whether superior or non-superior, can produce a concentrated mind, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena while producing a concentrated mind through exhalation and inhalation, he skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates phenomena that do not produce the concentrated mind of exhalation and inhalation, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena, whether superior or non-superior, can produce the concentrated mind of exhalation and inhalation, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to a concentrated mind, he is aware of the out-breath and in-breath, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplating it, and skillfully understanding it.

Even when he contemplates the Dharma and does not give rise to a concentrated mind, he is aware of the out-breath and in-breath, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully contemplating it, and skillfully understanding it.

If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of producing the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath of a concentrated mind, one should skillfully grasp its characteristics, skillfully contemplate it, and skillfully understand it.

A bhikṣu contemplates phenomena to produce a concentrated mind; whether he contemplates phenomena or does not contemplate them, he should associate with superior phenomena and not associate with non-superior phenomena.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while generating a concentrated mind and contemplating the inhalation and exhalation; if he does not generate [such a mind], he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he is mindful of the arising of a concentrated mind during exhalation and inhalation; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, he is not mindful of it. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he is aware of the arising of a concentrated mind and of the exhalation and inhalation while contemplating the Dharma; if it does not arise, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to those that are not superior. With a concentrated mind, he breathes out and breathes in, and through the awareness of breathing out and breathing in with a concentrated mind, he attains joy. This concludes the eleven matters concerning training in breathing out with a concentrated mind and training in breathing in with a concentrated mind.
What is meant by "training in exhaling with a liberated mind" and "training in inhaling with a liberated mind"?
Liberation means that the mind inclines toward that, honors that, leans toward that, and is liberated by means of that; this is called liberation.
For example, when a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to liberation, he correctly grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it.
Or, when contemplating the Dharma and not giving rise to a mind of liberation, he still correctly grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, correctly contemplates it, and correctly understands it.
If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of producing a mind of liberation, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.
When a bhikṣu contemplates a phenomenon and produces a mind of liberation, he skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If, when contemplating phenomena, one does not give rise to a mind of liberation, yet skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them;

or if, regarding phenomena that are either superior or non-superior, one can give rise to a mind of liberation, skillfully grasping their characteristics, skillfully contemplating them, and skillfully understanding them.

A bhikṣu, while contemplating the Dharma, breathes out and breathes in with a mind of liberation, skillfully grasping the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflecting upon it, and skillfully understanding it.

Or, while contemplating the Dharma, he breathes out and breathes in without a mind of liberation, yet still skillfully grasps the characteristics of the Dharma, skillfully reflects upon it, and skillfully understands it.

If, when focusing on phenomena that are either superior or non-superior, one generates a mind of liberation through exhalation and inhalation, skillfully grasping the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflecting, and skillfully understanding— then a bhikṣu,

while reflecting on phenomena and generating a mind of liberation through exhalation and inhalation, is aware of this, skillfully grasping the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflecting, and skillfully understanding.

If one contemplates phenomena and gives rise to the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath with a mind of liberation, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one gives rise to the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath with a mind of liberation regarding phenomena that are either superior or non-superior, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma so that the mind of liberation arises; he contemplates the Dharma when it does not arise, and does not contemplate the Dharma when there is no need for contemplation. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to those that are not superior.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma while exhaling and inhaling, his mind gives rise to liberation; if it does not arise, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he is mindful of the inhalation and exhalation as his mind attains liberation; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, he is not mindful of it. He draws near to the superior Dharma and does not draw near to that which is not superior.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. With a mind liberated, he exhales and inhales, and through the awareness of exhalation and inhalation with a liberated mind, he attains joy. This concludes the twelve matters concerning training in the exhalation and training in the inhalation of a liberated mind.
What is meant by training in the contemplation of impermanence while breathing out, and training in the contemplation of impermanence while breathing in?
What is meant by the perception of impermanence?
It is as when a bhikṣu, whether under a tree or in the open air, reflects in this way:
Form is impermanent; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are impermanent.
When a person of true reality forms a thought or recollective thought regarding this, it is called the perception of impermanence.
How does one contemplate it?
When a person of true reality observes, correctly observes, minutely observes, discriminates, understands, and penetrates, this is called "observation.
A bhikṣu contemplates phenomena and gives rise to the perception of impermanence; he skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If, when contemplating phenomena, one does not give rise to the perception of impermanence, yet skillfully grasps the characteristics of those phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them;

or if, whether the phenomena are superior or non-superior, one can give rise to the perception of impermanence, skillfully grasping their characteristics, skillfully contemplating them, and skillfully understanding them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates dharmas and gives rise to the perception of impermanence, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If, while contemplating dharmas, he does not give rise to the contemplation of impermanence, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of generating the contemplation of impermanence, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully reflects upon it, and skillfully understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena while generating the contemplation of impermanence regarding the out-breath and in-breath, he skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.

If, while contemplating phenomena, one does not give rise to the contemplation of impermanence regarding the out-breath and in-breath, yet skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them;

or if, whether the phenomena are superior or non-superior, one gives rise to the contemplation of impermanence regarding the out-breath and in-breath, skillfully grasping the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplating them, and skillfully understanding them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena and gives rise to the contemplation of impermanence regarding the awareness of exhaling and inhaling, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When he contemplates and does not give rise to the contemplation of impermanence regarding the awareness of exhaling and inhaling, he likewise skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one is able to generate the contemplation of impermanence regarding the out-breaths and in-breaths through superior or non-superior awareness, one will skillfully grasp the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), skillfully reflect, and skillfully understand.

When a bhikṣu reflects on phenomena and generates the perception of impermanence while reflecting on phenomena, yet does not generate the contemplation of impermanence or the reflection on phenomena, he draws near to superior phenomena and does not draw near to non-superior phenomena.
When a bhikṣu contemplates the arising of impermanence or does not contemplate it, he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the arising of impermanence while contemplating the out-breath and in-breath, or does not contemplate them and does not attend to those dharmas, he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to the contemplation of impermanence regarding the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation, he contemplates the Dharma; if it does not arise, he does not contemplate. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates that which is to be practiced and does not contemplate that which is not to be practiced; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. He observes impermanence while exhaling and inhaling; through observing impermanence while exhaling and inhaling, he becomes aware of and attains joy. This is called training in the observation of impermanence while exhaling and training in the observation of impermanence while inhaling; thus ends the thirteen matters.
What is meant by training in the observation of exhaling with dispassion and training in the observation of inhaling with dispassion?
What is meant by the perception of dispassion?
It is as when a bhikṣu, either under a tree or in the open air, reflects in this way:
If one perceives or recollects the exhaustion of craving, dispassion, nirvana, tranquility,
and the sublime excellence— as they truly are— this is called the perception of dispassion.
What is meant by "contemplation" (vipassanā)?
When a person of suchness contemplates, correctly contemplates, and minutely contemplates, discerning and penetrating [the truth], this is called contemplation.
A bhikkhu, reflecting on the Dharma, gives rise to the perception of nirvāṇa and detachment; he skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflects, and skillfully understands.
If, while contemplating phenomena, the thought of detachment does not arise, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.
If, while contemplating phenomena, the thought of detachment does not arise, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.
If a phenomenon, whether superior or non-superior, can give rise to the perception of detachment, one properly grasps its characteristics, properly contemplates it, and properly understands it.
When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena and gives rise to the contemplation of detachment, he properly grasps their characteristics, properly contemplates them, and properly understands them.
If one contemplates phenomena that do not give rise to the contemplation of detachment, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena—whether superior or non-superior—are able to give rise to the contemplation of detachment, one skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates dharmas and gives rise to the contemplation of exhalation and inhalation that leads to detachment, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When he contemplates dharmas and does not give rise to the contemplation of exhalation and inhalation that leads to detachment, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of producing the contemplation of the out-breath and in-breath that leads to dispassion, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

A bhikṣu, contemplating phenomena, gives rise to the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath through the contemplation of dispassion, skillfully grasping their characteristics, skillfully contemplating them, and skillfully understanding them.

If, while contemplating phenomena, one gives rise to the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath through the contemplation of dispassion (*vairāgya*), one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

Whether the phenomena are superior or non-superior, if they can give rise to the awareness of the out-breath and in-breath through the contemplation of dispassion, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, the thought of detachment arises; when he contemplates the Dharma and it does not arise, he does not contemplate that Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma that gives rise to the contemplation of detachment; he does not contemplate the Dharma that does not give rise to it. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to those that are not superior.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he gives rise to the contemplation of detachment regarding the out-breaths and in-breaths; if he does not give rise to it, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he gives rise to the contemplation of detachment and maintains awareness of the exhalation and inhalation while contemplating the Dharma; if it does not arise, he does not contemplate. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas; he observes the exhalation and inhalation with dispassion, and through observing the exhalation and inhalation with dispassion, he attains joy through clear comprehension. This concludes the fourteen matters concerning training in the observation of exhalation with dispassion and training in the observation of inhalation with dispassion.
What is meant by "training in the observation of exhaling and training in the observation of inhaling"?
What is meant by "the perception of cessation"?
It is as when a bhikṣu, either under a tree or in the open air, reflects in this way:
If one perceives the exhaustion of craving, nirvana, tranquility,
and the sublime as they truly are, whatever perception or mental recollection such a person has is called the "perception of cessation.
What is meant by "contemplation"?
When a person of true reality observes, observes correctly, observes minutely, and analyzes with discernment, this is called "observation.
A bhikṣu contemplates the perception of the arising and ceasing of phenomena; he skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.
If one contemplates the perception of non-arising and non-ceasing, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates the perception of arising and ceasing regarding phenomena that are either superior or non-superior, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.
A bhikṣu contemplates the arising and ceasing of phenomena, skillfully grasping their characteristics, skillfully reflecting upon them, and skillfully understanding them.
Or, he contemplates the non-arising and non-ceasing of phenomena, skillfully grasping their characteristics, skillfully reflecting upon them, and skillfully understanding them.

If a phenomenon is either superior or non-superior, one is able to generate the contemplation of arising and ceasing, skillfully grasping its characteristics, skillfully reflecting upon it, and skillfully understanding it.

A bhikṣu, while contemplating the arising and ceasing of phenomena during exhalation and inhalation, skillfully grasps their characteristics, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates the arising and ceasing of phenomena while observing the out-breath and in-breath, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.

If one contemplates the arising and ceasing of phenomena—whether those phenomena are superior or non-superior—while observing the out-breath and in-breath, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.

A bhikṣu contemplates the arising and ceasing of dharmas while being aware of the out-breath and in-breath, skillfully grasping the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully reflecting upon them, and skillfully understanding them.

Or, he contemplates the non-arising and non-ceasing of dharmas while being aware of the out-breath and in-breath, skillfully grasping the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully reflecting upon them, and skillfully understanding them.

If a phenomenon—whether superior or non-superior—is capable of producing the awareness of the observation of the out-breath and in-breath, one skillfully grasps its characteristics, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

A bhikṣu contemplates the phenomenon of the perception of arising and ceasing; whether he contemplates the phenomenon or does not contemplate it, he draws near to superior phenomena and does not draw near to non-superior phenomena.

A bhikṣu contemplates the arising and ceasing of phenomena; if he does not contemplate phenomena that do not arise, he does not contemplate them. He draws near to superior phenomena and does not draw near to inferior phenomena.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharma through the contemplation of the arising and ceasing of exhalations and inhalations; if he does not give rise to [such thoughts], he does not contemplate the dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas; he observes the cessation of exhalation and inhalation, and through observing the cessation of exhalation and inhalation, he attains joy through clear comprehension. This is called training in the observation of the cessation of exhalation and training in the observation of the cessation of inhalation. Thus ends the fifteenth section.
What is meant by training in the supramundane contemplation of exhaling and training in the supramundane contemplation of inhaling?
What is meant by the supramundane perception?
It is as when a bhikṣu, either under a tree or in the open air, reflects in this way:
The abandonment of all outflows, the extinction of craving, nirvana, tranquility, and the sublime excellence—
whatever perception or recollection a person of such reality has regarding these is called the supramundane perception.
What is contemplation?
When a person of reality contemplates, correctly contemplates, and minutely contemplates, analyzing, understanding, and piercing through [the truth], this is called contemplation.
A bhikṣu reflects upon the Dharma, giving rise to supramundane thoughts, skillfully grasping the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflecting, and skillfully understanding.
If, when contemplating dharmas, one does not give rise to supramundane thoughts, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If, whether the dharmas are superior or non-superior, one is able to give rise to supramundane thoughts, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of dharmas, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.
When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma and gives rise to supramundane insight, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.

If, while contemplating the Dharma, he does not give rise to supramundane insight regarding the out-breaths and in-breaths, he still skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully reflects upon them, and skillfully understands them.

If a phenomenon is either superior or non-superior, it can give rise to supramundane contemplation of the out-breath and in-breath; one skillfully grasps the characteristics of the phenomenon, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

When a bhikṣu contemplates phenomena and gives rise to supramundane contemplation of the out-breath and in-breath with full awareness, he skillfully grasps the characteristics of the phenomenon, skillfully contemplates it, and skillfully understands it.

If, when contemplating phenomena, one gives rise to supramundane observation of the out-breath and in-breath with clear comprehension, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

If phenomena, whether superior or non-superior, can give rise to supramundane observation of the out-breath and in-breath with clear comprehension, one skillfully grasps the characteristics of phenomena, skillfully contemplates them, and skillfully understands them.

When a bhikṣu contemplates dharmas, he gives rise to the thought of transcendence; if he does not give rise to it, he does not contemplate them. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, supramundane contemplation arises; when he does not contemplate the Dharma, it does not arise. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the arising of supramundane contemplation regarding the exhalation and inhalation, he contemplates the Dharma; if it does not arise, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to those that are not superior.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the Dharma, he gives rise to supramundane contemplation by being mindful of the exhalation and inhalation while contemplating the Dharma; if such contemplation does not arise, he does not contemplate the Dharma. He draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas.

A bhikṣu contemplates the dharmas that should be cultivated and does not contemplate those that should not be cultivated; he draws near to superior dharmas and does not draw near to inferior dharmas. Through supramundane contemplation of the out-breath and in-breath, and through the awareness gained from supramundane contemplation of the out-breath and in-breath, he attains joy. This is called training in the supramundane contemplation of the out-breath and training in the supramundane contemplation of the in-breath.
This is called the concentration on mindfulness of exhaling and inhaling.
What is meant by mindfulness of exhaling and inhaling?
Exhaling refers to the out-breath; inhaling refers to the in-breath.
Whether mindfulness takes the out-breath as its object or the in-breath as its object, it abides together with and ceases together with concentration.
If one binds the mind to the out-breath or binds the mind to the in-breath, the mind attains co-abiding; this is called the completion of the sixteen matters of mindfulness of breathing.
What is the perception of the impurity of the body?

It is when a bhikṣu contemplates his own body from the crown of the head to the feet, and from the feet to the crown of the head, seeing that everything down to the skin is impure—namely, bones, teeth, nails, hair; thin skin and thick skin; flesh, blood, sinews, and veins; the spleen, kidneys, heart, and lungs; feces, urine, mucus, saliva, pus, and blood; fat, marrow, brain, and membranes; tears, sweat, and bone marrow.
Just as a person with clear vision observes the various distinct grains in a granary— sesame, wheat, beans, and so forth—
so too does a bhikṣu observe his own body, from the crown of the head to the feet, as entirely impure.
If a person of suchness has a perception or a mental recollection, this is called the perception of impurity.

If one becomes concentrated on this perception, such that it arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with [the mind], this is called the concentration associated with the perception of impurity.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates bones, knows bones, understands bones, and accepts bones; and so on, up to contemplating tears and sweat, knowing tears and sweat, understanding tears and sweat, and accepting tears and sweat.
Whatever perception or mental recollection a person of such realization may have is called the "perception of the common impurity.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body composed of the four great elements: this body possesses the earth element, as well as the water, fire, and wind elements.
Just as a butcher or a butcher’s apprentice, having divided an ox into four quarters, sits or stands and contemplates these four parts;

so too does a bhikṣu contemplate this body composed of the four great elements—the earth element, the water, fire, and wind elements—observing how these various elements are mutually distinct. These elements within the body depend upon external elements; they are sustained by food and drink, yet they are frail, unsubstantial, and perishable from moment to moment, remaining for only a brief instant.
If a person of suchness forms a perception or recollection, this is called the "concentrated perception of universal impurity.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as entirely empty and universally empty, thoroughly knowing and practicing this through mindfulness.
Just as a bamboo thicket is entirely empty and altogether void,
so too does a bhikṣu contemplate the body as entirely empty and altogether void, through the practice of universal knowledge by means of mindfulness.
Whatever perceptions or recollections a person of such reality may have— even these are called the "concentrated perception of impurity."

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the body as like a festering ulcer. The body has nine openings for the discharge of fluids; all that flows out from them is impure discharge. It is the membrane of the womb, it is putrid, it is foul-smelling and filthy, it is a loathsome discharge: from the eyes flow the discharge of rheum, tears, pus, and blood; from the ears flow the discharge of earwax, pus, and blood; from the nose flow the discharge of mucus, saliva, pus, and blood; from the mouth flow the discharge of spittle, saliva, pus, and blood; and from the two lower orifices flow the discharge of excrement, urine, pus, and blood—just as when a person’s festering ulcer has been covered by a long-standing scab.
Thus, that which issues from these nine orifices of wounds and exudations is entirely impure exudation; it is the fetal membrane, it is putrid, it is foul and filthy, and it is a loathsome exudation.

Furthermore, as Mahākāśyapa has said: this body composed of the four great elements is characterized by decay and contradiction, a locus for secretions and outflows, an abode for manifold diseases, and a basis for manifold sufferings; one who cherishes this body is like one who cherishes a corpse, for its lifespan is brief.
If a person of such realization forms a perception or a mental recollection, this is called the "perception of the common impurity.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees a corpse discarded in a cemetery for one day up to three days, he contemplates his own body as having such a nature and such characteristics, not being exempt from this condition.
If a person of such a nature forms a perception or a mental recollection [of this], it is called the "perception of impurity shared with others.
Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees a corpse abandoned in a cemetery for one or two days, bloated and discolored blue-black;
One contemplates one's own body as having such qualities and such characteristics, not yet free from these dharmas.
Whatever perception or mental recollection a person of reality has, this is called the "concentrated perception of impurity."
Furthermore, a bhikṣu may see a corpse discarded in a cemetery for one to three days, being devoured by crows, birds, tigers, wolves, and various other beasts.
Observing one's own body as having such qualities and such characteristics, and not being free from these qualities—
whatever perception or mental recollection a person of reality (yathābhūta-pudgala) may have, even this is called the "concentrated perception of impurity" (aśubha-samādhi).
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees a corpse with its bones and joints still connected, bluish-red and festering, filled with impure pus and blood, foul-smelling, loathsome, and disgusting,
he contemplates his own body as having such a nature and such characteristics, not being apart from this condition.
If a person of such realization forms a perception or a mental recollection [of this], it is called the "perception of the common impurity.
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints are still connected, though the flesh and blood have already fallen away and only the tendons and veins remain unsevered.
Observing one's own body as having such qualities and such characteristics, and not being free from these qualities—
whatever perception or mental recollection a person of reality has therein, this is called the "concentrated perception of impurity."
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints have already fallen apart but have not yet left their original place,
he contemplates his own body as being of such a nature and such characteristics, and that it has not yet departed from this nature.
If a person of such reality forms a perception or a mental recollection [of this], it is called the "perception of the common impurity.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints have already disintegrated and moved from their original positions, with the feet, thighs, upper arms, hips, spine, ribs, hands, feet, shoulders, forearms, neck, and skull each lying in a different place.
Observing one's own body as having such qualities and such characteristics, and not being free from these qualities—
whatever perception or mental recollection a person of reality has therein, this is called the "concentrated perception of impurity" (aśubha-samjñā-samādhi).
Furthermore, when a bhikṣu sees a corpse whose bones and joints are old and weathered so that their color is white like a seashell, or blue like a pigeon, decayed and shattered;
he contemplates his own body as having such a nature and such characteristics, not being exempt from this law.
If a person of true realization forms a perception or recollection [of this], it is called the "concentrated perception of impurity.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates a skeleton in which the bones have swollen and become bluish-purple, with red, putrid parts falling away and scattering.
If a person of such realization forms a perception or recollection, this is called the "perception of impurity with its counterpart.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu knows the bones, understands the bones, and experiences the bones; he even contemplates their dissolution, knowing them as dissolved, understanding them as dissolved, and experiencing them as dissolved.
