If a person of true reality forms a perception or a mental recollection, this is called the "perception of the shared impurity" (*asubha-samādhi*).
What is meant by the perception of the shared impurity?

It is when a bhikṣu contemplates from the crown of the head to the feet, and from the feet to the crown of the head, that everything down to the skin is impure—namely, the bones, teeth, nails, hair, thin skin, thick skin, and even tears, sweat, marrow, and bone.
Just as a person with clear vision observes the various distinct grains in a granary— sesame, wheat, beans, and so forth—
so too does a bhikṣu observe his own body, from the crown of the head down to the feet, as entirely impure.
Whatever perception or mental recollection a person of such reality may have is called the perception of impurity.

Using this perception to subdue the mind, cultivating it until it becomes pliant and causing the concentrated mind to abide, is called the meditative absorption associated with the perception of impurity.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu contemplates the four great elements of the body, and even contemplates the bones, the joints of the bones, and the sensation of the bones; he even contemplates their dissolution, their dispersal, and the sensation of their dissolution and dispersal.
Whatever perception or mental recollection a person of suchness may have is called the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*).

By means of this perception, one subdues the mind and cultivates it until it becomes supple; having attained a concentrated mind that abides and dwells correctly, this is termed the meditative concentration on the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā-samādhi*).
What is meant by entering the fire concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*)?
It is as follows: a bhikṣu takes the internal fire element as fire, and takes the internal earth, water, and wind elements as fuel.

With the internal fire element and the internal earth, water, and wind elements, he contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; he contemplates flames, knows flames, understands flames, and experiences flames.
In this way, the bhikṣu observes with heedfulness, seeing the smoke and flames as a great mass of fire.
If, having cultivated this concentration, he perceives the smoke and flames as a great mass of fire, this is called entering the fire-concentration (tejodhātu-samādhi).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the internal fire element as the fire, and the external earth, water, and wind elements, along with grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, as the fuel.

With the internal fire element and the external earth, water, and wind elements, as well as the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, he contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; this is called entering the fire concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the internal fire element as the fire, and the external earth, water, and wind elements, along with grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, as the fuel.

With this internal fire element and these external earth, water, and wind elements, as well as the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, he contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; even this is called entering the fire-samādhi.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the external fire element as fire, and takes the internal earth, water, and wind elements as fuel.

With the external fire element and the internal earth, water, and wind elements, he contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; this is called entering the fire concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the external fire element as his fuel and the external earth, water, and wind elements, along with grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, as his kindling.

With this external fire element and these external earth, water, and wind elements, as well as the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, he contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; this is called entering the fire concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*).
Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the external fire element as his fire, and takes the internal and external earth, water, and wind elements, along with grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, as his fuel.

With the external fire element and the internal and external earth, water, and wind elements, as well as the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, he contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; this is called entering the fire samādhi.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the internal and external fire element as the fire, and takes the internal earth, water, and wind elements as the fuel.

With the internal and external fire element taken as the fire and the internal earth, water, and wind elements [as the fuel], he contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; this is called entering the fire-samādhi.
Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the internal fire element and the external earth, water, and wind elements as his fire; he takes the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves as his fuel.

With this internal fire element and these external earth, water, and wind elements—the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves—the bhikṣu contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; even this is called entering the fire-samādhi.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu takes the internal and external fire element as the fire; he takes the internal and external earth, water, and wind elements, as well as grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, as the fuel.

By means of the internal and external fire element and the internal and external earth, water, and wind elements, along with the grasses, trees, branches, and leaves, the bhikṣu contemplates smoke, knows smoke, understands smoke, and experiences smoke; even this is called entering the fire-samādhi.
What is the meditative concentration on the basis of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda-samādhi*) for common realization?

It is the meditative concentration on the basis of supernormal power achieved through the cultivation of the volitional formations of abandonment (*chanda-saṃskāra-udyoga-sampanna-ṛddhipāda*), as well as the meditative concentrations on the basis of supernormal power achieved through the volitional formations of abandonment of energy (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Through these, one experiences various supernormal powers: shaking the great earth; becoming many from being one and being one from being many; passing unhindered through mountains, walls, and barriers as if through open space; sitting cross-legged and traveling through the air like a bird; entering and emerging from the earth as if in water; walking upon water as if on land; emitting smoke and flames from the body like a great mass of fire; and touching the sun and moon with the hand, even attaining mastery of the body up to the Brahma-world.
What is the shaking of the earth?

It is as when a bhikṣu perceives a limited perception of earth and perceives an immeasurable perception of water; if he wishes to shake the earth, he shakes it, truly shakes it—just as he desires, according to his desire, and to the full extent of his desire.

It is like a wine merchant or a wine merchant’s apprentice who, having pressed the wine, throws the skin-sack into the great water; grasping the two corners with his hands, he lifts it up and drags it along at will, according to his desire, as he wishes, and to his heart's content.

In this way, a bhikṣu perceives a limited perception of earth and an immeasurable perception of water; if he wishes to move the earth, to shake it, or to cause it to shake thoroughly—just as he desires, according to his desire, and to the full extent of his desire—this is called the concentration on the shaking of the earth.
How does one become many from being one?

For example, when a bhikṣu has cultivated and extensively practiced meditative concentration, he gives rise to a mind within his own body to transform it into other physical bodies, complete with all limbs and members and with no deficiency in the sense faculties.
Just as a potter or a potter’s apprentice prepares well-kneaded clay to fashion various vessels, all of which he can successfully complete and thereby obtain profit;
so too does a bhikṣu, directing his mind toward his own body, transform it into another physical form, complete with all its limbs and joints and with no deficiency in its sense faculties.
He reflects thus:

"This emanated form-body produced from this four-element physical body is distinct from the four-element physical body; the emanated form-body is one thing, and the four-element physical body is another.
Within this four-element physical body, he gives rise to a mind that transforms it into another form-body, complete with all limbs and joints and with no deficiency in its sense faculties."
It is like a person taking a garment out of a chest and reflecting thus:
"This is the chest; this is the garment. The chest is one thing and the garment is another; it is because of the chest that the garment is taken out."
In this way, a bhikṣu contemplates this physical body composed of the four great elements and this emanated body:
the physical body composed of the four great elements is one thing, and the emanated body is another.

Within this physical body composed of the four great elements, one gives rise to a transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) to manifest other physical bodies, complete with all limbs and joints and lacking no sense faculties.

Whether manifesting two bodies, three bodies, or even up to a hundred or a thousand bodies, one manifests various bodies according to one's desire; this is called the meditative concentration of "making one into many."
What is meant by making the many into one?
It is as when a bhikṣu, having closely approached meditative concentration and practiced it extensively, transforms a manifold body through supernormal power and returns it to a single body.

Just as a person might scatter various kinds of grain seeds upon the ground and then gather them back into a single heap, so too does a bhikṣu, by means of his supernormal power (ṛddhi), manifest immeasurable bodies and then gather them back into a single body; this is called "making the many into one."
What is meant by "passing through without obstruction"?

It is as when a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, can pass through high mountains, walls, or barriers—whether near or far—without obstruction, as if moving through empty space.
"Near" refers to light that has reached the eye, which has not yet ceased or vanished, nor has it been removed or exhausted.
"Far" refers to light that has not reached the eye, does not appear before one, and has already ceased, vanished, been removed, or exhausted.
There are two kinds of mountains:
earthen mountains and rocky mountains; caves, sand, and stones—these are called mountains.
There are two kinds of walls: [brick walls and stone walls].
Wooden walls, earthen walls, whether near or far, high mountain walls— contemplate that all such high mountain walls are empty.
Just as a bhikṣu does not contemplate the mountains, the banks, thorny thickets, or the deep, perilous rivers of this earth, but contemplates only the equality of it all as being like the ground.
It is like stretching a cowhide over level ground and nailing it down so that there are no folds or wrinkles.

Because the bhikṣu observes thus with such heedfulness, he can pass through near and distant objects, high mountains, and walls without obstruction, as if moving through empty space; this is called the concentration of unobstructed penetration.
What is meant by sitting cross-legged and soaring through the air like a bird?

It is as when a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced meditative concentration, ascends into the empty space and sits cross-legged, traveling through the east, south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, just as a flying bird leaves the ground and reaches the sky.
In this way, because the bhikṣu observes with heedfulness, he sits cross-legged and travels through space like a bird; this is called the concentration of traveling through space.
What is meant by entering and exiting the earth as if emerging from and submerging in water?
Just as a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced meditative concentration, enters and exits the earth as if entering and emerging from water;
the bhikṣu contemplates earth as water, knows it as water, understands it as water, and accepts it as water.

In this way, because the bhikṣu observes with heedfulness, he enters and emerges from the earth as if it were water; this is called the meditative concentration of entering and emerging from the earth as if it were water.
What is meant by treading upon water as if it were earth?
Just as when a bhikṣu has closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, he walks upon water as if upon the earth;
the bhikṣu contemplates water as earth, knows it as earth, understands it as earth, and accepts it as earth.
Because a bhikṣu contemplates in this way with such heedfulness, he treads upon water as if it were solid ground; this is called the concentration of treading upon water as if it were solid ground.
How does his body emit smoke and flames like a great mass of fire?
Just as when a bhikṣu has closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, his body emits smoke and flames like a great mass of fire.
For this bhikṣu, the internal fire element becomes the fire, and the internal earth, water, and wind elements become the fuel.

By means of the internal fire element and the great elements of earth, water, and wind, one contemplates the emission of smoke, knowing the smoke, understanding the smoke, and experiencing the smoke; one contemplates the emission of flames, knowing the flames, understanding the flames, and experiencing the flames.

Because a bhikṣu contemplates in this way with such heedfulness, smoke and flames issue from his body like a great mass of fire; this is called the meditative concentration in which smoke and flames issue from the body like a great mass of fire.
How does one touch the majesty and power of the sun and moon with the hand?
It is like a bhikṣu who, having drawn near to meditative concentration and cultivated it extensively, touches the majesty and power of the sun and moon with his hand.

If a bhikṣu contemplates the sun and moon as being near, knows them to be near, understands them to be near, and perceives them as near, that bhikṣu, while staying on Jambudvīpa, would be able to stretch out his right hand and touch the sun and moon.

Furthermore, a bhikṣu generates a mind within his own body to transform it into another physical body, complete with all limbs and joints and lacking no sense faculties. With this transformation-body, he ascends to the realm of the Four Great Kings and touches the sun and moon with his hand. Again, with this physical body composed of the four great elements, he ascends to the realm of the Four Great Kings and touches the sun and moon with his hand. This is called the meditative concentration of touching the sun and moon with one's hand through their majestic power.
How does one attain mastery over the body up to the realm of Brahmā?
When a bhikṣu has closely approached meditative concentration and practiced it extensively, he attains mastery over the body up to the realm of Brahmā.

A bhikṣu, from his own body, gives rise to the mind to transform it into another physical body, complete with all limbs and joints and lacking no sense faculties. With this transformation-body, he goes to the Brahma Heaven to approach the Brahmā, dwelling together, sitting together, coming and going together, entering meditative absorption together, sharing knowledge and vision, and engaging in conversation. Furthermore, with this physical body composed of the four great elements, he flies to the Brahma Heaven to approach the Brahmā, dwelling together, sitting together, coming and going together, entering meditative absorption together, sharing knowledge and vision, and engaging in conversation. This is called the concentration of attaining mastery over bodies as far as the Brahma Heaven.

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration (samādhi), attains the concentration of fruition (vipāka-samādhi), then whether he has entered into concentration or not, he is able to perform various immeasurable supernormal powers (ṛddhi-pāda), such as shaking the earth up to the Brahma-world and attaining mastery over his body; this is called the concentration of supernormal power known through shared realization.
What is the concentration of the divine ear for shared realization?

It is when a bhikṣu, taking up the perception of the sound of wild reeds and rushes, withdraws his mind from the coarse sounds of the wild reeds and rushes and causes the mind to enter into the subtle sounds of the wild reeds and rushes.

By means of the subtle sounds of wild reeds and rushes, the bhikṣu harmonizes his mind and makes it supple, causing the mind to enter the realization of the divine ear-knowledge (*divya-śrotra-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*).
Through such heedful contemplation, he attains the shared realization of the divine ear and achieves a concentrated mind that abides in right dwelling.
Once the bhikṣu has attained concentration, he directs his mind toward human voices, wondering: "What are people discussing?
What are they saying? Thus observing with diligence, when the bhikṣu hears human voices, he hears everything that people discuss and say.

Just as when a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced meditative concentration, directs his mind toward the sounds of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, or devas—what do the devas discuss? What do they speak of?
When a bhikṣu observes with such heedfulness, he hears the voices of devas; he hears everything that is discussed and spoken.

When a bhikṣu has cultivated and frequently practiced meditative concentration, with the divine ear—purified and surpassing that of humans—he simultaneously hears two kinds of sounds: the voices of humans and non-humans.

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, attains the concentration of fruition, then whether he has entered into concentration or not, with his purified divine ear surpassing that of humans, he simultaneously hears two kinds of sounds:
the voices of humans and non-humans; this is called the divine-ear concentration of common realization.
What is the meditative concentration for the common realization of another’s mind?
It is when a bhikṣu takes up the characteristics of his own mind, considering: "By what cause does my mind arise? By what does it cease? What does it approach? What does it distance itself from?"
When a bhikṣu has thus grasped the characteristics of his own mind, he causes the mind to be directed toward the realization and knowledge of another's mind.
By observing with such heedfulness, the bhikṣu attains the concentration for the shared realization of another's mind; his mind abides and is rightly established.

Once a bhikṣu has attained meditative concentration, if he wishes to know what another person is thinking, what they are perceiving, and what they are contemplating, that bhikṣu, by observing with such heedfulness, is able to know the other's mind;
he knows it exactly as it is thought, as it is perceived, and as it is contemplated.

Suppose a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, desires to know the minds of beings in the hells, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts, and the heavens: what do they think, what do they perceive, and what do they contemplate?

When a bhikṣu observes with such heedfulness, he is able to know the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and devas; whatever is thought, whatever is perceived, and whatever is contemplated, he knows it all completely.
Just as a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced meditative concentration, is able to know the minds of others and other sentient beings:
he knows a mind with desire as it truly is—a mind with desire; he knows a mind without desire as it truly is—a mind without desire;
he knows a mind with hatred as it truly is—a mind with hatred; he knows a mind without hatred as it truly is—a mind without hatred.
When there is a deluded mind, he knows it as it truly is, "there is a deluded mind";
when there is no deluded mind, he knows it as it truly is, "there is no deluded mind.
He knows a sunken mind as it truly is, a scattered mind as it truly is, a limited mind as it truly is, an expansive mind as it truly is, an unconcentrated mind as it truly is.
He knows a concentrated mind as a concentrated mind, as it truly is; he knows an unconcentrated mind as an unconcentrated mind, as it truly is;
he knows a liberated mind as a liberated mind, as it truly is; he knows an unliberated mind as an unliberated mind, as it truly is; he knows a surpassable mind as a surpassable mind, as it truly is;
and he knows an unsurpassable mind as an unsurpassable mind, as it truly is.

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, attains the concentration of fruition (vipāka-samādhi), then whether he has entered that concentration or not, he is able to know the minds of others and other sentient beings. He knows a mind with desire as it truly is—a mind with desire; likewise, up to knowing a superior mind as it truly is—a superior mind, and a non-superior mind as it truly is—a non-superior mind. This is called the concentration of the shared realization of others' minds (paracitta-vijñāna-samādhi).
What is the meditative concentration for the common realization of past lives?
It is as follows: a bhikṣu contemplates the uninterrupted succession of the mind, wherein the subsequent mind and the preceding mind follow one another in continuous sequence.

By thus contemplating the uninterrupted succession of the mind, the bhikṣu attains the meditative concentration for the common realization of the uninterrupted succession of minds, abiding and dwelling correctly therein.
Once a bhikṣu has attained meditative concentration, he recollects one thought-moment, two thought-moments, three, four, five, ten, up to a hundred, a thousand, or even more.
Or, there may be the initial consciousness arising within a mother’s womb; the bhikṣu reflects thus:
"After which thought-moment has ceased does the initial consciousness arise in the mother’s womb?"
The bhikṣu causes the mind to incline toward the realization of past lives.
By observing with such heedfulness, the bhikṣu attains a concentrated mind that dwells rightly and remains established in the realization of past lives.
For a bhikṣu who has attained meditative concentration, mindfulness is not difficult to maintain.

He recalls his former births, his former existence, his former dwelling places, his former origins, and his former personal identity; whether it was at the point when he was about to end his life or after his mind had already ceased, he remembers receiving the initial consciousness within his mother’s womb.
If one cultivates this concentration, it is not difficult to recollect.
A bhikṣu reflects in this way: "What was my name in the past?
What was my clan? What was my birth? What was my food? What was my lifespan? What was my ultimate dwelling? And what suffering or pleasure did I experience?"

If a bhikṣu cultivates this concentration, he knows: "In the past, I had such a name, such a clan, such a birth, such food, such a lifespan, such a final dwelling, and such experiences of suffering and pleasure. This is called the concentration of recollecting past lives with shared realization.

Just as when a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, recollects one birth, two births, up to a hundred or a thousand births, or even beyond, or recalls having formerly dwelt in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva-deva).
Knowing that the immediate mind is obstructed because ordinary beings have not heard [this teaching], they say, "I was never there before; it has suddenly arisen of its own accord.

Because the noble ones have heard it, they thus contemplate their past lives and realize through the mind that there exists such a heaven—a dwelling place of form, non-perception, non-sensation, and no-mind.
A bhikṣu reflects thus: "If I recollect the forms of my past lives," the bhikṣu contemplates these uninterrupted forms,
wherein subsequent forms and preceding forms gradually become continuous.

When a bhikṣu contemplates the uninterrupted succession of forms in this way, he attains the concentration on the uninterrupted succession of past-life forms; his mind becomes settled and rightly established.
Once the bhikṣu has attained this concentration, it is not difficult for him to recollect [his past lives].
This is called the meditative concentration for the common realization of past lives.

For instance, when a bhikṣu has cultivated and frequently practiced the perception of concentration, he recollects one birth, two births, and so on, up to a hundred or a thousand births, or even more; or he may have previously dwelt in the formless heavens.
Because it is obstructed by uninterrupted matter and because ordinary persons have not heard [of it], they say, "I was never previously there; I have suddenly arisen of my own accord.

Because the noble ones have heard [of it], they thus contemplate their past lives through the evidence of matter: that there are such formless states, with perception, with sensation, or those belonging to the formless realm.
A bhikṣu reflects thus:
"If I recollect my past lives with the mind," the bhikṣu then contemplates the subsequent mind and the preceding mind, gradually and without interval.
When a bhikṣu thus contemplates with an uninterrupted mind, he attains a state of concentration that is continuous with his past-life consciousness, abiding and dwelling correctly therein.
Once the bhikṣu has attained this concentration, it is not difficult for him to recollect.
This is called the concentration of the recollection of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-samādhi*) which is commonly realized.
When a bhikṣu has cultivated and frequently practiced this concentration, he recollects various immeasurable past lives.

Whether he recollects one birth, two births, up to a hundred or a thousand births; whether it was during the formation of an eon (*vivarta-kalpa*), the destruction of an eon (*saṃvarta-kalpa*), or both the formation and destruction of an eon; he recollects: "I formerly existed there, with such a name, such a clan, and so forth, even experiencing such suffering and pleasure; when my life there ended, I was born there, and when my life there ended, I was born here."
In this attainment of practice, one recollects various and immeasurable past lives.

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration (*samādhi*), attains the concentration of fruition (*vipāka-samādhi*), then whether he has entered into concentration or not, he recollects various and immeasurable past lives, from a single birth up to this present attainment of practice; this is called the concentration of the knowledge of past lives shared with others (*sādhāraṇa-pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-samādhi*).
The Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra, Scroll Twenty-Nine.
