*Sūtra on the Stages of Meditation*, Part Two, Chapter on Concentration, Lower Section. What is the "concentration on the perception of light"?
It is as when a bhikṣu takes up various signs of light, namely: the light of fire, the light of the sun, moon, and stars, and the light of mani-jewels.

Having grasped the signs of light, whether under a tree or in the open air, one contemplates the light, knows the light, and experiences the light; whatever perception or mental recollection a person of true reality possesses in this regard is called the perception of light.
If this perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with that concentration, it is called the "concentration associated with clear perception" (*ālokasaṃjñā-samādhi*).

When a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced this concentration, dwells beneath a tree or in an open space, and with a pure mind, practices universal analytical application with a superior mind of clarity, whatever perception or mental recollection a person of true reality possesses is called "clear perception."
If this perception arises, abides, and ceases together with concentration, it is called the "concentration associated with clear perception" (*sāloka-samādhi*).

When a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced concentration, dwells beneath one tree, or two or three, or even up to ten trees, with a purified mind he attains a pervasive practice of clear and superior mental states; whatever perceptions or recollections such a person of true reality possesses, these are called "clear perceptions."
If this perception arises, abides, and ceases together with concentration, it is called the "perception of clarity accompanied by concentration.

When a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced concentration, perceives one, two, three, or even ten gardens with a pure mind, practicing universal comprehension and possessing a superior mind of clarity—just as a person of true realization forms perceptions and recollections—this is called the "perception of clarity."
If this perception arises, abides, and ceases together with concentration, it is called the "concentration associated with clear comprehension" (*sābhijñā-saṃjñāsamādhi*).

When a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced concentration, perceives one grove, two or three, or even up to ten groves with a pure mind, and through his pervasive analytical practice possesses a superior mind of clear comprehension—whatever perceptions or recollections such a person of true reality (*yathābhūta-pudgala*) may have, these are called "perceptions of clear comprehension."
If this perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with that concentration, it is called the "concentration associated with clear perception.

When a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced that concentration, perceives one village, two or three, or even up to ten villages with a pure mind, and through his pervasive understanding and practice possesses a superior mind of clear perception—such as the perceptions and recollections of a person who knows reality as it is—this is called "clear perception" (vidyā-saṃjñā).
If this perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with concentration, it is called the "concentration associated with clear comprehension" (*sābhijñā-samādhi*).

When a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced concentration, perceives one, two, three, or even ten gardens with a pure mind, and through his pervasive application of insight possesses a superior mind of clear comprehension—whatever perceptions or recollections such a person of true reality (*yathābhūta-pudgala*) may have, these are called "clear comprehension perceptions."

If this perception arises together with, abides together with, and ceases together with that concentration, it is called the "concentration associated with clear knowledge" (*sābhijñā-saṃjñāsamādhi*).

When a bhikṣu, having cultivated and frequently practiced this concentration, surveys the waters and the land on all sides with a pure mind, and through his pervasive understanding and practice possesses a superior mind of clear knowledge—whatever perceptions or recollections such a person of true reality (*yathābhūta-pudgala*) may have, these are called "perceptions of clear knowledge."
If one becomes concentrated on this perception such that it arises, abides, and ceases together with it, this is called the concentration on the perception of light.

For example, when a bhikṣu has become concentrated through close proximity and extensive cultivation, he sees with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, the birth and death of sentient beings—their beautiful and ugly forms, their good and bad destinations, and their lowly or exalted states.

He knows that sentient beings create karma: these sentient beings have accomplished evil conduct of body, speech, and mind; they have reviled the noble ones, held wrong views, and performed actions based on wrong views; thus, at the breaking up of the body after death, they fall into hell, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts.

These sentient beings have accomplished virtuous conduct of body, speech, and mind; they do not slander the noble ones, possess right view, and perform right actions of body; at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn among gods or humans.

Thus, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees beings passing away and being reborn—whether they are of beautiful or ugly appearance, and whether they are in good or evil destinations—and he knows the karma created by those beings.

Having cultivated this meditative concentration, one perceives with the divine eye—purified and surpassing that of humans—the birth and death of sentient beings, even to the point of knowing the karma they have created; this is called the "concentrated perception of shared luminosity."

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, attains the certainty of its fruition, then whether he has entered into concentration or not, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, he sees the birth and death of sentient beings and even knows the karma performed by those beings; this is called the "concentrated perception of shared clarity."
What is meant by the "uninterrupted concentration" (*ānantarya-samādhi*)?
A bhikṣu contemplates impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the tranquility of nirvāṇa, thereby attaining a concentrated mind that abides in stillness.

Having attained this concentration, he attains the first noble five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*). Because he has attained these first noble five faculties, he enters the supreme certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and leaves the stage of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*). It is impossible for him to die prematurely in the interim without having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*).
If one who has not yet attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) were to fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, such a thing is impossible.

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated this concentration, attains the "uninterrupted" concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*) directed toward the fruit of stream-entry, and upon the immediate cessation of this concentration attains the fruit of stream-entry, this is called "uninterrupted concentration."

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated meditative concentration, attains the concentration of immediate succession directed toward the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, and upon the immediate cessation of this concentration attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, this is called the concentration of immediate succession.

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated this concentration, attains the concentration of immediate succession directed toward the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), and upon the immediate cessation of this concentration attains the fruit of non-returning, this is called the concentration of immediate succession.

If a bhikṣu, having closely approached and extensively cultivated a concentration, attains the concentration of immediate succession directed toward the fruit of arhatship, and upon the immediate cessation of this concentration attains the fruit of arhatship, this is called the concentration of immediate succession.
What is the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*)?
When a trainee (*śaikṣa*), free from afflictions, enters the noble path with a noble mind, and possesses firm faith and firm dharma—this is called the faculty of concentration.
What is the faculty of concentration?

A practitioner who has abandoned the afflictions and whose noble mind enters the noble path—whether it be one possessing firm faith and firm Dharma, or others in the various realms of existence—who perceives the faults of conditioned formations, contemplates the tranquility of Nirvāṇa, and as a real person contemplates suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; desiring what has not yet been attained, desiring what has not yet been understood, and desiring what has not yet been realized, they cultivate the path to abandon the afflictions.

One sees those in training—whether stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners—who are fully endowed with the wisdom of contemplation; whether they abide on the plane of wisdom, or have liberated their minds through contemplation, or have attained the four fruits of asceticism: the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, or the fruit of non-returning.

An Arahant who is beyond training, desiring to attain the noble qualities not yet attained, is fully endowed with the wisdom of the path of cultivation; whether it be the stage of knowledge or the mind liberated through insight, he has already attained the fruit of Arahantship.

A person who acts according to reality, a person who proceeds toward reality, whose mind abides, is rightly established, is concentrated, and dwells upon its object; whose mind is unified and at ease, neither distracted nor abandoning it.

The mind relying on the intellect, the mind dwelling in solitude, concentration, the awakening factor of concentration, and right concentration—these are called the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*).
What is the power of concentration (*samādhibala*)?
The faculty of concentration is called the power of concentration.
What is the awakening factor of concentration?
The power of concentration is called the awakening factor of concentration.
What is right concentration?
If concentration is wholesome, compliant, and non-opposing, it is called right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*).
What is wrong concentration?
If concentration is unwholesome, non-compliant, and opposing, it is called wrong concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*).
What is noble concentration?
If concentration is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called noble concentration.
What is non-noble concentration?
If a concentration is with outflows, it is called non-noble concentration.
What is concentration with outflows?
If a concentration is defiled, it is called concentration with outflows.
What is untainted concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is free from defilement, it is called untainted concentration.
What is tainted concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*)?
If there is seeking within concentration, it is called "concentration with defilement.
What is "concentration without defilement"?
If there is no seeking within concentration, it is called "concentration without defilement."
What is concentration with seeking?
If concentration is to be grasped, it is called concentration with seeking.
What is concentration without seeking?
If concentration is not subject to grasping, it is called "concentration without seeking.
What is concentration subject to grasping?
If concentration involves grasping, it is called "concentration subject to grasping."
What is concentration that is not to be grasped?
If a concentration is without grasping, it is called concentration that is not to be grasped.
What is concentration with grasping?
If a concentration has something superior to it, it is called "concentration with grasping.
What is "concentration without grasping"?
If a concentration has nothing superior to it, it is called "concentration without grasping."
What is superior concentration?
If a concentration involves grasping, it is called superior concentration.
What is non-superior concentration?
If a meditative concentration does not surpass others, it is called "unexcelled concentration" (*anuttara-samādhi*).
Furthermore, if a concentration has other concentrations that surpass it in excellence and subtlety, it is called "surpassable concentration" (*sottara-samādhi*);
if a concentration has no other concentrations that surpass it in excellence and subtlety, it is called "unexcelled concentration."

Furthermore, if one has cultivated meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the Tathāgata attains unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena. By virtue of his power, supremacy, and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata achieves the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the four fearlessnesses (*catur-vaiśāradya*); through great loving-kindness and great compassion, he turns the wheel of Dharma and achieves mastery. Apart from this concentration, any other concentration is called "concentration with superior qualities" (*viśeṣa-samādhi*).
If the aforementioned concentration is eliminated, it is called "unexcelled concentration" (anuttara-samādhi).
What is "concentration of experience" (vedita-samādhi)?
If the concentration is internal, it is called "concentration of experience."
What is non-attained concentration?
If a concentration is external, it is called non-attained concentration.
What is internal concentration?
If concentration is associated with feeling, it is called internal concentration.
What is external concentration?
If concentration is not associated with feeling, it is called external concentration.
What is concentration with fixed retribution?
If a concentration is of a nature that entails retribution, it is called concentration with fixed retribution.
What is concentration without retribution?
If a concentration is either a result of maturation (*vipāka*) or neither a result nor a dharma subject to maturation, it is called "concentration without maturation" (*avipāka-samādhi*).
What is "concentration shared with ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana-sādhāraṇa-samādhi*)?

If a concentration is not entered into or emerged from by ordinary persons, yet is entered into and emerged from by ordinary persons as well, it is called "concentration shared with ordinary persons."
What is the concentration not shared with ordinary persons?
If a concentration is neither entered into nor emerged from by ordinary persons, it is called the concentration not shared with ordinary persons.
What is the concentration shared with those who are not ordinary persons?
If a concentration is entered into and emerged from by both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and non-ordinary persons, it is called a concentration shared with non-ordinary persons.
What is a concentration not shared with non-ordinary persons?

If a concentration is entered and exited by ordinary persons but not entered or exited by those who are not ordinary persons, it is called the "concentration not shared with those who are not ordinary persons.
What is the "concentration shared with śrāvakas"?
If a concentration is entered and emerged by both non-śrāvakas and śrāvakas, it is called a concentration shared with śrāvakas.
What is a concentration not shared with śrāvakas?
If a concentration is entered and emerged by non-śrāvakas but not entered or emerged by śrāvakas, it is called a concentration not shared with śrāvakas.
What is the concentration not shared with śrāvakas?
If a concentration that śrāvakas enter and emerge from is also entered and emerged from by those who are not śrāvakas, this is called the concentration not shared with śrāvakas.
What is the concentration not shared with śrāvakas?
If a concentration is such that śrāvakas enter and emerge from it, while non-śrāvakas do not enter or emerge from it, this is called the concentration not shared with śrāvakas.
What is the lightning-like concentration (*vidyut-sama-samādhi*)?
If a concentration abides for only a very brief duration—just as lightning abides for only a very brief duration—the concentration is likewise; this is called the lightning-like concentration.
What is the vajra-like concentration?

If a concentration dwells immeasurably, dwelling for immeasurable time, just as a vajra dwells immeasurably, dwelling for immeasurable time, so too is this concentration; this is called the vajra-like concentration.
Furthermore, if one has cultivated meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the portions of afflictions (*kleśa*) gradually diminish.

Just as lightning emerging from the clouds illuminates a small portion of darkness and then quickly vanishes, so too is this concentration; it is called "concentration like lightning" (*vidyut-sama-samādhi*).

If one has cultivated concentration such that all afflictions—whether coarse or subtle—are severed and extinguished without exception, it is like throwing a diamond at pearls and stones, which it destroys and shatters without fail;
concentration is likewise, and this is called the "diamond-like concentration" (vajropama-samādhi).
Furthermore, if one cultivates concentration and attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, or *anāgāmin*, this is called "concentration like lightning.
If one cultivates concentration and attains the fruit of *arhat*, this is called "concentration like a diamond (*vajra*)."

Furthermore, if one cultivates concentration to attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) up to the fruit of an arhat or the path of a pratyekabuddha, this is called the "concentration like lightning.

If one cultivates concentration such that one attains unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding all phenomena—by virtue of the power of supreme and unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; if the Tathāgata accomplishes the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, turns the wheel of Dharma with great kindness and great compassion, and achieves mastery—this is called the "diamond-like concentration" (*vajropama-samādhi*).
What is "attaining concentration through non-attainment"?
If one has attained concentration that is non-attained, difficult to attain, and difficult to maintain, this is called "attaining concentration through non-attainment.
What is "attaining concentration through attainment"?
If a concentration is attained with certainty, is definitely attained, is not difficult to attain, and is easy to maintain, this is called "concentration that is attained with certainty.
What is concentration that is difficult to maintain through application?

It is a concentration that is attained without certainty, is difficult to attain, and difficult to maintain; it lacks the power of mastery and sovereignty, does not accord with one's wishes, does not follow one's wishes, and does not fulfill one's wishes, such that there is difficulty in entering and emerging from it through application.
Just as a boat going against the current is difficult to move, so too is concentration; this is called "concentration that is difficult to maintain through effort" (*sasaṃkāra-duḥkhilā samādhi*).
What is "concentration that is easy to maintain without effort" (*asaṃkāra-sukhilā samādhi*)?

It is when concentration is attained—attained with certainty, not with difficulty, but easily—by means of power, mastery, and sovereignty, according to one's wish, in accordance with one's wish, and to the full extent of one's wish, entering and emerging from it without effort.
Just as a boat travels easily with the current, so too is concentration; this is called "concentration that is effortless and easy to maintain.
What is "one-sided cultivation of concentration"?
If, having cultivated concentration, one perceives light but does not see forms, or sees forms but does not perceive light, this is called "one-sided cultivation of concentration."
What is the cultivation of concentration with two factors?
If, having cultivated concentration, one perceives light and also sees forms, this is called the cultivation of concentration with two factors.

Furthermore, if, having cultivated concentration, one gives rise to knowledge but does not sever the afflictions, or if one severs the afflictions but does not give rise to knowledge, this is called the cultivation of concentration with one factor.
If, having cultivated concentration, knowledge arises and one is able to sever the afflictions, this is called the twofold cultivation of concentration.

Furthermore, if, having cultivated concentration, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises but not the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), this is called the singlefold cultivation of concentration.

If, having cultivated concentration, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) arise, this is called the cultivation of concentration with two parts.
What is concentration with an object?
If concentration possesses an objective referent, it is called concentration with an object.
What is the attainment of non-perception?
If an attainment is without objective referents, it is called the attainment of non-perception.
Furthermore, excluding the attainment of non-perception and the attainment of cessation, any other attainment is called the attainment with perception.
If one is in the attainment of non-conception or the attainment of cessation, this is called the attainment of non-conception.
What is the attainment according to the object (*yathābhūta-samādhi*)?

If a phenomenon is in accordance with its reality, its characteristics, its intrinsic nature, its arising in dependence on conditions, and its entering and exiting according to its marks, this is called the attainment according to the object.
What is the perception of recollection (saṃjñā-vitarka)?

If a phenomenon is according to its characteristic, its appearance, its intrinsic nature, and its arising in dependence on conditions; whether it enters or exits in accordance with its characteristic or not in accordance with its characteristic—this is called the perception of recollection.
What is the meditative absorption of the departure from the perception of form?

If one enters absorption having departed from the perception of form, or if one enters absorption while departing from the perception of form, this is called the meditative absorption of the departure from the perception of form.
What is the meditative absorption of the non-departure from the perception of form?

If one enters meditative absorption without being free from the perception of form, or if one enters meditative absorption while not being free from the perception of form, this is called the concentration that is not free from the perception of form (*arūpa-saṃjñā-vigata-samādhi*).
Furthermore, if the concentration belongs to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is called the concentration that is free from the perception of form (*rūpa-vigata-samādhi*).
If one is concentrated in the form realm and the noble states, this is called the concentration of non-separation from form.
What is the concentration of the spheres of mastery?
If one is concentrated in the eight spheres of mastery, this is called the concentration of the spheres of mastery.
What is the concentration of the universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*)?
If there are the ten universal bases, these are called the concentration of the universal bases.
What is the concentration with applied thought (*savitarka*)?

If a concentration is associated with applied thought (*vitarka*), arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called concentration with applied thought (*savitarka-samādhi*).
What is concentration without applied thought (*avitarka-samādhi*)?

If a concentration is not associated with applied thought, not arising together with it, not abiding together with it, and not ceasing together with it, this is called concentration without applied thought.
What is concentration with investigation (*savitarka-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is associated with investigation, arising together with it, abiding together with it, and ceasing together with it, this is called concentration with investigation.
What is concentration without investigation (*avitarka-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is not associated with insight (*vipaśyanā*), and does not arise, abide, or cease together with insight, it is called concentration without insight.
What is concentration with joy (*prīti*)?
If a concentration is associated with joy, arising together with joy, abiding together with joy, and ceasing together with joy, this is called concentration with joy.
What is concentration without joy?
If a concentration is not associated with joy, not arising together with joy, not abiding together with joy, and not ceasing together with joy, this is called concentration without joy.
What is concentration associated with relishing (*āsvādana-samādhi*)?
If concentration is associated with defilement (*kliṣṭa*), it is called concentration associated with relishing.
What is concentration associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is called concentration associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is concentration associated with patience (*kṣānti*)?
If a concentration arises, abides, and ceases together with patience, it is called concentration associated with patience.
What is concentration not associated with patience (*kṣānti*)?
If a concentration does not arise, abide, or cease together with patience, it is called concentration not associated with patience.
What is concentration associated with knowledge (*jñāna*)?
If concentration arises, abides, and ceases together with knowledge, it is called concentration associated with knowledge.
What is concentration not associated with knowledge?
If concentration does not arise, abide, and cease together with knowledge, it is called concentration not associated with knowledge.
What is the concentration that begins with patience (*kṣānti*)?
If it is a concentration that is noble and untainted (*anāsrava*), cultivated by those with firm faith and firm Dharma, this is called the concentration that begins with patience.
What is the concentration that begins with knowledge (*jñāna*)?
If a concentration is cultivated by one who possesses the noble, untainted vision of the path of seeing, it is called the "concentration at the beginning of knowledge.
What is the "concentration at the end of desire"?
If a concentration is associated with the final consciousness, it is called the "concentration at the end of desire."
What is the concentration of initial arising?
If a concentration is associated with the first consciousness, it is called the concentration of initial arising.
What is wholesome concentration?
If concentration is cultivated, it is called wholesome concentration.
What is unwholesome concentration?
If concentration is abandoned, it is called unwholesome concentration.
What is indeterminate concentration?
If a concentration experiences that which is neither retribution nor a dharma subject to retribution, this is called indeterminate concentration.
What is the concentration of one in training (śaikṣa)?
If a concentration is noble but not that of one beyond training, it is called the concentration of one in training (*śaikṣa-samādhi*).
What is the concentration of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is noble but not that of one in training, it is called the concentration of one beyond training.
What is concentration that is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner?
If a concentration is not noble (*ārya*), it is called concentration that is neither of the learner nor of the non-learner.
What is retributive concentration?
If it is determinate in its maturation or determinate in its wholesome retribution, this is called "determinate in retribution" (*vipāka-niyata*).
What is "determinate in retribution and stage" (*vipāka-bhūmi-niyata*)?
If it is determinate in having retribution, this is called "determinate in retribution and stage."
What is the state of concentration that is neither resultant nor productive of result?
If a concentration is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and not included within one’s own continuum, this is called the state of concentration that is neither resultant nor productive of result.
What is the state of concentration abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*)?
If a concentration is unwholesome and is not abandoned by insight, it is called a concentration abandoned by insight.
What is a concentration abandoned by cultivation?
If a concentration is unwholesome and is not abandoned by insight, it is called a concentration abandoned by cultivation.
What is concentration that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation?
If a concentration is wholesome or indeterminate and is not [abandoned by either], it is called concentration that is neither abandoned by vision nor abandoned by cultivation.
What is concentration whose cause is abandoned by vision?
If a concentration is abandoned through vision, or is the retribution of a dharma abandoned through vision, this is called "concentration whose cause is abandoned through vision.
What is "concentration whose cause is abandoned through cultivation"?
If a concentration is abandoned through cultivation, or is the retribution of a dharma abandoned through cultivation, this is called "concentration whose cause is abandoned through cultivation."
What is concentration that has neither the faculty of view nor the faculty of cultivation as its cause?

If it is wholesome concentration, or the fruition of wholesome dharmas, or that which is neither fruition nor a dharma leading to fruition, this is called concentration that has neither the faculty of view nor the faculty of cultivation as its cause.
What is inferior concentration?
If concentration is unwholesome, it is called inferior concentration.
What is middling concentration?
If concentration is indeterminate, it is called intermediate concentration.
What is superior concentration?
If concentration is wholesome, it is called superior concentration.
Furthermore, if concentration is unwholesome or indeterminate, it is called inferior concentration.
If concentration is non-noble and wholesome, it is called middling concentration.
If concentration is noble and untainted, it is called superior concentration.
What is coarse concentration?
If concentration is bound to the desire realm, it is called coarse concentration.
What is subtle concentration?
If concentration is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or is unbound, it is called subtle concentration (*sūkṣma-samādhi*).
What is minute concentration (*aṇu-samādhi*)?
If concentration is bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is called minute concentration.
Furthermore, if a concentration is bound to the desire realm or bound to the form realm, it is called coarse concentration.
If a concentration is bound to the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, or is unbound, it is called subtle concentration.
If concentration is bound to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is called subtle concentration.

Furthermore, if concentration is bound to the desire realm, the form realm, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, it is called coarse concentration.
If concentration is unconditioned by the realms of existence, it is called subtle concentration (*sūkṣma-samādhi*).
If concentration is conditioned by the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is called minute concentration (*aṇu-samādhi*).

As for concentration with directed thought and evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra*), concentration without directed thought but with evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra*), concentration without directed thought and without evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra*), and the concentrations of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), they are explained in detail within the Threefold Path of the Section on the Wings of Enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya*).
What are the three aspirations through which concentration is attained?
They are: concentration attained through the aspiration for results, concentration attained through the aspiration itself, and concentration attained through the aspiration for tranquility.
If a bhikṣu attains one or two concentrations—whether it be the concentration of emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness—the bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"I should personally approach and cultivate this concentration extensively, for I desire to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Thus, a bhikṣu approaches and cultivates concentration extensively, desiring to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.

A bhikṣu closely approaches and trains in concentration with the aspiration to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. If he attains concentration in this manner, it is called "concentration attained through the fruit of aspiration.
If a bhikṣu practices with diligence—whether there is desire or lack of desire, or progress or lack of progress—the bhikṣu reflects in this way:
"I should cultivate this desire and energy, drawing near to them and practicing them extensively.
A bhikṣu who draws near to and practices desire and energy extensively should be diligent, energetic, and concentrated in mind.
If one attains concentration in this manner, it is called "concentration attained through aspiration.
If a bhikṣu attains one or two concentrations that are difficult to attain and difficult to maintain, the bhikṣu reflects thus:
"I should draw near to and cultivate this concentration extensively, so that I may obtain mastery, power, and sovereignty over it."
If a bhikṣu closely approaches meditative concentration and practices it extensively, thinking, "May I obtain power, honor,
and sovereignty through this," and thus attains concentration, this is called attaining concentration with an unpacified aspiration.
These are called the three types of concentration attained through aspiration.
What are the concentrations not attained through aspiration?
They are: concentration attained without obtaining the fruit, concentration not attained through aspiration, and concentration not attained through the aspiration for tranquility.
If a bhikṣu attains one or two concentrations—whether the concentration of emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness—the bhikṣu does not reflect thus:
"I should draw near to and cultivate this concentration extensively," because he does not desire to attain the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
It is because a bhikṣu who closely approaches and frequently cultivates concentration does not aspire merely for the sake of attaining the fruits of śrāmaṇya;
rather, having closely approached and frequently cultivated concentration, the bhikṣu attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
If one attains concentration in this manner, it is called "attaining concentration through non-wishing for its fruit.
If a bhikṣu practices with diligence, whether there is desire or lack of desire, or effort or lack of effort, the bhikṣu does not reflect in this way:
"I should cultivate desire and effort, and approach them with frequent practice and study."
If a bhikṣu desires and exerts himself to cultivate and frequently practice [this], he should be diligent in concentration and mental focus.
If he thus attains concentration, this is called "attaining concentration without aspiration."
If a bhikṣu has recently attained one or two concentrations that are unstable, difficult to attain, and difficult to maintain, he should not think:
"I should not cultivate this concentration extensively; let me instead attain concentration through power, honor, and mastery."
If a bhikṣu closely approaches meditative concentration and practices it extensively, thinking,
"May I attain concentration through the power of my mastery," and thus attains concentration in this manner, it is called attaining concentration with an unpeaceful aspiration.
This is called concentration attained without the three aspirations.
What is the concentration of observing the internal body within the internal body?

If a bhikṣu observes all internal material forms comprised of the four great elements, or even those internal material forms comprised of the four great elements in a single location, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and remains rightly established—this is called the concentration of observing the internal body within the internal body.
What is the concentration on observing the external body?

If a bhikṣu, regarding all external material bodies comprised of the four great elements, or a single portion of external material bodies comprised of the four great elements, observes them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells rightly—this is called the concentration on observing the external body.
What is the concentration of observing the internal and external body by observing the internal and external body?

If a bhikṣu, regarding all internal and external material bodies comprised of the four great elements, or a single instance of an internal or external material body comprised of the four great elements, contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, thereby attaining concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established—this is called the concentration of observing the internal and external body by observing the internal and external body.
What is the concentration on observing internal feelings within internal feelings?

If a bhikṣu observes all internal feelings, or internal feelings in a single location, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells correctly, this is called the concentration on observing internal feelings within internal feelings.
What is the concentration on observing external feelings by observing external feelings?

If a bhikṣu observes all external feelings, or external feelings in a single location, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells correctly, this is called the concentration on observing external feelings by observing external feelings.
What is the concentration on the contemplation of internal and external feelings?

If a bhikṣu contemplates all internal and external feelings, or internal and external feelings in a single location, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and is rightly established, this is called the concentration on the contemplation of internal and external feelings.
What is the concentration of observing the internal mind with the internal mind?

If a bhikṣu observes all internal minds, or a portion of the internal mind, as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and remains rightly established, this is called the concentration of observing the internal mind with the internal mind.
What is the concentration of observing the external mind with respect to the external mind?

If a bhikṣu, regarding all external minds or a certain portion of external minds, observes them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains concentration such that the mind abides and dwells rightly—this is called the concentration of observing the external mind with respect to the external mind.
What is the concentration of observing the internal and external mind with respect to the internal and external mind?

If a bhikṣu, regarding all internal and external minds, or a single instance of internal and external mind, observes them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, and thereby attains a concentrated mind that abides and remains rightly established—this is called the concentration of observing the internal and external mind with respect to the internal and external mind.
What is the concentration on internal phenomena by observing internal phenomena?

If a bhikṣu, setting aside the phenomena comprised within the physical body of the four great elements, observes all other internal phenomena—whether the entirety of them or a single portion of them, such as feeling and mind—as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, thereby attaining a concentrated mind that abides and dwells correctly; this is called the concentration on internal phenomena by observing internal phenomena.
What is the concentration on external phenomena through the contemplation of external phenomena?

If a bhikṣu, setting aside the phenomena comprised by the physical body of the four great elements, contemplates all other external phenomena—whether the remaining aggregates of sensation, mind, and formations, or any single instance of an external phenomenon—as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, thereby attaining a concentrated mind that abides and dwells correctly; this is called the concentration on external phenomena through the contemplation of external phenomena.
What is the concentration on internal and external phenomena through the contemplation of internal and external phenomena?

If a bhikṣu, setting aside the phenomena comprised by the physical body of the four great elements, contemplates all other internal and external phenomena—whether they be feelings, the mind, or any remaining internal and external phenomena in a single location—as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, thereby attaining a concentrated mind that abides and dwells correctly, this is called the concentration on internal and external phenomena through the contemplation of internal and external phenomena.
What is concentration on internal objects?
If concentration arises through contemplating internal phenomena, this is called concentration on internal objects.
What is concentration on external objects?
If concentration arises from contemplating external phenomena, this is called concentration on external objects.
What is concentration on both internal and external objects?
If concentration arises from contemplating both internal and external phenomena, this is called concentration on both internal and external objects.
What is the concentration on the sphere of sentient beings?
There is no such thing as a concentration on the sphere of sentient beings.

Furthermore, if one contemplates sentient beings with thoughts of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, and thereby gives rise to concentration, this is called the concentration on the sphere of sentient beings.
What is concentration with form as its object?
When concentration arises through contemplating phenomena of form, this is called concentration with form as its object.
What is concentration without form as its object?
If concentration arises through contemplation of formless phenomena, this is called concentration with the formless as its object.
What is concentration with sentient beings as its object?
It is as explained above.
What is concentration on conditioned objects?
If one contemplates conditioned phenomena and concentration arises, this is called concentration on conditioned objects.
What is concentration on unconditioned objects?
If concentration arises through contemplation of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), this is called concentration on the object of the unconditioned.
What is concentration on the object of sentient beings?
It is as explained above.
What is concentration with a dharma-object?
If concentration arises through contemplation of dharmas, this is called concentration with a dharma-object.
What is concentration without an object?
There is no concentration without an object.
Furthermore, if concentration arises when one contemplates past or future phenomena, this is called concentration without an object.
What is limited concentration?
If concentration dwells for a short duration and for a brief interval, this is called "limited concentration" (paritta-samādhi).
What is "middling concentration" (majjhima-samādhi)?
If concentration dwells for a middling duration and for a middling interval, this is called "middling concentration."
What is immeasurable concentration (*apramāṇa-samādhi*)?
If a concentration dwells immeasurably and dwells for immeasurable intervals, it is called immeasurable concentration.
Furthermore, if a concentration dwells for a short time, is slight and weak, and has a limited object, it is called limited concentration (*parītta-samādhi*).
If one abides in concentration with a middling degree of stability, middling excellence, and middling objects, this is called middling concentration.
If one abides in concentration with immeasurable stability, immeasurable excellence, and immeasurable objects, this is called immeasurable concentration.
What is concentration with a limited object?

If a concentration arises by taking as its object a single sentient being, a single phenomenon, or a single mental formation—excluding the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa—it is called concentration with a limited object.
What is concentration with a middling object?

If concentration arises by taking as its object a limited number of sentient beings or a limited number of phenomena—excluding the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa—it is called concentration with a middling object.
What is the concentration with immeasurable objects?
If a concentration arises by taking as its object immeasurable sentient beings, immeasurable phenomena, the Tathāgata, and nirvāṇa, it is called the concentration with immeasurable objects.
What is limited concentration with a limited object?

It is when concentration arises by taking as its object a small, limited, and weak single sentient being, a single dharma, or a single practice; excluding the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa, this is called limited concentration with a limited object.
What is the object of limited concentration?

If concentration arises by taking as its object a limited, dwelling, weak, and measurable number of sentient beings or a limited number of phenomena—excluding the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa—this is called the object of limited concentration.
What is limited concentration with an immeasurable object?

If concentration arises by taking as its object a few beings, immeasurable dharmas, the Tathāgata, and nirvāṇa—abiding for a short time and being weak—it is called limited concentration with an immeasurable object.
What is the middle concentration with a limited object?

If a concentration arises by taking as its object one sentient being, one phenomenon, or one mental formation that abides in the middle and is of middling-weak intensity—excluding the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa—this is called the middle concentration with a limited object.
What is the middle object of the middle concentration?

It is that which arises because the concentration takes as its object beings who are middling, soft, and limited in number, as well as phenomena that are limited in number; excluding the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa, this is called the middle object of the middle concentration.
What is the middle concentration with immeasurable objects?

If a concentration arises by taking as its object those of middling capacity who dwell amidst the immeasurable sentient beings, immeasurable phenomena, Tathāgatas, and nirvāṇa that are of middling and soft degree, this is called the middle concentration with immeasurable objects.
What is immeasurable concentration with a limited object?

If a concentration takes as its object an immeasurable dwelling, an immeasurable excellence, or a single sentient being, a single dharma, or a single practice—excluding the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa—this is called immeasurable concentration with a limited object.
What is the objective sphere within the immeasurable concentrations?

If a concentration takes as its object that which is immeasurable—abiding, excellence, and immeasurable sentient beings and immeasurable phenomena—with the exception of the Tathāgata and nirvāṇa, this is called the objective sphere within the immeasurable concentrations.
What is the immeasurable concentration with immeasurable objects?

If a concentration takes as its object the immeasurable abiding in immeasurable excellence, immeasurable sentient beings, immeasurable phenomena, the Tathāgata, and nirvāṇa, this is called immeasurable concentration with immeasurable objects.
What is the concentration of brief duration?
If a concentration abides for a short interval—such as the snap of a finger or slightly more, but not as long as the milking of a cow or more—it is called the concentration of brief duration.
What is intermediate abiding concentration?
If one abides in concentration for a period between that of milking a cow or more, but not for seven days or more, this is called intermediate abiding concentration.
What is the concentration of immeasurable duration?
If a concentration abides for an immeasurable interval—such as seven days or more—it is called the concentration of immeasurable duration.
What is the concentration of short duration?

If concentration has a limited object and is weak, or if it abides for a short duration—such as for the snap of a finger or slightly more, but not for the time it takes to milk a cow or longer—this is called "limited concentration and limited abiding."
What is dwelling in a minor concentration?

If the concentration has a limited object and is weak, or if one dwells in the intermediate state for a duration such as the time it takes to milk a cow, or more, but not for seven days or more, this is called dwelling in a minor concentration.
What is "limited concentration with immeasurable abiding"?

If the concentration has a limited object and is limited and weak, yet one abides in it for an immeasurable duration—such as seven days or more—this is called limited concentration with immeasurable abiding.
What is "abiding briefly in intermediate concentration"?

If, within the state of concentration, the object is weak and one abides for only a short duration—such as the snap of a finger or slightly more, but not as long as the time it takes to milk a cow or more—this is called abiding briefly in intermediate concentration.
What is dwelling in the intermediate state of meditative concentration?

If the object within the concentration is weak and one dwells in the intermediate state for a duration such as the time it takes to milk a cow, or more, but not for seven days or more, this is called dwelling in the intermediate state of meditative concentration.
What is the intermediate immeasurable dwelling?
If within meditative concentration the object is moderate, and one dwells for an immeasurable interval of seven days or more, this is called the intermediate immeasurable dwelling.
What is "immeasurable concentration with brief abiding"?

It refers to a concentration that has immeasurable objects and immeasurable excellence, yet abides for only a short interval—such as the snap of a finger or slightly more—not for as long as it takes to milk a cow or more; this is called immeasurable concentration with brief abiding.
What is dwelling in the immeasurable concentration?

If one dwells for a brief interval—such as the time it takes to milk a cow, or slightly more—in a concentration whose objects are immeasurable and its excellence is immeasurable, yet not for seven days or more, this is called dwelling in the immeasurable concentration.
What is immeasurable concentration and immeasurable abiding?
If the concentration has immeasurable objects and immeasurable excellence, and one abides therein for seven days or more, this is called immeasurable concentration and immeasurable abiding.
What is past concentration?
If concentration has arisen and ceased, this is called past concentration.
What is future concentration?
If concentration has not yet arisen and has not yet emerged, this is called future concentration.
What is present concentration?
If concentration has arisen but has not yet ceased, this is called present concentration.
What is concentration with a past object?
If concentration arises through contemplation of past phenomena, this is called concentration with a past object.
What is concentration with a future object?
If concentration arises through reflecting on future phenomena, this is called concentration with a future object.
What is concentration with a present object?
If concentration arises through reflecting on present phenomena, this is called concentration with a present object.
What is concentration on an object that is neither past, nor future, nor present?
When concentration arises through contemplating phenomena that are neither past, nor future, nor present, this is called concentration on an object that is neither past, nor future, nor present.
What is concentration bound to the desire realm?
If a concentration is characterized by the outflows of desire and is tainted, it is called concentration bound to the desire realm.
What is concentration bound to the form realm?
If a concentration has the outflows of form (*rūpāsrava*) and is with outflows (*sāsrava*), it is called a concentration bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-samādhi*).
What is a concentration bound to the formless realm?
If a concentration has the outflows of the formless (*ārūpyāsrava*) and is with outflows, it is called a concentration bound to the formless realm.
What is non-bound concentration?
If a concentration is noble and untainted, it is called non-bound concentration.
What is concentration that is cultivated but not detached from?
If a concentration is non-noble and possesses retribution, it is called a concentration that is performed but not detached.
What is a concentration that is detached but not performed?
If a concentration is noble, possesses retribution, and is capable of severing afflictions, it is called a concentration that is detached but not performed.
What is the concentration of both application and detachment?
There is no single concentration that is either application or detachment;

rather, if it is a concentration of application, it is not detachment, and if it is a concentration of detachment, it is not application. This is called the concentration of both application and detachment.
What is the concentration that is neither produced nor abandoned?
With the exception of the produced and abandoned concentrations, any other concentration is called the concentration that is neither produced nor abandoned.

Furthermore, there is the produced concentration that is not abandoned; if a concentration belongs to the desire realm and has retribution, it is called the produced concentration that is not abandoned.

If a meditative concentration that is noble (*ārya*), possesses retribution (*savipāka*), and is capable of severing the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "the concentration of detachment that is not produced" (*niḥsaraṇa-samādhir akṛta*).

If one cultivates concentration to sever the afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and thereby receives existence (*bhava*) in the form and formless realms (*rūpārūpyadhātu*), it is called "the concentration of detachment that is produced" (*niḥsaraṇa-samādhiḥ kṛta*).
If a concentration has no retribution, or if it is a noble concentration that has retribution but does not sever afflictions, this is called neither-activated-nor-detached concentration.

There is concentration that is grasping but not emerging, concentration that is emerging but not grasping, concentration that both emerges and grasps, and concentration that neither emerges nor grasps. There is defiled concentration that is not detached from defilement, concentration that is detached from defilement but not defiled, concentration that is both defiled and detached from defilement, and concentration that is neither defiled nor detached from defilement.

There is concentration with yokes that is not free from yokes; concentration free from yokes that is not with yokes; concentration both with yokes and free from yokes; and concentration neither with yokes nor free from yokes; it is the same for these as well.
What is meant by "concentration that is a fruit of wisdom but not a fruit of abandonment"?

If one cultivates concentration and thereby gives rise to wisdom, yet this wisdom is not capable of abandoning the afflictions, this is called concentration that is a fruit of wisdom but not a fruit of abandonment.
What is meant by "concentration that is the fruit of abandonment but not the fruit of knowledge"?
If one cultivates concentration to abandon afflictions but does not give rise to knowledge, this is called concentration that is the fruit of abandonment but not the fruit of knowledge.
What is meant by "concentration that is both the fruit of knowledge and the fruit of abandonment"?
There is no fixedness regarding whether they are the fruit of knowledge or the fruit of abandonment;

that is, if it is the fruit of knowledge it is certainly not the fruit of abandonment, and if it is the fruit of abandonment it is certainly not the fruit of knowledge—this is called the fixedness of the fruits of knowledge and abandonment.
What is concentration that is neither the fruit of wisdom nor the fruit of abandonment?
Excluding concentration that is the fruit of wisdom and the fruit of abandonment, any other concentration is called concentration that is neither the fruit of wisdom nor the fruit of abandonment.

Furthermore, concentration that is the fruit of wisdom is certainly not the fruit of abandonment. If, by cultivating concentration, one attains the five supernormal powers of non-noble beings—whether one or two of them—this is called concentration that is the fruit of wisdom and not the fruit of abandonment.
If one cultivates meditative concentration and attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, this is called the concentration that is the fruit of abandonment, not the fruit of knowledge.

If one cultivates meditative concentration and attains the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *anāgāmin*, or *arhat*, these are called the concentrations that are both the fruits of knowledge and the fruits of abandonment.

If a concentration is either definitely without retribution or definitely with retribution, yet does not give rise to knowledge nor is capable of severing afflictions, it is called a concentration that is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the fruit of severance.

The same applies to the following: the concentration of the fruit of knowledge is not the concentration of the attainment of the fruit; the concentration of the attainment of the fruit is not the fruit of knowledge; the concentration of the fruit of knowledge is the concentration of the attainment of the fruit; and that which is neither the fruit of knowledge nor the concentration of the attainment of the fruit is likewise so.
What is the concentration of extinction that is not insight?
If one cultivates concentration to sever afflictions but does not give rise to wisdom, this is called the concentration of extinction that is not insight.
What is the concentration of insight that is not extinction?
If one cultivates concentration-born wisdom but does not sever the afflictions, this is called awakening to concentration but not its exhaustion.
What is the awakening to the exhaustion of concentration?
There is no single concentration that is either exhausted or awakened.
If concentration is exclusively cessation and not awakening, or if concentration is exclusively awakening and not cessation, this is called concentration of both cessation and awakening.
What is concentration that is neither cessation nor awakening?
With the exception of concentration of both cessation and awakening, any other concentration is called concentration that is neither cessation nor awakening.
Furthermore, if one cultivates meditative concentration and attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, this is called "concentration that is exhausted, but not awakened.

If one cultivates meditative concentration and attains the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) that are not noble—whether one or two of them—this is called "awakening that is concentrated, but not exhausted."

If one cultivates concentration and attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmin*), or the fruit of arhatship (*arhat*), this is called the concentration of the awakening of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna-samādhi*).

If concentration is neither a result of maturation (*avipāka*) nor possesses maturation, yet is unable to sever afflictions (*kleśa*) and does not give rise to wisdom (*jñāna*), this is called the concentration that is neither the exhaustion nor the awakening (*na-kṣaya-na-bodha-samādhi*).

It is certain that *śamatha* is not *vipaśyanā*, and it is certain that *vipaśyanā* is not *śamatha*; the cases where both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are present, and where neither *śamatha* nor *vipaśyanā* is present, are likewise.
What is the concentration of the stage of decline (*hānabhāgīya-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is unwholesome (*akuśala*), it is called the concentration of the stage of decline.
What is the concentration pertaining to maintenance (*sthityaṃśika-samādhi*)?
If a concentration is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), it is called the concentration pertaining to maintenance.
What is the concentration pertaining to growth (*vṛddhyaṃśika-samādhi*)?
If concentration is neither noble nor wholesome, it is called concentration conducive to growth (*vṛddhibhāgīya-samādhi*).
What is concentration conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-samādhi*)?
If concentration is noble, retributive, and capable of severing the afflictions, it is called concentration conducive to penetration.

Furthermore, if one cultivates concentration such that it declines, is not a noble wholesome state, does not abide, and does not increase, this is called concentration of the category of decline (*hāna-bhāgīya-samādhi*).

If one cultivates concentration such that it is not a noble wholesome state, abides, does not decline, but does not increase, this is called concentration of the category of maintenance (*sthiti-bhāgīya-samādhi*).
If a concentration is associated with the factor of shooting, it is called the concentration of the shooting portion (*śarabhaṅga-bhāgīya-samādhi*).
What is the concentration of the falling-back portion (*hāna-bhāgīya*) that is not the abiding portion (*sthiti-bhāgīya*)?
If a concentration involves falling back and does not involve abiding, it is called the concentration of the falling-back portion that is not the abiding portion.
What is concentration that is stabilizing but not regressive?
If a concentration is stabilizing and not subject to regression, it is called stabilizing concentration that is not regressive.
What is concentration that is both regressive and stabilizing?
There is no fixed distinction between the stage of decline and the stage of stability;

rather, that which is the stage of decline is not the stage of stability, and that which is the stage of stability is not the stage of decline—this is called the concentration of the stages of decline and stability.
What is the concentration that is neither conducive to decline nor conducive to maintenance?

With the exception of concentrations conducive to decline and conducive to maintenance, any other concentration is called the concentration that is neither conducive to decline nor conducive to maintenance.
What is concentration that belongs to the category of decline (*hānabhāgīya*) but not to the category of increase (*viśeṣabhāgīya*)?
If a concentration is subject to decline but not to increase, it is called concentration belonging to the category of decline but not to the category of increase.
What is concentration that belongs to the category of increase but not to the category of decline?
If concentration increases without declining, this is called concentration of the category of increase and non-decline (*vṛddhibhāgīyā-aparihāṇabhāgīya-samādhi*).
What is concentration of the category of decline and increase?
There is no single concentration that is both of the category of decline and the category of increase.
If it is a state conducive to decline and not conducive to growth, or if it is a state conducive to growth and not conducive to decline, this is called the concentration of decline and growth.
What is the concentration that is neither conducive to decline nor conducive to growth?

Excluding the stage of decline (*hānabhāgīya*) and the stage of increase (*viśeṣabhāgīya*), any other meditative concentration is called the concentration that is neither of the stage of decline nor of the stage of increase.
What is the concentration of the stage of decline that is not of the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
If a meditative concentration is subject to regression but not to progress, it is called a concentration of the regressive type (hānabhāgīya) and not of the progressive type (viśeṣabhāgīya).
What is a concentration of the progressive type and not of the regressive type?
If a meditative concentration is subject to progress but not to regression, it is called a concentration of the progressive type and not of the regressive type.
What is the concentration that is both subject to decline and subject to progress?
There is no single concentration that is simultaneously subject to decline and subject to progress.

If a concentration subject to decline is not a concentration subject to progress, or if a concentration subject to progress is not subject to decline, this is called the concentration that is both subject to decline and subject to progress.
What is the concentration that is neither of the category of decline nor of the category of progress?
Excluding the concentrations of decline and progress, any other concentration is called the concentration that is neither of the category of decline nor of the category of progress.
What is concentration that pertains to maintenance but not to increase?
If a concentration has maintenance but no increase, this is called concentration pertaining to maintenance but not to increase.
What is concentration that pertains to increase but not to maintenance?
If concentration were to increase, it would be called concentration of the stage of increase (*vṛddhibhāgīya-samādhi*) rather than concentration of the stage of stability (*sthitya-bhāgīya*).
What, then, is concentration of the stage of stability and the stage of increase?
There is no single concentration that is both of the stage of stability and the stage of increase.
If it is a concentration of the stage of abiding (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) but not of the stage of increase (*vṛddhi-bhāgīya*),
or if it is of the stage of increase but not of the stage of abiding, this is called the concentration of the stages of abiding and increase.
What is the concentration that is neither of the stage of abiding nor of the stage of increase?

Excluding the concentration of the stage of abiding (*sthiti-bhāgīya*) and the concentration of increase (*vṛddhi-bhāgīya*), any other concentration is called the concentration that is neither of the stage of abiding nor of increase (*naiva-sthiti-bhāgīya-na-vṛddhi-bhāgīya*).
What is the concentration of the stage of abiding that is not of the stage of penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*)?
If a concentration has stability but lacks progress, it is called a concentration of the stability portion and not the progress portion.
What is a concentration of the progress portion and not the stability portion?
If there is progress but no stability, it is called a concentration of the progress portion and not the stability portion.
What is the concentration of both the abiding portion and the analytical portion?
There is no single concentration that is both the abiding portion and the analytical portion.

If it is a concentration of the abiding portion but not the analytical portion, or if it is a concentration of the analytical portion but not the abiding portion, this is called the concentration of both the abiding portion and the analytical portion.
What is the concentration that is neither the "abiding portion" nor the "penetrating portion"?
Excluding the abiding portion and the penetrating portion concentrations, any other concentration is called the concentration that is neither the abiding portion nor the penetrating portion.
What is concentration that is of the nature of increase but not of the nature of penetration?
If a concentration possesses increase but lacks penetration, it is called concentration that is of the nature of increase but not of the nature of penetration.
What is concentration that is of the nature of penetration but not of the nature of increase?
If there is a concentration that is "shooting" but not "increasing," this is called concentration belonging to the category of shooting and not the category of increasing.
What is concentration belonging to both the categories of increasing and shooting?
There is no single concentration that belongs to both the category of increasing and the category of shooting.

If a concentration of the stage of increase is not a concentration of the stage of shooting, or if a concentration of the stage of shooting is not a concentration of the stage of increase, this is called the concentration of both the stage of increase and the stage of shooting.
What is the concentration that is neither of the stage of increase nor of the stage of shooting?

Excluding the concentration of the stage of increase and the concentration of the stage of application, any other concentration is called the concentration that is neither of the stage of increase nor of the stage of application.

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the four dhyānas, the four immeasurable minds, the four formless attainments, the four paths, the four fruits, the four meditative cultivations, the four abandonments; the five faculties, the five powers, the five entrances to liberation, the five elements of emergence, the five meditations on contemplation, the five factors for the arising of liberation; the six recollections, the six emptinesses, the six elements of emergence, the six factors conducive to clear knowledge, the six factors for gladdening the faculties, the six types of joyless right awakening; the seven factors of awakening, the seven perceptions, the seven requisites for concentration; the eightfold noble path, the eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery; the nine cessations, the nine successive cessations, the nine perceptions; the ten perceptions, the ten right dharmas, the ten totalities, and the eleven entrances to liberation—these are as extensively explained in the categories of the Path (*mārga-pakṣya*).
The Śāriputra Abhidharma Śāstra, Volume Thirty.
